stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea for 6 months, having had regular periods before this since the age of 13. Over the past few months she has occasionally been leaking milk from both breasts. Urine hCG is negative and thyroid function is normal. She has no past medical history and she is on no medication; physical examination is normal. Her serum prolactin level is 2400 mU/l. Which of the following best fits her condition?
options: She is likely to have a macroprolactinoma
She should be managed primarily with observation
Cabergoline is the treatment for the underlying condition
Surgery is the best treatment option
A visual field defect is likely
explanation:
Cabergoline is the treatment for the underlying condition
The treatment for the underlying condition. The diagnosis here is prolactinoma, the most common hormonesecreting pituitary tumours. Based on its size, a prolactinoma can be classified as a microprolactinoma (< 10 mm diameter) or a macroprolactinoma (>10 mm diameter); microprolactinomas are much more common than macroprolactinomas. Cabergoline is a potent dopamine-receptor agonist on D 2 receptors that has a direct inhibitory effect on pituitary lactotroph (prolactin) cells.

She is likely to have a macroprolactinoma
She is likely to have a macroprolactinoma is incorrect. Microprolactinomas are much more common.

She should be managed primarily with observation
She should be managed primarily with observation is incorrect. She has hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which should be treated to avoid sequelae of chronic hypooestrogenism.

Surgery is the best treatment option
Surgery is the best treatment option is incorrect. Medical treatment will shrink tumour size and she likely has a microadenoma, which will not cause any mass effect.

stem: A 45-year-old man with type II diabetes presents for review at the Diabetes Clinic. He is on maximal dosage of metformin and his HbA 1c is 62 mmol/mol (7.8%). You elect to add in dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor. Which of the following best describes the predominant mode of action of dapagliflozin?
options: It acts at the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-γ) receptor site, promoting
It acts by delaying gastric emptying
It acts by increasing peripheral insulin sensitivity
It acts by stimulating insulin output
It acts by increasing renal glucose excretion
explanation:
It acts by increasing renal glucose excretion
Dapagliflozin inhibits SGLT2 in the kidney. SGLT2 is a low-affinity, high-capacity glucose transporter located in the proximal renal tubules. It is responsible for 90% of glucose reabsorption. Inhibition of SGLT2 leads to lowering of blood glucose due to an increase in renal glucose excretion. This is dependent upon GFR and the class is therefore not recommended where there is significant renal impairment. Recent SGLT2 cardiovascular outcome studies, (EMPA-reg and CANVAS), have suggested a mortality benefit for the class.

It acts at the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-γ) receptor site, promoting
It acts at the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-γ) receptor site, promoting binding as a heterodimer with the retinoid X-receptor to DNA It acts at the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPAR-γ) receptor site, promoting binding as a heterodimer with the retinoid X-receptor to DNA is incorrect. That is how the glitazones work.

It acts by delaying gastric emptying
It acts by delaying gastric emptying is incorrect. Delayed gastric emptying is a function of GLP-1 monoagonists, in addition to stimulating glucose sensitive insulin release.

It acts by increasing peripheral insulin sensitivity
It acts by increasing peripheral insulin sensitivity is incorrect. The primary mode of action of glitazones is to increase insulin sensitivity in muscle and fat.

It acts by stimulating insulin output
It acts by stimulating insulin output is incorrect. That is how GLP1/DPP4/sulfonylureas work.

stem: An obese, 55-year-old patient with hypercholesterolaemia (low-density lipoprotein (LDL) 5.2 mmol/l, highdensity lipoprotein (HDL) 1 mmol/l), well-controlled type II diabetes (HbA1c 48 mmol/mol) and hypertension has been on a low-cholesterol diet for the last six months. His latest LDL level is 4.8 mmol/l and his triglycerides are within the normal range. In terms of primary prevention, what is the next therapeutic step in his cholesterol management?
explanation:
Add statins
NICE guidance recommends that atorvastatin 20 mg for the primary prevention of CVD should be offered to people with type II diabetes and who have a 10% or greater 10-year risk of developing CVD. The level of risk should be estimated using the QRISK2 assessment tool. Patients with elevated LDL cholesterol, despite lifestyle modification, should be offered 20 mg of atorvastatin as the first-line lipid-lowering programme, and reassessed in three months.

Add pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is a thiazolidinedione; it is recommended as add-on therapy in the first intensification in a patient already on metformin and with a rise in HbA1c to 58 mmol/mol or above. It is not recommended as first-line if lifestyle modification fails. Despite a favourable weight neutral or weight loss profile, when added to metformin therapy, pioglitazone is reserved as a second-line agent because of less favourable risks associated with its use, including the risk of fluid retention and oedema and an associated risk of bladder cancer in men. It is not indicated in this case as glycaemic control is the target.

Add gemfibrozil
Gemfibrozil is a fibrate that is sometimes used for the treatment of isolated hypertriglyceridaemia. It is an activator of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-alpha (PPARα), a nuclear receptor involved in the metabolism of carbohydrates and fats, as well as adipose tissue differentiation. However, it has only a very modest effect on LDL lowering and so would not be the best option in this case.

Add metformin
Metformin is recommended as the first-line glucose-lowering agent for patients with type II diabetes and who are not controlled with lifestyle adjustment alone. However, this patient has glycaemic control, which is the target, and therefore the greater risk for him at present is elevated non-HDL cholesterol.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of anorexia and weight loss, excess pigmentation and dizziness on standing. She has a previous history of autoimmune hypothyroidism that is managed with thyroxine. Examination reveals postural hypotension and skin discoloration. Initial investigations reveal hyponatraemia (Na 119 (135-145 mEq/l) and hyperkalaemia (K 5.5 (3.6-5.2). Which of the following tests will be most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Short Synacthen ® test
This woman has multiple signs and symptoms and abnormal biochemistry associated with adrenal failure.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is incorrect. ESR may be normal and is not specific.

Thyroid function tests
Thyroid function tests is incorrect. She has signs and symptoms and abnormal biochemistry associated with adrenal failure. Thyroid function tests can be abnormal in untreated Addison’s due to sick euthyroid state, usually with slightly lowered fT4. This should be re-tested after treatment is commenced.

Serum urea
Serum urea is incorrect. Although urea may be raised if she is volume depleted, it is not diagnostic.

Serum calcium
Serum calcium is incorrect. She has signs and symptoms and abnormal biochemistry associated with adrenal failure. Adrenal failure A diagnosis of adrenal failure is demonstrated by a failure of the plasma cortisol concentration to increase in response to adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Demonstration of a high plasma ACTH concentration indicates primary adrenal failure rather than secondary adrenal failure (due to pituitary insufficiency). The short corticotropin test is the ‘gold standard’ diagnostic tool to establish the diagnosis. If a short corticotropin test is not possible in the first instance, we recommend an initial screening procedure comprising the measurement of morning plasma ACTH and cortisol levels. Diagnosis of the underlying cause should include a validated assay of autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase. In autoantibody-negative individuals, other causes should be sought. Treatment is with once-daily fludrocortisone (median, 0.1 mg) and hydrocortisone (15–25 mg/d) in divided doses or prednisolone 3-5mg. Follow-up should aim at monitoring appropriate dosing of corticosteroids and associated autoimmune diseases, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease.

stem: A 74-year-old man with a history of ischaemic heart disease is treated with ramipril, amiodarone, furosemide, atorvastatin and warfarin. He has suffered two anterior myocardial infarctions over the past 10 years. Over the past two months he has lost 6 kg in weight, is hungry all the time and has diarrhoea. Over the past 48 h he has developed severe palpitations. On examination in the Emergency Department his BP is 105/72 mmHg, with pulse 130/min (atrial fibrillation). He has bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest, and bilateral pitting oedema affecting both lower limbs. There is a small smooth goitre and his TSH is <0.05 U/l. Thyroid autoantibodies are positive and a thyroid isotope scan shows diffuse uptake. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial way to manage his amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis?
explanation:
Propylthiouracil
This is a thionamide and reduces the conversion of inactive T 4 to active T 3, and is the first-line treatment option in the management of type-1 amiodarone-induced thyroiditis. Some cases of amiodarone-induced thyroiditis will show a mixed type-1 and type-2 picture and will require dual treatment with both steroids and propylthiouracil.

Lugol’s iodine
Lugol’s iodine is incorrect. Lugol’s iodine is used as an acute treatment for thyrotoxicosis in patients where progression to surgery is urgent and there is no time for other medical interventions. It can treat symptoms of thyrotoxicosis within a few days, to allow the patient to proceed to thyroidectomy.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Steroids are the treatment of choice in type-2 amiodarone-induced thyroiditis characterised by a destructive thyroiditis, absent uptake on an isotope scan and negative antibodies. This case describes a type-1 amiodarone-induced thyroiditis, as shown by increased uptake on the isotope scan and positive antibodies.

Radioiodine
Radioiodine is incorrect. Radioiodine is much less effective in amiodarone-induced thyroiditis because the patient is replete with iodine. In addition, radioiodine treatment is not appropriate in a symptomatic thyrotoxic patient as there is an increased risk of exacerbating the clinical picture or precipitating a thyroid storm.

Surgery
Surgery is incorrect. This patient would not be fit for a general anaesthetic or neck surgery given the thyrotoxic state and cardiac failure. The best option would be to manage the thyrotoxicosis abruptly to facilitate early definitive surgical management once the patient’s medical condition has been medically optimised and his thyroid status has improved.

stem: A 72-year-old man is discharged from the hospital the morning after presenting to the Emergency Department having collapsed with a blood glucose of 2.2 mmol/l. He has had type 2 diabetes for 6 years, and takes metformin, sitagliptin and gliclazide. A recent HbA1c was measured at 45 mmol/mol, he admits to up to two episodes of hypoglycaemia per week and does not check his blood sugars at home. Examination reveals a BP of 132/82 mmHg, with pulse 78/min and regular. His BMI is 28. Which of the following is the most appropriate step with respect to his diabetes management?
explanation:
Stop gliclazide
Gliclazide is a sulphonylurea and acts as an insulin secretagogue, and is associated with hypoglycaemia. Frequent hypoglycaemia and very tight glycaemic control has been shown to increase cardiovascular events and death from cardiovascular events (ACCORD study). As this patient is elderly and does not regularly check his sugars, he is at very high risk of significant morbidity related to hypoglycaemia. In addition to stopping his gliclazide medication, this patient should be advised to check his sugars regularly on leaving the hospital and to contact the diabetes team frequently.

Keep his medication unchanged
Keep his medication unchanged is incorrect. In this situation, leaving his medication unchanged puts him at significant risk of a further hypoglycaemic episode.

Stop sitagliptin
Stop sitagliptin is incorrect. Sitagliptin is a DPP4 inhibitor and acts to inhibit the normal gut enzyme DPP4, which breaks down GLP-1 hormone released after eating. By inhibiting this enzyme, DPP4 Chat inhibitors with AIallow Tutor longer duration of action of endogenous GLP-1. Sitagliptin is less commonly associated with hypoglycaemia compared to sulphonylurea treatment. GLP-1 normally stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner.

Start insulin
Start insulin is incorrect. Initiation of insulin in this case would be the incorrect decision. Firstly it would increase the risk of further and more severe hypoglycaemia and, secondly, this patient’s glycaemic control as shown by his HbA1c does not indicate a need for any additional hyperglycaemic agents.

Stop metformin
Stop metformin is incorrect. Metformin is a biguanide and the first drug treatment of choice after lifestyle modification for type 2 diabetes. It has a favourable profile, as it is weight neutral, capable of achieving a drop in HbA1c of 1–1.5% and is very rarely associated with hypoglycaemia. Diabetes - Type II You are asked to review a 54-year-old patient by his GP. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril. His BMI is 28 kg/m 2 which is unchanged since his last check up a year ago. He is currently well and has no symptoms of illness but a fasting glucose test carried out recently was elevated. The patient has a family history of type 2 diabetes. The GP carries out an oral glucose tolerance test.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has attended the Emergency Department on a number of occasions this year because of renal tract stones. She has also suffered depression during the last 2 years. She is found to have a serum calcium of 3.10 mmol/l (NR 2.2–2.6), a Cr of 138 µmol/l (NR 45––100) and an albumin of 40 g/l. She has previously been successfully treated with cabergoline for a prolactinoma. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)
The combination of hyperparathyroidism and pituitary tumour is suggestive of MEN1. This is associated with pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic tumours (the 3 P’s).

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This refers to the excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the parathyroid glands in response to hypocalcaemia, the opposite of the clinical picture in this case. It is usually associated with chronic kidney disease.

Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria
Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria is incorrect. This usually causes lifelong mild, asymptomatic hypercalcaemia, and is not associated with prolactinoma.

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. This would cause hypo- not hypercalcaemia. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (see link to Endocrine Society guidelines) MEN1 is an autosomal dominant disorder that is due to mutations in the tumour suppressor gene MEN1, which encodes a 610 amino acid protein, menin. Thus, the finding of MEN1 in a patient has important implications for family members, because first-degree relatives have a 50% risk of developing the disease and can often be identified by MEN1 mutational analysis. MEN1 is characterised by the occurrence of parathyroid, pancreatic islet, and anterior pituitary tumours; some patients may also develop carcinoid tumours, adrenocortical tumours, meningiomas, facial angiofibromas, collagenomas and lipomas. Patients with MEN1 have a decreased life expectancy, and the outcomes of current treatments, which are generally similar to those for the respective tumours occurring in non-MEN1 patients, are not as successful because of multiple tumours, which may be larger, more aggressive and resistant to treatment, and the concurrence of metastases. The prognosis for MEN1 patients might be improved by presymptomatic tumour detection and undertaking treatment specific for MEN1 tumours. Thus, it is recommended that MEN1 patients and their families should be cared for by multidisciplinary teams comprising relevant specialists with experience in the diagnosis and treatment of patients with endocrine tumours.

stem: He has a past history of ischaemic heart disease and his only medications include ramipril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg, aspirin 75mg and bisoprolol 5mg. Which of the following drugs are you most likely to prescribe?
explanation:
Linagliptin
Linagliptin is the correct answer. DPP-IV inhibitors are the best option for this man as they would likely bring his HbA1c to target, are associated with weight loss (approx 3–4 kg) and are not contraindicated in renal impairment.

Chlorpropamide
Chlorpropamide is incorrect. This is an old sulphonylurea that is not used or mentioned in guidelines due to its side-effect profile, which includes weight gain, rash and gastrointestinal (GI) upset.

Insulin glargine
Insulin glargine is incorrect. Insulin is not usually first-line treatment for Type 2 diabetes, as it is associated with hypoglycaemia and weight gain.

Rosiglitazone
Rosiglitazone is incorrect. Rosiglitazone is associated with increased heart failure and ischaemic heart disease, as well as weight gain, and is not commonly used due to these concerns. It is a thiazolidinedione, which works as an insulin sensitiser, by binding to the PPAR receptors in fat cells and making the cells more responsive to insulin.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Metformin is use is contraindicated at GFR < 30 ml/min, due to the risk of lactic acidosis.

stem: A 73-year-old woman presents with weight loss and is found to have a serum calcium concentration of 3.22 mmol/l. PTH is low and phosphate is just below the lower limit of normal. A skeletal survey is normal. She undergoes investigation for malignancy and is found to have a gastric carcinoma. Secretion of which of the following substances by the tumour is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Parathyroid hormone-related peptide
In patients with solid tumours, non-metastatic hypercalcaemia is most frequently the result of secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) by the tumour and is reported in association with gastric cancer.

Calcitonin
Calcitonin is incorrect. Secretion of calcitonin, either ectopically or by medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, is clinically silent and it does not disrupt calcium homeostasis.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol)
Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is incorrect. Unregulated production of calcitriol has been described in patients with lymphoma but is rare. Elevated calcitriol synthesis is seen in sarcoidosis and can cause hypercalcaemia.

Osteoclast-activating cytokines
Osteoclast-activating cytokines is incorrect. Although is an important cause of hypercalcaemia in patients with myeloma, but this is a relatively uncommon malignancy.

Parathyroid hormone
Parathyroid hormone is incorrect. PTH is appropriately low in this woman. PTHrP is being secreted by the tumour and acting similarly to PTH, and the raised calcium that this causes suppresses PTH.

stem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the clinic with her mother. They are concerned that she has not yet entered puberty. Past medical history of note includes a left inguinal hernia which was repaired in infancy. On examination her BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. Her height is 176 cm and her BMI is 21. She has normal breast development and normal external female genitalia, although there is an absence of secondary sexual hair. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Androgen insensitivity syndrome
Androgen insensitivity is associated with an XY genotype but with a mutation in the androgen receptor. This leads to the development of female external genitalia, but testes remain, and are undescended. Patients with AIS may often present with hernias in infancy.

Anorexia
Anorexia is incorrect. Anorexia is all but ruled out with a BMI of 21

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is incorrect. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is associated with clitoromegaly and a normal pattern of secondary sexual hair.

Klinefelter’s syndrome
Klinefelter’s syndrome is incorrect. Klinefelter’s is associated with male external genitalia Partial Androgen Insensitivity SyndromeA 55-year-old man who has a history of ischaemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes presents to the Emergency department with shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. On examination his BP is 155/82; pulse is 88 and regular. His BMI is 35. You confirm bilateral basal crackles consistent with heart failure on auscultation of the chest, and pitting oedema of both ankles. He takes a number of medications for his diabetes and hypertension. Which one is most likely to be associated with this patient's development of heart failure?

Turner’s syndrome
Turner’s syndrome is incorrect. Turner’s is associated with short stature and cardiovascular abnormalities including hypertension and coarctation of the aorta.

stem: A 46-year-old magazine columnist is referred by her GP with a history of tiredness and lethargy. There has been no weight loss. The GP found her serum sodium to be 128 mmol/l and 130 mmol/l (137–144 mmol/l) on two occasions (with a normal creatinine, calcium, glucose and lipid profile). The patient herself denies any weight loss or polydipsia, but does report that she is an anxious individual. Paired plasma and urine osmolalities are 255 mOsmol/kg (285–295 mOsmol/kg) and 95 mOsmol/kg (50–1200 mOsmol/kg), respectively. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A tumour of the posterior pituitary
explanation:
Psychogenic polydipsia
The diagnosis that is most compatible with the biochemical results in this scenario is psychogenic polydipsia. This is associated with low plasma and urine osmolalities owing to a very large throughput of water. It is more common in female patients and is frequently associated with a co-morbid psychiatric diagnosis of bi-polar disorder or anxiety.

A tumour of the posterior pituitary
A tumour of the posterior pituitary is incorrect. A tumour of the posterior pituitary is exceedingly rare. Hypothalamic tumours can either cause ADH excess or diabetes insipidus, with features that would not be explained by this biochemical and clinical picture.

Diabetes insipidus
Diabetes insipidus is incorrect. In diabetes insipidus the plasma osmolality is raised and the urine osmolality is inappropriately low. Typically, patients will also report polydipsia. This combination of biochemical and clinical features is not seen in this case, making the diagnosis unlikely.

Ectopic antidiuretic hormone (ADH) hypersecretion
Ectopic ADH hypersecretion is incorrect. In the syndrome of inappropriate ADH hormone secretion syndrome (SIADH), the urine osmolality is inappropriately raised in the face of low plasma osmolality. Diabetes Insipidus An obese, 55-year-old patient with hypercholesterolaemia (low-density lipoprotein (LDL) 5.2 mmol/l, highdensity lipoprotein (HDL) 1 mmol/l), well-controlled type II diabetes (HbA1c 48 mmol/mol) and hypertension has been on a low-cholesterol diet for the last six months. His latest LDL level is 4.8 mmol/l and his triglycerides are within the normal range. In terms of primary prevention, what is the next therapeutic step in his cholesterol management?

Pseudohyponatremia
Pseudohyponatremia is incorrect. Hyperlipidaemia or hyperglycaemia can cause pseudohyponatraemia when sodium is measured by flame photometry (because the lipid occupies a significant volume, but the sodium is only present in the water phase). The normal glucose and lipid results given in this clinical case make this diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 36-year-old woman who is 18 weeks' pregnant attends the Midwife Clinic for a pregnancy check. She is noted to have glycosuria and has a BMI of 30 kg/m 2 and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). You suspect that her mother has type 2 diabetes. What is her correct management plan?
options: Wait until 24–28 weeks gestation before testing for gestational diabetes
Commence insulin treatment as she has gestational diabetes
Perform a 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
Perform a fasting blood glucose: if it is over 7.0 mmol/l, then proceed to perform a 75 g oral glucose
explanation:
Perform a 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
As she has glycosuria, she has three risk factors for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): obesity, PCOS and family history. She is at high risk and should have testing for GDM, which involves a 75 g OGTT.

Wait until 24–28 weeks gestation before testing for gestational diabetes
Wait until 24–28 weeks gestation before testing for gestational diabetes is incorrect. She has glycosuria.

Commence insulin treatment as she has gestational diabetes
Commence insulin treatment as she has gestational diabetes is incorrect. The diagnosis should be confirmed first. If she does have GDM then dietary modification should be commenced, with consideration of metformin and insulin treatment.

Perform a fasting blood glucose: if it is over 7.0 mmol/l, then proceed to perform a 75 g oral glucose
Perform a fasting blood glucose: if it is over 7.0 mmol/l, then proceed to perform a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test Perform a fasting blood glucose: if it is over 7.0 mmol/l, then proceed to perform a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test is incorrect. She should have screening for GDM as she is at high risk, and oral glucose tolerance test is the gold standard screening test.

Perform a HbA1c
Perform a HbA1c is incorrect. It is not the gold standard screening test for GDM, and can be inaccurate in pregnancy. Gestational diabetes GDM complicates up to 12% of pregnancies. It is diagnosed according to the IADPSG (International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups) or WHO criteria. It is associated with increased maternal and foetal morbidity and mortality; these morbidities can be improved with optimisation of glucose levels and gestational weight gain. Screening for GDM is usually between 24 and 28 weeks; however, it should be carried out earlier if there is a high risk of GDM. The Hyperglycemia and Adverse Pregnancy Outcome (HAPO) study established a relationship between maternal hyperglycaemia and adverse outcomes, and a one-step approach to establishing the diagnosis of GDM using a 75 g, 2 h oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was proposed.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with unilateral gynaecomastia. He had breast reduction surgery on the other side ten years ago. On examination, he has sparse body hair in the axilla and pubic regions. Two testicles are identified, both small-volume. On further questioning you elucidate that he has a normal sense of smell. His blood tests reveal: testosterone 4 nmol/l (normal range 9–35 nmol/l), luteinising hormone (LH) and folliclestimulating hormone (FSH) both elevated, prolactin 300 mU/l (normal level is < 360 mU/l). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome (KS) results from two or more X chromosomes in males and results in a karyotype of 47XXY. The dominant symptom is primary testicular failure resulting in hypogonadism and premature elevation of FSH, LH. The severity of signs and symptoms can vary and include muscle weakness, lethargy, low libido, low testicular volume, reduced hair growth, gynaecomastia and reading difficulties. The diagnosis is made by a karyotype.

Kallmann syndrome
Kallmann syndrome is incorrect. This syndrome is caused by a lack of gonadotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus as a result of the GnRH releasing neurones not migrating into the correct location during embryonic development. Therefore, Kallmann syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and 50% of patients will also have loss of smell or anosmia. The elevated luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone and the normal sense of smell make Kallmann syndrome less likely compared with Klinefelter syndrome.

Hypothalamic hypogonadism
Hypothalamic hypogonadism is incorrect. It can be triggered by weight loss, stress, intercurrent illness or in some cases can be hereditary. Hypothalamic hypogonadism is characterised by low or normal gonadotropins which are inappropriate for a low testosterone level. As the LH and FSH levels are elevated in this case, the diagnosis is not fitting with secondary hypogonadism or hypothalamic hypogonadism.

Androgen insensitivity syndrome
Androgen insensitivity is incorrect and would be associated with a female phenotype and raised testosterone level. Therefore, this is not fitting with the clinical case described, where the testosterone is subnormal and the patient has a male phenotype. Klinefelter SyndromeA 45-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy, with an ejection fraction of 10%, takes amiodarone. He is doing well but on routine blood testing is found to have a free T4 of 38 (10-22) and TSH <0.01. With the information that has been given, what is the best first-line management for this patient’s thyrotoxicosis?

11ß-hydroxylase deficiency
11ß-hydroxylase deficiency is incorrect. This is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and is caused by an autosomal recessive inheritance of a mutation in the CYP11B1 gene that in its classic form can cause precocious puberty in males and females. Therefore, this diagnosis is not fitting with the above case.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents to the clinic with excessive sweating. He is found to have elevated growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and a GH suppression test is consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause for the excessive sweating?
explanation:
Sweat gland hyperplasia
Excessive growth hormone levels found in acromegaly are recognised as leading to sweat gland hyperplasia, which in turn leads to symptoms of excessive sweating.

Raised systolic blood pressure
Raised systolic blood pressure is incorrect. Raised systolic blood pressure is rarely associated with symptoms. Some patients do report headaches, altered vision and tinnitus.

Hyperglycaemia
Hyperglycaemia is incorrect. While hyperglycaemia is seen in association with acromegaly, it is associated with polyuria rather than excessive sweating.

Increased peripheral androgen production
Increased peripheral androgen production is incorrect. Increased peripheral androgen production is associated with polycystic ovarian syndrome, not with acromegaly.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: High-dose carbimazole therapy with thyroxine replacement
explanation:
Radioactive iodine therapy
Any patient with a solitary palpable nodule of > 1 cm in diameter will require an urgent ultrasound scan. Thyroid radionuclide uptake scanning may be performed in patients with thyrotoxicosis and a thyroid nodule. Toxic thyroid nodules preferentially take up radioactive iodine. This makes them particularly amenable to radioactive iodine treatment. A dose of 300–500 MBq is usually sufficient to cure thyrotoxicosis. If the nodule is shrinking at three months following treatment, then no further assessment is indicated.

Carbimazole
Carbimazole is used in the treatment of Graves’ disease. Any patient with severe clinical or biochemical thyrotoxicosis also requires immediate medical treatment, before definitive treatment decisions are taken.

Surgical excision
Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated in children and in women who are lactating or pregnant, as well as where the safety of cohabitants from the effects of radioactivity cannot be guaranteed. Surgery is the next best option for patients in whom radioiodine is contraindicated or refused. However, there are no obvious contraindications to radioactive iodine in this case.

Propranolol therapy
Propranolol therapy is commonly used to relieve symptoms of thyrotoxicosis but does not address the underlying problem.

stem: A 30-year-old man and his wife are referred to the Reproductive Endocrinology Clinic after failing to conceive for two years. The man admits to use of recreational drugs and anabolic steroids in the past. Examination of the man is as follows: height 189 cm, weight 95 kg (with central distribution of adipose tissue) and bilateral gynaecomastia. Ultrasound examination of the patient’s testes calculated a right testicular volume of 10.5 ml (right) and 10.1 ml (left). Which of the following investigations is most helpful in providing a diagnosis?
options: Computed tomography of the pituitary gland
explanation:
Chromosomal analysis
Klinefelter syndrome, the diagnosis here, is a genetic disorder in which affected people have an extra X chromosome, giving a genotype of XXY. It is usually diagnosed in late pubertal or early adult life because of delayed sexual development or infertility. In this case, the patient’s tall stature, gynaecomastia, small testicular volumes (normal testicular volume is 12.5–19 ml) and infertility (inability to conceive after one year of unprotected sexual intercourse) point towards Klinefelter syndrome. Diagnosis with chromosomal analysis is the only definitive test that will confirm the diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome.

Computed tomography of the pituitary gland
Klinefelter syndrome is associated with primary gonadal failure. No anatomical abnormality is expected with the pituitary gland. Computed tomography will be normal.

Measurement of serum gonadotropins
Primary hypogonadism of any cause is characterised by low testosterone levels, azoospermia and raised gonadotrophin levels (luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone). Elevated gonadotrophin levels in themselves are not specific to Klinefelter syndrome. Other possible causes of primary hypogonadism include undescended testis, mumps orchitis, haemochromatosis and myotonic dystrophy type 1.

Measurement of serum testosterone
Measurement of serum testosterone levels would not provide a diagnosis, as any hypogonadism (primary or secondary) causes low testosterone levels. 618 Klinefelter SyndromeA 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer visits you because she is keen to start on tamoxifen to reduce her risk of getting breast cancer. Which of the following statements best describes the mode of action of tamoxifen?

Semen analysis
Although Klinefelter syndrome is associated with a decreased sperm count, this would not help to narrow down the diagnosis, as there are many causes of a decreased sperm count.

stem: Which of the following is an associated risk of this condition?
explanation:
Neonatal hypoglycaemia
This patient has gestational diabetes, causing raised serum glucose, which leads to increased fetal insulin secretion. In the neonatal period the baby’s insulin remains high, and can lead to neonatal hypoglycaemia.

Down’s syndrome
Down’s syndrome is incorrect. This patient has gestational diabetes; although both Down’s syndrome and gestational diabetes are more common in older mothers, there is no direct link between the two. Gestational diabetes increases the risk of many fetal and maternal pregnancy complications, and can cause neonatal hypoglycaemia.

Fetal microsomia
Fetal microsomia is incorrect. This patient has gestational diabetes, which increases the risk of macrosomia, not microsomia. Gestational diabetes increases the risk of many fetal and maternal pregnancy complications, including heart and neural tube defects, placental abruption, and preterm labour. It also increases the risk of post-term complications such as neonatal hypoglycaemia.

HELLP syndrome
HELLP syndrome is incorrect. HELLP syndrome stands for haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count. This patient has gestational diabetes. HELLP syndrome is linked to pre-eclampsia, but there is no link to gestational diabetes. Gestational diabetes increases the risk of many fetal and maternal pregnancy complications, including heart and neural tube defects, placental abruption, and preterm labour. It also increases the risk of post-term complications such as neonatal hypoglycaemia. Diabetes in PregnancyPlacenta praevia
Placenta praevia is incorrect. Placenta praevia refers to the placement of the placenta in the lower half of the uterus, potentially obstructing the os. This patient has gestational diabetes; there is no specific link between placenta praevia and gestational diabetes, though gestational diabetes can increase the risk of placental abruption. Other complications seen in gestational diabetes include neonatal hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 27-year-old woman was admitted two days ago through the emergency department with seizures. She has a history of moderate alcohol use. Two weeks ago she received penicillin for secondary syphilis. She is complaining of muscle cramps, weakness and headache. She received 1 g of phenytoin on the day of admission and is now taking 100 mg three times a day. She is also taking paracetamol, multivitamins and tapering doses of chlordiazepoxide. There is a history of seizures in her family. She is 152 cm tall and weighs 55 kg. Her blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg, pulse 90 bpm. The rest of the physical examination is normal except for a round face, a short neck, short fourth and fifth metacarpals and bilateral cataracts. Abnormal lab results include a calcium of 1.5 mmol/l (normal range 2.2–2.6 mmol/l), phosphate 1.7 mmol/l (0.8–1.4 mmol/l) and an intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) of 200 pg/ml (15–65 pg/ml). Which of the following is most likely?
explanation:
Pseudohypoparathyroidism
The findings of Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy (short stature, brachydactyly and soft-tissue calcification) along with severe hypocalcaemia and elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) are diagnostic of pseudohypoparathyroidism (type IA). This is an autosomal dominant disorder resulting from a G-protein (Gs) defect, which leads to PTH resistance. Hypothyroidism and ovarian failure are also seen because G proteins are also involved in TSH and gonadotropin-receptor signalling. Learning disability is seen in 70% of cases.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. There are no signs of hypothyroidism given. She is of normal, stable weight and the short digits are more consistent with a diagnosis of pseudohypothyroidism.

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. The fact that PTH is markedly elevated in the face of a low serum calcium is much more consistent with pseudohypoparathyroidism.

Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism
Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism is incorrect. The phenotypic features of pseudohypoparathyroidism are seen in this condition, but with normal calcium and phosphate handling. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaA 25-year-old man, who is a well-known frequent attender with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), comes to the Emergency Department with severe vomiting and dehydration. His glucose levels are out of control and it is unclear if he has taken his insulin. His blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg; pulse is 105 bpm and regular. Investigations:

Hyperparathyroidism
Hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This is associated with hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, not the biochemical picture seen here.

stem: Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for his erectile dysfunction and loss of libido?
explanation:
Testosterone
The patient has a low testosterone, LH and FSH. The diagnosis is therefore hypogonadotropic (pituitary) hypogonadism. As such, in the presence of sexual symptoms, a trial of therapy is warranted. If a trial of treatment is indicated, discuss the different testosterone preparations available, for example daily topical gel, patch or regular or depot injections. It is appropriate to start treatment at the usual adult dose in patients with adult-onset hypogonadism, and continue for three months before determining clinical response.

Alprostadil
Alprostadil is incorrect. Alprostadil is a prostaglandin which can be given by intracavernosal injection, intraurethral application or topical application for the management of erectile dysfunction. In this case testosterone should be corrected first.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. A fasting blood sugar of 7.5 mmol/l is only just within the diabetic range, and metformin will not impact on erectile function.

Cabergoline
Cabergoline is incorrect. Cabergoline is the first-line dopamine agonist used in the treatment of microprolactinoma. The prolactin in this case is only slightly above the upper limit of normal and is not likely to be responsible for his symptoms.

stem: She is not keen on insulin therapy. How would you plan to manage her sugars?
options: Persuade her to accept twice-daily mixed insulin
Persuade her that a basal-bolus regime is the best thing for her
Start a 2-week trial of diet and lifestyle modification
explanation:
Start metformin
NICE guidelines recommend that immediate treatment with insulin, with or without metformin, as well as changes in diet and exercise, should be offered to women with gestational diabetes who have a fasting plasma glucose level of 7.0 mmol/litre or above at diagnosis. In this case, where the patient is reluctant to have insulin injections, metformin would be the most appropriate next choice. There is strong evidence for the effectiveness and safety of metformin in the management of gestational diabetes. As this patient is obese, it would therefore seem reasonable to begin with metformin in this case.

Persuade her to accept twice-daily mixed insulin
Persuade her to accept twice-daily mixed insulin is incorrect. Traditionally, management of gestational diabetes has centred on dietary management and insulin initiation, but two studies suggested that metformin might be a viable alternative in appropriate patients. One very large trial of metformin with or without insulin versus insulin alone reported similar outcomes with respect to a composite of various measures of fetal distress. Insulin should be offered as second-line treatment if metformin is unacceptable to the patient, or as add-on if targets are not reached within two weeks on metformin alone.

Persuade her that a basal-bolus regime is the best thing for her
Persuade her that a basal-bolus regime is the best thing for her is incorrect. Again, insulin therapy can be reserved for those patients who prefer insulin to metformin therapy or for those who do not manage to meet glycaemic targets on metformin therapy alone. If insulin therapy is initiated for patients, it would be important to determine whether fasting or postprandial sugars are causing the most concern, and tailor insulin therapy accordingly.

Start low-dose gliclazide
Start low-dose gliclazide is incorrect. The only sulphonylurea currently recommended for use in gestational diabetes is glebenclamide. NICE recommends that glibenclamide is considered for women with gestational diabetes in whom blood glucose targets are not achieved with metformin but who decline insulin therapy or who cannot tolerate metformin.

stem: A 61-year-old obese man with a history of Type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He is on 2g of metformin per day, yet has continued to gain weight and his HbA1c is elevated at 69.40 mmol/mol (8.5%). On examination his BMI is 32 and his BP is 155/82 mmHg. A trial of exenatide is planned. Which of the following correctly describes the mode of action of exenatide?
explanation:
GLP-1 agonist
Exenatide is a GLP-1 agonist, which accentuates the incretin effect leading to potentiation of insulin release following an oral glucose load. It also slows gastric emptying, leading to satiety and positive effects with respect to weight control.

AMP kinase activator
AMP kinase activator is incorrect. Metformin is an indirect AMP kinase activator leading to reduced hepatic glucose output.

DPPIV inhibitor
DPPIV inhibitor is incorrect. Sitagliptin is a DPPIV inhibitor, which reduces degradation of endogenous GLP-1.

SGLT-2 inhibitor
SGLT-2 inhibitor is incorrect. SLGT-2 inhibitors, such as dapaglifozin, reversibly inhibit sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal convoluted tubule to reduce glucose reabsorption and increase urinary glucose excretion.

stem: A 27-year-old woman on cabergoline for microprolactinoma becomes pregnant. What is the most appropriate management advice for this woman?
options: Continue cabergoline at the same dose
Visual field testing should be done every fortnight
Stop cabergoline as soon as the pregnancy is confirmed
Needs cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at least twice during pregnancy
explanation:
Stop cabergoline as soon as the pregnancy is confirmed
Prolactinomas are the most common hormone-secreting pituitary tumors. Based on its size, a prolactinoma can be classified as a: microprolactinoma (< 10 mm diameter) or a macroprolactinoma (>10 mm diameter). Microprolactinomas appear as a hypodense area on magnetic resonance imaging. Serum prolactin levels usually correspond to tumour size, often above 3000 mU/l in patients with macroadenomas. First line therapy is dopamine agonists to lower prolactin levels, decrease tumor size, and restore gonadal function for patients harbouring symptomatic prolactin-secreting microadenomas or macroadenoma. Cabergoline is used in preference to other dopamine agonists because it has higher efficacy in normalizing prolactin levels, as well as a higher frequency of pituitary tumor shrinkage. For symptomatic patients who do not achieve normal prolactin levels or show significant reduction in tumor size on standard doses of a dopamine agonist (resistant prolactinomas), the dose should be increased to maximal tolerable doses before referring the patient for surgery. Although cabergoline is thought to be safe in pregnancy, it is no longer needed once pregnancy occurs. It is clearly not needed to treat hypogonadism and it is not needed to control size of adenoma as microprolactinomas almost never spontaneously increase in size. Trans-sphenoidal surgery is reserved for symptomatic patients with prolactinomas who cannot tolerate high doses of cabergoline or who are not responsive to dopamine agonist therapy.

Continue cabergoline at the same dose
Continue cabergoline at the same dose is incorrect as although it is thought to be safe in pregnancy, it is no longer needed once pregnancy occurs. It is clearly not needed to treat hypogonadism and it is not needed control size of adenoma as microprolactinomas almost never spontaneously increase in size.

Visual field testing should be done every fortnight
Visual field testing should be done every fortnight is incorrect as microprolactinomas almost never spontaneously increase in size.

Switch to bromocriptine
Switch to bromocriptine is incorrect as it as treatment is not needed once pregnancy occurs. It is clearly not needed to treat hypogonadism and it is not needed control size of adenoma as microprolactinomas almost never spontaneously increase in size.

stem: A 21-year-old student nurse is admitted to the Emergency Department with hypoglycaemia. She was providing end-of-life care with her supervisor to an elderly woman when she collapsed. The cardiac arrest team was called, when she was found to have a blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/l on finger prick and responded to IV dextrose. This is apparently the third collapse over the past 4 months. There is no history of diabetes in the family and her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On review in the Emergency Department her BP is 110/82 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. She is sweating and tremulous, her blood glucose has recovered to 5.1 mmol/l. Which of the following is the best way to confirm the likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Insulin and glucose after a 24 h fast
Insulin and glucose after a fast and exercise provocation test
Insulin, glucose and c-peptide from the time of the attack
explanation:
Insulin, glucose and c-peptide from the time of the attack
Given the severity of the hypoglycaemia, and the circumstances in which it arose, the most likely diagnosis is exogenous administration of insulin. In this situation during the hypoglycaemic episode, insulin is high, glucose is low and c-peptide is low. In insulinoma (which of course is extremely rare at an incidence of 0.4 per 100,000 person-years), insulin and c-peptide are high and glucose is low. Whilst fasting and exercise testing are possibilities in evaluation of insulinoma, it remains a very unlikely diagnosis in this situation.

Insulin and glucose after a 24 h fast
Insulin and glucose after a 24 h fast is incorrect. Fasting and measuring insulin and glucose levels can help distinguish hyperinsulinaemia from other causes of hypoglycaemia.

Insulin and glucose after a fast and exercise provocation test
Insulin and glucose after a fast and exercise provocation test is incorrect. This will further stimulate the body in starvation to produce glucagon and release further glucose stores; normal patients should be able to maintain glucose levels, but patients with persistent suppression of gluconeogenesis, such as with consistently high insulin levels, would develop further hypoglycaemia.

Pancreatic MRI
Pancreatic MRI is incorrect. This would be appropriate if there was a history and laboratory findings suggestive of a pancreatic tumour, such as insulinoma. However, there are more likely alternative diagnoses.

Random insulin, dextrose and glucagon
Random insulin, dextrose and glucagon is incorrect. These tests would not be helpful as the values fluctuate and would not be able to demonstrate additional exogenous insulin. Hypoglycaemia Unrelated to DiabetesAn 18-year-old woman with primary amenorrhoea comes to the endocrine clinic for review. She is concerned that her periods have not started. Her only other history of note is bilateral inguinal hernia repair as an infant. On examination her BP is 122/82; pulse is 64 and regular. She is 1.82 m tall and has a BMI of 22.5. Breast development is normal, although she seems to have an absence of pubic and axillary hair.

stem: A 70-year-old man is admitted to hospital in a comatose condition. His wife gives a history of past episodes of sweating and palpitations, confusion, fits and occasional abnormal behaviour. He has gained approximately 4 kg in weight over the past 5 months due to persistent hunger. On examination his pulse is 92 bpm and his blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg. His BMI is 32. His plasma catecholamine level is normal and blood glucose is 1.9 mmol/l (normal range 3.0–6.0 mmol/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Insulinoma
The weight gain and hypoglycaemia seen here raise the possibility of insulinoma. The crucial path to diagnosis is measurement of insulin, glucose and C-peptide at the time of an attack, with both insulin and C-peptide elevated in the presence of hypoglycaemia.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2) is incorrect. MEN 1 is associated with pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, rather than MEN 2, which is associated with hyperglycaemia and increased risk of diabetes.

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. Phaeochromocytoma leads to episodes of hypertension and potentially hyperglycaemia, rather than the hypoglycaemia picture seen here.

Pseudodementia
Pseudodementia is incorrect. Pseudodementia is associated with features of depression including memory impairment, slowed thinking and lack of spontaneity. Hypoglycaemia is not a feature. InsulinomaEpilepsy
Epilepsy is incorrect. A primary neurological cause for the presentation is incorrect given the presence of hypoglycaemia on blood glucose testing.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is referred for an opinion. She was diagnosed with Type II diabetes 6 months ago, having had impaired fasting glucose before that, and is being treated with metformin. She reports that she has lost 5 kg in weight despite not attempting to lose any weight. Her GP is thinking about insulin therapy. Her lab results reveal HbA1c of 8.3% % (67.2 mmol/mol), Hb of 100g/l (NR 115–155), MCV of 86 fl (NR 80–96) and MCHC of 35g/dl (NR 33–36). On examination she has angular stomatitis and a well-demarcated erythematous rash in her groin, extending to her lower limbs, buttocks and perineum. What is the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Glucagonoma
The skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), glucose intolerance, a normochromic normocytic anaemia, weight loss and angular stomatitis are all highly suggestive of glucagonoma.

Poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes
Poorly controlled Type II diabetes is incorrect as her diabetes, although suboptimally controlled, would not cause her anaemia, rash and angular stomatitis.

Latent Type 1 diabetes
Latent Type I diabetes is incorrect as diabetes would not cause her anaemia, rash and angular stomatitis.

Somatostatinoma
Somatostatinoma is incorrect as these tumours, although they do cause diabetes and weight loss, present with different features: chronic diarrhoea, cholelithiasis, weight loss, steatorrhoea and diarrhoea, and hypochlorhydria.

Cushing’s disease
Cushing’s disease is incorrect as although it can be associated with Type II diabetes, it would not cause this rash or stomatitis; it typically presents with striae, weight gain, easy bruising, proximal myopathy and hypertension.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the Diabetic Clinic with amenorrhoea of six months’ duration. There is no family history of osteoporosis or fracture. She is a police officer. She smokes five cigarettes per day and drinks 15 units of alcohol per week. Her body mass index is 28 kg/m 2 and her blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg. Blood tests show: follicle-stimulating hormone 35 IU/l (post-menopausal level usually > 30 IU/l) and luteinising hormone 57 IU/l (post-menopausal level > 30 IU/l). Bone density measurements with a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scan are within normal limits. What is the main protective factor she has against developing osteoporosis?
options: Prior long-term use of progesterone-only contraceptive
explanation:
Body mass index 28 kg/m 2
In patients who are overweight without type II diabetes (body mass index 25–30 kg/m 2), the bone mineral density is increased. This may be due to increased levels of oestrone, which is produced in adipose tissue via conversion of thecal androgens.

Age 52
Bone resorption advances at around age 50, with roughly 14% of 50- to 59-year olds having osteoporosis.

Continued physical activity
Although this patient has a job involving exercise, carrying excess weight provides greater benefits, compared with physical activity.

Nulliparity
It is thought patients who are nulliparous to have 4-fold increased risk of osteoporosis, compared to those who are multiparous.

stem: A 21-year-old medical student presents with recurrent collapses. These have occurred on a number of occasions in association with stressful periods on the wards. Most recently she has been attached to the Emergency Department and has suffered two collapses during cardiac arrests of patients on the unit. Her father has type I diabetes on insulin therapy. You are on call with her overnight and she collapses again. You collect a blood sample, which shows: glucose 1.6 mmol/l, insulin 1261 pmol/l (normal levels are < 400 pmol/l), cpeptide 20 pmol/l (normal levels are < 75 pmol/l). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Illicit use of insulin
The marked elevation in insulin levels in the presence of a normal C-peptide suggests that illicit use of insulin is the most likely diagnosis. This coupled with the timing of the hypoglycaemic events which have no temporal relationship to fasting but seem to be associated with stressful events, relate to the patient’s working environment and may represent a defective coping mechanism.

Insulinoma
Insulinoma is incorrect. Collapse due to hypoglycaemia related to insulinoma is precipitated by a period of fasting with or without exercise and symptoms that are relieved by eating. This triad of hypoglycaemia with fasting, which is relieved by eating is referred to as Whipple’s triad. The diagnosis of an insulinoma biochemically is characterised by an inappropriately elevated insulin level and c-peptide level in the presence of a low serum glucose ( < 2.0 mmol/L). Typically, this diagnosis is made during an observed 72-hour fast and the patient is monitored closely for hypoglycaemia and testing performed when hypoglycaemia occurs.

Glucagonoma
A glucagonoma is incorrect. It is a rare neuroendocrine tumour of the pancreas characterised by the secretion of excess glucagon hormone. An excess of glucagon increases serum glucose levels by activating anabolic and catabolic processes including gluconeogenesis and lipolysis, respectively.

Phaeochromocytoma
A phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. It can cause episodic symptoms as described in this case and can cause mild hypoglycaemia due to the predominant β-adrenoreceptor stimulatory effect of excess catecholamines on the release of insulin. However, severe hypoglycaemia is rare with phaeochromocytoma and very high levels of insulin are not typical, making this an unlikely diagnosis. If marginal increases in insulin occur, there will be a corresponding elevation in insulin.

Illicit use of sulphonylureas
Illicit use of sulphonylureas is incorrect. It is commoner in relatives of patients with type 2 diabetes. Such use should be screened for using a urinary sulphonylurea screen if suspicious hypoglycaemic episodes are occurring in relatives of patients or patients themselves on sulphonylurea treatment. This would lead to an increase in endogenous insulin with a corresponding rise in c-peptide levels. Hypoglycaemia Unrelated to DiabetesA 29-year-old pregnant woman presents to her General Practitioner Antenatal Clinic for her 20-week review and is noted to have glycosuria. She is G2P1, with no significant previous medical history and no family history of note. A follow-up oral glucose tolerance test reveals a fasting glucose level of 6.6 mmol/l and a 2-hour level of 9.2 mmol/l. On examination, her blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg, heart rate is 65 bpm and regular and body mass index 25 kg/m 2. There is no concern for the fetus on the most recent ultrasound scan.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with worsening back and left hip pain. He is now finding it difficult to walk despite taking regular paracetamol and ibuprofen. He has a history of hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) for which he takes ramipril, indapamide and a high-dose Seretide inhaler. On examination you confirm lumbar spine tenderness and left hip pain. Which one of the following additional findings when existing without any other test abnormalities would suggest a diagnosis of Paget’s disease rather than metastatic disease?
options: Mixed sclerotic and lytic lesions on X-ray
Serum alkaline phosphatase activity five times the upper limit of normal
explanation:
Multinucleated osteoclasts on bone biopsy
The mixed lytic/sclerotic appearance of Paget’s disease may make it difficult to radiographically distinguish metastatic malignancy in some patients. A biopsy may sometimes be required if imaging studies, including computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), are unable to distinguish these conditions with sufficient confidence.

Mixed sclerotic and lytic lesions on X-ray
Mixed sclerotic and lytic lesions on X-ray is incorrect. The radiographic appearances of Paget’s and metastatic cancer can overlap, therefore this is not a differentiator in favour of Paget’s.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is uncommon as a feature of Paget’s, and is only really seen in Paget’s in patients who have had a prolonged period of immobilisation.

Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) 8 ng/l
Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) 8 ng/l is incorrect. Serum PSA of 8 is in a range where the possibility of prostatic carcinoma cannot be excluded. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaSerum alkaline phosphatase activity five times the upper limit of normal
Paget’s disease affecting one joint is common, particularly where the hip and pelvis is concerned. The most noticeable biochemical abnormality associated with Paget’s is a marked elevation in alkaline phosphatase, sometimes up to five times the upper limit of the normal range. However, ALP levels can also be elevated in metastatic cancer.

stem: A 20-year-old nursing student is admitted to the Emergency department for the 3rd time in 3 months having suffered a collapse on the ward where she is currently placed. Her glucose at the time is measured at 1.5 mmol/l. There is no past medical history of note and only medication currently is the progesterone only pill. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to differentiate insulin abuse from insulinoma?
options: Insulin and c-peptide at the time of an attack
Glucose at the time of an attack
explanation:
Insulin and c-peptide at the time of an attack
The most cost effective method of differentiating between exogenous insulin administration and an insulinoma is insulin, glucose and c-peptide measurement at the time of an attack. In exogenous administration, insulin levels are markedly elevated but c-peptide production is suppressed, whereas in insulinoma, both are elevated.

Glucose at the time of an attack
Glucose at the time of an attack is incorrect. In both conditions glucose will be low and insulin and c-peptide results are needed to differentiate the underlying cause.

72 hr fast
72 hr fast is incorrect. If possible, investment in an admission for fasting or fasting and exercise can be avoided if samples taken during or soon after a hypoglycaemic episode are available for insulin and c-peptide testing. For insulinoma in addition, a 72hr fast is rarely required; symptoms can be precipitated after a 24hr fast with exercise.

24 hr fast and exercise
24 hr fast and exercise is incorrect. A 24hr fast and exercise is required as screening for an insulin secreting tumour, this can be ruled out by measuring insulin, glucose and c-peptide at the time of an attack. InsulinomaInsulin: glucose ratio
Insulin: glucose ratio is incorrect. In both insulinoma and exogenous insulin administration, insulin levels are inappropriately high given the serum glucose.

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends the Diabetic Clinic for review. She has type I diabetes diagnosed 24 years ago and is currently managed with a basal-bolus regime. Other medication includes ramipril 5 mg once a day. She has recently undergone bilateral laser therapy for diabetic retinopathy. She drinks alcohol occasionally and smokes 10 cigarettes/day. On examination, her BP is 125/70 mmHg and her pulse is 75 bpm and regular. There is minor sensory loss affecting both feet, such that she was recently unable to feel a small cut on the sole of her foot. A recent glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) was measured at 52 mmol/mol. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol level is 2.5 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most important next step in this patient’s management?
explanation:
Stopping smoking
Cohort studies offer conflicting evidence as to whether stopping smoking reduces progression of nephropathy. However, patients with retinopathy are at significant lifetime risk of diabetic macrovascular disease, where smoking cessation has a potentially very large positive impact.

Gabapentin
Gabapentin would be useful for painful diabetic neuropathy, due to small fibre neuropathy. Here, the sensory loss is likely caused by large fibre neuropathy and gabapentin will not be effective.

Increasing long-acting insulin by 2 units
Increasing long-acting insulin, without knowing the patient’s glucose levels during a 24-hour period, could potentially put the patient at risk of hypoglycaemic episodes. HbA1c is reasonably controlled at 52 mmol/mol and little benefit will be gained from trying to intensify this blindly.

Starting aspirin 75 mg
Data on aspirin in primary cardiovascular prevention are much weaker, compared to use of aspirin in the secondary prevention population. It is therefore not recommended in National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines in this scenario.

Transferring to insulin pump
Transferring to an insulin pump is incorrect. HbA1c is reasonably controlled at 52 mmol/mol. Therefore, intensification of glucose control will have little added benefit on progression of complications of diabetes.

stem: A 62-year-old woman recently diagnosed with primary hyperparathyroidism has a serum calcium concentration of 2.9 mmol/l, with high PTH level. low phosphate, normal creatinine, high urinary calcium excretion. Sestamibi and ultrasound scan reveal a right-sided parathyroid nodule. She has a history of renal stones. Bone mineral density is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Long-term observation with regular blood tests
explanation:
Parathyroid adenectomy
In primary hyperparathyroidism, a patient with significantly elevated serum calcium should be referred for surgery, unless it is contraindicated for other reasons. Other indications for surgery include impaired renal function, renal stones, nephrocalcinosis, reduced bone mineral density, substantially elevated urinary calcium excretion.

Long-term observation with regular blood tests
Long-term observation with regular blood tests is incorrect as she has primary hyperparathyroidism complicated by renal stones, which should be treated by surgery.

Long-term bisphosphonates
Long-term bisphosphonates is incorrect as she has primary hyperparathyroidism complicated by renal stones, which should be treated by surgery.

Hormone replacement therapy
Hormone replacement therapy is incorrect as this will not lower her calcium. Indications for surgery for primary hyperparathyroidism Age under 50 Calcium 0.25 mm/l above the upper limit of normal Peri- or postmenopausal women and men age 50 and older who have a T-score of 2.5. In premenopausal women and in men under 50, the Z score of 2.5 is recommended as the cut-point below which surgery is advised. Fracture: If a vertebral fracture is present by x-ray or vertebral fracture assessment (VFA), surgery is recommended, even if there is no prior documentation. Creatinine clearance of 60 cc/min. Stones or nephrocalcinosis If marked hypercalciuria is present (ie, 400 mg/d), a more complete urinary biochemical stone profile should be considered. In the presence of abnormal findings indicating increased calcium-containing stone risk and marked hypercalciuria, a guideline for surgery is met.

stem: A 36-year-old woman sees her GP complaining of fatigue, a 4 kg weight gain, and dry hair and skin. On clinical examination she has a small diffuse goitre. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is 16 U/l (NR 0.5–4.5) and her free thyroxine (FT4) is 5 pmol/l (NR 10–22), her total cholesterol is 6.3 (< 5mmol/l) and other routine bloods are normal. She has two sisters who have thyroid disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the Western world. It is characterised by destruction of thyroid cells by cell- and antibody-mediated immune processes; this destruction results in hypothyroidism. It is found more often in women than in men. It is associated with positive thyroid antibodies and can sometimes be associated with a diffuse goitre, although not always. The gland is infiltrated with lymphocytes and patients can become hypothyroid.

de Quervain’s thyroiditis
de Quervain’s thyroiditis is incorrect. Patients usually have pain in the region of the thyroid, which is usually diffusely tender, and some have systemic symptoms. Also called subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, it is a transient inflammation of the thyroid. Hyperthyroidism often occurs initially, sometimes followed by transient hypothyroidism. Complete recovery usually occurs in weeks to months.

Follicular carcinoma
Follicular carcinoma is incorrect. It does not cause hypothyroidism and would cause a nodule, not a small diffuse goitre as in this case.

Graves’ disease
Graves’ disease is incorrect. It usually causes thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism.

Toxic multinodular goitre
Toxic multinodular goitre is incorrect. It says in the question that the woman had a smooth goitre, not nodular. In addition, toxic multinodular goitre usually causes thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism results from impaired production of thyroid hormones, thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). Primary hypothyroidism occurs when the thyroid gland is unable to produce thyroid hormones because of iodine deficiency or an abnormality within the gland itself. It is categorised as overt or subclinical hypothyroidism, depending on whether the free T4 is low (overt) or normal (subclinical) Causes of primary hypothyroidism: Iodine deficiency (developing world) Autoimmune thyroiditis (most common in Western world) Post-ablative therapy or surgery Drugs: iodine, amiodarone, lithium, interferons, rifampicin Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis Post-partum thyroiditis Thyroid infiltrative disorders: amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, tuberculosis, scleroderma Congenital hypothyroidism Useful external websites NICE. Hypothyroidism. Clinical Knowledge Summary (CKS). London: NICE, 2016. ( Jonklaas J, Bianco A C, Bauer A J, Burman K D, Cappola A R, Celi F S, et al. 2014. Guidelines for the treatment of hypothyroidism: Prepared by the American Thyroid Association Task Force on thyroid hormone replacement. Thyroid, 24, 12, 1670–1751.

stem: A 62-year-old woman undergoes subtotal thyroidectomy for goitre. Twelve hours after the operation, she calls the duty doctor and is found to be suffering from pins and needles in her hands and a carpopedal spasm; an urgently corrected calcium level is found to be 1.95 mmol/l. Which of the following statements is true regarding this patient?
options: She is likely to have permanent hypoparathyroidism due to surgery
Her hypocalcaemia is likely to be transient and due to local trauma at the time of surgery
Her hypocalcaemia is likely to be related to an acute fall in active thyroid hormone after thyroid gland
Her measured parathyroid hormone (PTH) at this time will be high
Her hypocalcaemia is predominantly due to coexistent vitamin D deficiency and is likely to respond
explanation:
Her hypocalcaemia is likely to be transient and due to local trauma at the time of surgery
The primary cause is due to secondary hypo-parathroidism following damage to or devascularisation of one or more parathyroid glands during surgery. Acute hypocalcaemia can be life-threatening, necessitating urgent treatment. In severe cases, intravenous calcium forms the mainstay of initial therapy, but it is essential to ascertain the underlying cause and commence specific therapy as early as possible. Signs and symptoms typically present when calcium acutely falls below 1.9mmol/l. These include: Perioral and digital paraesthesiae Positive Trousseau’s and Chvostek’s signs Tetany and carpopedal spasm Laryngospasm ECG changes (prolonged QT interval), arrhythmia Seizure Immediate treatment: 10–20 ml 10% IV calcium gluconate in 5% dextrose over 10 minutes, with ECG monitoring. This can be repeated until the patient is asymptomatic, and should be followed up with a calcium gluconate infusion.

She is likely to have permanent hypoparathyroidism due to surgery
She is likely to have permanent hypoparathyroidism due to surgery is incorrect. Post-operative hypocalcaemia is transient in the vast majority of cases.

Her hypocalcaemia is likely to be related to an acute fall in active thyroid hormone after thyroid gland
Her hypocalcaemia is likely to be related to an acute fall in active thyroid hormone after thyroid gland removal and she will recover Her hypocalcaemia is likely to be related to an acute fall in active thyroid hormone after thyroid gland removal and she will recover is incorrect. It is unrelated to thyroid hormone.

Her measured parathyroid hormone (PTH) at this time will be high
Her measured parathyroid hormone (PTH) at this time will be high is incorrect. It is likely to be low: the diagnosis is hypoparathyroidism from surgical trauma or inadvertent resection. Useful external websites Turner J, Gittors, N, Selby P; Society for Endocrinology. Society for Endocrinology endocrine emergency guidance: Emergency management of acute hypocalcemia in adults. Bristol: Society for Endocrinology, 2016. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaHer hypocalcaemia is predominantly due to coexistent vitamin D deficiency and is likely to respond
Her hypocalcaemia is predominantly due to coexistent vitamin D deficiency and is likely to respond to treatment with vitamin D Her hypocalcaemia is predominantly due to coexistent vitamin D deficiency and is likely to respond to treatment with vitamin D is incorrect. Although vitamin D deficiency may worsen post-operative hypoparathyroidism, it is not the predominant cause.

stem: A 48-year-old alcoholic presents to the Endocrine Clinic with loss of libido, erectile dysfunction and breast tenderness. On examination his BP is 110/70, pulse is 70 and regular. You confirm gynaecomastia and signs of chronic liver disease and his BMI is elevated at 30. Elevated oestrodiol and liver function tests consistent with cirrhosis are noted on laboratory testing. Which of the following is a direct precursor to oestradiol?
explanation:
Testosterone
Testosterone is derived from cholesterol and is converted to oestradiol by aromatase. Alcohol excess and obesity are known to increase aromatase activity, and may therefore account for feminisation in obese patients or those with alcoholism.

Dihydrotestosterone
Dihydrotestosterone is incorrect. 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.

Cortisol
Cortisol is incorrect. Cortisol is converted from deoxycortisol by 11-beta hydroxylase.

Progesterone
Progesterone is incorrect. Progesterone is a precursor to deoxycorticosterone. Impotence and Erectile DysfunctionA 25-year-old woman goes to her GP complaining of tiredness and thirst. She tells you that she has no significant history of previous medical problems, apart from two episodes of kidney stone. In terms of family history, her father had two of his parathyroid glands removed (because of high calcium levels) and recurrent pancreatitis when he was in his thirties, but this didn’t seem to cure the problem. On examination she looks well. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, her pulse is 75 bpm and her body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m 2. Investigations show:

Oestriol
Oestriol is incorrect. Oestriol is produced from oestradiol in the liver and placenta.

stem: A 19-year-old student nurse was admitted after her third collapse in recent months. She was noted to have a blood sugar of 0.9 mmol/l on finger-prick testing, and responded well to intravenous glucose therapy. At the time she was hypoglycaemic, with C-peptide 20 pmol/l (> 75) and insulin 8.1 mU/l (<3). What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Self-administration of a short-acting insulin
Low glucose, high insulin levels and suppressed c-peptide is suggestive of insulin administration. Patients with insulinoma and insulin secretagogue-induced hypoglycaemia can have plasma insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin values above or within the normal overnight fasting range.

Insulinoma
Insulinoma is incorrect. In this situation both C-peptide and insulin would be elevated in the presence of hypoglycaemia during an attack. The fact the C-peptide is suppressed is a pointer towards exogenous insulin administration.

Glucagonoma
Glucagonoma is incorrect. This is associated with hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia.

Occult administration of sulphonylureas
Occult administration of sulphonylureas is incorrect. This would be associated with elevated insulin but also with elevated c-peptide, rather than the scenario here where c-peptide is suppressed in the presence of elevated insulin and hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea. Past history of note includes bilateral inguinal hernias repaired in infancy. General physical examination reveals no abnormality. Her blood pressure is normal at 110/70, pulse is 70 and regular. Her BMI is 22. Breast development is normal, pubic and axillary hair is virtually absent. On karyotyping, she is found to have a 46,XY genotype. What is the most probable cause of her condition?
explanation:
Lack of dihydrotestosterone receptors
This girl is genotypically male and has testicular feminisation, wherein testosterone is being produced in adequate amounts by the testes located in the abdomen. The majority of cases occur due to a lack of androgen receptors to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is formed from testosterone by 5α-reductase and is responsible for the development of male secondary sex characteristics. In the absence of androgen receptors, the cells are more receptive to oestradiol, which is also produced from testosterone by the enzyme aromatase. Therefore, although the genotype is XY (male), these patients will have well-developed feminine secondary sex characteristics apart from pubic hair, which is driven by exposure to dihydrotestosterone and are likely to have been brought up female. Primary amenorrhoea is often the only symptom that brings these girls to medical attention.

Lack of testosterone formation
Lack of testosterone formation is incorrect. Testosterone levels are not low in this condition. Low levels of testosterone raise the possibility of defective sex steroid production or Leydig cell hypoplasia.

Decreased 5α-reductase
Decreased 5α-reductase is incorrect. 5α-reductase drives conversion of testosterone to DHT. Decreased levels of 5α-reductase would be associated with a male rather than a female phenotype.

Increased aromatase synthesis
Increased aromatase synthesis is incorrect. Aromatases convert androgens to oestrogens, although males with increased aromatase activity have elevated circulating levels of oestrogens, they remain phenotypically male. AmenorrhoeaA patient has a two-month history of intermittent flushing associated with tachycardia and wheezing. There have also been episodes of profuse watery diarrhoea. On examination the patient has facial plethora and is flushed. On examination BP is 160/80, cardiovascular examination reveals a pansystolic murmur which is louder on inspiration in keeping with tricuspid regurgitation, and abdominal examination reveals a palpable liver edge. Given the suspected diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate investigation?

Total absence of testes
Total absence of testes is incorrect. The bilateral inguinal hernias here are a clue to the diagnosis of androgen insensitivity; hernias in infancy due to testes are relatively common.

stem: An 81-year-old woman is referred to the thyroid clinic with a 9-month history of increasing size of a preexisting goitre.
