She has long-standing autoimmune hypothyroidism and has been on a dose of thyroxine of 100 mcg daily for many years. Her TSH is 3 U/l (NR 0.4–4) and FT4 12pmol/l (10–22). Which of the following primary thyroid cancers is she most likely to have?
explanation:
Thyroid lymphoma
Although it is rare, it is the most likely diagnosis in this case as it is known to be associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, occurs predominantly in elderly women and patients often have a pre-existing goitre and hypothyroidism.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer
Anaplastic thyroid cancer is incorrect. It usually presents with a rapidly enlarging mass and often has associated symptoms relating to mass effect or metastases. It is the most aggressive type of thyroid cancer and although it accounts for < 2% of thyroid cancers, it accounts for nearly half of thyroid cancer deaths.

Follicular thyroid cancer
Follicular thyroid cancer is incorrect. It is often subclinical and when picked up, appears as an irregular solid or cystic mass or nodule in an otherwise normal thyroid.

Medullary thyroid cancer
Medullary thyroid cancer is incorrect. It is an uncommon cause of thyroid cancer, accounting for only 4% of thyroid cancers, and in sporadic cases, it usually occurs in the 5th and 6th decades of life. It arises from within the C-cells of the thyroid, cells which produce calcitonin. It is commonly associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), together with primary hyperparathyroidism and phaeochromocytoma.

Papillary thyroid cancer
Papillary thyroid cancer is incorrect. It usually appears as an irregular solid or cystic mass or nodule in an otherwise normal thyroid.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with increased hair growth on her arms, legs and body. She describes a sixmonth history of weight gain, particularly in the abdominal region, and she has noted purple striae on her abdomen. Her menstrual pattern is normal, with a cycle every 30 days. There is no family history of type 2 diabetes and no one else in her family has suffered from hirsutism. Clinically there is no evidence of acanthosis nigricans, her BMI is 29 and there is evidence of coarse black hair growth on her arms, legs, chin and upper lip. Pigmented purple striae are evident on her abdomen, and there is no evidence of virilisation on examination of the female external genitalia. Which single investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
explanation:
Two 24 h urinary cortisol levels
Cushing syndrome commonly presents with hirsutism due to co-secretion of the adrenal androgen DHEA. The clinical description in this case of weight gain and pigmented striae is very suggestive of excess cortisol. The Endocrine Society guidelines recommend an initial screening test for Cushing syndrome with one of the following: a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, two midnight salivary cortisol levels or two 24 h urinary free cortisol levels.

Serum adrenal androgen level
Serum adrenal androgen level is incorrect. Adrenal androgens, including dehydroisoandrosterone and androstenedione, are released by the adrenal cortex and converted to testosterone. Excess adrenal androgens can occur due to adrenal adenomas, carcinomas or hyperplasia and will result in excess testosterone, which usually leads to a disturbed menstrual cycle and female virilisation. Therfore excess serum adrenal androgens is a less likely diagnosis in this case.

Serum oestrogen level
Serum oestrogen level is incorrect. Serum oestrogen level would not be helpful in the diagnosis of hirsutism in the presence of a normal menstrual cycle but should be measured in patients presenting with primary or secondary ammenorrhoea to rule out hypogonaidsm.

Karyotype
Karyotype is incorrect. A karyotype is an important consideration in patients with primary amenorrhoea or secondary menstrual disturbance. As there is no menstrual disturbance in this case, a karyotype would not be a helpful initial screening test.

Serum prolactin level
Serum prolactin level is incorrect. A prolactin level is an important consideration for patients with secondary amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea, as an elevated prolactin level can cause anovulation and menstrual disturbance at high serum levels. However, this is not the correct answer in this case as no menstrual disturbance is described.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with anxiety and weight loss, with increased appetite. Her blood results show an FT 4 of 44 nmol/l (NR 10–22 nmol/l) and a TSH of < 0.01 (NR 0.5–3.5). Which of the following findings would suggest most strongly that she has Graves’ disease?
options: High serum triiodothyronine (T3) concentration but normal thyroxine (T4) concentration
High titre of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-receptor autoantibodies
Nodular thyroid visible on ultrasound scan
explanation:
High titre of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-receptor autoantibodies
Graves’ disease (GD) is an autoimmune disorder in which thyrotropin-receptor antibodies (TRAbs) stimulate the TSH receptor, increasing thyroid hormone production. No further investigations are necessary for the diagnosis of GD.

High erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
High erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is incorrect. ESR is normal in GD and can be raised in thyroiditis.

High serum triiodothyronine (T3) concentration but normal thyroxine (T4) concentration
High serum triiodothyronine (T3) concentration but normal thyroxine (T4) concentration is incorrect. Both T3 and T4 will be high in GD.

Low thyroid uptake of technetium-99m
Low thyroid uptake of technetium-99m is incorrect. Low uptake is seen with thyroiditis. The confirmatory test for GD is autoantibody testing. Investigations in thyrotoxicosis Antibodies to the TSH receptor, thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin are found in the serum of the majority of patients with Graves’ disease, in which radioisotope uptake is typically increased. Low radioisotope uptake occurs in subacute (de Quervain’s) thyroiditis (in which the ESR is typically elevated). Elevated T3 with a normal T4 (‘T3 toxicosis’) can occur early in the course of thyrotoxicosis from any cause. The high concentrations of thyroid hormones suppress TSH secretion to very low levels in thyrotoxicosis due to thyroid disease; detectable (not always elevated) TSH in thyrotoxicosis suggests that this is caused by a pituitary adenoma secreting TSH.

stem: A 38-year-old psychiatric inpatient, who is being treated for depression, is admitted to a general ward with increasing confusion. His Na + is 122 mmol/l, with a plasma osmolality of 235 mosmol/kg (NR 278–305 mosm/kg); urine osmolality is 400 mosmol/kg (350-1000 mosm/kg). There is no evidence on examination of cardiac, renal or hepatic failure. Random plasma cortisol is 440 nmol/l, TSH 2.4 (NR 0.5–4.5) and FT4 is 15 (NR 10–22). Given the most likely diagnosis, which of the following statements best fits this condition?
options: The patient has reduced renal sodium excretion
Treatment with IV 0.9% saline will be beneficial
Urinary sodium concentration will be elevated
Psychiatric drugs are not related to the underlying condition
explanation:
Urinary sodium concentration will be elevated
The underlying diagnosis is syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), which is associated with high urinary sodium of > 20 mmol/l (reflecting relative increased concentration owing to reduced water loss).

The patient has reduced renal sodium excretion
The patient has reduced renal sodium excretion is incorrect. The underlying diagnosis is SIADH, which is associated with high urinary sodium of > 20 mmol/l.

Treatment with IV 0.9% saline will be beneficial
Treatment with IV 0.9% saline will be beneficial is incorrect. Treatment of SIADH involves fluid restriction; IV normal saline would not increase serum sodium.

Psychiatric drugs are not related to the underlying condition
Psychiatric drugs are not related to the underlying condition is incorrect. The underlying diagnosis is SIADH, which is associated with psychiatric drugs, including monoamine oxidase inhibitors, phenothiazines, carbamazepine or chlorpropamide.

The patient is hypovolaemic
The patient is hypovolaemic is incorrect. The underlying diagnosis is SIADH, which is associated with euvolaemia.

stem: A 74-year-old man who is maintained on metformin for type 2 diabetes presents to the Emergency Department acutely unwell. He is shocked, drowsy and confused. Blood testing reveals pH 7.23 (7.35-7.45), bicarbonate 14 mmol (22-26) with an anion gap of 24 mmol/l (8-16) and lactate 5 mmol/L (0.5-1) . Chest X-ray shows consolidation. ECG is normal. Ketones are not significantly elevated and random blood glucose is 8.7 mmol/l. What is the mainstay of treatment for his metabolic derangement?
explanation:
Intravenous isotonic fluid
This man has lactic acidosis from a combination of sepsis and metformin. The mainstay of treatment is rehydration.

Intravenous insulin therapy
Intravenous insulin therapy is incorrect. This is not immediately necessary given that his sugar and ketones are normal, and will not reverse his acidosis.

Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate is incorrect. There is no evidence that replacing bicarbonate is beneficial, and it may even be harmful.

Intravenous 10% dextrose
Intravenous 10% dextrose is incorrect. This will raise his blood sugars.

Intravenous hypertonic saline
Intravenous hypertonic saline is incorrect. This will neither rehydrate him nor treat his acidosis.

stem: A 42 year old undergoes pituitary surgery for a non functioning macroadenoma impinging on the optic chiasm. Post operatively he has panyhypopituitarism. He is treated with steroid replacement, testosterone and thyroxine and he has symptoms suggestive of growth hormone deficiency. A decision is made to replace his growth hormone. Which of the following is a well-recognised effect of this treatment?
options: Increase in fasting serum triglyceride concentration
Increase in serum total cholesterol concentration
explanation:
Increase in lean body mass
In GH-deficient adults, there is good evidence that exogenous GH administration increases muscle mass and decreases fat mass.

Decrease in bone mineral density
Decrease in bone mineral density is incorrect. It has been shown that GH treatment of men with GH deficiency increased BMD by 5 percent in the spine and 2 percent in the femoral neck.

Increase in fasting serum triglyceride concentration
Increase in fasting serum triglyceride concentration is incorrect. Studies have reported no change in LDL cholesterol in response to GH replacement, while others have reported a decrease. In one trial, serum total and LDL cholesterol concentrations fell during the first three months of therapy, but this effect was not maintained at 6 to 18 months.

Increase in fat mass
Increase in fat mass is incorrect. In GH-deficient adults, there is good evidence that exogenous GH administration increases muscle mass and decreases fat mass. Growth hormone deficiency The causes of growth hormone deficiency are the same as the causes of deficiencies of other pituitary hormones Adults who have GH deficiency exhibit increased fat mass, decreased lean body mass, decreased bone mineral density (BMD), less energy, and greater mortality. The evidence for worse cardiovascular risk factors is conflicting. A serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) concentration lower than the age-specific lower limit of normal in a patient who has organic pituitary disease confirms the diagnosis of GH. Normal aging is not a reason to evaluate for GH deficiency. The risks of human GH as an anti-aging intervention outweigh its benefits. In the United States, this off-label use of GH is illegal. Substantial evidence suggests that GH treatment in adults who acquired GH deficiency in adulthood results in an increase in muscle mass and a decrease in body fat, improvement in exercise capacity though not in muscle strength, improvement in BMD in men but not women, and improvement in some parameters of cardiac function. The evidence concerning improvements in the sense of well-being and serum lipids and other markers of cardiovascular risk is conflicting. Hypopituitarism And Growth Hormone Deficiency In AdultsIncrease in serum total cholesterol concentration
Increase in serum total cholesterol concentration is incorrect. Studies have reported no change in LDL cholesterol in response to GH replacement, while others have reported a decrease. In one trial, serum total and LDL cholesterol concentrations fell during the first three months of therapy, but this effect was not maintained at 6 to 18 months.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has been referred by her GP for admission because she has been complaining of frequent episodes of sweating and palpitations associated with a low blood glucose level. The family history reveals that she has a brother with Type 1 diabetes. A blood test shows the following results: glucose 1.1 mmol/l, insulin > 500 pmol/l (reference range 15–100 pmol/l) and C-peptide of < 0.2 nmol/l (reference range 0.2–1.4 nmol/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Factitious hypoglycaemia from insulin administration
The combination of hypoglycaemia, inappropriately high serum insulin and low C-peptide suggest insulin use. Patients with insulinoma and insulin secretagogue-induced hypoglycemia have plasma insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin values that are high or inappropriately normal for the degree of hypoglycaemia; in this case, the Cpeptide is low.

Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is incorrect. This would cause high, not low, glucose.

Insulinoma
Insulinoma is incorrect. Patients with insulinoma and insulin secretagogue-induced hypoglycaemia have plasma insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin values that are high or inappropriately normal for the degree of hypoglycaemia; in this case, the C-peptide is low.

Pancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. This can cause diabetes, which would cause high blood sugars.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a small lump on the left-hand side of her neck in the thyroid region. It has been present for several months and she has not noticed it changing in size. Thyroid function tests are normal; ultrasound classifies the nodule as ‘U4’, and fine needle aspiration biopsy reveals ‘Thy 5’– architecture suspicious of carcinoma of the thyroid. She undergoes hemithyroidectomy, which reveals a 1.5 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma; there is good margin clearance, no extrathyroidal extension or lymph node involvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?
options: Oral thyroxine therapy and radioiodine therapy
Total thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy with oral thyroxine replacement therapy
explanation:
Observation
This is a low-risk disease: risk stratification and the risk of recurrence guide treatment in thyroid cancer. If the risk of recurrence is very low, it cannot be reduced significantly further by additional surgery or radioiodine.

Oral thyroxine therapy and radioiodine therapy
Oral thyroxine therapy and radioiodine therapy is incorrect. She may not need thyroxine after a hemithyroidectomy, as there is residual functioning in the thyroid gland. The small tumour does not warrant radioiodine.

Total thyroidectomy
Total thyroidectomy is incorrect.

Total thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy with oral thyroxine replacement therapy
Total thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy with oral thyroxine replacement therapy is incorrect. She may not need thyroxine after a hemithyroidectomy, as there is residual functioning in the thyroid gland. The small tumour does not warrant radioiodine. She does need complete resection as the tumour has been completely resected, and she would be classified as low risk for recurrence.

Radioiodine therapy
Radioiodine therapy is incorrect. She would be classified as low risk for recurrence. Radioiodine does not further reduce the risk of recurrence when it is so low in the first place.

stem: A 18-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with episodes of shortness of breath on exercise. Her parents have always been reluctant to use medical services for themselves and their children, and therefore this patient has never been registered with a general practitioner. On examination her BP is 155/88; pulse is 82 and regular. She has a systolic murmur. You also note that she is of short stature with webbing of the neck. She tells you that she has never had a menstrual period. Which hormone is it most important to replace in this patient?
explanation:
Oestrogen
The clinical picture here is consistent with a diagnosis of Turner syndrome. Oestrogen replacement is required to develop secondary sexual characteristics, and to reduce the risk of long-term osteoporotic fracture.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. Although growth hormone may be useful for a limited period to increase final adult height, by age 18 the window for intervention may well have passed.

Progesterone
Progesterone is incorrect. Progesterone is usually introduced later, 2 years after oestrogen therapy is commenced.

Pulsatile GnRH
Pulsatile gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is incorrect. As patients with Turner syndrome have streak ovaries, there is no rationale for pulsatile GnRH therapy. AmenorrhoeaA 27-year-old yoga teacher comes to the clinic for review. She feels that she needs to drink 6-10 litres of water per day to remain hydrated, and complains that she is passing urine up to 5 times per night. She has no past medical history of note, and her only medication is the progesterone only pill. Examination reveals a BP of 120/80 mmHg, pulse is 65/min and regular. Her BMI is 21. Investigations reveal:

Luteinising hormone
Luteinising hormone (LH) is incorrect. There is no role for exogenous LH in the treatment of Turner syndrome because of the absence of ovaries.

stem: Which of the following is the best diagnostic investigation?
options: Insulin, glucose and C-peptide during an attack
explanation:
Insulin, glucose and C-peptide during an attack
There is a suspicion that this patient has recurrent hypoglycaemia. In practice, the risk of insulinoma as the underlying diagnosis is much lower than other potential causes such as abuse of insulin or sulphonylureas. The measurement of insulin, glucose and c-peptide levels during an attack is therefore the gold standard investigation, with a rise in insulin without rise in C-peptide indicating the possibility of exogenous insulin administration. If there is a rise in both insulin and C-peptide (indicating endogenous insulin secretion) during an attack, urinary assay for sulphonylureas might be considered.

Insulin levels after a 72-hour fast
Insulin levels after a 72-hour fast is incorrect. Insulin levels alone don’t inform as to whether the cause of the collapse is due to endogenous insulin production or exogenous insulin abuse. As such all three measures, insulin, glucose and c-peptide during an attack are needed to determine the diagnosis.

Fasting C-peptide
Fasting C-peptide is incorrect. Although this may be inappropriately elevated, given the attacks occur during exercise or stress, taking blood during an episode is much more useful.

HbA1c
HbA1c is incorrect. The HbA1c may be at the lower end of the normal range, although this is uninformative as to the underlying cause. Hypoglycaemia Unrelated to DiabetesGlucose during an attack
Glucose during an attack is incorrect. Glucose assayed during an attack without c-peptide or insulin is uninformative with respect to the underlying cause, for this reason all 3 elements must be measured.

stem: Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Semaglutide
As a glucagon-like peptide 1 type drug, semaglutide promotes weight loss. There is no caution in renal impairment and it is not contraindicated in inflammatory bowel disease.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is not a good choice for this patient. Sulfonylurea drugs have a tendency to promote weight gain. There is a moderate risk of hypoglycaemia, especially in older patients.

Lantus ®
Insulin would the patient’s diabetic control; however, there is a moderate to high risk of hypoglycaemia and a moderate chance of weight gain. Semaglutide tablets offer the best management for this patient.

Liraglutide
Liraglutide will promote modest weight loss, coupled with a reduction in glycated haemoglobin. There is also no dose reduction for renal failure. Liraglutide, however, is contraindicated in inflammatory bowel disease.

stem: You have referred a 17-year-old girl who is part of a family who avoid medical services wherever possible. Her mother is now concerned that her daughter is short for her age and has not commenced her periods. On examination she is below the 50th centile for height. She appears to have excess skin around her neck, and has not developed secondary sexual characteristics. There is an audible cardiac murmur. Chromosome analysis reveals a 45X picture. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Turner syndrome
Turner syndrome is associated with short stature, delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics and primary amenorrhoea. There may also be dyspraxia, poor spatial awareness or mild intellectual impairment. Cardiovascular defects include aortic stenosis and bicuspid aortic valve; coarctation of the aorta may also be present.

Noonan syndrome
Noonan syndrome is incorrect. Her karyotyping shows 45X. Although the presentation can be similar, Noonan syndrome is autosomal dominant.

Testicular feminisation
Testicular feminisation is incorrect. Short stature and webbed neck are typical of Turner syndrome, although this is a differential diagnosis in primary amenorrhoea.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is incorrect. All the features are consistent with Turner syndrome. CAH can present with salt wasting at birth, with failure to thrive or, later in life, with infertility, depending on the underlying defect.

Congenital lymphoedema
Congenital lymphoedema is incorrect. This usually presents with unilateral limb swelling. Turner syndrome Turner syndrome occurs in between 1 in 2500 and 1 in 5000 live births. It is a condition in which the female is missing or partly missing an X chromosome. Clinical features include slow linear growth, short stature, delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics and absence of menses. There may also be dyspraxia, poor spatial awareness or mild intellectual impairment. Associated cardiovascular defects include aortic stenosis, bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta. Girls with Turner syndrome also have an increased risk of hypothyroidism.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Endocrine Clinic with primary amenorrhoea. She represents her high-school in athletics and does train frequently. Physical examination is unremarkable, although her BMI is 18.5. Which of the following would be the most appropriate intervention for her?
options: Adequate diet with gradual weight increase
explanation:
Adequate diet with gradual weight increase
Delayed menarche in this patient may well be related to her low BMI of 18.5. She should be advised on a healthy eating plan which will drive gradual weight gain without interfering with her athletic training programme.

Oestrogen
Oestrogen is incorrect. Oestrogen replacement is of value in patients with Turner syndrome or in women with Kallmann syndrome.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone
Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is incorrect. GnRH is used in the treatment of Kallmann syndrome where restoration of fertility is desired. To restore fertility it is delivered in a pulsed fashion.

Gonadotropins
Gonadotrophins is incorrect. Gonadotrophin therapy is used to restore fertility in patients with pituitary failure/gonadotrophin deficiency.

Oestrogen and progesterone
Oestrogen and progesterone is incorrect. The combination is used in the treatment of Turner syndrome, although progesterone is commenced 1–2 years after oestrogen is started in such cases. AmenorrhoeaA 34-year-old woman with Graves’ disease has been treated with radioiodine.

stem: A 17-year-old boy who is 155 cm tall is worried that he might have stopped growing. Which hormone is chiefly responsible for epiphyseal fusion and cessation of growth?
explanation:
Oestrogen
The growth spurt at puberty is brought about by the secretion of androgens in the male and oestrogens in the female. However, it is oestrogens that ultimately terminate growth by causing the epiphyses in the long bones to fuse. Oestrogens rather than androgens are therefore responsible for skeletal maturation, epiphyseal fusion and cessation of growth in males and females.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. Growth hormone promotes longitudinal bone growth, but is not responsible for epiphyseal fusion.

Testosterone
Testosterone is incorrect. Testosterone both stimulates bone growth and increases bone mineral density, but does not drive epiphyseal fusion.

Somatostatin
Somatostatin is incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits bone fusion and growth, but does not terminate it. Delayed Puberty or Short StatureA 54-year-old man who has had previous surgery for acromegaly is receiving adjuvant treatment with lanreotide medical therapy because his growth hormone is persistently elevated on biochemical testing with measurement of insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) (54 ng/ml) The persistent elevation of growth hormone was confirmed by a glucose tolerance test and growth hormone measurement. His prolactin level is normal. What is the mode of action of lanreotide?

Thyroxine
Thyroxine is incorrect. T3 regulates bone turnover and bone mineral density, but does not cause epiphyseal fusion.

stem: Urinary ketones are positive (+++). Which one of the following is the most important next intervention?
explanation:
Intravenous fluids
In this situation, patients may be fluid depleted by 5 or more litres, early fluid replacement with stat 1litre of IV normal saline is crucial and can be instigated whilst an insulin pump is being set up. In the short term, it can help reduce acidosis by improving tissue perfusion, (although of course insulin is the most important step following initiation of IV fluid replacement).

Insulin
Insulin is incorrect. Insulin is the next step after IV fluid replacement is commenced, and modern thinking favours a fixed rate insulin infusion rather than use of a Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin infusion (VRIII). Fluid replacement combined with appropriate insulin dosing can reverse DKA over the course of a few hours.

Potassium
Potassium is incorrect. As insulin replacement is initiated in DKA, potassium levels can fall quite dramatically in a short period due to the effect of insulin on the intracellular shift of potassium. Therefore careful monitoring and correct replacement of potassium is a very important part of any DKA protocol and management.

Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is incorrect. The role of bicarbonate in DKA is controversial. The acidosis usually corrects itself once the fluid and electrolyte balance is restored. Some physicians administer bicarbonate if there is severe acidosis (pH < 7). However, rapid correction of acidosis might impair cardiac function. Furthermore there is an argument that bicarbonate supplementation has a beneficial role in the treatment of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis only. DKA is a common cause of a raised anion gap acidosis.

stem: A 18-year-old woman is seen at the Endocrine Clinic for review after recovering from anorexia nervosa, which she has suffered from over the past three years. Her periods have not yet commenced. Which of the following would be most typical of the first sign of onset of puberty?
explanation:
Breast-bud development
Breast-bud enlargement is the first sign of puberty in girls. This begins between the ages of 9 years and 12 years and continues to 12–18 years.

Pubic hair growth
Pubic hair growth is incorrect. Pubic hair growth commences at ages 9–14 years, and is complete at 12–16 years.

Height spurt
Height spurt is incorrect. Peak height velocity is reached earlier (10–13 years) and growth is completed much earlier than in boys.

Axillary hair growth
Axillary hair growth is incorrect. This mirrors pubic hair growth and commences between 9 and 14 years of age.

Menarche
Menarche is incorrect. Menarche occurs relatively late (11–15 years). Delayed Puberty or Short StatureA 28-year-old woman who is 3 months post-partum comes to the surgery complaining of tiredness: she has had no periods since the baby was born and she has been unable to breastfeed because of a lack of milk production. You notice in her case sheet that she required a blood transfusion after delivery for severe postpartum haemorrhage.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 3 months post-partum comes to the surgery complaining of tiredness: she has had no periods since the baby was born and she has been unable to breastfeed because of a lack of milk production. You notice in her case sheet that she required a blood transfusion after delivery for severe postpartum haemorrhage. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sheehan syndrome
It is hypopituitarism following pregnancy, complicated by haemorrhage at the time of delivery, and so fits with the clinical picture in this case. The post-partum haemorrhage and associated hypotension are thought to cause pituitary infarction. Patients fail to lactate (agalactorrhea) and remain amenorrhoeic after delivery, and also develop other pituitary hormone deficiencies of the thyroid and adrenal axis.

Empty sella syndrome
Empty sella syndrome is incorrect. Given that the patient had a significant post-partum haemorrhage, which is not associated with empty sella.

Hypophysitis
Hypophysitis is incorrect. Given that the patient had a significant post-partum haemorrhage and she has no history of infiltrative or granulomatous disease.

Prolactinoma
Prolactinoma is incorrect. The patient has had no milk production. Patients with prolactinoma on the other hand presents with galactorrhea (excessive milk production). In addition, she has fatigue, suggestive of other pituitary axis dysfunction (eg thyroid, adrenal), which does not usually occur in association with prolactinoma. Sheehan SyndromeSipple syndrome
Sipple syndrome is incorrect. This is another term for MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), which is associated with hyperparathyroidism, medullary thyroid tumours and phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents to the Endocrine Clinic. He had a history of type II diabetes, bladder cancer and hypertension. He is taking metformin. He is a smoker of 25 cigarettes per day. On examination, his height is 167 cm and he weighs 109 kg. Investigations show a glycated haemoglobin of 74.86 mmol/mol (9%) (normal value < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%)). Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention for this patient’s glucose control?
explanation:
Canagliflozin
With such a high risk factors for cardiovascular disease, canagliflozin is the next step in patients who have been treated with metformin. Patients should receive 100 mg once daily which is increased to 300 mg a day if it is tolerated and required. Patients should be advised to take their dose before breakfast. Canagliflozin also can have a positive impact of a patient's weight.

Alogliptin
Alogliptin is an example of a dipeptidyl peptidase type 4 inhibitor which is a useful adjunct to metformin. Considering this patient has a number of risk factors for cardiovascular disease, however, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence suggest sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors as the next step.

Glimepiride
Glimepiride, a sulfonylurea, is a reasonable consideration, but not when there is a significant risk of cardiovascular disease. Sulfonylurea drugs can also encourage weight gain which would be detrimental to this patient. Flozin therapy is indicated when there is significant risk of cardiovascular disease.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide does reduce blood glucose levels by stimulating insulin secretion from the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans; however, it is a sulfonylurea drug which is not suitable here due to the patient being at high risk of cardiovascular disease.

stem: A 61-year-old man with type II diabetes managed with metformin and a sulfonylurea presents to the Diabetic Foot Clinic for a review. His feet are warm and dusky pink in appearance. He has loss of vibration sense in his big toes and insensitivity to the 10 g monofilament on the soles of both his feet. There is a 1 × 1 cm shallow ulcer on the dorsal surface of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of his right foot. There is no sign of infection and debridement is planned. Glycated haemoglobin levels are 61.75 mmol/mol (normal value < 53 mmol/mol). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Non-removable casting
Non-removable casting should be used to offload the pressure on the uninfected forefoot and mid-foot diabetic ulcers. This allows time for the tissue to heal. Non-removable casts are used because adherence is low if removable devices are used. In addition to wound debridement and off-loading of the ulcer via non-removable casts, infection management and revascularisation procedures (when indicated) represent the best treatments for diabetic foot ulcers. Alternative offloading may be required while casts are made.

Electrical stimulation therapy
While trials of electrical stimulation therapy, such as shock-wave therapy (delivered using a handheld probe to deliver high-energy heart rates to the wound), showed early wound closure, compared to control populations, National Institute of Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend against its use. Some trials have shown greater efficacy from electrical stimulation therapy when compared to hyperbaric oxygen.

Epidermal growth factor
Epidermal growth factor has limited efficacy when reviewing the time to recovery for a diabetic ulcer, while increasing the risk of overall adverse events. Epidermal growth factor stimulates cell proliferation, differentiation and survival.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Several trials have reviewed the contribution of hyperbaric oxygen therapy to the speed of healing. Pressure is usually elevated to 2–3 atmospheres with 100% oxygen levels. The patient stays in the hyperbaric chamber for 45–120 minutes. There is limited evidence to support its use and guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommend against it.

Platelet-derived growth factor
Platelet-derived growth factor can be administered in a gel preparation locally. Although they are effective, they have high costs and are therefore not deemed an option by NICE. Platelet-derived growth factor plays a role in vasculature formation, thereby counteracting the effects of hyperglycaemia and microangiopathy (disease of small blood vessels).

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic with a history of hirsutism, acne and oligomenorrhoea. She has no children and there is no family history of similar symptoms. She is having difficulty losing weight, she has searched the Internet and now thinks she might have polycystic ovarian syndrome. She wants to discuss the implications of this. Her BMI is 29. Which of the following is the most important issue to discuss with her at this stage of her life?
options: Whether she wants to have children
explanation:
Whether she wants to have children
All the options are relevant issues in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and they should all be discussed. The most important issue in a woman of this age is fertility. Infertility occurs in 30% of women with PCOS. PCOS accounts for 75% of cases of anovulatory infertility. At age 37, this patient has limited time if she were to require assisted fertility. Clomiphene is commonly used. Ovulation induction with human menopausal gonadotrophin (hMG) or FSH results in 95% ovulation rate and up to 50% pregnancy rate. With obesity, the risk of spontaneous miscarriage is thought to be higher than in the general population. There is also increased risk of gestational diabetes.

Exercise regimens
Exercise regimens is incorrect. It is relevant with respect to her care, and will reduce her long term cardiovascular risk, but the most time pressing issue with respect to her diagnosis is fertility.

Her blood glucose level
Her blood glucose level is incorrect. Although her life time risk of diabetes is increased, again the most pressing short term issue to address is her fertility.

Treatment for her hirsutism
Treatment for her hirsutism is incorrect. Hirsutism and acne can be very difficult to deal with and can cause distress from a cosmetic point of view, but may be less important versus any wish for fertility. Options for medical therapy include androgen-receptor antagonists (cyproterone acetate, spironolactone, flutamide), insulin sensitiser (metformin), ovarian androgen suppressants (combined oral contraceptive pills), topical inhibitors (eflornithine). They may be combined with cosmetic treatments like waxing, shaving, plucking or electrolysis. 615 Excessive Hair GrowthWeight-reduction diets
Weight-reduction diets is incorrect. Weight reduction will positively impact on fertility, but may take time to do this, which at age 37, may not be acceptable versus other interventions to enable her to have children.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is seen in the Resuscitation Area of the Emergency Department. She was found collapsed at home by her mother. She has been diagnosed with type I diabetes. On examination, she has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15. She is sweating. A capillary blood glucose reads 1.1mmol/L. The patient does not have IV access. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Intramuscular glucagon
This patient is unconscious and sweating with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9, which suggests a hypoglycaemic episode, confirmed with bedside testing. Glucagon is the initial management of hypoglycaemia in patients unable to swallow who do not have IV access, and delivery should either be by intramuscular injection. The dose is 1 mg and if there is no positive response within 10 minutes, intravenous glucose must be given. Glucagon is only licensed for insulin-induced hypoglycaemia.

Oral dextrose gel
Oral dextrose gel is the first-line therapy in patients who are conscious and able to swallow, repeated up to three treatments in total, followed by a long-acting carbohydrate.

Intravenous glucose 5%
If there is IV access, or no response to glucagon after ten minutes (or if glucagon is not available), 10% or 20% glucose should be given via an intravenous drip.

Intravenous glucose 50%
An intravenous infusion of glucose 50% is not recommended as it is hypertonic, thereby increasing the risk of extravasation injury, and is viscous, making administration difficult.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with erectile dysfunction. He has no past medical history and is not taking any medications, recreational drugs or alcohol. Physical examination is normal. What is the commonest cause in this age group?
explanation:
Psychological factors
The most common cause of erectile dysfunction for young men is anxiety.

Alcohol
Alcohol is incorrect as although this is a cause of ED, it is not the most common cause.

Beta-blockers
Beta-blockers is incorrect as young men are rarely taking beta blockers

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect as diabetes is relatively rare in this age group (1 in 200) Erectile dysfunction Erectile dysfunction occurs in approximately 10% of all men and in > 50% of men over the age of 70 years. Common causes are psychological factors (20%), drugs (25%) and endocrine causes. Baseline investigations include serum testosterone, prolactin, fasting glucose, luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), thyroid function tests, liver and renal function tests, lipids and ferritin. Impotence and Erectile DysfunctionTesticular tumour
Testicular tumour is incorrect as this would usually not affect erectile function.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents for a routine check-up. He has a history of obesity and impaired fasting glucose. Routine bloods show a triglyceride concentration is 6 mmol/l, with normal high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels. What is the most likely cause of his clinical presentation?
explanation:
Familial hypertriglyceridaemia
The answer is Familial hypertriglyceridaemia (Option C). (type IV hyperlipoproteinaemia phenotype), in which triglyceride levels, but not cholesterol, are elevated as a result of excess hepatic production of very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL). It is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with moderate elevations in serum triglyceride concentration (2.3–5.6 mmol/l), and is often accompanied by insulin resistance, obesity, hyperglycaemia, hypertension and hyperuricaemia.

Secondary dyslipidemia
Secondary dyslipidemia is incorrect. There is no evidence of other disease (eg hypothyroidism).

Familial heterozygous hypercholesterolaemia
Familial heterozygous hypercholesterolaemia is incorrect. His low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is normal.

Dysbetalipoproteinaemia
Dysbetalipoproteinaemia is incorrect. This is associated with both elevated triglycerides and cholesterol.

Abetalipoproteinaemia
Abetalipoproteinaemia is incorrect. This causes an inability to absorb fats and is associated with failure to thrive and steatorrhoea. Familial hypertriglyceridaemia Patients with familial hypertriglyceridaemia are heterozygous for inactivating mutations of the LPL gene and, as noted above, typically have low serum HDL-C (hypoalphalipoproteinaemia). The common LPL mutations raise serum triglycerides by 20–80%; more marked elevations require some other factor, such as one of the drugs or acquired disorders noted above, and oestrogen replacement therapy in postmenopausal women. Familial hypertriglyceridaemia is associated with increased coronary risk and is common in patients with premature coronary heart disease (CHD). One report, for example, evaluated patients undergoing coronary arteriography before age 55 years: the prevalence of familial hypertriglyceridaemia with hypoalphalipoproteinaemia was 15%. Among first-degree relatives of affected patients, baseline serum triglycerides predict cardiovascular mortality, independent of serum total cholesterol. HypertriglyceridaemiaA 26-year-old man with Addison's disease presents with an acute onset of diarrhoea and vomiting over the past 6 hours. Apparently his two children have recently been ill with a 48-hour vomiting virus. He currently takes fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone steroid replacement.

stem: What advice would you give him regarding his medication while fasting (he insists on doing it)?
options: Take short-acting insulin for the evening meal
Switch to gliclazide twice a day
To change the timing of his metformin
Do not fast because he is at increased risk of hypogylcaemia
explanation:
To change the timing of his metformin
As metformin is not associated with hypoglycaemia, the patient should be reassured that, despite fasting, hypoglycaemia is low risk and continuation of treatment is important, given the history of microvascular complication and the fact that the fasting is a temporary and short-lived issue. Due to the fast, he may have to adjust the timings of his oral medication.

Stop metformin
Stop metformin is incorrect. Metformin is not associated with hypoglycaemia when used as monotherapy. It reduces hepatic glucose output and has its predominant effects on fasting plasma glucose. Therefore, it would not be advisable to discontinue therapy.

Take short-acting insulin for the evening meal
Take short-acting insulin for the evening meal is incorrect. This is not necessary to achieve adequate glycaemic control, and would increase the risk of hypoglycaemia.

Switch to gliclazide twice a day
Switch to gliclazide twice a day is incorrect. Gliclazide is a sulphonylurea that is an insulin secretagogue and can cause hypoglycaemia; this would increase the risk of hypoglycaemia and would not be recommended.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with weight loss, malaise and nausea. Tests reveal: sodium 126 mmol/l, potassium 5.8 mmol/l, haemoglobin 129 g/l, decreased T 4 9.6pmol/L and a low normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). The patient also reports reduced libido, shaving frequency and energy over the past two months, and a 9 am testosterone reveals a level of 5.5 nmol/l (normal: 8.7 - 29 nmol/L) with low normal gonadotrophin hormones (LH and FSH). He reports a head injury after a fall from a height approximately five months ago. On examination the patient is pale, there is no visual field defect on confrontation and the blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg, with a postural drop of 10 to 100/75 mmHg. Testicular examination reveals normal testicular volume. Which of the following investigations would be the most appropriate confirmatory test?
explanation:
Insulin stress test
The clinical case history and biochemistry is suggestive of hypopituitarism with suspicion of cortisol deficiency, a low T 4 but inappropriately low normal TSH and a low morning testosterone in a young male with an uncompensated or inappropriately low level of gonadotrophin hormones. This pattern suggests a deficiency of anterior pituitary function. An insulin tolerance test is the gold standard dynamic test for the diagnosis of ACTH and GH deficiency in patients with suspected hypopituitarism. The main risk associated with this test is symptomatic hypoglycaemia, and therefore an insulin tolerance test is contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures or epilepsy and in those with ischaemic heart disease, as it involves a weight-based dose of intravenous insulin to achieve a hypoglycaemia level below 2.2 mol/l.

Free thyroxine level
Free thyroxine level is incorrect. A free thyroxine level is useful in the setting of a high or suppressed TSH level to diagnose hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism. However, in this case with evidence of other anterior pituitary deficiencies, a free thyroxine level would not be the most suitable initial investigation as it must be interpreted alongside a TSH level to diagnose secondary hypothyroidism due to TSH deficiency in hypopituitarism.

Short Synacthen ® test
Short Synacthen ® test is incorrect. A Synacthen ® test is the dynamic test of choice for the diagnosis of cortisol insufficiency. It is based on the cortisol response to a 250 ng dose of tetracosactide or ACTH. The gold standard response for a normal test is a cortisol of >550 nmol/l 30 min post-ACTH stimulation. A Synacthen ® test can also be used as a screening test for ACTH insufficiency and, if the test is positive, an insulin tolerance test, (ITT) is usually recommended. In this case, as there is evidence of other anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies, an ITT with measurement of growth hormone reserve and cortisol would provide more information about the extent of hypopituitarism.

Oral glucose tolerance test
Oral glucose tolerance test is incorrect. The confirmatory test for suspected acromegaly is the oral glucose tolerance test. In this test the rise in glucose caused by a 75 g oral glucose load should suppress growth hormone secretion in the absence of autonomous GH production. The level of growth hormone should be <20 mU/l and decrease 2 h after the glucose load. It the level is high and fails to suppress, then acromegaly is confirmed. An oral glucose tolerance test is not useful in the diagnosis of suspected ACTH deficiency or hypopituitarism. Hypopituitarism And Growth Hormone Deficiency In AdultsA 56-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes presents with background diabetic retinopathy. His HbA1c has been consistently above 75 mmol/mol (9%) for the past 5 years. He is treated with metformin, liraglutide and basal insulin, but has history of non-compliance with medication. He is a smoker and has poorly controlled hypertension, with BP recorded at 154/90 mmHg. Which of the following factors would be most likely to worsen his diabetic retinopathy in the short term?

Water deprivation test
Water deprivation test is incorrect. A water deprivation test is the gold standard dynamic test for the diagnosis of suspected diabetes insipidus, and can differentiate between cranial DI and nephrogenic DI based on the inTutor response of urine osmolality to synthetic ADH (DDAVP). There is no history of polyuria or polydipsia this clinical case, and there is no role for the water deprivation test in the diagnosis of anterior hypopituitarism.

stem: A 56-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes presents with background diabetic retinopathy. His HbA1c has been consistently above 75 mmol/mol (9%) for the past 5 years. He is treated with metformin, liraglutide and basal insulin, but has history of non-compliance with medication. He is a smoker and has poorly controlled hypertension, with BP recorded at 154/90 mmHg. Which of the following factors would be most likely to worsen his diabetic retinopathy in the short term?
options: Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels
Long-term improvements in blood glucose control
explanation:
Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels
Rapid implementation of tight glycaemic control in the setting of retinopathy is associated with worsening of retinopathy.

Rapid improvement in blood pressure
Rapid improvement in blood pressure is incorrect. This will not worsen his diabetic retinopathy; lowering BP will reduce risk of progression of retinopathy.

Long-term improvements in blood glucose control
Long-term improvements in blood glucose control is incorrect. This has been shown to reduce risk of microvascular complications.

Triglyceride levels of 2.1 mmol/l
Triglyceride levels of 2.1 mmol/l is incorrect. This will not affect his retinopathy.

Continuing to smoke
Continuing to smoke is incorrect. This will not rapidly worsen his retinopathy. Summary of guidelines for screening and managing retinopathy (American Diabetes Association) Optimise glycaemic control to reduce the risk or slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy. Optimise blood pressure and serum lipid control to reduce the risk or slow the progression of diabetic retinopathy. Adults with Type 1 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist within 5 years after the onset of diabetes. Patients with Type 2 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of the diabetes diagnosis. If there is no evidence of retinopathy for one or more annual eye exams, then exams every 2 years may be considered. If any level of diabetic retinopathy is present, subsequent dilated retinal examinations for patients with Type 1 or 2 diabetes should be repeated at least annually by an ophthalmologist or optometrist. If retinopathy is progressing or sight-threatening, then examinations will be required more frequently. While retinal photography may serve as a screening tool for retinopathy, it is not a substitute for a comprehensive eye exam, which should be performed at least initially and at intervals thereafter as recommended by an eye-care professional. Eye examinations should occur before pregnancy or in the first trimester, and then patients should be monitored every trimester and for 1 year post-partum, as indicated by the degree of retinopathy. Treatment Promptly refer patients with any level of macular oedema, severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (a precursor of proliferative diabetic retinopathy) or any proliferative diabetic retinopathy to an ophthalmologist who is knowledgeable and experienced in the management and treatment of diabetic retinopathy. Laser photocoagulation therapy is indicated to reduce the risk of vision loss in patients with high-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy and, in some cases, severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor are indicated for centre-involved diabetic macular oedema, which occurs beneath the foveal centre and may threaten reading vision. The presence of retinopathy is not a contraindication to aspirin therapy for cardioprotection, as aspirin does not increase the risk of retinal haemorrhage.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has been prescribed emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg) following unprotected sexual intercourse. Her periods have been regular to date and her last period was 1 week ago. What is the most probable mechanism of action of emergency contraception in preventing conception in this case?
options: Decreasing tubal motility and ciliary activity
Rendering the endometrium unfavourable for implantation
Blocking the secretion of progesterone by the corpus luteum
explanation:
Delay ovulation
Delay ovulation is correct. The main mode of action of Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is to delay ovulation.

Thickening the cervical mucus
Thickening the cervical mucus is incorrect. Thickening of the cervical mucus is less likely to be effective, as sperm may already have entered the uterine cavity.

Decreasing tubal motility and ciliary activity
Decreasing tubal motility and ciliary activity is incorrect. The main mode of action of Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is to delay ovulation.

Rendering the endometrium unfavourable for implantation
Rendering the endometrium unfavourable for implantation is incorrect. Levonorgestrel used as emergency contraception has no significant effect on the favourability of the uterus for implantation. ContraceptivesBlocking the secretion of progesterone by the corpus luteum
Blocking the secretion of progesterone by the corpus luteum is incorrect. The emergency contraceptive pill does not block progesterone secretion by the corpus luteum.

stem: A 42-year-old man with long-standing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection presents for review. He has been taking antiretroviral therapy for 5 years and has been relatively free of associated disease. You notice on examination that he appears to have lost subcutaneous fat on his arms, legs and face, and has increased deposition of fat around his abdomen. His lipids are also abnormal, with a raised triglyceride level and a low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol level. What is the most likely cause of this clinical picture?
explanation:
Antiretroviral-related lipodystrophy
As the survival of HIV-positive people improves, more complications of antiretroviral therapy are becoming apparent. These include a lipodystrophy-type syndrome that is characterised by the loss of peripheral and facial subcutaneous fat, but with increased abdominal and visceral fat deposition. There is also an increase in the size of the dorsocervical fat pad (buffalo hump). This fat redistribution is associated with a group of abnormalities that is usually associated with insulin resistance, such as impaired glucose tolerance, low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels and high triglycerides. Glitazones can be used to treat the condition, although some small trials have proved equivocal.

HIV wasting
HIV wasting is incorrect. HIV wasting is when someone with a diagnosis of AIDS loses 10% of their weight. Since it is a complication of AIDS it is very unlikely in someone who is taking ART, it is associated with muscle rather than fat wasting and is not associated with further adipose deposition.

HIV-associated malignancy
HIV-associated malignancy is incorrect. HIV increases the risk of some malignancies such as Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and cervical cancer in the presence of immunosuppression (these are all AIDS defining). There is also a general increased risk of anal, hepatic and lung cancer, as well as Hodgkin’s lymphoma. With malignancy, there can be generalised weight loss and fat loss during cachexia, but there should not be further abdominal adiposity.

Gastrointestinal pathology
Gastrointestinal pathology is incorrect. There are no particular gastrointestinal symptoms to suggest gastrointestinal pathology. If there was diarrhoea then CMV infection should be considered, but again this is uncommon if the CD4 count and HIV viral load are both well controlled. HypertriglyceridaemiaAn inherited insulin-resistance syndrome
An inherited insulin-resistance syndrome is incorrect. Inherited insulin resistance would cause diabetes and present with symptoms and signs of this. Also, the age of presentation is usually much younger.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is taking alendronate for osteoporosis. She visits the clinic and is keen to discuss the mechanism of action of this class of drugs, as she has been studying various treatment options on the Internet. Which of the following options best describes the mode of action of the bisphosphonate class of agents?
options: Increases the bioavailability of vitamin D
explanation:
Inhibits osteoclast activity
Bone undergoes constant turnover and is kept in balance (homoeostasis) by osteoblasts creating bone and osteoclasts destroying bone. Bisphosphonates inhibit the digestion of bone by encouraging osteoclasts to undergo apoptosis, or cell death, thereby slowing bone loss.

Inhibits osteoblast activity
Inhibits osteoblast activity is incorrect as they do not affect osteoblasts, they inhibit osteoclasts.

Stimulates osteoblast activity
Stimulates osteoblast activity is incorrect as they do not affect osteoblasts, they inhibit osteoclasts. Teriparatide is the only licenced agent which stimulates osteoblasts and, to a lesser extent, osteoclasts.

Stimulates osteoclast activity
Stimulates osteoclast activity is incorrect as they inhibit osteoclasts.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner stating that he had met several people recently that he had not seen in years, and who mentioned that his appearance had changed a lot. He himself has noticed an increase in his shoe size. On clinical examination, he has enlarged hands and feet and macroglossia. Blood pressure is 152/95 mmHg. You suspect acromegaly. You order an IGF1 measurement and it comes back as raised. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm a diagnosis of acromegaly biochemically after initial screening?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGGT) with growth hormone measurement
explanation:
Oral glucose tolerance test (OGGT) with growth hormone measurement
In acromegaly, there is a failure to suppress growth hormone (GH) to < 2 mU/l in response to a 75 g oral glucose load. The normal response is GH suppression to undetectable levels.

Serial insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) measurement
Serial insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) measurement is incorrect. IGF-1 is useful as initial screening for acromegaly, as it provides an integrated measure of growth hormone levels over time. OGTT with GH measurement is diagnostic of growth hormone excess.

Morning growth hormone measurement
Morning growth hormone measurement is incorrect. GH is not useful in the diagnosis of acromegaly because, although normal people have undetectable growth hormone levels throughout the day, there are pulses of GH released which are impossible to differentiate from the levels seen in acromegaly.

Insulin tolerance test
Insulin tolerance test is incorrect. This test is used for growth hormone and ACTH deficiency.

Corticotropin-releasing hormone test
Corticotropin-releasing hormone test is incorrect. This is a test used for the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Acromegaly Acromegaly is a disorder of IGF-I excess, which occurs after growth plate cartilage fuses in adulthood. It is a rare but severe disease that is often diagnosed late, and so morbidity and mortality rates are high, particularly as a result of associated cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and respiratory disorders as well as malignancies. It is usually caused by pituitary adenomas; however, pancreatic, adrenal and ovarian tumours can occasionally secrete GH/GHRH. Clinical features Sweating is present in more than 80% of cases, hypertension in 40%, impaired glucose tolerance in 40% and type II diabetes in 20%. Coarse facial features, including prognathism, are often noticed by patients when they compare old photographs and enlargement of the hands and feet; soft-tissue swelling is another common feature. Treatment The treatment of choice is trans-sphenoidal resection; however, surgery has been found to cure 80% of microadenomas and 40% for macroadenomas with a recurrence rate of about 5%–10%. Somatostatin and dopamine analogues and GH receptor antagonists are the mainstay of medical treatment for GH excess and are generally used when primary surgery fails to induce complete remission. GigantismA 23-year-old with XY genotype but complete androgen insensitivity syndrome comes to the clinic for review.

stem: On examination she has angular stomatitis and a well-demarcated erythematous rash in her groin, which extends to her lower limbs, buttocks and perineum. What is the most suitable next step in her management?
explanation:
Measure plasma glucagon levels
There is a suggestion that this patient has a glucagonoma, a pancreatic alpha-cell tumour that secretes glucagon and 90% of cases causes a characteristic skin rash – necrolytic migratory erythema. The annual incidence of glucagonoma is estimated to be 1 in 20 million, with over 70% being malignant but, because of their indolent presentation, the diagnosis is often overlooked for many years. Over 90% of glucagonomas are also associated with impaired glucose tolerance as a result of insulin antagonism, and they eventually lead to weight loss due to protein catabolism. The surgical cure rate is as low as 5% because these tumours have often metastasised many years before the patient presents. Octreotide improves the skin rash but can have a detrimental effect on glucose control. Combination chemotherapy with streptozocin and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) gives good palliative results, as does hepatic embolisation.

Commence insulin treatment
Commence insulin treatment is incorrect. Although her HbA1C is raised, her clinical presentation is not attributable to her diabetes, she likely has a glucagonoma.

Commence GLP-1 analogue
Commence GLP-1 analogue is incorrect. Although her HbA1C is raised her clinical presentation is not attributable to her diabetes, she likely has a glucagonoma.

Refer for lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy
Refer for gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy is incorrect. The diagnosis in this case is glucagonoma, which will not be diagnosed using endoscopy. A microcytic rather than normocytic anaemia is an indication for endoscopies, particularly if there is also weight loss.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with difficult-to-treat hypertension; she is taking ramipril, atenolol and bendroflumethiazide, but her blood pressure in the clinic is still 150/100 mmHg; her serum potassium concentration in the clinic was 2.9 mmol/l. Her atenolol is stopped, her potassium is normalised with oral supplementation and then she undergoes further testing, which reveals a low plasma renin and an elevated aldosterone to renin ratio. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely to fit with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Conn syndrome
As this woman has secondary hypertension: the combination of hypokalaemia, suppressed renin and elevated aldosterone to renin ratio, is indicative of hyperaldosteronism. She should undergo secondary testing with saline suppression followed by adrenal venous sampling to localise the disease.

Adrenal Cushing’s
Adrenal Cushing’s is incorrect as Cushing’s would not cause suppressed renin and high aldosterone, although it can cause hypokalaemia.

Glucocorticoid-suppressible hyperaldosteronism
Glucocorticoid-suppressible hyperaldosteronism is incorrect as this is extremely rare, although the biochemistry would be similar. In this condition, aldosterone secretion is solely regulated by adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), the renin–angiotensin system is suppressed and there is an absence of the normal potassium-induced increase in aldosterone secretion. This dysregulation of aldosterone secretion by a hormone that is not sensitive to sodium balance explains the chronic, autonomous aldosterone production.

Aldosterone-producing carcinoma
Aldosterone-producing carcinoma is incorrect as this is extremely rare, although the biochemistry and presentation would be similar. HyperaldosteronismAdrenal incidentaloma
Adrenal incidentaloma is incorrect as this would mean a non-functioning adenoma, whereas this woman has abnormal biochemistry, suggesting a functioning adenoma or hyperplasia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to her GP with a history of weight loss, heat intolerance, poor concentration and palpitations. Which of the following is most likely to be associated with a diagnosis of thyroiditis associated with viral infection?
explanation:
Reduced uptake on 99mTc thyroid scintigraphy
The commonest cause of thyrotoxicosis is Grave’s disease, which accounts for 80% of cases. Less common causes include toxic multinodular goitre, solitary toxic adenoma and thyroiditis. In thyroiditis, stored thyroid hormone from within colloid is released. This results in excess free thyroxine (FT4) in the circulation. Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is suppressed through negative feedback. There is reduced uptake and iodine trapping in the colloid as synthesis of thyroid hormone is switched off. Thyroid scintigraphy with 99mTc or radioiodine shows reduced or absent uptake in all types of thyroiditis. In contrast, most other causes of thyrotoxicosis show increased uptake. In Graves’ disease, the increased uptake is diffuse. In toxic MNG or solitary adenoma, focal increase in uptake is seen.

Bilateral exophthalmos
Bilateral exophthalmos is incorrect. Thyroid eye disease is unique to and pathognomonic of Graves’ disease.

Diffuse, smooth goitre
Diffuse, smooth goitre is incorrect. Both Graves’ disease and thyroiditis can present with a diffuse, smooth, symmetrical goitre. In Graves’ disease, it may be accompanied by a bruit. In viral (de Quervain) thyroiditis, it may be painful and tender.

Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies
Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies is incorrect. TPO antibodies are not specific. It is present in a wide range of thyroid disorders, including Grave’s disease (70-80%) and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (95%). It may be positive in 20% of normal population. 616 Thyrotoxicosis

Pretibial myxoedema
Pre-tibial myxoedema is incorrect. Pre-tibial myxoedema is an uncommon dermatological manifestation of autoimmune thyroid disease. It is characterized by bilateral, asymmetric, non-pitting scaly thickening and induration of the skin, most commonly as one or a few well-demarcated papules or nodules several centimetres in diameter. The most frequent location of pretibial myxoedema is over the lower legs, especially the pretibial areas or the dorsum of the foot.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with well-managed type 1 diabetes is being monitored for other autoimmune disease and is found to have positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies, but is euthyroid. She has recent found out she is 6 weeks’ pregnant. It was an unplanned pregnancy. She is concerned about the implications of these antibodies. Which of the following potential consequences are associated with the presence of maternal thyroid autoantibodies?
options: Increased risk of transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis
explanation:
Higher risk of spontaneous abortions
The presence of maternal thyroid autoantibodies is strongly associated with miscarriage and pre-term delivery. There is evidence that treatment with levothyroxine can attenuates the risks. Meta-analysis of cohort studies showed the odds of miscarriage to be more than threefold in the presence of thyroid autoantibodies.

Increased risk of neonatal hypothyroidism
Increased risk of neonatal hypothyroidism is incorrect. There is no known association between maternal autoantibodies and neonatal hypothyroidism.

Increased risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension
Increased risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension is incorrect. There is no association between maternal autoantibodies and hypertension; this usually occurs with maternal diabetes.

Increased risk of macrosomia
Increased risk of macrosomia is incorrect. There is no association between maternal autoantibodies and macrosomia; this usually occurs with maternal diabetes. Association between thyroid autoantibodies and miscarriage and pre-term birth There is evidence that thyroid autoimmunity is an important risk factor for miscarriage and pre-term birth. The presence of thyroid autoantibodies is relatively common in women of reproductive age. In an ‘unselected’ population of women, the prevalence ranges from 6 to 20%, being even higher in women with a history of recurrent pregnancy loss, at around 17-33%, and in women with a history of subfertility, at around 10-31%. In the developed world, thyroid autoimmunity is the main cause of hypothyroidism, which itself results in poor obstetric outcomes. Even in women with biochemically normal thyroid function, studies have reported an association between the presence of thyroid autoantibodies, particularly thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage, pre-term birth and adverse neurodevelopmental sequelae in children. The exact mechanisms of these associations are unknown, though two have been proposed. First, the presence of thyroid autoantibodies in women with normal thyroid function could be associated with a subtle deficiency in the availability of thyroid hormones (a fall in circulating free thyroid hormones within the reference range) or a lower capacity of the thyroid gland to respond adequately to the demand for augmented synthesis of thyroid hormones required in pregnancy. Useful external weblinks Association between thyroid autoantibodies and miscarriage and pre-term birth: meta-analysis of evidence www.bmj.com/content/342/bmj.d2616 ( Diabetes - Type I A 54-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for her annual review. Her glycaemic control has deteriorated over the past year despite having taken part in the DAFNE programme, and she has evidence of early peripheral diabetic neuropathy. Her visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes. Which of the following findings on retinal photography would warrant making an urgent referral to an ophthalmologist?

Increased risk of transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis
Increased risk of transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis is incorrect. There is no known association between maternal thyroid peroxidase autoantibodies and neonatal thyrotoxicosis. This can occur with maternal Graves’ disease where there are positive TSH receptor antibodies; this is managed with beta blockers and anti-thyroid drugs and usually resolves within 12 weeks after birth.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to the clinic with difficult-to-treat hypertension. She takes ramipril 10 mg and amlodipine 10 mg, and currently has a blood pressure of 155/95 mmHg. She has noted that her face has become more rounded over the years, and she is having increasing trouble with both acne and hirsutism. Fasting blood glucose is 6.6mmol/l, renal function is normal and K + is 3.4 mmol/l. There has also been increasing problems with abdominal obesity, and she has noticed some purple stretch marks appearing around her abdomen. What test is most likely to be abnormal in this case?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement
explanation:
Overnight dexamethasone suppression test
The diagnosis here is most likley to be Cushing‘s syndrome, the screening test for which is an overnight lowdose dexamethasone suppression test. Cushing syndrome comprises a large group of signs and symptoms that reflect prolonged and inappropriate high exposure of tissue to glucocorticoids (Table 1). Whereas the most common cause is iatrogenic from medically prescribed corticosteroids, endogenous Cushing’s is an uncommon disorder: European populationbased studies reported an incidence of two to three cases per 1 million inhabitants per year (4, 5). Excess cortisol production, the biochemical hallmark of endogenous Cushing’s, may be caused by either excess adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion (from a pituitary or other ectopic tumour) or independent adrenal overproduction of cortisol. For the initial testing: Urine-free cortisol (UFC; at least two measurements) Late-night salivary cortisol (two measurements) 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST) Longer low-dose DST (2 mg/d for 48 h)

Urinary vanillylmandelic acid
Urinary vanillylmandelic acid is incorrect. That would be abnormal in phaeochromocytoma, of which there is no evidence in this case.

Plasma metanephrines
Plasma metanephrines is incorrect. That would also be abnormal in phaeochromocytoma, of which there is no evidence in this case. The diagnosis is likely to be Cushing syndrome in this scenario.

Plasma renin-to-aldosterone ratio
Plasma renin-to-aldosterone ratio is incorrect. This would be a screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism, rather than for Cushing syndrome.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful initial investigation to elucidate the underlying cause?
explanation:
IGF-1
The development of diabetes in an individual of relatively normal weight, coupled with skin tag formation, excessive acne and carpal tunnel syndrome, raises the possibility of acromegaly. The elevated prolactin and decreased TSH (just below the lower limit of normal), raise the possibility of pressure effects from a growth hormone -producing pituitary adenoma.

Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test is incorrect. This would have been the correct answer in order to localise the source of excess cortisol in elevated cortisol. Dexamethasone is given, which suppresses endogenous cortisol production, and ACTH and cortisol are measured. If ACTH is low and cortisol is not suppressed, then primary hypercortisolism, such as Cushing syndrome, is present. If ACTH is elevated and cortisol is not suppressed, then a ectopic ACTH syndrome is likely.

OGTT with growth hormone
OGTT with growth hormone is incorrect. The presence of an elevated IGF1 would indicate the need for an oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement. An MRI pituitary would then confirm the presence of the adenoma.

24 h urinary catecholamines
24 h urinary catecholamines is incorrect. This would have been the correct investigation if phaeochromocytoma was suspected. Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour. Presentation is usually with headache, profuse sweating, palpitations and tremor – occurring in episodes with increasing severity and frequency. CT can be used to confirm diagnosis by finding the underlying tumour, and surgical resection of the tumour is the best option, but preoperative alpha- and beta-blockade is needed to control blood pressure and to prevent an intra-operative hypertensive crisis. GigantismA 34-year-old woman, who is 22 weeks’ pregnant, comes to the Emergency Department complaining of increasingly severe tiredness, lethargy and cold intolerance, which has developed over the past 4 weeks. Although her General Practitioner did some blood tests, he told her that no treatment was indicated. There is no past medical history of note and she has two other healthy children. On examination, her BP is 105/75 mmHg and her pulse is 68 bpm and regular. She has a small smooth goitre, which is non-tender. Investigations:

24 h urinary free cortisol
24 h urinary free cortisol is incorrect. This would be an investigation for Cushing syndrome. The features of carpal tunnel syndrome and acne makes this a less likely diagnoses. Cushing syndrome is prolonged exposures to high levels of glucocorticoid steroids. This can be divided into ACTH-dependent or –independent Cushing. There is excessive ACTH production, either from the pituitary – Cushing’s disease – or ectopic production, e.g. lung cancer. In the latter case, the cause may be adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, or excess iatrogenic from steroid prescription. Presentation is an obese patient with full, plethoric face, proximal muscle wasting and weakness, as well hypertension and other problems. A 24 h urinary cortisol can confirm Cushing syndrome, to which an alternative is a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test. Pituitary MRI can then be used to look for a pituitary adenoma. Treatment depends on the cause; surgery and radiotherapy are options for Cushing’s disease.

stem: What is the likely cause for the patient’s symptoms and blood gas results?
explanation:
Addison’s disease
This patient is a young woman with abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, with a low-normal blood pressure. She has a mild metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap . This would be a typical presentation of Addison’s disease; it causes a metabolic acidosis due to the increased excretion of sodium and increased retention of hydrogen secondary to the relative lack of aldosterone. This is more likely than diabetic ketoacidosis (the only other option in the list to cause these symptoms with a metabolic acidosis) because DKA would cause a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap.

Conn’s syndrome
Conn’s syndrome is incorrect. Conn’s syndrome causes hyperaldosteronism, and usually presents incidentally with hypertension – this patient has a relatively low blood pressure. Hyperaldosteronism would typically cause a metabolic alkalosis, as aldosterone acts to excrete hydrogen ions, but this patient has a metabolic acidosis. This would be more typical for Addison’s disease, which can cause a mild metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap.

Cushing’s syndrome
Cushing’s syndrome is incorrect. Cushing’s syndrome causes a functional hyperaldosteronism (because the excess cortisol is active at the mineralocorticoid receptor). Hyperaldosteronism can cause a metabolic alkalosis, as aldosterone acts to excrete hydrogen ions; however, this patient has a metabolic acidosis. This would be more typical for Addison’s disease, which can cause a mild metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap.

Diabetic ketoacidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. Diabetic ketoacidosis could cause these symptoms, signs and a metabolic acidosis. However, you would expect to see a raised anion gap in diabetic ketoacidosis; here, the anion gap is normal. This makes Addison’s disease more likely; it can present with a mild metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap as seen here. Adrenal Insufficiency A 76-year-old woman with a history of thyroid cancer comes to see you seeking advice. This patient recently had an incidental finding of a 1 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma (with no capsular invasion, PT1 NO MO) in a multi-nodular goitre surgically removed because of compressive symptoms. A post-operative ultrasound shows no evidence of residual disease in the neck and no lymphadenopathy.

Persistent vomiting
Persistent vomiting is incorrect. Persistent vomiting could cause a metabolic alkalosis, due to the excretion of hydrogen ions in vomitus, but it would not cause a metabolic acidosis as seen here. This picture of abdominal pain and vomiting in a young woman, combined with a mild acidosis with normal anion gap, is suggestive of Addison’s disease.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with a history of thyroid cancer comes to see you seeking advice.
