This patient recently had an incidental finding of a 1 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma (with no capsular invasion, PT1 NO MO) in a multi-nodular goitre surgically removed because of compressive symptoms. A post-operative ultrasound shows no evidence of residual disease in the neck and no lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?
options: Surveillance and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) suppression with replacement thyroxine and
explanation:
Surveillance and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) suppression with replacement thyroxine and
Surveillance and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) suppression with replacement thyroxine and dynamic risk stratification Following initial treatment with total thyroidectomy, TSH should be suppressed to below 0.1 mU/l in all patients for 9–12 months. Dynamic risk stratification refers to the decision to relax TSH suppression below 1 mU/l, after determining response to treatment in the first 9–12 months post-treatment. This measure of response involves an ultrasound of neck, a stimulated thyroglobulin and in patients with previous radioiodine treatment, a nuclear imaging scan or cross-sectional imaging. Based on the results of the tests, patients are categorised as low, intermediate or high risk of recurrence and management personalised accordingly.

External-beam radiotherapy
Conventional external-beam radiotherapy is incorrect. It has a role in the treatment of gross residual disease in patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma as it can locoregional symptoms and recurrence. However, there is no indication for external-beam radiotherapy in a patient with a 1 cm tumour, which is surgically cured with no residual disease or lymphadenopathy.

Radioactive iodine
Radioactive iodine treatment is incorrect. It is a type of targeted radiotherapy. The treatment uses a radioactive form of iodine called iodine 131 (I-131), which is taken up by thyroid cancer cells and destroys them. Radioactive iodine (RAI) treatment is indicated in patients with pT2-pT4, pN0-pN1b disease. The recent British Thyroid Association guidelines on thyroid cancer recommend that there is no indication for RAI treatment in patients with tumours < 1 cm unifocal or multifocal, and on histology show classical papillary or follicular variant or follicular minimally invasion without angioinvasion and no invasion of thyroid capsule.

Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is incorrect. If disease recurrence occurs in the neck or distant metastases develop, targeted chemotherapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, can be considered as a treatment option in patients who are not responsive to first-line treatment with radioiodine. However, chemotherapy would not be a suitable treatment option in this case.

Discharge patient
Discharge patient is incorrect. Patients, even with a 1 cm intrathyroidal well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma as described in this case, have a modest risk of recurrence and follow-up is strongly recommended.

stem: A 61-year-old patient with a history of recent thyrotoxicosis underwent major surgery 1 week ago. He now presents with altered mental status, tachycardia, high-grade fever, vomiting and cardiac failure; a diagnosis of thyroid storm (crisis) is made. What is the most important next step in the management?
options: Transfer the patient to the intensive care unit
Avoid using chlorpromazine for the treatment of agitation
Potassium iodide should be given with propylthiouracil
Peritoneal dialysis should be started immediately
explanation:
Transfer the patient to the intensive care unit
A multimodal treatment approach to patients with thyroid storm should be used, including β-adrenergic blockade, antithyroid drug therapy, inorganic iodide, corticosteroid therapy, aggressive cooling with paracetamol and cooling blankets, volume resuscitation, respiratory support and monitoring in an intensive care unit. Thyroid storm Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis, or thyroid storm, is a rare, occasionally iatrogenic disorder characterised by multisystem involvement and a high mortality rate if not immediately recognised and treated aggressively. A high index of suspicion for thyroid storm should be maintained in patients with thyrotoxicosis associated with any evidence of systemic decompensation. Precise criteria for thyroid storm have been defined and include: tachycardia, arrhythmias, congestive heart failure, hypotension, hyperpyrexia, agitation, delirium, psychosis, stupor and coma; as well as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and hepatic failure. Precipitants of thyroid storm in a patient with previously compensated thyrotoxicosis include abrupt cessation of antithyroid drugs, thyroid or non-thyroidal surgery in a patient with unrecognised or inadequately treated thyrotoxicosis and a number of acute illnesses unrelated to thyroid disease. Thyroid storm also occurs, rarely, following radioactive iodine therapy: exposure to iodine from the use of iodine-containing contrast agents may be an additional factor in the development of thyroid storm in patients with illnesses unrelated to thyroid disease. Each pharmacologically accessible step in thyroid hormone production and action is targeted in the treatment of patients with thyroid storm. Management: A multimodal treatment approach to patients with thyroid storm should be used, including βadrenergic blockade, antithyroid drug therapy, inorganic iodide, corticosteroid therapy, aggressive cooling with paracetamol and cooling blankets, volume resuscitation, respiratory support and monitoring in an intensive care unit.

Avoid using chlorpromazine for the treatment of agitation
Avoid using chlorpromazine for the treatment of agitation is incorrect. This patient’s thyroid storm should be managed with β-adrenergic blockade, antithyroid drug therapy, inorganic iodide, corticosteroid therapy, aggressive cooling with paracetamol and cooling blankets, volume resuscitation, respiratory support and monitoring in an intensive care unit.

Avoid carbimazole treatment
Avoid carbimazole treatment is incorrect. This will form part of the treatment strategy.

Potassium iodide should be given with propylthiouracil
Potassium iodide should be given with propylthiouracil is incorrect. This patient’s thyroid storm should be managed with β-adrenergic blockade, antithyroid drug therapy, inorganic iodide, corticosteroid therapy, aggressive cooling with paracetamol and cooling blankets, volume resuscitation, respiratory support and monitoring in an intensive care unit.

Peritoneal dialysis should be started immediately
Peritoneal dialysis should be started immediately is incorrect. This is not used in managing thyroid storm.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with headaches, excessive sweating, galactorrhoea, polyuria and polydipsia. He says that he can no longer wear his wedding ring because his fingers have become swollen. Visual field examination reveals bitemporal hemianopia. His blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. His BMI is 24. Blood tests show: fasting glucose 9 mmol/l (normal range 3–6 mmol/l); prolactin 1200 mU/l (normally < 360 mU/l). What is the most probable underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Acromegaly
This patient most probably has acromegaly. Although the characteristic changes in appearance are not apparent in nearly half of cases, associating the different clinical features that occur in this condition usually results in the diagnosis. A pituitary tumour (often a mixed adenoma) is the most common cause. In 30% of patients, mild to moderate hyperprolactinaemia occurs. In some, the adenoma secretes both growth hormone and prolactin. The sweating, soft tissue swelling, hypertension and dysglycaemia, fit well with the diagnosis. Excessive levels of growth hormone (GH) secreted by the pituitary gland may influence the production of insulin in up to half of patients with acromegaly. Abnormalities in insulin action may result in elevated glucose levels, and some of these patients may go on to develop insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes mellitus, explaining the symptoms of thirst and polyuria.

Prolactinoma
Prolactinoma is incorrect. The suspicion, as indicated by the visual field defects, is of a macroadenoma. The prolactin is not elevated enough to indicate a macroprolactinoma, therefore the rise is most likely to be due to local pressure from another tumour type. The hypertension, dysglycaemia and soft tissue swelling fit better with acromegaly.

Diabetes mellitus type 2
Diabetes mellitus type 2 is incorrect. The other features. including hypertension and soft tissue swelling, coupled with a relatively normal BMI, count against type 2 diabetes as the underlying diagnosis.

Cushing’s disease
Cushing’s disease is incorrect. Cushing’s disease is associated with marked weight gain, which is not present here. Acromegaly

Craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma is incorrect. Craniopharyngiomas present with diabetes insipidus due to failure of vasopressin production.

stem: A driver with a history of type 2 diabetes has been changed from oral medication to insulin some nine months earlier. He wishes to begin driving group 2 vehicles (lorries). What does he need to prove so that he can drive a lorry?
options: Need to confirm he has no episodes of severe hypoglycaemia in the last 12 months
explanation:
Need to confirm he has no episodes of severe hypoglycaemia in the last 12 months
A patient with diabetes can continue to drive a heavy goods vehicle (HGV) while taking insulin, as long as the following criteria are satisfied: There has not been any severe hypoglycaemic event in the previous 12 months (this is defined as 'requiring assistance of another person') If they have only recently started insulin, they must show three months of blood glucose monitoring on insulin They have full hypoglycaemic awareness They can show adequate control of their diabetes by regular blood glucose monitoring, at least twice daily and at times relevant to driving They can demonstrate an understanding of the risks of hypoglycaemia There are no other debarring complications of diabetes.

He cannot drive a lorry
He cannot drive a lorry is incorrect. Although patients taking insulin were previously not permitted to drive a HGV, they are now permitted to as long as they can confirm stable glucose control.

He must wait three months
He must wait three months is incorrect. Patients must show they have three months of stable blood glucose control with no significant hypoglycaemia.

He must wait six months
He must wait six months is incorrect. Patients can drive a HGV as long as there is no history of severe hypoglycaemia in the previous 12 months.

He must wait one year
He must wait one year is incorrect. One year of stable glucose control is required, not a one-year prospective period of glucose monitoring. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the diabetes clinic for review. He has had Type 1 diabetes for 30 years, with suboptimal control, and his most recent HbA1c was 8.8%/73 mmol/mol. Recently, he has had a number of falls, which he describes as attacks of feeling ‘faint’. He has suffered from impotence for a number of years and takes anti-reflux medication. On examination he has a postural drop of 35 mmHg in his blood pressure. Which diagnosis fits best with this history and examination?
explanation:
Autonomic neuropathy
This man has many symptoms of diabetic autonomic neuropathy, including postural hypotension, impotence and gastroparesis in the setting of long-standing diabetes with suboptimal control

Transient ischaemic attacks (TIA)
Transient ischaemic attacks is incorrect because he does not have any symptoms of TIA, which would include unilateral weakness, numbness and visual loss. In addition, the large postural BP drop would go against TIA.

Arrhythmia
Arrhythmia is incorrect because this man has multiple symptoms of diabetic autonomic neuropathy, including postural hypotension, impotence and gastroparesis in the setting of long-standing diabetes with suboptimal control. If his faints were caused by intermittent arrhythmia, he would not have such a large postural BP drop.

Vasovagal syncope
Vasovagal syncope is incorrect because this man has multiple symptoms of diabetic autonomic neuropathy, including postural hypotension, impotence and gastroparesis in the setting of long-standing diabetes with suboptimal control. Vasovagal syncope is when a trigger, such as stress, micturition and heat, results in increased vagal tone and decreased sympathetic nervous system tone.

Neurocardiogenic syncope
Neurocardiogenic syncope, another term for vasovagal syncope, is incorrect because this man has multiple symptoms of diabetic autonomic neuropathy, including postural hypotension, impotence and gastroparesis, in the setting of long-standing diabetes with suboptimal control. Vasovagal syncope is when a trigger, such as stress, micturition and heat, results in increased vagal tone and decreased sympathetic nervous system tone.

stem: A 45-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy, with an ejection fraction of 10%, takes amiodarone. He is doing well but on routine blood testing is found to have a free T4 of 38 (10-22) and TSH <0.01. With the information that has been given, what is the best first-line management for this patient’s thyrotoxicosis?
explanation:
Antithyroid drugs and corticosteroids
The diagnosis here is amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT). Type 1 thyrotoxicosis is treated with high doses of anti thyroid drugs to block thyroid hormone synthesis. Type 2 thyrotoxicosis is treated with a relatively long course of glucocorticoids. In reality it is often hard to differentiate between the 2 causes. When the mechanism of hyperthyroidism is uncertain, a combination of glucocorticoids and thionamides is used as initial therapy. A rapid response suggests type 2 AIT; thionamides can be tapered. A poor initial response suggests type 1 AIT; the steroids can be tapered and the patient can be treated for type 1 AIT.

Radioiodine
Radioiodine is incorrect as it is not usually effective because of reduced uptake by the thyroid gland. Radioactive iodine can only be used in the rare patients with high radioactive iodine uptake.

Lugol's iodine
Lugol's iodine is incorrect as although it may in some cases thyroid function in AIT, it only works temporarily.

Thyroidectomy
Thyroidectomy is incorrect as although it remains an effective form of treatment, with euthyroidism being restored within a matter of days, is not a first-line therapy. Effort should be made to normalise thyroid function prior to surgery. Thyrotoxicosis

Discontinue amiodarone
Discontinue amiodarone is incorrect as discontinuing amiodarone does not control the thyrotoxic state quickly because of its long half-life, and in certain situations it may not be ideal.

stem: A 55-year-old man who has a history of ischaemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes presents to the Emergency department with shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance. On examination his BP is 155/82; pulse is 88 and regular. His BMI is 35. You confirm bilateral basal crackles consistent with heart failure on auscultation of the chest, and pitting oedema of both ankles. He takes a number of medications for his diabetes and hypertension. Which one is most likely to be associated with this patient's development of heart failure?
explanation:
Saxagliptin
In its post-marketing cardiovascular endpoint study, saxagliptin was shown to be associated with increased incidence of heart failure. The aetiology is unclear, but where it is seen, substitution with an alternative is advisable.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Although amlodipine is recognised to cause ankle oedema, because of peripheral venous dilatation, it is not strongly associated with increased risk of heart failure.

Dapagliflozin
Dapagliflozin is incorrect. This is an SGLT2 inhibitor which causes increased urinary glucose excretion. It also has a thiazide diuretic-like action and has modest BP lowering effects.

Indapamide
Indapamide is incorrect. Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic and as such reduces the risk of heart failure. 
Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Metformin does not increase risk of cardiac failure and may reduce the risk of ischaemic cardiovascular events over the long term.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with prognathism and interdental separation. His GP has found it increasingly difficult to manage his blood pressure control over the past 2 years and he is now taking 3 oral agents. In addition despite a BMI of only 25, he has recently been diagnosed with impaired glucose tolerance. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
options: Fasting glucose test including growth-hormone measurement
Glucose tolerance test including growth-hormone measurement
explanation:
Glucose tolerance test including growth-hormone measurement
This patient’s symptoms are entirely consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. Biochemical diagnosis is made by measuring growth hormone levels in response to a glucose challenge, in normal patients, the concentration of growth hormone should fall.

Basal growth hormone measurement
Basal growth hormone measurement is incorrect. Growth hormone is subject to diurnal variation, which means one off measurements may not reflect the underlying diagnosis.

Fasting glucose test including growth-hormone measurement
Fasting glucose test including growth-hormone measurement is incorrect. We already know this patient has diabetes, and it’s a failure to suppress growth hormone in response to a glucose challenge which helps confirm the diagnosis of acromegaly.

Serum prolactin measurement
Serum prolactin measurement is incorrect. Prolactin levels increase during sleep, in response to oestrogen and stress, but hyperprolactinaemia doesn’t result in hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance.

Thyroid function test
Thyroid function test is incorrect. TFTs may be abnormal as a result of a somatotroph adenoma, but hypo or hyperthyroidism isn’t the primary cause of the symptoms seen here. Acromegaly An 11-week-pregnant woman presents to hospital with hyperemesis gravidarum. Thyroid function tests are completed and she is found to have a free T 4 of 30 (10–22) and a TSH of 0.06 (0.5–3.5). She does not have a goitre. Thyroid antibodies are negative. She has no symptoms of hyperthyroidism.

stem: An 11-week-pregnant woman presents to hospital with hyperemesis gravidarum. Thyroid function tests are completed and she is found to have a free T 4 of 30 (10–22) and a TSH of 0.06 (0.5–3.5). She does not have a goitre. Thyroid antibodies are negative. She has no symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Which of the following is the best management step?
explanation:
Observe and wait for normalisation
This woman has transient hyperthyroidism of hyperemesis gravidarum. This is caused by high levels of hCG, a known stimulator of TSH receptors. In spite of the significant biochemical evidence for hyperthyroidism, signs and symptoms of hypermetabolism are mild or absent. Normalisation of hyperthyroxinaemia parallels the improvement in vomiting and weight gain, with most cases resolving spontaneously in 2-10 weeks.

Radioiodine
Radioiodine is incorrect. This is not safe in pregnancy and is not necessary; it is used for thyrotoxicosis not cured following medication or if there is medication intolerance.

Immediate surgical referral
Immediate surgical referral is incorrect. The condition will probablyly resolve spontaneously. Surgery is useful for thyrotoxicosis in the setting where radio-iodine is contra-indicated, eg Graves’ with opthalmopathy, or when medication is not effective.

Propylthiouracil
Propylthiouracil is incorrect. The condition will probably resolve spontaneously. Propylthioutacil is used to treat hyperthyroidism in early pregnancy. Thyrotoxicosis A 19-year-old female gymnast presents with complaints of headache and fatigue. She has had no significant previous medical history, but has been amenorrhoeic for the past four months. She tells you that her menstrual cycle began aged 15 and was regular up until the past six months when she started more competitive gymnastic training. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and her pulse is 55 bpm. Her body mass index (BMI) is 16 kg/m 2. Investigations:

Carbimazole
Carbimazole is incorrect. The condition will probably resolve spontaneously Carbimazole is used to treat hyperthyroidism.

stem: A 44-year-old man is surprised to find that he cannot easily get his feet into a pair of shoes that he last wore 5 years ago. He goes to buy a new pair and is told that his shoe size has increased. He searches on the Internet for an explanation and, deciding that he could have acromegaly, consults his GP. The GP has not seen him for several years and thinks his appearance has changed, so refers him to the Endocrine Clinic. Which of the following would be the most useful first-line test for investigating him?
options: Glucose tolerance test with measurement of growth hormone
Insulin hypoglycaemia test (insulin tolerance test, insulin stress test)
Measurement of serum growth hormone during sleep
Measurement of serum growth hormone following exercise
Measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) concentration
explanation:
Measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) concentration
In healthy individuals, growth hormone secretion is suppressed following the administration of glucose. Failure of suppression is diagnostic of excessive growth hormone secretion. As an initial screening test, however, it may be more practical to measure serum IGF-1 and to follow this with an oral glucose tolerance test if the results are abnormal.

Glucose tolerance test with measurement of growth hormone
Glucose tolerance test with measurement of growth hormone is incorrect. Whilst acromegaly is a disorder where growth hormone is part of the aetiology, measuring serum growth hormone is problematic due to fluctuations. An advantage of IGF-1 is that levels are relatively stable over time, making it a better choice.

Insulin hypoglycaemia test (insulin tolerance test, insulin stress test)
Insulin hypoglycaemia test (insulin tolerance test, insulin stress test) is incorrect. An insulin hypoglycaemia test involves measuring glucose and cortisol following IV administration of insulin. This test assesses the integrity of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis.

Measurement of serum growth hormone during sleep
Measurement of serum growth hormone during sleep is incorrect. Measuring growth hormone can be reliable if the production has been suppressed. This can be done by using a oral glucose tolerance test rather than measuring levels during sleep. The insulin hypoglycaemia test and measurement of growth hormone during sleep can be used in the investigation of suspected growth hormone insufficiency.

Measurement of serum growth hormone following exercise
Measurement of serum growth hormone following exercise is incorrect. The insulin hypoglycaemia test and measurement of growth hormone following exercise can be used in the investigation of suspected growth hormone insufficiency.

stem: Which of the following features is a potential complication of this condition?
explanation:
Cardiomegaly
Cardiomegaly can be a complication of myxoedema (severe hypothyroidism). This patient has hypothyroidism: she has a raised thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) with low T4 and low-normal T3. Patients with myxoedema can develop pericardial effusions, cardiomegaly and heart failure.

Glove and stocking peripheral neuropathy
Glove and stocking peripheral neuropathy is incorrect. This patient has hypothyroidism, as evidenced by her symptoms and the high TSH with low T4. Although hypothyroidism can cause nerve entrapment syndromes (e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome) it does not cause a length-dependent neuropathy (i.e. glove and stocking neuropathy). Severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema) can cause bradycardia, hypothermia, altered mental state and heart failure with pericardial effusions and cardiomegaly.

Gynaecomastia
Gynaecomastia is incorrect. Gynaecomastia is a rare complication of thyrotoxicosis. This patient has hypothyroidism, as evidenced by her symptoms, and the raised TSH with low T4. Gynaecomastia is not especially associated with hypothyroidism. Severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema) can cause bradycardia, hypothermia, altered mental state and heart failure with pericardial effusions and cardiomegaly.

Optic neuropathy
Optic neuropathy is incorrect. Graves’ disease can cause optic neuropathy (compressive, as a result of extraocular muscle swelling and apical obstruction). However, this patient has hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism, as evidenced by her symptoms and the high TSH with low T4. Severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema) can cause bradycardia, hypothermia, altered mental state and heart failure with pericardial effusions and cardiomegaly. Hypothyroidism

Pretibial myxoedema
Pretibial myxoedema is incorrect. Pretibial myxoedema is associated with Graves’ disease; i.e. with hyperthyroidism. This patient has hypothyroidism, as evidenced by her symptoms and the high TSH with low T4. Hypothyroidism can cause generalised swelling of the face, hands and feet, but it does not cause pretibial myxoedema (which is infiltrative). Severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema) can cause bradycardia, hypothermia, altered mental state and heart failure with pericardial effusions and cardiomegaly.

stem: A 61-year-old farmer with Type 1 diabetes for 35 years, and long-standing poor control, complains of a limp and an abnormally shaped ankle. Examination reveals a painless joint that is warm and swollen; there is crepitus and what appears to be palpable bone debris. There is no history of trauma. An X-ray reveals gross joint destruction and apparent dislocation. His C-reactive protein (CRP) and white cell count (WCC) are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Charcot arthropathy
In patients with diabetes mellitus, the loss of sensation to a joint from neuropathy can result in a chronic, progressive and destructive arthropathy. It is seen in patients with poor control and peripheral neuropathy, who may also have other microvascular complications: Charcot arthropathy is multifactorial, due to a combination of mechanical and vascular factors resulting from diabetic peripheral and autonomic neuropathy and metabolic abnormalities of bone. The pathology of this condition is thought to be related to an exaggerated local inflammatory response to trauma to the neuropathic foot, mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines, resulting in the osteoarthropathy.

Osteomyelitis
Osteomyelitis is incorrect as the X-ray findings, in combination with the normal bloods, in this patient with Type 1 diabetes with poor control, all suggest Charcot joint.

Old healed fracture
Old healed fracture is incorrect as there is no history of trauma and the joint destruction on X-ray, in this patient with Type 1 diabetes with poor control, all suggest Charcot joint.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect as the X-ray findings, in combination with the normal bloods, in this patient with Type 1 diabetes with poor control, all suggest Charcot joint.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect as this would not cause the dislocation on X-ray, or the skin changes. Charcot arthropathy Clinical features Patients classically present with sudden onset of unilateral warmth, redness and oedema over the foot or ankle, often with a history of minor trauma; the affected foot may be discernibly warmer to the touch than the contralateral foot. Sometimes, patients present instead with a slowly progressing arthropathy, with insidious swelling over months or years, and, occasionally, recurrent acute attacks may occur. The most frequently involved joints in patients with diabetes are the tarsus and tarsometatarsal joints, followed by the metatarsophalangeal joints and the ankle. Management Avoidance of weight bearing Tight glycaemic control Patients who do not respond adequately to other interventions should be referred for consultation with an orthopaedic surgeon with experience in the management of diabetic neuropathic arthropathy, to assess the individual risks and benefits of surgical stabilisation or other procedures The role of bisphosphonates and calcitonin in acute Charcot neuroarthropathy remains uncertain. Diabetes - Type I.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis leading to his acute presentation?
explanation:
Pituitary apoplexy
The hormone test results with which we are presented here indicate hypothyroidism, hypoandrogenism and probably hypocortisolism. The most likely underlying cause is a pituitary adenoma, but the history leading to his acute presentation is typical of pituitary apoplexy, characterised by sudden-onset retro-orbital headache, vomiting and relative hypotension, with diplopia and visual field defects. Magnetic resonance imaging is the best way to image the pituitary to support the diagnosis. Over the long term he is likely to require corticosteroid, testosterone and thyroid hormone replacement.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. Subarachnoid haemorrhage is normally associated with marked hypertension; the low normal blood pressure here is a much stronger pointer to pituitary apoplexy.

Migraine
Migraine is incorrect. The sodium just below the lower limit of normal, and potassium approaching the upper limit of normal fits better with metabolic derangement as a result of pituitary apoplexy.

Parietal lobe infarct
Pituitary lobe infarct is incorrect. This patient has little or no vascular risk factors and his blood pressure is normal, counting against a stroke.

Non-functioning pituitary adenoma
Non-functioning pituitary adenoma is incorrect. The sudden onset headache fits better with a haemorrhage and pituitary apoplexy rather than with the chronicity of a non-functioning adenoma.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with known multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome presents to her endocrinologist because of a recent diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes. She has also unintentionally lost 5 kg in weight. The endocrinologist notices a rash. What is the name of the rash that she most likely has?
explanation:
Necrolytic migratory erythema
The diagnosis here is glucagonoma, which is associated with this characteristic skin rash in 75% of cases. The lesion starts as an indurated erythema at the perineum, face and nose; within a few days blisters will cover the surface of the skin, which then crust and heal, leaving hyperpigmented skin. This process takes 7–14 days, with lesions developing in one area while others are resolving.

Erythema chronicum migrans
Erythema chronicum migrans is incorrect as the diagnosis here is glucagonoma, which is associated with a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema). Erythema chronicum migrans, on the other hand, is associated with Lyme disease.

Acanthosis nigricans
Acanthosis nigricans is incorrect as the diagnosis here is glucagonoma, which is associated with a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema). Acanthosis is associated with insulin resistance.

Panniculitis
Panniculitis is incorrect as the diagnosis here is glucagonoma, which is associated with a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema). Panniculitis is inflammation of subcutaneous adipose tissue and is associated with inflammatory disorders and leukaemias.

Ichthyosis
Ichthyosis is incorrect as the diagnosis here is glucagonoma, which is associated with a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema). Ichthyosis is a genetic condition of dry, thickened epithelium.

stem: How would you best manage him initially with respect to his phaeochromocytoma and episodes of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)?
explanation:
Phenoxybenzamine
The pharmacological options for treatment of this man’s SVT are severely limited until he is adequately alpha blocked with phenoxybenzamine. As such, phenoxybenzamine is the initial management of choice, with titration if possible to maximal dose. It is likely once sympathetic outflow is reduced that episodes of SVT may well disappear anyway

Metoprolol
Metoprolol is incorrect. Beta blockers may be used as additional therapy in patients who are not controlled on maximal alpha blockade, but initial therapy is not appropriate.

Digoxin
Digoxin is incorrect. Digoxin is appropriate for rate control in persistent AF, but is of no value here.

Amiodarone
Amiodarone is incorrect. In the presence of continued sympathetic outflow due to the phaeochromocytoma, amiodarone is unlikely to have a useful impact.

Verapamil
Verpamil is incorrect. Cardioselective calcium channel antagonists do positively affect blood pressure, but are used in combination with alpha blockade for phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 32-year-old lawyer presents with non-specific symptoms of tiredness. She is dissatisfied with her GP and arranges a private magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of her pituitary. Blood testing by her private physician reveals normal thyroid function (T 4 14.6 pmol/l and TSH of 1.7 mIU/L), 0800 h cortisol of 560 nmol/l, prolactin of 154 mIU/l and normal gonadotropin and growth hormone levels. Her pituitary scan reveals a 0.8 cm microadenoma with no suprasellar extension or compression of optic chiasm. This patient has normal visual fields on confrontation. Which of the following represents the most appropriate course of action?
explanation:
Observation and reassurance
This patient has a microadenoma and a normal pituitary screen. Her tiredness is probably functional and completely unrelated to the microadenoma. All of the proposed interventions in the list of options are associated with significant morbidity. Some autopsy series have suggested that the incidence of pituitary tumours in people with an unrelated cause of death could be as high as 27%. The Endocrine Society guideline for incidental pituitary adenoma recommends that patients who have an incidental finding of a pituitary adenoma should undergo baseline pituitary function tests as in this case to evaluate for hypopituitarism or hypersecretion. If baseline biochemistry is normal, the recommendation for follow-up is a six monthly MRI in a patient with a macroadenoma (adenoma > 1cm) and a 12-month repeat MRI for patients with a microadenoma ( < 1 cm). If the first follow-up MRI is normal, the recommendation is for three yearly MRI scans thereafter for the patient with a microadenoma. The recommendation for biochemical surveillance is annual testing of baseline pituitary function in patients with a macroadenoma, but no further biochemical testing is necessary for patients with incidental microadenomas if the clinical evaluation and history remain stable.

Treatment with dopamine agonist therapy
Dopamine agonist therapy is incorrect and is the gold standard treatment option for patients with a prolactinsecreting pituitary adenoma or prolactinoma. Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline or bromocriptine will result in tumour shrinkage, normalisation of prolactin, and restoration of gonadal function in the majority of patients. In this case the prolactin is normal and so a dopamine agonist is not indicated.

Somatostatin therapy
Somatostatin therapy is incorrect. This is used as an adjuvant treatment for patients with growth hormone (GH) secreting pituitary adenomas to control GH levels in patients pre-operatively or in patients with recurrence of GH post-trans-sphenoidal surgery. Somatostatin analogues are synthetic forms of the hormone somatostatin which stops GH action, and the use of somatostatin analogues in patients with acromegaly can achieve tumour shrinkage and normalisation of GH and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) levels in most patients.

Bilateral stereotactic pituitary irradiation
Stereotactic radiosurgery is incorrect. It provides an efficient, safe, and minimal invasive treatment option for patients with secretory pituitary adenomas, but there are risks associated with this treatment including the risk of permanent hypopituitarism. There is no indication to perform stereotactic irradiation in a patient with a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma.

Trans-sphenoidal resection of pituitary
Trans-sphenoidal resection of pituitary is incorrect. For a non-functioning pituitary adenoma, trans-sphenoidal surgery is only indicated if there is compression of the optic chiasm and risk of bitemporal hemianopia or invasion of the cavernous sinus causing cranial nerve damage. Useful Weblinks Pituitary Incidentaloma: An Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline dx.doi.org/10.1210/jc.2010-1048 ( Prolactinoma A 38-year-old woman, who has recently been diagnosed with Graves’ disease and is being treated with carbimazole, comes to the Emergency Department with double vision and loss of colour sensitivity. She has marked proptosis and lid lag and you suspect she has worsening thyroid eye disease (TED).

stem: A 42-year-old man with recurrent episodes of pancreatitis is found to have severe hypertriglyceridaemia. He is seen by a lipid specialist and is diagnosed with hyperlipoproteinaemia type IB. This condition is associated with mutations in the gene coding for which protein?
explanation:
Apolipoprotein CII (APO CII)
Deficiency of this protein causes hyperlipoproteinaemia type IB/familial apolipoprotein CII deficiency. It is associated with acute pancreatitis, lipemia retinalis, eruptive skin xanthomas and hepatosplenomegaly. Pathogenesis: Dietary triglycerides in cholesterol are packaged by gastrointestinal epithelial cells into large lipoprotein particles called chylomicrons. After secretion into the intestinal lymph and passage into the general circulation, chylomicrons bind to the enzyme lipoprotein lipase, which is located on endothelial surfaces. This enzyme is activated by a protein contained in the chylomicron, apolipoprotein CII, liberating free fatty acids and monoglycerides, which then pass through the endothelial cells and enter adipocyte or muscle cells. Complete inactivation of either lipoprotein lipase or apolipoprotein CII as a result of the inheritance of two defective copies of the relevant gene therefore results in an accumulation of chylomicrons (type I lipoprotein elevation), due to failure of conversion to the chylomicron remnant particle. Presentation: Patients with familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency usually present in infancy with recurrent attacks of abdominal pain caused by pancreatitis; they also have eruptive xanthomas resulting from triglyceride deposition. Treatment: This should consist of a low-fat diet that can be supplemented by medium-chain triglycerides, which are not incorporated into chylomicrons. Differential diagnosis: The absence of functional apolipoprotein CII, with consequent failure to activate lipoprotein lipase, presents with a similar phenotype, although the affected patients are typically detected at a somewhat later age than patients with familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

Apolipoprotein E (APO E)
Apolipoprotein E (APO E) is incorrect as defects in gene coding for this protein are associated with familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia.

Apolipoprotein AII (APO AII)
Apolipoprotein AII (APO AII) is incorrect as this apolipoprotein ( is found in high-density lipoprotein ( (HDL) cholesterol ( in plasma ( A patient with APO AII deficiency has been described, but this patient was largely unaffected in terms of lipid profile and appeared to be free of cardiovascular disease.

Lipoprotein B
Lipoprotein B is incorrect as deficiency in this protein is associated with impairments in LDL catabolism, resulting in increased levels of low-density lipoprotein in the blood. The clinical manifestations are similar to diseases produced by mutations of the LDL receptor, such as familial hypercholesterolaemia. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency HypertriglyceridaemiaA 21-year-old student nurse is admitted to the Emergency Department with hypoglycaemia. She was providing end-of-life care with her supervisor to an elderly woman when she collapsed. The cardiac arrest team was called, when she was found to have a blood glucose of 2.1 mmol/l on finger prick and responded to IV dextrose. This is apparently the third collapse over the past 4 months. There is no history of diabetes in the family and her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On review in the Emergency Department her BP is 110/82 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. She is sweating and tremulous, her blood glucose has recovered to 5.1 mmol/l.

Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor
Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor is incorrect as abnormalities associated with this receptor cause familial heterozygous or homozygous hypercholesterolaemia.

stem: You review a 52-year-old woman in the thyroid clinic. She has a thyroid mass. Her functional status is excellent. She has no significant previous illnesses and currently holds down a part-time job as a solicitor. Biochemical testing reveals normal thyroid function. Fine needle aspiration biopsy of the lesion reveals a thyroid lymphoma. Which of the following is the best choice of therapy in this case?
explanation:
Chemotherapy and external-beam radiotherapy
Unlike other forms of thyroid cancer, thyroid lymphoma is not treated by surgical excision of the thyroid gland. It is instead treated with chemotherapy, radiation treatment, or a combination of both. The standard therapy for thyroid lymphoma is the combination of R-CHOP (rituximab plus standard chemotherapeutic agents), and external-beam radiotherapy.

Suppressive treatment with thyroid hormone
Suppressive treatment with thyroid hormone is incorrect. Thyroid lymphoma is not responsive to suppressive treatment with thyroxine.

Radioiodine treatment
Radioiodine treatment is incorrect. Iodine-131 is a radioactive isotope of iodine that is selectively concentrated in the thyroid tissue and metabolised by the same pathways as naturally occurring iodine. This, together with its long half-life (eight days), allows it to deliver high doses of radiation to the thyroid gland that are sufficient to destroy thyroid follicular cells. It has no utility in the treatment of thyroid lymphoma.

External-beam radiotherapy
External-beam radiotherapy is incorrect. External-beam radiotherapy used in isolation is inadequate for the treatment of thyroid lymphoma.

Palliative measures
Palliative measures is incorrect. Given her excellent functional status, she is a good candidate for both radiotherapy and an R-CHOP chemotherapy regimen.

stem: A highly insulin-resistant, 56-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes has been taking 200 units total daily dose of subcutaneous insulin per day. His weight is increasing and his control worsening, with an HbA1c of 76 mmol/mol (9.1%). He wishes to discuss adding pioglitazone to his regimen as he has read that it may help reduce his insulin requirement. Which of the following statements best describes pioglitazone therapy?
options: Pioglitazone causes heart failure by exerting a direct toxic effect on the myocardium
Pioglitazone is associated with weight loss
Pioglitazone has no effect on bone mineral density
Heart failure can be precipitated in some patients taking glitazones due to fluid retention
Pioglitazone acts primarily at the site of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) receptor
explanation:
Heart failure can be precipitated in some patients taking glitazones due to fluid retention
This is a recognised side effect of this class of drugs, with approximately 5% developing oedema.

Pioglitazone causes heart failure by exerting a direct toxic effect on the myocardium
Pioglitazone causes heart failure by exerting a direct toxic effect on the myocardium is incorrect. Heart failure seen with these drugs is caused by excess fluid retention.

Pioglitazone is associated with weight loss
Pioglitazone is associated with weight loss is incorrect. Glitazones cause weight gain.

Pioglitazone has no effect on bone mineral density
Pioglitazone has no effect on bone mineral density is incorrect. Glitazones have been shown to be associated with accelerated bone loss and an increased risk of fracture. Glitazones/thiazolidenidiones These drugs act at the site of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-γ) receptor, promoting the transcription of genes predominantly linked to fatty acid metabolism. Metformin acts primarily by affecting hepatic insulin resistance, whereas glitazones act by improving insulin sensitivity and peripheral glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and fat. They have fallen out of favour due to effects on bone density and an increased fracture risk, along with an increased cardiovascular risk and fears over a link between bladder cancer and pioglitazone. Diabetes - Type II A 22-year-old man with diabetes mellitus comes to the clinic for review. He tells you he has recently moved to the area and been told that he has maturity onset diabetes of the young, (MODY). Which of the following features in his history would lead you to suspect that he is correct?

Pioglitazone acts primarily at the site of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) receptor
Pioglitazone acts primarily at the site of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α) receptor is incorrect. It acts at the site of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR-γ) receptor, promoting the transcription of genes predominantly linked to fatty acid metabolism.

stem: Magnetic resonance imaging reveals a 7 mm pituitary microadenoma. Which of the following hormones would you expect to be low?
explanation:
Luteinising hormone
This patient describes secondary amenorrhea and has biochemical evidence of an elevated prolactin and radiological evidence of a pituitary microadenoma. The overall diagnosis is in keeping with a pituitary microprolactinoma. Elevated levels of prolactin inhibit gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) through a negative feedback mechanism. Inhibition of GnRH results in reduced stimulation and secretion of the gonadotrophin hormones (FSH and LH) from the anterior pituitary, resulting in hypothalamic hypogonadism and secondary amenorrhea.

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is incorrect. ADH is released from the posterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary function is rarely affected by adenomas in the anterior pituitary, but can be damaged by hypothalamic tumours, infiltrative disorders such as sarcoidosis, histocytosis or Wegner’s granulamotosis. Therefore, ADH secretion is very unlikely to be affected in this case of pituitary microadenoma.

Cortisol
Cortisol is incorrect. Impaired ACTH secretion from the anterior pituitary can cause hypocortisolaemia in the setting of a macroadenoma, due to the compressive effects of a large adenoma on the normal pituitary tissue leading to hypopituitarism. However, this is very uncommon in the setting of a microadenoma and there are no clinical signs or symptoms of cortisol deficiency in this case.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. The sequential loss of pituitary hormones secondary to a mass effect is in the following order: growth hormone (GH), luteinising hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and prolactin. Therefore, if hypopituitarism occurs because of mass effect, growth hormone deficiency is often the first hormonal deficiency observed. In this case, the pituitary adenoma is a microadenoma and the risk of compression of normal pituitary tissue is minimal.

Thyroxine
Thyroxine is incorrect. An elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone in the setting of primary hypothyroidism can stimulate prolactin secretion through the effect of an elevated TRH. TRH can stimulate prolactin as well as TSH secretion from the anterior pituitary. An elevated prolactin level from a microprolactinoma, as in this case, is unlikely to affect thyroxine levels. If a patient had elevated prolactin because of a large macroprolactinoma, the compressive effects of a macroadenoma on normal pituitary tissue can cause hypopituitarism and lead to secondary hypothyroidism in this clinical setting.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is reviewed in the endocrinology clinic for a background of Graves’ disease on carbimazole 20 mg a day. She is clinically now euthyroid and her most recent thyroid function tests show a TSH of 1.79 miu/L and a T 4 of 13.6pmol/L. What is the most important side effect of carbimazole treatment about which all patients must be counselled?
explanation:
Agranulocytosis
Agranulocytosis is a rare but potentially catastrophic side effect of both carbimazole and propylthiouracil treatment. Agranulocytosis is an acute condition involving a severe and dangerous leukopenia. People with this condition are at very high risk of serious infections due to their suppressed immune system. Patients classically develop a sore throat with the onset of agranulcytosis, and therefore all patients should be counselled on this risk and advised to present to their GP for a full blood count if they develop a sore throat on this medication, and to discontinue the medication and seek advice.

Heart failure
Heart failure is incorrect. Both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism produce changes in cardiac contractility, myocardial oxygen consumption, cardiac output, blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance, and can lead to heart failure, but this effect on cardiovascular function is most commonly reversed with treatment and no direct link between carbimazole treatment and heart failure exists.

Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is incorrect. Osteoporosis is a risk associated with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism due to accelerated bone turnover and reduced bone density driven by excess thyroid hormone. However, this risk is again reversed with treatment and is not associated with carbimazole treatment.

Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is incorrect. Atrial fibrillation is commonly associated with thyrotoxicosis, and occurs in up to 15% of patients with hyperthyroidism compared to 4% of people in the general population; it is more common in men and in patients with triiodothyronine (T3) toxicosis. Also, subclinical hyperthyroidism is a risk factor associated with a threefold increase in development of AF. However, there is no risk of atrial fibrillation associated with carbimazole treatment. Thyrotoxicosis

Acute kidney injury
Acute kidney injury is incorrect. Carbimazole is hepatically cleared and is not associated with acute kidney injury. However, carbimazole is associated with liver dysfunction, typically causing a cholestatic pattern and requires discontinuation of the medication.

stem: A 31-year-old man is referred to the local Hypertension Clinic because of recently discovered hypertension that is labile and difficult to control. Which of the following features is most likely to suggest a genetic/familial syndrome is the cause for his hypertension?
options: Random blood glucose level of 9 mmol/l
A serum calcium level of 1.5 mmol/l
A family history of parathyroid hyperplasia
A family history of papillary thyroid neoplasia
explanation:
A family history of parathyroid hyperplasia
Among endocrine causes of hypertension, only phaeochromocytoma has a strong genetic heritability (MEN 2 association), and MEN 2 is associated with medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and primary parathyroid hyperplasia or multiple adenomas (with reducing incidence).

Serum potassium level of 3.9 mmol/l
A serum potassium level of 3.9 mmol/L is incorrect. Hypokalaemia may be a feature of primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome). More rarely, hypokalaemia is also seen with aggressive forms of Cushing’s syndrome as in ectopic ACTH production or functioning adrenal cancers. Hypokalaemia is also seen in Liddle’s syndrome, an inherited cause of hypertension, although a serum potassium below the lower limit of the normal range (<3.5 would be expected).

Random blood glucose level of 9 mmol/l
Random blood glucose level of 9 mmol/L is incorrect. Cushing’s syndrome, acromegaly and rarely phaeochromocytoma may be associated with hyperglycaemia. However, both hypertension and diabetes are common conditions in the general population. Their co-existence does not suggest a genetic/familial aetiology.

A serum calcium level of 1.5 mmol/l
A serum calcium of 1.5 mmol/L is incorrect. Hypocalcaemia has no known association with endocrine hypertension. Hypercalcaemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism could be a feature of both MEN 2 and MEN 1. 613 Phaeochromocytoma

A family history of papillary thyroid neoplasia
A family history of papillary thyroid neoplasia is incorrect. Medullary thyroid cancer is part of MEN2 but papillary thyroid cancer has no association.

stem: Cortisol level 30 min into a Synacthen ® test is 570 nmol/l. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
explanation:
Corticosteroid-related adrenal suppression
It is likely that he is using an over-the-counter inhaled nasal corticosteroid preparation, as well as his inhaled corticosteroids for asthma. The combination is likely to have led to a degree of adrenal suppression, as evidenced by postural hypotension, mild hyponatremia, coupled with a low baseline cortisol which returns to the normal range after administration of Synacthen . The treatment of choice is cessation of the inhaled nasal steroids, coupled with a strategy to reduce his asthma therapy corticosteroids, for instance by adding in a longacting ß 2-agonist and then stepping down the level of inhaled steroids. Once these strategies are in place, the Synacthen ® test should be repeated. ®

Iatrogenic Cushing
Iatrogenic Cushing is incorrect. The most common cause of Cushing syndrome is iatrogenic Cushing syndrome. This can be caused by long-term oral corticosteroid treatment of a variety of disorders such as asthma and rheumatoid arthritis, or in immunosuppression. Although adrenal suppression can occur from topical or inhaled steroid therapy, iatrogenic Cushing is less commonly caused by these therapies. This patient does not have any signs or symptoms of Cushing such as weight gain, hypertension, proximal myopathy, striae or bruising. Also of note, this patient has postural hypotension rather than hypertension, which is associated with Cushing.

Primary adrenal failure
Primary adrenal failure is incorrect. This patient has mild symptoms to suggest cortisol suppression, but his Synacthen ® test does not indicate overt adrenal failure with adequate cortisol response post-Synacthen ® stimulation.

Normal adrenal function
Normal adrenal function is incorrect. This patient describes fatigue and there is evidence of postural hypotension coupled with a low baseline cortisol, which responds to stimulation with ACTH, indicating that adrenal function is suppressed and not entirely normal. Adrenal Insufficiency A 31-year-old woman who is 22 weeks’ pregnant is referred to the diabetic clinic with glycosuria. It is her first pregnancy. On examination, her blood pressure is 139/80 mmHg and her body mass index (BMI) is 32 kg/m 2. She has no other medical history of note. Investigations show:

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH is incorrect. SIADH is characterised by the inappropriate secretion of ADH from the posterior pituitary, causing excess water retention and a dilutional hyponatremia. This patient has a mild hyponatremia coupled with postural hypotension. Postural hypotension is a very sensitive indicator of hypovolaemia, and SIADH is characterised by a euvolemic state. Furthermore, SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion after cortisol deficiency and hypothyroidism have been ruled out. Therefore, suppressed cortisol function or mild cortisol suppression is the correct answer in this case, and not SIADH.

stem: She is very distressed as she is on a college scholarship for rowing and her diabetes and glycaemic control is significantly affecting her training, despite excellent compliance and engagement with diabetes services. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange a continuous glucose monitor and consider an insulin pump device if evidence of severe
explanation:
Arrange a continuous glucose monitor and consider an insulin pump device if evidence of severe
Arrange a continuous glucose monitor and consider an insulin pump device if evidence of severe exercise-induced hypoglycaemia. In an attempt to best mimic the insulin delivery of a normal, healthy pancreas, insulin pumps were first developed in the late 1970s. Today’s mobile phone–size pumps are much more sophisticated and give both basal insulin doses (background insulin delivered every few minutes in small increments to cover the body’s general need for insulin) and boluses (larger doses given to cover meals and snacks or to lower elevated blood glucose at any time). Active people who use insulin need to make frequent adjustments in their diabetes regimen to maintain blood glucose within target range, especially when doing higher-intensity or longerduration exercise, and therefore an insulin pump allows more flexibility and less erratic glycaemic control.

Insulin aspart
Insulin aspart is incorrect. This is a manufactured form of human insulin, and involves the exchange of a single amino acid. This single amino acid change helps the fast-acting insulin analogue to be absorbed quickly into the bloodstream. As a result, it starts working in minutes, which allows one to take insulin and eat right away. However, this is the most common type of insulin used in a nutritional bolus regime and, therefore, is unlikely to offer any further benefit to this patient.

Insulin detemir
Insulin detemir is incorrect. Both insulin glargine and insulin detemir are long-acting insulin analogues, which have been primarily shown in type 1 diabetes to reduce nocturnal hypoglycaemia.

Insulatard ®
Insulatard ® is incorrect. Insulatard ® is a human insulin with gradual onset and long duration of action. It can cause hypoglycaemia due to long duration of action and therefore would not be appropriate for this patient.

NovoMix ® 50/50
NovoMix ® 50/50 is incorrect. NovoMix ® 50/50 is unlikely to be of much help in this patient, because it would still necessitate a twice-daily dosing regime and does not enable much flexibility for patients who frequently exercise. Diabetes - Type I.

stem: A 18-year-old student presents with intermittent weakness and feelings of tiredness. Her GP requested some blood tests and found her to have a potassium level of 2.8 mmol/l and bicarbonate of 32 mmol/l. Her blood pressure is 110/78. She is of short stature and tells you that she has always found sport and exercise difficult, with frequent admissions in childhood for dehydration/electrolyte abnormalities. You arrange renin and aldosterone levels and both are elevated. Urinary calcium excretion is elevated. Urinary diuretic screen is negative. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Bartter syndrome
Bartter syndrome is characterised by increased urinary calcium excretion, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and raised renin and aldosterone levels.

Diuretic abuse
Diuretic abuse is incorrect. Urinary diuretic screen is negative and aldosterone would be low.

Gitelman syndrome
Gitelman syndrome is incorrect. That syndrome is associated with hypocalciuria.

Liddle syndrome
Liddle syndrome is incorrect. She is normotensive.

Conn syndrome
Conn syndrome is incorrect. She is normotensive and renin is raised. Bartter syndrome Bartter syndrome is characterised by increased urinary calcium excretion, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and raised renin and aldosterone levels. The age at onset varies, depending on the severity of the causative mutation – most patients present in childhood, but some can present later in adolescence as is the case here. Bartter syndrome is caused by a mutation in the Na +-K +-2Cl – co-transporter, the ATP-regulated potassium channel or the kidney-specific basolateral chloride channel. This impairs sodium and chloride reabsorption and causes an increase in the production of renal prostaglandin E 2. Hyperplasia of the juxtaglomerular apparatus is seen on renal biopsy. Potassium Imbalance Exposure to darkness is found to increase melatonin secretion. You are considering recommending it for use in a 17-year-old man with severe autism who is awake for much of the night.

stem: Exposure to darkness is found to increase melatonin secretion. You are considering recommending it for use in a 17-year-old man with severe autism who is awake for much of the night. What is the most common mechanism by which melatonin is naturally synthesised?
options: Blockade of noradrenaline release from sympathetic nerve terminals
Increased intracellular cAMP in the hypothalamus
explanation:
Increased serotonin N-acetyltransferase
Melatonin is synthesised and secreted by the pineal gland from serotonin: N-acetyltransferase + acetyl-CoA converts serotonin to N-acetyl serotonin, which is then converted by hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase to melatonin. Exposure to darkness causes activation of the hypothalamus by the retinohypothalamic nerves. This results in increased noradrenaline secretion by the postganglionic sympathetic nerves (nervi conarii) that innervate the pineal gland. Noradrenaline acts via α-adrenergic receptors in the pineal gland to increase the intracellular levels of cAMP, which then causes an increase in N-acetyltransferase activity.

Decreased activity of suprachiasmatic nuclei
Decreased activity of suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) is incorrect. Increased activity of the SCN helps drive melatonin production.

Decreased hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase activity
Decreased hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase activity is incorrect. This is responsible for the second step in melatonin production.

Blockade of noradrenaline release from sympathetic nerve terminals
Blockade of noradrenaline release from sympathetic nerve terminals is incorrect. Increased noradrenalin release from nerves which innervate the pineal gland drives N-acetyltransferase activity and subsequent melatonin production.

Increased intracellular cAMP in the hypothalamus
Increased intracellular cAMP in the hypothalamus is incorrect. It is increased levels of cAMP in the pineal gland that drive melotonin production.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the endocrine clinic with a rapidly enlarging left thyroid nodule. Histology of this lesion suggests that it is a medullary thyroid carcinoma. Her blood pressure is also elevated at 155/90. Which of the following would you consider as the most likely cause of her hypertension?
explanation:
Phaeochromocytoma
The presence of medullary thyroid carcinoma raises the possibility of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A. MEN2A is associated with hyperparathyroidism, medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.

Coarctation of the aorta
Coarctation of the aorta is incorrect. Coarctation of the aorta is associated with Turner’s syndrome, rather than with medullary thyroid cancer.

Hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism
Hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism is incorrect. Conn’s syndrome is not a feature of MEN-2a.

Liddle’s syndrome
Liddle’s syndrome is incorrect. Liddle’s syndrome is caused by in inherited mutation of the epithelial sodium channel and is not associated with MEN-2a.

Renal artery stenosis
Renal artery stenosis is incorrect. Renal artery stenosis associated with fibromuscular dysplasia is common in patients of African origin, and not associated with MEN-2a. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia A 27-year-old woman on cabergoline for microprolactinoma becomes pregnant.

stem: You elect to start a GLP-1 analogue or glucagon-like petide-1. Which of the following is a contraindication to treatment with a GLP-1 analogue?
explanation:
A history of gastroparesis
Glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) analogues can delay gastric emptying and can therefore exacerbate theTutor symptoms of gastroparesis and are contraindicated in patients with a history of gastroparesis.

Increased body mass index
Increased body mass index is incorrect. NICE guidelines recommend that GLP-1 analogues should only be considered in patients with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes defined as a HbA1c of > 7.5% (58 mmol/mol) a BMI > 35 because of the additional potential for weight loss with this class of drugs.

A history of hypoglycaemia
A history of hypoglycaemia is incorrect. One advantage of this class of drug over older insulin secretagogues, such as sulfonylureas or meglitinides, is that they have a lower risk of causing hypoglycaemia is low compared with GLP-1 analogues as insulin is only secreted in a glucose dependant manner. However, this advantage is lost if GLP-1 analogues are used in conjunction with insulin or sulphonylurea treatment.

Background retinopathy
Background retinopathy is incorrect. There is no contraindication to the use of GLP-1 analogues in this condition. In fact, improved glycaemic control will aid in the prevention of microvascular complication of type 2 diabetes.

Smoking history
Smoking history is incorrect. GLP-1 analogues are not contraindicated in patients with a smoking history, although all patients with type II diabetes should be advised on lifestyle modification to minimise cardiovascular complications and smoking cessation advice and guidance should be provided to every patient during a clinical visit. Diabetes - Type II You are reviewing a 45-year-old man who has type 2 diabetes. He works a varying shift pattern as a taxi driver and has not tolerated metformin therapy due to gastrointestinal side effects. You decide that the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin is the most appropriate therapy choice.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis given the findings?
explanation:
Phaeochromocytoma
We have evidence of end-organ damage, with both retinal changes and proteinuria. Additionally, the degree of hypertension, hypokalaemia and evidence of raised blood glucose also point to the possibility of phaeochromocytoma. Increased epinephrine concentrations in the plasma secreted by pheochromocytoma induce hypokalemia through stimulation of beta 2 receptors causing activation of sodium potassium-ATPase in skeletal muscles and subsequent intracellular shift of potassium.

Tension headache
Tension headache is incorrect. Tension headache is not associated with fundal changes.

Essential hypertension
Essential hypertension is incorrect. This lady has severe hypertension with end-organ damage and is likely to have an underlying cause.

Benign intracranial hypertension
Benign intracranial hypertension is incorrect. Benign intracranial hypertension is associated with papilloedema, which is not seen here. Phaeochromocytoma

Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. Diabetic retinopathy would be expected to appear up to 10 years after the onset of diabetes, so is not an appropriate diagnosis here.

stem: Which of the following is the management of choice?
explanation:
Parathyroidectomy
This patient has symptomatic hyperparathyroidism, as evidenced by polyuria and polydipsia, history of renal colic, and increased creatinine. In addition her T score is <-2.5 and technetium scanning reveals a discrete adenoma, so as such progression to surgery is the best option.

Cinacalcet
Cinacalcet is incorrect. Cinacalcet is useful with respect to treating the metabolic abnormalities associated with hyperparathyroidism, but does not reduce bone turnover or BMD, and therefore this is a secondary option in those who will not tolerate surgery for medical reasons.

Observation
Observation is incorrect. She needs treatment and has symptomatic hyperparathyroidism with osteoporosis and a parathyroid adenoma.

Raloxifene
Raloxifene is incorrect. Selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERMs) such as raloxifene are not be the first line option in this case. They are an alternative to bisphosphonates for osteoporosis where they are not tolerated.

Risedronate
Risedronate is incorrect. In those who do not meet the criteria for surgery or refuse it, a bisphosphonate may be a reasonable option for bone protection. This is wrong in this case as there is no obvious contraindication to surgery, so she shoud be offered it.

stem: A 42-year-old man is referred to the Hypertension Clinic for advice. He is currently taking atenolol, bendroflumethiazide and ramipril and his blood pressure is currently 165/105 mmHg. His potassium is 3.0 mmol/l, with a serum bicarbonate concentration of 31 mmol/l. His BMI is 24, with a normal hip:waist ratio. What is the best next management step?
options: Measure the ratio of aldosterone to renin
Wash out as many of his antihypertensive agents as possible for a period of 2 weeks, then review
Add in a further agent and review in 12 months
explanation:
Measure the ratio of aldosterone to renin
The suspicion here – with hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and resistant hypertension despite being on 3 agents – is that he has primary hyperaldosteronism. Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism due to an aldosterone-secreting adenoma. Recent guidelines suggest taking a baseline random renin and aldosterone to calculate ratio is a worthwhile initial screen even in the presence of interfering medications. If the aldosteronerenin ratio is <800 (using units of pmol/ml/hr for renin and pmol/L for aldosterone) then Conn syndrome is extremely unlikely and the patient should be investigated for other causes of secondary hypertension and hypokalaemia. An aldosterone-renin ratio of >800 should prompt medication review and formal evaluation. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II-receptor blockers and spironolactone/eplerenone need to be stopped for at least 4 weeks before re-testing. Beta-blockers and other diuretics need to be stopped 2 weeks before testing. Patients may need to start alternative agents to maintain safe BP control. This requires careful involvement of the GP and patient in arranging safe BP and serum potassium monitoring before planning investigations. Although calcium channel blockers may also interfere with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway, in practice this is not clinically apparent. Alpha-blockers (such doxazosin) and calcium channel blockers (such as amlodipine) are thus routinely recommended for BP control during investigation of possible Conn syndrome. The protocol for this test usually requires the patient to lie recumbent and resting for 30 minutes, can be taken at any time of day, and with a normalised potassium concentration (using supplementation) if possible.

Wash out as many of his antihypertensive agents as possible for a period of 2 weeks, then review
Wash out as many of his antihypertensive agents as possible for a period of 2 weeks, then review is incorrect. The initial investigation should be a random aldosterone:renin ratio, preceding to a test off all antihypertensives if the initial results are suggestive of primary hyperaldosteronism.

Measure his 24-hour blood pressure
Measure his 24-hour blood pressure is incorrect. This patient warrants further investigation for secondary hypertension as he is still hypertensive on 3 different BP agents, and has biochemical abnormalities.

Arrange 24-hour urinary free cortisol collection
Arrange 24-hour urinary free cortisol collection is incorrect. This is one of the initial screening tests for Cushing syndrome. This causes hypertension and can cause hypokalaemia, but you would also expect to find central obesity on examination.

Add in a further agent and review in 12 months
Add in a further agent and review in 12 months is incorrect. This patient warrants further investigation for secondary hypertension as he is still hypertensive on 3 different BP agents, and has biochemical abnormalities.

stem: Which of the following is the best initial investigation to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
IGF-1
The diagnosis to exclude here is clearly acromegaly. Growth hormone production is cyclical; therefore, a random sample is not particularly useful. On the other hand, IGF-1 is elevated in acromegaly and has a very long halflife; therefore, this is the initial outpatient screening blood test of choice.

Insulin tolerance test
Insulin tolerance test (ITT) is incorrect. This is used in the assessment of pituitary/growth hormone insufficiency, but is now rarely used because of potential alternative methods of investigation, and risks of hypoglycaemia associated with ITT.

Random growth hormone
Random growth hormone is incorrect. Growth hormone is subject to diurnal variation and has a short half-life; random sampling is therefore not useful in the assessment of acromegaly.

24hr urinary free cortisol
24hr urinary free cortisol 24-hour urinary-free cortisol is incorrect. This is most useful in the assessment of Cushing’s disease.

Visual field testing
Visual field testing is incorrect. Although it may be required in the event that a pituitary tumour is identified, this should take place after the biochemical diagnosis of acromegaly has been confirmed.

stem: A 48-year-old man is referred by his GP with suspected acromegaly to the Endocrine Clinic. He has difficult-tocontrol hypertension, and has been troubled with sweating over the past few months. He can no longer wear his wedding ring. On examination in the clinic he has prognathism, large hands and feet. He confirms that his appearance has changed versus photographs taken of him from a few years earlier. Which of the following would be the most useful initial investigation?
options: Glucose tolerance test with measurement of growth hormone
Measurement of serum basal growth hormone concentration
Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration during sleep
Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration following exercise
Measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-1)
explanation:
Measurement of serum insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-1)
Acromegaly is caused by excessive growth hormone secretion after the fusion of the epiphyses, and is usually the result of a pituitary adenoma. Ectopic secretion of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) is a rare cause. IGF-1 is valuable in monitoring for recurrence after treatment and as an initial investigation because IGF1 is elevated in acromegaly, has a long half-life, and can be measured at any time of the day.

Glucose tolerance test with measurement of growth hormone
Glucose tolerance test with measurement of growth hormone is incorrect. A glucose tolerance test is a useful next step in biochemical investigation of acromegaly, and a failure of growth hormone to suppress to below 0.3 μg/l indicates possible acromegaly.

Measurement of serum basal growth hormone concentration
Measurement of serum basal growth hormone concentration is incorrect. Isolated (basal, unstimulated) growth hormone levels are often raised in acromegaly, but because the hormone is secreted sporadically and has a short half-life, levels may not always be elevated.

Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration during sleep
Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration during sleep is incorrect. Measurement of growth hormone concentration during sleep is clearly impractical; IGF-1, a single measurement in the clinic is a superior option.

Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration following exercise
Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration following exercise is incorrect. Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration following exercise is not useful, as growth hormone is a counter-regulatory hormone which rises in response to exercise.

stem: A 49-year-old woman is investigated to determine the cause of Cushing syndrome following the demonstration of hypercortisolaemia by a high 24-hour urinary cortisol excretion and failed dexamethasone suppression test. Her midnight plasma cortisol concentration is elevated. Her 0900-h plasma cortisol concentration falls to 50% of the baseline value after a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test. The plasma cortisol concentration increases by 25% after she is given intravenous corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cushing’s disease (pituitary-dependent Cushing syndrome)
Incomplete suppression of cortisol following high-dose dexamethasone (2 mg 6-hourly for 48 hours) is typical of Cushing’s disease. There is typically no suppression in patients with Cushing syndrome that is not pituitarydependent. An increase in cortisol following the administration of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is also suggestive of Cushing’s disease, but with other causes there is usually no response. The use of CRH in this setting is based on the principle that pituitary tumors respond to exogenous CRH, whereas ectopic and adrenal tumors do not.

Adrenal adenoma
Adrenal adenoma is incorrect. Adrenal Cushings as if the adrenals were the source of hypertcortisolism there would be no suppression after high dose dexamethasone and no increase in cortisol following the administration of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).

Adrenal carcinoma
Adrenal carcinoma is incorrect. If the adrenals were the source of hypertcortisolism there would be no suppression after high dose dexamethasone and no increase in cortisol following the administration of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).

ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (AIMAH)
ACTH-independent macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (AIMAH) is incorrect. If the adrenals were the source of hypertcortisolism there would be no suppression after high dose dexamethasone and no increase in cortisol following the administration of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).

Ectopic secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
Ectopic secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is incorrect. High dose dexamethasone exerts negative feedback on pituitary neoplastic tumours causing Cushing's disease but not on ectopic ACTHproducing cells or adrenal adenoma.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated in the Endocrinology Clinic because of increased urine output. She weighs 60 kg and has a 24 h urine output of 3500 ml. Her basal urine osmolality is 210 mOsmol/kg. She undergoes a fluid deprivation test and her urine osmolality after fluid deprivation (loss of weight 3 kg) is 510 mOsmol/kg. A subsequent injection of subcutaneous DDAVP (desmopressin acetate) did not result in any further significant rise of urine osmolality after 2 h (520 mOsmol/kg). Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary polydipsia
DI is suspected when the urine output is >50 ml/kg per day (3000 ml for a 60 kg female). If the basal urine osmolality is <300 mOsmol/kg, this suggests an osmotic diuresis. If fluid deprivation causes a urine osmolality >300 mOsmol/kg, this suggests psychogenic (primary) polydipsia. This condition can be difficult to diagnose, and confirmation using a fluid deprivation test is sometimes required. It is more common in females then males and is more common in patients with a psychiatric history.

Normal
Normal is incorrect. This patient has a significant urinary output and a dilute urine concentration. At the very least, this patient should be tested using a paired serum and urine osmolarity but, as the diagnosis can be difficult, a water deprivation test is often required to confirm a diagnosis and is the gold standard test for the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus (DI).

Syndrome of inappropriate ADH
