Syndrome of inappropriate ADH is incorrect. This is characterised by euvolaemic hyponatremia and concentrated urine, usually >350 mmol/kg, caused by the inappropriate secretion of ADH and water retention rather than excretion.

Pituitary DI
Pituitary DI is incorrect. This is caused by a deficiency of ADH hormone production from the posterior pituitary, and leads to polyuria and polydipsia. It can be either hereditary or acquired and is more common in patients post-neurosurgery or head trauma. Fluid deprivation will fail to induce a urine concentration of >300 mOsmo/kg in patients with cranial DI. However, this disorder can be diagnosed by the administration of subcutaneous desmopressin acetate (DDAVP), which causes an increased urine osmolality to >300 mOsmol/kg in pituitary DI.

Nephrogenic DI
Nephrogenic DI is incorrect. Nephrogenic DI is rare and can be either hereditary or acquired and is caused by insensitivity or resistance of the cells in the collecting duct of the nephron to the action of ADH. Again patients will fail to concentrate the urine to greater than 300mosmo/kg after fluid deprivation. However unlike cranial DI patients with nephrogenic DI will not concentrate urine after administration of subcutaneous DDAVP.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with 13 months of amenorrhoea. For the past few months she has been experiencing hot flushes, night sweats, mood changes and pain on intercourse. Clinical examination is unremarkable. Her follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level has been > 40 IU/l on two separate occasions, her serum oestradiol level is 45 pmol/l (> 100) and testosterone is 1.0 nmol/l(0.3–1.7). The thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is normal; the fasting blood glucose is normal; a pregnancy test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI)
The amenorrhoea in combination with menopausal blood tests (persistently high FSH and low oestrogen) in a 24-year-old suggests premature ovarian insufficiency.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)
Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is incorrect. FSH would be normal/low and oestradiol would be normal.

Androgen-secreting adrenal tumour
Androgen-secreting adrenal tumour is incorrect. She does not have hyperandrogenism and her FSH is elevated; it would be normal with an androgen-secreting tumour.

Pituitary failure
Pituitary failure is incorrect. This would result in gonadotropin deficiency, ie low FSH/LH, and hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism – the opposite picture to the hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism in this case. Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) The blood picture of elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), low oestradiol and prolonged amenorrhoea fits the diagnosis of premature ovarian failure. There are no standardised diagnostic criteria for POI, but a practical definition is four or more months of ‘disordered menses’ in association with menopausal FSH levels, in a woman before the age of 40 years. The difference from menopause is that there is varying and unpredictable ovarian function in 50% of women diagnosed with POI, and 5–10% of those women go on to conceive a viable pregnancy following their diagnosis. Autoimmune disease is responsible for 20% of cases of premature ovarian failure: it occurs in 10% of women with Addison’s disease and in 25% of women with autoimmune thyroid disease. However, all women presenting with POI should be tested for the FMR1 premutation (fragile X) regardless of their family history. Approximately 1 in 100 women in the general population develops POI, whereas approximately 20% of women who carry the FMR1 premutation develop the condition. Treatment involves HRT and monitoring bone mineral density. Useful external websites Nelson L M. 2009. Clinical practice. Primary ovarian insufficiency. New England Journal of Medicine, 360, 6, 606–614. AmenorrhoeaA 46-year-old woman with a history of cluster headache, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, controlled schizophrenia and reflux oesophagitis, who is taking a number of medications, comes to the clinic for review. She complains of milk leakage on minimal stimulation, including when she has sexual intercourse with her husband, and problems with vaginal dryness. On examination her BP is 132/72 mmHg, pulse is 73 beats per min and regular. Neurological examination is unremarkable. You are able to elicit milk leakage on palpation of her nipples. Investigations reveal:

Hypothalamic amenorrhoea (HA)
Hypothalamic amenorrhoea (HA) is incorrect. The picture in HA would be gonadotropin deficiency, ie low FSH/LH, and hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism – the opposite picture to the hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism seen in this case.

stem: Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of her clinical picture?
explanation:
Haloperidol
This woman has drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia. A number of medications are recognised to cause this, including Haloperidol. Other causes include dopamine receptor antagonists, eg domperidone, neuroleptics, antidepressants, verapamil, methyldopa, opiates, protease inhibitors, fibrates and H2 antagonists. If possible the medication should be withdrawn.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol is associated with increased risk of impaired glucose tolerance in patients who are obese at baseline, it isn’t a cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is incorrect. Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant, used in the treatment of bile acid diarrhoea, and isn’t a cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

Pizotifen
Pizotifen is incorrect. Pizotifen is used for the treatment of migraine and if anything is associated with a reduction in prolactin. Hyperprolactinaemia and Prolactinoma A 26-year-old woman, who is 20 weeks’ pregnant with her first child, presents to the Emergency Department with an episode of severe hypoglycaemia whilst shopping in the local supermarket. This is the third episode over the past two weeks, and she admits to increased nausea and difficulty maintaining her weight. Her type 1 diabetes has previously been well controlled using an insulin pump, and a most recent HbA1c was 45 mmol/mol (6.3%). On examination in the Emergency Department her BP is 110/60 mmHg, with pulse 95/min and regular. Her glucose is 9.1 mmol/dl after 10% dextrose administered by the ambulance crew. Investigations:

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect. Statins do not increase prolactin levels. The main concern with their use is of course the development of myositis.

stem: Which of the following tests would you do next?
explanation:
24hr urinary free cortisol
24hr urinary free cortisol 24 h urinary free cortisol is one of the investigations used in the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome. Other initial investigations include late night salivary cortisol levels and dexamethasone suppression tests. The most important diagnosis to exclude is Cushing syndrome, given the presence of obesity, hypertension, dysglycaemia and hypokalaemia. Random cortisols are not particularly useful in confirming the diagnosis, due to diurnal variation in cortisol production. 24 h urinary free cortisol can be followed by low-dose dexamethasone suppression test and imaging. Conn syndrome is less likely than Cushing given the presence of other features of the latter, such as obesity and dysglycaemia.

Abdominal USS
Abdominal USS is incorrect. It is not the appropriate investigation for patients with suspected Cushing.

Glucose tolerance test
Glucose tolerance test is incorrect. This is used in the investigation of diabetes mellitus and acromegaly.

Pituitary MRI
Pituitary MRI is incorrect. In the initial investigation of Cushing syndrome, imaging is not carried out until the diagnosis is confirmed. The source is then the next investigation route to be taken.

Renin / aldosterone ratio
Renin/aldosterone ratio is incorrect. This is useful in suspected cases of hyperaldosteronism, and would be another important consideration in this patient given the biochemistry and resistant hypertension, but the cushingoid signs are more prominent.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with her husband to the endocrine clinic. She has distressing symptoms of sweating, and her husband noticed increased prominence of her jaw compared to old photos that he was looking through. Last year she was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes and hypertension; other past history of note is that she has recently been operated on for carpal tunnel syndrome. She takes atenolol 100 mg, atorvastatin 10 mg and metformin 2 g. Which of the following fits best with her condition?
options: Random growth hormone level will be < 1 ng/ml
Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels will be normal
Growth hormone (GH) levels will remain above 1 ng/ml after a 75 g glucose load
Her cardiac risk is similar to the general population
Hypertension coexists in 10% of patients with this condition
explanation:
Growth hormone (GH) levels will remain above 1 ng/ml after a 75 g glucose load
The diagnosis here is acromegaly, or growth hormone excess, which is diagnosed when GH levels are > 1ng/ml after an oral glucose tolerance test. Normal subjects will exhibit suppression of GH to undetectable values (< 0.3) during the test.

Random growth hormone level will be < 1 ng/ml
Random growth hormone level will be < 1 ng/ml is incorrect. The diagnosis here is acromegaly, which will be associated with a high growth hormone.

Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels will be normal
Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) levels will be normal is incorrect. The diagnosis here is acromegaly, which will be associated with high IGF-1 levels. GH stimulates the production of (IGF-1), which is produced in the liver and many other tissues; IGF-1 is the main mediator of the actions of GH.

Her cardiac risk is similar to the general population
Her cardiac risk is similar to the general population is incorrect. Cardiovascular morbidity and mortality are increased in acromegaly. Biventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction occur in acromegaly, leading to an impaired systolic function, ending in heart failure if the disease is untreated. Abnormalities of cardiac rhythm and of valves have also been described in acromegaly. Acromegaly Acromegaly is a disorder of IGF-I excess that occurs after the growth plate cartilage fuses in adulthood. It is a rare but severe disease that is often diagnosed late, and so morbidity and mortality rates are high, particularly as a result of associated cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and respiratory disorders, as well as malignancies. It is usually caused by pituitary adenomas; however, pancreatic, adrenal and ovarian tumours can rarely secrete GH/growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH). Clinical features Sweating is present in more than 80% of cases, hypertension in 40%, impaired glucose tolerance in 40% and Type 2 diabetes in 20%. Coarse facial features, including prognathism, are often noticed by patients when they compare old photographs, and enlargement of the hands and feet, and soft-tissue swelling are also common features. Treatment The treatment of choice is transsphenoidal resection; however, surgery has been found to cure only approximately 60% of patients with acromegaly. Somatostatin and dopamine analogues, and GH receptor antagonists are the mainstays of medical treatment for GH excess, and are generally used when primary surgery fails to induce complete remission. Acromegaly A 20-year-old nursing student is admitted to the Emergency department for the 3rd time in 3 months having suffered a collapse on the ward where she is currently placed. Her glucose at the time is measured at 1.5 mmol/l. There is no past medical history of note and only medication currently is the progesterone only pill.

Hypertension coexists in 10% of patients with this condition
Hypertension coexists in 10% of patients with this condition is incorrect. Hypertension is an important complication of acromegaly, contributing to the increased morbidity and mortality of this condition, and prevalence of hypertension in patients with acromegaly is about 40%, higher than in the general population.

stem: A 25-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department having consumed 20tablets of propranolol. He is hypotensive with a blood pressure of 80/50, his pulse is 32 and regular. An infusion of glucagon is prescribed. What is the main mechanism of action of glucagon with respect to resolving bradycardia?
options: Promotes the formation of cyclic AMP
explanation:
Promotes the formation of cyclic AMP
Glucagon acts by bypassing the blocked ß-receptor, thus activating adenyl cyclase and promoting the formation of cyclic AMP from adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Cyclic AMP in turn exerts a direct ß-stimulant action on the heart. Although all the other options are actions of glucagon, they are not essential for reversing the effect of excess propranolol ingestion.

Stimulates lipolysis
Stimulates lipolysis is incorrect. Although lipolysis is an action of glucagon, it is not essential with respect to the mode of action in β-blocker overdose.

Increases glycogenolysis
Increases glycogenolysis is incorrect. Although glycogenolysis is important with respect to resolving hypoglycaemia, it does not play a significant role in resolving bradycardia and hypotension.

Promotes gluconeogenesis
Promotes gluconeogenesis is incorrect. Like glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, plays its main role in resolving hypoglycaemia. Beta-Blocker Overdose

Alters protein kinase A activity
Alters protein kinase A activity is incorrect. Protein kinase A is cyclic AMP-dependent kinase; in the hepatocyte it drives glucose production, but it does not modulate tachycardia.

stem: He is commenced on an insulin infusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
IV Normal saline
This patient likely has first presentation type 1 diabetes mellitus, given his high blood glucose, age and metabolic acidosis. Priority is rehydration in these patients and it is the most important thing to get right. In all likelihood, this man is presenting with a new diagnosis of type I diabetes. As such, the key steps in managing him successfully are delivery of IV insulin and aggressive IV fluid rehydration in the first instance with normal saline. Guidelines recommend delivery of 1 l of normal saline during the first 60 min. In contrast to previous practice around the use of a Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin infusion (VRIII), modern guidelines recommend commencing with a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion (0.1 unit/kg/h).

IV 5% dextrose
IV 5% dextrose is incorrect. This is used only when the blood glucose is dropping rapidly or has dropped too low.

IV Sodium bicarbonate
IV sodium bicarbonate is incorrect. This is not routinely used to treat acidosis or DKA.

IV Cephalosporin
IV cephalosporin is incorrect. This is useful if an infection is suspected as the trigger for presentation, but is not the appropriate next step.

Surgical review
Surgical review is incorrect. This should be considered if surgical abdomen is suspected. In this scenario, his abdomen is soft and the cause is diabetic ketoacidosis, but if pain persists this would be advised. Diabetic Ketoacidosis A 24-year-old adopted man presents with transient left-sided weakness of his arm, which resolves after a few hours. His only other history of note is reduced libido and inability to maintain erections. On examination he appears to have a spotty skin pigmentation. You notice a heart murmur, and there is suggestion of a left atrial mass on echocardiography. His prolactin is elevated at 2000 μmol/l.

stem: A 24-year-old adopted man presents with transient left-sided weakness of his arm, which resolves after a few hours. His only other history of note is reduced libido and inability to maintain erections. On examination he appears to have a spotty skin pigmentation. You notice a heart murmur, and there is suggestion of a left atrial mass on echocardiography. His prolactin is elevated at 2000 μmol/l. What is the most likely diagnosis
explanation:
Carney complex
It is an autosomal dominant condition caused by an inactivating mutation of protein kinase A on chromosome 17. The diagnosis of Carney complex can be made if there are two features out of the following, or one feature and an affected first-degree relative: Spotty skin pigmentation Myxoma Endocrine tumours – the commonest is primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, but it is also associated with Sertoli cell tumours, growth hormone- or prolactin-producing pituitary adenomas, thyroid adenomas and ovarian cysts Psammomatous melanotic schwannoma (PMS)

Left atrial myxoma
Left atrial myxoma is incorrect. This patient does have a probable atrial myxoma, but the combination of other symptoms makes Carney complex the more likely answer.

Prolactinoma
Prolactinoma is incorrect. This patient does have a probable prolactinoma given his raised Prolactin, reduced libido and difficulty maintaining erections, but the combination of other symptoms makes Carney complex the more likely answer.

Protein C deficiency
Protein C deficiency is incorrect. Protein C deficiency usually presents with venous thromboembolism. These commonly affect the lower limbs and/or lungs. Prolactinoma

Somatic symptom disorder
Somatic symptom disorder is incorrect. This used to be known as somatisation disorder but has been renamed in the DSM-5 criteria. Patients present with a variety of cardiac, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neurological and urogenital symptoms where no physical cause is found. This patient has abnormalities on his blood tests and echocardiography so this is not a somatic symptom disorder.

stem: A 21-year-old university student presents for review. She is distressed by the fact that she is overweight, and she has acne, loss of scalp hair and troublesome facial hair. She has a BMI of 27kg/m 2; she had menarche at age 16 and has irregular menses; her mother has Type 2 diabetes. Which pattern of blood tests fits with the likely underlying diagnosis in this case?
options: High LH, high FSH, normal oestradiol, high testosterone
Normal LH, normal FSH, high testosterone, high prolactin
Low LH, high FSH, normal testosterone, normal oestradiol
High LH, low FSH, high oestradiol, high SHBG
High LH, normal FSH, normal oestradiol, high testosterone
explanation:
High LH, normal FSH, normal oestradiol, high testosterone
The answer is High LH, normal FSH, normal oestradiol, high testosterone (Option E). The underlying diagnosis here is polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), which is usually associated with: high levels of luteinising hormone (LH), due to an abnormal gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pulse generator that preferentially secretes LH over follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH); low or normal FSH; normal oestradiol; and hyperandrogenaemia.

High LH, high FSH, normal oestradiol, high testosterone
High LH, high FSH, normal oestradiol, high testosterone (Option A) is incorrect as the diagnosis here is PCOS, which is associated with high levels of LH, low or normal FSH, normal oestradiol and high testosterone.

Normal LH, normal FSH, high testosterone, high prolactin
Normal LH, normal FSH, high testosterone, high prolactin (Option B) is incorrect as the diagnosis here is PCOS, which is associated with high levels of LH, low or normal FSH, normal oestradiol and high testosterone. High prolactin is not associated with PCOS, although this fact is debated.

Low LH, high FSH, normal testosterone, normal oestradiol
Low LH, high FSH, normal testosterone, normal oestradiol (Option C) is incorrect as the diagnosis here is PCOS, which is associated with high levels of LH, low or normal FSH, normal oestradiol and high testosterone. High prolactin is not associated with PCOS, although this fact is debated.

High LH, low FSH, high oestradiol, high SHBG
High LH, low FSH, high oestradiol, high sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) (Option D) is incorrect as the diagnosis here is PCOS, which is associated with high levels of LH, low or normal FSH, normal oestradiol and high testosterone. High prolactin is not associated with PCOS, although this fact is debated as low SHBG is often seen in PCOS Polycystic ovarian syndrome This woman has polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). The prevalence of PCOS is estimated to range from 8% to 22% of women; oligo/amenorrhoea is present in 70%, hirsutism in 60%, obesity in 35% and infertility in 30%. Laboratory features Luteinising hormone (LH) is usually markedly raised, as is the ratio of LH to follicle-stimulating hormone (LH:FSH). Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is low in 50%, due primarily to hyperinsulinaemia. Testosterone and DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) levels are also usually raised. Up to 40% of women with PCOS have impaired glucose tolerance, and up to 10% develop frank Type 2 diabetes mellitus; the insulinresistant state is also associated with dyslipidemia. Management Management is usually with weight loss and lifestyle advice. Metformin is a useful treatment for insulin resistance and can help to restore ovulation, although it has not been proven to increase live birth rate; clomiphene is proven to induce ovulation. Creams and laser electrolysis might have a useful role to play if the primary complaint is one of hirsutism, while anti-androgens, such as in certain oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) and spironolactone, will also help hirsutism.

stem: A 40-year-old woman was brought unconscious to the Emergency Department. On recovery she is found to have impaired visual acuity (RVA 6/24, LVA 6/36). Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Her electrolytes are abnormal, with a sodium level of 130.0 mmol/l and a potassium level of 6.5 mmol/l. Her previous medical history includes amenorrhoea for the last 5 years. What treatment should be administered urgently?
explanation:
Intravenous hydrocortisone
The clinical picture is suggestive of pituitary apoplexy. She has a low blood pressure, low sodium levels and elevated potassium levels suggesting an addisonian crisis. Intravenous hydrocortisone is the life-saving therapeutic intervention and must be administered urgently.

Intravenous aciclovir
Intravenous aciclovir is incorrect. Aciclovir is an antiviral agent which is indicated in herpes simplex virus encephalitis. The clinical picture is not suggestive of encephalitis.

Intravenous cefuroxime
Intravenous cefuroxime is incorrect. As per the history there is no evidence of an infection, thus an antibiotic is not indicated.

Intravenous phenytoin
Intravenous phenytoin is incorrect. There is no evidence of a seizure in the history. 693 Adrenal Insufficiency A 35-year-old woman presented with a 2 day history of vomiting and abdominal pain. She had a background of anorexia nervosa with diuretic abuse, though she was currently engaging well in a treatment programme. On examination, her pulse rate was 86bpm and blood pressure 102/76mmHg. She weighed 55kg. Investigations:

Intravenous thiamine
Intravenous thiamine is incorrect. There is no evidence of hypoglycaemia associated with chronic starvation or alcoholism that will warrant administration of intravenous thiamine before dextrose infusion.

stem: Which of the following investigations is most likely to reveal a further complication from the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Prolactin
The combination of parathyroid disease and insulinoma is suggestive of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1). This is caused by an inherited mutation in the menin gene and can cause primary hyperparathyroidism, pituitary adenomas and neuroendocrine tumours of the pancreas. Pituitary adenomas may be found in almost 20% of MEN 1 patients. A raised prolactin level may suggest this here.

BRCA gene testing
Breast cancer rates are doubled in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 patients, compared to the normal population. This increased risk is probably associated directly with a menin gene mutation, rather than with a different gene mutation.

Cancer antigen-125
Cancer antigen-125 is a tumour marker associated with ovarian tumours, and less frequently with breast and endometrial cancers. It is not useful in screening for other tumours in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

Spot calcium : creatinine ratio test
A low urinary calcium excretion on a 24-hour collection or spot calcium : creatinine ratio test indicates familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria, an autosomal dominant mutation of the calcium receptor-sensing gene. It leads to reduced calcium excretion and consequent mild to moderate hypercalcaemia. Patients are usually asymptomatic or picked up incidentally. Surgery has no role in management, and the diagnosis can be confirmed by genetic testing. Patients rarely have calcium levels as high as the value given in this case and are rarely as symptomatic. The family history of an insulinoma is not in keeping with familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria and should prompt suspicion of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

Urinary metanephrines
The dominant features of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A) are medullary thyroid carcinoma, hyperparathyroidism and phaeochromocytoma. Plasma fractionated metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines and normetanephrines are useful in the screening for phaeochromocytoma. These would not be expected in MEN 1, except in rare cases. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia A 66-year-old male patient with an extensive smoking history is being investigated for a suspected primary lung malignancy on a recent chest X-ray. He has been complaining of weakness in his leg and upper arm muscles. He describes difficulty standing up from a seated position, and in combing his hair. He reports weight gain of 8 kg over the past four months and has noted that his skin appears darker and that his gums appear stained also. At present he is taking no regular medication but reports that he took a week-long course of steroids two months ago for an unresolving chest infection. Four years previously, this gentleman received radiotherapy for a head and neck cancer related to his smoking history. Routine investigations reveal a potassium of 2.9 mmol/l. A 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test has revealed an 8 am cortisol of 199 mmol/l. A paired 8 am ACTH was 430 nmol/l (< 350 nmol).

stem: Thyroglobulin level is low and measures of thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO) and TSH receptor antibodies (TRAB) are negative. Scintigraphy showed low or absent uptake in the gland. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Thyrotoxicosis factitia
The combination of low thyroglobulin, decreased uptake on scintigraphy and raised T 4 can only really be thyrotoxicosis factitia. Given that this patient is a pharmacist, she is likely to have access to thyroid hormone. Management is likely to be challenging, with appropriate psychological support and counselling the mainstay of therapy.

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is incorrect. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune cause of primary hypothyroidism. Patients will have an elevated TPO antibody titre, and will usually be symptomatic with fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. The biochemistry will reveal a low T 4 and a correspondingly elevated TSH level. Therefore, this is not the correct diagnosis for this case.

Graves' disease
Graves’ disease is incorrect. Graves’ disease is an autoimmune cause of thyrotoxicosis. The TPO and TRAB antibodies are frequently positive and a patient would have an elevated thyroglobulin due to increased release of thyroid hormone from the thyroid gland. Scintigraphy in patients with Graves’ thyrotoxicosis usually reveals a diffuse uptake. Therefore, Graves’ disease is not the correct diagnosis in this case.

Toxic multinodular goitre
Toxic multinodular goitre is incorrect. This is more common in elderly patients, and is characterised by autonomous production of thyroid hormone from one or more hyperfunctioning thyroid nodules in a multinodular gland. Typically, the thyroglobulin will be elevated and scintigraphy will reveal a dotted appearance of increased uptake in certain nodules rather than a reduced or absent uptake, as in this case.

TSHoma
TSHoma is incorrect. A TSHoma is a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, and is rare. It is characterised biochemically by an elevated T 4 in the presence of an inappropriately elevated or normal TSH level. The thyroglobulin level would be elevated in this case due to the increased release of thyroid hormone from the gland.

stem: You suspect he may have a phaeochromocytoma. Which of the following is the initial investigation of choice?
explanation:
24hr urinary catecholamines
Urine testing for catecholamines has both a high sensitivity and specificity for phaeochromocytoma, but it does not however localise the tumour. It is the first investigation of choice both because it is non invasive and because it reduces the chance of imaging detecting a lesion which may turn out to be an incidentaloma.

CT abdomen
CT abdomen is incorrect. CT is useful for localizing the phaeochromocytoma, only after it has been biochemically confirmed.

MIBG scan
MIBG scan is incorrect. MIBG scanning are useful in determining the site of the phaeochromocytoma, like CT, only once it has been biochemically confirmed.

Ultrasound abdomen
Ultrasound abdomen is incorrect. Ultrasound abdomen is rarely sensitive enough to detect a tumour.

Selective venous sampling
Selective venous sampling is incorrect. Selective venous sampling is very rarely used unless extra-adrenal tumours are suspected and identification at the time of surgery has proved unsuccessful.

stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes had an anterior myocardial infarction five years ago. He is receiving aspirin 150 mg once daily and twice daily insulin. A baseline screen revealed a body mass index (BMI) of 34 kg/m 2, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, HbA1c 51.91 mmol/mol (6.9 %), serum cholesterol 3.6 mmol/l (normal < 5.1 mmol/l). Which of the following measures would delay deterioration in renal function most?
options: Increase insulin frequency to four times daily
Increase aspirin from 150 mg to 300 mg daily
explanation:
Ramipril
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors reduce proteinuria by relaxing the efferent arterioles in the glomerulus, and slow the development of both nephropathy and retinopathy. Some evidence points to specific beneficial effects in nephropathy, in addition to the lowering of blood pressure. ACE inhibitors do not worsen blood glucose or lipids, and may have a small positive effect on insulin sensitivity.

Orlistat
Orlistat is incorrect. Although orlistat may have modest effect on weight control, there is little evidence it has an impact on progression of nephropathy.

Increase insulin frequency to four times daily
Increase insulin frequency to four times daily is incorrect. HbA1c is already well controlled at less than 52 mmol/mol, hence increasing insulin frequency will have little impact on nephropathy progression.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect. Statins primarily impact on the risk of macrovascular disease. Diabetes - Type II A 72-year-old woman who has suffered an episode of hypoglycaemia on the orthopaedic ward is administered glucagon. She has type 2 diabetes but has been taking insulin for the past 7 years. Which of the following actions of glucagon are most associated with rapid reversal of hypoglycaemia?

Increase aspirin from 150 mg to 300 mg daily
Increase aspirin from 150 mg to 300 mg daily is incorrect. Increasing aspirin further doesn’t significantly impact on risk of macrovascular events, but does impact with respect to increased risk of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.

stem: A 72-year-old woman who has suffered an episode of hypoglycaemia on the orthopaedic ward is administered glucagon. She has type 2 diabetes but has been taking insulin for the past 7 years. Which of the following actions of glucagon are most associated with rapid reversal of hypoglycaemia?
options: Promotes the formation of ATP from cyclic AMP
explanation:
Activates adenylate cyclase
Adenylate cyclase is a key enzyme involved in the breakdown of glycogen polymers to increase availability of glucose. Activation of this and other enzymes is responsible for restoring blood glucose levels in the short term in patients administered glucagon for the treatment of hypoglycaemia.

Increases glycogenolysis in muscle
Increase glycogenolysis in muscle is incorrect. The predominant action with respect to glycogenolysis is in the liver.

Induces the synthesis of phosphofructokinase
Induces the synthesis of phosphofructokinase is incorrect. Insulin induces the synthesis of phosphofructokinase, which increases glycolysis, and stimulates acetyl-CoA carboxylase to increase the synthesis of fatty acids.

Stimulates acetyl-CoA carboxylase
Stimulates acetyl-CoA carboxylase is incorrect. Action of acetyl-CoA carboxylase is stimulated indirectly via insulin rather than glucagon action. Diabetes - Type II A 42-year-old woman with a history of weight loss and palpitations over the past few months is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic by her GP. Her thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is suppressed at <0.05mU/l (normal range 0.4-5). Other past history of note includes asthma for which she takes a Salbutamol inhaler. Which of the following features would most suggest a diagnosis of Graves’ disease as the underlying cause of her hyperthyroidism?

Promotes the formation of ATP from cyclic AMP
Promotes the formation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) from cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP) is incorrect. Glucagon acts via cyclic AMP to stimulate lipolysis, producing free fatty acids that can act as a major source of energy, rather than promoting the formation of ATP.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a history of weight loss and palpitations over the past few months is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic by her GP. Her thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is suppressed at <0.05mU/l (normal range 0.4-5). Other past history of note includes asthma for which she takes a Salbutamol inhaler. Which of the following features would most suggest a diagnosis of Graves’ disease as the underlying cause of her hyperthyroidism?
explanation:
Pre-tibial myxoedema
Pre-tibial myxoedema occurs due to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans. This occurs in about 40% of patients with Graves' disease. It causes non-pitting pink/purple plaques of oedema just above the lateral malleolus.

Goitre
Goitre is incorrect. Goitre is a non-specific finding in hyperthyroidism. It is also seen in toxic multinodular goiter, and neck tenderness is seen in patients suffering from subacute thyroiditis.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. Hypertension non-specific, and may be primary or associated with secondary causes such as Conn’s or Cushing’s. It isn’t usually a feature of hyperthyroidism.

Lid lag
Lid lag is incorrect. Lid lag is a feature of sympathetic over activity, and is not specific to Grave’s.

Tachycardia
Tachycardia is incorrect. Like lid lag, tachycardia is a feature of sympathetic over activity consistent with hyperthyroidism per se, rather than being specific to Grave’s. Thyrotoxicosis A 36-year-old woman sees her GP complaining of fatigue, a 4 kg weight gain, and dry hair and skin. On clinical examination she has a small diffuse goitre. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is 16 U/l (NR 0.5–4.5) and her free thyroxine (FT4) is 5 pmol/l (NR 10–22), her total cholesterol is 6.3 (< 5mmol/l) and other routine bloods are normal. She has two sisters who have thyroid disease.

stem: What would be the most appropriate treatment for his loss of libido?
explanation:
Testosterone replacement
This patient, with signs of liver disease, diabetes and joint pain most probably has a diagnosis of hereditary haemochromatosis. Iron overload causes endocrine dysfunction, particularly on the pituitary axis. Hypogonadotrophic hypogadism is a classical complication of the condition. Although venesection is the treatment of choice for hereditary haemochromatosis, this will not correct testicular atrophy or hypopituitarism, either or both of which can contribute to a loss of libido. Testosterone replacement is often helpful in these patients.

Desferrioxamine
Desferrioxamine is incorrect. This is an option for patients who cannot tolerate venesection (because of severe cardiac disease or anaemia).

Sildenafil
Sildenafil is incorrect. Sildenafil treats erectile dysfunction and is unlikely to be effective in the context of testosterone below the lower limit of normal.

Insulin therapy
Insulin therapy is incorrect. The underlying cause of low testosterone is related to iron deposition, as such insulin therapy will not affect the outcome with respect to loss of libido.

Liver transplant
Liver transplantation is incorrect. Although liver transplantation is a treatment for end-stage cirrhosis, it is unlikely to reverse testicular atrophy or hypopituitarism to any great extent, and hence does not affect libido where it is due to low testosterone.

stem: A 28-year-old woman attends the diabetes clinic with her two children. This is her third pregnancy and this time she has been diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus. Her mealtimes and portion sizes are erratic. Recent fasting plasma glucose levels have been in the range of 5–6 mmol/l and she is taking twice-daily mixed insulin. Later that evening she collapses while shopping and is brought to the Emergency Department with a blood glucose of 2.4 mmol/l. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management in this patient?
options: Reduce her dose of twice-daily mixed insulin by 50%
Reduce her dose of twice-daily mixed insulin by 20%
Check a random cortisol to rule out Addison’s disease
Change her to a basal-bolus regimen
Advise her to increase the size and regularity of her meals
explanation:
Change her to a basal-bolus regimen
This woman’s fasting plasma glucose levels are appropriate, but taking a twice-daily mixed insulin regimen is probably not appropriate to her lifestyle. A basal-bolus regimen would give her more flexibility in varying the insulin dose. The co-existence of Addison’s is unlikely and increasing the size of her meals would only promote excess weight gain and worsen insulin resistance. Ideally she should be managed with a pump regimen, but not everyone feels they are able to manage pump therapy.

Reduce her dose of twice-daily mixed insulin by 50%
Reduce her dose of twice-daily mixed insulin by 50% is incorrect. Reducing her insulin dose by 50% risks a significant deterioration in her fasting blood glucose, and as such is not advised.

Reduce her dose of twice-daily mixed insulin by 20%
Reduce her dose of twice-daily mixed insulin by 20% is incorrect. Although this will reduce the risk of hypoglycaemic events, it will lead to a deterioration in her HbA1c.

Check a random cortisol to rule out Addison’s disease
Check a random cortisol to rule out Addison’s disease is incorrect. Although Addison’s isn’t impossible, hypoglycaemia as a result of her insulin regimen is much more likely. Diabetes in PregnancyA 25-year-old woman develops hyperthyroidism 6 weeks after delivery. On examination she has painless, firm enlargement of the thyroid gland; TSH-receptor antibody testing is negative. Which of the following statements is most correct with regards to the probable diagnosis?

Advise her to increase the size and regularity of her meals
Advise her to increase the size and regularity of her meals is incorrect. This may result in significant weight gain during the course of her pregnancy and lead to a deterioration in potential outcomes of the pregnancy, particularly with respect to modes of delivery.

stem: A 25-year-old woman develops hyperthyroidism 6 weeks after delivery. On examination she has painless, firm enlargement of the thyroid gland; TSH-receptor antibody testing is negative. Which of the following statements is most correct with regards to the probable diagnosis?
options: The condition is more likely in those in whom thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies were positive
Most patients will have lifelong hypothyroidism
It is less common in patients with a history of Type 1 diabetes
Around 20% of women have some degree of thyroid dysfunction post-partum
It is associated with intense fibrosis of the thyroid gland
explanation:
The condition is more likely in those in whom thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies were positive
The condition is more likely in those in whom thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies were positive before delivery In a prospective study of pregnant women, those with positive thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies in the first trimester were 27 times more likely to develop post-partum thyroiditis than those with negative serology.

Most patients will have lifelong hypothyroidism
Most patients will have lifelong hypothyroidism is incorrect. The classic triphasic pattern is thyrotoxicosis at 1–6 months post-partum, followed by hypothyroidism and return to euthyroidism at 9–12 months post-partum.

It is less common in patients with a history of Type 1 diabetes
It is less common in patients with a history of Type 1 diabetes is incorrect. It is twice as common in these patients.

Around 20% of women have some degree of thyroid dysfunction post-partum
Around 20% of women have some degree of thyroid dysfunction post-partum is incorrect. This occurs in up to 10% of pregnancies. Thyrotoxicosis

It is associated with intense fibrosis of the thyroid gland
It is associated with intense fibrosis of the thyroid gland is incorrect. It is not associated with fibrosis but inflammation.

stem: A 32-year-old patient is being investigated for polydipsia. There has been no recent loss of weight, and she takes no regular medications. Investigations showed that sodium, potassium, calcium glucose, urea, and creatinine were all normal, as were the serum and urine osmolalities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
explanation:
Psychogenic polydipsia
This patient has psychogenic polydipsia. Their serum and urine osmolalities are in the normal range. In patients with polydipsia and polyuria, in whom calcium and glucose levels are normal, diabetes insipidus (DI) is much rarer than ‘psychogenic’ or primary polydipsia. Patients with DI normally present with some degree of dehydration, with urea levels above the upper limit of the normal range.

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Nephrogenic DI is incorrect. In the absence of medications known to cause nephrogenic DI, it would be unusual for a patient to present for the first time at age 32. The fact that electrolytes and osmolalities are normal also makes the diagnosis unlikely.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is incorrect. SIADH is associated with hyponatraemia in patients who are euvolaemic.

Cranial diabetes insipidus
Cranial DI is incorrect. Inappropriately dilute urine, even in the presence of water deprivation would be expected, and in cranial DI at least some electrolyte disturbance on routine testing would be usual. Diabetes Insipidus A 52 year old woman visits your surgery wishing to discuss hormone replacement therapy (HRT). She is suffering from severe hot flushes, sweats and vaginal dryness. She is requesting further information about the side effects of HRT.

Water intoxication
Water intoxication is incorrect. Water intoxication results in hyponatraemia, rather than the normal electrolytes seen here.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step with respect to her diabetes therapy?
explanation:
Change Gliclazide for Sitagliptin
This nurse has two problems: shift changes have precipitated episodes of hypoglycaemia, and these in turn have precipitated over-eating and weight gain. Overall her diabetes control is acceptable, but discontinuing her sulphonylurea (SU) without starting an alternative will precipitate a deterioration in HbA1c. The most appropriate option is to substitute the SU with a dipeptidylpeptidase IV (DPPIV) inhibitor such as Sitagliptin, which is weight neutral or may promote modest weight loss, and does not result in hypoglycaemia.

Add Liraglutide
Add Liraglutide is incorrect. Liraglutide is a GLP-1 agonist, it is a once a day subcutaneous injectable and as such is usually reserved for patients who fail on alternative oral therapies.

Change Gliclazide for Liraglutide
Change Gliclazide for Liraglutide is incorrect. Given this is an injectable and HbA1c is relatively well controlled, orals would be preferred first.

Reduce Gliclazide
Reduce Gliclazide is incorrect. This would reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia and the stimulus to eat, although it is also likely to drive a deterioration in HbA1c, hence switching to sitagliptin is preferred. Diabetes - Type II A 62-year-old woman undergoes subtotal thyroidectomy for goitre. Twelve hours after the operation, she calls the duty doctor and is found to be suffering from pins and needles in her hands and a carpopedal spasm; an urgently corrected calcium level is found to be 1.95 mmol/l. Which of the following statements is true regarding this patient?

Reduce Metformin
Reduce Metformin is incorrect. Metformin does not promote hypoglycaemia or weight gain, hence there is no rationale to reduce the metformin dose.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with episodes of headaches, tremor and sweating which can last for a considerable period of time. He has a history of epilepsy since childhood, for which he takes two different antiepileptics. On examination his pulse is 135 bpm and his blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. He has a large portwine naevus on one side of his face. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Sturge–Weber syndrome
Sturge–Weber syndrome is associated with an extensive port-wine naevus on one side of the face (usually in the distribution of a division of the Vth cranial nerve). Phaeochromocytoma is associated with Sturge–Weber, although with a lower associated risk compared to other conditions like multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A syndrome (MEN 2A).

von Recklinghausen’s disease
Von-Recklinghausen’s disease (VRD) is incorrect. VRD is also known as neurofibromatosis type 1, and is associated with phaeochromocytoma in up to 5% of patients, but it is associated with skin neurofibromas, and multiple café au lait spots occur in peripheral neurofibromatosis.

von Hippel–Lindau disease
Von Hippel–Lindau disease is incorrect. This is associated with haemangioblastomas and increased risk of phaeochromocytoma. In type 1 the risk is less than 10%, but in type 2 the lifetime risk is up to 10%.

Ataxia telangiectasia
Ataxia telangiectasia (AT) is incorrect. The most increased risk in AT is of haematological malignancy including leukaemia and lymphoma. Phaeochromocytoma A 23-year-old South African woman who has recently started the oral contraceptive pill for contraceptive purposes comes to the dermatology clinic. She is concerned because the skin on her hands and forearms has become increasingly fragile and she has a bullous rash. In addition, she has increased pigmentation and some hair growth on her face. On examination of her mucous membranes, there is no abnormality. Investigations show:

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is incorrect. HHT is associated with increased risk of arteriovenous malformations and bleeding, rather than increased risk of phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 65-year-old woman was referred to clinic after an incidental finding of hypercalcaemia was made. She did not have any symptoms. She had a history of hypothyroidism for which she took levothyroxine. In which of the following conditions would you find hypercalcaemia?
explanation:
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
After a long period of secondary hyperparathyroidism (as in chronic kidney disease), the parathyroid glands become autonomous, and this leads to inappropriately high parathyroid hormone levels, resulting in demineralisation of bone and increased calcium resorption and retention, leading to hypercalcaemia.

DiGeorge syndrome
DiGeorge syndrome is incorrect. DiGeorge syndrome, caused by microdeletions on chromosome 22, causes a hypocalcaemia through hypoparathyroidism, not hypercalcaemia. You would expect to find hypercalcaemia in tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

Polyglandular syndrome type 1
Polyglandular syndrome type 1 is incorrect. Polyglandular syndrome type 1 causes hypoparathyroidism (leading to hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia), recurrent candidiasis, and Addison’s disease. It does not cause hypercalcaemia. You would expect to find hypercalcaemia in tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism describes an appropriately high parathyroid hormone level in response to a low serum calcium level, therefore you would not find hypercalcaemia in this condition. However, in tertiary hyperparathyroidism, resulting from a long period of secondary hyperparathyroidism, you would expect to find hypercalcaemia.

Tumour lysis syndrome
Tumour lysis syndrome is incorrect. The classic biochemical findings of tumour lysis syndrome are hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and hyperuricaemia. You would expect to find hypercalcaemia in tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 40-year-old man is identified at a well man clinic appointment as having obesity, impaired fasting glucose and hypertension, with a blood pressure of 155/95. The hypertension is confirmed over the course of 3 months, and his BMI is stuck at 33. Which of the following antihypertensive drugs should you most avoid in this patient?
explanation:
Hydrochlorothiazide
Thiazide diuretics and β-blockers have been shown in large interventional studies and meta-analyses to negatively impact on progression to diabetes in patients with obesity/impaired glucose tolerance. As such in this case therefore hydrochlorthiazide should be avoided.

Losartan
Losartan is incorrect. Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are indicated in patients with diabetes to reduce progression of nephropathy, and have no negative impact on glucose tolerance.

Lisinopril
Lisinopril is incorrect. Like ARBs, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have been shown to impact on both micro- and macrovascular outcomes in the diabetes population, and do not negatively impact on glucose control.

Indapamide
Indapamide is incorrect. Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic which does not carry the same negative impact on glucose tolerance as thiazides themselves. Diabetes - Type II

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is incorrect. Although non-selective β-blockers have a potentially significant negative impact on glucose tolerance, this is not the case for cardioselective β-blockers such as bisoprolol or carvedilol.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with a blood glucose of 29 mmol/l; she is known to have Type 1 diabetes. Her pH is 7.12, with a serum bicarbonate of 11 mmol/l, and urinalysis shows +4 ketones. Which of the following statements about diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is true in adolescents and adults?
options: Myocardial infarction is the precipitating factor in up to 5% of cases of DKA
Infection is the precipitating cause in 70% of cases of DK
Bicarbonate levels can be normal in DKA
Blood glucose can be normal in DKA
Non-compliance with insulin causes 5% of cases of DKA
explanation:
Blood glucose can be normal in DKA
The answer is Blood glucose can be normal in DKA (Option D). Euglycaemic ketoacidosis is rare, occurring in approximately 1% of DKA – seen when there has been prolonged fasting, or during pregnancy or with interruption of insulin delivery with insulin pump therapy. It is also a rare complication of taking SGLT2 inhibitors.

Myocardial infarction is the precipitating factor in up to 5% of cases of DKA
Myocardial infarction is the precipitating factor in up to 5% of cases of DKA (Option A) is incorrect. It is the precipitant in < 1% of cases of DKA, although it is important to consider this, especially in elderly patients.

Infection is the precipitating cause in 70% of cases of DK
Infection is the precipitating cause in 70% of cases of DKA (Option B) is incorrect. It is the Chat precipitant inTutor 30–40% with AI of cases of DKA.

Bicarbonate levels can be normal in DKA
Bicarbonate levels can be normal in DKA (Option C) is incorrect. DKA involves metabolic acidosis and low bicarbonate by definition. Diabetic ketoacidosis Precipitating factors leading to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) are: Infection (30–40%) Non-compliance with treatment (25%) Alterations to insulin dose (13%) Newly diagnosed diabetes (10–20%) Myocardial infarction (< 1%) The American Diabetes Association categorises DKA in adults into one of three stages of severity: Mild:blood pH mildly reduced to between 7.25 and 7.30 (NR 7.35–7.45); serum bicarbonate reduced to 15–18 mmol/l (NR > 20); the person is alert Moderate:pH 7.00–7.25; bicarbonate 10–15; mild drowsiness may be present Severe:pH below 7.00; bicarbonate below 10; stupor or coma may occur Diabetic Ketoacidosis

Non-compliance with insulin causes 5% of cases of DKA
Non-compliance with insulin causes 5% of cases of DKA (Option E) is incorrect. It is the precipitant in 25% of cases of DKA.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the clinical findings?
explanation:
Pseudo-Cushing syndrome
Pseudo-Cushing’s syndrome occurs in response to prolonged heavy alcohol consumption and obesity. It is associated with an elevation in cortisol but not to the extent of that seen with Cushing’s syndrome itself. Management is with weight control and a reduction of alcohol consumption.

Cushing's syndrome
Cushing’s syndrome is incorrect. His risk factors for pseudo-Cushing’s mitigate against this. It’s likely that 24hr urinary free cortisol would only be slightly above the normal range.

Hyperaldosteronism
Hyperaldosteronism is incorrect. Hyperaldosteronism is highly unlikely given that the potassium is in the middle of the normal range, and hyperaldosteronism isn’t associated with significant weight gain.

Intermittent prednisolone use
Intermittent prednisolone use is incorrect. Intermittent steroid use is not likely to cause such significant blood pressure elevation and is a less important contributor to his symptoms compared with alcohol comsumption.

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. There is no reason to consider phaeochromocytoma given the other pointers towards pseudo-Cushing’s syndrome.

stem: A 54-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes presents to the clinic. He has had diabetes for the past 4 years and currently takes metformin 1g BD. Unfortunately his HbA1c has deteriorated over the past few months and was most recently measured at 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%). On examination his BP is 155/82 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular and his BMI is 34. He works as a taxi driver and is concerned about hypoglycaemia and further weight gain, so you elect to start him on sitagliptin. Which of the following correctly describes the mode of action of sitagliptin?
explanation:
DPPIV inhibitor
GLP-1 is cleaved by DPPIV, which leads to its inactivation. This means that the half-life of native GLP-1 is very short. DPPIV inhibitors were developed to prolong the half-life of native GLP-1, which leads to an improvement in insulin release in response to an oral glucose load, the so called incretin effect. This is however glucose dependent, such that DPPIV inhibitors do not carry the same concerns about hypoglycaemia as sulphonylureas. Unlike GLP-1 agonists such as liraglutide, DPPIVs do not raise GLP-1 to supraphysiological levels and therefore do not inhibit gastric emptying. As such they do not carry the same benefit with respect to weight loss.

AMP Kinase activator
AMP Kinase activator weight Tutor AMP Kinase activator is incorrect. Metformin is an indirect activator of AMP kinase leading to modest loss and reduced hepatic glucose output.

Glucokinase activator
Glucokinase activator is incorrect. Glucokinase activators remain in development but development is hampered by tachyphylaxis to glucose lowering effects.

SGLT2 inhibitor
SGLT2 inhibitor is incorrect. An example of an SGLT-2 inhibitor is dapagliflozin. These drugs reduce glucose reabsorption in the kidney leading to modest calorie loss and positive effects on weight and sodium excretion. Diabetes - Type II

GLP-1 agonist
GLP-1 agonist is incorrect. Liraglutide is a GLP-1 agonist. This drives GLP-1 to supraphysiological levels leading to greater benefits with respect to glucose reduction and weight control.

stem: Urinary calcium excretion is increased on a 24 h collection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyrodisim is characterised by high calcium and a correspondingly high or, inappropriately, normal parathyroid hormone level. It is usually caused by autonomous parathyroid hormone production from one parathyroid adenoma or, less commonly, from multiple parathyroid gland hyperplasia as part of a hereditary endocrine syndrome (multiple endocrine neoplasia). Patients can present with the complication of hypercalcaemia including fatigue, constipation, depression, abdominal pain and renal stones. In the long term it can lead to osteopenia or osteoporosis. The treatment is surgical removal of the overactive parathyroid gland.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This occurs in patients with chronic kidney disease and reduced glomerular filtration rate because of ineffective phosphate excretion and vitamin D deficiency. It causes excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by the parathyroid glands in response to hypocalcaemia. This is unlikely in this case as the kidney function is normal and there is no history of chronic kidney disease.

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. Hypoparathyroidism is characterised by low levels of parathyroid hormone and calcium. It is most commonly caused iatrogenically following neck surgery or radiotherapy, but can be genetic as part of a syndrome called DiGeorge syndrome. The high calcium and parathyroid hormone levels in this case make this diagnosis unlikely.

Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria
Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria is incorrect. Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria is an autosomal dominant mutation of the calcium receptor-sensing gene. It leads to reduced calcium excretion and consequent mild to moderate hypercalcaemia. Patients are usually asymptomatic or picked up incidentally. Surgery has no role in the management, and the diagnosis can be confirmed by genetic testing or confirmation of a low urinary calcium excretion on a 24 h collection or spot calcium creatinine ratio test. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaA 54-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes presents to the clinic. He has had diabetes for the past 4 years and currently takes metformin 1g BD. Unfortunately his HbA1c has deteriorated over the past few months and was most recently measured at 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%). On examination his BP is 155/82 mmHg, pulse is 85/min and regular and his BMI is 34. He works as a taxi driver and is concerned about hypoglycaemia and further weight gain, so you elect to start him on sitagliptin. Which of the following correctly describes the mode of action of sitagliptin?

Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia is incorrect. Osteomalacia is caused by vitamin D deficiency and can result in hypocalcaemia and calcium resorption leading to inadequate bone mineralization. If severe, patients can develop proximal myopathy and a characteristic waddling gait. The treatment involves replacement of vitamin D and calcium. A high calcium level in this case makes this diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has a 6-month history of weight gain. She is otherwise well and takes no medication. On examination her body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m 2, her blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg and she has a round, red face and slight atrophy of her arm muscles. Renal function tests and urinalysis are normal. What is the next step in obtaining the diagnosis?
options: A low-dose overnight dexamethasone suppression test
explanation:
A low-dose overnight dexamethasone suppression test
This patient presents with clinical features suggestive of cortisol excess or Cushing syndrome, including a sixmonth history of weight gain, hypertension (170/100 mm Hg), proximal myopathy as suggested by atrophy of her arm muscles, facial plethora and a rounded face. Other sensitive clinical features include hypokalaemia due to the mineralocorticoid action associated with excess cortisol levels, pigmented abdominal striae and easy bruising. Importantly the history notes that she is not taking any medications such as exogenous steroids that might have accounted for these clinical features. If there is a clinical suspicion of Cushing syndrome, the Endocrine Society guidelines recommend an initial screening test using either a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test or two measurements of either late night salivary cortisol or 24 h urinary free cortisol. A lowdose dexamethasone suppression test involves the administration of 1 mg of dexamethasone at midnight and a 9 am cortisol measurement the following day. Exogenous dexamethasone should suppress the endogenous production of cortisol from the adrenal cortex, and a cut-off of <50 nmol/l is the gold standard for a normal test. In the setting of autonomous or excess cortisol secretion, exogenous dexamethasone will fail to suppress cortisol to <50 nmol/l, indicating a positive test.

Urinary catecholamine collection
Urinary catecholamine collection is incorrect. Urinary catecholamine testing is the screening test used for the diagnosis of a phaeochromocytoma. A phaeochromocytoma is a tumour of the adrenal medulla that secretes inappropriate levels of caetacholamine hormones. Patients can present with hypertension, as in this case; however, additional clinical symptoms would include arrhythmias, pallor, headaches, weight loss and anxiety. The hypertension and symptoms caused by a phaeochromcoytoma are often episodic in nature and different to the symptoms described in this clinical scenario.

Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) collection
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) collection is incorrect. Urinary 5-HIAA is the screening test utilised in the diagnosis of suspected carcinoid syndrome. Carcinoid syndrome is caused by a neuroendocrine tumour that is secreting vasoactive serotonin. Carcinoid tumours usually originate in the gastrointestinal tract. Normally the liver controls the effect of serotonin unless the tumour metastasizes to the liver, in which case the secretion of serotonin is no longer controlled and the patient will become symptomatic. Symptoms associated with serotonin secretion include flushing, diarrhoea, bronchoconstriction and occasionally right-sided heart failure, and are not in keeping with the symptoms described in this case.

Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound is incorrect. An abdominal ultrasound would not be a useful diagnostic test in this scenario as the initial diagnosis is made by a biochemical screening test.

CT of the abdomen
CT of the abdomen is incorrect. CT of the abdomen has low sensitivity and specificity as an initial screening test in suspected Cushing syndrome. However, it may be useful if a biochemical diagnosis of excess cortisol is made in conjunction with suppressed ACTH, indicating that ACTH from the pituitary is not driving the source of excess cortisol. In this scenario, CT of the abdomen may be useful to locate an adrenal tumour secreting excess cortisol.

stem: An obese 38-year-old man presents with rapid weight gain and the development of extensive abdominal striae, and his midnight cortisol is found to be elevated. He has hypertension with a BP of 155/82 mmHg, type 2 diabetes currently treated with metformin, and has recently suffered a left Colles’ fracture. Which of the following would best differentiate between a pituitary adenoma and ectopic ACTH production as a cause of hypercortisolism?
explanation:
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test
The high-dose dexamethasone suppression test involves the administration of 2 mg dexamethasone 6-hourly for a 48-hour period. In patients with Cushing’s disease, the cortisol falls by more than 50% of the basal value, though it should be noted that 10% of patients with Cushing’s disease fail to suppress. A reduction of more than 90% in basal urinary free cortisol levels confirms Cushing’s disease due to a pituitary adenoma as the underlying cause. Where cortisol levels fail to reduce, ectopic ACTH production is suggested.

Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test is incorrect. While a low-dose dexamethasone test is the usual test to follow 24-hour urinary free cortisol, it doesn’t add incrementally to our knowledge versus the high-dose alternative, or midnight cortisol, as it doesn’t differentiate between pituitary and non-pituitary causes of Cushing’s.

Synacthen® test
Synacthen test is incorrect. The Synacthen test is used for evaluation of potential Addison’s disease, rather than Cushing syndrome.

24-hour urinary cortisol collection
24-hour urinary cortisol collection is incorrect. This won’t add significantly to the information already obtained from the midnight cortisol.

Basal adrenocorticotropic hormone levels
Basal adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels are incorrect. There is overlap between pituitary and nonpituitary dependent causes with respect to basal ACTH levels.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is being investigated for suspected multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2B, after a first degree relative was diagnosed with the syndrome. She is noted to have marfanoid features on clinical examination. What will be the most likely finding if this patient has MEN 2B?
explanation:
Elevated metanephrines
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B) with a marfanoid phenotype is associated with phaeochromocytoma and medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. Parathyroid hyperplasia is not well described in association with MEN2B. Out of the options given, elevated metanephrines are most likely to be found.

Elevated serum calcium
Elevated serum calcium is incorrect. Elevated serum calcium is most likely to be seen in parathyroid hyperplasia which is seen in MEN2A.

Elevated thyroxine
Elevated thyroxine is incorrect. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is of calcitonin producing, rather than thyroxine-producing cells.

Decreased parathyroid hormone
Decreased parathyroid hormone is incorrect. No change in parathyroid hormone is expected in MEN2B.

Elevated glucagon
Elevated glucagon is incorrect. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours are a feature of MEN1 rather than MEN2 syndromes.

stem: A patient has a two-month history of intermittent flushing associated with tachycardia and wheezing. There have also been episodes of profuse watery diarrhoea. On examination the patient has facial plethora and is flushed. On examination BP is 160/80, cardiovascular examination reveals a pansystolic murmur which is louder on inspiration in keeping with tricuspid regurgitation, and abdominal examination reveals a palpable liver edge. Given the suspected diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) collection
The biologically active metabolite characteristically produced by metastatic carcinoid tumours is 5hydroxytryptamine (5-HT, serotonin), which is synthesised from the amino acid tryptophan. 5-HT plays a part in the pathogenesis of some of the symptoms of the carcinoid syndrome, particularly diarrhoea and bronchoconstriction. It is metabolised to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which accounts for 95% of the urinary excretion of 5-HT.

Dexamethasone suppression test
Dexamethasone suppression test is incorrect. This is the recommended screening test for the diagnosis of suspected Cushing syndrome and is based on the failure of autonomous cortisol production to fall to <50 nmol/l after a 1 mg dexamethasone tablet taken at midnight the night before a morning cortisol measurement. It is not useful in the diagnosis of suspected carcinoid syndrome.

Urinary catecholamine collection
Urine catecholamine collection is incorrect. This is a screening test for patients with suspected phaeochromocytoma, a tumour that arises from the adrenal medulla and sceretes catecholaimes, which can be measured in the urine. A phaeochromocytoma is associated with episodic symptoms, most commonly pallor, palpitations and headaches. It is not the correct diagnosis here as it is not associated with wheezing or diarrohea.

Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound is incorrect. An abdominal ultrasound may be helpful in the diagnosis of liver metastases, which are usually present in carcinoid syndrome. The primary tumour is most often in the GI tract and the secreted serotonin and kallikrein are inactivated in the liver; manifestations of carcinoid syndrome do not occur until there are metastases to the liver or when the cancer is accompanied by liver failure (cirrhosis).

Fasting gastrin
Fasting gastrin is incorrect. Gastrin is measured in patients in whom a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumour of the duodenum or pancreas is suspected. This type of tumour is most commonly diagnosed in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. It causes severe gastric and duodenal ulceration due to markedly elevate gastrin levels, and can lead to perforation of the stomach or duodenum. However, a gastrinoma does not predispose to flushing or bronchoconstriction.

stem: A 24-hour urine collection shows 350 mg/day of calcium excretion (normal 100–200 mg/day). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
The patient has a prolactinoma of the pituitary, for which he is on cabergoline, a dopamine agonist that inhibits the release of prolactin from the anterior pituitary. He has now presented with primary hyperparathyroidism, likely secondary to a parathyroid tumour. Hyperparathyroidism can remain subclinical for years; however, it has led to recurrent kidney stones. The excess parathyroid hormone has led to hypophosphataemia. Vitamin D deficiency is commonly seen in patients with hyperparathyroidism. Alkaline phosphatase is often within the normal range in primary hyperparathyroidism. Given the patient’s prolactinoma, and now suspected parathyroid tumour, this is in keeping with Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is dominantly inherited and associated with an increased susceptibility to parathyroid adenomas, pituitary tumours and enteropancreatic endocrine tumours, due to mutations in the multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 gene.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) does present with hypercalcaemia, but the patient’s calcium excretion is normal. The patient also has a prolactinoma of the pituitary, for which he is prescribed cabergoline. This is not associated with FHH.

Hypophosphataemia
Although elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) is associated with increased phosphate excretion, the features here are most consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism where the parathyroid gland is inappropriately excreting too much PTH, leading to hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) is dominantly inherited and associated with a susceptibility to medullary thyroid cancer, parathyroid adenomas and phaeochromocytomas, due to mutations in the RET gene. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) is subdivided into MEN2A and MEN2B. MEN2B is associated with mucosal neuromas of the lips and tongue, distinctive facies with enlarged lips, ganglioneuromatosis of the gastrointestinal tract and a ‘marfanoid’ body habitus. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia

Pseudohypoparathyroidism
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is a failure to respond to PTH; therefore, PTH levels may be high or normal. The patient, however, is hypercalcaemic, rather than hypocalcaemic.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with a history of poorly controlled Type II diabetes comes to the clinic for review. She is treated with BD mixed insulin but is concerned about weight gain and wonders if she can take something alongside the insulinthat will not cause her to gain weight. Other problems include ischaemic heart disease and renal impairment, and she takes a number of concomitant cardiovascular medications. Her BMI is 33 and her estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 28 ml/min per 1.73 m 2. Which of the following is a suitable agent to add in to her insulin therapy?
explanation:
Linagliptin
The drug has been extensively studied in patients with renal impairment, and no dose adjustment is required. It is 80% excreted in the faeces, which accounts for the lack of need for dose adjustment in renal impairment. With regard to weight, DPP-IV (Dipeptidyl peptidase IV) inhibitors like linagliptin also have significant advantages when compared with pioglitazone and sulfonylureas because they do not increase the risk for hypoglycaemia or weight gain.

Exenatide
Exenatide is incorrect. Exenatide is ruled out in patients with a creatinine clearance <30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2. There is no experience of use of exenatide in this population and there have been rare reports of kidney disease in association with exenatide use.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Gliclazide is of limited efficacy late in Type 2 diabetes and will not limit weight gain.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Metformin is of limited efficacy late in Type 2 diabetes and will not limit weight gain. ( Diabetes - Type II A 27-year-old man with a new diagnosis of Kallman syndrome is in the Endocrine Clinic. He has a family history and has been found to have a mutation in the Kal1 gene. He has low LH, FSH and testosterone. Other pituitary hormones are normal. He is not keen on having children. Which would be the most appropriate treatment at this stage?

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Although it improves glycaemic control, is associated with weight gain and risk of heart failure; as such it is also best avoided here.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent heavy periods and pain associated with her monthly cycle. A fall in which of the following hormones is most commonly associated with shedding of the endometrium during menstruation?
explanation:
Progesterone
Involution of the corpus luteum results in a decrease in progesterone and oestradiol secretion. This occurs around day 24 of a 28-day menstrual cycle. The loss of hormonal support causes endometrial shedding.

Luteinising hormone
Luteinising hormone (LH) is incorrect. A peak in LH occurs around the time of ovulation; during the remainder of the menstrual cycle LH is at a lower level.

Follicle-stimulating hormone
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is incorrect. There is a peak in FSH which occurs at the time of ovulation, with a lower level during the remainder of the menstrual cycle.

Gonadotropin-releasing hormone
Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is incorrect. The peak in GnRH occurs to drive LH and FSH around the point of ovulation with lower levels at other time points in the menstrual cycle.

Oestrone
Oestrone is incorrect. Oestrone is synthesised both in the ovaries and the liver, but a fall in estrone does not play a primary role in endometrial shedding.

stem: A 41-year-old heavy smoker is referred by his GP with a serum sodium level of 125 mmol/l (132-145). He feels generally unwell and apathetic but is orientated and has no seizure activity. He is not taking any medications. Clinically he is euvolaemic. Chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass. Serum osmolarity is 268 mosm/kg (275–295), urine sodium is 55mmol/L (<20), urine osmolality 110mOsm/L (<100). Random cortisol is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management of his fluid balance?
explanation:
Fluid restriction
The patient likely has SIADH. He has euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with inappropriately elevated urinary sodium. Although there is little to no formal evidence that fluid restriction increases serum sodium concentration more than placebo in SIADH, clinical experience generally supports its use, provided fluid restriction is strictly adhered to.

Slow IV normal saline infusion
Slow IV normal saline infusion is incorrect as this will not increase serum sodium.

Desmopressin
Desmopressin is incorrect as this will reduce sodium further.

Intravenous glucocorticoid
Intravenous glucocorticoid is incorrect as there is no suggestion of underlying cortisol deficiency. Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone

Perform fluid deprivation test
Perform fluid deprivation test is incorrect as this is a test for diabetes insipidus.

stem: Her main complaint is of hirsutism and acne. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Co-cyprindiol (cyproterone acetate and ethinylestradiol)
The diagnosis here is polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Co-cyprindiol (cyproterone acetate and ethinylestradiol; brand name Dianette) blocks androgen receptors (via the cyproterone component), and reduces androgen production via negative feedback because of the presence of ethinylestradiol. It is particularly effective in reducing androgenic acne and is therefore the logical choice here. Weight loss is extremely important in the management of PCOS and the patient should also be encouraged to follow intensive life style and diet intervention.

Clomifene
Clomifene is incorrect. Clomifene is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, it is used to stimulate ovulation in patients with PCOS, and as such is not useful to relieve symptoms of PCOS here.

Combined OCP
Combined OCP is incorrect. The combined OCP is useful in regulating ovulation, but is less useful in managing symptoms of hyperandrogenism versus co-cyprindiol.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Metformin promotes a small amount of weight loss and improves insulin sensitivity. It was previously considered as an option to stimulate ovulation but this is ineffective versus clomifene.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Pioglitazone improves ovarian insulin sensitivity and restores ovulation, although it has multiple side effects including fluid retention, weight gain and loss of bone mineral density and as such it is not recommended.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus has had two episodes of dizziness associated with driving a car. She currently administers insulin. Her glucose was 2.1 mmol/l on one of these occasions, which improved after intravenous glucose. Her insulin dose was reduced. On further questioning she admits to one collapse where she later came round on the kitchen floor. What is the next important step?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
explanation:
Advise not to drive
If loss of awareness of hypoglycaemia is confirmed, then driving must stop. Although she gives only some reports of dizziness, it is likely that her driving ability has been significantly impaired. Driving can resume provided reports show awareness of hypoglycaemia has been regained, confirmed by a GP or consultant report. If frequent hypoglycaemic episodes continue if the diabetes is poorly controlled, then driving should cease until satisfactory control is re-established.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
