Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain is incorrect. MRI is not indicated here as the primary reason for the episodes of dizziness is hypoglycaemia.

72-hour observation in hospital
72-hour observation in hospital is incorrect. A 72-hour period in hospital is inappropriate. Inactivity associated with a period in hospital is likely to reduce the probability of further episodes of hypoglycaemia.

Psychiatric referral
Psychiatric referral is incorrect. There is a likely physical cause for this patient’s symptoms, psychiatric referral is therefore not warranted. Diabetes - Type I A 39-year-old woman with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis presents to the clinic for review. Her Hashimoto’s is managed with replacement thyroxine 125 µg/day. She presents to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of bilateral loin pain. Investigations reveal:

Better diabetes education
Better diabetes education is incorrect. Although this is useful with respect to use of insulin and hypoglycaemia, the most pressing need at this point is to reduce insulin dose.

stem: A KUB (kidney, ureter, bladder) X-ray study shows evidence of nephrocalcinosis. A renal ultrasound reveals no abnormality. Urine dipstick analysis reveals no abnormality. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Renal tubular acidosis type I
Renal tubular acidosis type I (hypokalaemic distal renal tubular acidosis) can occur in association with a number of autoimmune conditions, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), vasculitis and autoimmune hypothyroidism. Other causes include drugs such as amphotericin B and lithium, chromosomal abnormalities such as Marfan syndrome, and conditions such as chronic pyelonephritis and obstructive uropathy. Treatment includes oral supplementation with potassium and bicarbonate.

Renal tubular acidosis type 4
Renal tubular acidosis type 4 is incorrect. Type 4 renal tubular acidosis is associated with hyperkalemia and a normal anion gap acidosis typically caused by a hypo-reninaemic hypo-adlosteronism. As this patient has a hypokalemia, this diagnosis is not correct.

Medullary sponge kidney
Medullary sponge kidney is incorrect. This is a congenital disorder which causes cystic dilatation of the collecting tubules in one or both kidneys, increasing the risk for kidney stones and urinary tract infection. However, this abnormality would be evident on KUB and/or ultrasound and so is unlikely in this case.

Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. Polycystic kidney disease can present with loin pain and is an autosomal dominant condition caused by inheritance of the PKD1 gene, which leads to the development of multiple renal cysts. These cysts are picked up by renal ultrasound, making this diagnosis unlikely in this clinical case. Hypothyroidism

Chronic interstitial nephritis
Chronic interstitial nephritis is incorrect. This is a form of chronic inflammation affecting the interstitium of the kidneys, and is typically associated with non-visible haematuria. The absence of any haematuria on the urine analysis testing makes the diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 21-year-old woman presents for review. She is concerned on this occasion because she has not had a period for 5 months; she had menarche aged 13 and regular periods up to recently. Her BMI is 17.6 kg/m 2, and she is a long distance runner. A pregnancy test is negative and thyroid function testing is normal. Which diagnosis fits best with this woman’s clinical picture?
explanation:
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea (FHA)
This is because she had previously regular periods and is an athlete with a low BMI, all of which point to hypothalamic amenorrhoea. Many women who diet or who exercise at a high level do not take in enough calories to expend on their exercise as well as to maintain their normal menstrual cycles.

Panhypopituitarism
Panhypopituitarism is incorrect as, given that she is thin and a long distance runner, functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea is much more likely. FHA is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea with low oestrogen, and is much more common than prolactinoma.

Hyperprolactinaemia
Hyperprolactinaemia is incorrect. Given that she is thin and a long distance runner, functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea is much more likely.

Premature ovarian insufficiency
Premature ovarian insufficiency is incorrect. She is thin and a long distance runner, making functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea more likely. AmenorrhoeaPolycystic ovarian syndrome
Polycystic ovarian syndrome is incorrect. She is thin, with menarche at a normal age and regular cycles for many years; PCOS is usually present from puberty.

stem: An 18-year-old man with meningococcal septicaemia treated with high-dose ceftriaxone develops gangrene in four toes, which necessitates amputation. Post-operatively, he complains of flank pain and is now becoming drowsy and lethargic. His blood pressure is 90/45 mmHg and his peripheries are cool. Plasma creatinine is 96 μmol/l, urea is 9.6 mmol/l, K + is 6.7 mmol/l, Na + is 119 mmol/l and bicarbonate is 17 mmol/l; spot urine Na + is 30 mEq/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
options: Acute interstitial nephritis secondary to ceftriaxone
explanation:
Adrenal insufficiency
Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage may occur in the setting of severe sepsis and provide explanation for the electrolyte derangement. This was initially described in patients with meningococcaemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC; Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome), although in a recent series, Pseudomonas infection was the most common cause. The combination of hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia and metabolic acidosis should always suggest hypoadrenalism. Adrenal insufficiency results in mineralocorticoid deficiency, potentially life-threatening salt-wasting and a failure to excrete potassium.

Acute interstitial nephritis secondary to ceftriaxone
Acute interstitial nephritis secondary to ceftriaxone is incorrect. Cephalosporins may provoke tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN), but the hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia and hypotension are typical of a hypoadrenal crisis.

Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is incorrect. Ischaemic ATN secondary to hypotension, as described in this case, may result from meningococcal infections; however, the concurrent onset of hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia, along with the relative preservation of renal function, argue against this.

Septic shock
Septic shock is incorrect. Septic shock secondary to hypotension, as described in this case, may result from meningococcal infections; however, the concurrent onset of hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia, along with the relative preservation of renal function, argue against this. Adrenal Insufficiency Following a head injury, a 24-year-old patient develops polyuria and polydipsia and is suspected of having cranial diabetes insipidus. He undergoes a water deprivation test. Which one of the following responses would be diagnostic of cranial diabetes insipidus?

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is incorrect. Urine sodium concentration would be higher (> 40, typically 50–100 mEq/l) in SIADH. ADH secretion in a septic, hypotensive patient could not be clearly defined as being inappropriate.

stem: A 27-year-old man is found to have oligospermia. He has a normal male phenotype including secondary sexual characteristics. Blood tests show: testosterone 30 nmol/l (normal range 9–35 nmol/l), luteinising hormone 10 IU/l (1–10 IU/l) and follicle-stimulating hormone 0.5 IU/l (1–7 IU/l). Which of the following is most likely to be the cause of the oligospermia?
explanation:
Decreased androgen-binding proteins
This patient has isolated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) deficiency. Normal levels of luteinising hormone (LH) suggest that there is no hypothalamic disorder. FSH stimulates the Sertoli cells in the testes to produce ABPs and inhibin. ABP is responsible for binding testosterone and making it available for spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules. In the absence of FSH, ABP is not produced and this causes oligospermia.

Increased inhibin
Increased inhibin is incorrect. Inhibin is secreted in response to FSH as part of a negative feedback loop. As such, reduced levels of FSH would actually drive reduced levels of inhibin.

Decreased dihydrotestosterone
Decreased dihydrotestosterone is incorrect. Deficiency of DHT or androgen receptors would cause testicular feminisation, FSH levels would be normal in these cases, and external phenotype would be female.

Deficiency of androgen receptors
Deficiency of androgen receptors is incorrect. Deficiency of androgen receptors results in testicular feminisation.

Hypothalamic disorder
Hypothalamic disorder is incorrect. A hypothalamic disorder such as Kallmann syndrome would result in both LH and FSH deficiency.

stem: An overweight patient with type II diet-controlled diabetes is seen in the outpatient clinic. Despite following an appropriate diet and increased exercise four times a week, his blood glucose is still not well controlled. There is a strong family history of cardiovascular disease and the patient is anxious to modify his cardiovascular risk. His most recent HbA1C is 50 mmol/mol, sodium 140 mmol/l, potassium 4.0 mmol/l, creatinine 85 µmol/l; his BMI on examination is 29 and blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg. What would be the first-line treatment?
explanation:
Metformin
Metformin is a biguanide used as a first-line treatment in type 2 diabetes, particularly in overweight people when diet and exercise have failed to control blood sugar levels. It can also be used in combination with other antidiabetic medicines to provide better control of blood sugar. It reduces hepatic glucose output and has its predominant effects on fasting plasma glucose. Data from a landmark study ? UKDPS ? showed that intensive glucose control with metformin appears to decrease the risk of diabetes-related end points in overweight diabetic patients, and is associated with less weight gain and fewer hypoglycaemic attacks than are insulin and sulphonylureas; it may be the first-line pharmacological therapy of choice in these patients.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Pioglitazone is a thiazolidinedione, recommended as add-on therapy in the first intensification in a patient already on metformin with a HbA1c rise to 58 mmol/mol or above. It is not recommended as first line if lifestyle modification fails. Despite a favourable weight-neutral or -loss profile, when added to metformin therapy, pioglitazone is reserved as a second-line agent because of less favourable risks associated with its use. In particular, pioglitazone has recently been associated with an increased risk of bladder cancer in men.

GLP-1 analogue
GLP-1 analogue is incorrect. GLP-1 analogue is a type of medication called an incretin. It stimulates the secretion of insulin in a glucose-dependent manner, delays gastric emptying and signals satiety, resulting in an overall effect of weight loss in most patients. The NICE guidelines recommend that GLP-1 analogues should only be considered in patients with poorly controlled type II diabetes defined as a HbA1c of >7.5% (58 mmol/mol) and BMI >35, because of the additional potential for weight loss with this class of drugs. Weight loss in excess of 10 kg has been anecdotally reported, and studies suggest a minimum of 3?5 kg weight loss with this class of drugs. Furthermore, recent cardiovascular outcome studies found that the risk of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal myocardial infarction or non-fatal stroke among patients with type II diabetes mellitus was lower in patients taking GLP-1 analogues compared to placebo.

Long-acting insulin
Long-acting insulin is incorrect. Long-acting insulin analogues, such as insulin glargine and detemir, are reserved for patients with poorly controlled type II diabetes despite maximum escalation of oral hyperglycaemic agents. Insulin should not be considered as first line for patients with confirmed type II diabetes, because of the associated weight gain and existing insulin-resistant phenotype in patients with this condition.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Gliclazide is a sulphonylurea that acts as an insulin secretagogue and therefore can cause weight gain. As this patient is already significantly overweight, it would be imperative to avoid medications that might exacerbate this and further increase the insulin-resistant phenotype. Furthermore, sulphonylureas are recommended as second-line or add-on therapy after metformin according to the NICE guidelines.

stem: An obese (BMI = 30) 53-year-old woman presents with a myocardial infarction. Her mother has type II diabetes. Her cholesterol is 5.1 mmol/l. Current medication includes metformin, ramipril and aspirin. Examination reveals some evidence of left ventricular failure. A recent HbA1c was measured at 64 mmol/mol. Which one of the following interventions is the most likely to prolong her survival?
explanation:
Empagliflozin
SGLT-2 inhibitors like empagliflozin both reduce the risk of cardiac failure and ischaemic cardiovascular events. As such they are the most appropriate intervention here for a patient presenting with a myocardial infarction with evidence of cardiac failure against a background of uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Although sulphonylureas like gliclazide do glycaemic control, they have no effect on cardiovascular outcome, with cardiovascular disease the most likely cause of death in this population.

Saxagliptin
Saxagliptin is incorrect. Gliptins do not positively impact on cardiovascular outcomes and may actually increase the risk of left ventricular failure in some patients with ischaemic cardiovascular disease. As such they are not an appropriate option here.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Pioglitazone leads to worsening of cardiac failure in patients with ischaemic heart disease. It is therefore not the most appropriate intervention here. It is also associated with increased risk of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Diabetes - Type II A 54-year-old man with a 40-year history of type I diabetes comes to the Emergency Department with vomiting and feeling generally unwell. He has hypertension and smokes 30 cigarettes per day. His glucose level is 45 mmol/l and he has features of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). After initial fluid replacement and a fixed-rate insulin infusion, he is still unwell. His BP is 105/80 mmHg and his pulse is 68 bpm and regular. There are crackles at both bases on auscultation of the chest, consistent with pulmonary oedema. Investigations after initial treatment:

Acarbose
Acarbose is incorrect. Although acarbose is associated with an improvement in outcomes with respect to ischaemic cardiovascular disease, it doesn’t have the same impact on cardiac failure as empagliflozin, which makes this a more correct answer.

stem: Which of the following is the optimal step in her management?
options: Reassure her that everything is ok
explanation:
Arrange a short Synacthen test
This patient has adrenal insufficiency. There are a number of clues that point towards a diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency here, with the tiredness and lethargy, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, and surprisingly good diabetes control for a person with 20 years+ diabetes. Random cortisol levels should be taken in the acutely unwell patient in whom adrenal insufficiency is suspected immediately before emergency treatment commences. In the subacute patient, a Synacthen test should be performed before treatment starts.

Start thyroxine 50mcg
Start thyroxine 50 mcg is incorrect. TSH is often elevated in adrenal insufficiency, and falls once steroid replacement is instituted.

Stop her ramipril
Stop her ramipril is incorrect. The coexistence of the low sodium counts towards a diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency and against a diagnosis of ramipril-related hyperkalaemia. Although her BP is low, and the ramipril could be temporarily suspended, it is more important in this case to rule out/confirm the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency. Therefore the optimal next step would be to check for adrenal insufficiency.

Check her T3/T4
Check her T 3/T 4 is incorrect. TSH is often elevated in adrenal insufficiency, and falls once steroid replacement is instituted. TSH and free thyroxine should be tested together in all patients suspected of having thyroid dysfunction. Adrenal Insufficiency

Reassure her that everything is ok
Reassure her that everything is ok is incorrect. This patient is presenting with symptoms that require further investigation.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents with tiredness and headaches, coupled with loss of libido over the past few months. He continues to hold down a job as a salesman but is finding this increasingly demanding. There is no past medical history of note, he smokes 10 cigarettes per day and drinks one bottle of wine per week. On examination his BP is 110/60 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. The only abnormal finding is a bitemporal hemianopia. Which of the following diagnoses would you consider most likely?
explanation:
Pituitary adenoma
The loss of libido and tiredness suggest disruption of the anterior pituitary hormone axis, with possible decreased testosterone, low TSH or low growth hormone. The hemianopia is due to compression of the optic chiasm by the underlying tumour.

Craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma is incorrect. Cranopharyngioma is a slow growing, and is more likely to be associated with an inferior quadrantanopia.

Glioblastoma
Glioblastoma is incorrect. It is a fast growing tumour more likely to present with focal neurological deficit.

Meningioma
Meningioma is incorrect. Meningiomas are rare in a 29 year old man, and like glioblastoma more likely to present with symptoms of local compression than with pituitary dysfunction alone.

Pituitary metastases
Pituitary metastases is incorrect. This would be a highly unlikely explanation for the patients symptoms in the absence of other pointers towards disseminated carcinoma.

stem: Islet cell, glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) and insulin antibodies are all negative. Urine and blood ketone measurements are negative, but urinary dipstick shows 3+ glucosuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
MODY (maturity-onset diabetes of the young)
MODY is characterised by: Raised high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels Preserved insulin sensitivity Low renal threshold for glucose (glycosuria). MODY has an age of onset usually between 10 and 30 years, and can be managed in many patients with the use of sulphonylureas alone. The strong family history of early-onset diabetes without a history of insulin resistance or elevated BMI is also suggestive of MODY, as is the marked glucosuria described in this case.

Type I diabetes
Type I diabetes is incorrect. The absence of antibodies and the absence of ketosis, despite an elevated blood glucose as well as the subacute presentation, make the diagnosis of type I diabetes unlikely. This can, however, be difficult to distinguish and patients are frequently started on insulin therapy. Patients who have maturityonset diabetes of the young (MODY) and are mistaken for patients with type I diabetes will have extremely low insulin requirements and appear to have a prolonged or exaggerated ‘honeymoon period’.

Type II diabetes
Type II diabetes is incorrect. The low BMI and a very strong family history at a young age despite a low BMI and the absence of an insulin-resistant phenotype, clinically makes the diagnosis of type II diabetes unlikely.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. Addison’s disease is an autoimmune condition caused by destruction of the adrenal gland by circulating antibodies. It can present with a low BMI. However, hypoglycaemia rather than hyperglycaemia is a feature, due to low or absent cortisol levels. Diabetes - Type II

LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood)
LADA (latent autoimmune disease of adulthood) is incorrect. This is a late-onset diabetes of adulthood or ageing, characterised by the presence of antibodies directed against pancreatic islet cells. These patients will eventually require insulin therapy, but can sometimes be managed with oral agents initially until insulin production ceases. The absence of antibodies in this case and the young age makes the diagnosis unlikely.

stem: A 54-year old woman is seen for the first time in the Diabetes Clinic. She is obese, plethoric and has marked bruising on her limbs and fresh striae over her abdomen. She has developed a dorsal kyphosis following a vertebral collapse earlier in the year. Which of the following results will help to pinpoint the diagnosis if you suspect Cushing syndrome secondary to adrenal adenoma?
options: 0900-h serum cortisol of 200 nmol/l after an overnight dexamethasone test
explanation:
Undetectable serum adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) level
Functioning adrenal adenomas produce excessive levels of cortisol, which suppresses the ACTH production from the pituitary gland by negative feedback.

Normal 0900-h serum cortisol level
Normal 0900-h serum cortisol level is incorrect. There is wide variation of ‘normal’ cortisol. A single measurement of cortisol cannot be used to diagnose Cushing’s syndrome.

Serum potassium of 2.2 mmol/l
Serum potassium of 2.2 mmol/L is incorrect. Low serum potassium is seen in Cushing’s syndrome with very high cortisol levels, particularly with ectopic ACTH production in paraneoplastic syndrome and in adrenal cancer.

0900-h serum cortisol of 200 nmol/l after an overnight dexamethasone test
0900-h serum cortisol of 200 nmol/l after an overnight dexamethasone test is incorrect. In normal individuals, cortisol is suppressed to <50 nmol/L after administration of dexamethasone, a very potent glucocorticoid. Failure to suppress with dexamethasone occurs in all types of Cushing’s syndrome; it is not unique to that due to an adrenal adenoma.

Raised urine cortisol:creatinine ratio
Raised urinary cortisol:creatinine ratio is incorrect. There are no validated normal values for cortisol:creatinine ratio to make the diagnosis. A high ratio is consistent with Cushing’s syndrome but it does not distinguish between adrenal adenoma and other causes. Measurement of 24-hour urinary cortisol is a recognised screening test for Cushing’s syndrome.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with concerns that he is not entering puberty. His only past medical history of note is a decreased sense of smell. On examination, his testes are located in the scrotum and are small and soft. He has only sparse axillary and pubic hair. Testosterone is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Kallmann syndrome
Kallmann syndrome is attributed to isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) deficiency. It is often familial and X-linked. Kallmann syndrome is associated with hypogonadism (with testosterone < 6 nmol/l), although fertility can be restored with the use of GnRH analogue therapy.

Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome is incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome is not associated with decreased sense of smell, although testosterone is of course reduced.

Mumps orchitis
Mumps orchitis is incorrect. Most individuals are now vaccinated against mumps; rates of infection are therefore low and patients usually remember the infective episode. The disease is associated with low testosterone but not loss of sense of smell.

Hyperprolactinaemia
Hyperprolactinaemia is incorrect. Hyperprolactinaemia is associated with loss of libido and erectile function in a patient who is likely to have entered puberty normally.

Cryptorchidism
Cryptorchidism is incorrect. This is ruled out by the presence of testes within the scrotum.

stem: A 42-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic because a 0.9cm pituitary tumour was discovered on CT scanning, after he was knocked unconscious falling off his bike. Pituitary function and visual field testing is entirely normal. You plan to review in 12 months time. Which of the following is the most likely occurrence?
explanation:
No change in his condition
This is likely an incidental finding. This patient has no signs or symptoms of a pituitary tumour. You are also reassured by the scenario in which pituitary function is described as normal. Increased use of CT scanning has resulted in increased pick-up rates for pituitary ‘incidentalomas’. A number of published case series provide evidence of longitudinal sequelae, and in the majority of cases no changes in size, endocrine pathology or in symptoms from local pressure occur. Increase in size >10% was seen in 40% of those followed. Symptoms were noted in approximately 25% of individuals, including visual field loss and panhypopituitarism.

Bitemporal hemianopia
Bitemporal hemianopia is incorrect. Visual testing would have revealed visual loss in the temporal fields of each eye.

Development of acromegaly
Development of acromegaly is incorrect. Acromegaly has typical symptoms of excess growth hormone including large hands, obstructive sleep apnoea, hypertension and enlarged jaw, amongst many. The scenario gives no indication of this.

Pituitary apoplexy
Pituitary apoplexy is incorrect. Pituitary function would be abnormal. Prolactinoma You are reviewing a 52-year-old woman who has a history of type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease and coeliac disease. Her daughter has been researching autoimmune disease on the Internet and has been learning about the association between certain HLA types and disease. Which of the following HLA subtypes is most strongly associated with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes?

Development of symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia
Development of symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia is incorrect. Firstly, this patient is asymptommatic. Symptoms you would look for would include gynaecomastia, galactorrhoea, mood changes, decreased libido and infertility.

stem: Table: Findings of a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test After two weeks of dietary modification, her fasting plasma glucose is still elevated at 6.8 mmol/l. Which is the appropriate next step in management of this patient?
explanation:
Metformin therapy
A strict definition of diabetes mellitus is applied in pregnancy because glucose excursions are known to be associated with increased rates of both intra-uterine death and inherited abnormalities (particularly musculoskeletal). Studies reported the successful use of glibenclamide in mild gestational diabetes and use of metformin before starting insulin therapy in appropriate patients. Indeed, in the metformin study, there were better treatment satisfaction scores for women randomised first to metformin therapy and it is now recommended as a potential option by NICE guidelines on the management of diabetes in pregnancy. Of course, many Chat patients needTutor insulin with AI adding in to their metformin therapy, but in this case weight gain during the pregnancy is often less versus insulin alone. Gestational diabetes is associated with an increased lifetime risk of the development of type 2 diabetes, and advice should be given about adhering to lifestyle measures.

Glipizide therapy
Glipizide therapy is incorrect. Glipizide should not be used because it has not been trialled in pregnancy and it is likely to promote hypoglycaemia and weight gain.

Soluble insulin
Soluble insulin is incorrect. Metformin may be effective for a period of weeks in controlling blood sugar, thus limiting overall weight gain during the pregnancy before insulin is started.

Low calorie diet
Low calorie diet is incorrect. A low calorie diet may negatively impact on the health of the pregnancy, and in this situation a low carbohydrate diet alone is unlikely to achieve target blood sugars, given the fasting value is already 7.0 mmol/l.

Repeat OGTT in four weeks
Repeat OGTT in four weeks is incorrect. This risks significant exposure to elevated blood glucose levels, and harm to the pregnancy. Useful external weblinks www.nice.org.uk/guidance ( www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0707193 ( Diabetes in PregnancyA 30-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of polyuria and polydipsia. Her only other history of note was increasing joint pains, and one visit to the GP with depression and constipation some six months before. Examination was unremarkable. Investigations show: glucose 4.1 mmol/l, urea 5.2 mmol/l, creatinine 80 µmol/l, corrected serum calcium 3.1 mmol/l, serum phosphate 0.7 mmol/l, parathyroid hormone 6.2 pmol/l (normal range 0.9–5.4 pmol/l).

stem: A 30-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of polyuria and polydipsia. Her only other history of note was increasing joint pains, and one visit to the GP with depression and constipation some six months before. Examination was unremarkable. Investigations show: glucose 4.1 mmol/l, urea 5.2 mmol/l, creatinine 80 µmol/l, corrected serum calcium 3.1 mmol/l, serum phosphate 0.7 mmol/l, parathyroid hormone 6.2 pmol/l (normal range 0.9–5.4 pmol/l). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this clinical picture?
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism
This woman has normal renal function in the presence of hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Parathyroid hormone levels are just above the normal range, but any elevation in this scenario would be suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. This condition is twice as common in women and the prevalence increases with increasing age. About 85% of cases are related to a single parathyroid adenoma; 15% are related to multiple gland hyperplasia. Familial cases can occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes (MEN 1 or MEN 2A). Treatment is by surgical removal of the abnormal parathyroid gland after localisation using a combination of either parathyroid ultrasound or technetium-99m sestamibi scanning.

Occult malignancy
Occult malignancy is incorrect. It can cause hypercalcaemia due to humoral-mediated release of calcium and direct calcium release from destructive bone metastasis. Importantly, this type of hypercalcaemia is not mediated by parathyroid hormone and as a result the parathyroid hormone is often suppressed in response to the elevated serum calcium. Therefore, occult malignancy is not the correct diagnosis in this case as the parathyroid hormone is elevated.

Hypervitaminosis D
Hypervitaminosis D is incorrect and uncommon. This is caused by excess vitamin D, which increases calcium levels. However, hypercalcaemia caused by excess vitamin D would be parathyroid hormone independent and would cause a reduction in serum parathyroid hormone by negative feedback. Therefore, hypervitaminosis is not the correct diagnosis in this case as there is evidence of an elevated parathyroid hormone level.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect and is driven by low vitamin D levels in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is usually accompanied by a high phosphate level caused by the inability of the kidney in chronic kidney failure to excrete phosphate. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is the incorrect diagnosis in this case as the phosphate is low and the patient has normal renal function. Useful mnemonic for hypercalcaemia: VITAMINS TRAP V = vitamins A & D I = immobilisation T = thyrotoxicosis A =Addison's disease M = milk-alkali syndrome I = inflammatory disorders N = neoplastic diseases S = sarcoidosis T = thiazides and other drugs R = rhabdomyolysis A = AIDS P = Paget's disease, parenteral nutrition, parathyroid disease Hyperparathyroidism

Pseudohypoparathyroidism
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is incorrect. It is a rare disorder of parathyroid hormone resistance caused by a defect in a G-coupled protein receptor. The associated biochemistry would reveal a low-serum calcium and a high phosphate level in the presence of an elevated parathyroid hormone. Therefore, pseudohypoparathyroidism is not the correct diagnosis in this case as there is an elevated serum calcium.

stem: A 35-year-old woman visits you in the paediatric diabetes clinic with her 2-year-old son, who has recently developed type 1 diabetes. He has an identical twin brother and she is concerned about his risk of developing diabetes. What advice would you give regarding the twin’s future risk?
options: He has a 100% future risk of developing type 1 diabetes
A trial of low-dose insulin in the unaffected child will reduce his future risk of diabetes
Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of
He has an approximately 50% future risk of developing type 1 diabetes
IA-2 antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of diabetes
explanation:
He has an approximately 50% future risk of developing type 1 diabetes
Concordance rates for type 1 diabetes are higher in monozygotic than dizygotic twins, which is consistent with a role for genetic factors determining the disease. Nevertheless, ∼50% of monozygotic twins are discordant for type 1 diabetes, providing strong evidence that non-genetically determined factors also influence susceptibility to disease.

He has a 100% future risk of developing type 1 diabetes
He has a 100% future risk of developing type 1 diabetes is incorrect. He has an approximately 50% future risk.

A trial of low-dose insulin in the unaffected child will reduce his future risk of diabetes
A trial of low-dose insulin in the unaffected child will reduce his future risk of diabetes is incorrect. This would not stop the autoimmune process and could be dangerous.

Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of
Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of diabetes Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of diabetes is incorrect. It has been shown that antibodies in the unaffected child increase the likelihood that he/she will go on to develop type 1 diabetes. Genetic risks for developing diabetes Type 1 diabetes Twin studies have suggested that the future risk of diabetes in the unaffected child is 30–50%. The presence of GAD, islet cell or IA-2 antibodies in the unaffected child increases the likelihood that he/she will go on to develop type 1 diabetes. Children of type 1 diabetic patients have a slightly increased risk of developing the disease (3–6% risk where the father is diabetic, 2–3% where the mother is diabetic). Twin studies in type 2 diabetes have suggested that if one identical twin develops the disease, the risk in the unaffected twin rises to 50% or greater. Diabetes - Type I A 50-year-old woman with resistant hypertension is investigated for an underlying secondary cause. She has found to have hypercortisolaemia, after testing reveals a high 24-hour urinary cortisol excretion and failed dexamethasone suppression test. Which one of the following clinical findings would suggest most strongly that ectopic secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is the cause of the condition?

IA-2 antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of diabetes
IA-2 antibodies in the unaffected child are not predictive of the risk of diabetes is incorrect. It has been shown that antibodies in the unaffected child increase the likelihood that he/she will go on to develop type 1 diabetes.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with resistant hypertension is investigated for an underlying secondary cause. She has found to have hypercortisolaemia, after testing reveals a high 24-hour urinary cortisol excretion and failed dexamethasone suppression test. Which one of the following clinical findings would suggest most strongly that ectopic secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is the cause of the condition?
explanation:
Weight loss
Ectopic Cushing’s syndrome is associated with underlying malignancy. For this reason it is recognised to occur in conjunction with weight loss. Other features such has muscle wasting and hyperglycaemia are also seen.

Hyperglycaemia
Hyperglycaemia is incorrect. This can occur with Cushings from any cause, it is not specific to any underlying cause.

Worsening hypertension
Worsening hypertension is incorrect. This can occur with Cushings from any cause, it is not specific to any underlying cause.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. This can occur with Cushings from any cause, it is not specific to any underlying cause.

Muscle wasting
Muscle wasting is incorrect. This can occur with Cushings from any cause, it is not specific to any underlying cause.

stem: A 44-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department after sustaining a head injury. A CT brain does not show any trauma; however, it does show an enlargement of the pituitary fossa. Subsequent MRI shows a 1.5-cm pituitary adenoma confined to the pituitary fossa. She does not have any medical history and denies feeling in any way unwell prior to the accident. Neurological exam reveals a bitemporal homonymous hemianopia. Which of the following hormones is most likely to be being secreted in excess?
explanation:
Prolactin
Prolactinomas are the most frequently occurring functional pituitary tumours. In addition prolactin secretion can be increased in patients with other pituitary tumours because of the interruption of the inhibitory effect of dopamine secreted by the hypothalamus.

Adrenocorticotropin (ACTH)
Adrenocorticotropin (ACTH) is incorrect. Prolactinomas are the most frequently occurring functional pituitary tumours.

Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is incorrect. Prolactinomas are the most frequently occurring functional pituitary tumours. FSHomas are uncommon.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. Prolactinomas are the most frequently occurring functional pituitary tumours. Acromegaly is rare. Pituitary tumours Prolactinomas are the most frequently occurring functional pituitary tumours. Prolactin secretion can be increased in patients with other pituitary tumours because of the interruption of the inhibitory effect of dopamine secreted by the hypothalamus. Adrenocorticotropin hormone- (ACTH-) secreting and growth hormone-secreting tumours both occur less frequently and thyroid-stimulating hormone- (TSH-) and folliclestimulating hormone- (FSH-) secreting tumours are uncommon. Non-functional tumours can occur at any age but are more frequent in the elderly. Hyperprolactinaemia and Prolactinoma A 25-year-old woman who is in the 20th week of her first pregnancy comes to the endocrine clinic for review. She is finding it increasingly difficult to maintain her weight, feels constantly anxious and tremulous, and has taken to opening the windows at night in the middle of winter in a bid to keep cool. She has a history of type 1 diabetes, which is well controlled with insulin pump therapy, but is otherwise well. On examination her BP is 105/70 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. She has a fine tremor at rest. Abdominal palpation is consistent with a 20-week pregnancy, although she is slim, with a BMI of only 21. There is a small, smooth goitre on neck palpation. Investigations reveal:

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is incorrect. Prolactinomas are the most frequently occurring functional pituitary tumours. TSHomas are extremely rare, incidence is less than one in a million.

stem: A 56-year-old lady presents with a sensation of choking and difficulty in swallowing large, solid foods. She had a recent endoscopy, which revealed no abnormality of the oesophagus or stomach. On examination there is a diffuse nodular goitre but no thyroid bruit or dysthyroid eye disease. Biochemistry reveals a T 4 of 16.9 pmol/l and a TSH of 3.25 mIU/l. What is the most appropriate next investigation for determining the volume of the thyroid gland?
explanation:
Ultrasound
Ultrasound is useful in determining thyroid size accurately. It can determine the gland volume and is the most sensitive imaging modality for evaluating thyroid nodules. It doesn’t involve exposure to ionising radiation and is therefore the preferred next step here.

Thyroid isotope uptake (Technetium-99m)
Thyroid isotope uptake (Technetium-99m) is incorrect. This is most useful for differentiating between a thyroiditis and other causes of hyperthyroidism. In thyroiditis there is gland destruction and there will be reduced uptake of Technetium-99m on the uptake scan. This differs from the result expected with Graves’ disease, where there is global diffuse increased uptake or an autonomous nodule, which will have focal uptake. It is less helpful at determining gland volume.

X-ray of the neck
X-ray of the neck is incorrect. This provides very little information about the thyroid gland and is rarely used, except occasionally for determining whether a multinodular goitre is causing compression of adjacent structures, but is much less sensitive and specific compared to CT of the neck.

CT neck
CT neck is incorrect. A CT scan does provide information about gland volume but involves exposure to ionising radiation, making ultrasound a more favourable modality for determining gland volume. CT scan of the neck is used for determining retrosternal extension or tracheal compression caused by a large, multinodular goitre.

MRI neck
MRI neck is incorrect. MRI is rarely used in the evaluation of the thyroid gland. Occasionally MRI may be used in the evaluation of suspected infiltration of the thyroid by infection, or suspected thyroid lymphoma. It certainly isn’t done in this situation ahead of an ultrasound scan.

stem: A 54-year-old pub owner is referred by his GP for endocrine assessment. He is obese, with a body mass index (BMI) of 32 kg/m 2, and has hypertension, which is poorly controlled on atenolol and bendroflumethiazide; a recent fasting blood glucose test was 9.2mmol/l. On examination he is cushingoid and his BMI is 32 kg/m 2. You order a 24-hour urine-free cortisol (UFC), which comes back slightly above normal range; an overnight dexamethasone suppression test is 30 nmol/l (NR < 50). Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pseudo-Cushing syndrome
Obese patients who consume alcohol to excess over a prolonged period can acquire a cushingoid appearance; in this case, this man’s occupation as a publican suggests that he will have easy access to alcohol. His two screening tests for Cushing’s disease (the dexamethasone suppression test and the 24-hour urine-free cortisol) are effectively normal, which effectively rules this out.

Cushing’s disease
Cushing’s disease is incorrect. There is no biochemical evidence of cortisol excess on the two screening tests. Cushings disease is excess ACTH from the anterior pituitary, as opposed to Cushings syndrome, which occurs due to excess cortisol from any source.

Simple obesity
Simple obesity is incorrect. The mild elevation in UFC suggests pseudo-Cushing’s.

Cushing’s syndrome
Cushing’s syndrome is incorrect. There is no biochemical evidence of cortisol excess on the two screening tests.

Primary aldosteronism
Primary aldosteronism is incorrect. His hypertension is likely essential.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department via ambulance in an unconscious state; her daughter found her on the floor. On examination she is found to have a core temperature of 33°C, BP 133/80 mmHG and pulse 52 bpm, and thorough clinical examination reveals signs of congestive cardiac failure. Her blood glucose level is 5.7 mmol/l and random cortisol is 450 nmol/l. Routine bloods and blood gas are otherwise normal; however, her thyroid function reveals a TSH of 43 (0.5–3.5) and FT 4 of 0.8 (10–22). Which diagnosis fits best with this woman’s clinical picture?
explanation:
Myxoedema coma
This woman has a greatly reduced FT 4 concentration, is hypothermic, unconscious and in heart failure, all of which are associated with profound hypothyroidism, or myxoedema coma.

Euglycaemic ketoacidosis
Euglycaemic ketoacidosis is incorrect. She is not acidotic on blood gas and her grossly abnormal thyroid function test (TFTs) make hypothyroidism the obvious underlying problem.

Hypocortisolaemia
Hypocortisolaemia is incorrect. Her cortisol is not low.

Panhypopituitarism
Panhypopituitarism is incorrect. Her cortisol is normal and her TFT picture is of primary, not secondary, hypothyroidism. Profound hypothyroidism Mortality associated with this condition used to be as high as 50%, but survival has improved with modern intensive care management. Management Free triiodothyronine (T3) is usually given via a nasogastric tube or intravenous injection, at the rate of 2.5–5 µg every 8 hours, with conversion to free thyroxine T4 after the patient regains consciousness. There is a risk of precipitating heart failure if larger doses are given in the initial period. Other supportive measures include oxygen therapy, intravenous hydrocortisone therapy and glucose infusion, but none of these has been proved to be effective in the setting of a randomised controlled trial. Hypothyroidism

Sepsis
Sepsis is incorrect. Her blood tests reveal no signs of sepsis and her grossly abnormal TFTs make hypothyroidism the obvious underlying problem. Hypothermia in the elderly can obviously be a sign of sepsis, so it is important to make sure and rule out infection.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 6-month history of secondary amenorrhoea; she also has noted some galactorrhoea. Her GP has checked some bloods and her FSH is 2.3 (NR3–10), LH is 2 (NR 3–12) and oestradiol is 90 (NR 100–600). Physical examination is normal. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Microprolactinoma
The combination of galactorrhoea and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is indicative of prolactinoma.

Turner syndrome
Turner syndrome is incorrect because it would not cause galactorrhoea and would present earlier, usually with primary amenorrhoea.

Polycystic ovarian disease (PCOS)
Polycystic ovarian disease (PCOS) is incorrect because it would not cause galactorrhoea and is associated with high LH levels, normal/low FSH and normal oestradiol. It is debated whether PCOS is associated with raised prolactin, but most experts feel it is not, so raised prolactin should always undergo further investigation.

Sheehan syndrome
Sheehan syndrome is incorrect because it would not cause galactorrhoea and is caused by post-partum haemorrhage, which then causes hypopituitarism. Galactorrhoea Galactorrhoea is the non-puerperal expression of milk. Hyperprolactinaemia causes galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea, which can result from a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour or hyperplasia. Hypothyroidism is a cause of raised prolactin levels. In acromegaly a third of patients have mild elevation of prolactin levels, resulting in galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and decreased libido. Similar elevation of prolactin levels occurs in a small percentage of patients with primary hypothyroidism. Prolactinoma A patient comes to the endocrine clinic for review. He has autosomal dominant diabetes and has been identified as having an HNF1-alpha mutation. Which of the following cells is most likely to be affected by this mutation in this individual?

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect because although it can occasionally cause minor elevation in prolactin, it does not usually cause hypogonadism.

stem: A patient comes to the endocrine clinic for review. He has autosomal dominant diabetes and has been identified as having an HNF1-alpha mutation. Which of the following cells is most likely to be affected by this mutation in this individual?
explanation:
Beta cells of the pancreas
The HNF1-alpha mutation is a recognised cause of maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY). The HNF1alpha gene is found on chromosome 12, and is responsible for differentiation of beta cells. Mutations lead to reduced beta cell mass and/or defective insulin release. Treatment with sulfonylureas is often effective in controlling blood glucose levels.

Alpha cells of the pancreas
Alpha cells of the pancreas is incorrect. Alpha cells of the pancreas are responsible for producing glucagon. Congenital hyperinsulinism is well described, although congenital hyperglucagonaemia is not.

Hepatocytes
Hepatocytes is incorrect. MODY5 in particular, due to a defect in HNF1-beta, is associated with hepatic and renal cyst formation.

Fat cells
Fat cells is incorrect. Insulin sensitivity of fat cells is regulated by PPAR-gamma, which is a target for treatment of glitazones. Diabetes - Type II A 19-year-old nursing student is referred to the endocrinology clinic with frequent dizzy spells and collapses. These seem to happen at times of stress. She tells you she feels hungry beforehand, and feels like she has to eat something. The frequency of attacks is increasing and she is now having one or two a day. Once or twice they seem to have happened after she has been jogging. She has a family history of type 2 diabetes. On examination, her blood pressure is 115/72 mmHg and her pulse is 70 bpm. General examination is unremarkable. Investigations show:

Delta cells of the pancreas
Delta cells of the pancreas is incorrect. Delta cells are responsible for producing somatostatin.

stem: A 26-year-old woman attends her GP complaining of feeling tired all the time for the last few months. She describes 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. Her mother has autoimmune hypothyroidism and her maternal uncle has type 1 diabetes. She has had no periods for six months and has been feeling dizzy first thing in the morning. Which of the following clinical signs would the GP be most likely to find if the diagnosis was thought to be adrenal failure?
explanation:
Postural hypotension
Postural hypotension is a hallmark of adrenal failure because the disease involves deficiencies in both mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids. Mineralocorticoid deficiency leads to sodium loss and decreased blood volume, which contributes to low blood pressure, particularly noticeable when changing positions. Glucocorticoid deficiency impacts the cardiovascular system's responsiveness to catecholamines, exacerbating hypotension. Given the patient's symptoms, including dizziness first thing in the morning, postural hypotension is a strong indicator of adrenal insufficiency and warrants further evaluation and treatment with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.

Buccal ulceration
Buccal ulceration is not associated with adrenal failure. Instead, adrenal insufficiency presents with buccal pigmentation rather than ulceration. Hyperpigmentation occurs due to elevated levels of ACTH, which also increases melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). The woman might experience oral changes, but ulceration is not characteristic of adrenal failure.

Diminished body hair
Diminished body hair is more indicative of hypogonadism rather than adrenal failure. While secondary sexual hair loss might occur due to hypothalamic dysfunction stemming from weight loss and low BMI, it is unlikely to present diminished body hair as a primary feature. Adrenal insufficiency primarily impacts glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid production rather than directly affecting body hair. Thus, diminished body hair does not align with the typical symptoms of adrenal failure.

Pallor
Pallor is more commonly seen in conditions involving hypopituitarism, which results in normochromic, normocytic anaemia and lack of MSH. In adrenal insufficiency, ACTH levels are typically elevated, which conversely leads to hyperpigmentation rather than pallor. The patient's symptoms align more closely with adrenal insufficiency, where hyperpigmentation would be expected due to the elevated ACTH. Pallor due to a lack of ACTH is, therefore, not a fitting characteristic of primary adrenal failure. Adrenal Insufficiency A 74-year-old man with type II diabetes is reviewed in the Cardiology Department six weeks after a myocardial infarction. He has a history of ulcerative colitis and hypertension. His current therapy includes metformin and azathioprine. On examination, his blood pressure is 152/82 mmHg, his chest is clear and he has a body mass index of 40 kg/m 2. Investigations:

Optic atrophy
Optic atrophy is unrelated to adrenal failure. The most common causes of optic atrophy in young adults are conditions like multiple sclerosis rather than hormonal deficiencies. Adrenal insufficiency directly affects steroid hormone production and does not impact the optic nerve. Therefore, optic atrophy should not be expected in a patient with symptoms pointing to adrenal insufficiency.

stem: A 17-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes presents with confusion, hyperventilation and dehydration. On examination she is hyperventilating, smells of pear drops and has a blood pressure of 95/50 mmHg and a pulse of 105 bpm. Arterial blood gas measurement reveals a pH of 7.2. You suspect that she has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). What is the primary cause of ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes?
explanation:
Lipolysis
Lipolysis increases the availability of free fatty acid substrate for hepatic metabolism, which leads to accumulation of acid intermediate- and end-products (ketoacids and ketones such as acetoacetate, ßhydroxybutyrate and acetone). Ketones are also seen in some situations of acute energy deficit.

Lipogenesis
Lipogenesis is incorrect. Lipogenesis is the process by which acetyl-CoA is converted to fatty acids. The former is an intermediate stage in metabolism of simple sugars, such as glucose. Through lipogenesis and subsequent triglyceride synthesis, energy can be efficiently stored in the form of fats. This does not lead to ketone formation.

Gluconeogenesis
Gluconeogenesis is incorrect. Gluconeogenesis is one of the mechanisms used by humans and many other animals to maintain blood glucose levels, and to avoid hypoglycaemia. This is the mechanism that is inhibited by metformin, and does not contribute to ketogenesis.

Glycolysis
Glycolysis is incorrect. This is a metabolic pathway which involves the conversion of glucose to pyruvate in order to produce ATP or energy, and is a process used by almost every cell in the body for energy production, but does not lead to ketone production. Diabetic Ketoacidosis You have referred a 17-year-old girl who is part of a family who avoid medical services wherever possible. Her mother is now concerned that her daughter is short for her age and has not commenced her periods. On examination she is below the 50th centile for height. She appears to have excess skin around her neck, and has not developed secondary sexual characteristics. There is an audible cardiac murmur. Chromosome analysis reveals a 45X picture. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?

Glycogenolysis
Glycogenolysis is incorrect. Glycogenolysis is a mechanism of glucose production through the breakdown of glycogen in the liver and muscle, and it is particularly important in maintaining glucose levels in states of sympathetic over activation.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a history of polycystic ovarian syndrome comes to the clinic for review. She is obese with a BMI of 31, has a BP of 145/82 mmHg, facial acne, and excess hair around her beard line. She tells you that she wishes to become pregnant and her appearance if possible, and has read about using metformin to achieve her aims. Which of the following most closely represents the primary action of metformin in the treatment of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)?
explanation:
Increases insulin sensitivity
By increasing insulin sensitivity, including potentially within the ovary itself, metformin is thought to the chances of ovulation in women suffering from PCOS. Whilst it’s onset of action and effectiveness in inducing ovulation is inferior to clomiphene, it remains an option for some women who prefer to use it for the potential ancillary effects on their general health.

Reduces insulin secretion
Reduces insulin secretion is incorrect. Insulin secretion is reduced in association with metformin therapy, although this is secondary to mprovements in insulin sensitivity.

Reduces circulating oestrogen levels
Reduces circulating oestrogen levels is incorrect. By improving insulin sensitivity and reducing weight, metformin improves the balance between oestrogen and androgen levels.

Reduces circulating testosterone levels
Reduces circulating testosterone levels is incorrect. The reduction in testosterone levels occurs as a secondary effect of improvement in insulin sensitivity.

Reduces appetite
Reduces appetite is incorrect. Metformin does not significantly reduce appetite.

stem: He is recommended to start a low phosphate diet. Which other intervention would you commence?
explanation:
1-alpha calcidol
The answer is Calcium and 1-alpha calcidol (Option D). Calcium and 1-alpha Calcidol supplementation, usually with weekly 1-alpha Calcidol dosing, is the most appropriate initial step and conforms with current guidelines on management of secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Lanthanum carbonate
Lanthanum carbonate (Option A) is incorrect. Phosphate binders, including lanthanum carbonate, can be unpleasant to take, and as such reduction of phosphate intake, following a low phosphate diet should be instigated first.

Alendronate
Alendronate (Option B) is incorrect. Alendronate is a bisphosphonate which is a pyrophosphate analogue and should not be used if the eGFR <30, which is likely here.

Calcitonin
Calcitonin (Option C) is incorrect. Calcitonin is associated with malignancy and has been withdrawn from the market. Hyperparathyroidism

Cinacalcet
Cinacalcet (Option E) is incorrect. Cinacalcet is reserved for patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism or tertiary hyperparathyroidism who are on maintenance dialysis therapy and unable to undergo parathyroid surgery.

stem: Which of the following is likely to be the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Plasma VIP
A VIPoma is suspected, given the metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. It is also called pancreatic cholera syndrome, Verner-Morrison syndrome or WDHA syndrome. These patients present with profuse watery diarrhoea, mild abdominal pain and dehydration. The watery diarrhoea, coupled with a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis is very suggestive of VIPoma. Levels of VIP are usually between 2 and 10 times the normal range. The anti-endomyseal antibody and faecal fat results count against significant malabsorption.

24hr catecholamines
24hr catecholamines 24 h catecholamine is incorrect. This would be considered in suspected phaeochromocytoma.

24hr urinary 5-HIAA
24hr urinary 5-HIAA 24 h urinary 5-HIAA is incorrect. This is the main metabolite of serotonin; it is useful in investigation of carcinoid syndrome.

D-xylose absorption test
D-xylose absorption test is incorrect. This is useful in the investigation of bacterial overgrowth syndrome, which is the not the clinical suspicion here. Such patients would have nausea, bloating and weight loss. D-xylose absorption is abnormal in diseases that result in intestinal malabsorption, such as Whipple’s disease.

Hydrogen breath test
Hydrogen breath test is incorrect. This is useful in the investigation of bacterial overgrowth syndrome, which is not the clinical suspicion here.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the fertility clinic for review. Her partner has three children from a previous relationship, yet despite trying for a child for a year she is unable to get pregnant. She is keen to learn more about timing of ovulation. Which of the following investigations is most likely to indicate that ovulation is imminent?
options: Follicle size of 20 mm on ultrasound scan
explanation:
Raised LH level
A sudden increase in luteinising hormone (LH) levels – the LH surge – is of particular significance because it indicates that ovulation will occur about 24 hours after the LH peak.

Follicle size of 20 mm on ultrasound scan
Follicle size of 20 mm on ultrasound scan is incorrect. Follicle size is usually around 22 mm prior to ovulation, but an ultrasound scan gives no indication that ovulation is about to occur.

Increase in basal body temperature
Increase in basal body temperature is incorrect. An increase in basal body temperature occurs after ovulation – it doesn’t pre-date its occurrence.

Positive Spinnbarkeit test
Positive Spinnbarkeit test is incorrect. A positive Spinnbarkeit test is used to demonstrate oestrogenic activity of the cervical mucus – elasticity of the cervical mucus is greatly enhanced prior to ovulation, but does not provide a clue as to when ovulation will occur.

Secretory changes on endometrial biopsy
Secretory changes on endometrial biopsy is incorrect. Secretory changes on endometrial biopsy are seen after ovulation has occurred.

stem: A 40-year-old woman who has been prescribed metoclopramide for persistent nausea comes to the surgery for review. She says that her symptoms of nausea have resolved, but she now has milk leakage from both breasts, a loss of libido, and has not had periods for the last four months. What is the mechanism of action of metoclopramide that has driven these symptoms?
options: Stimulates dopamine release by the hypothalamus
Direct stimulatory effect on pituitary lactotropes
Binds to D 2-receptors on pituitary lactotropes
Inhibits luteinising hormone secretion by the anterior pituitary
explanation:
Binds to D 2-receptors on pituitary lactotropes
This patient has developed hyperprolactinaemia due to metoclopramide therapy. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that binds to D 2-receptors on pituitary lactotropes. This stimulates the release of prolactin by the anterior pituitary, resulting in galactorrhoea. Prolactin inhibits gonadotropin-releasing hormone and gonadotropin secretion and so oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea can occur.

Stimulates dopamine release by the hypothalamus
Stimulates dopamine release by the hypothalamus is incorrect. It is prolactin release by the anterior pituitary that is stimulated by D 2-receptor binding.

Direct stimulatory effect on pituitary lactotropes
Direct stimulatory effect on pituitary lactotropes is incorrect. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist rather than an agonist.

Promotes pituitary adenoma growth
Promotes pituitary adenoma growth is incorrect. Dopamine antagonists have no effect on adenoma growth. Hyperprolactinaemia and Prolactinoma A 21-year-old man who is marfanoid in appearance is referred by his GP for review. He has been suffering from acute headaches and panic attacks and is unable to continue his course work at university. On examination his blood pressure is 148/98 mmHg and you notice a number of neuromas around his lips. His 24-hour urinary catecholamine levels are raised. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?

Inhibits luteinising hormone secretion by the anterior pituitary
Inhibits luteinising hormone (LH) secretion by the anterior pituitary is incorrect. It is prolactin which inhibits LH secretion, this is not a direct effect of metoclopramide.

stem: You are asked by a GP to review a 18-year-old girl who presents with primary amenorrhoea. On examination, she appears to have minimal pubic hair but normal breast development; examination also reveals a blind-ended vagina. Biochemistry reveals an increased luteinising hormone (LH) level, a normal follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level, and raised oestradiol and testosterone levels. Which diagnosis fits best with this history and examination?
explanation:
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is a condition that results in the partial or complete inability of the cell to respond to androgens, which impairs the masculinisation of male genitalia in the developing fetus, as well as the development of male secondary sexual characteristics at puberty. In AIS, the gonads are testes that produce normal androgens. The lack of functional androgen tissue receptors results in sparse or no pubic and axillary hair, but patients with androgen insensitivity typically have normal breast development because of the peripheral conversion of the circulating androgens to oestrogens. They may have a small lower vagina or a normal vaginal length; however, no uterus or cervix is present because of the in utero production of a Müllerian-inhibiting substance by the testes. In pubertal girls, the diagnosis between androgen insensitivity and Müllerian agenesis can be made by assessing serum testosterone levels, followed by karyotype analysis; results will indicate levels in the pubertal male range, the XY karyotype and patients’ infertility. Orchidectomy is advised due to a risk of testicular malignancy.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome
Polycystic ovarian syndrome is incorrect. The lack of pubic hair and blind-ended vagina, which suggest AIS.

Turner syndrome
Turner syndrome is incorrect. The normal breast development and high androgen and LH levels. Women with Turner syndrome usually have short stature and a webbed neck.

Asherman syndrome
Asherman syndrome is incorrect. The hormonal abnormalities and lack of pubic hair. Asherman syndrome is intrauterine adhesions/scarring from previous infection/scarring. AmenorrhoeaA 64-year-old man with type 1 diabetes for 45 years presents for review. He has poor control, HbA1C 75 mmol/mol (9%) and he takes a multiple daily injection regimen of insulin. He complains of multiple areas of skin changes on his abdomen. On examination, he has areas of severe lipohypertrophy.

Kallmann syndrome
Kallmann syndrome is incorrect. This causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, unlike the high LH, oestradiol and testosterone seen in this case.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with Graves’ disease has been treated with radioiodine. What is the best advice for the patient during the post-radioiodine period?
options: It is safe for her to try and conceive after 3 months
She should not have close contact with young children and pregnant women for about 10 days after
There is no need to monitor her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level
She will never need further doses of radioiodine
She can be in close contact with children within 1 day
explanation:
She should not have close contact with young children and pregnant women for about 10 days after
She should not have close contact with young children and pregnant women for about 10 days after treatment Although the amount of radioiodine during the treatment is small and there is no evidence that the radiation from this amount of radioiodine will cause any problem, it makes sense to take steps to minimise exposure to others, no matter how small.

It is safe for her to try and conceive after 3 months
It is safe for her to try and conceive after 3 months is incorrect. It is recommended to wait at least 6 months before attempting to conceive.

There is no need to monitor her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level
There is no need to monitor her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is incorrect. There is a high chance she will become hypothyroid and could relapse, so her thyroid function tests (TFTs) should be monitored carefully.

She will never need further doses of radioiodine
She will never need further doses of radioiodine is incorrect. Thyrotoxicosis

She can be in close contact with children within 1 day
She can be in close contact with children within 1 day is incorrect. She should not have close contact with young children and pregnant women for about 2 weeks after treatment, due to the risk of exposing them to radiation.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism is being treated with thyroxine replacement, the dose of which is being titrated against the results of biochemical thyroid function tests. Five days after the last increase in dose, the results of thyroid function tests are: FT 4 28 pmol/l (NR 9–26 pmol/l), TSH 14 mU/l (NR 0.2–5.0 mU/l). Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: A decrease in the dose of thyroxine
A further increase in the dose of thyroxine
No change in dose at this time
Question the patient’s compliance with medication
explanation:
No change in dose at this time
It is too soon after the last change in dose for a new steady state to have been achieved: it is usual to wait for a month before reviewing the response. When thyroxine replacement is started, the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration often falls to normal more slowly than the free thyroxine (FT 4) concentration increases. Free thyroxine concentrations in clinically euthyroid patients on thyroxine replacement are often high-normal, or even slightly elevated, reflecting the lack of production of triiodothyronine (T3) by the thyroid – peripheral metabolism of thyroxine is the only source of T3. Irregular medication could explain these results but should not be considered until sufficient time has elapsed for the data to reliably reflect the effects of replacement.

A decrease in the dose of thyroxine
A decrease in the dose of thyroxine is incorrect. It is too soon after dosage change to interpret the results.

A further increase in the dose of thyroxine
A further increase in the dose of thyroxine is incorrect. It is too soon after dosage change to interpret the results.

Question the patient’s compliance with medication
Question the patient’s compliance with medication is incorrect. It is too soon after dosage change to interpret the results. Thyroxine replacement therapy (American Thyroid Association guidelines) Dose adjustments are guided by serum TSH determinations 4–8 weeks following initiation of therapy, dosage adjustments or change in the L-thyroxine preparation. While TSH levels may decline within a month of initiating therapy with doses of L-thyroxine, such as 50 or 75 µg, making adjustments with smaller doses may require 8 weeks or longer before TSH levels begin to plateau. Increment changes of 12.5–25 µg/d are initially made, but even smaller changes may be necessary to achieve goal TSH levels. Useful external websites Garber J R, Cobin R H, Gharib H, Hennessy J V, Klein I, Mechanik J I, et al. 2012. Clinical practice guidelines for hypothyroidism in adults: Cosponsored by the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the American Thyroid Association. Endocrine Practice, 18, 6, 988–1028. ( Hypothyroidism

Replace thyroxine with triiodothyronine
Replace thyroxine with triiodothyronine is incorrect. This is usually only used in very severe hypothyroidism, when a rapid response to treatment is required.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with fever, marked anxiety, palpitations, muscle weakness, sweating and diarrhoea. On examination she has a small goitre, and ECG shows fast atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 135 bpm. Blood tests reveal an elevated white cell count (WCC) and C-reactive protein (CRP). Thyroid function testing reveals a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of < 0.05 mU/l. Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Thyroid storm
This patient presents with features of severe hyperthyroidism. This, along with elevated inflammatory markers and remarkably suppressed TSH, is in keeping with thyroid storm.

Systemic infection
Systemic infection is incorrect. Although she has signs of infection, the overwhelming issue here is thyroid storm, which is obvious from her suppressed TSH, in combination with fast Afib and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.

Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation is incorrect. Her suppressed TSH, in combination with fast Afib and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, are all suggestive of thyroid storm, which is causing her atrial fibrillation.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. Her suppressed TSH, in combination with fast Afib and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, are all suggestive of thyroid storm.

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. Her suppressed TSH, in combination with fast Afib and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, are all suggestive of thyroid storm. Thyrotoxicosis A 54-year-old obese woman has been referred because of poor diabetic control despite being on gliclazide 160 mg twice a day. She has a history of hypertension that is managed with ramipril 10 mg daily and indapamide. Her body mass index (BMI) is 35 kg/m 2. There is also a history of irritable bowel syndrome. Biochemistry results show: mildly raised urea, creatinine 180 µmol/l, alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyltransferase both normal, HbA1c 79.24 mmol/ (9.4%).

stem: A 54-year-old obese woman has been referred because of poor diabetic control despite being on gliclazide 160 mg twice a day. She has a history of hypertension that is managed with ramipril 10 mg daily and indapamide. Her body mass index (BMI) is 35 kg/m 2. There is also a history of irritable bowel syndrome. Biochemistry results show: mildly raised urea, creatinine 180 µmol/l, alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyltransferase both normal, HbA1c 79.24 mmol/ (9.4%). Which of the following would you do next?
explanation:
Add dulaglutide
In this situation obesity and poor glycaemic control, both a reduction in HbA1c and weight management is desirable. As such, addition of a glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) agonist, which may require a reduction in SU dose is the preferred option. This will drive improved blood glucose control against a background of modest (up to 3%) weight reduction. Note that while some GLP-1 agonists must be used with caution when there is concomitant renal impairment, such as exenatide, this does not apply to all drugs within this class. Dulaglutide specifically has been shown to be safe and effective for patients with T2DM and CKD. In the BNF, there are no cautions for the use of this drug with renal impairment.

Add acarbose
Add acarbose is incorrect. Acarbose is effective in reducing absorption of carbohydrates from the gut, but has only a modest effect in reducing blood glucose and weight control.

Switch to repaglinide
Switch to repaglinide is incorrect. Repaglinide is less effective than gliclazide in reducing HbA1c and is therefore not an option here.

Add metformin
Add metformin is incorrect. Metformin only lowers HbA1c by between 0.7 and 1%. As such it won’t achieve adequate HbA1c lowering, and has only a very small effect on weight. Diabetes - Type II A 30-year-old man and his wife are referred to the Reproductive Endocrinology Clinic after failing to conceive for two years. The man admits to use of recreational drugs and anabolic steroids in the past. Examination of the man is as follows: height 189 cm, weight 95 kg (with central distribution of adipose tissue) and bilateral gynaecomastia. Ultrasound examination of the patient’s testes calculated a right testicular volume of 10.5 ml (right) and 10.1 ml (left). Which of the following investigations is most helpful in providing a diagnosis?

Add pioglitazone
Add pioglitazone is incorrect. Pioglitazone drives weight gain in the context of obesity and may drive a reduction in bone mineral density. As such it isn’t an ideal choice here.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer visits you because she is keen to start on tamoxifen to reduce her risk of getting breast cancer. Which of the following statements best describes the mode of action of tamoxifen?
options: It is a mixed oestrogen-receptor antagonist and partial agonist
explanation:
It is a mixed oestrogen-receptor antagonist and partial agonist
While tamoxifen is commonly known as an anti-oestrogen, this is not an accurate description of its clinical activity. In actual fact, tamoxifen has both oestrogenic and anti-estrogenic properties depending on the target tissue.

It is a progesterone-receptor agonist
It is a progesterone-receptor agonist is incorrect. Tamoxifen is a mixed oestrogen-receptor antagonist and partial agonist.

It is a progesterone-receptor antagonist
It is a progesterone-receptor antagonist is incorrect. Tamoxifen is a mixed oestrogen-receptor antagonist and partial agonist.

It is an oestrogen-receptor agonist
It is an oestrogen-receptor agonist is incorrect. Tamoxifen is a mixed oestrogen-receptor antagonist and partial agonist.

It is an oestrogen-receptor antagonist
It is an oestrogen-receptor antagonist is incorrect. Tamoxifen is a mixed oestrogen-receptor antagonist and partial agonist. Tamoxifen While tamoxifen is commonly known as an anti-estrogen, but this is not an accurate description of its clinical activity. In actual fact, tamoxifen boasts both oestrogenic and anti-estrogenic properties depending on the target tissue. Due to this dual action, tamoxifen is better described by the term selective oestrogen receptor modulator (SERM). Tamoxifen has a complex mechanism of action owing to its molecular structure. It is chemically very similar to oestrogen/estradiol, but the latter is a small, carbon-rich steroid and tamoxifen has an extra chain that is important for its antagonistic action. Tamoxifen’s pro- and anti-oestrogenic actions are mediated by its competitive binding to oestrogen receptors, which then undergo a conformational change. The nuclear complexes thus formed change the expression of oestrogen-dependent genes to generate multiple growthpromoting signals both inside and outside the nucleus. For example, the prolonged binding of tamoxifen to specific genes can lead to a blockage of the proliferative actions of endogenous oestrogen on mammary epithelium, by reducing DNA polymerase activity, blocking oestradiol uptake and eventually dampening the oestrogen response.

stem: A 54-year-old man who has had previous surgery for acromegaly is receiving adjuvant treatment with lanreotide medical therapy because his growth hormone is persistently elevated on biochemical testing with measurement of insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) (54 ng/ml) The persistent elevation of growth hormone was confirmed by a glucose tolerance test and growth hormone measurement. His prolactin level is normal. What is the mode of action of lanreotide?
options: Inhibition of the growth hormone receptor
explanation:
Stimulation of the somatostatin receptor
The somatostatin receptor is a 7-transmembrane G-protein receptor. Lanreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue. Stimulation of the somatostatin receptor leads to inhibition of the production of a number of hormones, including gastrin, cholecystokinin, glucagon, growth hormone, insulin and secretin. Somatostatin analogues are used for the medical treatment of acromegaly, either pre-surgery or after surgery or radiotherapy for persistently elevated growth hormone levels. They are also used for symptomatic relief of the carcinoid syndrome. Side-effects include gastrointestinal side-effects of diarrhoea and abdominal cramping and somatostatin analogues can precipitate gallstone formation.

Inhibition of the somatostatin receptor
Somatostatin analogues are synthetic forms of the hormone somatostatin which acts to block the action of growth hormone. Inhibition of the somatostatin receptor is incorrect and would potentiate the effect of growth hormone.

Inhibition of the growth hormone receptor
Inhibition of the growth hormone receptor is incorrect. Inhibition by an agent called pegvisomant is a treatment option for patients with acromegaly who have failed to respond to surgery or treatment with somatostatin analogues. Pegvisomant blocks the action of growth hormone at the growth hormone receptor and reduces production of IGF-1, which helps in the control of symptoms.

Stimulation of the dopamine D 2-receptor
