The pain may begin focally and spread throughout the gland over several weeks; patients may have malaise, low-grade fever and fatigue in addition to the symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. The thyroid is firm and painful to palpation. In addition to laboratory evidence of thyrotoxicosis, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein is elevated, and mild anaemia is common. RAIU is low, and thyroid ultrasonography shows diffuse heterogeneity and decreased or normal color flow Doppler, rather than the enhanced flow characteristic of GD. (American Thyroid Association guidelines) Patients with mild symptomatic subacute thyroiditis should be treated initially with beta-adrenergic-blocking drugs and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Those failing to respond, or those with moderate-to-severe symptoms, should be treated with corticosteroids.

Commence carbimazole
Commence carbimazole is incorrect. TThe likely diagnosis here is thyroiditis, and so the hyperthyroidism will likely be transient, and rarely requires active treatment. Treatment in subacute thyroiditis is analgesia, anti inflammatories, and beta blockers to treat anxiety and palpitations.

Commence propylthiouracil
Commence propylthiouracil is incorrect. Carbimazole and Propylthiouracil are thionamides which are the most commonly used treatment for hyperthyroidism. However subacute thyroiditis is the likely diagnosis in this scenario, and the hyperthyroidism will therefore likely be transient and rarely requires active treatment.

Commence Eltroxin®
Commence Eltroxin® is incorrect. She is not hypothyroid and Eltroxin® would worsen her condition. Thyrotoxicosis

Radioactive iodine treatment
Radioactive iodine treatment is incorrect. The likely diagnosis here is thyroiditis, and so the hyperthyroidism will likely be transient. Radioactive iodine is taken up by the thyroid and has a destructive effect to the active cell, ultimately reducing the amount of thyroxine produced and sometimes reducing the size of the gland. It is often used in Graves disease, toxic nodular hypothyroidism, and to decrease size of goitres if present.

stem: Which of the following is the the most appropriate management for this ulcer?
explanation:
Non-removable casting
Non-removable casting should be used to offload pressure on the uninfected forefoot and mid-foot diabetic ulcers. This allows time for the tissue to heal.

Electrical stimulation therapy
While trials of electrical stimulation therapy, such as shock wave therapy (delivered using a handheld probe to deliver high-energy heart rates to the wound), showed early wound closure, compared to control populations, National Institute for Health Care and Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend against its use.

Epidermal growth factor
According to a Cochrane review, epidermal growth factor has limited efficacy when reviewing time to recovery for a diabetic ulcer, while increasing the risk of overall adverse event rates. National Institute for Health Care and Excellence guidelines recommend against its use.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Several trials have reviewed the contribution of hyperbaric oxygen therapy to the speed of healing. There is limited evidence to support its use and NICE guidelines recommend against it.

Platelet-derived growth factor
Platelet-derived growth factor can be administered in a gel preparation locally. Although they are effective, they have a high cost and are therefore not deemed an option by NICE.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a renal calculus. She has recurrent episodes of headache and sweating. Physical examination reveals a thyroid nodule but no clinical signs of thyrotoxicosis. Which one of the following investigations would be most useful in arriving at a diagnosis for the headaches?
options: Free triiodothyronine (T3), free thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels
explanation:
24-h urine collection for metanephrines
Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2 is associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, hyperparathyroidism and phaeochromocytoma. The most useful investigation would be a 24-h urine collection for metanephrines; plasma and urinary catecholamines can also be measured directly. The hyperparathyroidism has likely led to elevated calcium levels leading to the renal stones.

24-h urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid excretion
24-h urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid excretion is incorrect. Estimation of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is done for carcinoid syndrome; it is not part of MEN2. Carcinoid syndrome is where a carcinoid tumour releases excessive serotonin. About 1200 patients are diagnosed with a carcinoid tumour per year in the United Kingdom, and less than one-tenth will have carcinoid syndrome. This presents with diarrhoea, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, facial flushing, tachycardia, breathlessness and wheeze.

Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
Serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is incorrect. ALP levels would be raised in hyperparathryoidism, but it would not lead to the diagnosis of MEN2.

Serum calcium level
Serum calcium level is incorrect. Detection of hyperparathyroidism would not lead to the diagnosis of MEN2, so serum calcium would not be helpful in this regard. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia

Free triiodothyronine (T3), free thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels
Free triiodothyronine (T3), free thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels is incorrect. Thyroid function is normal in MEN2; therefore, measuring T3, T4 and TSH levels would not be helpful.

stem: What is the most likely cause for the more frequent nocturnal hypoglycaemic episodes?
explanation:
Exercise-induced hypoglycaemia
Exercise-associated hypoglycaemia results from many factors, including improved insulin sensitivity, impaired glucagon secretion and counter-regulatory hormonal response. All patients should be advised to intake extra carbohydrates before exercising or reduce the dose of insulin before exercising. In this case the patient’s hypoglycaemic episodes are occurring at night and she is exercising in the evening, explaining why these episodes are commonly occurring at night. She needs to be educated on the importance of carbohydrate loading prior to exercise and her insulin doses will need to be modified if this is not effective in reducing hypoglycaemic episodes.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. This is an important consideration in any patient with type 1 diabetes who develops new, frequent hypoglycaemic episodes. As type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition, patients with this form are also at risk of other autoimmune conditions such as Hashimoto’s thyroid disease and Addison’s. However, the normal sodium and lack of postural hypotension described in this case makes a diagnosis of Addison’s less likely.

‘Honeymoon’ period
‘Honeymoon’ period ‘Honeymoon period’ is incorrect. The honeymoon period refers to the time in the initial diagnosis of type 1 diabetes where the pancreatic islet cells are still capable of making small amounts of endogenous insulin. This insulin production can be unpredictable and therefore dosing of exogenous insulin can be difficult in attempting to avoid hypoglycaemia. However, this patient has a diagnosis for over 8 years as per the case history and so is very unlikely to be in the ‘honeymoon period’.

Factitious hypoglycaemia
Factitious hypoglycaemia is incorrect. This is an important consideration; occasionally young patients will selfadminister excess insulin in an attempt to cause deliberate hypoglycaemia and self-harm. There is no history of self-harm or anxiety or mental health issues described in this passage. Furthermore, frequent self-dosing with excess insulin can lead to weight gain, and the patient described in this case has lost weight. Diabetes - Type I

Lipohypertrophy
Lipohypertrophy is incorrect. It is important always to examine injection sites because of the risk of lipohypertrophy over time if patients do not rotate their insulin injection sites. This can lead to variable absorption of insulin and, as doses change, it can cause erratic glycaemic control and hypoglycaemia. The normal injection site exam described in this case makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 52-year-old man is sent by his General Practitioner for an urgent review. He has had type II diabetes for ten years and is treated with metformin, sitagliptin and gliclazide. His HbA1c is 90 mmol/mol (10.4%). For the past week, he has had feelings of severe aching pain and paraesthesiae in his thighs; he also complains of anorexia and a 3 kg weight loss. On clinical examination, there is proximal muscle weakness. Which of the following best fits the underlying condition in this case?
options: 80% of patients recover fully from this condition
Commencing insulin therapy is the mainstay of treatment
Recovery from this condition will occur over one year
The condition is more common in type I diabetes
Weight loss is unlikely to be related to the diagnosis
explanation:
Commencing insulin therapy is the mainstay of treatment
Good glycaemic control through the adjustment of diabetes medication (eg oral agents, insulin) is of paramount importance in diabetic amyotrophy, which is the diagnosis in this case. The patient in this case is already on 3 oral agents and has very poor glycaemic control; insulin is the next-line treatment to glucose control.

80% of patients recover fully from this condition
80% of patients recover fully from this condition is incorrect as good functional recovery within 12–24 months is expected in 60% of patients with diabetic lumbosacral plexopathy, although mild weakness, discomfort and stiffness often persist for years; occasional relapses can occur.

Recovery from this condition will occur over one year
Recovery from this condition will occur over one year is incorrect as good functional recovery within 12–24 months is expected in 60% of patients with diabetic lumbosacral plexopathy, although mild weakness, discomfort and stiffness often persist for years; occasional relapses can occur.

The condition is more common in type I diabetes
The condition is more common in type I diabetes is incorrect as it is seen in both type I and type II diabetes.

Weight loss is unlikely to be related to the diagnosis
Weight loss is unlikely to be related to the diagnosis is incorrect as weight loss is a frequent feature of this condition. Diabetic amyotrophy/proximal neuropathy/lumbosacral plexopathy Proximal neuropathy in diabetes mellitus is a condition in which patients develop severe aching or burning and lancinating pain in the hip and thigh. This is followed by weakness and wasting of the thigh muscles, which often occur asymmetrically. It usually has its onset during or after middle age (although it can occur in younger individuals). Concomitant distal, predominantly sensory, neuropathy may exist. The results of most electrodiagnostic studies are consistent with the presence of a neurogenic lesion that could be associated with lumbosacral plexopathy, radiculopathy or proximal crural neuropathy. Good glycaemic control through the adjustment of diabetes medication (eg oral agents, insulin) is of paramount importance in diabetic amyotrophy.

stem: You suspect that she might have retrosternal thyroid extension. Which of the following would be the investigation of choice for this patient to determine the degree of retrosternal involvement?
explanation:
Computed tomography of the chest
CT provides detailed information about the size, shape and extent of the goitre, and defines its relationship to other structures, in particular the trachea, and is able to produce serial transverse sections giving crosssectional information about tracheal calibre, making it the best investigation for the preoperative assessment of a patient with a large multinodular goitre and suspected retrosternal extension.

Chest X-ray
Chest X-ray is incorrect. Although a plain radiograph can be used to demonstrate retrosternal thyroid extension and tracheal deviation, computed tomography of the chest is more sensitive and specific in determining the extent of disease.

Thyroid ultrasound
Thyroid ultrasound is incorrect. Thyroid ultrasound is most useful for determining the nature of intrathyroid lesions, and can detect extension of the thyroid gland into the thorax, in addition to tracheal deviation or narrowing, but cannot give precise anatomical detail on the severity of retrosternal extension.

Thoracic inlet X-ray
Thoracic inlet X-ray is incorrect. Again this may demonstrate tracheal deviation, but will not give sufficient anatomical information to determine the need for surgical management or to plan a surgical intervention.

Radioisotope scan
Radioisotope scan is incorrect. This is useful in determining the uptake of thyroid hormone and thus the underlying diagnosis behind thyrotoxicosis, or in identifying cold nodules within the gland that might raise the suspicion of an underlying neoplasm, but has no role in a euthyroid patient with a compressive goitre.

stem: You are investigating a new insulin receptor modulator which is thought to insulin sensitivity by binding to the insulin receptor downstream of the insulin binding site. When looking at cellular processes, which of the following enzymes is most likely to be inhibited by improving insulin action?
explanation:
Pyruvate carboxylase
Pyruvate carboxylase drives a key step in gluconeogenesis, promoting the synthesis of phosphoenolpyruvate from pyruvate within mitochondria. It is then exported into the cytosol where conversion into glucose occurs.

Glucokinase
Glucokinase is incorrect. Glucokinase activity is upregulated by insulin; it is a key step in driving glycogen production via the formation of glucose-6-phosphate.

Glycogen synthetase
Glycogen synthetase is incorrect. Glycogen synthetase activity is upregulated by insulin; it binds to a growing chain of synthesised glycogen and adds UDP-glucose to the 4-hydroxyl group of the glucosyl residue.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is incorrect. This enzyme is upregulated by insulin action to increase glycolysis.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase is incorrect. Pyruvate dehydrogenase drives the formation of acetyl-CoA, and is upregulated by insulin.

stem: A 72-year-old woman comes to see you with chronic back pain, which worsened one week ago. She has been wheelchair-bound for six months because of severe osteoporosis with multiple lumbosacral spine fractures. She has severe rheumatoid arthritis, which has required large doses of glucocorticoids for many years. The patient reports progressive loss of height and kyphosis over the past year. Other medications include omeprazole for severe reflux oesophagitis. Her T score is -3.5. She is not keen on very frequent regular injectable therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Denosumab
Denosumab is a RANKL ligand inhibitor which is endorsed by NICE guidance for the treatment of severe osteoporosis, (T score -3.5 or worse). Although it is an injectable option for the treatment of osteoporosis, it is given only once every 6 months and is therefore tolerated by patients who don’t want a daily subcutaneous injection

Calcitonin
Calcitonin is incorrect. Chronic use of calcitonin is not recommended because of the association of use of the drug with osteosarcoma.

Calcium and vitamin D
Calcium and vitamin D is incorrect. This is inadequate therapy for the treatment of severe osteoporosis.

Risedronate
Risedronate is incorrect. Risedronate is a bisphosphonate and is therefore likely to precipitate worsening of existing oesophagitis.

Teriparatide
Teriparatide is incorrect. Although this synthetic parathyroid hormone (PTH) analogue is an effective option for the treatment of severe osteoporosis, it is a daily injectable and therefore not considered by many patients, particularly those who don’t like injectables.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic with painful oral ulcers, anorexia and gradual weight loss over the past few months. Her periods ceased when she was 21 years old. Her mother had a history of thyroidectomy for autoimmune thyroid disease. Examination reveals a BP of 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 72 beats/min and regular. Which of the following would suggest polyglandular syndrome type 1?
explanation:
Hypocalcaemia
Polyglandular syndrome type 1 is an autosomal recessive condition associated with: Hypoparathyroidism (in around 90%) Mucocutaneous candidiasis Adrenal insufficiency (in around 60%) Primary gonadal failure Primary hypothyroidism Hypopituitarism/diabetes insipidus (rarely) There might be associated malabsorption, pernicious anaemia, chronic active hepatitis or vitiligo. Polyglandular syndrome type 2 can be autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant or polygenic in its pattern of inheritance. Features can include: Adrenal insufficiency (in all patients) Hypothyroidism Type 1 diabetes Gonadal failure Diabetes insipidus (DI) (rare) Associated conditions include vitiligo, myasthenia gravis, alopecia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura and pernicious anaemia.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease is not associated with polyglandular syndrome type 1.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Type 1 diabetes mellitus is associated with polyglandular syndrome type 2.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. Hyperparathyroidism is associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia, not autoimmune polyglandular syndrome.

Diabetes insipidus
DI is incorrect. DI is rarely associated with polyglandular syndrome type 2, rather than type 1.

stem: A 68-year-old man attends his GP, on the insistence of his wife, because his left forefoot has become increasingly swollen, misshapen and unstable when he walked. He has a 20-year history of poorly controlled Type 2 diabetes, complicated by retinopathy and nephropathy. He is managed with multiple daily injections of insulin, and his most recent HbA1c is 86 mmol/mol (10%). Which of the following best describes the pathology or management of this man’s foot condition?
options: Tight glucose control is unlikely to be of benefit in this condition
This condition is unrelated to trauma
This is not related to diabetic neuropathy
Plain radiography is normal in this condition
The pathology of this condition is thought to be related to an exaggerated local inflammatory
explanation:
The pathology of this condition is thought to be related to an exaggerated local inflammatory
The pathology of this condition is thought to be related to an exaggerated local inflammatory response to trauma to the neuropathic foot The diagnosis here is diabetic neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy. In patients with diabetes mellitus, the loss of sensation to a joint may result in a chronic, progressive and destructive arthropathy. It is multifactorial, due to a combination of mechanical and vascular factors resulting from diabetic peripheral and autonomic neuropathy and metabolic abnormalities of bone. Trauma to the neuropathic foot may trigger an exaggerated local inflammatory response, mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines, resulting in the osteoarthropathy. As an example, lack of proprioception secondary to peripheral neuropathy may result in ligamentous laxity, increased range of joint movement, instability and damage by minor trauma, to which the relatively insensitive neuropathic foot is prone. In addition, the resulting change in the architecture of the foot causes a change in weight bearing and subsequent localised trauma. Finally, autonomic neuropathy may result in vasomotor changes and in the formation of arteriovenous shunts; these, in turn, result in reductions in effective skin and bone blood flow, despite the good and sometimes bounding foot pulses in these patients.

Tight glucose control is unlikely to be of benefit in this condition
Tight glucose control is unlikely to be of benefit in this condition is incorrect. Glycaemic control is important to promote wound healing.

This condition is unrelated to trauma
This condition is unrelated to trauma is incorrect. Often there is a history of minor trauma. Trauma to the neuropathic foot may trigger an exaggerated local inflammatory response, mediated by pro-inflammatory cytokines, resulting in the osteoarthropathy.

This is not related to diabetic neuropathy
This is not related to diabetic neuropathy is incorrect. The diagnosis is Charcot foot, or diabetic neuropathic arthropathy. Charcot Arthropathy Clinical features Patients classically present with sudden onset of unilateral warmth, redness and oedema over the foot or ankle, often with a history of minor trauma; the affected foot may be discernibly warmer to the touch than the contralateral foot. Sometimes, patients present instead with a slowly progressing arthropathy, with insidious swelling over months or years, and, occasionally, recurrent acute attacks may occur. The most frequently involved joints in the diabetic patients are the tarsus and tarsometatarsal joints, followed by the metatarsophalangeal joints and the ankle. Management Avoidance of weight bearing Tight glycaemic control Patients who do not respond adequately to other interventions should be referred for consultation with an orthopaedic surgeon with experience in the management of diabetic neuropathic arthropathy, to assess the individual risks and benefits of a surgical stabilisation or other procedures The role of bisphosphonates and calcitonin in acute Charcot neuroarthropathy remains uncertain. Diabetes - Type II

Plain radiography is normal in this condition
Plain radiography is normal in this condition is incorrect. Although plain radiographs can be normal in the early stages of the disease, later on they show joint destruction, osteolysis, joint reorganisation and subluxation.

stem: A 26-year-old man with Addison's disease presents with an acute onset of diarrhoea and vomiting over the past 6 hours. Apparently his two children have recently been ill with a 48-hour vomiting virus. He currently takes fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone steroid replacement. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Intravenous fluids and intravenous hydrocortisone
Patients with Addison's disease are dependent on steroid replacement to manage their condition, and during times of physiological stress, such as illness, their steroid requirements increase. Vomiting and diarrhoea can prevent the absorption of oral medications, making it crucial to administer hydrocortisone intravenously to ensure adequate levels. Intravenous fluids are also necessary to correct any dehydration caused by the vomiting and diarrhoea, which can exacerbate the risk of adrenal crisis. Prompt administration of intravenous hydrocortisone and fluids is essential to stabilise the patient's condition and prevent potentially life-threatening complications.

Intravenous cyclizine
IV cyclizine is incorrect because while it may help alleviate nausea and vomiting, it does not address the underlying need for increased steroid replacement in Addison's disease. Patients with Addison's disease require additional steroids during times of illness or stress to prevent adrenal crisis. Relying solely on an anti-emetic will not provide the necessary steroid support that the patient needs. Therefore, cyclizine alone is insufficient and inappropriate in this scenario.

Intravenous ondansetron
IV ondansetron is incorrect for similar reasons to cyclizine. Although ondansetron can help control nausea and vomiting, it does not replace the essential steroids that the patient is unable to take orally. Without addressing the steroid deficiency, the patient remains at high risk for adrenal crisis. Additionally, focusing on anti-emetics without steroid replacement can delay the critical treatment the patient needs, potentially worsening their condition.

Increase fludrocortisone by 50%
Increasing fludrocortisone by 50% is incorrect because it primarily addresses mineralocorticoid needs, not the glucocorticoid needs that are crucial in this situation. During acute illness or stress, it is the glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) dose that needs to be significantly increased to manage the body's heightened requirements. Fludrocortisone adjustments are typically not sufficient to prevent adrenal crisis in these circumstances. Therefore, this option does not provide the necessary increase in glucocorticoid levels needed for this patient. Adrenal Insufficiency

Increase oral hydrocortisone by 50%
Increasing oral hydrocortisone by 50% is incorrect because the patient is experiencing vomiting and may not be able to retain or absorb oral medications effectively. In cases where oral intake is compromised, intravenous administration of hydrocortisone is necessary to ensure that the patient receives the required dose. Simply increasing the oral dose does not guarantee adequate steroid replacement and leaves the patient at risk of adrenal crisis. Therefore, this approach is not appropriate given the patient's current inability to take medications orally.

stem: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is diagnosed and, therefore, restrict their fluid intake. His sodium falls further to 119 mmol/l the following day. His drowsiness has increased. A computerised tomography (CT) head is arranged. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management for him?
explanation:
Give hypertonic saline (3%)
The European guidelines for the management of severe symptomatic hyponatraemia recommend the use of intravenous hypertonic saline (3%) as an initial bolus of 300 ml with repeat serum sodium measurement every 20 minutes, ideally in a critical care unit with very close observation. Intravenous bolusing of hypertonic saline should be continued at 20-minute intervals at a rate of 150 ml over 20 minutes until an increase of 5 mmol/l of serum sodium is achieved. The serum sodium should not be increased faster than of 10 mmol/l during the first 24-hours and an additional 8-mmol/l during every 24-hours thereafter until the serum sodium concentration reaches 130 mmol/l.

Continue fluid restriction
Continue fluid restriction is incorrect. This patient has severe symptoms with worsening hyponatraemia despite implementation of fluid restriction. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia is a potentially life-threatening condition and urgent escalation of treatment with hypertonic saline is required at this point to prevent further cerebral oedema and to allow a slow measured restoration of serum sodium levels.

Start dexamethasone
Give dexamethasone is incorrect. Dexamethasone can exacerbate salt and water retention further and has no role in the management of acute severe hyponatraemia.

Give normal saline 0.9%
Give normal saline 0.9% is incorrect. Intravenous normal saline would further increase water retention and cause further dilutional hyponatraemia and worsen the clinical condition and serum sodium.

Give demeclocycline
Give demeclocycline is incorrect. Demeclocycline is an efficient oral treatment for syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which fails to respond to intake restriction. Like all tetracyclines it leads to an increase in the excretion of water, leading to a rise in serum sodium levels. However, it is only indicated in the setting of less severe hyponatraemia if the patient is clinically stable with no neurological symptoms and would not be a suitable treatment as the initial management of this critically unwell patient.

stem: You review a 32-year-old woman with relapsed Graves’ disease. The thyroid-stimulating hormone level (TSH) is less than 0.05 mU/l, with a free thyroxine (FT 4) of 52.5 pmol/l. She has severe bilateral thyroid eye disease, with marked orbital oedema and proptosis. She is a smoker. You are considering definitive treatment as she has relapsed twice after drug treatment. Which of the following statements about the management of her thyroid eye disease is most accurate?
options: Systemic steroids are of no value in managing the eye disease
Subtotal thyroidectomy is the best treatment option for her
Stopping smoking will make no difference to her clinical course now that she has established thyroid
Radioiodine treatment is the best treatment option for her
Total thyroidectomy is the best treatment option for her
explanation:
Total thyroidectomy is the best treatment option for her
Her thyroid eye disease might be worsened by radioiodine treatment: she has severe thyroid eye disease and is a smoker, so she is at high risk for worsening disease with radioiodine. In addition, she has relapsed twice despite medical treatment: patients with Graves’ hyperthyroidism and active moderate-to-severe or sightthreatening ophthalmopathy should be treated with either medications or surgery.

Systemic steroids are of no value in managing the eye disease
Systemic steroids are of no value in managing the eye disease is incorrect. Steroids have been shown to be of benefit in severe active Graves’ ophthalmopathy (GO).

Subtotal thyroidectomy is the best treatment option for her
Subtotal thyroidectomy is the best treatment option for her is incorrect. Subtotal surgery will not cure her Graves’, which affects the entire thyroid gland.

Stopping smoking will make no difference to her clinical course now that she has established thyroid
Stopping smoking will make no difference to her clinical course now that she has established thyroid eye disease Stopping smoking will make no difference to her clinical course now that she has established thyroid eye disease is incorrect. Smoking is the most important known risk factor for the development or worsening of GO – unrelated to type of therapy for GO – and consistent data from several studies show a detrimental effect of smoking on GO in patients treated with radioactive iodine. The risk is proportional to the number of cigarettes smoked per day, and former smokers have significantly lower risk than current smokers, even after adjusting for lifetime cigarette consumption.

Radioiodine treatment is the best treatment option for her
Radioiodine treatment is the best treatment option for her is incorrect. She has severe thyroid eye disease and is a smoker, so she is at high risk for worsening disease with radioiodine treatment.

stem: A 34-year-old accountant is referred to you with a history of diabetes mellitus since the age of 16 years. He is a methodical man and appears always to have striven to maintain reasonable metabolic control of his condition, while managing a normal lifestyle. What is the most likely finding on examination and routine testing?
options: A raised albumin to creatinine ratio in the urine (microalbuminuria)
explanation:
Background retinopathy
The risk of developing retinopathy progressively increases with increasing duration of diabetes. Standardised methods of assessing retinopathy, including retinal photography, have revealed that 97% of insulin-dependent diabetics have some evidence of retinopathy (background changes at the least) 15 years after diagnosis. Half have proliferative changes 20 years after diagnosis.

A raised albumin to creatinine ratio in the urine (microalbuminuria)
A raised albumin to creatinine ratio in the urine (microalbuminuria) is incorrect. Although microalbuminuria is likely in this patient, the chance of seeing it is less compared to the chances of detecting background retinopathy. Around 25–30% of people develop some degree of diabetic nephropathy by the time they have had diabetes for 10–20 years.

Absent ankle jerks
Absent ankle jerks is incorrect. A peripheral sensory neuropathy is more likely to be seen in patients with diabetes mellitus, rather than a loss of motor function.

Anti-thyroid antibodies
Anti-thyroid antibodies is incorrect. Although other autoimmune pathologies are significantly more likely to occur in patients with Type 1 diabetes, the frequency of autoantibody detection is very much lower versus the risks of diabetic retinopathy or nephropathy. Diabetes - Type I A 28-year-old, single machinist, who describes herself as always being anxious, presents because she is concerned about weight loss (59 to 50 kg), tiredness and amenorrhoea over the past year. Examination reveals: pallor, pulse 96 bpm and regular (lying down), blood pressure 110/78 mmHg lying and 92/66 mmHg standing, tendon reflexes slightly slow to relax. There is a normochromic, normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin 99 g/l). Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, plasma glucose and serum calcium are all normal, apart from a potassium just above the upper limit of normal. Her 9 am cortisol is 53 mmol/l, she has a normal prolactin, a low T 4 of 6.9 pmol/l, a low normal TSH and undetectable gonadotrophin hormone levels.

Macroproteinuria on dipstick urine testing
Macroproteinuria on dipstick urine testing is incorrect. It is very unlikely a patient with significant proteinuria would be referred to you late in the disease without symptoms precipitating them presenting to the clinic.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with a prolactin of 2000 mU/l. Medication of note includes ramipril for hypertension and orlistat for weight loss. She tells you that her periods have been rather heavy over the past few months but she puts this down to the menopause. On examination in the clinic her BP is 155/72 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Her BMI is 31, she admits to not having managed to lose any weight over the past few months. Her visual field examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is often forgotten as a cause of raised prolactin, and the difficulty in losing weight coupled with menorrhagia support this diagnosis. Measurement of TSH is the next obvious step in investigating this patient.

Drug induced hyperprolactinaemia
Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is incorrect. Hyperprolactinaemia is not listed as a side effect of either ramipril or orlistat.

Microprolactinoma
Microprolactinoma is incorrect. Prolactin levels would be expected to be much higher in a patient with a prolactinoma.

Macroprolactinoma
Macroprolactinoma is incorrect. Prolactin levels would be expected to be much higher in a patient with a prolactinoma. The patient may also present with visual field loss. Hypothyroidism

Non-functioning pituitary adenoma
Non-functioning pituitary adenoma is incorrect. Non-functioning pituitary adenomas can compress the pituitary gland, causing hypopituitarism. Large pituitary tumours can cause a mild elevation in prolactin due to compression of the pituitary stalk.

stem: A 28-year-old, single machinist, who describes herself as always being anxious, presents because she is concerned about weight loss (59 to 50 kg), tiredness and amenorrhoea over the past year. Examination reveals: pallor, pulse 96 bpm and regular (lying down), blood pressure 110/78 mmHg lying and 92/66 mmHg standing, tendon reflexes slightly slow to relax. There is a normochromic, normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin 99 g/l). Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, plasma glucose and serum calcium are all normal, apart from a potassium just above the upper limit of normal. Her 9 am cortisol is 53 mmol/l, she has a normal prolactin, a low T 4 of 6.9 pmol/l, a low normal TSH and undetectable gonadotrophin hormone levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypopituitarism
Hypopituitarism causes pallor, due to loss of the melanocyte-stimulating properties of adrenocorticotropic hormone, and a moderate normochromic, normocytic anaemia which responds to thyroid and steroid replacement. Postural hypotension occurs due to adrenocortical underactivity, tiredness and slow-reacting reflexes due to hypothyroidism, and amenorrhoea due to loss of gonadotropins.

Microprolactinoma
Microprolactinoma is incorrect. A microprolactinoma can cause secondary ammenorhoea due to the production of prolactin from a small pituitary adenoma (<1 cm). Elevated prolactin levels cause anovulation. Most patients with microprolactinoma are well, apart from amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, and the normal prolactin level in this case makes the diagnosis unlikely.

Primary hypothyroidism
Primary hypothyroidism is incorrect. The thyroid function results in this case are not in keeping with primary hypothyroidism. Despite a low free T 4, there is an inappropriately low TSH, suggesting an inability at the level of the pituitary to produce TSH to stimulate thyroxine production. Furthermore, in primary hypothyroidism, a low T 4 is usually detected in the presence of an elevated TSH. Although weight loss and a normochromic anaemia can occasionally be found in hypothyroidism, weight gain, menorrhagia and macrocytic anaemia are more common.

Anorexia nervosa
Anorexia nervosa is incorrect. It is unusual for patients with anorexia nervosa to present concerned about their health. Others often initiate the call for help. It is often a diagnosis of exclusion after pathological causes for weight loss, such as hypopituitarism, have been excluded.

Thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotoxicosis is incorrect. The thyroid function test results provided in this case are not in keeping with thyrotoxicosis; you would expect an elevated T 4 in the presence of a suppressed TSH. Hypopituitarism.

stem: You suspect that she has thyrotoxicosis. Which of the following fits best with the action/effects of excess thyroxine?
explanation:
Decreased oestrogenisation
Excess thyroxine can lead to a cessation of menses (amenorrhoea), and as such is associated with decreased oestrogenisation and increased risk of osteoporosis.

Decreases myocardial oxygen demand
Decreased myocardial oxygen demand is incorrect. Excess thyroxine hormone is associated with increased myocardial oxygen demand, which leads to presentation with angina in some patients with thyrotoxicosis. For this reason, caution should also be used when escalating the dose of thyroxine replacement in elderly patients or patients with a history of cardiovascular disease with hypothyroidism.

Increased prolactin release
Increased prolactin release is incorrect and occurs in hypothyroidism due to the effect of excess thyrotropinreleasing hormone in the setting of a low free T 4 in a hypothyroid state, on prolactin secretion.

Decreased heart rate
Decreased heart rate is incorrect. Thyroxine regulates the body’s basal metabolic rate. An increased level of thyroxine leads to an increased metabolic rate leading to an increased heart rate, weight loss, and an increased temperature. Excess thyroid hormones increase heart rate, cardiac contractility and cardiac output. They also promote vasodilation, which leads to enhanced blood flow to many organs. Thyrotoxicosis

Leads to increased bone mass
Leads to increased bone mass is incorrect. Excess thyroid hormone reduces bone mineral density and is a risk factor for osteoporosis.

stem: A 40-year-old woman, who has been prescribed thyroid replacement therapy, has routine thyroid function tests (TFTs). She is currently well, takes no medication apart from thyroid hormone, and has a stable weight. On examination she appeared clinically euthyroid with no abnormal findings. Her TFTs revealed: thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH) 3.2 mU/l (normal range 0.38–5.33 mU/l), free T 4 2.6 pmol/l (7.9–14.4 pmol/l) and free tri-iodothyronine (T 3) 4.9 nmol/l (3.8–6.0 nmol/l). Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Her thyroid hormone replacement is adequate
Investigation of pituitary function is required
explanation:
Her thyroid hormone replacement is adequate
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) measurements are used as the standard method to monitor thyroid hormone replacement. She is clinically euthyroid and her TSH is within the normal range. Tri-iodothyronine (T 3) and tetra-iodothyronine (T 4) exist in a state of dynamic equilibrium, so although her free T 4 is low, her T 3 is within the normal range. Many patients who have adequate thyroid hormone replacement do still complain of symptoms of tiredness, lethargy, and mental slowing. It has been postulated that the addition of some replacement in the form of T 3 might these symptoms. A randomised controlled trial of T 4 + T 3 replacement vs T 4 replacement alone reported positive effects on mood in some patients with hypothyroidism.

Investigation of pituitary function is required
Investigation of pituitary function is required is incorrect. This patient’s weight is stable. She feels well and takes no medication apart from thyroid hormone. Given the T 3 is at the upper end of the normal range, and TSH is in the normal range, no further investigation is needed.

She has tertiary hypothyroidism
She has tertiary hypothyroidism is incorrect. Tertiary hypothyroidism occurs due to failure of thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) production, a low TSH in the presence of low T 3 would be expected.

She has subacute thyroiditis
She has subacute thyroiditis is incorrect. Subacute thyroiditis results in elevated T 3 and T 4 and suppression of TSH due to acute release of thyoid hormone. Hypothyroidism A previously fit 30-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of weight loss, tiredness, and nausea. He has no past medical history of note. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 78 beats/min and regular. There is a postural blood pressure drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Investigations:

She has sick euthyroid syndrome
She has sick euthyroid syndrome is incorrect. This is associated with low levels of T 3 in the presence of significant intercurrent illness.

stem: Which of the following would be the most useful diagnostic investigation?
explanation:
Short Synacthen®test
The clues here include the nausea, tiredness, weight loss over the past few months, coupled with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, and the postural hypotension. These features are all strong pointers towards a diagnosis of Addison’s disease, and a short Synacthen test, where a rise in cortisol indicating normal adrenal function rules out the diagnosis.

Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody titre
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody titre (anti-TPO) is incorrect. Although the TSH is mildly elevated, this is commonly seen in patients with adrenal crisis due to Addison’s disease, the more likely diagnosis here.

Insulin tolerance test
Insulin tolerance test is incorrect. Insulin tolerance testing is considered for evaluation of growth hormone deficiency. In the situation of adrenal insufficiency, it may also be a particularly dangerous investigation.

Free thyroxine concentration
Free thyroxine concentration is incorrect. Hypothyroidism alone wouldn’t produce the abnormal U&E seen here. In patients with adrenal insufficiency, Free T4 levels are low to normal, however, thyroid stimulating hormone levels may elevated. This usually resolves with steroid replacement

Thyroid-releasing hormone test
Thyroid-releasing hormone test (TRH) is incorrect. TRH testing is used to differentiate between thyroid hormone resistance and a TSH-oma, which is relevant here given the abnormal U&E pointing towards adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal Insufficiency A 55-year-old-woman presents with the clinical features of Cushing syndrome. She is on no medication. The results of routine biochemical investigations are normal. Her 0900-hours cortisol concentration is 800 nmol/l (normal 150-650) and ACTH 80 ng/ml (normal <50). Following a high dose dexamethasone the previous evening, a repeat 0900-hours cortisol concentration is 380 nmol/l.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with hypertension that his GP is finding difficult to manage. There are a number of metabolic abnormalities found on investigation and he is concerned about the possibility of Conn syndrome. The blood picture is one of metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia and low renin and high aldosterone levels. What diagnosis fits with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Gordon syndrome
Also known as pseudohypoaldosteronism, this is a condition that mimics hypoaldosteronism. The condition is due to a failure of response to aldosterone, and levels of aldosterone are actually elevated due to a lack of feedback inhibition. This syndrome is characterised by short stature, intellectual impairment, dental abnormalities, muscle weakness, severe hypertension by the third decade of life, low fractional excretion of sodium, normal renal function, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and low renin and elevated aldosterone levels. Hyperkalaemia, another hallmark of this syndrome, may be a function of diminished sodium delivery to the cortical collecting tubules.

Bartter syndrome
Bartter syndrome is incorrect. Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive hypokalaemic salt-wasting tubulopathy. Clinically, Bartter demonstrates almost the opposite biochemistry, with low potassium and high renin and aldosterone. Management is supportive and aimed at correcting, or minimising, electrolyte disturbances and extracellular volume depletion.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. Addison’s disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, is characterised by inadequate production of cortisol and aldosterone resulting in adrenal insufficiency. Symptoms are insidious, except in the case of adrenal crisis, and include abdominal pain and gastrointestinal abnormalities, weakness, weight loss and hypotension, not hypertension, as here.

Conn syndrome
Conn syndrome is incorrect. Conn syndrome, or primary hyperaldosteronism, is due to the excess production of aldosterone from the adrenal glands. This results in low renin levels, hypertension, and hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia, as here. Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System

Gitelman syndrome
Gitelman syndrome is incorrect. Gitelman syndrome isan autosomal recessive hypokalaemic salt-wasting tubulopathy. This is characterised by hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypocalciuria, and hypomagnesaemia. Management is supportive and aimed at correcting, or minimising, electrolyte disturbances and extracellular volume depletion.

stem: You see a 71-year-old female resident of a nursing home. Her complaints include a poor appetite, weight loss, cramps and weakness. She was diagnosed with Crohn's disease 10 years ago but is not taking any medications. Five months ago she had a mammogram and flexible sigmoidoscopy, both of which were normal. Because her examination was normal, she was given a 1-month return appointment and sent for blood tests. At the end of the day, your lab calls urgently to report a value of calcium of 1.4 mmol/l (normal range 2.2–2.6 mmol/l) with an inorganic phosphate of 0.58 mmol/l (0.8–1.5 mmol/l). She has a creatinine of 80 µmol/l (60– 110 µmol/l), the albumin is 35 g/l (37–49 g/l) and the alkaline phosphatase is 250 U/l (42–98 U/l). Which of the following diagnoses is most compatible with these results?
explanation:
Vitamin D deficiency
In vitamin D deficiency, decreased intestinal absorption of calcium leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism, which increases renal tubular loss of phosphate. Vitamin D deficiency can result from inadequate dietary intake, lack of sun exposure and malabsorption (in this case due to the long-standing Crohn’s disease).

Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. In hypoparathyroidism, there is reduced mobilisation of calcium from bone, reduced renal reabsorption of calcium (along with decreased phosphaturia) and reduced formation of 1,25hydroxy-vitamin D, resulting in reduced intestinal absorption of calcium. Consequently, the hypocalcaemia is accompanied by hyperphosphataemia. Hypoparathyroidism can be congenital or acquired, (eg post-thyroid surgery).

Hypomagnesaemia
Hypomagnesaemia is incorrect. Hypomagnesaemia causes deficient secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) and consequent functional hypoparathyroidism.

Kidney disease
Kidney disease is incorrect. Kidney disease impairs hydroxylation of 25-hydroxy-vitamin D, which results in the malabsorption of calcium. The body compensates by increased secretion of PTH, leading to increased mobilisation of calcium from bone. Kidney disease is characterised by an abnormal serum creatinine, whereas renal dysfunction is not the critical pathogenetic feature of the other forms of hypocalcaemia. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaDietary calcium deficiency
Dietary calcium deficiency is incorrect. Given she is a nursing home resident, dietary calcium deficiency is unlikely as her meals will be provided to her. Malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D is much more likely.

stem: A 31-year-old lady was recently diagnosed with an insulinoma. She tells you that her mother had a perforated duodenal ulcer at a young age, from ‘too much acid’, and her maternal aunt has a pituitary tumour. Which other features would you expect to find in this hereditary syndrome?
explanation:
Parathyroid hyperplasia
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common feature of MEN1, with 90% penetrance by age 65 in patients who have a mutation in the Menin gene. The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN1 is parathyroid hyperplasia rather than a parathyroid adenoma.

Hirschprung’s disease (HSCR)
Hirschprung’s disease (HSCR) is incorrect. HSCR, or aganglionic megacolon, occurs due to the congenital absence of parasympathetic neuronal ganglia in a segment of the hindgut, resulting in malfunction of the affected segment. There is an association between Hirschprung’s and MEN2.

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. Phaeocromocytoma occurs as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, due to an activating mutation in the RET gene. Patients with this mutation can develop bilateral phaeochromocytoma.

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect. Medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs as part of MEN2 syndrome caused by mutations in the RET gene. Other manifestations of this syndrome include primary hyperparathyroidism and phaeochromocytoma. The precursor to medullary thyroid carcinoma is hyperplasia of the thyroid c-cells. Phaeochromocytoma

Mucosal neuromas
Mucosal neuromas is incorrect. This is a dermatological manifestation unique to MEN2B, caused by a mutation affecting specific codons of the RET gene. Mucosal neuromas are the most consistent and distinctive feature, appearing in 100% of patients, and are numerous yellowish-white, sessile, painless nodules on the lips or tongue. MEN2B is also associated with a more aggressive phenotype than MEN2A and an earlier presentation with medullary thyroid carcinoma.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents for assessment at the fertility clinic; she has been unable to conceive for 18 months despite regular intercourse. She had menarche aged 16 and has always had irregular periods. On clinical examination she has a BMI of 32 kg/m2 and hirsutism; thyroid function tests are normal. Which of the following fits best with her diagnosis?
options: Luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels are likely to be approximately the same
Sex hormone-binding globulin is frequently low in this condition
Fertility is usually unaffected by this condition
Measured dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) will be normal or low
explanation:
Sex hormone-binding globulin is frequently low in this condition
Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is a protein that binds to both testosterone and oestradiol; it is reduced in insulin resistance, which is common in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Many women with PCOS have a high-normal or even a normal total testosterone, but a low SHBG because they have insulin resistance. Its amount can vary widely in patients, and if the SHBG is either low or high, the amount of active (bioavailable) testosterone can vary widely.

Luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels are likely to be approximately the same
Luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone levels are likely to be approximately the same is incorrect. PCOS is associated with an elevated LH:FSH ratio – usually to more than 3 : 1 – serum LH is raised, with that of FSH relatively lower than in a normal menstrual cycle.

Androstenedione level is normal
Androstenedione level is normal is incorrect. It is an androgen that will be elevated in PCOS.

Fertility is usually unaffected by this condition
Fertility is usually unaffected by this condition is incorrect. It is associated with anovulatory infertility. Polycystic ovarian syndrome This woman has PCOS, the prevalence of which is estimated to range from 8% to 22% of women. Oligo/amenorrhoea is present in 70%, hirsutism in 60%, obesity in 35% and infertility in 30%. Laboratory features Luteinising hormone (LH) is usually markedly raised, as is the ratio of LH to follicle-stimulating hormone (LH:FSH). Sex hormone-binding globulin is low in 50%, due primarily to hyperinsulinaemia. Testosterone and DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) levels are also usually raised. Up to 40% of women with PCOS have impaired glucose tolerance, and up to 10% develop frank Type 2 diabetes mellitus; the insulin-resistant state is also associated with dyslipidemia. Management Management is usually with weight loss and lifestyle advice. Metformin is a useful treatment for insulin resistance and can help to restore fertility, although clomiphene might also be required for ovulation induction. Creams and laser electrolysis might have a useful role to play if the primary complaint is one of hirsutism; antiandrogens, such as in certain oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) and spironolactone, will also help hirsutism.\nMeasured dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) will be normal or low
Measured dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) will be normal or low is incorrect. It is an androgen that will be elevated in PCOS.

stem: Given the suspected diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
2 × 24 h urinary free cortisol
The diagnosis to be excluded here is Cushing syndrome. An ideal initial test is 2 × 24 h urinary free cortisol because it can be done as an outpatient and is non-invasive. The false-positive rate for the test 1%AIand Chatis with Tutorthe false-negative rate is 5–10%. Because the false-negative rate approaches 10%, however, it is never used alone as a screening test for Cushing syndrome and should be followed by an overnight dexamethasone suppression test if clinical suspicion is high. If both of these tests are normal, then Cushing syndrome can effectively be ruled out. Midnight salivary cortisol levels might be an additional useful test in some cases, to demonstrate the loss of circadian rhythm of cortisol secretion.

Aldosterone levels
Aldosterone level is incorrect. An aldosterone level is measured along with a renin level in patients with suspected Conn syndrome, or hyperaldosteronism. This is caused by autonomous secretion of aldosterone from an adrenal adenoma and is characterised by an elevated aldosterone and suppressed renin. Patients with hyperaldosteronism can present with hypertension and hypokalemia, as in this case, but weight gain, striae and proximal myopathy are not a feature of Conn and raise the possibility of Cushing syndrome.

Insulin tolerance test
Insulin tolerance test is incorrect. An insulin tolerance test is used for the diagnosis of ACTH deficiency and growth hormone deficiency in suspected hypopituitarism, and therefore would provide no information about suspected autonomous cortisol production, which is likely in this case.

Short Synacthen ® test
Short Synacthen ® test is incorrect. A short Synacthen ® test is the gold standard for the diagnoses of cortisol deficiency or adrenal failure. It involves a basal cortisol measurement followed by an intramuscular injection of Synacthen ®. Synacthen ® acts to stimulate cortisol production, and a repeat cortisol level of <500 nmol/l postSynacthen ® test is indicative of cortisol deficiency. As the suspicion here is of excess cortisol, this answer is not correct.

High-dose dexamethasone suppression test
High-dose dexamethasone suppression test is incorrect. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent Cushing due to a pituitary adenoma from ectopic ACTH production from an occult malignant tumour (most commonly small cell lung cancer). Failure to suppress cortisol to <50 nmol/l on a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test suggests an ectopic source of ACTH. This test is not used first line in suspected Cushing syndrome and therefore is not the correct answer.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to her GP with a history of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. She is keen to become pregnant and has been trying to conceive for nine months, without success. She is of normal weight and has no other constitutional symptoms. Her thyroid function shows a TSH of 2.6 mIU/l and a free T 4 of 16.7 pmol/l. Her BMI is 23 and she has no evidence of hirsutism or acne. Which of the following is most likely to be the reason for her symptoms?
options: Drug treatment she is on for asthma
explanation:
Pituitary microadenoma
This woman’s symptoms are consistent with hyperprolactinaemia. Raised prolactin has many causes, including a microadenoma or macroadenoma. This patient’s amenorrhea and anovulation are likely to be reversed with treatment using dopamine agonists; dopamine agonists such as cabergoline will normalise prolactin levels within a short period in most patients. A macroadenoma more commonly presents with symptoms due to hypopituitarism, compressive effects due to optic chiasm compression, or cavernous sinus invasion.

Drug treatment she is on for asthma
Drug treatment she is on for asthma is incorrect. Steroid drug treatment, either inhaled or oral, can cause adrenal failure due to prolonged exogenous steroid use. This can lead to symptoms of adrenal insufficiency such as fatigue, weight loss and postural hypotension. These symptoms are not evident in this case.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. Hypothyroidism can cause a rise in prolactin usually less than 1000 mIU/L. This is caused by an increase in thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus in response to a low free T 4. This stimulation in TRH in turn stimulates prolactin, leading to a mild increase in prolactin. However in Tutor this case the TSH and free T 4 are normal.

Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is incorrect. Hyperthyroidism can cause oligomennorrhea or amenorrhea, which resolve with treatment. However, in this case the thyroid function is normal and the patient has no other symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.

PCOS
PCOS is incorrect. Polycystic ovarian syndrome can cause a mild elevation in prolactin due to the stimulation of GnRH in patients with PCOS. Stimulation of GnRH in PCOS is believed to be caused by relative oestrogen deficiency in PCOS. GnRH can, in turn, stimulate prolactin but levels are rarely greater than 1000 mIU/l. PCOS is usually associated with other clinical features such as acne, hirsutism and raised BMI, and this clinical phenotype is not evident in this case.

stem: A 54-year-old man with long-standing Type 2 diabetes presents for review. He has a history of hypertension and smoking; his recent HbA1c results have averaged 74 mmol/mol (8.9%). He wore deck shoes without socks on a recent holiday in Spain and one day his wife noticed a large ulcer over the big toe on his left foot. On examination there is obvious loss of sensation – probing of the depth of the ulcer elicits no pain; his foot appears warm, with a bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, and there is some toe clawing. What is the likely underlying aetiology of his ulcer?
explanation:
Neuropathic ulceration
The combination of a painless ulcer in a pressure area in someone with poorly controlled diabetes and neuropathy is suggestive of a neuropathic ulcer.

Simple trauma
Simple trauma is incorrect. He has signs of ulceration.

Arterial ulcer
Arterial ulcer is incorrect. These are usually painful and not located in pressure areas, such as in this case; there is also no history of claudication or signs of ischaemia.

Vasculitis
Vasculitis is incorrect. This is not a common cause of ulcers.

Charcot arthropathy
Charcot arthropathy is incorrect. This is the term given to bony destruction in a patient with diabetes and neuropathy; it is not associated with skin ulceration. The diabetic foot (American Diabetes Association) The lifetime risk of a person with diabetes developing a foot ulcer may be as high as 25%, whereas the annual incidence of foot ulcers is 2%. Up to 50% of older patients with Type 2 diabetes have one or more risk factors for foot ulceration. A number of component causes, most importantly peripheral neuropathy, interact to complete the causal pathway to foot ulceration: the most common triad of causes that interact and ultimately result in ulceration has been identified as neuropathy, deformity and trauma. Foot Care Recommendations For all patients with diabetes, perform an annual comprehensive foot examination to identify risk factors predictive of ulcers and amputations. The foot examination should include inspection and assessment of foot pulses. Patients with insensate feet, foot deformities and ulcers should have their feet examined at every visit. Provide general foot self-care education to all patients with diabetes. A multidisciplinary approach is recommended for individuals with foot ulcers and high-risk feet (eg dialysis patients and those with Charcot foot, prior ulcers or amputation). Refer patients who smoke, have a loss of protective sensation (LOPS), structural abnormalities or a history of prior lower-extremity complications to foot-care specialists for ongoing preventive care and lifelong Initial screening for peripheral arterial disease (PAD) should include a history for claudication and an assessment of the pedal pulses. Refer patients with significant claudication or a positive ankle -brachial pressure index (ABPI) for further vascular assessment and consider exercise, medications and surgical options. Amputation and foot ulceration, which are consequences of diabetic neuropathy and/or PAD, are common and represent major causes of morbidity and disability in people with diabetes. Loss of 10 g monofilament and reduced vibration perceptions predict foot ulcers. Early recognition and management of risk factors can prevent or delay adverse outcomes.

stem: A 42-year-old man presented with headache and blurred vision for a few weeks. Investigation showed serum prolactin of 21 500 mU/L. On further questioning he admitted loss of interest in sexual intercourse over the past few months and general feelings of lethargy. Computerised tomography (CT) brain scan showed a large pituitary mass encroaching on the optic chiasm with evidence of midline shift. What is the next appropriate treatment?
options: Dopamine agonist and review in 4 weeks with respect to proceeding to surgery
explanation:
Dopamine agonist and review in 4 weeks with respect to proceeding to surgery
It is likely that this man has a macroprolactinoma, characterised by the markedly raised prolactin level and the symptoms of tiredness and lack of sexual interest. Symptoms of macroprolactinoma include galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea in women, and hypogonadism and impotence in men. Macroprolactinomas may also be associated with headaches, visual field defects and generalised hypopituitarism. Some debate exists as to whether there is value in treatment with dopamine-agonist therapy in this case or if early progression to surgery is the better option. Case series suggest that even in cases of macroprolactinoma, up to 80% of tumours see some response to dopamine agonists.

Adenomectomy
Adenomectomy is incorrect. In this case, a trial of dopamine agonist therapy would be indicated first before more invasive measures.

Hypophysectomy
Hypophysectomy is incorrect. In this case, a trial of dopamine agonist therapy would be indicated first before more invasive measures.

Pituitary irradiation
Pituitary irradiation is incorrect. In this case, a trial of dopamine agonist therapy would be indicated first before more invasive measures. Prolactinoma A 54-year-old man with long-standing Type 2 diabetes presents for review. He has a history of hypertension and smoking; his recent HbA1c results have averaged 74 mmol/mol (8.9%). He wore deck shoes without socks on a recent holiday in Spain and one day his wife noticed a large ulcer over the big toe on his left foot. On examination there is obvious loss of sensation – probing of the depth of the ulcer elicits no pain; his foot appears warm, with a bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, and there is some toe clawing. What is the likely underlying aetiology of his ulcer?

Somatostatin
Somatostatin is incorrect. Synthetic analogues of somatostatin (growth hormone-inhibiting hormone) are used in the treatment of carcinoid syndrome and acromegaly, but not prolactinoma.

stem: A 28-year-old machinist presents to her GP with weight loss despite a good appetite, palpitations and excess sweating. The GP suspects thyrotoxicosis and confirms this by finding a free T 4 of 58 pmol/l (10–22 pmol/l) with an undetectable thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level. On examination she has a normal-sized thyroid gland with a suggestion of bulkiness on the right-hand side. A technetium uptake scan reveals a single ‘hot’ nodule in the right lobe of the thyroid with suppression of activity elsewhere. Antibody testing reveals normal thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and thyroid-stimulating antibody (TRAB) antibody levels. Which of the following clinical features would she be most likely to have?
explanation:
Lid retraction and lid lag
Lid retraction and lag are signs of sympathetic overactivity, and occur in any thyrotoxic state (thyroxine potentiates the action of catecholamines). This patient has negative antibodies and signs of an autonomous thyrotoxic nodule on isotope scanning, and therefore should not have any of the clinical features associated with autoimmune Graves’ disease.

Corneal ulceration
Corneal ulceration is incorrect. Corneal ulceration can develop in severe Graves’ dysthyroid eye disease caused by exopthalmus, ocular muscle inflammation and inability to completely shut the eyelid, leading to prolonged corneal exposure to light and corneal ulceration. This patient has no features of autoimmune Graves’ thyroid Tutor disease, and therefore Graves’ opthalmopathy would not be a feature of this patient’s presentation.

Periorbital oedema
Periorbital oedema is incorrect. Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSH-R) is an antigen found in orbital fat and connective tissue, and is a target for autoimmune assault. In patients with Graves’ disease and elevated TRAB antibodies, Graves’ opthalmopathy can develop which includes periorbital inflammation leading to erythema and oedema.

Pretibial myxoedema
Pretibial myxoedema is incorrect. This is also known as Graves’ dermopathy, and is usually always preceded by Graves’ opthalmopathy. It characteristically affects the shins.

Unilateral exophthalmos
Unilateral exophthalmos is incorrect. This is caused by inflammation of the extraocular eye muscles in Graves’ opthalmopathy and is usually bilateral, but can be asymmetrical. Again, as this patient has no evidence of Graves’ disease, this is not the correct answer. Thyrotoxicosis A 42-year-old man with long-standing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection presents for review. He has been taking antiretroviral therapy for 5 years and has been relatively free of associated disease. You notice on examination that he appears to have lost subcutaneous fat on his arms, legs and face, and has increased deposition of fat around his abdomen. His lipids are also abnormal, with a raised triglyceride level and a low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol level.

stem: Following a head injury, a 24-year-old patient develops polyuria and polydipsia and is suspected of having cranial diabetes insipidus. He undergoes a water deprivation test. Which one of the following responses would be diagnostic of cranial diabetes insipidus?
options: A rise in plasma osmolality to 302 mosmol/kg during water deprivation
Failure to concentrate the urine during water deprivation, but achievement of urine osmolality of 720
Failure to concentrate the urine either with water deprivation or following the administration of
Failure to concentrate the urine with a plasma osmolality of 280 mosmol/kg at the end of the period
Weight loss of 2% during the investigation
explanation:
Failure to concentrate the urine during water deprivation, but achievement of urine osmolality of 720
Failure to concentrate the urine during water deprivation, but achievement of urine osmolality of 720 mosmol/kg following the administration of desmopressin The effect of desmopressin here confirms that the kidneys are still responsive to ADH, and the failure to concentrate urine during the deprivation test indicates diabetes insipidus.

A rise in plasma osmolality to 302 mosmol/kg during water deprivation
A rise in plasma osmolality to 302 mosmol/kg during water deprivation is incorrect. The rise in plasma osmolality must be paired with an inappropriately dilute urine (> 50%) following desmopressin to diagnose cranial diabetes insipidus. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the rise in urine osmolality is less than 45% following desmopressin.

Failure to concentrate the urine either with water deprivation or following the administration of
Failure to concentrate the urine either with water deprivation or following the administration of desmopressin Failure to concentrate the urine either with water deprivation or following the administration of desmopressin is incorrect. Failure to concentrate urine after water deprivation or desmopressin injection is suggestive ofTutor nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Failure to concentrate the urine with a plasma osmolality of 280 mosmol/kg at the end of the period
Failure to concentrate the urine with a plasma osmolality of 280 mosmol/kg at the end of the period of water deprivation Failure to concentrate the urine with a plasma osmolality of 280 mosmol/kg at the end of the period of water deprivation is incorrect. Osmolality will rise above the normal range.

Weight loss of 2% during the investigation
Weight loss of 2% during the investigation is incorrect. Weight loss >3% weight is a positive test, and it is recommended to stop the test if this occurs.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with a 10-year history of well-controlled Type 1 diabetes, treated with an insulin pump, presents for her routine diabetes appointment. She has been talking to a patient in the waiting room who is on dialysis for diabetic nephropathy, and she has a number of questions regarding her risk of renal disease. Which of the following statements best describes renal disease in patients with Type 1 diabetes?
options: Microalbuminuria usually occurs within 2 years of the diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes
Diabetes is the number one cause of end-stage renal disease in Europe and the US
After the serum creatinine level reaches 200 µmol/l, a fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 0.5
Chronic kidney disease usually occurs within 5 years of the onset of albuminuria
People with overt diabetic nephropathy have a 10 times higher mortality rate than age- and sexmatched controls
explanation:
Diabetes is the number one cause of end-stage renal disease in Europe and the US
Over 40% of people entering dialysis in the US/UK has diabetic nephropathy.

Microalbuminuria usually occurs within 2 years of the diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes
Microalbuminuria usually occurs within 2 years of the diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes is incorrect. Microalbuminuria typically occurs after 5 years in Type 1 diabetes.

After the serum creatinine level reaches 200 µmol/l, a fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 0.5
After the serum creatinine level reaches 200 µmol/l, a fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 0.5 ml/minute per month might be expected After the serum creatinine level reaches 200 µmol/l, a fall in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 0.5 ml/minute per month might be expected is incorrect. Data from the MDRD Study during an average 2-year follow-up show that the average rate of decline in GFR was approximately 4 mL/min/year and was not related to the baseline level of GFR or creatinine.

Chronic kidney disease usually occurs within 5 years of the onset of albuminuria
Chronic kidney disease usually occurs within 5 years of the onset of albuminuria is incorrect. Microalbuminuria typically occurs after 5 years; however, overt nephropathy, with urinary protein excretion higher than 300 mg/day, often develops after 10–15 years, and chronic kidney disease develops within 10 years of developing overt nephropathy. Nephropathy in Diabetes Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is typically defined by macroalbuminuria (urinary albumin excretion of more than 300 mg in a 24 hour collection) or macroalbuminuria plus abnormal renal function (abnormal serum creatinine, calculated creatinine clearance or glomerular filtration rate). Diabetes has become the primary cause of chronic kidney disease in the Western world. Useful external websites American Diabetes Association. 2004. Nephropathy in diabetes. Diabetes Care, 27, Suppl. 1, S79–S83. ( Diabetes - Type I

People with overt diabetic nephropathy have a 10 times higher mortality rate than age- and sexmatched controls
People with overt diabetic nephropathy have a 10 times higher mortality rate than age and sex-matched controls is incorrect. The combination of diabetes and nephropathy increases cardiovascular disease risk by 20– 40-fold.

stem: A 16-year-old adolescent is seen in the Endocrinology Clinic because he feels he is failing to enter puberty like his peers. On examination, pubic hair growth is minimal; facial hair growth is absent, and the external genitalia are small. Both testes are normal in size and located in the scrotum. Which of the following hormones most drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics?
explanation:
Dihydrotestosterone
The hormone has a two- to threefold higher level of affinity for the androgen receptor, and a fivefold higher propensity to activate the androgen receptor, compared to testosterone. In adults, it has a primary role in driving the growth of hair associated with secondary sexual characteristics. Dihydrotestosterone is also important in the development and maintenance of the prostate gland and seminal vesicles.

Testosterone
Testosterone is incorrect. Testosterone is the primary sex hormone in men and plays an important role in the development of male genitalia, development of the prostate and maintenance of spermatogenesis. Testosterone is also involved in mood and behaviour. Testosterone does contribute to the development of muscle and bone mass, as well as body hair growth.

Androstenedione
Androstenedione is incorrect. Androstenedione is a weak androgen, compared to dihydrotestosterone or testosterone itself, and therefore does not play a primary role in the development of secondary sexual characteristics. Androstenedione is a precursor to testosterone and some oestrogens such as estrone. It has some oestrogenic activity. There is a rise in androstenedione level produced during adrenarche.

Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)
Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) is incorrect. DHEA is produced by the adrenals and primarily acts as an intermediate for the production of other steroid hormones. DHEA is produced in the zona reticularis of the adrenal glands. DHEA is a weak oestrogen and has effects on the central nervous system, with receptor modulation of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors.

Androsterone
Androsterone is incorrect. Like androstenedione, androsterone is a weak androgen and also acts as an intermediate for conversion into other sex steroid hormones. It is a metabolite of testosterone and has effects on the central nervous system, as well as anticonvulsant effects. Androsterone is found in the urine and sebaceous glands.

stem: A 23-year-old with XY genotype but complete androgen insensitivity syndrome comes to the clinic for review. Which of the following is the most likely phenotype of this patient?
options: Normal pattern of secondary sexual hair, female genitalia but with clitoromegaly
Male genitalia with small testes and scanty secondary sexual hair
Normal female genitalia with absence of secondary sexual hair
Normal female genitalia with short stature
explanation:
Normal female genitalia with absence of secondary sexual hair
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome is associated with female external genitalia and cryptorchidism, where testes may often present as inguinal hernias when these individuals are infants.

Normal pattern of secondary sexual hair, female genitalia but with clitoromegaly
Normal pattern of secondary sexual hair, female genitalia but with clitoromegaly is incorrect. Partial androgen insensitivity may lead to clitoromegaly, as may 21-hydroxylase deficiency in genetic females.

Male genitalia with small testes and scanty secondary sexual hair
Male genitalia with small testes and scanty secondary sexual hair is incorrect. Male genitalia with small testes and scanty secondary sexual hair may indicate Klinefelter’s syndrome.

Normal male genitalia
Normal male genitalia is incorrect. Complete androgen insensitivity is associated with female, not male, genitalia.

Normal female genitalia with short stature
Normal female genitalia with short stature is incorrect. Normal female external genitalia with short stature may be an indication of possible Turner’s (XO genotype).

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the Reproductive Endocrinology Clinic with a history of being unable to conceive after two years of using no contraception. It is thought that she might have polycystic ovarian syndrome. Which one of the following is most likely to be associated with this condition?
options: Low sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and raised free androgen index
explanation:
Low sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and raised free androgen index
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrinopathy in women of reproductive age. Joint European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology and American Society of Reproductive Medicine consensus on the diagnostic criteria (Rotterdam criteria) require at least 2 out of 3 of the following: hyperandrogenism (clinical and biochemical), oligo-/amenorrhoea, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound and exclusion of other disorders.

A 28-day menstrual cycle
A 28-day menstrual cycle is incorrect. Almost all patients with PCOS have irregular menstrual periods.

Hirsutism and virilisation
Hirsutism and virilisation is incorrect. Hirsutism occurs in PCOS as a result of hyperandrogenaemia. However, virilisation (deepening of voice, male pattern baldness, cliteromegaly, increased muscle bulk) suggests high androgen levels. Causes other than PCOS, e.g. congenital adrenal hyperplasia or androgen-producing tumours, should be excluded.

Low levels of circulating insulin
Low levels of circulating insulin is incorrect. PCOS is characterised by increased insulin resistance and hyperinsulinaemia.

Normal BMI (body mass index)
Normal BMI (body mass index) is incorrect. Obesity, insulin resistance and hyperinsulinaemia are involved in the pathogenesis of PCOS.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of steroid-treated sarcoidosis presents with extreme thirst and nocturia five times per night.
