Her serum calcium concentration is 2.3 mmol/l, glucose is 4.6 mmol/l and potassium is 3.5 mmol/l. After an overnight fast including water restriction, her serum Na + is 149 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Cranial diabetes insipidus
Cranial diabetes insipidus is correct and psychogenic polydipsia is incorrect – The differential diagnosis of polyuria and polydipsia, in the absence of hyperglycaemia, lies between diabetes insipidus (DI) and psychogenic polydipsia (compulsive water drinking). In diabetes insipidus, massive water loss drives thirst by pushing up the tonicity (osmolality) of serum and stimulating the antidiuretic hormone (ADH)/thirst axis (the hormonal side of which may be unresponsive). In psychogenic polydipsia, thirst drives polyuria; the tonicity of serum tends to be pushed downwards while there is free access to water. Sarcoidosis is one of the principal causes of central (cranial) diabetes insipidus, with destruction of the posterior pituitary or hypothalamic tracts. Head injury, autoimmune hypophysitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Langerhans’ cell histiocytosis (in up to 40% of cases) are other important causes. Diagnosis is confirmed using the water deprivation test: if water is restricted, either using a formal water deprivation test or an overnight fast, urine output drops in response to appropriate rises in plasma ADH. This means that if the ADH axis is intact and access to water is restricted, the plasma osmolality does not rise above 295 mosmol/kg – this roughly equates to a serum Na + concentration of 145 mmol/l. If the plasma osmolality rises above 295 mosmol/kg with water restriction, or the serum Na+ concentration rises above 145 mmol/l, this implies that the ADH/thirst axis is damaged and that compulsive water drinking cannot explain the symptoms.

Chronic cystitis
Chronic cystitis is incorrect. The more common renal manifestations of sarcoidosis include nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis and interstitial nephritis rather than chronic cystitis, unless as a secondary complication.

Hypokalaemia-induced polyuria
Hypokalaemia-induced polyuria is incorrect – The patient’s serum potassium is insufficiently low to produce this effect. Hypokalaemia produces polyuria only when there is insufficient potassium in the renal tubules to allow the Na-K-Cl cotransporter pumps to resorb sodium from the tubular lumen and thereby provoke diuresis.

Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency
Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency is incorrect – The response to an overnight water deprivation test is sufficiently diagnostic for DI to rule out adrenal insufficiency as the most likely answer.

Psychogenic polydipsia
Cranial diabetes insipidus is correct and psychogenic polydipsia is incorrect – The differential diagnosis of polyuria and polydipsia, in the absence of hyperglycaemia, lies between diabetes insipidus (DI) and psychogenic polydipsia (compulsive water drinking). In diabetes insipidus, massive water loss drives thirst by pushing up the tonicity (osmolality) of serum and stimulating the antidiuretic hormone (ADH)/thirst axis (the hormonal side of which may be unresponsive). In psychogenic polydipsia, thirst drives polyuria; the tonicity of serum tends to be pushed downwards while there is free access to water. Sarcoidosis is one of the principal causes of central (cranial) diabetes insipidus, with destruction of the posterior pituitary or hypothalamic tracts. Head injury, autoimmune hypophysitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Langerhans’ cell histiocytosis (in up to 40% of cases) are other important causes. Diagnosis is confirmed using the water deprivation test: if water is restricted, either using a formal water deprivation test or an overnight fast, urine output drops in response to appropriate rises in plasma ADH. This means that if the ADH axis is intact and access to water is restricted, the plasma osmolality does not rise above 295 mosmol/kg – this roughly equates to a serum Na+ concentration of 145 mmol/l. If the plasma osmolality rises above 295 mosmol/kg with water restriction, or the serum Na + concentration rises above 145 mmol/l, this implies that the ADH/thirst axis is damaged and that compulsive water drinking cannot explain the symptoms. Diabetes Insipidus A 55-year-old chronic smoker presents with polyuria, polydipsia and altered sensation for the past two days. He is known to be suffering from squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung. On examination he is lethargic and confused. His blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg, pulse is 85 beats/min and regular. Electrocardiography shows a narrowed QT interval.

stem: A 60-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. He has noted an increase in his shoe size and his wedding ring no longer fits him. He has noted he has been sweating a lot and his wife complains that he is snoring more at night. He also has impaired fasting glucose of 6.8 mmol/l. His BP is 155/90 mmHg and his BMI is 30 kg/m 2. Which of the tests below is most useful for confirming the underlying diagnosis?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement
explanation:
Oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement
The soft tissue swelling, impaired glucose tolerance and raised blood pressure are indicative of acromegaly. A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is the gold standard test for diagnosing acromegaly. In normal people, the growth hormone (GH) level is suppressed during the test, but in patients with acromegaly, it is not. This is because insulin and GH are antagonistic hormones.

Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 level
Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is an excellent screening test for the diagnosis of acromegaly. Random levels of IGF-1 are likely to be raised, but as there is a wide range of normal, a single measurement is not sufficient to make the diagnosis. A dynamic test (OGTT) is required.

Skull X-ray
A skull X-ray will most likely be abnormal in acromegaly, as frontal bossing occurs through the action of IGF-1 on cell growth. However, it cannot confirm acromegaly.

Random growth hormone level
Growth hormone (GH) is a pulsatile hormone, so a random GH level is not a good screening tool for the diagnosis of acromegaly. IGF-1 has improved sensitivity as a screening tool, with OGTT as a confirmatory test. Acromegaly

MRI of the pituitary fossa
Pituitary tumours in acromegaly are usually macroadenomas. As other secretory and non-secretory tumours of the pituitary can also be macroadenomas, these tests would not confirm that the patient had acromegaly, but they would be used in the diagnostic workup.

stem: A 55-year-old chronic smoker presents with polyuria, polydipsia and altered sensation for the past two days. He is known to be suffering from squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung. On examination he is lethargic and confused. His blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg, pulse is 85 beats/min and regular. Electrocardiography shows a narrowed QT interval. What is the most probable metabolic abnormality?
explanation:
Hypercalcaemia
Paraneoplastic syndromes in bronchogenic carcinoma can cause several electrolyte abnormalities. The features in this case are suggestive of hypercalcaemia. As well as shortening of the QT, J waves with notching of the QRS are also seen. Hypercalcaemia occurs as a result of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) production.

Hypernatraemia
Hypernatraemia is incorrect. No significant changes on the ECG are seen in response to hypernatraemia.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is incorrect. Hypokalaemia is associated with PR prolongation, T wave flattening and inversion, and ST depression.

Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is incorrect. Like hypernatraemia, hyponatraemia has no significant impact on the ECG. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaHyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia is incorrect. Hyperkalaemia is associated with peaked T waves and progressive flattening of P waves with widening of the PR segment.

stem: You review a 58-year-old patient with type 1 diabetes that has been given a 5 unit transfusion of blood in response to an upper GI bleed some 2 weeks earlier. You examine his home blood glucose monitoring diary and see that he appears to have a problem with hypoglycaemia in the late afternoon, but is running high on his morning fasting sugars. You want to refer to an HbA1c to see what is happening over time. How long will you wait until you next check this patient's HbA1C level?
explanation:
3 months
This represents the time taken for HbA1c to equilibrate and is therefore the correct answer here.

2 weeks
2 weeks is incorrect. Red blood cells have a lifespan of approximately 120 days, and HbA1c is thought to take around 3 months to equilibrate. Any measurement after 2 weeks will significantly under-estimate glycaemic burden.

4 weeks
4 weeks is incorrect. Given that HbA1c takes 3 months to equilibrate, a measure at 4 weeks will significantly under-estimate HbA1c.

2 months
2 months is incorrect. It would be most appropriate to wait an interval of around 3 months before measuring haemoglobin A1C again. Measurement after 2 months may under-estimate true HbA1c by up to 30%. Diabetes - Type I

5 months
5 months is incorrect. Haemoglobin A1C is a measure of glucose control over the previous 3 months, related to the rate of red cell turnover. Waiting 5 months to test HbA1c risks unnecessary exposure to high blood glucose levels without intervention.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with weight loss and is found to be biochemically hyperthyroid. She is started on carbimazole but after 2 weeks describes progressive visual blurring. Her corrected visual acuities are 6/12 bilaterally and she has impairment of colour vision bilaterally. There is evidence of bilateral proptosis, pupillary reactions appear normal. What are her symptoms most likely to be due to?
explanation:
Optic nerve compression
This patient has thyroid eye disease. Swelling of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat predisposes the optic nerve to compression at the orbital apex. Optic nerve compression may occur in the absence of proptosis, and classically causes reduced vision with colour desaturation, disc oedema and a visual field defect with enlargement of the blind spot.

Adverse drug reaction
Adverse drug reaction is incorrect. There are no ophthalmic side-effects of carbimazole.

Embolic phenomena
Embolic phenomena is incorrect. Embolic phenomena would present with rapid stepwise deterioration and would be very unlikely to present with symmetrical impairment.

Infiltration of the optic nerve
Infiltration of the optic nerve is incorrect. The optic nerve itself is not infiltrated in thyroid eye disease.

Optic atrophy
Optic atrophy is incorrect, although optic atrophy may occur after a number of weeks of compression.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. She reports increased sweating and swelling of hands and feet to the point that she can no longer wear her wedding ring. She complains also that her sleep quality is poor and that her husband reports snoring and occasionally he reports that she stops breathing for a few seconds when sleeping. You suspect a new diagnosis of acromegaly and associated insulin resistance. In a patient with hyperglycaemia and suspected acromegaly, which of the following tests would confirm the diagnosis of acromegaly?
options: Insulin tolerance test (ITT) and GH levels
Glucose tolerance test (GTT) and GH levels
explanation:
Glucose tolerance test (GTT) and GH levels
The confirmatory test is the oral glucose tolerance test. In this test the rise in glucose caused by a 75 g oral glucose load, should suppress growth hormone secretion in the absence of autonomous GH production. The level of growth hormone should be < 20 mU/l and should decrease two hours after the glucose load. If the level is high and fails to suppress, then acromegaly is confirmed.

Random growth hormone (GH) level
An isolated random growth hormone (GH) level is inaccurate because levels vary with the time of day, so a random level cannot be interpreted with any accuracy.

Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) level
Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is incorrect. This is a good screening test because this reflects GH secretion in the previous 24 hours, but it does not confirm acromegaly. It is used to monitor patients with GH deficiency on replacement GH or to monitor patients at risk of hypopituitarism who may develop GH deficiency. However, it is only useful as a screening test and confirmatory dynamic testing is necessary using either an insulin tolerance test to diagnose growth hormone deficiency or a glucose tolerance test with GH measurements to diagnose acromegaly.

Urinary cortisol level
Two 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels is incorrect. These are one of the screening tests of choice in the diagnosis of suspected Cushing syndrome. The other screening tests include a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by a 0900 h cortisol measurement or two midnight salivary cortisol measurements. Urinary cortisol has no role in the diagnosis of suspected acromegaly. Diabetes - Type II

Insulin tolerance test (ITT) and GH levels
An insulin tolerance test (ITT) is incorrect. This is the gold standard dynamic test for the diagnosis of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and GH deficiency in patients with suspected hypopituitarism. An insulin tolerance test is contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures or epilepsy and in patients with ischaemic heart disease as it involves a weight-based dose of intravenous insulin to achieve a hypoglycaemia below 2.2 mol/l.

stem: You are drawing up guidelines for the management of oral blood glucose-lowering agents for a patient’s postmyocardial infarction (MI). Looking at a summary of the available evidence, which of the following pieces of advice would you give?
options: Pioglitazone should be started in patients post-MI
Metformin should be stopped in all patients post-MI
All patients should be transitioned to permanent insulin therapy
Metformin should be stopped in patients who have an unstable circulation post-MI
Sulphonylureas should be commenced in all patients
explanation:
Metformin should be stopped in patients who have an unstable circulation post-MI
Unstable circulation post MI, increases the risk of hypoperfusion and acute kidney injury. Hypoperfusion and acute kidney injury are risk factors for the development of lactic acidosis in patients on metformin, and thus should be avoided in these patients.

Pioglitazone should be started in patients post-MI
Pioglitazone should be started in patients post-MI is incorrect. Glitazones are generally not used in patients at risk of fluid retention because of the risk of heart failure, which includes some patients who have had a myocardial infarction.

Metformin should be stopped in all patients post-MI
Metformin should be stopped in all patients post-MI is incorrect. Metformin was originally ruled out in all patients who suffered an MI, but is continued by many clinicians now unless there is evidence of significant circulatory impairment or raised creatinine.

All patients should be transitioned to permanent insulin therapy
All patients should be transitioned to permanent insulin therapy is incorrect. The DIGAMI-2 study was generally disappointing with respect to demonstrating any benefits of insulin therapy, and for this reason permanent insulin therapy is no longer recommended post-MI if pre-MI glycaemic control was adequate.

Sulphonylureas should be commenced in all patients
Sulphonylureas should be commenced in all patients is incorrect. Sulphonylureas are insulin secretagogues and are associated with an increased risk of hypoglycaemia. Hypoglycaemia causes the release of counterregulatory hormones, including cortisol and catecholamines, and can exacerbate cardiac function in the setting of a recent MI. Therefore, sulphonylureas are usually avoided or used with caution in patients post-MI. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: You review a 51-year-old man on the cardiology ward. He is recovering from an inferior myocardial infarction and is about to be discharged. A fasting plasma glucose has confirmed the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and you elect to start metformin monotherapy. His creatinine on admission was 102 micromol/l and has remained stable throughout his hospital stay. In regards to metformin which of the following should you warn him about?
options: He should stop it if his creatinine rises above 110 micromol/l
He should stop it if angiography is planned
He should stop it if he gets symptoms of IBS after starting the medication
It increases the risk of myopathy in conjunction with statins
explanation:
He should stop it if angiography is planned
Metformin is now well recognised as increasing the risk of contrast nephropathy, and as such it should be stopped approximately 48 h before injection of contrast media is planned.

He should stop it if his creatinine rises above 110 micromol/l
He should stop it if his creatinine rises above 110 micromol/l is incorrect. According to the summary of product characteristics, metformin is not recommended when GFR falls below 60 ml/min although many clinicians continue to use it at a reduced dose until the GFR falls below 30; 60 ml/min GFR corresponds to a creatinine of approximately 135 micromol/l for an average man. As metformin is renally excreted, its accumulation can occur in association with impaired renal function and this increases the risk of lactic acidosis.

He should stop it if he gets symptoms of IBS after starting the medication
He should stop it if he gets symptoms of IBS after starting the medication is incorrect. GI symptoms are the most commonly tolerated side effect with metformin therapy. Patients can develop diarrhoea in the first week or two of treatment, which in most patients is self-limiting. There are subsets of patients who will have persistent GI side effects and who will be unable to tolerate metformin therapy.

It may cause hypoglycaemia
It may cause hypoglycaemia is incorrect. Metformin is a biguanide that acts to inhibit hepatic gluconeogenesis. One of the benefits of metformin therapy is that it is very seldom associated with hypoglycaemia. Diabetes - Type II You are drawing up guidelines for the management of oral blood glucose-lowering agents for a patient’s postmyocardial infarction (MI). Looking at a summary of the available evidence, which of the following pieces of advice would you give?

It increases the risk of myopathy in conjunction with statins
It increases the risk of myopathy in conjunction with statins is incorrect. Metformin does not interact with the cytochrome P450 hepatic enzyme and does not influence the risk of myopathy associated with statin therapy.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with primary hyperparathyroidism. It emerges that she has been treated previously for a prolactinoma. She tells you that her mother was affected by a similar condition some years earlier. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
The history of primary hyperparathyroidism and a pituitary tumour in this patient is highly suggestive of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1). This is an autosomal dominant disorder that is caused by mutations in the MEN1 gene on 11q13. The MEN1 gene encodes a tumour suppressor protein called menin. It is characterised by tumours of the parathyroid glands, pituitary and pancreatic islet cells. About 90% of patients develop parathyroid hyperplasia or adenoma. Pituitary tumours are seen in about 60% of patients and include prolactinomas, growth hormone-producing tumours and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-producing tumours. Between 50% and 75% of patients with MEN1 develop pancreatic islet cell tumours that include gastrinoma, insulinoma, glucagonoma and VIPoma.

Familial parathyroid hyperplasia
Familial parathyroid hyperplasia is incorrect, although the presence of a pituitary tumour is consistent with this as the underlying diagnosis.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is incorrect as this is associated with café au lait spots, axillary freckling and cutaneous neurofibromas.

Polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type 1
Polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type 1 is incorrect as this is associated with hypoparathyroidism, Addison’s disease, mucocutaneous candidiasis, Type 1 diabetes and premature ovarian failure. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia

von Hippel–Lindau syndrome
von Hippel–Lindau syndrome von Hippel-Lindau syndrome is incorrect as this leads to phaeochromocytoma, haemangioblastoma, and formation and increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.

stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman presents to her General Practitioner Antenatal Clinic for her 20-week review and is noted to have glycosuria. She is G2P1, with no significant previous medical history and no family history of note. A follow-up oral glucose tolerance test reveals a fasting glucose level of 6.6 mmol/l and a 2-hour level of 9.2 mmol/l. On examination, her blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg, heart rate is 65 bpm and regular and body mass index 25 kg/m 2. There is no concern for the fetus on the most recent ultrasound scan. Which of the following is the most appropriate next therapy for the patient?
options: Trial of exercise and diet control
explanation:
Trial of exercise and diet control
The patient has been diagnosed with gestational diabetes without complications (normal recent fetal scan). As her fasting blood glucose level is < 7 mmol/l, she should be trialled with 1–2 weeks of lifestyle, diet and exercise alterations. The patient should be referred to a dietician. If on review, there continues to be evidence of poor glycaemic control, the patient should first be offered metformin, off label.

Insulin
As per the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance, the patient should immediately be offered insulin therapy if her initial fasting glucose level is > 7 mmol/l. This can be with or without metformin. Insulin should also be offered as first-line treatment in patients who present with a fasting blood glucose level of between 6 and 6.9 mmol/l, with complications such as macrosomia or hydramnios.

Insulin and aspirin
There is no indication to start insulin therapy or aspirin at this stage. Aspirin is used in patients who have one high-risk indicator for pre-eclampsia or more than one moderate risk factor. High-risk indicators required) Chat (one with include: chronic kidney disease autoimmune diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome diabetes hypertension or hypertension in a previous pregnancy. Moderate risk factors (more than one required) include: first pregnancy age 40 years or older pregnancy interval of > 10 years body mass index > 35 kg/m 2 family history of pre-eclampsia multi-pregnancy.

Insulin and metformin
Insulin, with or without metformin, should be used in patients who present with a fasting glucose level of > 7 mmol/l or if the patient’s blood glucose levels fail to be controlled with metformin alone.

Metformin
As per guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, the patient has confirmed gestational diabetes from a glucose tolerance test. Her fasting glucose level is < 7 mmol/l, so a trial of lifestyle, diet and exercise changes is appropriate. The patient should then be reviewed in 1–2 weeks. If she continues to have poor glycaemic control, she should be offered metformin. The guidance suggests using metformin, as an off-licence medication, unless not acceptable to the patient or contraindicated.

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department after chasing thieves who were stealing her car. Her blood pressure is noted to be 185/110 mmHg on admission. She admits to having episodic headaches and to feeling stressed and anxious. She is of normal appearance. Her serum calcium on admission is 2.95 mmol/l with normal renal function. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a possible adrenal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
MEN 2A
Medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs in almost all MEN 2A patients. Phaeochromocytoma occurs in 30-50% of patients. Hyperparathyroidism occurs in about 20% of patients. This patient has hypertension and symptoms of headache and anxiety suggestive of catecholamine excess. The likely cause of this is phaeochromocytoma, especially given the ultrasound findings. Her calcium is also high, which is suggestive of hyperparathyroidism. Correct management of this patient includes: Appropriate α- and ß-blockade prior to surgical removal of the phaeochromocytoma Screening for medullary thyroid carcinoma, initially with ultrasound scan and calcitonin assay. Intravenous pentagastrin test should be considered if serum calcitonin and thyroid ultrasound scan are all normal in a patient from an MEN2 family Probable thyroidectomy and parathyroidectomy in the hands of an experienced surgeon

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. The patient does have symptoms suggestive of a phaeochromocytoma but the presence of hypercalcaemia suggests hyperparathyroidism, making a diagnosis of MEN 2A more likely.

Carcinoid syndrome
Carcinoid syndrome is incorrect. The symptoms of carcinoid syndrome include flushing, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, palpitations, hypotension and wheeze.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1) is incorrect. MEN 1 consists of hyperparathyroidism (in 80% of patients), pancreatic tumours (in 70% of patients), pituitary adenomas (in 30-50% of patients) Chatand with angiofibromas.

MEN 2B
MEN 2B is incorrect. MEN 2B consists of medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma (which can be bilateral) and Marfinoid habitus. The patient is this scenario has a normal appearance.

stem: 17-OH-progesterone is 1.4 times the upper limit of normal. Normal bilateral ovaries and uterus were visualised on pelvic ultrasound. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia is a cause of hyperandrogenism in up to 1 in 1000 females, particularly those of Hispanic, Yugoslavian or Eastern European Jewish descent. The clinicalChat picture be withcan confusing because patients might complain of no other symptoms apart from primary amenorrhoea. Management involves glucocorticoid supplementation in juveniles; flutamide (used as an anti-androgen) might be the only treatment required in adults with mild symptoms.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome
Polycystic ovarian syndrome is incorrect. 17-OH-progesterone is not significantly elevated in polycystic ovarian syndrome.

Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia is incorrect. Classical adrenal hyperplasia is diagnosed at birth.

Turner syndrome
Turner syndrome is incorrect. The normal ultrasound with respect to ovaries and uterus, is inconsistent with Turner’s where streak ovaries are seen. Congenital Adrenal HyperplasiaTesticular feminisation
Testicular feminization is incorrect. Testicular feminization is associated with female external genitalia and cryptorchidism.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with a history of thirst, polyuria and a recent 3.2 kg (7 lb) weight loss. His glucose is 33.4 mmol/l and his urine contains +1 ketones on dipstick. Which of the following features would suggest he has Type 2 rather than Type 1 diabetes?
options: A body mass index (BMI) of 23 kg/m2
explanation:
High circulating insulin level
Type 2 diabetes is associated with insulin resistance and high insulin levels.

A body mass index (BMI) of 23 kg/m2
A body mass index (BMI) of 23 kg/m 2 is incorrect. People with Type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) more commonly have a high BMI.

HLA type DR3
HLA type DR3 is incorrect. This is associated with Type 1 diabetes.

Positive islet cell antibodies
Positive islet cell antibodies is incorrect. This seen in Type 1 diabetes.

Plasma bicarbonate level of 8 mmol/l Plasma bicarbonate level of 8 mmol/l is incorrect. This severe acidosis would be associated with diabetic ketoacidosis, which would make Type 1 diabetes the most likely underlying cause.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in his management?
explanation:
Intravenous (IV) 0.9% saline
Chatblood with IV 0.9% saline is the initial intervention of choice for management of DKA. Even when systolic pressure is 90 mmHg or above, an aggressive fluid replacement prescription is recommended: 0.9% sodium chloride (NaCl) 1 litre over 1 st hour 0.9% NaCl 1 litre with potassium chloride (KCl) over next two hours 0.9% NaCl 1 litre with KCl over next four hours 0.9% NaCl 1 litre with KCl over next six hours.

Fixed-rate insulin infusion (FRII)
Although a FRII is now the preferred way to treat DKA, patients with DKA are severely dehydrated. As such, the Joint British Diabetes Societies guidelines recommend IV saline fluid replacement as the initial intervention of choice. Insulin is infused at a rate of 0.1 U/kg/h. For a 70-kg man, seven units of insulin per hour would be infused.

IV calcium chloride
Even though this patient’s K + is above the upper limit of normal at 5.8 mmol/l, it will fall rapidly with fluid replacement and insulin infusion. Myocardial protection with calcium chloride is therefore not required.

IV sodium bicarbonate
Although this patient is acidotic, rapid correction of the metabolic acidosis with fluid replacement and insulin infusion is to be expected. Bicarbonate is thought to increase the risk of cerebral oedema associated with DKA, and may delay any fall in blood lactate.

Sliding-scale insulin therapy
Sliding-scale insulin therapy is no longer recommended for the treatment of DKA because it may drive dangerous fluctuations in blood sugar, with swings from hypo- to hyperglycaemia. This has driven the change to a FRII. An initial bolus of insulin is only indicated when there is a delay to starting the FRII.

stem: A 52-year-old man is referred to the clinic with rapid weight gain, increased acne and a recent diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes. There is a past history of hypertension, the control of which has worsened over the past few months. On examination his BP is 155/95 mmHg, pulse is 78/min and regular. There is evidence of acne, his BMI is 34 and abdominal striate are visible. You suspect Cushing’s disease. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities would you expect to see?
explanation:
Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Cushing’s disease is associated with glucocorticoid excess, and this excess leads to potassium depletion and sodium and water retention, at the expense of increased excretion of chloride. The result is a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

Hypochloraemic metabolic acidosis
Hypochloraemic metabolic acidosis is incorrect. Metabolic alkalosis with reduced urinary chloride excretion is seen in cases of severe vomiting.

Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis
Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis is incorrect. Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis is seen in Addison’s and severe small bowel volume depletion, for instance in association with cholera.

Hyperchloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Hyperchloraemic metabolic alkalosis is incorrect. Hyperchloraemic metabolic alkalosis is not common. A villous adenoma can cause hypokalaemia. Acid-base disorders may also occur: this is a hyperchloraemic acidosis if bicarbonate is the principal anion lost, or a metabolic alkalosis if chloride is the predominant anion lost.\nRespiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis is incorrect. Respiratory alkalosis is seen in the early stages of aspirin overdose.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the endocrine clinic for review. She has had no menstrual period for the past five months and has lost her libido. In addition she is particularly distressed by the fact that she has developed milk leakage on minimal stimulation of her breasts during sexual intercourse. There is no past medical history of note, apart from mild depression for which she takes sertraline. On examination her BP is 122/82 mmHg, with pulse 65/min and regular. Her BMI is 22. Neurological examination including visual fields is normal. You confirm leakage of milk on minimal breast stimulation. Prolactin is elevated at 2000 mU/l; other bloods including thyroid function are normal. An MRI reveals a 0.9 cm area of low attenuation in the pituitary. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Microprolactinoma
This is a case of a microprolactinoma, and the patient has all the symptoms of excess prolactin including galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and low libido. Treatment is with a dopamine agonist, typically cabergoline, to achieve normalisation of prolactin levels.

Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia
Drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is incorrect. Elevations in prolactin up to around 1000 mU/l are possible in relation to drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia, of which anti-depressants including SSRIs are a potential cause.

Macroprolactinoma
Macroprolactinoma is incorrect. The MRI reveals an adenoma, which is less than 1 cm, namely a microprolactinoma. A macroprolactinoma would typically cause much higher levels of prolactin and would be greater than 1 cm.

Non-functioning pituitary adenoma
Non-functioning pituitary adenoma is incorrect. Occasionally very large non-functioning pituitary adenomas can cause an elevation in prolactin up to and around 1000 mU/l. This is because of what is termed the ‘stalk effect’, which refers to the compressive effect of a large pituitary adenoma on the pituitary stalk, affecting the inhibitory signal of dopamine from the hypothalamus on prolactin secretion.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome
Polycystic ovarian syndrome is incorrect. PCOS can cause elevation in prolactin due to the low oestrogen stimulating GnRH, which in turn stimulates the anterior pituitary hormones including prolactin. However, the elevation in prolactin in PCOS rarely exceeds 1000 mU/l.

stem: You are examining the effect of an insulin receptor antibody which binds at a location separate to insulin itself and you are hoping it will upregulate insulin sensitivity. Upregulation of which glucose transporter (GLUT) would you expect to see?
explanation:
GLUT-4
GLUT-4 is a 400-kDa glucoprotein coded for on the short arm of chromosome 19. Insulin binding at the cell membrane receptor site results in tyrosine kinase activation and initiation of a cascade of secondary intracellular processes. One of these is the migration of the GLUT-4 receptor to the cell surface. GLUT-4 is the channel through which glucose is taken up into muscle and adipose tissue cells following stimulation of the insulin receptor.

GLUT-1
GLUT-1 is incorrect. The GLUT-1 receptor enables basal non-insulin-stimulated glucose uptake into cells.

GLUT-2
GLUT-2 is incorrect. GLUT-2 transports glucose into beta-cells (allowing for glucose sensing).

GLUT-3
GLUT-3 is incorrect. GLUT-3 enables non-insulin-mediated glucose uptake into brain neurons.

GLUT-5
GLUT-5 is incorrect. GLUT5 is a fructose transporter expressed on the apical border of enterocytes in the small intestine.

stem: A 37-year-old man presents for a routine pre-employment check-up. He is found to have triglycerides of 5.5mmol/l (NR 1.8–2.2 mmol/l), with normal high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels. He has a BMI of 31kg/m 2 and no past medical history. Which of the following statements best fits his abnormal lipid picture?
options: Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) levels will be elevated
Has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance
He is at risk for acute pancreatitis
explanation:
Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) levels will be elevated
The diagnosis in this case is familial hypertriglyceridaemia (type IV hyperlipoproteinaemia phenotype), in which triglyceride, but not cholesterol, levels are elevated as a result of excess hepatic production of VLDL. It is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with moderate elevations in the serum triglyceride concentration (2.3– 5.6 mmol/l).

Usually improved by glucocorticoids
Usually improved by glucocorticoids is incorrect as steroids, if anything, will worsen the lipid profile.

Usually improved by alcohol
Usually improved by alcohol is incorrect as alcohol will increase triglyceride levels further.

Has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance
Has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance is incorrect as familial hypertriglyceridaemia (type IV hyperlipoproteinaemia phenotype) is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with moderate elevations in the serum triglyceride concentration (2.3–5.6 mmol/l).

He is at risk for acute pancreatitis
He is at risk for acute pancreatitis is incorrect as pancreatitis related to hypertriglyceridaemia occurs at very high triglyceride levels, usually > 11 mmol/l.

stem: Antinuclear antibodies were positive. She notes that a similar episode occurred a few years previously when she took a specific antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda
This patient’s clinical picture is very typical of porphyria cutanea tarda. Antinuclear antibodies are frequently seen in patients with this condition. Oestrogens can precipitate development of the condition, hence her presentation shortly after commencing the oral contraceptive pill. A history of a similar episode in response to an antibiotic is also suspicious for porphyria cutanea tarda. Urinary porphyrins are raised in porphyria cutanea tarda; the cause is congenital deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). Assay of red blood cells for UROD activity is now available in many hospital laboratories. She should be encouraged to find another form of contraception.

Polycystic ovarian syndrome
Polycystic ovarian syndrome is incorrect. OCP is often used in patients with PCOS and irregular menses in order to regulate the menstrual cycle and supplement oestrogen levels for bone health. This patient does have acne, which can be a feature of PCOS-associated hyperandrogenaemia. However, the reaction to OCP described in this case and resultant bullous rash are very atypical for PCOS.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Stevens-Johnson syndrome is incorrect. Stevens?Johnson syndrome is a dermatological emergency characterised by widespread bullous formation or the typical ‘target’ lesions affecting the trunk and face, and one or more mucous membrane erosions. It is believed to be mediated by immune complex deposition and can be triggered by an infection or medication. There is no mucosal membrane involvement in this case and the bullous rash is limited to the hands, making this an unlikely diagnosis.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is incorrect. This is another severe blistering condition and is a dermatological and medical emergency. It is a rare, life-threatening skin condition that is usually caused by a reaction to drugs or, less commonly, an atypical infection. It causes the epidermis to detach from the dermis and is commonly widespread at presentation affecting the entire body. This results in severe dehydration, difficulty with thermoregulation and susceptibility to severe systemic infection. This is unlikely in this case given the localised and less severe bullous reaction.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is incorrect. This is an autoimmune systemic condition caused by circulating antibodies, which can affect kidneys, eyes, skin, heart, muscle, joints and liver. Most commonly patients present with painful and swollen joints, fever, chest pain, hair loss, mouth ulcers, swollen lymph nodes, feeling tired and a red or ‘butterfly’ rash, which is most commonly on the face. Often there are periods of illness, called flares, and periods of remission when there are few symptoms. Antinuclear antibodies can be positive in lupus but are not specific to the condition, and additional antibody testing including anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies is more specific. The presentation is often less acute then the presentation described in this case, and follows a waxing and waning course. This diagnosis is unlikely in this case as there are no systemic features described.

stem: Which of the following findings would you also anticipate on laboratory testing?
explanation:
Decreased FSH
Low body mass index, as seen here, leads to a fall-off in production of gonadotrophins and subsequent secondary ovarian failure. Gain in weight to normal BMI leads to a restoration of menses. Of significant concern in this patient is under-oestrogenisation and potential risk of osteoporosis.

Decreased prolactin
Decreased prolactin is incorrect. The prolactin in patients with anorexia nervosa is usually normal or slightly elevated.

Raised LH
Raised LH is incorrect. Raised gonadotrophins are seen in primary ovarian failure. In severe weight loss gonadotrophins are reduced.

Raised FSH
Raised FSH is incorrect. Raised gonadotrophins are seen in primary ovarian failure. In severe weight loss gonadotrophins are reduced.

Raised testosterone
Raised testosterone is incorrect. Raised testosterone levels may be seen in PCOS, unlikely given the scenario seen here.

stem: A 27-year-old man with a new diagnosis of Kallman syndrome is in the Endocrine Clinic. He has a family history and has been found to have a mutation in the Kal1 gene. He has low LH, FSH and testosterone. Other pituitary hormones are normal. He is not keen on having children. Which would be the most appropriate treatment at this stage?
options: Pulsatile subcutaneous administration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
Regular injections of human chorionic gonadotropin
explanation:
Testosterone patches
If fertility is not required, there is no need to stimulate spermatogenesis with gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) or gonadotropins; only testosterone replacement is required. Testosterone undecanoate is available for oral use, but frequent dosing is required. In addition, because of poor absorption, the plasma concentrations that can be achieved are often subnormal with oral preparations. Testosterone injections, implants or patches are more reliable. Should he require fertility in the future, then pulsed therapy with GnRH analogues is required to achieve this.

Oral testosterone replacement
Oral testosterone replacement is incorrect. Testosterone undecanoate is poorly absorbed with frequent dosing required and the plasma concentrations that can be achieved are often subnormal with oral preparations.

Pulsatile subcutaneous administration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
Pulsatile subcutaneous administration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is incorrect. Fertility is not required at present, as such there is no need to stimulate spermatogenesis with gonadotropin-releasing hormone.

Regular injections of human chorionic gonadotropin
Regular injections of human chorionic gonadotropin is incorrect. It would not treat his hypogonadism.

Regular injections of gonadotropins
Regular injections of gonadotropins is incorrect. There is no need to stimulate spermatogenesis with gonadotropins.

stem: Which of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?
explanation:
72-hour supervised fast
Although rare, an insulinoma is a possibility in this patient and a supervised 72 h fast is now seen as the definitive investigation. In the presence of a negative sulphonylurea screen, the test is considered positive if hypoglycaemia (<3.3 mmol/l) is revealed, although some also include criteria for c-peptide, Chat proinsulin with AI and Tutor insulin levels (being suggestive of the diagnosis if c-peptide exceeds 2.5 ng/ml, proinsulin levels are >25% of those for immunoreactive insulin, and insulin levels >166% of the upper limit of normal). To reduce the need for inpatient stay, many units now employ three separate 15 h fasts with glucose measurement.

Glucagon stimulation test
Glucagon stimulation test is incorrect. A glucagon stimulation test is used to measure pituitary function, e.g. growth hormone production.

Sulphonylurea assay
Sulphonylurea assay is incorrect. Sulphonylurea assay is helpful in conjunction with the 72 h fast.

Calcium stimulation test
Calcium stimulation test is incorrect. The calcium stimulation test, the selective intra-arterial calcium stimulation test, has greatly facilitated the precise regionalisation of insulinomas smaller than 2 cm, which non-invasive techniques (ultrasound [US], computed tomography [CT] and magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) often fail to localise.

Exercise provocation test
Exercise provocation test is incorrect. Provocation tests to induce hypoglycaemia are rarely required, and simple observation during fasting is sufficient.

stem: An 18-year-old woman with primary amenorrhoea comes to the endocrine clinic for review. She is concerned that her periods have not started. Her only other history of note is bilateral inguinal hernia repair as an infant. On examination her BP is 122/82; pulse is 64 and regular. She is 1.82 m tall and has a BMI of 22.5. Breast development is normal, although she seems to have an absence of pubic and axillary hair. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her amenorrhoea?
explanation:
Androgen insensitivity syndrome
AIS is associated with bilateral inguinal hernias, presenting in infancy, the usual cause being testes in the inguinal canal. The fact that breast development is normal (due to peripheral androgen conversion), yet pubic hair is absent, also fits with AIS. Confirming male karyotype is an obvious first step in evaluation.

Autoimmune ovarian failure
Autoimmune ovarian failure is incorrect. Autoimmune ovarian failure is usually seen as a cause of secondary amenorrhoea, and occurs with increased incidence in patients with other autoimmune diseases.

Kallmann syndrome
Kallmann syndrome is incorrect. The most prominent feature of Kallmann syndrome is anosmia, which is not reported here.

Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome is incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome is associated with a male phenotype, hence it cannot be the correct answer here.

Turner syndrome
Turner syndrome is incorrect. The phenotype described here does not fit with Turner syndrome, which is associated with short stature and a webbed neck.

stem: A 24-year-old man with learning disability presents for review. He complains of a sudden deterioration of vision in his left eye. His past history of note includes a deep vein thrombosis. On examination he appears tall and slim and almost marfanoid in appearance. He has a markedly elevated urinary homocysteine. Which enzyme defect is most likely to be responsible for this clinical picture?
explanation:
Cystathionine synthase
This presentation is consistent with type 1 homocystinuria, where a defect in cystathionine synthase is responsible. Patients present with mild-to-moderate learning disability, a Marfan-like syndrome and thrombotic episodes. The sudden visual deterioration could either be due to a thrombotic episode or to the lens dislocation associated with this condition.

Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase is incorrect. Although deficiency in this enzyme causes high homocysteine levels, it presents with seizures, gait dysfunction and developmental delay. The diagnosis here is type 1 homocystinuria, where a defect in cystathionine synthase is responsible.

Histidase
Histidase is incorrect. Deficiency in this enzyme does not usually cause any symptoms. The diagnosis here is type 1 homocystinuria, where a defect in cystathionine synthase is responsible.

Homogentisic acid oxidase
Homogentisic acid oxidase is incorrect. Deficiency in this causes alkaptonuria, which causes black urine, discolored sclera and cartilage.

Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase is incorrect. Abnormalities in this enzyme cause maple syrup urine disease. Infants with this disease seem healthy at birth but quickly deteriorate, often with severe brain damage, which may be permanent; without prompt treatment, they will die from cerebral oedema. Homocystinuria Homocystinuria can also be associated with defects in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (type 2 homocystinuria), but individuals with this condition rarely survive the neonatal period or, if they survive longer than this, they often have more severe learning disability.

stem: A 29-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department. He was found unconscious by the ambulance service, having collapsed at a darts match. His family history reveals a brother with type I diabetes. A blood test shows the following results: glucose 1.1 mmol/l, insulin > 500 pmol/l (normal range 15–100 pmol/l) and Cpeptide of < 0.2 pmol/l (normal range 0.2–1.4 pmol/l). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Factitious hypoglycaemia
Factitious insulin-induced hypoglycaemia is as common in previously healthy subjects as in insulin-dependent diabetics and is due to deliberate, but concealed injection of insulin. The history and laboratory findings are consistent with significant hypoglycaemia; they reveal high plasma insulin and low C-peptide (and proinsulin) concentrations, which can only fit with exogenous insulin administration.

Insulinoma
Insulinoma is incorrect. Insulinoma is associated with hypoglycaemia and hyperinsulinaemia, but C-peptide is also high because the excess insulin is endogenously produced.

Type I diabetes mellitus
Type I diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Type I diabetes mellitus presents with hyper, rather than hypoglycaemia; the only explanation here can be exogenous insulin administration.

Type II diabetes mellitus
Type II diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Type II diabetes is associated with hyperinsulinaemia during the early stages of the disease and elevated C-peptide due to increased insulin resistance, rather than the low C-peptide seen here. Hypoglycaemia is also very rarely seen unless the patient is prescribed insulin.

Insulin resistance
Insulin resistance is incorrect. Insulin resistance is associated with normal or hyperglycaemia in the presence of elevated insulin and C-peptide levels.

stem: A 36-year-old man is referred by his GP with likely acromegaly. Comparing his current features to old photographs you note a significant change in his appearance, with prominent macrognathia, macroglossia, large hands and feet. IGF1 is elevated and oral glucose tolerance test does not suppress growth hormone so acromegaly is confirmed. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals a microadenoma. Which of the following would usually be the treatment of choice?
options: Medical treatment with a growth hormone-receptor antagonist
Medical treatment with a somatostatin analogue
explanation:
Transsphenoidal surgery
The treatment of choice in acromegaly is transsphenoidal resection. However surgery has been found to cure only approximately 60% of patients with acromegaly. Somatostatin, dopamine analogues and GH receptor antagonists are the mainstays of medical treatment for GH excess and are generally used when primary surgery fails to induce complete remission.

Medical treatment with a growth hormone-receptor antagonist
Medical treatment with a growth hormone-receptor antagonist is incorrect. This is not first line treatment, surgery is.

Medical treatment with a somatostatin analogue
Medical treatment with a somatostatin analogue is incorrect. This is not first line treatment, surgery is, although this has been used to shrink large tumours prior to surgery.

Radiotherapy
Radiotherapy is incorrect. This is not first line treatment, although it can be used as an adjunct to surgery.

Transfrontal surgery
Transfrontal surgery is incorrect. The pituitary is accessed transphenoidally. Acromegaly Acromegaly is a disorder of IGF-I excess which occurs after the growth plate cartilage fuses in adulthood. It is a rare but severe disease that is often diagnosed late, and so morbidity and mortality rates are high, particularly as a result of associated cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and respiratory disorders as well as malignancies. It is usually caused by pituitary adenomas, however pancreatic, adrenal, and ovarian tumors can rarely secrete GH/GHRH. Clinical features Sweating is present in more than 80% of cases, hypertension in 40%, impaired glucose tolerance in 40% and type 2 diabetes in 20%. Coarse facial features, including prognathism, are often noticed by patients when they compare old photographs and enlargement of the hands and feet and soft-tissue swelling are also common features. Treatment The treatment of choice is trans-sphenoidal resection. However surgery has been found to cure only approximately 60% of patients with acromegaly. Somatostatin and dopamine analogues and GH receptor antagonists are the mainstays of medical treatment for GH excess and are generally used when primary surgery fails to induce complete remission.

stem: A 21-year-old woman is reviewed on the ward some 36 h after admission with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). She is well but has minimal residual acidosis. Which of the following molecules is most likely to be responsible?
explanation:
Beta-hydroxybutyrate
This compound is likely to be the lingering acid causing a mild acidosis after 36 h. A range of ketoacids are formed in DKA, including acetone, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetic acid. It is acetone that is responsible for the characteristic pear drop smell associated with DKA. At the 36 h time point it is most likely that levels of acetoacetate, the parent compound for acetone and beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone itself will have fallen towards the normal range. Acetaldehyde is metabolised to acetone and is therefore not a contributor to acidosis here. Formaldehyde is not seen in DKA, and malic acid is found in rhubarb.

Acetaldehyde
Acetaldehyde is incorrect. Acetaldehyde would have been metabolised to acetone after 36 h of treated DKA.

Acetone
Acetone is incorrect. The breakdown product of acetoacetate, this should have fallen after 36 h.

Formaldehyde
Formaldehyde is incorrect. Formaldehyde is not involved in DKA.

Malic acid
Malic acid is incorrect. Malic acid is found in rhubarb, but not in DKA.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with palpitations and shortness of breath. Recent thyroid function tests on the hospital computer reveal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of < 0.05 mU/l and a markedly elevated total thyroxine (T 4). You arrange blood gas testing. Which of the following findings would be most consistent with Graves’ disease?
explanation:
Decreased PaCO 2
Compared with normal subjects, hyperthyroid patients show significantly lower resting arterial CO 2 tension, tidal volume and significantly higher mean inspiratory flow and PaO 2. This can, of course, lead to misdiagnosis of patients with hyperthyroidism as having hyperventilation syndrome. Patients with hyperthyroidism also show a greater ventilatory response to hypoxia than normal patients. These ventilatory changes are significantly correlated with tri-iodothyronine (T 3) levels.

Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis is incorrect. Decreased PaCO 2 drives a respiratory alkalosis that may be mistaken for hyperventilation syndrome.

Decreased PaO 2
Decreased PaO 2, is incorrect. PaO 2 is normal; tidal volume is increased in patients with hyperthyroidism, which may well be reflective of increased basal metabolic rate.

Increased PaCO 2
Increased PaCO 2 is incorrect. PaCO 2 is likely to be decreased.

Decreased pH
Decreased pH is incorrect. pH is usually normal in patients with hyperthyroidism, although it may be increased because of respiratory alkalosis.

stem: A 44-year-old patient with a 15-year history of bipolar disorder is referred to an endocrinologist for an opinion. She is noted to have a Na + concentration of 144 mmol/l (NR 135–145), with a urea of 12 mmol/l and a Cr of 140 µmol/l; urine osmolality is 250 mosmol/l (NR 350–1000), and fasting plasma glucose and calcium are normal. The nurses have monitored her intake and output: oral intake is 2.5 litres and urine output is 4.4 litres in 24 hours. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Psychiatric drugs are unlikely to have played a part in her condition
If this patient underwent a water deprivation test, desmopressin would cause a rise in her urine
Cranial diabetes insipidus is the most likely underlying diagnosis
Desmopressin is an appropriate treatment for her condition
Lithium is the likely underlying cause of her condition
explanation:
Lithium is the likely underlying cause of her condition
The likely underlying cause of her condition, because this patient has nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which in the setting of chronic bipolar disorder, is commonly from lithium treatment.

Psychiatric drugs are unlikely to have played a part in her condition
Psychiatric drugs are unlikely to have played a part in her condition is incorrect. Lithium treatment is the likely underlying cause of her nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

If this patient underwent a water deprivation test, desmopressin would cause a rise in her urine
If this patient underwent a water deprivation test, desmopressin would cause a rise in her urine osmolality If this patient underwent a water deprivation test, desmopressin would cause a rise in her urine osmolality is incorrect. In the setting of a water deprivation test, desmopressin would cause a rise in urine osmolarity in cranial, not nephrogenic, diabetes insipidus.

Cranial diabetes insipidus is the most likely underlying diagnosis
Cranial diabetes insipidus is the most likely underlying diagnosis is incorrect. In the setting of chronic bipolar disorder, the most likely underlying diagnosis is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from lithium.

Desmopressin is an appropriate treatment for her condition
Desmopressin is an appropriate treatment for her condition is incorrect. Desmopressin is effective treatment in cranial, not nephrogenic, diabetes insipidus. Diabetes insipidus This patient has diabetes insipidus, probably renal in origin and related to the use of lithium as treatment for manic depression. Decompensated diabetes insipidus shows features of dehydration (as in this case), with an inappropriately low urine osmolality. Diabetes insipidus (DI) is defined as the passage of large volumes (> 3 l/24 h) of dilute urine (< 300 mOsm/kg). It has the following two major forms: Central (neurogenic, pituitary or neurohypophyseal) DI, characterised by decreased secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH; also referred to as arginine vasopressin [AVP]) Nephrogenic DI, characterised by decreased ability to concentrate urine because of resistance to ADH action in the kidney The urine remains dilute in cases of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, despite a rising plasma osmolality and failure of the urine to concentrate after desmopressin. Desmopressin is unlikely to be effective in this case – it is effective in cranial diabetes insipidus – NSAIDs might be effective. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus can have an autosomal recessive or X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance, whereas cranial diabetes insipidus is inherited only with an autosomal dominant pattern. Psychogenic polydipsia is ruled out by the water deprivation test, with urine osmolality rising appropriately in response to the lack of oral intake.

stem: A male cousin was seen in the clinic at the age of 8 years with precocious puberty. Which blood marker is most likely to be abnormal in this girl?
explanation:
17-hydroxyprogesterone
The likely underlying diagnosis for this girl is non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), because of her amenorrhoea, clinical hyperandrogenism, clitoromegaly and family history. The accumulation of excess precursor hormones and, as such, the distinguishing characteristic of 21-hydroxylase deficiency, is a high serum concentration of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (usually > 1000 ng/dl).

Sodium
This is simple virilising CAH, not salt wasting, so her sodium will be normal.

Potassium
Given that this is simple virilising CAH, not salt wasting, so her potassium will be normal.

Cortisol
It is normal in non-classic CAH. Given the block in the cortisol biosynthesis pathway, measured cortisol will not be high.

Human chorionic gonadotropin
This is a hormone produced by the embryo after implantation and will not be elevated in CAH.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her worsening glucose control?
explanation:
Adrenal insufficiency
With her auto-immune history and low sodium with high potassium, Addison’s disease should certainly be considered. Adrenal insufficiency is associated with episodes of hypoglycaemia; the sodium below the lower limit of normal, and the potassium at the upper end of the normal range, support the diagnosis, as does the nausea over the past two weeks. Onset of Addison’s in pregnancy is relatively rare, although incidence is of course increased in patients with a background of other autoimmune pathology such as type 1 diabetes. The raised MCV may represent concurrent B 12/folate deficiency, and raises the possibility of occult coeliac disease in addition.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. This is another possible diagnosis, but not directly the cause of worsening glucose control. No history of diarrhoea is given.

Increased fetal insulin production
Increased fetal insulin production is incorrect. This has no bearing on maternal glycaemic control, the amount of insulin produced by the fetus is minimal in comparison to exogenous insulin replacement.

Increased insulin resistance
Increased insulin resistance is incorrect. Type 1 DM is due to lack of insulin secondary to pancreatic beta cell destruction, whereas insulin resistance is what occurs in type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Folate deficiency
Folate deficiency is incorrect. This is not the cause of her presentation but should also be considered as an additional diagnosis given her MCV. Adrenal insufficiency is associated with episodes of hypoglycaemia; the sodium below the lower limit of normal, and the potassium at the upper end of the normal range support the diagnosis, as does the nausea over the past 2 weeks. Onset of Addison’s in pregnancy is relatively rare, although incidence is of course increased in patients with background of other autoimmune pathology such as Type 1 diabetes. The raised MCV may represent concurrent B12/folate deficiency, and raises the possibility of occult coeliac disease in addition.

stem: What is the most likely cause for her hyperkalaemia?
explanation:
Addison’s disease
This patient has a mild hyponatraemia and mild hyperkalaemia which is typical for Addison’s disease. Combined with her presenting symptoms and age, this is highly suggestive of Addison’s disease.

Bartter syndrome
Bartter syndrome is incorrect. Bartter syndrome is an autosomal recessive renal condition causing hypokalaemia (not hyperkalaemia), metabolic alkalosis, and hypochloraemia. There is excessive renal loss of sodium, potassium and chloride. This patient’s symptoms, combined with her mild hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, are suggestive of Addison’s disease.

Conn’s syndrome
Conn’s syndrome is incorrect. Conn’s syndrome is hyperaldosteronism, leading to hypertension (not seen here) and sodium retention with potassium loss. This patient has the opposite; hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. This, combined with her symptoms, is much more suggestive of Addison’s disease.

Diuretic abuse
Diuretic abuse is incorrect. Unless the patient was abusing spironolactone, diuretic abuse would cause hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia. This patient is engaging well in a treatment programme, which makes diuretic abuse less likely. Furthermore, diuretic abuse would not explain her abdominal pain and vomiting. A much more likely explanation, which would also account for the laboratory findings of mild hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, would be Addison’s disease.

Renal tubular acidosis type 1
Renal tubular acidosis type 1 is incorrect. Renal tubular acidosis type 1 causes hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia. This patient’s combination of symptoms, mild hyperkalaemia and mild hyponatraemia are more suggestive of Addison’s disease.

stem: A 19-year-old student is brought to the Emergency Department by his flatmates. He had been playing squash that afternoon, and while out for an Italian meal he complained of generalised weakness: he was unable to stand and had to be carried in by his friends. His potassium level was noted to be 2.6 mmol/l; urine screens for diabetes and laxative abuse were negative. Apparently, there is a family history of such events; he has had multiple previous episodes since childhood. The symptoms were aborted by potassium chloride. Which of the following types of mutation is most likely to be responsible?
options: Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated chloride channel
Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated potassium channel
Mutation in a renal potassium channel
Mutation in a renal chloride channel
Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated calcium channel
explanation:
Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated calcium channel
The diagnosis here is hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, which is related to muscle calcium-channel mutation (CACLN1A3). There are two types based on the causative gene, CACNA1 (calcium channel) and SCN4A (αsubunit of the sodium channel).

Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated chloride channel
Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated chloride channel is incorrect. The diagnosis here is hypokalaemic periodic paralysis type 1, which is related to muscle calcium-channel mutation. Voltage gated chloride channel mutations are associated with epilepsies.

Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated potassium channel
Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated potassium channel is incorrect. The diagnosis here is hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, which is related to muscle calcium-channel mutation. Mutations in the voltage gated potassium channel result in familial epilepsy.

Mutation in a renal potassium channel
Mutation in a renal potassium channel is incorrect. The diagnosis here is hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, which is related to muscle calcium-channel mutation. ROMK mutations result in forms of Bartter’s syndrome.

Mutation in a renal chloride channel
Mutation in a renal chloride channel is incorrect. The diagnosis here is hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, which is related to muscle calcium-channel mutation. Renal chloride channel mutations are a recognised cause of nephrocalcinosis.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has been diagnosed with a pericardial effusion. Her BMI is 31, and her hair is thinning on examination. She also reports recent cold intolerance and constipation. She has no medical history and takes no medications. She denies any recent viral prodrome. Her sister has a history of autoimmune thyroid disease. On examination she has dry skin and loss of the outer third of both eyebrows. There is no palpable goitre. Her blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg. Her cardiovascular examination reveals muffled heart sounds and a cardiac rub. Which endocrine disease is most likely to be associated with this finding?
explanation:
Hypothyroidism
Clinically silent pericardial effusion is common in untreated hypothyroidism; it may be seen in hyperthyroidism but the incidence is lower. The effusion itself has high cholesterol content, which can lead to an unusual secondary pericarditis with cholesterol deposits of ‘gold paint’ appearance. The pericardial effusion very rarely needs to be treated in its own right, and subsides when thyroid replacement therapy is given. The symptoms of cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation are a sign of reduced metabolic rate, also associated with hypothyroidism.

Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is associated with tachycardia due to increased basal metabolic rate and predisposes patients to the development of atrial fibrillation. Heart failure can develop as a result of arrythmias and tachycardia, but hyperthyroidism is less commonly associated with pericardial effusion compared to hypothyroidism.

Phaeochromocytoma
Phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. A phaeochromocytoma is a tumour of the adrenal medulla that secretes catecholamines. This tumour can be associated with dilated cardiomyopathy due to severe uncontrolled tachycardia, and patients can also develop a ‘takotsubo’ cardiomyopathy. The cardiovascular effects of excess catecholamine production are most commonly reversed with treatment and removal of the tumour, and phaeochromocytoma is rarely associated with a pericardial effusion.

Chronic renal insufficiency
Chronic renal sufficiency is incorrect. Chronic kidney disease and an elevated urea can lead to pericarditis and reduced effective fluid excretion, and also to hypervolaemia and a pericardial effusion. However, the symptoms of cold intolerance, hair loss and constipation present in this case would not be typical for chronic kidney disease.

Hypogonadism
Hypogonadism is incorrect. Hypogonadism can cause hair thinning and is most commonly observed in postmenopausal women. However, hypogonadism, either primary or secondary, is not associated with the development of pericardial effusions.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 10 weeks’ pregnant presents to the endocrine clinic with a suppressed thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH) level of less than 0.05, and a marked elevation in T4. She has positive anti-thyroid antibodies and a smoothly enlarged thyroid on palpation of the neck. She has an increased resting pulse rate of 95 beats per minute and a fine tremor at rest. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention in this case?
explanation:
Propylthiouracil
Propylthiouracil is the intervention of choice and should be used at a dose which keeps thyroid hormone levels in the upper third of the normal range. It should not be used late in pregnancy (patients are often switched to carbimazole), because of the risk of maternal liver toxicity.

Carbimazole and thyroxine (block replace)
Carbimazole and thyroxine (block replace) is incorrect. Block replace is not indicated because it risks hypothyroidism in the fetus, as thyroxine is less able to cross the placenta.

Radioactive iodine
Radioactive iodine is incorrect. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy, because of the risk of inducing fetal hypothyroidism.

Propranolol
Propranolol is incorrect. Untreated hyperthyroidism runs the risk of premature miscarriage; symptomatic relief alone is therefore not appropriate here.

Surgical resection
Surgical resection is incorrect. Surgery would usually be considered if thyroid suppressive agents are not tolerated or it is not possible to gain control of thyrotoxicosis.

stem: A 74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department in an acute confusional state. He is clinically euvolaemic. He has a chest X-ray with a suspicious-looking mass. His serum sodium concentration is 105 mmol/l and serum osmolality is 230 mosmol/kg. SIADH is suspected. Which of the following biochemical findings in this patient would best support this diagnosis?
options: Random plasma cortisol concentration of 548 nmol/l
Random urine sodium concentration of 10 mmol/l
explanation:
Random urine osmolality of 380 mosmol/kg
A urine osmolarity level that is higher than serum, in the setting of euvolaemia, establishes impaired water excretion. This is part of the essential criteria for SIADH.

Random plasma cortisol concentration of 548 nmol/l
Random plasma cortisol concentration of 548 nmol/l is incorrect. This simply means that he does not have cortisol deficiency; it does not mean that he has SIADH.

Random urine sodium concentration of 10 mmol/l
Random urine sodium concentration of 10 mmol/l is incorrect. Low urine sodium would suggest that hyponatraemia was due to sodium depletion.

Fraction of excreted sodium of 0.5%
Fraction of excreted sodium of 0.5% is incorrect. FENA would be higher (0.5%) in SIADH.

Serum urea concentration of 2.1 mmol/l
Serum urea concentration of 2.1 mmol/l is incorrect. Low urea is found with many underlying diagnoses of water overload.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of headaches and sweating. Her mother had renal calculi and died of a tumour in her neck. On examination, a nodule is felt in the patient’s neck in the region of the thyroid gland. Routine bloods are unremarkable; histology reveals small round cells which stain positively for calcitonin. A surgeon advises complete thyroidectomy. What is the most important investigation the surgeon must undertake prior to surgery?
explanation:
24-h urinary metanephrines and catecholamines
This patient probably has medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, which may be associated with phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism as part of the multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A syndrome (MEN 2A). Phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery. If present, the effect of catecholamines must be blocked prior to surgery using high-dose phenoxybenzamine +/− additional β-blockade according to blood pressure control.

Serum thyroxine
Serum thyroxine is incorrect. Thyroxine is normal because this is a cancer affecting C-cells, which produce calcitonin.

Serum calcium
Serum calcium is incorrect. Serum calcium is likely to be elevated due to hyperparathyroidism, but this is not as essential to test versus screening for a phaeochromocytoma.

24-h urine test for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA)
24-h urine test for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is incorrect.This is a screening test for carcinoid syndrome.

Serum calcitonin
Serum calcitonin is incorrect. Calcitonin may be elevated, but it does not affect prognosis of surgery versus the risks associated with a phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with a history of panic attacks, palpitations, sweating, headache and flushing. On examination his pulse rate is 120 bpm and his blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. Urinary catecholamines are elevated over a 24-h period, with noradrenaline most elevated. Initial ultrasound scan of the abdomen reveals no masses. A CT scan of the abdomen does not show an adrenal mass. Which of the following tests would be most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
options: Genetic testing for RET proto-oncogene mutation
explanation:
[131I], metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan
This patient most probably has a phaeochromocytoma. The presence of a raised noradrenaline usually indicates an extra-adrenal tumour. Scanning with [131I]metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) demonstrates specific uptake in sites of sympathetic activity with about 90% success. This scan is particularly useful with extra-adrenal tumours when CT or MRI of adrenal glands is negative.

Repeat ultrasound scan after interval
Repeat ultrasound scan is incorrect. An ultrasound scan is least sensitive with respect to identifying a phaeochromocytoma and would therefore be considered least useful.

Genetic testing for RET proto-oncogene mutation
Genetic testing for RET proto-oncogene mutation is incorrect. MEN2 is associated with mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. Whilst there is a high probability of a pheochromocytoma in this case, there is no suspicion of medullary thyroid cancer or parathyroid tumours. The likelihood of a diagnosis of MEN2, therefore, seems low.

Magnetic resonance imaging
Magnetic resonance imaging is incorrect. Whilst MRI is more sensitive compared with CT for identifying adrenal tumours, and is useful with respect to identifying anatomy prior to surgery, but is less useful with respect to extra-adrenal tumours than a MIBG scan.

Renal arteriography
Renal arteriography is incorrect. Given the tumour is extra-adrenal, this will not be helpful in identifying the location.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her?
options: High-dose carbimazole combined with thyroxine replacement
Low-dose carbimazole achieving thyroid hormones in the upper third of the normal range
Mid-dose carbimazole achieving TSH in the upper third of the normal range
explanation:
Low-dose carbimazole achieving thyroid hormones in the upper third of the normal range
This history and biochemistry with the positive antibodies is consistent with Graves’ disease and, as this patient is symptomatic, treatment should be initiated. As low a dose of carbimazole as possible is preferable to prevent fetal hypothyroidism. T 4 and T 3 are the best indicators of response in pregnancy as TSH may be suppressed in part because of beta-HCG levels. Carbimazole is often avoided in the first trimester because of the risk of congenital abnormalities such as cutis aplasia. Propylthiouracil is therefore preferred in the first trimester if antithyroid medication is needed.

High-dose carbimazole combined with thyroxine replacement
High-dose carbimazole combined with thyroxine replacement is incorrect. Thyroxine does not cross the placenta, but anti-thyroid medications do. This means that a conventional block replace approach will lead to significant fetal hypothyroidism.

Mid-dose carbimazole achieving TSH in the upper third of the normal range
Mid-dose carbimazole achieving TSH in the upper third of the normal range is incorrect. TSH may be suppressed in part because of beta-HCG levels in pregnancy; it is therefore preferable to use measurement of T 4 and T 3 for monitoring.

Radioiodine
Radioiodine is incorrect. Radioiodine is not appropriate in pregnancy because of the risk of damaging the developing thyroid in the fetus. In fact, most female patients are counselled not to become pregnant for at least 3-6 months post-radioactive iodine treatment.

Surgery
Surgery is incorrect. This is a last resort and would be reserved for patients who fail to respond to anti-thyroid medication or those with a compressive goitre requiring urgent surgery. If surgery is required it is preferable to perform surgery in the second trimester, due to the lower risk of harming the pregnancy.

stem: A 30-year-old man is referred by the Emergency Department after a road traffic accident. He has suffered from gradually increasing tiredness over the past 4 months. He has also split from his long-term girlfriend after problems with erectile dysfunction. On examination his blood pressure is 110/70; pulse is 75 and regular. BMI is 22. He has a bitemporal hemianopia. Blood tests reveal a testosterone level of 7 nmol/l (normal range 9–35 nmol/l). Prolactin is 4900 mcg/l. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 12-mm pituitary tumour. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Prolactinoma
Estimates suggest up to two-thirds of pituitary tumours are lactotroph (prolactin-producing) tumours. A prolactinoma is suggested by the low testosterone and problems with erectile dysfunction over the past few months and confirmed by the significant elevation in prolactin. The visual field defects are suggestive of a macroadenoma.

Somatotroph adenoma
Somatotroph adenoma is incorrect. Growth hormone-secreting tumours are much less common than prolactinomas and are associated with soft tissue swelling, macroglossia, prominent jaw and other features, including abnormal glucose tolerance and hypertension.

Basophil adenoma
Basophil adenoma is incorrect. Basophilic adenomas are reconised to produce ACTH, TSH, LH or FSH. There are no symptoms to suggest thyrotoxicosis or Cushings, and LH/FSH-producing tumours do not normally lead to symptoms.

Non-functioning pituitary tumour
