Non-functioning pituitary tumour is incorrect. Non-functioning pituitary tumours usually present when they are very large because of either pressure effects driving pan hypopituitarism, or a marked visual field defect.

Craniopharyngioma
Craniopharyngioma is incorrect. Craniopharyngiomas usually present with diabetes insipidus because of a failure of production of vasopressin.

stem: Ultrasound of the pelvis shows polycystic ovaries. What is the best initial management?
options: Stop lithium and replace with lamotrigine
explanation:
Stop lithium and replace with lamotrigine
The answer is to stop lithium after consultation with her psychiatrist. Long-term treatment with lithium can produce frank hypothyroidism, as in this case. Lithium is concentrated by the thyroid and inhibits thyroidal iodine uptake. It also inhibits iodotyrosine coupling, alters thyroglobulin structure, and inhibits thyroid hormone secretion. The best management in this case would be to discontinue the lithium therapy and replace it with another agent (after consulting the patient’s psychiatrist) – carbamazepine, sodium valproate or lamotrigine could all be alternative agents for mood stabilisation. Lamotrigine is the preferred option, assuming pregnancy is desired.

Dopamine agonist
Dopamine agonist is incorrect. The raised prolactin is likely to be related to a combination of lithium therapy and hypothyroidism.

Thyroxine
Thyroxine is incorrect. Thyroxine may be required, although thyroid function should be re-tested following a period off lithium to allow for a recovery in iodotyrosine coupling and thyroglobulin levels.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Although metformin may induce modest weight loss in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and glucose tolerance, removal of lithium is the most important next step.

Thyroxine and dopamine agonist
Thyroxine and dopamine agonist is incorrect. Removal of the lithium is the initial step, because this will result at least in partial resolution of the hypothyroidism.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is diagnosed with acromegaly. She has probably suffered from symptoms for two years before her presentation. Transsphenoidal surgical removal of the adenoma is proposed. Increased incidence of which cancer is associated with acromegaly?
explanation:
Colorectal cancer
A number of diseases are associated with increased risk of colorectal cancer. In acromegaly the increased risk is thought to result from a rise in IGF-1 and by changes in the enterohepatic circulation and bile salt loss into the GI tract. A number of familial cancer conditions such as familial adenomatous polyposis are also associated with colorectal cancer, and long-standing inflammatory bowel disease is recognised to increase risk.

Breast cancer
Breast cancer is incorrect. Although increased breast cancer cases may be associated with acromegaly, the risk is less well described than that for colorectal cancer.

Endometrial cancer
Endometrial cancer is incorrect. Endometrial cancer is associated with hyperinsulinaemia, although like breast cancer, no strong link to acromegaly has yet been described.

Lung cancer
Lung cancer is incorrect. Lung cancer is not associated with acromegaly, the link is, of course, strongest for smoking.

Oesophageal cancer
Oesophageal cancer is incorrect. The strongest risk factors for oesophageal cancer are cigarette smoking and alcohol consumption.

stem: Plasma osmolality was 261 mosmol/kg (275–295 mosm/kg), and thyroid function testing and cortisol were normal. Urine testing revealed an osmolality of 560 mosmol/kg (500-850 mosm/kg) and a sodium concentration of 55 mmol/l (<20mmol/l). What is the most likely cause of his hyponatraemia?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
explanation:
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) may be secondary to pneumonia. This patient has euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with inappropriately elevated urinary sodium, and normal thyroid and adrenal function, which is diagnostic of SIADH.

Addison’s disease
His potassium is normal, he is euvolaemic and he has SIADH biochemically, making Addison’s disease unlikely.

Kidney disease
Kidney disease is incorrect. Creatinine is normal.

Cardiac failure
This patient is euvolaemic, making cardiac failure unlikely.

Cirrhosis
This patient has no signs of cirrhosis, there are no signs of fluid overload and he has SIADH biochemically.

stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the clinic for review some two weeks after an emergency attendance at the hospital with symptoms of angioedema, for which he received intramuscular (IM) adrenaline and corticosteroids. He was diagnosed with type II diabetes six months earlier and consequently takes several medications, including ramipril, amlodipine, linagliptin, dapagliflozin, atorvastatin and aspirin. This is his third episode of angioedema and he is awaiting referral to the Allergy Clinic. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these episodes of angioedema?
explanation:
Ramipril
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have around five times the risk of angioedema of sodium– glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors, reported in around 1% of patients prescribed them in clinical trials. Episodes of angioedema occur because ACE inhibitors interfere with the metabolism of bradykinin. It is important to note that angioedema can occur at any time after ACE inhibitors are initiated, and it does not necessarily need to occur soon after therapy has commenced. Switching to angiotensin receptor blockers significantly reduces the risk of angioedema occurring.

AmlodipineAspirin
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) including aspirin are associated with angioedema, but this is thought to be less common as a cause than ACE inhibition, because ACE inhibitors prevent metabolism of bradykinin, directly increasing the baseline risk of angioedema. Some epidemiology studies have suggested asthma and nasal polyposis are more prevalent in patients with NSAID/aspirin-related angioedema.

Atorvastatin
The primary concerns about statin use are the development of myositis, which may be subclinical and contribute to increased risk of developing diabetes, or where metabolism is impaired by a drug–drug interaction, clinical myositis with pain and a significant rise in creatinine kinase. In the case of atorvastatin, the main concern is CYP3A4 interaction.

stem: A 37-year-old woman has been brought to the Emergency Department (ED) by her partner with a one day history of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and vomiting. She has a history of type I diabetes mellitus and pernicious anaemia. Her partner tells you that her General Practitioner (GP) has recently prescribed amoxicillin for a chest infection and that she has lost 12.5 kg (nearly 2 stone) in weight over the last few months. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. On examination, she is ﬂushed, disorientated, agitated and jaundiced. Her temperature is 42.1 °C. Her pulse is 180 beats per minute (bpm) and irregular. Her blood pressure (BP) is 180/70 mmHg. You detect a third heart sound, her chest is clear and her abdomen generally tender. Her legs are weak proximally and all reﬂexes brisk. She has some pitting oedema of her lower limbs. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 103 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 17.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 90 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 131 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 2.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 165 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.82 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Bilirubin 64 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l ALT 140 U/l 5–30 U/l ALP 210 U/l 30–150 U/l Glucose 19.8 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Neutrophils 12.6 × 109/l 2.5–7.58 × 109/l MCV 102.4 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ Results of an electrocardiogram (ECG) shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Thyroid storm Her past history of diabetes mellitus and pernicious anaemia makes it more likely that she has a further autoimmune disorder. The history of weight loss suggests an underlying thyroid disorder, with the thyroid storm being precipitated by her chest infection. Thyroid storm is a sudden, life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis. Some series suggest a mortality rate of between 30 and 75%. Its manifestations are due to the action of excess thyroid hormone. Fever is the most characteristic feature, with the temperature often rising above 41°C. There may be evidence of organ damage. The clinical picture is frequently clouded by a secondary infection such as pneumonia or a viral infection. Death may be caused by cardiac arrhythmia (the ECG here shows fast atrial ﬁbrillation), congestive heart failure, hyperthermia or other unidentiﬁed factors. The diagnosis of thyroid storm is made entirely on clinical grounds. The results of thyroid function tests will rarely be available soon enough to make the diagnosis. Propylthiouracil followed by a stable iodine preparation (eg Lugol’s iodine) is usually given. Propranolol, intravenous ﬂuids, dexamethasone and cooling are also often required. Finally, one must remember to treat the precipitating cause. A Atypical pneumonia This is caused by ‘atypical’ pathogens such as M. pneumoniae, Legionella spp, C. pneumonia and C. psittaci. Absence of cough and respiratory signs on physical examination makes this diagnosis unlikely. Incubation period is usually within 10 days, and onset of illness to presentation time is usually within a week. B Diabetic ketoacidosis Diabetic ketoacidosis usually evolves within 24 h. It is characterised by the triad of metabolic acidosis (7.25 or bicarbonate ≤15 mmol/l), hyperglycaemia (>13.9 mmol/l) and ketonemia, (≥3 mmol/l). D Gastroenteritis Symptom onset is usually acute (≤14 days) and weight loss can occur if the diarrhoea becomes persistent (>14–30 days) or chronic (>30 days). E Adverse drug reaction Drug reactions to pencillins are either IgE-mediated or nonIgE-mediated, presenting as immediate (within minutes to hours) or delayed reactions (after days to weeks), respectively. Delayed reactions are more common than immediate reactions. Pruritic or non-pruritic maculo-papular eruptions are a common feature of both types of reaction. Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening immediate reaction that requires emergency treatment. It is characterised by difﬁculty in breathing, bronchospasm, throat tightness, voice change, recurrent vomiting, light-headedness and hypotension.

stem: A 40-year-old man visits an Infertility Clinic on account of inability to sustain an erection. He does have an early morning erection, but when he tries to penetrate his partner, the erection is either too short-lived or too soft to achieve adequate penetration. He has suffered from type 1 diabetes for 30 years. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 155/90 mmHg. He has a normal distribution of pubic and axillary hair, and a normal penis and testes on examination. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 110 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Cholesterol 5.2 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l Triglyceride 2.1 mmol/l 0–1.5 mmol/l HbA1c 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%) < 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Urine Microalbuminuria Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for him?
explanation:
A Sildenaﬁl Given the duration of this patient’s diabetes, the most likely cause of his erectile dysfunction is microvascular disease. As such, moving to oral therapy to improve penile blood ﬂow is an appropriate intervention. In diabetes, high doses of PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenaﬁl may be needed to achieve a therapeutic effect. B Transdermal testosterone Given this man is 40 and has morning erections and normal penis, testes and sexual hair, he is unlikely to be signiﬁcantly

testosterone deﬁcient. Of course it is appropriate to assess testosterone levels as part of the work- up for him, but given it’s likely these are in the normal range, an impact on sexual function wouldn’t be expected. C Psychosexual counselling Although counselling has an important role in managing sexual dysfunction, he is also appropriate for medical intervention. D Additional blood glucose lowering therapy Although tight glycaemic control can stay progression of microvascular disease, reversal of existing damage isn’t seen. E Referral for penile implant This is obviously an intervention of last resort in patients who fail to respond to PDE5 inhibitors and prostaglandinbased therapies.

stem: A 49-year-old woman presents complaining of polydipsia, fatigue and weight loss. She was successfully treated medically for a prolactinoma 3 years ago. It is suspected that she might have type 1 multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN1). Which of the following underlying conditions is she most likely to have?
explanation:
Hyperparathyroidism
In MEN1, hyperparathyroidism is the most common presenting feature, occurring in about 95% of cases. It results from tumours or hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands, which leads to an overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Elevated PTH levels cause increased calcium levels in the blood, leading to symptoms such as polydipsia, fatigue, and weight loss. These symptoms align closely with the patient's complaints, which makes hyperparathyroidism the most likely underlying condition.

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect. This type of cancer is primarily associated with type 2 multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2), not MEN1. MEN2 is characterised by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and primary hyperparathyroidism. Since the question specifically refers to a suspicion of MEN1, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is less relevant to this patient's presentation.

Pancreatic islet cell tumour
While these tumours, including insulinomas and gastrinomas, are part of the MEN1 spectrum, they occur less frequently than hyperparathyroidism. Around 40% of MEN1 patients develop pancreatic islet cell tumours. Although these tumours can cause a variety of symptoms based on the hormones they secrete, the prevalence rate is significantly lower than that of hyperparathyroidism in MEN1, making it a less likely diagnosis in this context.

Pituitary non-functioning adenoma
Although pituitary adenomas are seen in MEN1, they are typically functioning adenomas such as prolactinomas, as evidenced by the patient's history of a prolactinoma. Non-functioning adenomas are less common and often do not cause specific symptoms unless they grow large enough to exert mass effects. Given the patient's previous medical history and current symptoms, hyperparathyroidism or another more common MEN1 manifestation is more likely.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. She has a goitre, palpitations and weight loss, and has most recently developed some blurring of vision. Her TSH is suppressed at <0.05 mU/l. On examination, her BP is 132/82 mmHg, with pulse 90/min and regular. She has a fine tremor and is perspiring at rest. She has significant bilateral proptosis with lid lag and diplopia on lateral gaze. Which of the following therapies for her Graves’ thyroiditis is most likely to worsen her eye disease?
explanation:
Radioiodine
Radioiodine is recognised to worsen thyroid eye disease and, as such, is best avoided until eye disease is stable.

Carbimazole
Carbimazole is incorrect. Carbimazole should not worsen thyroid eye disease significantly, particularly when used as part of a block replace regimen as is usual for Graves’ disease.

Potassium perchlorate
Potassium perchlorate is incorrect. Potassium perchlorate is used as an acute treatment for thyrotoxicosis prior to emergency surgery.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Prednisolone is commonly used to treat thyroid eye disease to reduce inflammation which is worsening the patient’s symptoms. Steroid-sparing agents may be used as an alternative, as may ciclosporin, and there are emerging data to support the use of agents such as rituximab.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with a six month history of headache and visual disturbance. He has a past medical history of poorly controlled hypertension for which he takes multiple agents. He is diagnosed with acromegaly. What would be an appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Cabergoline
Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist that binds the D2 receptor and prevents growth hormone hypersecretion. Alongside somatostatin analogues such as octreotide and lanreotide, it is one of the medical therapies for acromegaly. The definitive and optimum treatment is transphenoidal tumour resection.

Carbimazole
Carbimazole is incorrect. Carbimazole is used in the treatment of hyperthyroidism, and prevents the iodination of thyroglobulin. It has no role in the treatment of acromegaly, for which the definitive management is surgery, but medical options include somatostatin analogues or dopamine agonists (such as carbergoline).

Ketoconazole
Ketoconazole is incorrect. Ketoconazole is an antifungal agent that can be used to prevent cortisol secretion by the adrenal glands. It is therefore one of the medical therapies for Cushing’s syndrome. It has no role in the treatment of acromegaly, for which the definitive management is surgery, but medical options include somatostatin analogues or dopamine agonists (such as carbergoline).

Metyrapone
Metyrapone is incorrect. Metyrapone is occasionally used in the treatment of Cushing’s syndrome as it reduces cortisol secretion by the adrenal glands. It has no role in the treatment of acromegaly, for which the definitive management is surgery, but medical options include somatostatin analogues or dopamine agonists (such as carbergoline).

stem: A 62-year-old man presents to his GP with a 1-year history of bony pain, particularly affecting his left femur, pelvis and lower back; he is otherwise well. Blood tests reveal a serum calcium level of 2.3 mmol/l (NR 2.15– 2.55), phosphate of 1.1 mmol/l (NR 0.8–1.4) and ALP of 192 IU/l (30–130). Full blood count, renal and liver profiles are all normal. X-rays of the femur and pelvis reveal mixed lytic and sclerotic change, with accentuated trabecular markings; chest X-ray is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paget’s disease
High ALP levels, and mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions in a man that is otherwise systemically well. Paget’s disease Paget’s disease is thought to be present in 2% of the population aged over 55 years, with 90% being asymptomatic. It is more common in White populations and rare in populations of African descent. Three phases of radiological changes have been described in Paget’s disease: early disease is said to be primarily lytic, then there are mixed lytic and sclerotic changes, progressing later to primarily sclerotic change with increasing bony thickening. Treatment The goals of treatment are to: Normalise bone turnover Maintain the ALP level within the normal range Minimise symptoms Prevent long-term complications (deafness, which occurs in up to 50% of patients with skull-based Paget’s disease and, very rarely, osteogenic sarcoma) The mainstay of treatment for Paget’s disease has been use of the bisphosphonates.

Metastatic renal cell carcinoma
Metastatic renal cell carcinoma is incorrect. This typically causes lytic lesions. In addition, the man is systemically well and not anaemic.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. This appears radiologically as multiple destructive lytic lesions of the skeleton, as well as severe demineralisation, not mixed lytic and sclerotic lesions. In addition, his calcium is normal; hypercalcaemia is common in myeloma.

Hyperparathyroidism
Hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. His serum calcium and phosphate are normal; in hyperparathyroidism, calcium is high and phosphate is usually low.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 11β-hydroxylase attends the clinic with oligomenorrhoea and hirsutism. She asks you which hormone is responsible for excess coarse hair growth. Which of the following hormones is responsible for hirsutism in non-classical CAH?
explanation:
Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)
Non-classical CAH caused by a deficiency in the enzyme11β-hydroxylase results in the accumulation of adrenal sex steroids, most notably DHEA. Because of the shared pathways of cortisol, mineralocticoids and androgens, patients with CAH present with symptoms due to reduced production of cortisol and either over- or underproduction of mineralocticoids and androgens, depending on the exact enzyme deficiency. With 11βhydroxylase deficiency there is overproduction of androgens.

GnRH
GnRH is incorrect. GnRH elevation is a trigger for puberty itself, when the gland becomes less sensitive to negative feedback from female sex steroids. This promotes a rise in LH and FSH. Low GnRH occurs in hypothalamic hypogonadism due to stress, weight restriction or excessive exercise, and can cause secondary amenorrhoea but not hirsutism.

Oestrogen
Oestrogen is incorrect. Stimulation of oestrogen by LH and FSH surges occurs in puberty but is not involved in hirsutism. A low oestrogen due to primary or secondary hypogonadism can cause oligomenorrhoea and eventually amenorrhoea.

Cortisol
Cortisol is incorrect. Cortisol does not play a role in hirsutism, but patients with Cushing can develop hirsutism. In the presence of excess cortisol or Cushing syndrome, hirsutism can occur due to co-secretion of DHEA.

stem: A 35-year-old man is diagnosed with phaeochromocytoma after being admitted to the Emergency department with severe headaches and worsening blood pressure control. On examination his BP is 185/95 mmHg, despite taking Ramipril 10mg daily. Creatinine is recorded at 135 micromol/l. He is listed for surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention with respect to achieving blood pressure control?
explanation:
Phenoxybenzamine
Full alpha blockade is crucial before surgery to remove a phaeochromocytoma is attempted. Phenoxybenzamine is the agent of choice and should be started at least 7-10 days before surgery.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Calcium channel blockers are not the first choice agent for control of blood pressure in phaeochromocytoma. They would not minimize the potential for catecholamine surge driving severe hypertension, and therefore should only be used after alpha blockade has been initiated.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. If blood pressure control is not achieved with alpha blockade alone, a suitable beta blocker can be added. If beta blockade is started too early then un-opposed alpha stimulation may then precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

Doxazosin
Doxazosin is incorrect. Doxazosin is a less potent alpha blocker than phenoxybenzamine, which is a nonreversible alpha blocker. As such it is not the preferred agent for phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 56-year-old lifelong smoker presents to his GP with a history of cough, breathlessness and weight loss. A chest X-ray is abnormal, with a mass at the right hilum. Which of the following results is most likely to suggest the tumour is a small-cell lung tumour?
explanation:
Serum sodium of 123 mmol/l
Paraneoplastic syndrome in small cell lung cancer can secrete a number of hormones, including antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH). Excess ADH causes SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion). SIADH is characterised by hyponatraemia, low plasma osmolality (normal range is 275-295 mOsm/kg), inappropriately high urinary osmolatlity (>100 mOsm/kg), high urinary sodium (> 30 mmol/L) in the face of clinical euvolaemia.

Serum calcium of 3.3 mmol/l
Serum calcium of 3.3 mmol/l is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia from secretion of parathyroid hormone related protein (PTHrP) is a feature of squamous cell rather than small cell lung cancer.

Serum potassium of 5.5 mmol/l
Serum potassium of 5.5 mmol/L is incorrect. Hyperkalaemia is not a direct manifestation of a paraneoplastic syndrome, but is seen as a result of adrenal metastases.

Plasma osmolality of 335 mOsm/kg
Plasma osmolality of 335 mOsm/kg is incorrect. SIADH causes low osmolality. Serum osmolality can be calculated using the formula: 2 (Na + K +) + urea + glucose. Low sodium in SIADH gives low serum osmolality of <275 mOsm/kg.

Urine osmolality of 80 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality of 80 mOsm/kg is incorrect. In SIADH, there is retention of free water due to ADH. This causes concentration of urine. Urine osmolality could be frankly elevated (>500 mOsm/kg). When serum is very dilute, physiological adaptation would be to excrete even more dilute urine so as to restore serum osmolality. Any urine osmolality greater than 100 mOsm/kg is therefore ‘inappropriate’. The 100 mOsm/kg cut-off is a diagnostic criterion for SIADH. Urine osmolality of 80 mOsm/kg is ‘appropriate’ excretion of dilute urine. The picture is suggestive of psychogenic polydipsia.

stem: A 51-year-old man presents to Emergency Department with altered consciousness. His blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, his skin is pigmented and he has a past history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. His family says that he has been tired for several months and has been losing weight and complaining of abdominal pain. Which of the following results is most likely to be found on investigation?
explanation:
Serum sodium level of 116 mmol/l
The clinical picture of an unwell patient with weight loss, abdominal pain, low blood pressure, mucocutaneous pigmentation and history of an autoimmune disease is highly suggestive of Addison’s disease. The classical biochemistry is hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, raised urea (due to dehydration) and hypoglycaemia. Addison’s disease may be associated with eosinophilia.

Laboratory glucose level of 12.3 mmol/l
Laboratory glucose level of 12.3 mmol/l is incorrect. Addison’s disease is often complicated by hypoglycaemia.

Flattened T waves on electrocardiography
Flattened T waves on electrocardiography ‘Flattened T waves on electrocardiography’ is incorrect. Hyperkalaemia is a feature of Addison’s disease and are more likely to present as peaked T waves.

Serum potassium level of 2.4 mmol/l
Serum potassium level of 2.4 mmol/l is incorrect. Hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia, is a feature of Addison’s disease.

Serum urea level of 3.2 mmol/l
Serum urea level of 3.2 mmol/l is incorrect. Addison’s disease is associated with volume depletion and dehydration through loss of salt and water. Vomiting is often a feature of an acute crisis, leading to further dehydration.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents for review 6 months after first being diagnosed with type 2 diabetes; he has been taking metformin 2.5g/day since diagnosis. His body mass index (BMI) is 30 kg/m 2. Despite having intentionally lost about 7 kg in weight, his morning blood sugars are still around 9 mmol/l; HbA1c is 68 mmol/mol (8.4%). He is hypertensive and dyslipidemic, and is taking ramipril and atorvastatin. Which of the following therapies would be the best choice for his hyperglycaemia and obesity in addition to the metformin?
explanation:
Dapagliflozin
This man is obese and has suboptimally controlled diabetes on metformin. Dapagaliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, will glycaemic control, in addition to promoting weight loss, lowering blood pressure and improving lipid profile.

Insulin degludec
Insulin degludec is incorrect as insulin is usually fourth-line therapy in type 2 diabetes. It will not benefit his obesity as it will cause weight gain.

Glibenclamide
Glibenclamide is incorrect as this is an old sulphonylurea with a poor side-effect profile that is no longer routinely prescribed.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect as although it can be used second-line in type 2 diabetes, it will promote weight gain, not weight loss.

Acarbose
Acarbose is incorrect as it is very poorly tolerated and has been removed from treatment guidelines. SGLT2 is a protein in humans that facilitates glucose reabsorption in the kidney; SGLT2 inhibitors block the reabsorption of glucose in the kidney, increase glucose excretion and lower blood glucose levels. SGLT2 is a low-affinity, high-capacity glucose transporter located in the proximal tubule in the kidneys; it is responsible for 90% of glucose reabsorption. Inhibition of SGLT2 leads to the decrease in blood glucose due to the increase in renal glucose excretion. The mechanism of action of this new class of drugs also offers further glucose control by allowing increased insulin sensitivity and uptake of glucose in the muscle cells, decreased gluconeogenesis and improved first-phase insulin release from the beta cells. Vaginal yeast infections and urinary tract infections are the most common side-effects. They also cause significant lowering of HbA1c without increased risk of hypoglycaemia, reduction of body weight and reduction of systolic blood pressure. In addition, the EMPA-REG trial showed that empagliflozin significantly reduced deaths among individuals with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease when compared with placebo.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to her GP after the birth of her second child. She complains of extreme tiredness and a persistent hoarse voice that she is having problems shaking off. Although she is breastfeeding her child, she is failing to lose her pregnancy weight. Thyroid autoantibodies are negative; her thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH) level is 12 mU/l, with a free T4 (FT 4) of 5 pmol/l. There is no thyroid tenderness on examination. Her GP notes that her pulse is only 52 bpm. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Post-partum thyroiditis
She is hypothyroid, after the birth of her child, with negative antibodies, all of which is suggestive of postpartum thyroiditis. Post-partum thyroiditis may also be with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. Given the symptoms and history of recent pregnancy will definitely go for post-partum thyroiditis.

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is incorrect as she is post-partum and her thyroid autoantibodies are negative.

Toxic multinodular goitre
Toxic multinodular goitre is incorrect as this is associated with hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

Iodine deficiency
Iodine deficiency is extremely rare and does not occur in the Western world.

Graves’ disease
Graves’ disease is incorrect as this is associated with hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. Post-partum thyroiditis Post-partum thyroiditis is a common thyroid disorder that presents during the first post-partum year. It is the occurrence of either transient hyperthyroidism, transient hypothyroidism or transient hyperthyroidism followed by transient hypothyroidism. Most, but not all, women are euthyroid 1 year post-partum. It is an exacerbation of an underlying autoimmune thyroiditis, aggravated by the immunological rebound that follows the partial immunosuppression of pregnancy. Women who express human leukocyte antigen haplotypes DR3, DR4 and DR5 have an increased risk for post-partum thyroiditis. In women who develop post-partum thyroiditis, CD4 +/CD8 + and CD4 + 2H4 + ratios are elevated throughout pregnancy and post-partum. Histologically, thyroid aspirates reveal either a lymphocytic infiltrate or diffuse destruction, changes similar to those seen in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Treatment Hyperthyroidism: Symptomatic treatment with beta blockers. Hypothyroidism: Consider T4 treatment if symptomatic or TSH > 10. Useful external websites Stagnaro-Green A. 2002. Postpartum thyroiditis. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, 87, 9, 4042– 4047.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with extreme lethargy 6 weeks after the birth of her third child. Her pregnancy was uneventful, but she has a history of hypothyroidism and post-partum depression. She complains of fatigue, nausea and dizziness, along with symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI). The GP prescribes antibiotics; however, 3 days later she is brought to the Emergency Department via ambulance after collapsing at home. She is found to have a blood pressure of 80/52 mmHg, a Na + concentration of 127 mmol/l, a K + concentration of 5.9 mmol/l and a urea of 12 mmol/l. You note increased skin pigmentation. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Addison’s disease
She has evidence of primary hypoadrenalism. Her hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia are suggestive of both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. Secondary adrenal insufficiency from a central cause (ie in Sheehan syndrome) would not cause hyperkalaemia as aldosterone production is intact. Other clues to the diagnosis are the intercurrent illness (UTI), which has caused the Addisonian crisis, and her history of autoimmune hypothyroidism.

Sheehan syndrome
Sheehan syndrome is incorrect. The hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypotension are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency. Secondary adrenal insufficiency from a central cause would not cause hyperkalaemia as aldosterone production is intact.

Prolactinoma
Prolactinoma is incorrect. She has no galactorrhoea. In addition, the acute and severe nature of her symptoms does not fit with prolactinoma.

Postnatal depression
Postnatal depression is incorrect. This is because of her abnormal blood tests and severe physical symptoms.

Thyrotoxicosis
Thyrotoxicosis is incorrect. Her abnormal blood tests and severe acute illness do not fit with thyrotoxicosis. Primary adrenal insufficiency (PAI) PAI is defined by the inability of the adrenal cortex to produce sufficient amounts of glucocorticoids and/or mineralocorticoids. PAI is a severe and potentially life-threatening condition, due to the central role of these hormones in energy, salt and fluid homoeostasis. Acute management of adrenal crisis Patients with suspected adrenal crisis should be treated with an immediate parenteral injection of 100 mg hydrocortisone, followed by appropriate fluid resuscitation and 200 mg (50–100 mg/m2 for children) of hydrocortisone/24 h (via continuous IV therapy or 6-hourly injection) Long-term treatment The mainstay of treatment is steroid replacement – hydrocortisone (15–25 mg) or cortisone acetate (20–35 mg) – in two or three divided oral doses per day; the highest dose should be given in the morning at waking, the next in the early afternoon. In addition, all patients with confirmed aldosterone deficiency receive mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone. Clinical features of Adrenal Insufficiency and Adrenal Crisis Signs Routine Laboratory Tests Fatigue Hyperpigmentation (primary only), particularly of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, mucosal membranes, scars, areola of breast Hyponatremia Weight loss Low blood pressure with increased postural drop Hyperkalemia Postural dizziness Failure to thrive in children Uncommon: hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia Symptoms Adrenal insufficiency Adrenal crisis Severe weakness Hyponatremia Syncope Hypotension Hyperkalemia Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting; may mimic acute abdomen Abdominal tenderness/guarding Hypoglycemia Back pain Reduced consciousness, delirium Hypercalcemia Confusion Useful external websites Bornstein S R, Allolio B, Arlt W, Barthel A, Don-Wauchope A, Hammer, G D, et al. 2016. Diagnosis and treatment of primary adrenal insufficiency: An Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, 101, 2, 364–389.

stem: A 52 year old woman visits your surgery wishing to discuss hormone replacement therapy (HRT). She is suffering from severe hot flushes, sweats and vaginal dryness. She is requesting further information about the side effects of HRT. What is the most frequently recorded side effect of HRT?
explanation:
Breast tenderness
This is a common side effect of oestrogen treatment, along with bloating, nausea, leg cramps, headache.

Breast cancer
Breast cancer is incorrect as the lifetime risk of developing breast cancer significantly increases with current long-term HT when it is started in women aged 50 years or older and relative risk is 1.35. It is not the most common side effect.

Decreased bone mineral density
Decreased bone mineral density is incorrect as bone mineral density increases with HRT.

Venous thromboembolism
Venous thromboembolism is incorrect as this is relatively rare. The risk of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in 15 per 10,000 women per year.

Cholelithiasis
Cholelithiasis is incorrect as the annual incidence for any gallbladder event was 78 events per 10,000 personyears for women taking estrogen-only preparations versus 47 events per 10,000 person-years for placebo. He takes regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatories for osteoarthritis of both knees. He is tanned with multiple spider naevi across the upper chest and one finger breadth hepatomegaly. stem: A 26-year-old man is referred for gastroscopy because of a history of several months of dyspepsia, for which he has been taking over the counter antacids. His primary care physician carries out routine blood tests and he is found to have a serum calcium level of 3.2 mmol/l (NR 2.1–2.7 mmol/l) with a venous bicarbonate level of 33 mmol/l (NR 18–23 mmol/l); phosphate levels, renal and liver function, and chest X-ray are all normal. What is the most likely cause of his hypercalcaemia?
explanation:
Milk–alkali syndrome
Milk–alkali syndrome is the most likely cause of hypercalcaemia in this patient. This syndrome results from the excessive intake of calcium and absorbable alkali, often due to the overuse of calcium-containing antacids for dyspepsia. The elevated bicarbonate level (33 mmol/l) is indicative of metabolic alkalosis, which is a hallmark of milk–alkali syndrome. Additionally, the patient's young age and the absence of other significant symptoms or abnormalities in renal and liver function tests support this diagnosis.

Myeloma
Myeloma is unlikely in this patient due to several factors. First, myeloma typically presents in older individuals, and this patient is only 26 years old. Additionally, myeloma often presents with symptoms such as bone pain, anaemia, and renal impairment, none of which are noted in this case. Furthermore, the elevated bicarbonate level does not align well with the metabolic profile usually seen in myeloma patients, who often have renal dysfunction and hypercalcaemia due to bone resorption.

Metastatic malignancy
Metastatic malignancy is an improbable cause in this young patient. Most cases of hypercalcaemia due to metastatic malignancy are found in older patients with known primary cancer, which this patient does not have. Symptoms commonly associated with malignancy, such as weight loss, fatigue, or localised pain, are not reported here. Additionally, the normal chest X-ray and other blood tests do not support the presence of a malignancy causing hypercalcaemia.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is less likely, given the patient's normal phosphate levels. Typically, primary hyperparathyroidism presents with hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. Although primary hyperparathyroidism can occur in younger individuals, especially in the context of MEN1 syndrome, it is more commonly diagnosed in older adults. The patient's elevated bicarbonate level also does not fit well with the usual biochemical profile of primary hyperparathyroidism.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is an unlikely cause, given the patient's normal chest X-ray. Sarcoidosis often presents with bilateral hilar adenopathy, which is not observed here. Severe hypercalcaemia, such as a serum calcium level of 3.2 mmol/l, is uncommon in sarcoidosis. Furthermore, sarcoidosis typically affects individuals between the ages of 20 and 40, but the lack of other clinical signs or symptoms associated with sarcoidosis, such as respiratory issues or skin lesions, makes this diagnosis less probable. stem: A 40-year-old man is having routine blood tests completed as part of pre-employment health screening; he is well with no complaints. He is noted to have serum calcium concentration of 2.85 mmol/l (NR 2.2–2.6), normal phosphate, urea, Cr, vitamin D and PTH levels. His urinary calcium excretion is 12 mg/24 h (NR 100–250 mg/24 h). There is no history of renal stones, pancreatitis, depression or any prior illness. He is referred to an endocrine surgeon for consideration of parathyroidectomy. Which one of the following is true regarding the diagnosis this case?
options: Surgery is the appropriate treatment to cure his condition
It is unusual that he does not have any symptoms of hypercalcaemia
Inheritance of his condition is autosomal dominant
Acute pancreatitis is commonly associated with his condition
His calcium receptors have increased ability to sense raised calcium levels
explanation:
Inheritance of his condition is autosomal dominant
The diagnosis in this case is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH), because of his moderately high calcium in combination with low urinary calcium excretion. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia Hypercalcaemia is a potentially life-threatening condition; however, FHH is a rare, lifelong, benign condition. It is important to separate this condition from other causes of hypercalcaemia, such as hypercalcaemia of malignancy and primary hyperparathyroidism. Most cases are associated with loss-of-function mutations in the CaSR gene, which encodes a calcium-sensing receptor expressed in parathyroid and kidney tissue. The perceived lack of calcium levels by the parathyroid leads to constitutively high levels of parathyroid hormone and therefore hypercalcaemia; however, PTH can be normal. It has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. No treatment is generally required, as bone demineralisation and kidney stones are relatively uncommon in the condition. Useful Mnemonics/memory tools CHIMPANZEES for causes of hypercalcaemia.

Surgery is the appropriate treatment to cure his condition
Surgery is the appropriate treatment to cure his condition is incorrect. The diagnosis in this case is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, which is not treated with surgery; surgical treatment should be reserved for patients with severe complications.

It is unusual that he does not have any symptoms of hypercalcaemia
It is unusual that he does not have any symptoms of hypercalcaemia is incorrect. His hypercalcaemia is moderate and lifelong, and patients with FHH often have no symptoms.

Acute pancreatitis is commonly associated with his condition
Acute pancreatitis is commonly associated with his condition is incorrect. Pancreatitis is rare in FHH. There have been case reports, but the majority of people have mild/moderate hypercalcaemia with few symptoms. Calcium Homeostasis, Vitamin D and HypercalcaemiaHis calcium receptors have increased ability to sense raised calcium levels
His calcium receptors have increased ability to sense raised calcium levels is incorrect. The opposite is true, he likely has FHH, in which calcium sensing receptors do not sense changes in serum calcium.

stem: A 52-year-old businessman undergoes a routine medical examination as part of his company's health programme. He has no symptoms, although he is obese with a BMI of 31. His blood tests, performed on a fasting venous sample, show a serum glucose concentration of 7.1 mmol/l. This is repeated by his GP 2 days later and again is 7.1 mmol/l. How would you interpret this result?
explanation:
Diabetes mellitus
This patient has a fasting plasma glucose consistently above 7.0 mmol/l. Although he has no symptoms, this most likely represents a diagnosis of Type 2 diabetes given his significant obesity. A random sample greater than 11.1 or a glucose level >11.1 mmol/l, 2 h after a meal, is also consistent with a diagnosis of diabetes. An HbA1c level of >48mmol/mol (>6.5%) has now been added as an additional diagnostic criterion.

Normal results
Normal results is incorrect. A fasting plasma glucose >6.0 mmol/l is considered abnormal.

Impaired glucose tolerance
Impaired glucose tolerance is incorrect. Impaired glucose tolerance is defined as a blood glucose value between 7.8 and 11.1 mmol/l, 2 h after an oral glucose tolerance test.

Impaired fasting glucose
Impaired fasting glucose is incorrect. Impaired fasting glucose is defined as a glucose level between 6.1 and 6.9 mmol/l.

Simple obesity
Simple obesity is incorrect. The elevated fasting glucose seen here is inconsistent with simple obesity. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A patient with long-standing type 2 diabetes is found to have a urinary albumin excretion rate of 300 mg/l. His diabetes is well controlled on metformin and he is normotensive with a blood pressure of 122/82. His pulse is 65 and regular. Abdomen is soft and non-tender; BMI is elevated at 32. HbA1c is 56 mmol/mol. What of the following medications is most useful in reducing further progression of nephropathy?
explanation:
Lisinopril
Treatment with ACE inhibitors in patients with type 1 diabetes who are normotensive to slow progression of nephropathy is long established clinical practice. Smaller studies have also demonstrated in Type 2 diabetes that, even in normal blood pressure, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have similar benefit. As such it is the most appropriate intervention here.

Diltiazem
Diltiazem is incorrect. Diltiazem has been shown to reduce proteinuria in patients with diabetic nephropathy, but would be an alternative choice in patients who are unable to tolerate an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), or where these are contraindicated.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Sulfonylureas in this situation may exacerbate further weight gain and increase the risk of hypoglycaemia, with relatively limited benefit in further reducing HbA1c.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is incorrect. Dihydropyridine calcium antagonists are much less effective in reducing proteinuria versus ACE inhibitors, verapamil or dilitiazem.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Glitazones have a disadvantage in this situation that they would exacerbate weight gain. There are, however, data to suggest a modest positive impact on progression of renal disease in patients with Type 2 diabetes. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A 22-year-old man with diabetes mellitus comes to the clinic for review. He tells you he has recently moved to the area and been told that he has maturity onset diabetes of the young, (MODY). Which of the following features in his history would lead you to suspect that he is correct?
options: Failure to respond initially to gliclazide
explanation:
Family history of diabetes
A strong family history of diabetes is almost always seen. MODY3 is common, and results from HNF-1alpha mutation.

BMI of 32
BMI of 32 is incorrect. MODY occurs in individuals of normal weight

Failure to respond initially to gliclazide
Failure to respond initially to gliclazide is incorrect. Patients with MODY 3 may be controlled for a significant period of time with sulphonylureas, and indeed some of those miss-diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes can be transferred back from insulin to sulphonylurea therapy.

Frequent admissions with DKA
Frequent admissions with DKA is incorrect. MODY is not usually associated with symptoms of insulinopaenia.

Initial requirement for insulin therapy
Initial requirement for insulin therapy is incorrect. Patients with MODY may be managed initially with diet or oral hypoglycaemics before progression to insulin therapy. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: You are reviewing a 45-year-old man who has type 2 diabetes. He works a varying shift pattern as a taxi driver and has not tolerated metformin therapy due to gastrointestinal side effects. You decide that the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin is the most appropriate therapy choice. Which of the following is correct with regard to SGLT2 inhibitor therapy?
options: It acts by reducing hepatic glucose output
It acts primarily by reducing peripheral insulin resistance
It is associated with slightly increased blood pressure
It is useful in type 1 diabetes
It is associated with reduced cardiovascular risk
explanation:
It is associated with reduced cardiovascular risk
In the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial, the effects of empagliflozin were examined on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes at high risk for cardiovascular events. Patients with type 2 diabetes at high risk for cardiovascular events who received empagliflozin, as compared with placebo, had a lower rate of the primary composite cardiovascular outcome and of death from any cause when the study drug was added to standard care.

It acts by reducing hepatic glucose output
It acts by reducing hepatic glucose output is incorrect. SGLT2 inhibitors block the reabsorption of glucose in the kidney, increasing glucose excretion.

It acts primarily by reducing peripheral insulin resistance
It acts primarily by reducing peripheral insulin resistance is incorrect. SGLT2 inhibitors block the reabsorption of glucose in the kidney, increasing glucose excretion.

It is associated with slightly increased blood pressure
It is associated with slightly increased blood pressure is incorrect. It causes modest blood pressure reduction.

It is useful in type 1 diabetes
Whilst there have been several trials in type 1 diabetes, there is a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis which has prevented the widespread use of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents to the clinic with diabetes mellitus which was identified after he visited the GP with tiredness and lethargy. His fasting glucose was measured at 9.2 mmol/l and on further questioning he admits to nocturia. On examination his BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. His BMI is 26 kg/m 2. Urinalysis reveals ketonuria. Which of the following is the strongest pointer towards a diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes?
explanation:
Ketonuria
Ketonuria is indicative of insulinopaenia, and thus a strong indication of a diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes.

Age
Age is incorrect. Type 1 diabetes is increasingly diagnosed in the older population, and Type 2 diabetes is now recognised in children as young as 5 years of age, such that age is not a strong pointer as to the underlying pathology.

Anti-GAD antibodies
Anti-GAD antibodies is incorrect. Single autoantibody positivity is not necessarily indicative of a diagnosis of Type 1 diabetes, two or three antibody positivity being a much stronger pointer towards significant autoimmune beta cell destruction.

BMI
BMI is incorrect. Whilst loss in weight is indicative of insulinopaenia, baseline BMI is not a strong pointer to either Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes.

Nocturia
Nocturia is incorrect. Nocturia is not differentiating and is merely a sign of hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis. Diabetes - Type I.

stem: A 51-year-old woman presents to her GP for routine assessment of her diabetes. She was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes 9 months ago and has been treated with metformin 2 g. Past history of note is an inferior myocardial infarction some five years earlier. Her BMI is 32 kg/m 2; BP is 152/92, her HbA1c is measured at 64 mmol/mol (8%). Which would be an appropriate choice for this woman’s diabetes management?
explanation:
Commence an SGLT2 inhibitor
In a patient with hypertension, a previous MI and who is significantly overweight / obese, an SGLT-2 inhibitor has the advantage of reducing glucose, modest positive effects on weight loss, and some blood pressure lowering effects and is therefore the optimal choice.

Commence long-acting basal insulin
Commence long-acting basal insulin is incorrect. Insulin is third- or fourth-line treatment for Type 2 diabetes, and in this situation would drive significant weight gain and may even then not achieve blood glucose target.

Commence a GLP-1 agonist
Commence a GLP-1 agonist is incorrect. This would potentially be an option in this patient in the event they failed to gain glycaemic control on a second oral agent.

Commence a DPP-IV inhibitor
Commence a DPP-IV inhibitor is incorrect. This is an alternative to an SGLT-2 inhibitor, but the SGLT-2 inhibitor is preferred because it is associated with modest weight loss and BP lowering and may have positive effects on CV outcomes.

Commence a sulphonylurea
Commence a sulphonylurea is incorrect. This would be an inappropriate choice of medication in this case because of increasing the risk of weight gain and hypoglycaemia. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: His vision is 6/6 bilaterally and fundoscopy reveals neovascularisation at the optic disc. Which of the following is the most important next step in his clinical management?
explanation:
Referral for laser photocoagulation
Although tighter blood pressure and glucose control might reduce the risk of further deterioration with respect to microvascular complications, this patient is at imminent risk of a vitreous haemorrhage as a result of newvessel formation. Laser photocoagulation to reduce the development of friable new vessels is the optimal intervention here, followed by modification of risk factors for both macrovascular and future microvascular complications. This should involve smoking cessation advice, blood pressure control, optimisation of lipid profiles and glycaemic control.

Smoking cessation advice
Smoking is a very important and established risk factor for both microvascular and macrovascular disease. Smoking cessation should be offered at every clinical appointment, and specialist referral to smoking cessation services offered when possible. In this setting the risk of an imminent retinal haemorrhage, calls for immediate referral to ophthalmology and vascular risk factor modification should be initiated at a later date.

Transition to insulin therapy
According to the NICE guidelines on the management of type II diabetes, there are additional options using add-on or alternative oral hyperglycaemic agents for the management of suboptimal glycaemic control before transitioning to insulin therapy. In this clinical scenario, the priority is urgent laser photocoagulation to prevent a retinal haemorrhage and irreversible visual loss.

Add indapamide to his regime
Although this patient could benefit from further tightening of blood pressure control, the imminent risk of vitreal haemorrhage drives us towards laser therapy as the most appropriate next step. For blood pressure control addition of indapamide is an appropriate option.

Add doxazosin to his regime
Blood pressure control to a target of 140/80 mmHg, and a target of 130/80 mmHg for patients with established nephropathy or renal disease, is warranted in all patients with type II diabetes as per NICE guidance. In this case a blood pressure of 145/85 mmHg was recorded. As ‘white coat’ hypertension is common, it would be preferable to arrange serial blood pressure readings or a 24 h blood pressure monitor, to confirm suboptimal blood pressure before escalating treatment. Furthermore, the priority in this case is urgent ophthalmology assessment and treatment. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to you for a repeat prescription. She has had hypertension since her last pregnancy at the age 30 and has been maintained on clonidine 0.2 mg twice a day. She gets headaches, dyspnoea on exertion; swelling of her feet and orthopnoea, but denies chest pain. Her father is also being treated for hypertension. She does not smoke. She is five foot seven inches tall and weighs 95 kg. Her BP is 180/110 mm Hg, pulse is 92 bpm. The rest of her examination is remarkable for hypertensive retinopathy, bibasilar rales and 1+ pitting oedema bilaterally. Initial lab results were normal except for a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/l (normal range 3.5–5.0 mmol/l) and serum bicarbonate of 33 mmol/l (22–28 mmol/l). You correct the hypokalaemia and obtain a random serum aldosterone level of 25 ng/dl (5–30 ng/dl) with a plasma renin activity of 0.5 ng/ml/h (1.6–7.4 ng/ml/h) while the patient is on a normal diet. What additional tests might be appropriate?
options: Adrenal computed tomography, adrenal vein sampling and 18-hydroxycorticosterone testing
explanation:
Adrenal computed tomography, adrenal vein sampling and 18-hydroxycorticosterone testing
Primary aldosteronism, a disorder characterised by hypertension, hypokalaemia, suppressed plasma renin activity and increased aldosterone secretion, affects 0.05–2% of the hypertensive population. This disorder should be suspected in hypertensive patients in whom spontaneous or easily provoked hypokalaemia develops that is slow to correct after discontinuation of diuretics. As important as recognising the presence of primary aldosteronism is the differentiation of lesions that are surgically curable (60–70% of the cases in some series) from those that are best treated medically. In this patient, the presence of hypertension, hypokalaemia and alkalosis appropriately triggered screening for hyperaldosteronism, which led to the findings of an aldosterone–renin ratio of greater than 30, which constitutes a positive screening test. Aldosteronism can be confirmed by the finding of a 24-hour urine aldosterone secretion of 12 µg in the salt-replete state. Adrenal imaging is the next step to differentiate adrenal adenoma from adrenal hyperplasia, although adenomas smaller than 1.5 cm can be missed and so mistaken for hyperplasia. In confusing cases, adrenal vein sampling for aldosterone measurements is used to localise adenoma (with 95% accuracy). The finding of a lateralising 10 : 1 aldosterone ratio in the presence of a symmetrical adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) induced cortisol rise diagnoses and localises an adenoma. Other features suggestive of adenoma include a plasma 18-hydroxycorticosterone of 100 ng/dl or more, spontaneous hypokalaemia of less than 3 mmol/l and an anomalous postural decrease of plasma aldosterone concentration. Saline loading would be inappropriate in this patient because of her heart failure and hypertensive retinopathy.

Adrenal computed tomography
Adrenal computed tomography (CT) is incorrect. Adrenal CT may demonstrate an adenoma, but without adrenal vein sampling it’s inadequate to confirm a diagnosis of Conn’s.

Adrenal vein sampling
Adrenal vein sampling is incorrect. Adrenal vein sampling is invasive and wouldn’t be considred without confirmatory radiology.

18-Hydroxycorticosterone
18-hydroxycorticosterone is incorrect. 18-hydroxycorticosterone is a confirmatory test, but should be used in the context of radiology and adrenal vein sampling.

Saline loading test
Saline loading test is incorrect. Saline loading should be avoided, given that this patient has a history of heart failure. Potassium Imbalance A 61-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease presents to the clinic with worsening bony aches and pains over the past few months. He has a history of hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction and takes Lisinopril, Amlodipine, Rosuvastatin and BD mixed insulin. His BP is 148/90 mmHg, pulse is 74/min and regular, there are no heart murmurs. His chest is clear and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Investigations;.

stem: A 64-year-old man with type 1 diabetes for 45 years presents for review. He has poor control, HbA1C 75 mmol/mol (9%) and he takes a multiple daily injection regimen of insulin. He complains of multiple areas of skin changes on his abdomen. On examination, he has areas of severe lipohypertrophy. Which of the following is the likely cause of his lipohypertrophy?
options: Repeated insulin injection into the same site
explanation:
Repeated insulin injection into the same site
Repeated injection of insulin into the same sites results in local lipohypertrophy and consequent erratic absorption of the drug. This in itself can lead to poor diabetic control. Patients should be encouraged to rotate their sites.

Formation of anti-insulin antibodies
This is an adverse immunological side effect of insulin therapy is incorrect. Lipoatrophy, not hypertrophy, is an adverse immunological side effect of insulin therapy. This is seen infrequently nowadays with the advent of recombinant and analogue insulins.

Incorrect injection depth
Injection depth has no relevance with respect to risk of lipohypertrophy. It’s repeated injection into the same site which leads to the problem.

Concomitant use of metformin
There is limited evidence to support use of metformin in patients with type 1 diabetes. In patients with type 2 diabetes who are maintained on insulin it may help limit some of the associated weight gain.

Local pressure from clothing
Local pressure from clothing has no impact on the development of lipohypertrophy. Diabetes - Type I.

stem: A 27-year-old woman, with Type 1 diabetes mellitus since the age of 3, attends for her routine review and says she wishes to become pregnant. She has a HbA1c of 79 mmol/mol (9.4%). She has a history of mild nonproliferative retinopathy and sensory neuropathy. She has a microalbumin:creatinine ratio of 2.3. Her only medication is an insulin pump. Which of the following factors would be most likely to result in a poor pregnancy outcome if she were to become pregnant?
options: She has not been taking folic acid
explanation:
HbA1c of 79 mmol/mol (9.4%)
Observational studies show an increased risk of diabetic embryopathy, especially anencephaly, microcephaly and congenital heart disease, which increases directly with elevations in HbA1C. Spontaneous abortion is also increased in the setting of uncontrolled diabetes.

Mild non-proliferative retinopathy
Mild non-proliferative retinopathy is incorrect. Although pregnancy has been shown to be associated with progression of retinopathy, it is elevated HbA1C at baseline and the magnitude of improvement of glucose control that are associated with a higher risk of progression of retinopathy. She should be counselled about obtaining excellent metabolic control before conception to avoid this increase in risk, not to avoid pregnancy because of the retinopathy.

She has not been taking folic acid
She has not been taking folic acid is incorrect. Although preconception high-dose folic acid is important to reduce risk of congenital malformations, her very high HbA1C will likely result in a poor pregnancy outcome and is the most important factor.

Microalbumin:creatinine ratio of 2.3
Microalbumin:creatinine ratio of 2.3 is incorrect. This is a normal ratio. Nephropathy can also progress during pregnancy, but microalbuminuria would not be a contraindication to pregnancy.

Sensory neuropathy
Sensory neuropathy is incorrect. Although this can progress during pregnancy, it would not be a contraindication to pregnancy. Diabetes in pregnancy (see American Diabetes Association [ADA] guidelines) Pregestational diabetes confers greater risk on both mother and baby: all women of childbearing age with diabetes should be counselled about the importance of strict glycaemic control before conception and throughout pregnancy. Observational studies show an increased risk of diabetic embryopathy, especially anencephaly, microcephaly, and congenital heart disease, which increases directly with elevations in A1c. For women with pre-existing Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes who become pregnant, the following are recommended as optimal glycaemic goals, if they can be achieved without excessive hypoglycaemia: Pre-meal, bedtime and overnight glucose 3.3–5.4 mmol/l Peak postprandial glucose 5.4–7.1 mmol/l A1c < 6.0% Useful external websites American Diabetes Association. 2015. 12. Management of diabetes in pregnancy. Diabetes Care, 38, Suppl. 1, S77–S79. ( Diabetes - Type I A 63-year-old woman who is treated with long-term haemodialysis for renal failure related to type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. She complains of persistent tiredness and lethargy, and generalised bony aches and pains. She also has extreme thirst, which means it is very hard for her to stick to her fluid intake limit. She takes a number of medications including vitamin D, calcium supplements and a phosphate binder. She is pale and thin, with a BMI of 21. Her BP is 155/85 mmHg. Investigations;.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for her annual review. Her glycaemic control has deteriorated over the past year despite having taken part in the DAFNE programme, and she has evidence of early peripheral diabetic neuropathy. Her visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes. Which of the following findings on retinal photography would warrant making an urgent referral to an ophthalmologist?
options: Hard exudates five disc diameters lateral to the optic disc
More than five blot haemorrhages anywhere in the retina
More than five microaneurysms in the macular area
explanation:
Neovascularisation near the optic disc
New vessels near the disc are likely to rupture and cause vitreous haemorrhage. They warrant urgent, not routine, referral to an ophthalmologist with a view to laser photocoagulation treatment.

Hard exudates five disc diameters lateral to the optic disc
Hard exudates five disc diameters lateral to the optic disc is incorrect. Hard exudates are a feature of background diabetic retinopathy. They do not specifically require ophthalmological referral unless they are within one disc diameter of the macula, because in this case they can be associated with macular oedema and considered sight threatening. Treatments for macular oedema include both laser photocoagulation and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitors.

More than five blot haemorrhages anywhere in the retina
More than five blot haemorrhages anywhere in the retina is incorrect. Like hard exudates, blot haemorrhages are considered a feature of background diabetic retinopathy.

More than five microaneurysms in the macular area
More than five microaneurysms in the macular area is incorrect. Microaneurysms are considered a sign of background retinopathy; as such they do not require emergency referral here unless there are also hard exudates.

Scattered cotton-wool spots
Scattered cotton-wool spots is incorrect. These are consistent with background diabetic retinopathy. In this case tighter control of blood pressure and blood glucose are most important. Diabetes - Type I.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of deteriorating physical performance at work, associated with dysarthria and clumsiness. On examination he looks anaemic and has hepatomegaly and Kayser–Fleischer rings in the cornea. What would be the next appropriate investigation to support the suspected clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Serum caeruloplasmin level
Serum caeruloplasmin can be measured enzymatically (copper oxidase), by radial immunodiffusion or by reverse passive haemagglutination. The activity and concentration of this glycoprotein is reduced or absent (<200 mg/l) in 95% of patients with Wilson’s disease. It is a sensitive, minimally invasive test and so is the preferred screening test.

CT of the brain
CT of the brain is incorrect. MRI is superior to CT for the detection of basal ganglia abnormality in Wilson’s disease, and therefore CT is not a sensitive screening test.

MRI of the brain
MRI of the brain is incorrect. MRI can show some abnormalities in patients with Wilson’s disease, due to deposition of copper in the basal ganglia. Typical MRI features include; bilateral T 2 hyperintensity involving putamen, thalami and brainstem. However, this is not always present and so is not a sensitive screening test.

Liver biopsy
Liver biopsy is incorrect. In the absence of Kayser-Fleischer rings or neurological abnormalities, a liver biopsy for quantitative copper determination would be essential to establish a diagnosis of Wilson’s disease, but this would probably not be necessary here given the typical clinical picture.

C-reactive protein level
C-reactive protein level is incorrect. C-reactive protein is sensitive but has low specificity, as it can be elevated in infection or any form of chronic or acute inflammation, and so would not be helpful here. Wilson’s.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with deteriorating vision affecting his right eye over the past 24 h. He has a history of type 2 diabetes for which he takes metformin and gliclazide, and is also medicated for hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. On examination he has count fingers vision in his right eye, and 6/12 vision in his left eye. His BP is 155/85 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Fundoscopy reveals a segmental pattern of flame-shaped haemorrhages limited to the lower outer quadrant of the retina. Rare cotton wool spots are seen in the same region. Optic disc appears normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Branch retinal vein occlusion
Branch retinal vein occlusions (BRVO) are three times more common than central retinal vein occlusion. The segmental nature of the haemorrhages seen here fits best with this diagnosis. BRVO is seen more commonly in systemic conditions, which increase the risk of thromboembolism including diabetes. Management of the condition where there is coincident macular oedema includes triamcinolone injections, anti-VEGF and photocoagulation. Outcome for vision is relatively good over the medium term due to development of collateral veins, although new vessel formation six months or more after the original insult increases the risk of haemorrhage.

Background diabetic retinopathy
Background diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. This is the first stage of diabetic retinopathy and can only be picked up by fundoscopy as patients are generally asymptomatic. The characteristic sign on fundoscopic examination is micro-aneurysms. These are not described in this case so this diagnosis is unlikely.

Branch retinal artery occlusion
Branch retinal artery occlusion is incorrect. Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) is a rare retinal vascular disorder in which one of the branches of the central retinal artery is obstructed; it is diagnosed by fluorescein angiography demonstrating sudden diminution of dye at the site of occlusion. It is not the correct diagnosis for this case.

Hypertensive retinopathy
Hypertensive retinopathy is incorrect. Hypertensive retinopathy is possible in this case as this patient is hypertensive; however, the classic signs on fundoscopy in hypertensive retinopathy are AV nipping and silver wiring. These signs are not described in this case, making the diagnosis unlikely.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is incorrect. This is characterised by the production of vascular growth factors stimulated by microvascular ischemia, and leads to global retinal neovascularization and the risk of vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment. It requires treatment with laser photo coagulation. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: Liver function tests were normal; arterial blood gas measurements showed: pH 7.3, Pco 2 5.1 kPa and bicarbonate 17 mmol/l, lactate 3.5 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most detrimental in these circumstances and should be stopped?
explanation:
Metformin
Metformin is a biguanide used as a blood glucose lowering agent. The major toxicity of metformin is lactic acidosis, which is more likely to occur with reduced renal excretion of metformin in renal impairment. Decreasing renal function can cause metabolic acidosis, and these are both contraindications for treatment with metformin. It should not be used in patients with renal insufficiency who have a GFR <45 mmol/l, any form of acidosis, congestive heart failure, liver disease or severe hypoxia. As it is metabolised in the liver, it is contraindicated in patients with liver disease or a high alcohol intake. It is recommended that metformin is stopped in patients with a GFR of <30 mmol/L.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Ramipril, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEI), is indicated for the treatment of diabetic nephropathy with albuminuria. It should be used under specialist supervision if the creatinine concentration is >150 µmol/l, and the renal function and potassium levels should be monitored. In most circumstances this medication would be held in acute kidney injury but continued in chronic stable renal impairment.

Insulin
Insulin is incorrect. Insulin is not contraindicated in renal impairment, but doses may need to be adjusted as the kidneys excrete insulin and renal impairment could lead to accumulation of insulin and cause hypoglycaemia. The pulsatile pharmokinetic profile of insulin analogues makes them more favourable in end-stage kidney disease due to the reduced risk of hypoglycaemia. Insulin is not associated with metabolic acidosis.

Alcohol
Alcohol is incorrect. This patient should be counselled on the importance of alcohol cessations. Alcohol use can increase the risk of hypoglycaemia in patients with diabetes.. However, alcohol is unlikely to be contributing to metabolic acidosis or renal impairment in this case.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. This is a thiazide diuretic and is contraindicated in neither kidney disease nor metabolic acidosis. The most common side effect is hypovolaemic hyponatremia. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents to his family doctor complaining of excessive sweating, weight loss and palpitations over the past 6 months. On examination his BP is 125/82 mmHg, he is relatively tachycardic at rest with a pulse of 88/min. You note a fine tremor. There is no goitre. BMI is 22. Thyroid function tests are performed: serum TSH concentration is normal, but the concentrations of both free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine are elevated. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these results?
options: The presence of heterophilic antibodies in the patient’s serum
explanation:
A TSH-secreting pituitary tumour
TSH-secreting pituitary tumours are uncommon, but are a recognised cause of hyperthyroidism. They are slow growing (accounting for the gradual onset of symptoms here) and sometimes co-secrete growth hormone, excessive secretion of which is also a cause of sweating. A pituitary MRI is the next investigation of choice, with other pituitary function testing including an IGF-1 measurement. The key fact here is that the thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) should be suppressed in thyrotoxicosis where the thyroid is the primary cause. As the TSH is in the normal range, it this confirms a TSH secreting tumour must be the underlying cause.

Graves’ disease
Graves’ disease is incorrect. Graves’ disease is associated with a TSH below the lower limit of normal, the high levels of thyroid hormones suppressing TSH production via negative feedback.

Self-administration of thyroxine
Self-administration of thyroxine is incorrect. Much like Graves’ disease, exogenous administration of thyroxine should drive suppression of TSH.

The presence of heterophilic antibodies in the patient’s serum
The presence of heterophilic antibodies in the patient’s serum is incorrect. Heterophilic antibodies are antibodies in the patient’s serum that react with animal-derived antibodies used in the immunoassay that can lead to bizarre results. The clinical picture does however fit well with thyrotoxicosis.

Thyroid hormone resistance
Thyroid hormone resistance is incorrect. Thyroid hormone resistance is recognised in patients with G-proteincoupled receptor mutations, although the clinical picture described here is clearly of thyrotoxicosis, making this an unlikely diagnosis. She is taking metformin 500 mg twice a day, plain insulin 10 U at night, ramipril 2.5 mg once a day and bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg once a day. She drinks a glass of whisky to help her sleep at night. stem: A 42-year-old woman is diagnosed with phaeochromocytoma. Screening with pentagastrin testing suggests that she has medullary thyroid carcinoma, and you plan a thyroidectomy. What antihypertensive medication should be started before surgery for a patient with phaeochromocytoma?
explanation:
Phenoxybenzamine
Phenoxybenzamine is a more potent α-blocker than doxazosin and is the recommended choice for initial antihypertensive medication in phaeochromocytoma where surgery is contemplated. It should be given in divided doses, at 20 mg initially, increasing to 80 mg. Patients should then be considered for additional βblockade with propranolol, again in divided doses up to 240 mg/day. Always start with α-blockade first, as initial use of ß-blockers can worsen hypertension. Labetalol is not recommended. An experienced surgeon and anaesthetist are crucial for this operation.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Beta blockade deployed as monotherapy is not indicated in phaeochromocytoma. It may precipitate a significant rise in blood pressure and tachycardia.

Labetalol
Labetalol is incorrect. Although labetalol has some alpha activity, it also must not be deployed as monotherapy, because it is predominantly a ß-blocker and doesn’t achieve adequate α blockade when used alone.

Ramipril
Ramipril is incorrect. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor therapy doesn’t adequately reduce operative risk when compared to alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine.

Doxazosin
Doxazosin is incorrect. Phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible alpha-blocker and is therefore preferred to doxazosin, a less powerful agent used in the management of hypertension.
