He has background diabetic retinopathy and currently takes metformin 500 mg three times a day, as well as ramipril 10 mg and aspirin 75 mg. Investigations.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden loss of vision in his right eye. His only past history of note is a previous cerebellar haemorrhage. On examination he has evidence of bilateral retinal angiomas, and a partial retinal detachment in his right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
von Hippel–Lindau disease
Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease is characterised by: Central nervous system (CNS) and retinal haemangioblastomas (the presenting feature in 40% of patients) Renal cysts and carcinomas (occurring later) Phaeochromocytoma (20% of affected families, bilateral in 40% of patients), although the incidence is much higher in those with von Hippel Lindau type 2 Pancreatic tumours (50% are non-functioning) The diagnostic criteria is a family history of VHL with one of the above tumours, or no family history with ≥2 CNS/retinal haemangioblastomas plus visceral tumour. The prevalence is 1 in 39,000 with a mean age at presentation of 27 years. Renal cysts occur later, with 70% of patients having them by age of 60 years. Ideally, genetic testing in affected families should take place around the age of 5 years. Affected individuals then require yearly urinary metanephrines and fluorescein angiography and 3-yearly brain and spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging.

Simple traumatic retinal detachment
Simple traumatic retinal detachment is incorrect. The scenario gives no history of trauma and retinal angiomas would not be seen in simple retinal detachment.

Clotting disorder
Clotting disorder is incorrect. A clotting disorder such as haemophilia could increase the risk of cerebellar haemorrhage, but would not be associated with retinal angiomas.

Bleeding due to hypertension
Bleeding due to hypertension is incorrect. There is no reference to the patient having a high blood pressure and this wouldn’t be associated with retinal angiomas.

McCune–Albright syndrome
McCune–Albright syndrome is incorrect. McCune-Albright syndrome consists of at least 2 of: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia Café-au-lait skin pigmentation Autonomous endocrine hyperfunction (including precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism and Cushing’s syndrome Von Hippel–Lindau.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is referred to the general medical clinic with weight loss of 6 kg over six months. She admits to being lethargic and off her food. Her blood pressure is 122/80 mmHg, there is a postural drop on standing. Investigations show a low free tri-iodothyronine (T 3), low free tetra-iodothyronine (T 4) and low thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), sodium is also just below the lower limit of the normal range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anterior hypopituitarism
The answer is anterior hypopituitarism. There is a strong suspicion that this patient has suffered anterior pituitary failure. Isolated secondary hypothyroidism would not usually be associated with weight loss. The weight loss of 6 kg over 6 months raises the possibility of anterior pituitary failure. Thyroid function testing confirms secondary hypothyroidism, and this patient should also be screened for Addison’s disease. If the 0900 h cortisol and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels are low, this would point towards a diagnosis of pituitary failure. The investigation of choice to elucidate the cause is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa to exclude a pituitary tumour.

Secondary hypothyroidism
Secondary hypothyroidism is incorrect. Isolated secondary hypothyroidism would be unusual in the context of weight loss. The weight loss is therefore more consistent with generalised pituitary failure.

Hypothalamic hypothyroidism
Hypothalamic hypothyroidism is incorrect. This is rare, and related to failure of thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) production, other features of hypothalamic dysfunction would also be expected. Hypothalamic dysfunction features includes severe obesity, increased risk of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, attention deficit, and multiple endocrine abnormalities.

Primary hypothyroidism
Primary hypothyroidism is incorrect. Primary hypothyroidism is associated with an elevation in TSH, not seen here.

Sick euthryroid syndrome
Sick euthyroid syndrome is incorrect. Sick euthyroid syndrome is usually seen in the context of critical illness, with a reduction in T 3 and T 4. Hypopituitarism.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an abnormal chest X-ray revealing a right hilar mass. There is a history of 40 years of cigarette smoking. He is noted to have a markedly raised corrected calcium level of 3.25 mmol/l. Apart from a mildly raised urea level due to dehydration, his other renal function testing is normal. He also has a normochromic normocytic anaemia, with a haemoglobin of 100 g/l. Phosphate and vitamin D are normal and PTH is low. Which of the following is likely to be the underlying cause of his hypercalcaemia?
explanation:
Raised parathyroid hormone-related protein
The most common cause of hypercalcemia in patients with non-metastatic solid tumors and in some patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma is secretion of PTHrP; this condition, also called humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy (HHM), accounts for up to 80% of patients with hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Patients with HHM most often have squamous cell carcinomas (lung, head and neck) or renal, bladder, breast or ovarian carcinomas. They typically have advanced disease and a poor prognosis.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for 90% of the causes of hypercalcaemia. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the overproduction of PTH by the parathyroid gland. This results in hypercalcaemia, low phosphate and a high or inappropriately normal PTH, rather than the picture here. The mainstay of treatment is parathyroidectomy whilst cinacalcet can be used in patients who are not surgical candidates.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs when the parathyroid gland appropriately responds to a reduced calcium by increasing PTH. Thereafter serum calcium is increased through intestinal or bone resorption resulting in an elevated PTH and normal or low calcium concentrations. This can occur in patients with renal failure and vitamin D deficiency, which is not the case here.

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This occurs in patients with end stage renal failure, which is not the case here. PTH is high due to parathyroid hyperplasia, which results in hypercalcaemia.

Pseudo-hypoparathyroidism
Pseudo-hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. Pseudo-hypoparathyroidism is due to end organ resistance to parathyroid hormone. This is characterised by low calcium and high PTH. Calcium Homeostasis,.

stem: You are reviewing a 52-year-old woman who has a history of type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease and coeliac disease. Her daughter has been researching autoimmune disease on the Internet and has been learning about the association between certain HLA types and disease. Which of the following HLA subtypes is most strongly associated with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes?
explanation:
HLA-DR3
The DR-DQ haplotypes conferring the highest risk are DRB1, DQA1 and DQB1. HLA-DR3 is associated with diabetes mellitus, autoimmune hepatitis, dermatitis herpetiformis, Graves’ disease, membranous glomerulonephritis, myasthenia gravis, Addison’s disease, Sjögren syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

HLA-B47
HLA-B47 is incorrect. This is associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

HLA-B27
HLA-B27 is incorrect. This is associated with seronegative arthropathies.

HLA-A28
HLA-A28 is incorrect. This is associated with schizophrenia.

HLA-DR7.

stem: A 16-year-old male comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He is as tall as his peers but his parents are concerned because he does not appear to have entered puberty. Lack of a sense of smell has been noted, although this was thought to have at least in part been related to a rugby injury a few years earlier. Examination reveals normal height (1.7m). His BP is 105/80 mmHg; pulse is 66/min and regular. He has small testes (volume around 4ml). There is decreased facial and body hair. Which of the following would you consider as the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Kallmann’s syndrome
The lack of sense of smell and the fact that this child is of normal height steers us away from constitutional delayed puberty and towards Kallmann’s syndrome. The diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating deficient sex hormones (testosterone or oestradiol), inappropriately low or normal LH and FSH (in the context of primary gonadal failure).

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is incorrect. Boys with classical CAH present with early virilisation at the age of 2-4 years, rather than the picture seen here.

Constitutional delayed puberty
Constitutional delayed puberty is incorrect. Constitutional delayed puberty is associated with short stature and delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics rather than the tall stature seen here.

Kleinfelter’s syndrome
Kleinfelter’s syndrome is incorrect. The lack of sense of smell steers us away from a diagnosis of Kleinfelter’s syndrome, although the small testes and presence of at least some facial and body hair would fit with the diagnosis.

Testicular feminisation
Testicular feminization is incorrect. This is associated with androgen insensitivity, and patients present with a female phenotype and primary amenorrhoea. They also often give a history of bilateral inguinal hernias in infancy. On examination she looks a little hirsute and has evidence of facial acne. She is within her predicted adult height range and has normal breast and external genitalia development, although there is excess hair over her lower abdomen and around her nipple area. stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to reduce progression to type 2 diabetes?
explanation:
Diet and exercise
In the various diabetes prevention trials (Finnish, US and Indian), diet and exercise were associated with a reduction in progression to type 2 diabetes of around 50%. Even switching from refined (white) rice has been shown to reduce progression to diabetes by approximately 30% in high-risk individuals.

Acarbose
Acarbose is incorrect. Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor which blocks the breakdown of complex carbohydrates. It has been shown to reduce progression to diabetes by approximately 25% in the STOPNIDDM trial.

Liraglutide
Liraglutide, is incorrect. Liraglutide is licensed for the treatment of obesity at the 3mg dose. It has been shown to reduce progression to diabetes by 80% in the SCALE pre-diabetes study. It should however be considered in patients who are unable to lose weight by other means.

Orlistat
Orlistat is incorrect. Orlistat does reduce progression to diabetes by approximately 40%, as demonstrated by the XENDOS trial. Its use is however limited by its side effect profile, and it is usually reserved for patients who can’t lose weight by other means.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Whilst pioglitazone improves insulin sensitivity, it also leads to weight gain and loss of bone mineral density, as such it is potentially best avoided in this situation. It does however reduce progression to diabetes by approximately 50%. Diabetes in PregnancyA 50-year-old woman who has been diagnosed by her GP some 6 months earlier as suffering from type 2 diabetes comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. Over the past few months she has begun to suffer from increasing problems with sweating, early morning sleepiness and bilateral pins and needles in both hands, particularly in the early hours of the morning. On examination, her BP is 152/88 mmHg and pulse is 78/min and regular. She has multiple skin tags over both axillae, and greasy skin with facial acne. Her BMI is 27. Investigations.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a long history of Type 1 diabetes, microalbuminuria and diabetic eye disease presents for review. She has been amenorrhoeic for 12 months and recent home pregnancy tests have been negative. She has a healthy 1-year-old child, but had a post-partum haemorrhage just after his birth. Over the past few months she has also been increasingly tired and has noticed thinning of her pubic and axillary hair. On examination she is slim and pale, with small breasts and thin, or largely absent, pubic and axillary hair. Her early morning cortisol, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinising hormone (LH) levels are all low, and her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is just below the normal range. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary gland reveals an empty sella. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Sheehan syndrome
It is hypopituitarism following pregnancy complicated by haemorrhage at the time of delivery, and so fits with the clinical picture in this case. The post-partum haemorrhage and associated hypotension are thought to cause pituitary infarction: patients fail to lactate and remain amenorrhoeic after delivery, and also develop other pituitary hormone deficiencies of the thyroid and adrenal axis.

Prolactinoma
Prolactinoma is incorrect. There is no tumour visible on MRI, and this does not cause adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)/TSH deficiency.

Weight-related pituitary failure
Weight-related pituitary failure is incorrect. Her bloods show panhypopituitarism; weight loss can cause suppression of gonadotropins only.

Polyglandular syndrome
Polyglandular syndrome is incorrect. Hypopituitarism is not a feature of these syndromes.

Hypophysitis
Hypophysitis is incorrect. This is associated with infiltrative disorders (sarcoid, TB), of which there is no evidence in this case. Sheehan syndrome Sheehan syndrome is well known to occur in women who have had a post-partum haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock, but the risk of it occurring is increased in women with Type 1 diabetes who have microvascular disease, and in patients with sickle cell anaemia; it occurs in 1 in 10 000 deliveries. Initial management includes immediate steroid therapy followed by a full endocrine assessment and replacement of pituitary-dependent hormones (eg thyroxine) as required. Subsequent conception can be difficult and requires pulsed gonadotropin therapy to restart ovulation. Diabetes insipidus is not usually associated with the syndrome. Sheehan SyndromeYou review a 17-year-old girl who has had type 1 diabetes for eight years. She is currently managed with an insulin glargine/NovoRapid ® basal-bolus regime. Her parents tell you that they occasionally hear her crying in the night and go in to find her having a hypoglycaemic attack. This patient has lost weight recently through exercise, and her parents report that she has recently started attending the gym regularly in the evenings. On examination, the patient has a normal blood pressure of 120/80, with no postural drop. Her BMI is 24 kg/m 2 and there is no abnormality on examination of the injection sites. Investigations show.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Gliclazide
This woman has a strong family history of diabetes mellitus, with absence of ketones and negative antibodies. This raises the possibility that she may have maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY). One form of MODY, MODY-3, which occurs due to HNF-1 alpha mutation, is particularly sensitive to treatment with sulphonylureas; as such, gliclazide is an appropriate initial therapy for her. She should of course be warned about the need to present urgently if she suffers significant osmotic symptoms or weight loss, and at least in the initial stages should be considered for urine ketone monitoring.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. Agents which reduce hepatic glucose output such as metformin are rarely successful in the treatment of MODY.

Basal-bolus insulin
Basal-bolus insulin is incorrect. Basal bolus insulin is considered when patients fail to achieve glycaemic control on sulphonylurea therapy alone.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Pioglitazone increases peripheral insulin sensitivity, which isn’t a primary problem in MODY.

BD mixed insulin
BD mixed insulin is incorrect. Given this patient’s age, if insulin is required, a BD regimen is unlikely to achieve effective glycaemic control. Diabetes - Type II A woman presents with secondary amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. She has normal visual fields on confrontation. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg with no postural deficit. You are concerned that she might have a prolactinoma. Investigations.

stem: How would you best investigate this patient?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary
explanation:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary
This lady has a high TSH, causing high T 4 and T 3. Rarely, thyrotoxicosis is due to a pituitary tumour that is producing thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). This is associated with raised TSH and elevated T 3 and T 4 levels, as seen here. There is a diffuse, smoothly enlarged thyroid due to TSH stimulation. MRI of the pituitary is the next investigation of choice, with pituitary function testing. Trans-sphenoidal resection of the tumour is the therapy of choice.

Thyroid ultrasound
Thyroid ultrasound is incorrect. Given TSH, T3 and T4 are all elevated, a primary thyroid cause for hyperthyroidism is effectively ruled out, (TSH would be suppressed in this case).

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of thyroid
Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the thyroid is incorrect. FNA would almost certainly show normal tissue as this is TSH driven hyperthyroidism.

Thyroid isotope scan
Thyroid isotope scan is incorrect. It is expected that thyroid uptake would be normal or only slightly increased in pituitary driven thyrotoxicosis.

Thyroid autoantibodies
Thyroid autoantibodies is incorrect. Thyroid autoantibodies are likely to be negative and not informative as to the aetiology of this patient’s disease. He takes regular seretide for asthma and uses intermittent oral prednisolone for exacerbations, but has no other medical history of note. On examination his BP is 170/100 mmHg, with pulse 76 beats per min and regular. His BMI is 33 and he has significant abdominal adiposity. Investigations reveal.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is referred by the Emergency Department after attending with a Colles’ fracture, the second in the last 3 years. She underwent a radical hysterectomy at the age of 38 for carcinoma. Bone densitometry confirms osteoporosis. Calcium and parathyroid hormone assays are normal. Which of the following is the most likely to be true concerning the underlying pathophysiology?
options: She has suffered predominantly cortical bone loss
She has probably suffered an equal mix of cortical and trabecular bone loss
She has probably suffered predominantly trabecular bone loss
explanation:
She has probably suffered predominantly trabecular bone loss
This woman has osteoporosis, which is a bone disease in which the amount of bone is decreased and the structural integrity of trabecular bone is impaired.

She has suffered predominantly cortical bone loss

stem: A 21-year-old man who is marfanoid in appearance is referred by his GP for review. He has been suffering from acute headaches and panic attacks and is unable to continue his course work at university. On examination his blood pressure is 148/98 mmHg and you notice a number of neuromas around his lips. His 24-hour urinary catecholamine levels are raised. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B
MEN 2B is characterised by a marfanoid habitus, visceral and intestinal ganglioneuromas (which can occur around the lips and tongue), adrenal tumours and medullary thyroid carcinoma; parathyroid hyperplasia occurs much more rarely than in MEN2a. Adrenal tumours leading to Cushing syndrome and phaeochromocytoma (70% bilateral) can occur.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is incorrect. MEN1 is associated with neoplasms of the pituitary gland, the parathyroid gland and the pancreas. This man has signs of phaeochromocytoma.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A is incorrect. This is not associated with mucocutaneous neuroma.

Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. This is not associated with a marfanoid appearance, although it is associated with phaeochromocytoma.

Carcinoid syndrome
Carcinoid syndrome is incorrect. This man has signs of phaeochromocytoma. Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome comprising the signs and symptoms that occur secondary to carcinoid tumours. The syndrome includes flushing and diarrhoea and, less frequently, heart failure and bronchoconstriction. Type 2 multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN2) MEN 2B is characterised by a marfanoid habitus, visceral and intestinal ganglioneuromas (which can occur around the lips and tongue), adrenal tumours and medullary thyroid carcinoma; parathyroid hyperplasia occurs much more rarely than in MEN2a. Adrenal tumours leading to Cushing syndrome and phaeochromocytoma (70% bilateral) can occur. Screening is recommended for people with MEN2: The pentagastrin test is used to screen for medullary thyroid carcinoma with measurement of calcitonin (total thyroidectomy in childhood is often recommended for those with a known gene defect). Monitor calcium. The best screen for phaeochromocytoma is 24 h urinary catecholamine estimation or plasma catecholamines. Phaeochromocytoma A 26-year-old woman presented to the outpatient clinic with anxiety and weight loss of 2 months duration. She also reported fatigue, but she attributed this to breastfeeding her 3 month old baby. She had a history of diabetes mellitus type 1. She has a heart rate of 90 beats per minute at rest and has a fine tremor. Investigations.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his vomiting?
explanation:
Domperidone
This patient has diabetic gastroparesis, a well-described microvascular complication of long-standing or poorly controlled diabetes, which is characterised by often unpredictable vomiting and regurgitation of partially digested food because of disordered gastrointestinal motility. Domperidone, a prokinetic anti-emetic, is the initial therapy of choice.

Codeine phosphate
Codeine phosphate is used to treat diarrhoea associated with autonomic neuropathy, not gastroparesis, which is the most likely diagnosis here. It is usually started at a lower dose of 15 mg up to four times per day and can be titrated according to symptom improvement.

Metoclopramide
Although metoclopramide is a prokinetic anti-emetic that has been previously used for the treatment of diabetic gastroparesis, it is no longer recommended because of well-described long-term neurological side-effects associated with its use. Domperidone is a first-choice agent with erythromycin a potential alternative.

Metronidazole
Metronidazole is used for the treatment of bacterial overgrowth syndrome (BOS). BOS would be unusual as a cause of vomiting alone and is much more likely to be associated with intermittent abdominal bloating, indigestion and diarrhoea. Rifaximin is also used for BOS.

Ondansetron
Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. It is a centrally-acting agent, meaning that it is much less effective at treating symptoms of nausea and vomiting related to gastroparesis than a prokinetic agent such as domperidone. Diabetes - Type I A 39-year-old woman of South Asian origin comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She is 3 months post the birth of her third child, and has suffered from gestational diabetes mellitus in her last two pregnancies. She wants advice about how to reduce her future risk of type 2 diabetes. On examination her BP is 152/82 mmHg; pulse is 80/min and regular. Her BMI is 29. Investigations.

stem: A 62-year-old man with obesity and Type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. Current therapy includes Metformin 1g BD, Ramipril 10mg and Amlodipine 10mg. On examination his BP is 148/82 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. His BMI is 36. An HbA1c checked one week before the clinic appointment is 68 mmol/mol (8.4%). You elect to start Sitagliptin. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of Sitagliptin?
explanation:
DPP-IV inhibitor
DPP-IV inhibitors inhibit breakdown of naturally occurring peptides including GLP-1, a gut peptide produced along with GIP in the incretin response. The incretion response occurs in response to a meal / carbohydrate challenge, and results in enhanced insulin release, feelings of satiety and slowed gastric emptying. DPPIV inhibitors result in a reduction in HbA1c of between 0.6 and 0.9% depending on baseline, and are either weight neutral or promote a slight reduction in weight. They also reduce degradation of a number of other peptides; the effect of this is currently under investigation.

GLP-1 agonist
GLP-1 agonist is incorrect. GLP-1 agonists deliver supra-physiological doses of peptides that stimulate the GLP-1 receptor. Examples include Exenatide and Liraglutide. They result in a larger reduction in HbA1c versus DPPIV inhibitors, and modest weight reduction of approximately 3% over a 6 months period.

Glinide
Glinide is incorrect. Glinides bind an ATP dependent potassium channel on beta cells, resulting in insulin release but are shorter acting versus SUs, and are therefore less likely to cause hypoglycaemia.

SGLT-2 inhibitor
SGLT-2 inhibitor is incorrect. SGLT-2 inhibitors promote renal glucose excretion. This drives modest improvement in HbA1c and also reduces blood pressure because of a thiazide like diuretic effect. They also promote weight loss in some patients.

Sulphonylurea
Sulphonylurea is incorrect. Sulphonylureas bind to ATP dependent potassium channels on beta cells, this is not glucose dependent, and may therefore result in hypoglycaemia and weight gain. Diabetes - Type II A 58-year-old taxi-driver comes to the Diabetes Clinic for review. He has suffered from Type 2 diabetes mellitus for the past 6 years for which he currently takes metformin 1g BD. He admits to difficulties exercising because of his job and transgressions with his diet, which have led to an increase in weight. On examination his BP is 152/82 mmHg, pulse is 80/min and regular, his BMI is 34. Investigations.

stem: Which of the following is the likely cause of the thyroid mass and the biochemistry seen here?
explanation:
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
This patient has symptoms of hypercalcaemia, which is confirmed on blood tests along with a raised PTH, suggesting hyperparathyroidism. The thyroid mass may suggest underlying medullary thyroid cancer, both of which occur in MEN2.

Addison’s disease
This patient has symptoms of hypercalcaemia, and blood tests reveal hypercalcaemia and hyperparathyroidism. Addison’s disease can be associated with hypoparathyroidism as part of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2; it is not associated with hyperparathyroidism. Medullary thyroid cancer can be associated with hyperparathyroidism as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

Di George syndrome
DiGeorge syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 22. It leads to thymic aplasia or hypoplasia, cardiac defects, and hypoparathyroidism. However, this patient has hyperparathyroidism, as evidenced by the symptoms of hypercalcaemia, and investigations showing hypercalcaemia and raised PTH. Hyperparathyroidism can be associated with medullary thyroid cancer as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1
This patient has hyperparathyroidism, as evidenced by the raised PTH and hypercalcaemia. Hypoparathyroidism is associated with mucocutaneous candidiasis in autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, but hyperparathyroidism is not associated. Hyperparathyroidism can be associated with medullary thyroid cancer in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

Magnesium deficiency
Magnesium is required for the release of parathyroid hormone, and also promotes PTH action on target tissues; therefore magnesium deficiency leads to a functional hypoparathyroidism. This patient has a hyperparathyroidism however; he has symptoms of hypercalcaemia, and blood tests reveal hypercalcaemia and raised PTH. Hyperparathyroidism can be associated with medullary thyroid cancer in multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2. Magnesium deficiency would also not explain the thyroid mass seen here. stem: Which of the following represents the most appropriate additional medication for him?
explanation:
Dapagliflozin
This is an SGLT2 inhibitor. SGLT-2 inhibitors work by increasing renal excretion of glucose and sodium. This leads to a reduction in HbA1c, modest effects on weight and positive effects on blood pressure. It also has positive outcomes data in diabetes, heart failure and in patients with chronic kidney disease, making it the most appropriate choice here.

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. The history of myocardial infarction and the bipedal oedema on examination may point towards mild congestive cardiac failure, and therefore treatment with pioglitazone would not be recommended as all thiazolidinedione treatment is contraindicated in suspected heart failure. Pioglitazone and has also been associated with a possible increased risk of bladder cancer in men, and male patients started on this medication need to be advised of this possible association.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Gliclazide is a sulphonylurea, which acts as an insulin secretagogue and therefore can cause weight gain. As this patient is already significantly overweight, it would be imperative to avoid medications that could exacerbate this and further increase the insulin resistant phenotype. Furthermore, this patient is a nurse and may have to work frequent night shifts, so medications that could potentially cause hypoglycaemia should also be avoided if possible.

Bedtime insulin glargine
Bedtime insulin glargine is incorrect. This is a long-acting insulin analogue and again would lead to weight gain and potential hypoglycaemia in this individual, and so would not be the best add-on therapy at this time.

GLP-1 analogue
GLP-1 analogue is incorrect. GLP-1 analogues stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner and therefore are not associated with hypoglycaemia. They do, however, delay gastric empting and are contraindicated in patients with suspected gastroparesis. Recent cardiovascular outcome studies have suggested that GLP-1 analogues including liraglutide and dulaglutide reduce major adverse cardiovascular outcomes in patients with diabetes. A normochromic normocytic anaemia is noted.

stem: A 66-year-old male patient with an extensive smoking history is being investigated for a suspected primary lung malignancy on a recent chest X-ray. He has been complaining of weakness in his leg and upper arm muscles. He describes difficulty standing up from a seated position, and in combing his hair. He reports weight gain of 8 kg over the past four months and has noted that his skin appears darker and that his gums appear stained also. At present he is taking no regular medication but reports that he took a week-long course of steroids two months ago for an unresolving chest infection. Four years previously, this gentleman received radiotherapy for a head and neck cancer related to his smoking history. Routine investigations reveal a potassium of 2.9 mmol/l. A 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test has revealed an 8 am cortisol of 199 mmol/l. A paired 8 am ACTH was 430 nmol/l (< 350 nmol). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion
The most common cause of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, commonly referred to as Cushing disease. However, paraneoplastic ACTH production can occur outside the pituitary in the setting of malignancy, with small cell lung cancer being the most common malignancy associated with ectopic ACTH production, accounting for 50-75% of cases. Ectopic ACTH production can also stimulate production of glucocorticoid or cortisol hormone from the zona fasciculata in the adrenal cortex. ACTH is a cleavage product of the pro-hormone pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which also produces other hormones, including α-MSH that stimulates the production of melanin leading to skin hyperpigmentation as depicted in this case.

Adrenocortical tumour
Adrenocortical tumour is incorrect. In a patient with an adrenocortical tumour that is secreting cortisol, the with cortisol excess can cause clinical signs such as myopathy and weight gain; however, cortisolChat secretion from an adrenocortical tumour would be ACTH independent and in fact the ACTH would be suppressed due to feedback in the hypothalamic?pituitary?adrenal axis (HPA), and therefore the skin pigmentation associated with ACTH stimulation of the melaoncytes would not be present.

Radiation side-effects
Radiation side effects is incorrect. Radiation dermatitis is a side effect of external-beam ionising radiation used in the treatment of a number of malignancies, including head and neck, lung and breast. The skin changes are confined to the area exposed to the radiation and the dermatitis is often well demarcated.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus can occur as a metabolic complication in patients with cortisol excess or ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, but would not explain the symptom complex outlined in this clinical scenario.

Side-effects of steroids
Side effects of steroids is incorrect. Exogenous steroids can, with chronic use, cause weight gain, myopathy and skin atrophy. However, exogenous steroids lead to suppression of ACTH via feedback through the HPA axis and therefore would not be associated with skin hyperpigmentation.

stem: You review a 36-year-old woman who presents to the Emergency Department with anxiety and palpitations. She has an 8-month-old child. Over the past 4 months, she has lost 5 kg in weight but puts this down to all the work looking after her baby. You notice she has obvious chemosis and her facial appearance isshown below. Which of the following best ﬁts the underlying diagnosis of her systemic condition?
explanation: A Graves’ disease There is obvious proptosis and lid retraction which, along with chemosis, is consistent with Graves’ ophthalmopathy and thyrotoxicosis. Graves’ ophthalmopathy occurs due to local accumulation of glycosaminoglycans; 75% of Graves’ patients develop the disease within 1 year of ophthalmopathy occurring. The condition can be worsened by smoking and by hypothyroidism post-radioiodine treatment. If visual impairment, with blurring or visual ﬁeld loss, or pain occurs, then this is a sign of optic neuropathy, and the patient should be referred to an ophthalmologist for treatment. Standard therapy involves a portfolio of treatment modalities that may include systemic corticosteroids, radiotherapy or orbital decompression, or a combination of treatments. In patients with thyroid eye disease undergoing radioiodine treatment, post- radioiodine hypothyroidism should be avoided because of the risk of worsening Graves’ eye disease. For this reason, patients are stabilised on a block–replace regimen before moving to radioiodine therapy. D Toxic thyroid adenoma Toxic thyroid adenoma is associated with thyrotoxicosis, but not with the eye signs seen here which are related to Graves’. B Hashimoto’s thyroiditis Hashimoto’s disease is associated with goitre, but not with thyroid eye disease, and leads to hypothyroidism not thyrotoxicosis. C Riedel’s thyroiditis This leads to ﬁbrotic disease of the thyroid gland and to hypothyroidism rather than thyrotoxicosis. E Postpartum thyroiditis While postpartum thyroiditis may be associated with a transient period of thyrotoxicosis and TSH-r antibodies, eye signs consistent with Graves’ are not a feature of the condition.

stem: A 27-year-old woman attends the GP 3 months after the birth of her second child. She complains of an increasing inability to cope over the past few months and frequent tearfulness. On examination, her BP is 132/72 mmHg, her pulse is 66/min and regular, her BMI is 28 and she tells you she has gained weight over the past 2-3 weeks. Investigation Result Normal values TSH 8.5 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Free Thyroxine (FT4) Anti TPO antibodies 6.5 pmol/l + 10 - 22 pmol/l Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: C Post-partum thyroiditis Postpartum thyroiditis is said to develop some 3–7 months after pregnancy and is often associated with mild symptoms such as tiredness or depression. It is said to occur to varying degrees in 5–7% of women, and in 30– 52% of cases anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Permanent hypothyroidism is said to develop in around 40% of patients, with increased frequency in patients with positive anti-TPO antibodies. Standard treatment for postpartum hypothyroidism is low-dose thyroxine (around 50 μg), with a withdrawal period after 6 months to measure recovery of thyroid function. A Grave’s disease Graves’ disease is associated with thyrotoxicosis rather than the picture of hypothyroidism seen here. B Hashimoto’s thyroiditis This is the major differential, but the timing of her symptoms means that postpartum thyroiditis is potentially more likely, and there is potential to recover from the hypothyroidism seen here. D Sub-acute thyroiditis Subacute thyroiditis is associated with ﬂu-like symptoms and pain over the thyroid gland rather than the picture seen here. E Riedel’s thyroiditis This is associated with dense ﬁbrosis of the thyroid gland and notable changes in the anterior neck, not seen in this patient, and not associated with the post-pregnancy period.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents for review with concerns about his sexual function. He has recently begun a relationship with a woman and is unable to become sexually aroused. Past history of note includes repair of cleft lip and palate. On examination, he is normal height and is thin. He has failure of development of secondary sexual characteristics. Other history of note includes a lack of sense of smell, which he puts down to an accident as a toddler. He wishes to settle down with this woman and may start a family soon. Investigations: Investigation Result TSH Normal Luteinizing hromone (LH) Low FSH Low Testosterone Low Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
C Pulsed GnRH therapy This patient is thought to have Kallmann syndrome and a failure of GnRH, and hence LH, FSH secretion. The history of cleft palate defect and lack of sense of smell both ﬁt best with this as the most likely diagnosis. It is due to disordered migration of GnRH-producing neurones to the hypothalamus. It has an incidence of 1 in 10,000 males, with a male to female ratio of 4:1. Anosmia is present in 75% and there is an increased association with cleft lip and palate. Pulsed GnRH treatment is needed to restore LH and FSH release. It needs to be continued for as long as fertility is required. Once his family is complete, switching to testosterone therapy may be more convenient for him. B Continuous GnRH therapy As natural GnRH release is pulsatile, continuous therapy fails to lead to LH and FSH release. A Testosterone supplementation Although this restores secondary sexual characteristics, it doesn’t restore fertility and is therefore not appropriate here. D FSH therapy FSH can be used to induce fertility, but it is thought to be potentially less effective than pulsed GnRH therapy. Long-acting preparations of FSH do exist, though, which may be more convenient with respect to administration. E LH therapy LH can be used in conjunction with FSH to induce fertility in women with Kallmann syndrome.

ENDOCRINO 773-5 Acid-base disorders Overview Key Facts  Blood arterial pH is closely regulated between 7.35–7.45 in healthy individuals.  The kidneys and the lungs are intimately involved in the regulation of hydrogen ion concentration.  Respiratory acid-base disorders are primarily due to changes in CO2.  Metabolic acid–base disturbances arise from abnormalities in the regulation of bicarbonate and other buffers in the blood.  Acidosis ultimately results in an increase in H+ concentration and alkalosis a fall in H+.  The pH is the negative logarithm of H+ – a small change in pH represents a large change in H+ concentration. Metabolic Acidosis  The metabolic acidoses are classified on the basis of the anion gap.  The anion gap is the sum of the two major cations minus the sum of the two major anions and is represented by the equation:  anion gap = (Na+ + K+) - (Cl- + HCO3-)  The normal anion gap is 10–18mmol/l, which represents the excess of negative charge (unmeasured anions) present on albumin, phosphate, sulphate and other organic acids eg lactic acid.  Calculating the anion gap can help determine the cause of metabolic acidosis where a clinical cause is uncertain.  In an acidosis in which anions other than chloride are increased (eg lactate, ketones, salicylate), the anion gap is increased.  In an acidosis due to loss of bicarbonate (eg renal tubular acidosis), the plasma chloride concentration is increased and the anion gap is normal. Causes of metabolic acidosis (in relation to anion gap)  Normal anion gap:  diarrhoea (or other GI loss)  renal tubular acidosis  hypoaldosteronism  treatment of ketoacidosis.  Increased anion gap:  lactic acidosis  ketoacidosis (diabetes/starvation)

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  acute kidney injury and advanced CKD  hepatic failure  toluene ingestion.  Intoxications, eg methanol, aspirin, ethylene glycol. Metabolic alkalosis  Metabolic alkalosis is less common than metabolic acidosis as metabolic processes produce acids as by-products, and renal excretion of excess bicarbonate is very efficient.  Many causes of metabolic alkalosis are associated with hypokalaemia. Causes of metabolic alkalosis  Gastrointestinal hydrogen ion loss:  vomiting/pyloric stenosis  nasogastric suction  antacids (in CKD).  Intracellular shift of hydrogen ion:  hypokalaemia.  Alkali administration  Renal hydrogen ion loss:  mineralocorticoid excess, eg Cushing syndrome  loop or thiazide diuretics  post-hypercapnic alkalosis  hypercalcaemia and the milk-alkali syndrome.  Contractional alkalosis:  volume depletion. Respiratory acidosis  This is a reduced pH due to increases in CO2.  It is an indication of type II respiratory failure, which may be due to:  lung disease  asthma  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease  pneumonia  pulmonary fibrosis  obstructive sleep apnoea.  neuromuscular disease:  myasthenia gravis  Guillain-Barré syndrome  polio  cervical cord lesion  paralysis of the diaphragm.  reduced respiratory drive: ENDOCRINO 773-5  trauma  central nervous system tumour  sedative medications.  thoracic wall disease  kyphoscoliosis  flail chest. Respiratory alkalosis  This is due to reduced CO2 as a result of hyperventilation.  Causes include:  anxiety  drugs eg salicylate overdose  mild/moderate asthma  pulmonary embolism  stroke  meningitis  subarachnoid haemorrhage. Acromegaly Acromegaly is a rare condition that is almost always due to a growth hormone secreting pituitary tumour. Overview Key Facts  Acromegaly is a rare condition that is almost always due to a GH (growth hormone)-secreting pituitary tumour.  Common features include:  hand and foot enlargement  coarse facial features  lower jaw enlargement.  Associated with many complications that need careful monitoring such as diabetes, colon cancer, and cardiovascular disease.  It is diagnosed with raised IGF-1 (and confirmed by an oral glucose tolerance test).  Treatment of choice is the resection of the pituitary tumour via the trans-sphenoidal approach. Epidemiology  The incidence in the UK is approximately 3 per million per year. There is no gender preference.  5% is associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome.

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Aetiology  Acromegaly is almost always due to a growth hormonesecreting pituitary tumour (95%).  Rarely, the condition is due to ectopic GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) secretion from a tumour (typically carcinoid) which stimulates the normal pituitary (no discrete tumour seen on MRI).  Several of rare conditions associated with acromegaly, these include:  McCune Albright syndrome  neurofibromatosis  Multiple endocrine neoplasia.  Another familial cause identified is termed familial isolated pituitary adenoma (FIPA), associated with a mutation of the aryl-hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein (AIP) gene.  Patients with AIP gene mutation tend to be younger and have larger, more invasive tumours. Pathophysiology  Excess GH is secreted by the GH-secreting pituitary tumour.  GH excess can cause acral overgrowth, insulin antagonism and increased risks of colon cancer.  Elevated IGF-1 is secreted by hepatocytes in response to excess GH. Clinical Presentation  The common features of acromegaly are well known:  hand and foot enlargement  coarse facial features  overbite of the lower jaw as the lower jaw enlargement is more typical, splaying of the teeth).  Other features include:  diabetes  arthropathy – often pseudogout  sleep apnoea  headache  carpal tunnel syndrome  multinodular goitre  increase in malignancies, especially colonic polyps  hypertension  two-fold increase in death from cardiovascular disease  cardiomyopathy  left ventricular hypertrophy  enlarged testes  renal stones (hypercalciuria) ENDOCRINO 773-5  raised phosphate  raised prolactin, galactorrhoea, menstrual change  raised triglycerides. Acromegaly hand on the right: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Acromegaly_hands.JPEG Author: Philippe Chanson and Sylvie Salenave This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license. Acromegaly facial features: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/10/Acromegaly_ facial_features.JPEG Differential Diagnosis  Pseudo-acromegaly due to insulin resistance associated with hyperinsulinaemia/minoxidil. Diagnosis/Investigation  The first-line investigation to confirm the diagnosis is raised IGF-1 levels.  Oral glucose tolerance test can then be used for confirmation.  MRI scan to detect pituitary tumours.  Visual fields and acuity testing.  Cardiac assessment – ECG and echocardiography. Management  First-line treatment is trans-sphenoidal surgery to resect the pituitary tumour (or transcranial surgery if there is a large suprasellar extension of the tumour).  The cure rate is very variable (40–80%), and is dependent on the extent of lateral and superior extension and the skill of the surgeon.  Alternative therapies if surgery is unsuccessful or patient is unsuitable for surgery includes:  dopamine agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline, quinagolide, pergolide, which reduce GH secretion in approximately 20% of cases)  somatostatin analogues (octreotide, which inhibit GH secretion)  GH antagonists (pegvisamant, which blocks GH)  pituitary radiotherapy (may take years to take effect and can result in hypopituitarism). Prognosis  After successful treatment of acromegaly, most physical features do not regress, although some soft-tissue effects do.

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  Patients who are successfully treated generally have a normal life expectancy.  Life expectancy may be reduced by up to 10 years in patients whose GH levels remain uncontrolled. Acute Pancreatitis Pancreatitis describes inflammation of the pancreas. Overview Key Facts  Pancreatitis describes inflammation of the pancreas.  There are two types of pancreatitis:  acute  chronic.  Acute pancreatitis is an acute inflammation of the pancreas and can be divided into different classifications.  mild acute pancreatitis:  characterised by the absence of complications (local or systemic) or organ dysfunction.  moderately severe:  local complications and/or organ dysfunction which resolves within 48 hours.  severe:  persistent organ dysfunction leading to local complications (such as pancreatic necrosis, abscess and pseudocyst formation) is potentially fatal.  Scoring systems such as the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II, Ranson’s criteria or the Glasgow criteria aim to identify patients at high risk.  Pancreatitis is classed as a severe attack if more than three factors are present within 48 hours and requires consideration for admission to the High-Dependency Unit (HDU) or Intensive Care Unit (ICU).  Obstruction of the pancreatic duct by gallstones accounts for over 50% of cases; the majority of the remainder are alcoholrelated. All other causes are rare.  Management depends on the severity and may include oxygen, analgesia, fluid resuscitation, antibiotics and surgical intervention.  Early endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) decompression should be considered in patients with acute gallstone pancreatitis.  The majority of patients with acute pancreatitis will improve within 3–7 days of conservative management.  Acute pancreatitis usually resolves and pancreatic function is left intact. ENDOCRINO 773-5  It may progress to recurrent acute pancreatitis or chronic pancreatitis; the risk of this is higher among smokers and alcoholics.  Mortality in hospital remains at 7–10%, usually due to multiorgan failure or peripancreatic sepsis. Epidemiology  There are approximately 56 cases of acute pancreatitis per 100 000 per year in the United Kingdom.  Eighty per cent of patients with acute pancreatitis will have mild acute pancreatitis.  Worldwide, the annual incidence of acute pancreatitis is 13–45 cases per 100 000. Aetiology  The aetiology of acute pancreatitis can be remembered by the mnemonic GET SMASHED:  G Gallstones (50%)  E Ethanol  T Trauma  S Steroids  M Mumps/coxsackie B (viral – 4%)  A Autoimmune  S Scorpion sting  H Hyperlipidaemia, Hypercalcaemia, Hypertriglyceridaemia (metabolic disorders)  E Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)  D Drugs – azathioprine, oral contraceptive pill, steroids, anti-retrovirals, fibrates, thiazide diuretics. Pathophysiology  Acute inflammation and resultant oxygen-free radicals are thought to mediate tissue injury.  Intra-pancreatic activation of pancreatic enzymes due to:  pancreatic ductal outflow obstruction, eg gallstones  direct pancreatic acinar cell injury, eg alcohol or drugs.  Enzymatic autodigestion of parenchyma of the pancreas.  Inflammatory cells, eg neutrophils or macrophages, go to the parenchyma and release inflammatory cytokines, leading to pancreatic inflammation.  Pancreatic enzymes cause vascular injury which leads to vasodilatation and increased vascular permeability.  This causes a shift of fluid from the intravascular space into the interstitial space (third-space loss).  This leads to hypotension, tachycardia and distributive shock.

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  Uncorrected hypotension and third-space loss facilitate decreased organ perfusion, leading to multi-organ dysfunction (mainly renal) and pancreatic necrosis. Clinical Presentation  Severe epigastric pain may radiate to the back.  Pain may also be experienced in the left upper quadrant and may be worse after meals; it improves on leaning forwards.  Nausea and vomiting.  Tachycardia, hypotension and oliguria.  Epigastric tenderness.  Abdominal distension/guarding.  Ileus/reduced bowel sounds.  Ascites.  Cullen’s sign and Grey Turner’s sign are rare and show discolouration around the umbilicus and flank, respectively; a sign of haemorrhagic pancreatitis. Cullen's sign: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cullen%27s_sign.jpg This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license. Grey Turner’s sign: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hemorrhagic_pancreatitis_ -_Grey_Turner%27s_sign.jpg This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license. Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for acute pancreatitis include:  chronic/acute on chronic pancreatitis  perforated peptic ulcer or peptic ulcer disease  intestinal obstruction  ischaemic bowel  ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)  myocardial infarction/acute coronary syndrome  gallstone disease  oesophageal spasm. Overview Key Facts  Diabetes insipidus is a rare condition characterised by excessive thirst and polyuria.  Two main classes of diabetes insipidus (DI) are cranial DI and nephrogenic DI.  Diabetes insipidus (DI) is caused either by a failure to secrete vasopressin from the posterior pituitary (central or cranial DI) or resistance to the action of vasopressin in the kidney (nephrogenic DI).  Common causes of nephrogenic DI include electrolyte derangements (hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia) and lithium.  Diagnosis is made with a water deprivation test.  Cranial DI is managed by treating the underlying cause and ensuring adequate hydration. Diabetic Ketoacidosis Diabetic ketoacidosis is a medical emergency characterised by acidosis, hyperglycaemia and ketonaemia. Overview Key Facts  Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a medical emergency characterised by:  acidosis  hyperglycaemia (marked but may be normal in children or young people on insulin)  ketonaemia.  Triggered by infection, inadequate treatment, trauma, surgery, other medical conditions and drugs.  Should be considered in all patients with type I diabetics and patient with hyperglycaemia with unexplained vomiting, abdominal pain, signs of dehydration, polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, shock, lethargy/coma, or pear-drop ketotic breath.  Usually occurs in T1DM, very rarely T2DM.  Diagnosis is based on:  acidaemia (venous blood pH < 7.3 or HCO3- < 15 mmol/L)  hyperglycaemia (blood glucose > 11) or known DM  Ketonaemia (> 3 mmol/L) or urine ketones more than 2++ on dipstick.  Management is via the ABC approach, and then focusing on fluid replacement. Insulin infusion and potassium replacement. Epidemiology  The condition occurs most commonly in patients with type I diabetes.  A small number of patients with type I diabetes present with DKA.  Incidence is estimated to be around 1 in 2000.  The condition accounts for up to 15% of all diabetes related hospital admission and a similar percentage of diabetes related mortality. Aetiology  DKA is triggered by numerous cause including:  infection (up to 405)  first presentation (acute insulin deficiency)  inadequate treatment/poor compliance ENDOCRINO 773-5  trauma  surgery  emotional stress  other medical conditions eg pancreatitis  drugs (corticosteroids, clozapine). Pathophysiology  Ketoacidosis is an alternative metabolic pathway to normal carbohydrate metabolism, causing ketones to be produced as a by-product.  This occurs when there is a lack of insulin to drive glucose into cells for normal carbohydrate metabolism.  Accumulation of ketones overflow into urine causing ketonuria and metabolic acidosis, with resultant lowering of pH and bicarbonate levels.  Glucosuria leads to a diuresis, dehydration and hyperosmolarity, with resultant electrolyte disturbance. Clinical Presentation  DKA should be considered in all patients with type I diabetics and patient with hyperglycaemia with:  unexplained vomiting  abdominal pain  signs of dehydration  polyuria  polydipsia  weight loss  dehydration  shock,  lethargy/coma  pear-drop ketotic breath.  Kussmaul breathing (deep sighs).  Note DKA is often the first presentation of patients with type I diabetes. Differential Diagnosis  Other causes of metabolic acidosis eg salicylate overdose.  Sepsis.  Hyperosmolar coma.  Appendicitis.  Pancreatitis. Diagnosis/Investigation Diagnosis is based on:  Acidaemia (venous/arterial blood pH < 7.3 or HCO3- < 15 mmol/L.  Hyperglycaemia (blood glucose > 11) or known DM.  Ketonaemia (> 3 mmol/L) or urine ketones more than 2++ on dipstick.

Diabetic Neuropathy Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common complications of diabetes and is correlated with poor diabetic control and duration. Overview Key Facts  Diabetic neuropathy is one of the most common complications of diabetes and is correlated with poor diabetic control and duration.  The most common form of diabetic neuropathy is distal symmetric polyneuropathy, referred to as sock and glove distribution.  Autonomic neuropathy secondary to diabetes can lead to cardiac autonomic neuropathy, gastrointestinal dysmotility, diabetic cystopathy and impotence. ENDOCRINO 773-5  Treatment consists of slowing progression by improving glucose control. Epidemiology  Approximately half of the patients with diabetes develop neuropathy and there is a correlation between patients with a chronically high blood glucose level and a long duration of diabetes. Pathophysiology  Risk factors for diabetic neuropathy include duration of diabetes, glycated haemoglobin levels, insulin resistance and hypertension. Other factors associated with the development of diabetic neuropathy include triglyceride levels, low high-density lipoprotein levels and abdominal (central) obesity.  The underlying pathology of diabetic neuropathy is still not fully understood; however, there are a number of areas that have been identified as contributing to the peripheral sensory axon loss.  Diabetic neuropathy affects the longest sensory neurones first, leading to the peripheral sensory loss, due to a retraction of the terminal sensory axons. Schwann cells are targeted by hyperglycaemia, and features of demyelination can be seen in some cases, although diabetic neuropathy is not considered a demyelinating condition.  Hyperglycaemic state is believed to lead to oxidative stress of neurones with increased advanced glycation end products, activation of PKC isoforms, altered mitochondrial function and overactivity of the hexosamine pathway. Glucose metabolism may also lead to increased production of oxygen free radicals. Nerve ischaemia may also occur secondary to the microvascular changes seen with diabetes. Clinical Presentation Diabetic neuropathy exists in different clinical syndromes, the most common of which are:  Distal symmetric polyneuropathy  most common neuropathy  presents with progressive distal sensory loss in a ‘glove and stocking’ distribution  sensory loss tends to account for the majority of cases. Painful neuropathy (burning/stabbing) is slightly less common  results in axonal loss in nerve conduction studies  motor involvement can occur in severe cases.  Autonomic neuropathy  causes postural hypotension, gastroparesis, gustatory sweating, generalised sweating, altered bowel habit  the earliest clinical sign may be a resting tachycardia.  Diabetic amyotrophy (diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy)  non-systemic microvasculitis causes a lumbosacral plexopathy which can affect nerve roots

Overview Key Facts  Gitelman syndrome (also known as familial hypokalaemiahypomagnesaemia) is a rare genetic salt-wasting nephropathy.  It is caused by a loss of function in the sodium chloride cotransporter (NCCT) in the distal convoluted tubule of the nephrons.  This defect results in impaired transport of potassium, calcium, sodium, chloride and magnesium.  Difficult to distinguish clinically from Bartter syndrome.  Symptoms mimic thiazide toxicity and are secondary to metabolic disturbance.  Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis but is generally not needed.  The mainstay of treatment is a high-salt diet with lifelong magnesium and potassium supplements and regular monitoring of serum electrolyte levels.  Complications are rare but include chondrocalcinosis, rhabdomyolysis, growth retardation, arrhythmias and chronic renal failure. There is an excellent long-term prognosis with treatment. Epidemiology  Affects men and women equally.  Typically presents during adolescence or early adulthood.  The prevalence of heterozygotes (one gene mutation) is 1% of the European population. Aetiology  Eighty per cent of cases are caused by inactivating mutations in the SLC12A3 gene.  SLC12A3 encodes the thiazide-sensitive NCCT in the apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule.  Mutations of the SLC12A3 gene result in loss of function of this transporter.  It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Pathophysiology  The NCCT is responsible for the reabsorption of sodium and chloride at the distal convoluted tubule.  Abnormal functioning results in a failure to reabsorb sodium and chloride.  Water then moves down the concentration gradient, resulting in salt and water wasting and volume depletion.

Menopause and Hormone Replacement Therapy Menopause is defined as a stage in a woman's life where menstrual periods cease permanently due to the loss of ovarian follicular activity. Overview Key Facts  Menopause is defined as a stage in a woman's life where menstrual periods cease permanently due to the loss of ovarian follicular activity.  It occurs with the final menstrual period, however is usually diagnosed clinically after 12 months of amenorrhoea.  Although the menopause can cause symptoms which may be unpleasant, it is not a disease per se, and occurs as part of the normal aging process.  Perimenopause is the period of waning fertility before the menopause when the endocrinological, biological, and clinical features of approaching menopause begin.  Premature menopause (premature ovarian insufficiency/failure) is defined as menopause occurring before the age of 40 years.

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  Alterations in hormonal levels during menopause result in common menopausal symptoms.  Vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes and night sweats) are the most commonly reported symptoms (75% of postmenopausal women).  Biochemical measurements, hormonal tests,, and ultrasound tests are not useful in the routine diagnosis of menopause.  FSH measurement may be indicated if there are atypical symptoms or if premature ovarian failure is suspected.  Symptoms may be managed effectively with lifestyle changes eg:  regular exercise  avoiding triggers for hot flushes  good sleep hygiene.  Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) may be useful in some patients where lifestyle modification alone is ineffective; risks versus benefits should be considered on an individual basis.  Specific therapies targeting individual symptoms may also be used instead of HRT.  Symptoms may resolve in 2–5 years without intervention, but can take up to 10 years. Epidemiology  The mean age of the natural menopause in the UK is 51 years.  This varies between different ethnic groups. Aetiology  Menopause is a natural stage in a woman's life.  Women have a finite number of oocytes (eggs) at birth.  The number of oocytes is greatest before birth and declines with each menstrual cycle.  The menopause is characterized by the eventual depletion of the oocyte store and the associated cessation of menstruation. Pathophysiology  With advancing age, ovarian follicular activity declines.  Initially, ovulation fails, no corpus luteum forms, and no progesterone is secreted by the ovary.  Therefore, the premenopausal menstrual cycles are often anovulatory and irregular.  Later, Graffian follicles also fail to develop, oestrogenic activity is reduced, and endometrial atrophy leads to amenorrhoea. ENDOCRINO 773-5  Cessation of ovarian activity and a fall in the oestrogen and inhibin levels cause a rebound increase in the secretion of FSH and LH by the anterior pituitary gland in an attempt to stimulate follicles within the ovary to mature.  With further advancing years, gonadotropin activity of the pituitary gland also ceases, and a fall in FSH level eventually occurs. Clinical Presentation  Symptoms of the menopause can begin before cessation of regular menstruation and can persist for several years.  The course is highly variable in individual patients.  Symptoms associated with menopause include:  hot flushes/night sweats: 75% of women report vasomotor symptoms with 25% reporting severe symptoms  irregular bleeding  mood changes  musculoskeletal symptoms: joint and muscle aches and pain  urinary and vaginal symptoms: vaginal discomfort and dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent lower UTI  sexual disorder: loss of libido  sleep disturbance. Pancreatic Cancer Pancreatic tumours are predominantly adenocarcinomas and have a high incidence between the ages of 65 and 75 years. Overview Key Facts  Pancreatic tumours are predominantly adenocarcinomas and have a high incidence between the ages of 65 and 75 years.  Smoking increases the risk of developing pancreatic cancer two- to threefold.  Diabetes is also associated with increased risk of pancreatic cancer; it has been suggested that diabetes may be an early symptom.  Tumours may invade the common bile duct and duodenum.  Surgical resection is curative; however, disease is often diagnosed at a late stage and 5-year survival is less than 1%. Epidemiology  9 000 new diagnoses of pancreatic cancer occur each year in the United Kingdom (UK).  The incidence of pancreatic carcinoma is 110–120 per million.  Incidence increases to 800–1 000 per million in those over the age of 75 years.  70–80% of pancreatic carcinoma arise in the head of the pancreas. Carcinomas in the tail often present at an advanced stage.  More than 6 000 deaths per year are attributed to pancreatic cancer in the UK. Aetiology  Risk is increased two- to threefold in smokers and there is a higher risk in those with diabetes.

Overview Key Facts  Phaeochromocytomas are rare catecholamine-secreting tumours (adrenaline/noradrenaline) of the adrenal medulla or ganglia of the sympathetic nervous system.  It occurs sporadically or in association with other genetic diseases, such as multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome.  They follow the ‘tumour of 10% rules’:  10% are outside the adrenal glands – paragangliomas (including the organ of Zuckerkandl)  10% are multiple (eg bilateral)  10% are malignant  10% are familial.  Triad of headache, profuse sweating and palpitations are almost always present.  Surgical resection is the treatment of choice. ENDOCRINO 773-5  Pre-operative blood pressure control with alpha and betablockers is important to avoid hypertensive crisis during surgery. Triad of Phaeochromocytoma: MRCP notes pages 131 & 132 Epidemiology  Between 0.5 and 2 in 1 000 patients with hypertension have phaeochromocytoma, but patients may have normal or labile blood pressure.  There is no sex difference. Aetiology  Phaeochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine-secreting tumour that is derived from chromaffin cells.  It is usually found in the adrenal medulla; however, occasionally extra-adrenal tumour also occurs.  Familial phaeochromocytoma occurs in:  MEN syndrome (bilateral tumours in 70% of cases)  neurofibromatosis (1% incidence)  Von–Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease. Pathophysiology  Excessive catecholamines secreted (intermittent or continuous secretion) by the tumour result in various clinical manifestations.  Examples of the typically secreted catecholamines are noradrenaline and adrenaline; dopamine is also secreted by some tumours.  Catecholamines stimulate alpha-adrenergic receptors that result in  increased blood pressure  increased cardiac contractility  gluconeogenesis  glycogenolysis  relaxation of the intestines.  Beta-adrenergic receptors are also stimulated resulting in increased heart rate and contractility.  The tumour is autonomous, ie unregulated catecholamine secretion, unlike in the healthy adrenal medulla which is regulated by neural stimulation. Clinical Presentation  Symptoms occur intermittently and may vary from once monthly to a few times in a day.  The symptoms can last from seconds to hours.  The frequency and severity of the symptoms increases over time.

Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome Polycystic ovarian syndrome is a common endocrine disorder, with presentation from menarche onwards.

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Overview Key Facts  Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder, with presentation from menarche onwards.  It is the main cause of anovulatory infertility.  It is associated with insulin resistance, increased cardiovascular risk and excess ovarian androgen production.  Clinical features include hirsutism (facial, increased bodily and midline), acne and oligo/amenorrhoea.  Treatment involves weight loss and management of clinical symptoms alongside prevention of cardiovascular complications and endometrial carcinoma.  PCOS is a chronic condition that may require treatment throughout a woman’s ‘pre-menopausal life’; however, mortality is not increased in patients with PCOS. Epidemiology  Prevalence: approximately 10% of women (figures vary from 2% to 25%).  It affects women of all ethnicities. Aetiology  Aetiology is unknown.  There are likely many factors including environmental and genetic.  Long term use of sodium valproate is associated with increased risk of developing the condition. Pathophysiology  Many have insulin resistance and subsequent hyperinsulinaemia which may lead to the problems of:  reduced hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin production, causing higher ‘free’ active bodily testosterone  increased androgen production, preventing ovarian follicular development, thus causing anovulation and oligo/amenorrhoea  weight gain which may lead to the patient being 'stuck in a cycle' of consequential insulin resistance and worsening symptoms. Clinical Presentation  Age range of presentation: teenagers through to 20s (ie post-menarche). Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis is based on two out of three criteria being present. 1. Clinical features and/or biochemical evidence. 2. Anovulation/oligo-anovulation. 3. Ultrasound scan (USS) (transvaginal best).  Oligomenorrhoea:  hypothyroidism  premature ovarian failure  hyperprolactinaemia and prolactinoma  simple obesity.  Other causes of infertility:  structural (eg endometriosis)  issues with the male partner  hormonal.  Hyperandrogenism:  Cushing syndrome  late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Overview Overview Key Facts  The normal range for potassium in the serum is 3.55mmol/l.  Abnormalities in potassium levels are: Hyperkalaemia (> 5 mmol/l)  Levels greater than 6.5 mmol/l is classed as a medical emergency and requires urgent intervention due to risk of cardiac hypersensitivity leading to ventricular fibrillation and arrest.  Causes:  renal failure (oliguric)  drugs (ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics)  rhabdomyolysis  potassium excess  artefact (haemolysis of sample, contamination, delay in analysis)  burns  large blood transfusions.  Clinical presentation:  palpitations  tachycardia  irregular pulse  chest pain ENDOCRINO 773-5  weakness  dizziness and collapse  ECG changes include tall T waves, widened QRS, VF and asystole.  Treatment is dependent on underlying cause and urgency:  address underlying causes if possible  low sodium diet and/or sodium bicarbonate may be considered in mild hyperkalaemia  potassium over 6.5 or over 6 with ECG changes requires emergency treatment  actrapid 10 units with 50 ml 20% glucose (drives potassium into cells as a temporary measure), as can beta 2 agonists  intravenous (IV) calcium gluconate (cardioprotective)  urgent dialysis may be required for hyperkalaemia unresponsive to medical intervention. Hypokalaemia (< 3.5 mmol/l)  Levels less than 2.5 mmol/l requires urgent treatment  Causes:  GI losses – vomiting/diarrhoea/pyloric stenosis  diuretics  laxative abuse  excess liquorice  renovascular disease  accelerated-phase hypertension  Cushing syndrome  renin-secreting tumour  malnutrition  insulin administration  Liddle syndrome (hypertension, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, autosomal dominant inheritance)  Gitelman syndrome (autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant inheritance; hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia)  Barter syndrome (severe hypokalemia due to salt wasting, autosomal recessive inheritance).  Clinical presentation (from mild to severe hypokalaemia):  mild hypokalaemia is often asymptomatic  muscle cramps/weakness  constipation  hypotonia/hyporeflexia  palpitations, arrhythmias and dizziness  tetany  respiratory failure  direct tubular cell injury/interstitial nephritis  ECG changes include flat T waves, prolonged PR interval, ST depression and tall U waves.

Overview Key Facts  Hyperprolactinaemia is the most common pituitary disturbance and is defined by a raised serum prolactin level.  There are various causes, most commonly:  prolactinoma (benign pituitary gland tumour)  hypothyroidism  drug-induced/iatrogenic cause. ENDOCRINO 773-5  Prolactinomas are the most common functioning pituitary tumours:  microadenoma (< 10 mm) – approximately 90% of all prolactinomas  macroadenoma (> 10 mm) – approximately 10% of all prolactinomas  giant pituitary adenoma  malignant prolactinoma (very rare).  Prolactinomas may occur as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 (MEN1), an autosomal dominant genetic disorder:  pituitary adenomas (most often prolactinomas) occur in association with parathyroid and pancreatic islet cell tumours.  Patients with prolactinoma may be asymptomatic, or present with signs or symptoms of galactorrhoea, hypogonadism (osteoporosis, disturbed sexual function, amenorrhoea, subfertility) or mass effect (headaches and visual disturbance).  Diagnosis is made by measuring an increase in serum prolactin and the detection of a pituitary lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).  Treatment of prolactinoma is with dopamine agonists if the patient is symptomatic; surgical removal is usually reserved for those who are not responding to dopamine agonists.  Recurrence is common, especially if there are remnants visible on MRI post-treatment.  Therefore follow-up for both enlargement and recurrence is mandatory. Epidemiology  The most common cause of hyperprolactinaemia is a pituitary disorder.  Prolactinomas are the most common hormone-secreting pituitary tumours.  40% of all pituitary tumours are prolactinomas.  They occur very rarely in children. Aetiology  Pregnancy can be associated with rapid enlargement of tumours.  Prolactinomas occur in about 20% of patients with MEN1. Overview Key Facts  Thyroid eye disease (TED) is an autoimmune reaction against orbital tissue, causing inflammation and oedema of orbital tissue leading to anterior displacement of the eye (exophthalmos).  Also known as ‘Graves’ ophthalmopathy’, it most commonly affects people with Graves’ disease.  More common in women and smokers.  There is thought to be cross-reactivity against shared antigens in thyroid and orbital tissue.  An autoimmune reaction against orbital tissue stimulates orbital fibroblasts to produce glycosaminoglycans and causes increased T lymphocytes, which leads to inflammation and oedema, increasing the volume of extraocular muscles and connective tissue which can cause exophthalmos.  Eye signs are usually bilateral and include diplopia, eye pain, eyelid retraction and lid lag, photophobia, eyewatering, blurred vision and proptosis.  Diagnosis is made based on clinical history, examination and CT or MRI imaging.

Dopamine infusion Norm  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) raised in subacute thyroiditis.  Imaging:  ultrasound scan of the gland to check for nodules, consistency and extension of the goitre  thyroid uptake scans to determine the activity of lesions.
