Thyroid storm is a medical emergency; symptoms include fever tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, diarrhoea and vomiting, agitation, and delirium and coma. Differential Diagnosis Broad differential diagnoses depending on the symptoms present (not exhaustive):  Premature menopause if hot intolerance and amenorrhoea.  Cardiac arrhythmias if palpitational.  Malignancy if weight loss.  Anxiety attack. Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  TFT (TSH & free T4): mal TSH (applies to both normal and raised) secreting pituitary tumour (TSHoma) oid hormone resistance (receptor defect) adrenalism e psychiatric illness mittent T4 therapy (poor compliance) ute overdose (TSH normal) ering anti-T4/T3 antibody (TSH normal) lial dysalbuminaemic hyperthyroxinaemia (TSH normal) mal  Autoantibodies:  TSH-receptor antibodies (98% sensitivity and 99% specificity)  antithyroglobulin antibodies  antimicrosomal antibodies (present in around 75% of Grave’s diseases). ENDOCRINO 773-5 Management Non-pharmacological  Encourage to stop smoking if the patient smokes.  Thyroid storm is a medical emergency and suspicion warrants urgent admission.  Patients with suspected thyroid malignancy warrants referral via the 2-week cancer pathway.  Referral for endocrinology assessment. Pharmacological  Carbimazole and propylthiouracil.  Side effects:  common – rash, leukopenia  rare – agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, hepatitis, fever, arthralgia, vasculitis (propylthiouracil).  Beta-blockers/calcium channel blockers are used for rapid control of symptoms.  Radio-iodine treatment is used for uncontrolled Grave’s disease and those with toxic nodular hyperthyroidism. Surgical  Subtotal/total thyroidectomy is indicated in patients who do not show optimal response to anti-thyroid medication or radioiodine.  it is also a choice in patients who are pregnant  complications:  haemorrhage, hypothyroidism hypoparathyroidism and vocal cord paralysis. Prognosis  Up to 30% of patients with Grave's may resolve without treatment.  Relapse is common.  Thyroid storm is a rare complication but is potentially life threatening. It may occur in patients with untreated/poorly controlled disease following trauma, childbirth, surgery, and infection.  Surgery and radioactive iodine require close TFTs followups as they can cause hypothyroidism.  Untreated hyperthyroidism exposes patients to increased risks of death from osteoporotic fractures and cardiovascular disease such as heart failure, coronary heart disease, and arrhythmia.  Pregnant patients with hyperthyroidism include increased risk of maternal and fetal adverse outcomes. Turner Syndrome Turner syndrome is a genetic condition that affects women, defined as 45,XO (a missing or partial X chromosome).

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Overview Key Facts  Turner syndrome is a genetic condition that affects women, defined as 45,XO (a missing or partial X chromosome).  It occurs in about 1 in 2000 female births.  There is a wide variation in clinical features.  Characteristic features include:  short stature – often the primary feature of Turner syndrome:  roughly 20 cm shorter than women without Turner syndrome.  ovarian failure:  minimal pubertal development  primary amenorrhoea  infertility.  other characteristics affect about one-third of patients:  webbed neck.  Karyotyping is required for a definitive diagnosis.  There is no cure for Turner syndrome but there are supportive treatments for associated problems.  The life expectancy is reduced slightly due to the comorbidities associated with Turner syndrome. Congenital cardiac defects are a major cause of mortality. Epidemiology  It affects 1 in 2000 women.  99% of conceptions with the Turner syndrome karyotype end in stillbirth or miscarriage.  15% of spontaneous abortions have Turner syndrome karyotype.  < 10% of cases are diagnosed antenatally; 10% are diagnosed in adulthood with secondary amenorrhoea.  Mostly diagnosed in 10–16 year olds during puberty, with characteristic features becoming more prominent. Aetiology  Turner syndrome is a chromosomal abnormality.  There is no known cause or factors that predispose the development ofTurner syndrome.  It is usually a sporadic event.  It is not inherited and there are no associated environmental risks or risks based on a mother’s age:  having a child with Turner syndrome does not increase the risk of having another child with Turner syndrome.  Pathophysiology  There are two chromosomal variations:  classic Turner syndrome:  45,XO – one entirely missing X chromosome ENDOCRINO 773-5  mosaic Turner syndrome:  majority of cells have a partial or missing X chromosome  other cells may have only one or sometimes two X chromosomes.  Usually a random event:  non-disjunction  mosaic.  Very rarely can be inherited:  partial deletion of X chromosome that can pass down from generations.  Haploinsufficiency for PAR1 genes:  homologous regions of the X or Y sex chromosomes are known as pseudo-autosomal regions (PARs):  act like autosomes  genes that escape X-inactivation.  PAR1 genes are implicated in Turner syndrome.  Specific pathophysiology behind the phenotypes is not well understood:  impaired bone growth/short stature  haploinsufficiency on gene SHOX in PAR  normally encodes for bone growth. Clinical Presentation  Patients commonly present with the following symptoms.  Common characteristics:  short stature:  roughly 20 cm shorter than women without Turner syndrome  underdeveloped ovaries:  minimal pubertal development  primary amenorrhoea  infertility.  Other features:  short, webbed neck  broad chest  widely spaced nipples  wide carrying angle  downwards slanting eyes  low-set ears  low hairline  swollen hands and feet.  Associated problems:  cardiac problems:  bicuspid aortic valve  coarctation of the aorta  partial anomalous venous drainage  aortic abnormalities (dilatation/dissection/rupture)

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  kidney problems:  increased risk of UTIs  hypertension.  hypothyroidism  diabetes  obesity  lymphoedema  skeletal problems:  osteoporosis  scoliosis  fourth metacarpal bone shorter.  cognitive problems:  difficulties with spatial visualisation  weaker non-verbal skills  usually normal intelligence.  infertile.  Turner syndrome: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Neck_of_girl_with_Turner _Syndrome_(before_and_after).jpg Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses can include:  Noonan syndrome  hypopituitarism  delayed puberty  complete androgen insensitivity  46,XX gonadal dysgenesis  46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. Diagnosis/Investigation  Turner syndrome may be picked up prenatally or postnatally. Prenatal diagnosis  < 10% of cases are diagnosed antenatally.  Amniocentesis.  Chorionic villous sampling.  Ultrasound abnormalities:  cardiac defects  kidney abnormalities. Postnatal diagnosis  Usually due to characteristics presented at birth (20% in infancy).  If not picked up until later, it is usually picked up due to short stature or late puberty features:  primary amenorrhoea ENDOCRINO 773-5  not fully developed breasts  infertile.  It can also be picked up in adulthood, but only about 10% are diagnosed in adulthood:  secondary amenorrhoea.  Karyotyping  Definitive diagnosis of Turner syndrome.  Karotyping – 45,XO:  Source: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/th umb/1/1b/45%2CX.jpg/440px-45%2CX.jpg  Other investigations to consider  Audiology testing:  conductive/sensorineural hearing loss.  Echocardiogram.  Cardiac MRI:  all girls by age 12 should have one.  Bone age/skeletal survey:  radiology.  Blood tests:  serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) – elevated  anti-Mullerian hormone – low or absent  thyroid function tests (TFTs)  liver function tests (LFTs)  fasting glucose and HbA1c  serum lipids  IgA and tTg for coeliac disease.  Pelvic ultrasound.  Renal ultrasound.  The diagnostic criteria of Turner syndrome  30 cells or more on karyotyping with defective or missing second sex chromosome.  Short stature:  < 2.5th percentile or > 2 SD below expected for midparental height.  Premature ovarian failure or congenital heart defects:  ovarian failure:  early menopause  absent of development  elevated gonadotropins.  heart defects:  bicuspid aortic valve  aortic coarctation. Management Non-pharmacological  Regular health checks are necessary to identify any problems that arise:

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  endocrinologist  psychologist  gynaecologist  geneticist  nephrologist  cardiologist  ENT specialist.  Pharmacological  Treating associated problems:  hypertension – antihypertensives  otitis media – antibiotics  hypothyroidism – levothyroxine  diabetes – antidiabetics  osteoporosis – bisphosphonates.  Replacement of hormones:  growth hormone (GH, somatropin) – to increase adult height to enable independence  oxandrolone if GH is not appropriate or obtainable:  adjunct.  oestrogen and progesterone – to induce puberty.  Surgical  Surgical treatment is indicated for associated problems:  eg cardiac defects.  For future fertility problems:  assisted conception techniques – IVF.  Breast implantation.  `  Patients with Turner syndrome have a shorter life expectancy due to the associated conditions.  Congenital cardiac defects are a major cause of mortality.  Preventative treatment will help with the patient’s prognosis and quality of life. Urinary Tract Infection – Lower The urinary tract is usually sterile and so bacterial translocation can lead to infiltration and infection. Overview Key Facts  The urinary tract is usually sterile and so bacterial translocation can lead to infiltration and infection. ENDOCRINO 773-5  A urinary tract infection (UTI) can be classed as lower (cystitis – bladder infection, prostatitis – infection of the prostate in males) or upper (acute pyelonephritis – ureters and kidneys), dependent on location.  Symptoms of lower UTI often include dysuria, frequency and malodour/dark coloured urine.  Urine cultures confirm a diagnosis of UTI and guide antibiotic management.  The most common cause in adults is E.coli infection.  Lower UTI in men is less common; however, incidence increases in elderly men.  Antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment. Definitions/Classification  A UTI implies the presence of characteristic symptoms and significant bacteriuria from kidneys to bladder – generally threshold is 105.  Complicated UTIs occur in patients with abnormal urinary tracts (stones, obstruction, ileal conduits, Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR), neuropathic bladder), catheterised patients, and patients with concurrent chronic kidney disease (CKD) or renal transplant patients.  Bacteriuria refers to the presence of bacteria in urine. This may be symptomatic or asymptomatic.  Bacteriuria does not equate to a UTI (and does not require treatment if asymptomatic unless the patient is pregnant).  Recurrent UTI is defined as repeated UTI, which may be due to relapse or reinfection, and may be defined as three or more UTIs in the last 12 months, or two or more episodes of confirmed UTI in the last six months. Epidemiology  Acute UTI occurs in up to 50% of women.  Incidence of cystitis is 0.5% per year in sexually active women with a recurrence rate of 40%.  The incidence in men is considerably lower, at 1 in 1 000.  UTIs are more common in women due to a shorter urethra; 1 in 3 women will have had at least one episode of cystitis by 24 years old. Aetiology  Nearly all cases of urinary tract infections are bacterial in nature; however, Candida species can cause fungal UTI also and are associated with diabetes mellitus.  The most common causative pathogens are bacterial Coliforms, usually from the gastrointestinal tract:  escherichia coli (80%)  staphylococcus saprophyticus (4%)  klebsiella pneumoniae (4%)  proteus mirabilis (4%).

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com Pathophysiology  UTI results from pathogenic organisms gaining access to the urinary tract and not being effectively eliminated.  Entry of bacteria into the urinary tract may be:  direct from insertion of a catheter into the bladder, instrumentation, or surgery  via the blood stream (more likely in immunocompromised)  retrograde, ascending through the urethra into the bladder.  Risk factors predisposing to urinary tract infections include:  female sex  abnormal urinary tract, eg:  calculi  VUR  reflux nephropathy  analgesic nephropathy  obstruction  atonic bladder  ileal conduit  BPH.  recent instrumentation of renal tract  incomplete bladder emptying eg prostatic obstruction in men  antibiotic use (women) – causing changes in vaginal flora  in-dwelling catheter  pregnancy  impaired host defences, eg immunosuppression and diabetes  atrophic vaginitis  virulent organisms, eg urease-producing Proteus sp.  sexual intercourse  family history of UTI in mother  history of UTI in childhood  urinary incontinence  cystocoele. Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for a lower UTI include:  dysuria  frequency  urgency  nocturia (having to urinate during the night more frequently than usual)  suprapubic pain ENDOCRINO 773-5  nausea and/or vomiting  acute confusional state.  Clinical signs include:  suprapubic tenderness  odorous urine  cloudy urine  haematuria  rigors. Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for men include:  bladder or renal malignancy  epididymitis  pyelonephritis  sexually transmitted infections (STI’s)  urethritis.  Differential diagnoses for women include:  pyelonephritis  lichen sclerosis/planus  urolithiasis  interstitial cystitis  reactive arthritis or Bechet syndrome  gynaecological or urological malignancy such as ovarian cancer  STIs, eg chlamydia, gonorrhoea, herpes, candida  infection with tuberculosis/schistosomiasis  trauma from procedures, intercourse, abuse or activity, eg cycling  adverse drug reactions, eg cyclophosphamide, opioids and nifedipine. Diagnosis/Investigation  A urine dipstick should be performed on a suitable sample to help the diagnosis in women under 65 years old.  In men and women over 65 years old, and for patients with catheters, urine dipstick is not indicated.  This may be treated as bacterial if there are positive results for nitrite and/or leukocytes.  In symptomatic men, diagnosis is confirmed through urine culture and sensitivity via mid-steam urine (MSU) or catheter specimen of urine (CSU).  A UTI is usually indicated by:  at least 103 CFU/ml of Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus saprophyticus  at least 104 CFU/ml of a single organism  at least 105 mixed growth with one predominant organism.  Blood tests and cultures should also be requested if suspecting sepsis, eg full blood count, urea and electrolytes, and C-reactive protein.

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  Imaging: X-ray for gas-forming type, computed tomography (CT) for localisation of abscess. Management Non-pharmacological  Admission may be required if there are systemic symptoms:  vomiting  fever  rigors  confusion.  Otherwise:  simple analgesia, such as paracetamol  encourage intake of enough fluids to avoid dehydration  in those with recurrent cystitis, attention to hygiene, post-coital micturition and fluid intake  asymptomatic bacteriuria requires no treatment unless pregnant  provide appropriate information and advice, eg patient information leaflets  urology referral should be considered for recurrent UTI (especially men)/suspected underlying cause or risk factor/ongoing symptoms despite treatment  urgent cancer pathway referral should be considered for:  men over 45 years old with unexplained visible haematuria without signs of infection or persistent after treatment  men over 60 years old with non-visible haematuria + dysuria/raised white cell count (WCC). Pharmacological  Men (lower UTI) – take into account previous MC and S results and previous antibiotic use and then prescribe either:  trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily (BD) for seven days OR  nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for seven days  for acute prostatitis, prescribe a quinolone.  Women (lower UTI) – consider need for antibiotics if no visible haematuria not pregnant or catheterised, base reasoning on severity of symptoms, risk of complications and previous urinary tract infection history.  If required use:  trimethoprim 200 mg BD for three days or  nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for three days  second line: pivmecillinam 400 mg once, then 200 mg three times daily (TDS) for three days  fosfomycin 3 g single dose.  Recurrent (long-term antibiotic regimen): ENDOCRINO 773-5  trimethoprim 200 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 100 mg at night  nitrofurantoin 100 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 50–100 mg at night  second line: amoxicillin 500 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 250 mg at night  cefalexin 500 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 125 mg at night.  consider intra-vaginal oestrogen pessary in postmenopausal women with atrophic vaginitis.  Catheterised patients:  nitrofurantoin 100 mg (modified-release) BD for seven days OR  trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily for seven days OR  amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for seven days  pivmecillinam — an initial dose of 400 mg, then 200 mg TDS for a total of seven days  if acute prostatitis is suspected, prescribe a quinolone antibiotic.  Pregnant patients:  nitrofurantoin (avoid at term) 100 mg BD for seven days  second line: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for seven days  cefalexin 500 mg BD for seven days.  For all patients, advise to seek review if symptoms worsen if there is no improvement in 48 hours of starting antibiotics, or if sensitivities suggest a change of antibiotics. Surgical  Surgical intervention may be required for underlying causes or complications of UTI, eg bladder outlet obstruction or urinary calculi. Prognosis  Acute, uncomplicated lower UTI usually resolves within a few days.  Approximately 25–35 % of women with UTI have a recurrent infection within 3–6 months and approximately 44% within 12 months.  The main complication is ascending infection leading to:  pyelonephritis  renal and peri-renal abscess  urosepsis  impaired renal function and failure  parenchyma renal scarring  UTI in pregnant patients can lead to preterm labour and low birthweight. Other  Acute bacterial prostatitis:  patients present with symptoms of cystitis and the prostate is swollen and tender  there will be pyuria and a positive urine culture

555-493 jameelalrajhi@gmail.com  the most common pathogens are the Gramnegative bacilli, E. coli, and Proteus and Klebsiella spp  antibiotic treatment is needed for one month.  Chronic prostatitis:  manifest by recurrent UTIs with the same organism  it is characterised by a qualitative difference in the first voided urine (no pyuria), compared with that passed after prostatic massage (0.10 white blood cells per high-power field, bacterial colony count 10-fold greater)  treatment is with quinolone antibiotics for 1–3 months.  Urethral syndrome:  ‘abacterial’ cystitis  causes include true recurrent UTIs (but with low bacterial counts) and genital (eg Chlamydia sp.), vaginal (eg Trichomonas or Candida sp.) or fastidious organism (eg Ureaplasma or Lactobacillus sp.) infections.  Tuberculosis UTI:  tuberculosis reaches the urinary tract via haematogenous spread  most patients are aged 20–40 years old, with men affected twice as commonly as women  25% of patients are asymptomatic; a further 25% have asymptomatic pyuria or non-visible haematuria, and painless visible haematuria is common  hypertension is unusual, but genital involvement (epididymitis and prostatitis in men, salpingitis and pelvic pain in women) is commonly associated  in the early stages, ulcerating lesions and granulomas are seen in the renal pyramids and collecting systems; renal histology shows chronic interstitial nephritis with granulomas  prolonged anti-tuberculosis therapy can render the calcified, caseous masses (cement kidney) sterile. stem: A 60-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of persistent loose stools and gradual weight loss over the past 3 months. On examination, she is tachycardic – her heart rate is 110 beats per minute (bpm) - and she has a ﬁne tremor. Her eyes have a bulging appearance, shown below: The patient also reports sweating despite it being winter. Her GP suspects Graves’ Disease. Which autoantibody is she most likely to have in her blood?
explanation: E Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor stimulating antibody (TSAb) TSAb antibodies are usually present in Graves’ disease, and result in stimulation of the stimulating thyroid hormone (TSH) receptor, which leads to overproduction of thyroid hormones. The causes the symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, such has tremor, tachycardia, sweating etc. The TSH receptor is also expressed in the orbital ﬁbroblasts and adipocytes, which leads to the eye symptoms associated with Graves’ disease (building appearance). These do not occur when other nonautoimmune causes of thyrotoxicosis, such as a multinodular goitre, are present. C Islet antigen 2 (IA-2) antibody These antibodies are associated with type I diabetes mellitus, as they target the beta islet cells of the pancreas. A 21-Hydroxylase antibody This autoantibody is most commonly found in patients with primary hypoadrenalism (Addison’s disease). It occurs in 8090% of patients with this condition and is not involved in the aetiology of Graves’ disease. B Gastrin receptor antibody Gastrin receptor antibodies are associated with pernicious anaemia and not with Graves’ disease. The gastric parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which is needed for the absorption of vitamin B12 and therefore, antibodies against these cells result in vitamin B12 deﬁciency and anaemia. D Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor blocking antibody (TBAb) TBAb antibodies are associated with autoimmune hypothyroidism, eg Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. They target the TSH receptor and block their activation, which leads to hypothyroidism.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with complaints of excruciating abdominal pain in the epigastric region that radiates to his back. He has had four episodes of vomiting in the past two hours and is unable to eat solid foods. The patient does not smoke or consume alcohol. On examination, his blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 106 bpm. There is severe tenderness on palpation of the epigastric region. The patient appears dehydrated. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Urea 7.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 122 µmol/l 50–120µmol/l Amylase 1284 U/l < 200 U/l Lipase 1100 U/l < 140 U/l Triglycerides (TGL) 11.6 mmol/l < 1.5 mmol/l Low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) 4.8 mmol/l < 3.5 mmol/l After initial stabilisation of the patient with intravenous hydration, which of the following is the best line of management?
explanation: C Initiation of atorvastatin and fenoﬁbrate This patient has clinical features of pancreatitis, along with biochemical evidence (elevated amylase and lipase levels). The cause of pancreatitis is likely due to severe hypertriglyceridaemia (triglycerides (TGL) > 11.5 mmol/l). In addition, the low-density lipoprotein level is slightly elevated. In these patients, it has been found that initiation of a combination of statin and ﬁbrate, along with dietary modiﬁcation, decreases the future risk of pancreatitis and premature atherosclerosis. A Initiation of atorvastatin Initiation of statin alone in a patient with pancreatitis secondary to hypertriglyceridaemia is unlikely to achieve an adequate reduction of triglycerides to sufﬁciency reduce the risk of future repeat episodes. B Initiation of evolocumab Evolocumab, a proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin type 9 inhibitor, is being investigated as part of a clinical trial but is not recommended as standard of care in a patient with pancreatitis secondary to severe hypertriglyceridaemia (TGL = 11.5 mmol/l). D Initiation of fenoﬁbrate and gemﬁbrozil Initiation of two ﬁbrates does not confer an added beneﬁt and may increase the incidence of hepatitis. E Initiation of omega-3 fatty acids While omega-3 fatty acids may be useful, in addition to statins and ﬁbrates, they are not recommended as monotherapy as the minor reduction in triglyceride levels is unlikely to result in a sufﬁcient reduction of the risk of repeat episodes.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She has been suffering from intermittent tachycardia and panic attacks for several days. There is no significant medical history. She takes several vitamin and mineral supplements. On examination, there are no ocular signs and no obvious goitre. The thyroidstimulating hormone level is < 0.05 mIU/l (0.5–5.0 mIU/L), and that of free tri-iodothyronine (T3) is 40 (10–22). What is the most likely cause of this patient’s thyrotoxicosis?
explanation:
Graves’ disease
Graves’ autoimmune hyperthyroidism is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis, especially in young women. The presence of goitre is not necessary, although usually there is a small palpable goitre. Thyrotoxicosis affects 2% of women and 0.2% of men in their lifetime. Graves’ disease is responsible for around 80% of cases of thyrotoxicosis (toxic multinodular goitre is the next most common cause). Patients with Graves’ disease may be offered radioiodine treatment or a period of medical therapy with anti-thyroid drugs and thyroxine replacement. Patients who then fail on medical therapy are offered radiotherapy or surgery.

Excess iodine ingestion
Consuming excess iodine can cause iodine-induced hyperthyroidism. This is usually mild and transient. Excess iodine ingestion is rare and Graves’ disease is more common. Iodine excess can lead to subclinical orAI overt Tutor hyperparathyroidism. Excess iodine is ingested orally, although it is included in many topical ointments such as betadine.

Excess thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion
Excess thyroid secreting hormone (TSH) secretion is normally associated with low T4 and T3 levels, eg in hypothyroidism. This is because low T4 and T3 levels lead to an increase in thyrotropin-releasing hormone and subsequent TSH. Alternatively, if there was inappropriate excess TSH secretion, as seen in patients with TSHsecreting pituitary adenomas, then the measured TSH level would still be raised, which is not seen in this case.

Solitary toxic nodule
Approximately 5% of solitary thyroid nodules have thyroid function that acts independently from the thyroid. Graves’ disease is more common. A thyroid uptake and scan can be used to identify a solitary toxic nodule. Given the single toxic nodule, surgical resection may be a more appropriate option to preserve function of the remaining thyroid gland. Thyrotoxicosis A 45-year-old woman presented with a four month history of tiredness, poor concentration, and widespread pruritus. She had no other past medical history. On examination her pulse was 64bpm, and her blood pressure was 136/88mmHg. She was overweight, with dry skin. Investigations:

Toxic multinodular goitre
Toxic multinodular goitre occurs more commonly in the over-60 year group. Graves’ disease occurs most commonly in women aged 20 and 50 years. Toxic multinodular goitre is the second most common cause of hyperthyroidism. This requires radioactive iodine treatment. Spontaneous remission is rare.

stem: A 38-year-old woman, who has recently been diagnosed with Graves’ disease and is being treated with carbimazole, comes to the Emergency Department with double vision and loss of colour sensitivity. She has marked proptosis and lid lag and you suspect she has worsening thyroid eye disease (TED). Which of the following is the underlying cause of TED?
explanation:
Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) deposition
Fibroblasts are stimulated both by anti-TSH receptor antibodies and activated T cells and are responsible for deposition of GAG. Because GAG is hydrophilic, it draws in water from surrounding tissues leading to significant oedema, and the visual changes seen here are due to pressure on the optic nerve. Immune modulation with corticosteroids is the initial intervention of choice, and mycophenolate mofetil may also be effective. Teprotumumab is an insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-1 inhibitor which has also shown promise in treating TED.

Apoptosis of fibroblasts
Hyperstimulation of fibroblasts rather than apoptosis is what drives the changes seen in patients with TED. This may well be because of cross-reactivity between thyroid-stimulating antibodies and growth receptors, including for those for IGF-1 on the surface of fibroblasts. Activated T cells also play a directChat rolewith in stimulation of fibroblast activity.

Iatrogenic hypothyroidism
Although iatrogenic hypothyroidism is not the primary cause of TED, it may worsen symptoms by exacerbating soft tissue oedema. For this reason, most patients with Graves’ disease are initially treated with a block-replace regimen to establish stable thyroid status using high-dose carbimazole and thyroxine replacement. More intensive monitoring is also instituted around the time of radioiodine treatment.

Inflammatory optic neuritis
Inflammatory optic neuritis is not a prominent feature of TED. The effects on colour vision and visual acuity are due to pressure from accumulation of GAG and fluid at the back of the eye. Thyroid Eye Disease You review a 52-year-old woman in the thyroid clinic. She has a thyroid mass. Her functional status is excellent. She has no significant previous illnesses and currently holds down a part-time job as a solicitor. Biochemical testing reveals normal thyroid function. Fine needle aspiration biopsy of the lesion reveals a thyroid lymphoma.

Immunoglobulin (IgG) deposition
Immunoglobulin deposition is not the primary cause of the pressure effects seen on the optic nerve in TED. However, autoantibodies do play a role in stimulating fibroblast activity potentially via cross-reactivity against IGF-1 receptors on the fibroblast cell surface.

stem: A 34-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with a history of thyrotoxicosis. At her first appointment she is found to have a smooth goitre, lid lag and bilateral exophthalmos with puffy eyelids and conjunctival injection. She wants to discuss the treatment of her thyroid problem as she is keen to become pregnant. What is the most likely treatment you would advise?
options: A combination of anti-thyroid drugs and thyroxine
explanation:
12–18 months of thionamide therapy
There are two thionamides licensed for use in the UK: carbimazole and propylthiouracil. The former is far more commonly used in treatment of thyrotoxicosis. Historically, propylthiouracil used to be preferred in women who are either pregnant or are planning to become pregnant because unlike carbimazole, it is not associated with aplasia cutis or ompholocele. However, recent concerns about hepatotoxicity has led to calls that its use should be restricted to the first trimester with close (monthly) monitoring of liver function.

Beta-blockers alone
Beta-blockers alone is incorrect. Beta-blockers may be effective in controlling autonomic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis but untreated thyrotoxicosis increases the risk of fetal loss. Beta-blockers should given in Chat not withbe pregnancy or lactation unless absolutely essential. While there is no direct evidence of teratogenicity, beta blockers reduce placental perfusion, which may result in intra-uterine fetal death, immature and premature deliveries. In addition, adverse effects (especially hypoglycaemia and bradycardia in the neonate and bradycardia in the fetus) may occur. There is an increased risk of cardiac and pulmonary complications in the neonate in the post-natal period.

A combination of anti-thyroid drugs and thyroxine
A combination of anti-thyroid drugs and levothyroxine is incorrect. The ‘block and replace’ regimen is often used for patients who have ‘brittle thyrotoxicosis’ (i.e. with fluctuating antibodies and therefore variable activity). It must not be used in pregnancy. Levothyroxine does not cross the placenta whereas carbimazole does. This would lead to the fetal hypothyroidism.

Radioactive iodine
Radioactive iodine is incorrect. It is a very effective treatment for thyrotoxicosis but is contraindicated in women of childbearing age who are contemplating pregnancy within 6 months. It should also be avoided with unstable/severe eye disease.

Thyroidectomy
Thyroidectomy is incorrect. Surgery is an option for people with a large goitre, or for people who fail on other treatments but would not be first choice in a young, otherwise healthy woman. If surgery is necessary in a pregnant woman (i.e. due to an adverse reaction to medication such as neutropenia or liver toxicity), it is best performed during the second trimester.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful next intervention?
explanation:
Bendroflumethiazide
The diagnosis here is of drug induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, due to lithium therapy, which can cause permanent impairment of tubular function. Initial therapy is to stop the offending medication, if possible, and instigate a low salt diet. In the presence of a low sodium diet use of a thiazide can reduce urine output by 50% or more, it from Chatreducing with 10 litres to less than 5 litres. This can obviously have a significant impact on quality of life. Non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), inhibiting renal prostaglandin synthesis, can further reduce urine output. It is important to note that the nephrogenic DI induced by lithium may persist even after withdrawal of therapy and in some cases appear irreversible though the likelihood of this outcome may depend on the duration (and dose) of lithium therapy.

Demeclocycline
Demeclocycline is incorrect. Demeclocycline is used to drive free water excretion in patients with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). As such this is inappropriate here.

Furosemide
Furosemide is incorrect. Loop diuretics are less effective than thiazides or amiloride in reducing urine output in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Sildenafil
Sildenafil is incorrect. Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor which can be used in X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Diabetes Insipidus

V2 receptor antagonist
V2-receptor antagonist is incorrect. V2 receptor antagonists are investigational drugs used in the treatment of X-linked nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

stem: You review a 28-year-old woman who has been referred with amenorrhoea. She is noted on routine screening to have a raised prolactin level. She has read about her condition on the internet and has some questions about prolactin physiology. Thinking of hormones in general, which of the following hormones is under continuous inhibition?
explanation:
Prolactin
Prolactin is under predominantly inhibitory control by dopamine. Prolactin levels are known to rise during pregnancy, lactation, severe stress, sleep and coitus. Mildly increased prolactin levels in the range of 400–600 mU/l can be physiological, but higher levels require to be investigated. Levels above 1000 mU/l might raise the possibility of a microprolactinoma, and levels above 5000 mU/l imply the presence of a macroprolactinoma. Drug causes of hyperprolactinaemia are, not surprisingly, the dopamine antagonists, which include metoclopramide, domperidone and the phenothiazines. Clinical features of hyperprolactinaemia in women include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido, subfertility and features of androgen deficiency.

Growth hormone
Growth hormone is incorrect. Growth hormone secretion is pulsatile. It is suppressed by somatostatin, and pulses of growth hormone release correspond to periods when somatostatin levels fall.

Adrenocorticotropic hormone
Adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) is incorrect. ACTH release is reduced in response to a reduction of corticotropic-releasing hormone (CRH) and proopiomelanocortin (POMC) transcription, which primarily occurs because of increased levels of corticosteroids.

Thyroid-releasing hormone
Thyroid releasing hormone (TRH) is incorrect. TRH is released in pulsatile fashion, and is under negative feedback via tri-iodothyronine (T 3) and tetra-iodothyronine (T 4).

stem: A 51-year-old White man was recently diagnosed with a solitary 2.7-cm papillary cancer of the thyroid with no invasion of the capsule, no lymphadenopathy and no distant metastases. He has no history of head and neck irradiation, hoarseness, pain, dysphagia or haemoptysis. His physical examination is otherwise normal, with no laboratory test abnormalities. Which of the following measures is most appropriate for his management?
options: Partial thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine treatment
Near-total thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine treatment
Partial thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine treatment and thyroid hormone treatment
Near-total thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine treatment and thyroid hormone treatment
explanation:
Near-total thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine treatment and thyroid hormone treatment
The most common type of thyroid cancer is papillary cancer, which accounts for approximately 70% of all thyroid cancers. It is two to three times more common in females and peaks in the third and fourth decades of life. Papillary cancer is usually non-encapsulated and sometimes multifocal and it tends to spread by the lymphatic route. The first line of treatment of thyroid cancer consists of surgical resection. Although the optimum procedure is not known, the more aggressive tumours should be managed with more extensive procedures (near-total or total thyroidectomy, with or without lymph node dissection). Radioactive iodine (RAI) ablation should be considered when residual or metastatic disease is present. Finally, thyroid hormone treatment should be used with a goal of keeping the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level as low as possible without causing overt hyperthyroidism. RAI ablation and thyroid hormone suppression have been shown to reduce recurrence of thyroid cancer. In this patient, age and tumour size predict a poor outcome. Treatment should, therefore, consist of near-total thyroidectomy, RAI ablation and thyroid hormone treatment.

Partial thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine treatment
Partial thyroidectomy followed by RAI treatment is incorrect. This is inadequate, because it risks leaving cancer tissue in situ and hypothyroidism post-radioiodine.

Near-total thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine treatment
Near-thyroidectomy followed by RAI treatment is incorrect. This risks hypothyroidism, and not suppressing with exogenous thyroid hormone is considered inadequate therapy.

Thyroid hormone treatment
Thyroid hormone treatment is incorrect. This is clearly incorrect because it doesn’t even propose surgery as a treatment intervention. Thyroid Cancer An obese (BMI = 30) 53-year-old woman presents with a myocardial infarction. Her mother has type II diabetes. Her cholesterol is 5.1 mmol/l. Current medication includes metformin, ramipril and aspirin. Examination reveals some evidence of left ventricular failure. A recent HbA1c was measured at 64 mmol/mol. Which one of the following interventions is the most likely to prolong her survival?

Partial thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine treatment and thyroid hormone treatment
Partial thyroidectomy, RAI treatment and thyroid hormone treatment is incorrect. As much as is with possible of the Chat thyroid tissue surrounding the cancer should be removed because of potential lymphatic spread.

stem: A 17-year-old girl with Addison’s disease is intolerant of her hydrocortisone treatment, which she takes at a dose of 20 mg in the morning and 5 mg in the evening. Which of the following doses of prednisolone would provide an approximately equivalent daily dose to her hydrocortisone?
explanation:
6.5 mg
Equivalent dose of prednisolone vs hydrocortisone therapy is usually about 25% of the hydrocortisone dose. Adequacy of steroid replacement is normally assessed by clinical wellbeing and restoration of normal (not excessive) weight. Cortisol levels during the day are only a useful assessment if the patient is on hydrocortisone. Patients normally require therapy with mineralocorticoids as well as glucocorticoid therapy. Standard therapy is with fludrocortisone 50–300 micrograms/day, and effectiveness is assessed by serum electrolytes, postural change in blood pressure and suppression of plasma renin activity to normal levels.

1 mg
1 mg is incorrect. 1 mg is the dose of dexamethasone roughtly equivalent to 7.5 mg of prednisolone.

10 mg
10 mg is incorrect. 10 mg of prednisolone represents a chronic overdose and may drive the development of Cushingoid features over time.

12.5 mg
12.5 mg is incorrect. Like 10 mg, 12.5 mg of prednisolone represents a potential chronic overdose of steroid hormone.

15 mg
15 mg is incorrect. 15 mg of prednisolone may be the dose administered during a period of significant intercurrent illness to prevent adrenal crisis.

stem: A 56-year-old woman is commenced on carbamazepine, an anti-epeleptic medication, for suspected complex seizures. She is not taking any other medication and is otherwise well. Within 10 days of starting this new medication, the patient complains of feeling dizzy and unsteady on her feet. She is brought to hospital by her husband with severe confusion and vomiting. Clinically, she is euvolaemic. Her investigations show: sodium 124 mmol/l, potassium 3.7 mmol/l, creatinine 88 µmol/l. Her spot urine sodium is 65 mmol/l and urinary osmolarity is 495 mOsmo/l. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyponatraemia?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
explanation:
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
SIADH is defined as the inappropriate release of ADH from the posterior pituitary; the excess ADH acts on the distal convulted tubule in the kidney to cause excess water retention without affecting solute resorption, resulting in dilution of sodium and hyponatremia. There are a number of causes of hyponatremia, including drugs, and anti-epileptics such as carbamazepine mentioned in this case can cause SIADH. The diagnosis of SIADH relies on the diagnosis of clinical euvolaemia, the exclusion of other conditions including hypothyroidism and cortisol insufficiency, and biochemical evidence of sodium wasting reflected by a urinary sodium >50 mmol/l and concentrated urine indicating water resorbtion, determined by a urinary concentration which is greater than the serum concentration, or sometimes defined as a urine osmolarity > 100 mOsmo/L during hypotonicity.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. Addison’s disease is unlikely in this clinical scenario, as this causes a state of hypovolaemia that would result in a clinically hypovolaemic patient. Addisons disease is an autoimmune condition that is more common in younger patients, and the presentation is often less acute then the case Chat before with described above. However, it is important to eliminate Addison’s diease or cortisol insufficiency a diagnosis of SIADH can reliably be made, and all patients with suspected SIADH should first have thyroid function tests and a baseline 9 am cortisol or Synacthen test to rule out thyroid dysfunction and cortisol insufficiency.

Vomiting
Vomiting is incorrect. Dehydration is a common cause of hyponatermia in the elderly, who may less able to regulate water and salt balance. Howver vomiting leads to a state of volume depletion and salt preservation at the level of the kidneys, resulting in a clinically hypovolemic patient and a low urinary sodium.

Cerebral salt wasting (CWS)
Cerebral salt wasting (CSW) is incorrect. CSW is a rare disorder of renal salt wasting that is caused by a traumatic head injury or a cerebral haemorrhage. The biochemistry in CSW does mimic that of SIADH, as urinary sodium levels are high in CSW (>50 mmol/l), due to renal salt wasting. However the important distinguishing factor between CSW and SIADH is that patients with the former will be clinically hypovolaemic. A diagnosis of CSW does not fit with this clinical case, as there is no history of head trauma or cerebral haemorrhage and the patient is euvolaemic.

Seizures
Seizures is incorrect. Hyponatremia can lower the seizure threshold, making it even more important to resolve this electrolyte abnormality; however, seizures do not cause hyponatremia.

stem: A 55-year-old woman is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes after being treated on the Emergency take with cellulitis affecting her left lower limb. She has a past history of asthma for which she takes a salbutamol inhaler, but is on no other regular medication. On examination, her BP is 132/82; pulse is 80 and regular. Her chest is clear. Her abdomen is soft and nontender, with a BMI of 34. Creatinine is normal; HbA1c is 67 mmol/mol. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial intervention for controlling her blood sugar?
explanation:
Metformin
Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output rather than stimulating insulin release, and is associated therefore with modest weight loss. It also has positive effects on blood lipids and vascular inflammation, which may account for the observed positive effect it has on cardiovascular outcomes. Given its generic status it is therefore the default first-line agent for the treatment of Type 2 diabetes.

Empagliflozin
Empagliflozin is incorrect. Although SGLT-2 inhibitors do have positive effects on glucose control, weight and blood pressure, which appears to translate into improved cardiovascular outcomes, they areChat not with yet the first choice intervention for diabetes because of higher acquisition cost versus metformin and still evolving clinical data. It is an alternative choice in patients who cannot tolerate metformin.

Gliclazide
Gliclazide is incorrect. Sulfonylureas should be avoided in this case because they are likely to promote both weight gain and hypoglycaemia. Their glucose-lowering effect, although strong initially, begins to wane after 2– 3 years.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin is incorrect. Sitagliptin is a DPPIV inhibitor and represents an alternative choice to metformin in patients who cannot tolerate it. Diabetes - Type II

Pioglitazone
Pioglitazone is incorrect. Pioglitazone is a glitazone, which promotes an increase in peripheral insulin sensitivity. It is no longer widely used because of its effects in increasing body mass, and risks including fluid retention and a reduction in bone mineral density.

stem: What is the screening test for the most likely underlying diagnosis in this case?
options: Ratio of aldosterone to plasma renin activity after holding medication
explanation:
Ratio of aldosterone to plasma renin activity after holding medication
The most likely diagnosis is Conn syndrome, which is the most common cause of secondary hypertension and causes an elevated ratio of aldosterone to plasma renin activity. In addition, there is evidence of hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, and the woman does not appear cushingoid or acromegalic on examination. Conn syndrome occurs in 5–15% of patients with hypertension, and may occur in an even greater percentage of patients with treatment-resistant hypertension, which may be underdiagnosed. Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia is the most common cause, followed by adenoma.

Overnight dexamethasone suppression test
Overnight dexamethasone suppression test is incorrect. This is the screening test for Cushing’s disease, which is not the diagnosis here as the patient is not cushingoid.

Renal magnetic resonance angiography
Renal magnetic resonance angiography is incorrect. This is to image the renal arteries looking for renal artery stenosis, which is not the underlying diagnosis here because it is not the most common cause of secondary hypertension and the woman shows signs of hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

Urinary vanillylmandelic acid
Urinary vanillylmandelic acid is incorrect. It is a test for phaeochromocytoma, which is a rare cause of secondary hypertension. It is an end-stage metabolite of the catecholamines, epinephrine and norepinephrine.

Urinary catecholamines.

stem: The patient is very compliant with medication. The past medical history is significant for hypokalaemia, which was picked up two years ago on routine screening and left ventricular hypertrophy on a recent echocardiogram. You suspect Conn syndrome. Which of the following would be the first-line investigation of choice to investigate primary hyperaldosteronism?
explanation:
Aldosterone:renin ratio
An elevated aldosterone in the presence of a suppressed renin confirms the diagnosis of hyperaldosteronism or Conn syndrome. However, certain antihypertensives can affect the interpretation of the result and ideally the test should be done following a period off medication, although the test may still be useful if only some of the antihypertensive medications can be discontinued, such as β blockers which suppress renin and ACE inhibitors which cause a falsely low aldosterone reading.

Computed tomography of the abdomen
Cross sectional imaging is incorrect. It is useful after a biochemical diagnosis has been confirmed and localisation or lateralisation is needed (ie bilateral adrenal hyperplasia vs adenoma). Performing a CT scan prior to biochemical confirmation can lead to false positive results as non-functioning adrenal adenomas are very common with a reported prevalence of 4% in radiological series.

Saline suppression test
A saline suppression test is incorrect. It is used as a confirmatory test in patients with an equivocal aldosterone : renin ratio. A saline load using 0.9% saline, in the seated position with aldosterone : renin measurements before and after intravenous saline, will demonstrate if aldosterone levels are suppressed by saline as would be physiologically expected. In the presence of autonomous aldosterone production (Conn syndrome), the aldosterone will not suppress with saline. This test would not be the first line and therefore is not the correct answer for this case.

Urinary catecholamines
Urinary catecholamines is incorrect. They are a useful diagnostic screening test for phaeochromocytoma. Phaeochromocytoma can cause uncontrolled hypertension and lead to end-organ effects as depicted in this case. Although in theory catecholamine excess from phaechromocytoma can cause hypokalaemia, it isn't seen in clinical practice as described in this case. The patient does not report many of the other common symptoms of a phaeochromocytoma, including pallor, palpitations, anxiety and headaches.

24-hour urinary cortisol
24-hour urinary cortisol is incorrect.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is undergoing investigations for subfertility. She is overweight with a body mass index of 29, suffers from acne, hirsuitism and has heavy periods only once every 3–4 months. You wish to determine whether or not she is ovulating normally. Which of the following hormone levels rises most as an indicator of ovulation?
explanation:
Luteinising hormone
There is a sudden rise in LH which occurs in females and is responsible for ovulation induction. As such it is the optimal hormone to measure from the list given, to confirm ovulation. A rise in progesterone also occurs and is an alternative to measuring LH.

Oestradiol
Oestrodiol is incorrect. A gradual increase in oestradiol levels occurs during the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle; as such it is less useful to measure versus the sudden rise in LH that occurs.

Testosterone
Testosterone is incorrect. The history raises the possibility of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), which is associated with elevated testosterone, although this is not predictive of ovulation.

Follicle-stimulating hormone
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is incorrect. The rise in FSH seen at or just before ovulation is smaller than the rise seen for LH.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with tiredness and loss of libido. This is leading to problems with her relationship. She has had no periods for the past 4 months and has taken three pregnancy tests, all of which have been negative. She takes no medication and currently works as a solicitor. There is a past history of a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 5 years earlier after a return ﬂight to the UK from Australia. She does not have any current plans for pregnancy. On examination, her BP is 122/70 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. Her BMI is 22. Visual ﬁelds are normal. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 130 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 201 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 115 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Prolactin 1500 u/l 59 - 619 u/l Pituitary MRI Micro-adenoma Which of the following is the optimal way to manage her?
explanation: B Cabergoline Dopamine agonists are the intervention of choice for microprolactinoma. A meta-analysis suggested that cabergoline is more efﬁcacious than bromocriptine in normalising prolactin, with a better side effect proﬁle, and it is therefore the treatment of choice for this patient. D Domperidone Domperidone is a dopamine antagonist, which is a cause of hyperprolactinaemia. A Trans-sphenoidal resection Surgery is not indicated for microprolactinoma unless there is a failure of symptoms to respond to medical intervention or there is signiﬁcant optic chiasm compression from a macroadenoma. C Bromocriptine Bromocriptine has a slightly less favourable adverse event proﬁle versus cabergoline, but greater evidence exists for safe use in early pregnancy. It is therefore the preferred option in women who are considering starting a family. E Combined oral contraceptive pill Combined oral contraceptives are an option for women with a microprolactinoma who don’t require the return of fertility, although in this case they are best avoided with the previous history of deep vein thrombosis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to see you with a history of cold intolerance, weakness and constipation for three months. Her periods are regular but scanty; she has never been pregnant. Her history is significant for hypertension and peptic ulcer disease and her family history includes hypertension and diabetes. She takes ranitidine 150 mg at bedtime, sustained-release nifedipine 60 mg daily and docusate sodium 100 mg three times a day. Her pulse is 58 bpm and her blood pressure is 135/90 mmHg. Her skin is dry and scaly and she has hung-up reflexes. The rest of her examination is normal and tests show: normal serum biochemistry except for a creatine kinase of 300 U/l (normal range 26–140 U/l); full blood count normal; free thyroxine (T 4) 6.4 pmol/l (10–22 pmol/l) and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.2 mIU (0.3–5.0 mIU). Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying cause of her problems?
explanation:
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging
This patient has central hypothyroidism and should be evaluated for pituitary and end-organ function as well as the presence of a pituitary tumour. The T 4 is low and a compensatory rise in TSH has not occurred. The prolactin level should be measured and the pituitary–adrenal –gonadal and –growth hormone axes assessed. The presence of a pituitary tumour can be determined by imaging the pituitary gland with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT). Where appropriate, this should be followed by evaluation of the visual fields. The treatment of choice for most pituitary adenomas is trans-sphenoidal resection, although microprolactinomas can be managed successfully with dopamine agonist therapy.

Free tri-iodothyronine (T 3)
Free tri-iodothyronine is incorrect. the symptoms of hypothyroidism and low T 4 and T 3 is also likely to be low, but won’t help detail the underlying cause of her thyroid disorder.

Thyroid ultrasound scan
Thyroid ultrasound scan is incorrect. There is no sign of intrinsic thyroid disease and the low TSH implies central rather than thyroid-mediated hypothyroidism.

Thyroid uptake scan
Thyroid uptake scan is incorrect. Thyroid uptake scanning is most useful in the evaluation of thyroiditis, and therefore has little additional value here.

Anti-thyroid antibodies.

stem: Luteinising hormone (LH, 73.4 U/l) and FSH (30.6 U/l) are both markedly elevated. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Premature ovarian failure
This woman has had at least two periods that she reports, so this is secondary amenorrhoea. The raised FSH and LH levels are suggestive of premature ovarian failure. The most likely cause is an autoimmune ovarian failure, given the family history suggestive of autoimmune thyroid disease and premature ovarian failure in her mother. Hormone replacement is essential to avoid osteoporosis in the longer term.

Hypothalamic hypogonadism
Hypothalamic hypogonadism is incorrect. Hypothalamic hypogonadism is more common in patients who are weight restricting or in athletes undertaking extreme training. It results from reduced secretion of gonadotropinreleasing hormone from the hypothalamus, resulting in reduced stimulation of LH and FSH in the anterior pituitary. Therefore this diagnosis is incorrect in this case as both LH and FSH are markedly raised.

Prolactinoma
Prolactinoma is incorrect. A prolactinoma can cause hypothalamic ammenorhea due to the negative feedback through gonadotrophin-releasing hormone causing a low or normal LH and FSH. Therefore the presence of a normal prolactin and elevated LH and FSH make this an unlikely diagnosis.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. Hypothyroidism typically causes menorrhagia and hyperthyroidism; if severe, it can also cause oligomennorhoea and secondary ammenorhoea. There is a family history of hypothyroidism in this case, but the normal TSH makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

Sheehan syndrome.

stem: A 57-year-old woman presents a feeling of shortness of breath and choking when she lies down. Some 4 months earlier she had been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and was started on aspirin and digoxin by her GP. On examination her GP could feel an irregular nodular goitre. Plain radiography confirmed retrosternal extension. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is <0.05 mU/l, fT4 33 (10-22); thyroid autoantibodies are negative. What diagnosis best fits with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Toxic multinodular goitre
The combination of hyperthyroidism and a n irregular nodular goitre in a middle-aged woman is typical of a toxic nodular goitre; her atrial fibrillation might well be related to this. Her goitre is obstructing, with significant retrosternal extension, and surgery is the treatment of choice. Initially, however, she should be rendered euthyroid with antithyroid drugs, such as carbimazole.

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is incorrect as this causes hypothyroidism, is associated with positive autoantibodies and causes a small goitre, typically.

Thyroglossal cyst
Thyroglossal cyst is incorrect as this does not cause abnormal thyroid function.

Follicular thyroid carcinoma
Follicular thyroid carcinoma is incorrect as this does not cause abnormal thyroid function and is usually associated with a single, not diffuse, nodules.

Graves’ disease.

stem: A 39-year-old man is seen for a follow-up appointment in the Endocrinology Clinic. He has Graves’ disease, managed with a block-and-replace regimen. He has a goitre, without tracheal compression, and is being considered for subtotal thyroidectomy. What is the most common post-operative complication following subtotal thyroidectomy?
explanation:
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is correct. Hypothyroidism occurs in about 10% of patients within one year of surgery. This percentage increases with time, and a high proportion of patients become hypothyroid in the long term (40% over ten years) and require levothyroxine indefinitely. Many patients will require replacement doses of levothyroxine on discharge from hospital. Risk factors for permanent hypothyroidism include seropositive antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, high-normal preoperative thyroid-stimulating hormone levels and histologyconfirmed thyroiditis.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy is incorrect. Laryngeal nerve palsy, which typically presents with hoarseness, changes in vocal pitch and noisy breathing, occurs in 1% of cases. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve. It supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx, except the cricothyroid muscles. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation of the airway below the larynx.

Chronic hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism is incorrect. Transient hypocalcaemia occurs in up to 10% of patients, and may present with paraesthesiae, muscle twitches/cramps or tetany – fortunately, permanent hypoparathyroidism is Tutor seen in < 1% of patients. The parathyroid gland is approximately the size of a grain of rice and they are commonly found glands on the posterior of the thyroid.

Recurrent hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism occurs in up to 10% of patients after subtotal thyroidectomy. Recurrence rates after antithyroid medication is increased in younger patients, severe biochemical disease, high concentrations of thyrotropin-binding inhibitor immunoglobulin, large goitre and smoking.

Tracheal compression.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is referred by her General Practitioner (GP), who is concerned that she might have an underlying endocrine problem. The girl had been taken to the GP by her mother. She is very studious and has just won a place at university. She weighs only 38 kg (6 stone) and is 1.78 m (5 ft 10 in) tall; her skin is dry and she has excessive growth of fine, soft hair; she has been amenorrhoeic for nine months; her thyroid function is normal; she is anaemic and has associated reduced white cell and platelet counts. What would you predict her hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis bloods will show?
options: Low LH, high FSH, normal oestradiol
High LH, normal FSH, normal oestradiol
Low LH, low FSH, normal oestradiol
High LH, high FSH, low oestradiol
Low LH, low FSH, low oestradiol
explanation:
Low LH, low FSH, low oestradiol
The diagnosis here is anorexia nervosa, with associated hypothalamic amenorrhoea, which is associated with low gonadotropins and, therefore, low oestradiol.

Low LH, high FSH, normal oestradiol
Low LH, high FSH, normal oestradiol is incorrect as the diagnosis here is anorexia nervosa, with associated hypothalamic amenorrhoea, which is associated with low gonadotropins and, therefore, low oestradiol.

High LH, normal FSH, normal oestradiol
High LH, normal FSH, normal oestradiol is incorrect as this would be the biochemical picture in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), not hypothalamic amenorrhoea.

Low LH, low FSH, normal oestradiol
Low LH, low FSH, normal oestradiol is incorrect as the diagnosis here is anorexia nervosa, with associated hypothalamic amenorrhoea, which is associated with low gonadotropins and, therefore, low oestradiol.

High LH, high FSH, low oestradiol.

stem: The GP requests you to assess her hormone levels. Which of the following hormones do you most expect to be elevated?
explanation:
Cortisol
In weight restricted adults, cortisol levels are often high due to a permanent state of physical stress on the body related to a starvation or catabolic state. In certain circumstances, cortisol may even fail to suppress on low dose overnight dexamethasone suppression test.

Oestrogen
Oestrogen is incorrect. Patients who are weight restricted or who lose a dramatic amount of weight can develop a hypothalamic hypogonadism with a low or normal LH and FSH level and a low or normal oestraidol level. This can result in secondary amenorrhea and transient infertility. Weight gain will lead to a restoration of the normal menstrual cycle.

Luteinising hormone
Luteinising hormone is incorrect. Luteinising hormone will be low or normal in keeping with a hypothalamic hypogonadism picture.

Prolactin
Prolactin is incorrect. Prolactin levels are usually normal or slightly elevated in weight restriction. On the contrary prolactin levels are often elevated in patients with high BMI, insulin resistance and PCOS. In this instance, the high prolactin is believed to be driven by high oestraidol levels in PCOS.

Thyroid hormones.

stem: A 40-year-old man with long-standing type II diabetes is found to have a urinary albumin excretion rate of 400 mg/l. His diabetes is well controlled, recent HbA1C 48 mmol/mol (6.5%), his fasting lipids are at target and he is normotensive (120/80). A neurological examination reveals abnormal pin prick and vibratory sense peripherally and peripheral pulses are palpable. Creatinine is normal at 88 umol/l, and potassium is 4.0 mmol/l. What additional drug should he be prescribed?
explanation:
Lisinopril
In a combined analysis of one European and one American study (total n = 225) patients with type 1 diabetes with a mean entry blood pressure of 122/77 mmHg, an adjusted risk reduction of 63% (95%CI, 16–84%; P = 0.017) was shown for the development of clinical nephropathy when the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor captopril (100 mg/day) was compared to placebo. Three smaller studies in normotensive type 2 patients have reported a similar reduction in the rate of development of clinical nephropathy. Blockade of the renin–angiotensin system by any means therefore appears to confer benefit.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. The current 2013 guideline recommendations of the American Diabetes Association (ADA) suggest aspirin therapy for primary prevention in patients with either type I or II diabetes and who have an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. They do not recommend aspirin therapy in men under years of age Chat50 with or most women under 60 years of age that have a low risk of cardiovascular disease, because the risk of bleeding outweighs the potential benefits of aspirin treatment. In this patient the cardiovascular risk is low and the most pressing issue is the microalbuminuria, which needs to be treated to prevent progression.

Atenolol
Atenolol is incorrect. Atenolol is not a first-line antihypertensive agent in patients with diabetes, and may increase the risk of erectile dysfunction in men. It should be reserved for those patients with left ventricular dysfunction who my benefit from rate control in addition to the antihypertensive effects of atenolol.

Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is incorrect. Clopidogrel is not recommended for primary prevention in patients with diabetes unless they are intolerant to aspirin therapy.

Sitagliptin
Sitagliptin is incorrect. Sitagliptin is a DPP4 inhibitor and acts to inhibit the normal gut enzyme DPP4, which breaks down GLP-1 hormone released after eating. By inhibiting this enzyme, DPP4 inhibitors allow a longer duration of action of endogenous GLP-1. Sitagliptin is less commonly associated with hypoglycaemia compared to sulphonylurea treatment, GLP-1 normally stimulates insulin secretion in a glucose-dependent manner. This medication is used as a second-line agent after metformin if glycaemic control is not achieved with metformin monotherapy; sitagliptin can then be added. In this case the most pressing issue is the microalbuminuria, as his diabetes is reportedly well controlled. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: Which of the following would the next step to reveal the underlying diagnosis?
options: Plasma renin:aldosterone ratio post-BP medication washout
Magnetic resonance imaging of the adrenal glands
explanation:
Plasma renin:aldosterone ratio post-BP medication washout
An elevated aldosterone in the presence of a suppressed renin confirms the diagnosis of hyperaldosteronism or Conn syndrome. However, certain antihypertensives can affect the interpretation of the result and ideally the test should be done following a period off medication. The test may still be useful if only some of the antihypertensive medications can be discontinued such as beta-blockers. Beta-blockers suppress renin and can cause a false positive test and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors can suppress aldosterone, and therefore ACE inhibitors can cause falsely low aldosterone reading.

24-hour urinary catecholamines
Urinary catecholamines is incorrect. They are a useful diagnostic screening test for phaeochromocytoma. Phaeochromocytoma can cause uncontrolled hypertension as depicted in this case. However, a phaeochromocytoma would not lead to hypokalaemia as described in this case and the typical radiological appearance of a phaeochromocytoma would not be consistent with an adrenal adenoma as described in this case.

Metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan
A metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan is incorrect. It is used in the localisation or characterisation of a suspected phaeochromocytoma or for the localisation or screening of metastases in a case of suspected metastatic phaeochromocytoma. MIBG is taken up by the norepinephrine receptor on chromaffin cells, making it a useful nuclear imaging modality for this reason, although false negatives can occur and occasionally false positives as MIBG can be taken up physiologically by the adrenal medulla of a healthy adrenal. MIBG would not be a useful test in this clinical scenario.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the adrenal glands
Magnetic resonance imaging of the adrenal glands is incorrect. No further additional radiological characterisation is required in this case as we know from the CT that this patient has a 3-cm adrenal lesion which contains fat or lipid and therefore is likely to be a benign adrenal adenoma. The , which would affect the management for this patient, is whether the adrenal adenoma is secreting hormone. The most likely hormone hypersecretion in this case would be aldosterone, given the low potassium and hypertension; therefore, no additional information would be provided by an MRI scan at this time.

Saline suppression test.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is due to undergo a hysterectomy. She has a history of hypertension, headaches and panic attacks over the past few years. She currently takes ramipril for her blood pressure. Preoperative examination revealed a blood pressure of 150/85 mmHg, normal renal function and calcium concentration. An electrocardiogram showed mild left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). During the operation, as the surgeon attempts to mobilise her uterus, her blood pressure rises to 210/110 mmHg, her pulse rises to 130 bpm and she suffers an acute myocardial infarction. What is the most likely cause of her intraoperative hypertension and myocardial infarction?
explanation:
Undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma
Given her history, she is likely to have been suffering paroxysms of catecholamine release (headaches, ‘panic attacks’). Mobilisation of the uterus is likely to have precipitated an acute release of large amounts of catecholamines, causing her catastrophic rise in blood pressure and intraoperative myocardial infarction.

Essential hypertension
Essential hypertension is incorrect. She has signs and symptoms of catecholamine excess suggesting phaeochromocytoma.

Occult coronary artery disease
Occult coronary artery disease is incorrect. She has signs and symptoms of catecholamine excess suggesting phaeochromocytoma. Occult myocardial infarction would not cause that degree of hypertension and sinus tachycardia.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is incorrect. MEN1 is associated with neoplasms of the pituitary gland, the parathyroid gland and the pancreas, not phaeochromocytoma, which is the clinical picture in this case.

Renal artery stenosis.

stem: Creatinine is raised at 190 μmol/l. He is taking metformin for his diabetes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
options: Hyperkalaemia due to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE)
explanation:
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic coma
The investigations suggest that this patient has hyperosmolar hyperglycemic . The bicarbonate level and blood pH would both be low if he had diabetic ketoacidosis. The anion gap, just above the upper limit of normal, is almost certainly contributed to by metformin and his degree of renal impairment. Rehydration with IV fluids is the intervention of choice. Although insulin is required in the acute phase of the illness it may notwith beAI requied long term.

Diabetic ketoacidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. The normal bicarbonate and pH of 7.35 don’t fit with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis.

Drug overdose
Drug overdose is incorrect. There is no reason to suspect drug overdose in this case, and the blood picture seen here fits well with a diagnosis of non-ketotic hyperosmolar coma.

Acute stroke
Acute stroke is incorrect. The blood picture seen here and relative hypotension are inconsistent with a diagnosis of stroke.

Hyperkalaemia due to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACE)
Hyperkalaemia due to ACE inhibitor is incorrect. The potassium is at the upper end of the normal range, likely to be related to dehydration as a result of hyperosmolar, non-ketotic state rather than because of the ACE inhibitor script. Diabetes - Type II.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presenting with polyuria is found to have diabetes insipidus after a motorcycle accident which resulted in a head injury. Which part of the nephron is most affected in this condition?
explanation:
Cortical and medullary collecting tubules
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) plays a central role in urinary concentration by increasing the water permeability of the normally impermeable cortical and medullary collecting tubules. In the absence of ADH, little water is reabsorbed in the collecting tubules and dilute urine is excreted.

Proximal tubule
Proximal tubulen is incorrect. Sodium and water reabsorption in the proximal tubule is primarily via active reabsorption across the basolateral membrane via the Na/K/ATPase pump.

Distal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) is incorrect. Although aquaporin 2 expression is increased in the DCT as well as in cortical and medullary collecting tubules, the DCT expression contributes less to overall fluid balance.

Thin ascending loop of Henle
Thin ascending loop of Henle is incorrect. The thin ascending loop of Henle is impermeable to water.

Glomerular efferent arterioles.

stem: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction
Although vascular disease is less prevalent in type I, compared to type II, diabetes, this patient has ECG changes and has developed symptoms of LVF. This is unusual, given that patients with DKA are usually significantly volume-depleted. The likely cause of his symptoms and persistent acidosis due to poor tissue perfusion is an NSTEMI and while uncommon, patients with diabetes can present without chest pain.

Mesenteric ischaemia
This patient is still significantly acidotic, although ketone levels have fallen significantly. This raises the possibility that the acidosis is stemming from tissue ischaemia, rather than from continued severe ketoacidosis. Although mesenteric angina is possible in a patient with vascular disease, the T-wave changes on the ECG and the fact that this patient has developed symptoms of left ventricular failure (LVF) is a better pointer to a non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI).

Pre-renal failure
The combination of persistent acidosis despite fluid replacement and worsening LVF is a pointer to ‘pump failure’ due to an NSTEMI, rather than due to pre-renal failure because of persistent hypovolaemia. Urgent Cardiology review is the most appropriate next step.

Viral myocarditis
Viral myocarditis can coexist with DKA, although the limited ECG changes consistent with anterior territory ischaemia are more consistent with an NSTEMI, rather than with myocarditis. In myocarditis, more widespread T-wave inversion and some prodromal symptoms of a viral infection might be expected.

Pulmonary embolism.

stem: A 18-year-old man comes to the diabetes clinic for review. He has had multiple episodes of penile thrush and been feeling increasingly tired over the past few months. A fasting glucose was then noted to be 11.1 mmol/l. A number of members of his family also have diabetes, some which appears to be classical Type 2, others have presented like him at a young age. On examination his BP is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. His BMI is 22. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his diabetes?
explanation:
HNF 1-alpha mutation
Mutation of the hepatocyte nuclear factor (HNF) 1-alpha gene is responsible for up to 70% of cases of maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY), and is the commonest cause in the Northern European population. Patients with MODY due to HNF 1-alpha mutation are often very sensitive to sulphonylureas, and as little as 20 mg of gliclazide once to twice daily can be adequate in achieving excellent glycaemic control, which means that patients can be managed with oral therapies for their diabetes for a considerable period of time.

HNF 4-alpha mutation
HNF 4-alpha mutation is incorrect. HNF 4-alpha mutations account for 5?10% of cases of MODY.

Glucokinase mutation
Glucokinase mutation is incorrect. Glucokinase mutations are responsible for MODY2, the second commonest cause of MODY, where rises in glucose may be quite modest.

IPF 1 mutation
IPF 1 mutation is incorrect. Insulin promoter factor (IPF) 1 accounts for <1% of cases of MODY and is associated with pancreatic agenesis in homozygotes.

HNF 1-beta mutation.

stem: A 65-year-old woman known to have chronic low-back pain notices a severe sharp pain in the left groin after a minor fall and is unable to walk. She was born in Nigeria but has been living in the UK for 15 years. She has a BMI of 31kg/m 2. Left neck of femur fracture is identified on radiological examination. Routine laboratory evaluation discloses a serum calcium concentration of 2.01 (NR 2.15–2.6) mmol/l, a serum phosphate concentration of 0.68 (0.8–1.4) mmol/l, parathyroid hormone (PTH) level of 80 (11–54 pg/ml) and renal function is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Vitamin D deficiency
The combination of hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, along with fracture, points to the diagnosis of osteomalacia and vitamin D deficiency. She is at high risk for Vitamin D deficiency because of her ethnicity and obesity.

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect as this would be associated with high calcium levels.

Hypervitaminosis D
Hypervitaminosis D is incorrect as this would be associated with high calcium levels.

Paget’s disease of bone
Paget’s disease of bone is incorrect as this would be associated with a normal calcium level.

Idiopathic osteoporosis.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with episodes of tremor, sweating and incoordination, particularly when he first wakes in the morning. He has put on 4 kg in weight over the course of the last 6 months. Examination in the clinic is unremarkable. His BP is normal at 123/82 mmHg, pulse is 65 and regular. His BMI is 25. What would be the most useful investigation(s) to establish a diagnosis of an insulinoma?
options: An insulin hypoglycaemia test (insulin stress test)
Simultaneous measurement of fasting blood glucose and serum insulin and C-peptide
explanation:
Simultaneous measurement of fasting blood glucose and serum insulin and C-peptide
