Simultaneous measurement of fasting blood glucose and serum insulin and C-peptide concentrations during an episode. In insulinoma, levels of insulin fail to fall during a period of fasting. This results in increased risk of symptomatic hypoglycaemia and potentially accounts for his presentation. In patients presenting with elevated insulin and cpeptide with hypoglycaemia, sulfonylurea abuse should also be excluded. Gradual weight gain also fits with the diagnosis of insulinoma.

An insulin hypoglycaemia test (insulin stress test)
An insulin hypoglycaemia test (insulin stress test) is incorrect. Insulin stress testing is utilised in the evaluation of growth hormone insufficiency.

An oral glucose tolerance test
An oral glucose tolerance test is incorrect. An oral glucose tolerance test is used in the diagnosis of diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance.

Measurement of glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c)
Measurement of glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) is incorrect. HbA1c is an insensitive marker of insulinoma and is only really useful in evaluation of hypoglycaemia associated with diabetes therapy.

Measurement of serum 3-hydroxybutyrate.

stem: Urinalysis shows glucose++ and ketones+. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Basal-bolus insulin regimen
This patient has a diagnosis of type I diabetes. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend that a basal-bolus regimen should be offered for optimal management due to the patient's high glucose level. This approach enables patients to be flexible and work treatment around their schedule. For the basal insulin, patients would receive one or more separate injections of intermediate-acting insulin or longacting insulin analogue daily. This would be in addition to multiple bolus injections of short-acting insulin prior to the patient's meals.

Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin infusion
Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin infusion to This is a new presentation of type I diabetes. The patient does not have diabetic ketoacidosis. It is reasonable consider a basal-bolus insulin regimen, rather than a Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin infusion (VRIII).

Nocturnal long-acting insulin
Nocturnal long-acting insulin is not enough to control blood sugars regularly during the day.

Pre-meal short-acting insulin
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend against offering a non-basal-bolus regimen to newly diagnosed adults with type I diabetes. Basal-bolus insulin should be used, typically at night.

Twice-daily mixed insulin regimen.

stem: Which of the following treatments should be commenced first?
explanation:
Intravenous sodium chloride
This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a condition still associated with mortality in patients with type I diabetes mellitus. Having poorly controlled diabetes mellitus is a risk factor for developing DKA. The diagnostic criteria are as follows: ketonaemia ≥ 3mmol/l or > 2+ ketones on urine dipstick blood glucose > 11 mmol/l bicarbonate < 15 mmol/l and/or venous pH < 7.3. Patients will be fluid-deplete as a result of osmotic diuresis due to hyperglycaemia, vomiting commonly associated with DKA and decreased fluid intake due to altered consciousness. A patient may have a water deficit of 100 ml/kg. The most important initial treatment, therefore, is appropriate fluid replacement with intravenous 0.9% saline. The main aims of initial fluid replacement are to correct hypotension, replenish the intravascular deficit and counteract the effects of osmotic diuresis. After commencing fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, in the form of a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion, should be started.

Fixed-rate insulin infusion
Although a fixed-rate insulin infusion calculated at 0.1 U/kg should be prescribed for patients with DKA, this should be done following the commencement of intravenous fluids. The aim of insulin therapy is to suppress ketogenesis, reduce blood glucose and correct electrolyte imbalances.

Haemodialysis
Although this patient is showing a deranged renal profile and significant acidaemia, it is most likely secondary to DKA, given the history of poorly controlled type I diabetes. The mainstay treatment of DKA includes aggressive fluid resuscitation, followed by early and concomitantly intravenous insulin.

Intravenous antibiotics
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) may be precipitated by concurrent infection and antibiotics, therefore, may be indicated in some cases. As there are no signs of sepsis, or indeed any infection here, antibiotics should not be given before initiating treatment for DKA.

Intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

stem: A 71-year-old man with established sarcoidosis presents for review. On his routine bloods it is discovered that his serum calcium concentration is 2.95 mmol/l (NR 2.15–2.65). He complains of constipation and bone pain. His renal function, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase levels are all normal, and the parathyroid hormone level is low. What is the most likely cause of his hypercalcaemia?
explanation:
Increased hydroxylation of vitamin D
The hypercalcaemia in this case is related to sarcoidosis. It also frequently causes an increase in 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D, the active metabolite of vitamin D, which is usually hydrolysed within the kidney; however, in sarcoidosis patients, hydroxylation of vitamin D can occur outside the kidneys, namely inside the macrophages found in the granulomas that the condition produces. Interferon gamma produced by activated lymphocytes and macrophages plays a major role in the synthesis of 1 alpha,25-dihydroxy vitamin D 3 (1 alpha, 25(OH)2D3).

Primary hyperparathyroidism
Primary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is low.

Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy
Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy is incorrect. There is no evidence of malignancy.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. He does not have kidney disease, which is the main cause of secondary hyperparathyroidism.

Milk–alkali syndrome.

stem: A 40-year-old man is receiving lithium for a bipolar disorder. He now complains of increased urinary frequency and nocturia. He has taken the medication for some 7 years, he also takes risperidone and has gained 7 kg in weight over the past year. Post water deprivation test his plasma osmolality has risen to 320 and urine osmolality is 280. What is the most likely cause for his symptoms?
explanation:
Development of resistance to vasopressin
This patient’s water deprivation test is consistent with a diagnosis of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which is recognised as a long-term consequence of therapy. Often only partial reversal occurs with withdrawal of lithium therapy.

Deficiency of vasopressin
Deficiency of vasopressin is incorrect. Although lithium causes diabetes insipidus, this is not due to deficiency of vasopressin.

Reduced creatinine clearance
Reduced creatinine clearance is incorrect. Renal impairment is a recognised cause of lithium intoxication, but reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is not the cause of the presentation here.

Onset of thyrotoxicosis
Onset of thyrotoxicosis is incorrect. Lithium-related thyroid dysfunction does occur, and hypothyroidism may lead to syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), rather than the diabetes insipidus picture seen here.

Excessive water intake.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred by her GP to the hospital because of recurrent episodic headaches, which tend to come on at times of stress or exercise; she also complains of intermittent anxiety, palpitations and problems with sweating. He has tried her on a course of antidepressants, which only seemed to make her symptoms worse. Her 24-hour urinary catecholamines show markedly raised normetanephrine and metanephrine; CT imaging reveals a mass in the right adrenal medulla her blood pressure in the clinic is 145/95 mmHg. What is the best definitive management plan for this woman’s condition?
options: Urgent ß blockade, then unilateral adrenalectomy
Urgent α blockade, then ß blockade, if required, and unilateral adrenalectomy
Urgent ß blockade, then α -blockade, if required, and unilateral adrenalectomy
Urgent α blockade, then ß blockade, if required, and bilateral adrenalectomy
explanation:
Urgent α blockade, then ß blockade, if required, and unilateral adrenalectomy
This woman has a phaeochromocytoma of the right adrenal medulla.

Urgent ß blockade, then unilateral adrenalectomy
Urgent ß blockade, then unilateral adrenalectomy is incorrect. Use of β-adrenergic receptor blockers in the absence of an α-adrenoceptor blocker is not recommended, because of the potential for hypertensive crisis due to unopposed stimulation of α-adrenergic receptors.

Urgent adrenalectomy
Urgent adrenalectomy is incorrect. Surgery without blockade can precipitate adrenergic crisis.

Urgent ß blockade, then α -blockade, if required, and unilateral adrenalectomy
Urgent ß blockade, then α -blockade, if required, and unilateral adrenalectomy is incorrect. Use of β-adrenergic receptor blockers in the absence of an α-adrenoceptor blocker is not recommended, because of the potential for hypertensive crisis due to unopposed stimulation of α-adrenergic receptors.

Urgent α blockade, then ß blockade, if required, and bilateral adrenalectomy.

stem: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies are positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Weight gain due to lifestyle changes
explanation:
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
This patient has recent weight gain, increased total cholesterol and triglycerides and a raised thyroidstimulating hormone (TSH), with low-normal T 3 and T 4 and a small goitre. This picture is entirely consistent with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Thyroid hormone replacement is probably indicated in this case, with the aim of improving symptoms and restoring the TSH to the normal range.

Graves’ disease
Graves’ disease is incorrect. Graves’ disease is a cause of thyrotoxicosis.

Viral thyroiditis
Viral thyroiditis is incorrect. Her symptoms are too prolonged for a diagnosis of viral thyroiditis.

Sick euthyroid syndrome
Sick euthyroid syndrome is incorrect. She does not have any comorbid illnesses; her symptoms are due to hypothyroidism.

Weight gain due to lifestyle changes.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner, as he is concerned that he has not been experiencing signs of puberty like his peers. He denies any other symptoms and has no past medical history of note. On examination, he is tall but has underdeveloped muscles, and he lacks any facial hair. He has small testicles that measure 4 cm2 on orchidometry, and there is little surrounding pubic hair. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Luteinising hormone (LH) 0.5 mIU/ml 1.3–8 mIU/ml Testosterone 2 nmol/l 10–30 nmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Kallmann syndrome

Kallmann syndrome is a cause of delayed puberty due to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which is caused by a failure in the development of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurones in the hypothalamus. Along with delayed puberty, reﬂected in this patient’s presentation of small testicles and little pubic hair, patients most typically demonstrate anosmia. E Klinefelter syndrome Klinefelter syndrome is a reasonable differential diagnosis. It is associated with the 47,XXY karyotype and presents with tall stature, lack of secondary characteristics and infertility. However, Klinefelter syndrome is a cause of primary hypogonadism and in such patients, LH levels would be raised. In contrast, this patient's blood results demonstrate hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. A Anabolic steroid abuse Anabolic steroid abuse can cause secondary hypogonadism. However, there is nothing in this history to suggest this is the cause. This patient has underdeveloped muscles; if this were the cause, you would expect overdeveloped muscles. B Congenital adrenal hypoplasia Congenital adrenal hypoplasia is a rare cause of secondary hypogonadism. It presents in childhood with failure to thrive and salt-wasting, which leads to severe disease, resulting in severe volume depletion and electrolyte abnormalities. It is highly unlikely that a patient would reach adolescence without having been previously diagnosed. C Haemochromatosis Haemochromatosis may cause iron deposition in the pituitary gland, which can lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (as demonstrated by this patient’s blood results). Typically, haemochromatosis presents after the age of 40 in men and therefore does not tend to cause delayed puberty.

stem: A 50-year-old retired bank manager attended a ‘Well Man’ Clinic. He has always enjoyed good health, but has recently developed a dry cough. He takes daily over-the-counter multivitamin tablets. On examination, he is extremely well, with no abnormality detected. Screening investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal Values Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 5.0 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Hb 120 g/l 135 - 175 g/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l WCC 9.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l
explanation: B Primary hyperparathyroidism Plasma PTH is the best single test for differentiating between hypercalcaemia due to parathyroid overactivity and that due to non-parathyroid causes. Primary hyperparathyroidism can be associated with a plasma PTH level within the normal range. The normal response to hypercalcaemia is suppression of plasma PTH to below the lower reference limit. Levels within the reference limit are inappropriately high and suggestive of parathyroid disease. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is a hereditary disease with autosomal dominant transmission and is characterised by moderate chronic hypercalcaemia and normal or moderately elevated plasma PTH concentrations. The fractional excretion of calcium is lower than in primary hyperparathyroidism, and the urine calcium/creatinine ratio is usually < 0.01. The importance of this condition is that hypercalcaemia rarely leads to signiﬁcant clinical signs and parathyroidectomy is unsuccessful as therapy. A Multiple myeloma Plasma PTH levels would not be in the normal range and would be reduced. Hypercalcaemia is a common feature in multiple myeloma where there is frequently calcium elevation, renal insufﬁciency, anaemia and bone disease. Ten to 15% of patients present with hypercalcaemia in multiple myeloma. The cause is multifactorial, but bone destruction from osteolytic tumour lesions is the main contributing factor. C Prolonged tourniquet application This would not be a cause because PTH and corrected calcium were repeated on an uncuffed sample, with persistent hypercalcemia. D Sarcoidosis Plasma PTH levels would not be in the normal range and would be reduced. Hypercalcemia is common in sarcoidosis. This is due to an uncontrolled synthesis of 1,25dihydroxyvitamin D3 by macrophages. 1,25- dihydroxyvitamin D3 leads to an increased absorption of calcium in the intestine and an increased resorption of calcium in the bone. E Vitamin D excess Plasma PTH levels would not be in the normal range and would be reduced. Vitamin D excess is associated with hypercalcaemia because there is an increased absorption of calcium in the intestine and an increased resorption of calcium in the bone.

stem: A 54-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents for his annual review. Over the past couple of years, he has suffered problems with early satiety, indigestion and regurgitation of food matter but has not lost weight, and now requests investigations. His diabetes is relatively well controlled, with a recent HbA1c of 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%), his Hb is normal at 130 g/l and his ESR is 13 mm/h. You note that he does have a postural drop of 35 mmHg on blood pressure measurement. Which of the following actions is most useful with respect to his GI symptoms?
options: Trial of proton pump inhibitor therapy
explanation:
B Isotope gastric motility studies This patient likely has diabetic autonomic neuropathy, manifest in postural hypotension and delayed gastric emptying. Isotope gastric motility studies are the most appropriate way to assess gastric emptying, and treatments involve prokinetic agents such as domperidone, metoclopramide or erythromycin, although response to treatment is generally poor. Treatment of postural hypotension involves mechanical

measures such as bedhead elevation and wearing of support stockings. Intake of sodium chloride should be adequate, and ﬂudrocortisone may be added starting at a dose of 50 μg/day, increased up to 400 μg as required. Diuretics, vasodilators and tricyclic antidepressants may exacerbate the condition and, for this reason, review of current medications that may exacerbate postural hypotension is important before commencing further therapy. C Upper GI endoscopy Upper GI endoscopy is required as part of the work-up symptoms of indigestion in this patient, but won’t reveal the underlying cause. A Oesophageal pH monitoring Oesophageal pH monitoring is most useful for evaluating symptoms of oesophageal reﬂux disease. Although there is a degree of reﬂux here, it’s driven by dysmotility rather than by excess acid production. D Trial of anti-acids Although anti-acids may offer some relief, given dysmotility is the primary problem, they are unlikely to bring complete resolution of symptoms. E Trial of proton pump inhibitor therapy PPIs may reduce stomach acid, but they won’t impact on regurgitation of undigested food.

stem: A 48-year-old man who was previously seen in the Endocrinology Clinic for abdominal obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia presents six months later for review after having lost 42 lbs in weight. On examination in the clinic, his blood pressure (BP) is 155/92 mmHg and his body mass index (BMI) is 28 kg/m2. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 139 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 230 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Low densitylipoprotein (LDL) 4.4 mmol/l < 3.5 mmol/l Triglycerides 3.5 mmol/l 0–1.5 mmol/l High-density lipoprotein (HDL) 0.7 mmol/l > 1.0 mmol/l Fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/l (< 6.1) < 7 mmol/l Which of the following is true in this case?
options: His cardiovascular risk is not increased
He does not require anti-hypertensive therapy
It would be reasonable to treat him with a statin
He should be considered for gastric reduction surgery
He is not at increased risk of development of diabetes
explanation: C It would be reasonable to treat him with a statin Of particular concern in this patient is the typical lipid pattern seen in insulin-resistant states, with low HDL cholesterol and high triglycerides. Given his increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease, it would therefore be sensible to treat him with a statin. B He does not require anti-hypertensive therapy A blood pressure (BP) of 155/92 in a patient with signs of insulin resistance means that intervention with anti- hypertensive therapy is warranted. A His cardiovascular risk is not increased This patient has signs of insulin resistance, and a low HDL which drives a raised LDL : HDL ratio; as such, cardiovascular risk is increased in this patient. D He should be considered for gastric reduction surgery This patient has already lost a signiﬁcant amount of weight. As such, gastric reduction surgery isn’t warranted. E He is not at increased risk of development of diabetes A fasting glucose of 6.8 is on the cusp of diabetes, meaning that conversion is likely over the next few years.

stem: A 64-year-old woman with type II diabetes comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for investigation of chronic diarrhoea. She is taking metformin 2.5 g per day and gliclazide 160 mg. Additional medication includes simvastatin 40 mg and aspirin 75 mg. On examination, she has a body mass index (BMI) of 28 kg/m2 and looks well. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. Her blood pressure (BP) is 145/82 mmHg, with no postural drop. There is no evidence of peripheral neuropathy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 139 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 229 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Albumin 40 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 35 U/l 5–30 U/l ESR 13 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Small bowel biopsy normal and colonoscopy is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Bile salt malabsorption High-dose metformin is thought to interfere with the enterohepatic circulation of bile salts, leading to reduced reabsorption of bile salts from the ileum. Diarrhoea, in association with metformin therapy, can often be avoided with slow up-titration of the dose. A Autonomic neuropathy Given the lack of peripheral neuropathy and no postural drop in blood pressure, signiﬁcant autonomic neuropathy is very unlikely. C Chronic pancreatitis Clinically signiﬁcant chronic pancreatitis is associated with malabsorption. The albumin of 40 counts against signiﬁcant malabsorption. D Coeliac disease Coeliac disease is associated with anaemia and evidence of malabsorption on biochemistry, neither of which is seen here. The small bowel biopsy effectively rules this out. E NSAID related colitis Abnormalities on colonic biopsy would be expected in patients with NSAID-related colitis.

stem: A 17-year-old boy attends the clinic. He is worried as he has failed to enter puberty. He would like to form relationships with women but at the current time this is impossible. On examination he is 6ft 2 inches in height and has absent secondary sexual hair, a small penis and testes. On further questioning he admits to not having any sense of smell to speak of. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 231 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Testosterone Very low FSH Low LH Low Given the likely diagnosis, what appearance would you expect to see on cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)?
explanation: D Absent olfactory bulbs Absent olfactory bulbs, correct. This boy is likely to have Kallmann syndrome, as evidenced by hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and absent sense of smell. Absent olfactory bulbs are present on 75% of MRI scans in these patients. The syndrome results in an isolated gonadotrophin (GNRH) deﬁciency and, in turn, gonadal deﬁciencies. This causes loss of libido, loss of secondary sexual hair and amenor- rhoea/erectile dysfunction. B Hypothalamic damage on MRI This patient should be managed with androgen replacement therapy. Fertility can be restored in the majority of patients with either pulsed GNRH or gonadotrophin therapy. Assessment of bone age and bone mineral density is also essential in these patients. A Normal result Although with this condition the absence of olfactory bulbs is more common. This is because Kallman syndrome is usually an x-linked mutation in the KAL-1 gene which encodes anosmin-1, causing loss of smell. C Empty sella This is more often associated with a defect in the diaphragm and extension into the subarachnoid space (a congenital abnormality), following a pituitary infarction or pituitary tumour treatment. E Hypertrophied olfactory bulbs Kallman syndrome is associated with absent, not hypertrophied, olfactory bulbs.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. Over the past year, she has noticed a change in her facial appearance and has been suffering from headaches. Her General Practitioner (GP) has also found it difﬁcult to control her blood pressure and has recently diagnosed her with pre-diabetes. Her blood pressure is 155/88 mmHg; her pulse is 74 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 24 kg/m2.
explanation: C IGF-1 The picture here shows prognathism (prominent lower jaw) and widening of the nose, consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. IGF-1 has a long half-life and is elevated in patients with acromegaly. It therefore represents the ideal initial blood test. B Computed tomography (CT) head Because of the risk of brain imaging detecting an incidentaloma, a biochemical diagnosis of acromegaly is usually made before proceeding to pituitary imaging. Out of the two options, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is preferred to CT. A Abdominal ultrasound scan Ninety-ﬁve per cent of cases of acromegaly are related to a pituitary adenoma. An abdominal ultrasound is therefore not a ﬁrst-line investigation. Even in cases where acromegaly is conﬁrmed and a pituitary scan is negative, an ultrasound scan is unlikely to be sensitive enough to detect a tumour. D Random growth hormone Growth hormone release is pulsatile, and growth hormone itself has a very short half-life. This means that a random growth hormone measurement can miss a diagnosis of acromegaly. E 24-hour urinary free cortisol Urinary free cortisol is an initial outpatient investigation for Cushing syndrome, characterised by obesity and impaired glucose tolerance, rather than the changes in facial appearance seen here.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department after being found confused by her home help. She has problems with mobility and type II diabetes, and takes a number of medications. According to the carers, she has been increasingly chesty with a cough productive of bloodstained sputum over the past four days. On arrival in the Emergency Department, her blood pressure is 132/88 mmHg, pulse 84 bpm and regular and temperature 38.1 °C. There are signs of right-sided consolidation on auscultation. She is drowsy and confused and suffers a short (40 s) tonic– clonic seizure just after you complete your physical examination. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 11.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 199 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 112 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 108 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 9.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l CRP 189 mg/l < 5 mg/l Chest X-ray: Right lower lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention on top of antibiotic therapy?
explanation: C Hypertonic saline This is an emergency situation that cannot wait for ﬂuid restriction or demeclocycline to take effect because of the presence of a signiﬁcantly reduced conscious level and seizure activity. Bolus 150 mL of 3% NaCl over 20 minutes, 2- 3 times as needed, checking Na every 20 minutes. This may be enough acutely to prevent further seizures from occurring. The hypertonic saline must be administered in the High Dependency Unit (HDU) setting, so that close monitoring of serum sodium level can take place to avoid a rapid rise. B Fluid restriction Fluid restriction will correct the sodium level too slowly in this situation where the patient is obtunded and has suffered a seizure. Hypertonic saline under controlled conditions is the most appropriate option to correct his sodium level. A Demeclocycline Demeclocycline results in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and can correct syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) where there is a poor response to ﬂuid restriction. It is not used in this emergency situation. D Isotonic saline SIADH is euvolemic hyponatremia and it is a common misconception that isotonic saline will result in a signiﬁcant increase in serum sodium level. When urine osmolality is signiﬁcantly elevated, isotonic saline is a source of free water and can actually worsen hyponatraemia. E Lithium Although lithium results in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, it is not used as a medication in an acute situation for raising serum sodium levels.

stem: A 63-year-old HGV driver comes to the clinic for review. He has recently been diagnosed with type II diabetes. Past history of note includes poorly controlled hypertension. He is known to have missed a number of general practitioner (GP) appointments for follow-up. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 132/82 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. His BMI is 34. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 182 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 189 micromol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glomerular ﬁltration rate (GFR) Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l HbA1c mmol/mol (7.6%) <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: C Linagliptin The answer is Linagliptin - This patient has obesity, renal impairment and Type 2 diabetes. In this situation an agent that won’t lead to further weight gain is most appropriate. Linagliptin is a DPPIV inhibitor subject primarily to hepatic metabolism. This means it can be safely used in patients down to severe renal impairment. It may promote modest weight loss and does not increase the risk of hypoglycaemia; as such it is the default option here. A Basal bolus insulin Basal bolus insulin is incorrect, it is not indicated because it will lead to further weight gain and is associated with increased risk of hypoglycaemia. Starting insulin would mean he could not continue driving the HGV until he could demonstrate stable diabetes control. B Gliclazide Gliclazide is incorrect, increases weight gain and is associated with hypoglycaemia, so as such it should be avoided here. D Metformin Metformin is incorrect, this does not increase weight gain, and does not cause hypoglycaemia; it is however contra-indicated according to the prescribing information and NICE guidelines because GFR is almost at the level where it should be discontinued, (<30). E Pioglitazone Pioglitazone is incorrect, this promotes weight gain and ﬂuid retention, and so because of the weight gain, DPPIV inhibitors are preferred here.

stem: A 46-year-old presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of thirst and lethargy. He had been discharged some two weeks earlier after his third episode of acute pancreatitis in the past year. He admits to alcoholism, drinking three bottles of whisky and at least 30 pints of beer each week. On examination, he looks dehydrated and underweight. His blood pressure is 125/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 92 bpm, his body mass index is 21. Respiratory, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 9.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 232 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 185 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 26.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Amylase 400U/l < 200 U/l Urine ketones -ve He agrees to begin a detox regime. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage his diabetes?
explanation: E Insulin Diabetes associated with pancreatitis is due to damage to the endocrine pancreas and associated lack of insulin. This pathophysiology is consistent with the patient’s presentation: he is thin, with symptoms of insulinopaenia. As such, exogenous insulin replacement is the only appropriate intervention here. C Acarbose Acarbose reduces absorption of complex carbohydrates from the gut. In this case it won’t impact on glucose control and will actually worsen diarrhoea. A Metformin Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and is therefore expected to have no signiﬁcant impact on blood glucose levels in this patient. B Gliclazide Although gliclazide will have a stimulatory effect on remaining endogenous insulin production, it’s unlikely to achieve blood glucose control. D Sitagliptin Sitagliptin reduces degradation of endogenous incretins; these, however, have little effect on increasing insulin production from a failing pancreas.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes presents for review. He currently takes metformin 2 g/day and gliclazide 160 mg/day, and a recent HbA1c was 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%). His complaint is of weight loss, burning proximal muscle pain and weakness. On examination there is left-sided quadriceps wasting. Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for his diabetes and associated complications?
explanation: C Transition to insulin therapy The aetiology of diabetic amyotrophy, the diagnosis here, is unknown. It affects the lumbar sacral plexus lower motor neurones. Transition to insulin therapy is recommended because it is likely to improve his glucose control, and may impact progression of neuropathy. Recovery of diabetic amyotrophy happens over 3–4 months, but only 50% achieve complete recovery. Trials of immunomodulatory agents in managing the condition have been disappointing. A Increased metformin dose There is little evidence that increasing metformin dose above 2 g/day has any additional impact on glycaemic control. B Increased gliclazide dose Like metformin, the dose response curve for gliclazide is relatively ﬂat at high doses. The increment in glucose control between 160 and 320 mg/day is therefore small. D Amitriptyline Amitriptyline, although effective in treating neuropathic pain, won’t impact on progression of neuropathy. E Tramadol Opiate-based analgesics aren’t recommended for the treatment of diabetic neuropathy because they are less effective than agents such as tricyclic anti-depressants, and are addictive.

stem: An 18-year-old man with mild learning disability is referred to the Emergency Department for review. He has recently moved into sheltered accommodation in the area and is noted by staff to have made multiple complaints about muscular weakness and pins and needles affecting both hands. He has been noted by the GP to have hypocalcaemia and a raised level of parathyroid hormone. On examination, there is obvious subcutaneous calciﬁcation and he has a short ﬁfth metacarpal on each hand. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for this patient?
explanation: C Calcium and vitamin D supplementation This individual has pseudohypoparathyroidism. It is associated with short stature, short metacarpals, subcutaneous calciﬁcation and variable intellectual impairment. The G-proteincoupled receptor for PTH becomes unresponsive to the hormone, hence patients become hypocalcaemic in the face of normal or elevated PTH levels. Variable degrees of resistance involving other G-protein-mediated receptors, such as those linked to TSH, luteinising hormone (LH) and FSH activity, may also be seen. Calcium and vitamin D is the intervention of choice. Calcium levels should be monitored frequently during treatment as rapid rises may occur. A Parathyroidectomy The hypocalcaemia seen here is consistent with parathyroid resistance rather than functional parathyroid excess; hence parathyroidectomy is not appropriate. B Calcium supplementation Calcium supplementation alone is inadequate to restore normal calcium levels. D Parathyroid hormone administration Given this is a syndrome of parathyroid hormone resistance, supplementation of PTH will not restore normal calcium metabolism. E Calcitonin administration Calcitonin is used IV as a treatment for acute hypercalcaemia.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with limited exposure to medical services presents to the Endocrinology Clinic. She has never had a period and previously felt this was due to having a short height, but she has recently decided to seek advice. On examination, she is signiﬁcantly shorter than would be expected, given her parental height; her nipples are widely spaced and there is a suspicion of a high-arched palate. There appears to be a failure of secondary sexual characteristics. Her blood pressure is elevated at 149/90 mmHg. Investigations reveal a FSH level of > 40 IU/l on at least two occasions. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most likely complication in this patient?
explanation:
E Osteoporosis There is a strong suspicion that this patient has Turner syndrome and that access to health services has been patchy. Features include short stature, webbing of the neck, micrognathia, low-set ears, a high-arched palate, widely spaced nipples and cubitus valgus, some of which are clearly present here. Turner syndrome occurs due to the complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, and diagnosis is by lymphocyte karyotyping. Turner syndrome is associated with a number of other associated abnormalities, including aortic coarctation and other leftsided congenital heart defects, osteoporosis, hypothyroidism, lymphoedema, skeletal abnormalities and congenital malformations of the renal tract. Due to the genetic defect in Turner syndrome, cortical bone is thin, putting patients at greater risk of osteoporosis. Furthermore, in this patient who has been diagnosed with Turner syndrome later in life and who has not received any treatment with oestrogen, her risk of reduced bone density and osteoporosis is higher. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scanning should be completed for this patient. C Graves’ disease Autoimmune thyroid disease is found in up to half of patients with Turner syndrome and therefore, thyroid function should be measured. However, this is more commonly Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, rather than Graves’ disease. A Aortic dissection

Patients with Turner syndrome are at risk of aortic dissection, although the mechanism for this is poorly understood, and not necessarily related to the recognised risk of hypertension and cardiac abnormalities in patients with Turner syndrome. Cardiovascular screening is given high priority in affected patients. However, the risk of aortic dissection is lower than that of osteoporosis. B Gonadoblastoma Some patients with Turner syndrome may have a fragmented Y chromosome-speciﬁc sequence identiﬁed on karyotyping and this puts them at risk of gonadoblastoma, which is a benign tumour. The risk of this is lower than osteoporosis. D Hepatitis Thirty to 40% of patients with Turner syndrome have elevated transaminases, and treatment with oestrogen may decrease liver enzymes. However, the risk of hepatitis is lower than that of osteoporosis.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with hypertension that is refractory to multiple antihypertensive medications. He has no other past medical history of note. His regular medications include amlodipine, ramipril and indapamide. He reports a family history of early-onset hypertension and ischaemic stroke. His temperature is 36.7 °C, his heart rate is 70 bpm and regular and his BP is 165/95 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and his oxygen saturation is 98% on air. Investigation Result Normal value Na+ 145 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 2.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.0 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 70 µm/l 50–90 µmol/l Aldosterone 50 pmol/l 100–800 pmol/l Renin 0.2 pmol/ml/hour 0.5–3.5 pmol/ml/hour
explanation:
D Liddle syndrome Liddle syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by a genetic defect in the epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) found in the renal collecting tubules that results in increased Na+ reabsorption. The syndrome presents with a biochemical picture of hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Patients will also have low renin and aldosterone activity in a physiological effort to reduce BP. A Bartter syndrome Bartter syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the NKCC2 cotransporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle. This causes loss of Na+, K+ and chloride in the urine. Fluid loss associated with Na+ excretion leads to activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system that promotes potassium and H+ exchange for Na+ and bicarbonate reabsorption in the distal tubules, hence causing metabolic alkalosis and worsening hypokalaemia. Bartter syndrome is not in keeping with this patient’s presentation. B Cushing syndrome Excess levels of serum cortisol cause Cushing syndrome. It is characterised by central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump and abdominal striae. Patients can also present with hypertension. Biochemically, there is hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Since cortisol has some mineralocorticoid activity, Na+ retention and K+ excretion can also be present. The lack of physical characteristics makes Cushing syndrome unlikely. C Gitelman syndrome Gitelman syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that belongs to the family of salt-losing tubulopathies. It is caused by a mutation in the SLC12A3 gene encoding the thiazidesensitive sodium chloride transporter, and its presentation mimics thiazide diuretic use, with hypomagnesaemia and hypercalcaemia being additional features. The condition typically presents in adulthood, and other symptoms and signs include abdominal pain and nocturia, as well as other features including excessive thirst, tetany and chondrocalcinosis. This patient’s clinical presentation is not in keeping with Gitelman syndrome. E Primary hyperaldosteronism Primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn syndrome, is characterised by excessive production of aldosterone, leading to hypertension, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and low plasma renin activity. It is a very important differential diagnosis to consider for this patient. However, the blood results demonstrate low aldosterone and renin levels, making prima-

ry hyperaldosteronism unlikely.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted via the Emergency Department (ED) complaining of weakness, nausea, and malaise. Unfortunately, she has not brought all of her regular medications with her. She tells you that she is a tablet-controlled diabetic, with high blood pressure (BP) and kidney problems. She has with her a packet of lisinopril which she takes at 10 mg/day. In addition, she has a packet of gliclazide which she takes at 80 mg/day. She takes several other tablets, which she left on the sideboard at home when the ambulance collected her. She attended an outpatient appointment two weeks ago when she was prescribed a new medication. She does not know the name of this medication and does not have it with her; she was told that it was a medication also used to treat people with liver problems and had been taking one tablet a day. On examination, she is overweight and appears unwell. She has evidence of mild biventricular cardiac insufﬁciency, with elevated jugular venous pressure and pitting oedema of her ankles. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.An electrocardiogram (ECG) shown below. Urgent biochemical analysis revealsthe following: Investigation Result Normal Value Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 7.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 11.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 146 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Appropriate treatment is instigated. What is the most likely cause for this patient's presentation on this occasion?
options: A recent 2-day course of ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily (tid)/as required (prn) for backache
Recent commencement of digoxin 62.5 µg once daily (od)
Recent commencement of bisoprolol fumarate 2.5 mg od
Recent commencement of amiloride hydrochloride 5 mg twice daily (bd)
explanation:
B Recent commencement of spironolactone 50 mg This woman has life-threatening hyperkalaemia, with evidence of cardiotoxicity on ECG (tall tented T waves), requiring urgent intervention to prevent potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias. All of the drugs listed can be associated with hyperkalaemia. However, we know that this lady has renal disease. In addition, we know that she is already taking an angiotensinconverting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. Following the Randomised Aldactone Evaluation Study (RALES) clinical trial, when it was shown that aldosterone antagonists can reduce mortality in severe chronic congestive cardiac failure when given in conjunction with an ACE inhibitor, the prescription rates of spironolactone increased, along with hospital admission rates and deaths from hyperkalaemia. Although this medication can be given safely with ACE inhibitors, and indeed be beneﬁcial, there is a risk of causing lifethreatening hyperkalaemia, particularly in those with renal impairment. The combination of ACE inhibitor therapy with spironolactone therefore needs to be carefully considered and monitored to avoid signiﬁcant side-effects. The standard dose used for heart failure is at a lower level than that seen here (around 25– 50 mg daily). A A recent 2-day course of ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily (tid)/as required (prn) for backache Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents can be associated with hyperkalaemia in the context of renal impairment, although we might expect this with a longer duration of use if this were the cause in this case. C Recent commencement of digoxin 62.5 µg once daily (od) Digoxin toxicity can be increased by hypokalaemia, although it is hyperkalaemia which is seen here. D Recent commencement of bisoprolol fumarate 2.5 mg od Non-selective b blockade can lead to hyperkalaemia by decreasing the uptake of potassium from extracellular into intracellular spaces. This would not be expected with the highly selective b1 blocker bisoprolol. E Recent commencement of amiloride hydrochlo-

ride 5 mg twice daily (bd) Amiloride can cause hyperkalaemia in similar situations; however, it is not so commonly used in current practice.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the clinic with palpitations. Approximately 3 weeks ago she had suffered with ﬂu and since then she has been getting occasional palpitations, anxiety attacks and loose bowel motions. Her weight has remained stable and she has previously been ﬁt and well. Examination reveals a tender thyroid, but no enlargement or focal masses. Her pulse rate is 110/min and regular. Thyroid function tests: Investigation Result Normal values TSH 0.3 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l T4 190 nmol/l 58 - 178 nmol/l T3 3.21 nmol/l 1.07 - 3.18 nmol/l ESR 45 mm/h 1 - 20 mm/h What is the next most appropriate management step?
explanation: C Ibuprofen Subacute thyroiditis is transient inﬂammation of the thyroid, which typically occurs in females in the fourth and ﬁfth decade. Patients can have a preceding viral infection followed by mild symptoms of hyperthyroidism. The thyroid gland is usually tender by this time. If bloods are taken early, the patient can display a low thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and raised T4/tri-iodothyronine (T3). The mainstay of treatment is management of pain over the thyroid with NSAIDs. Prednisolone can be used if NSAIDS are ineffective. The symptoms should resolve but can take weeks to a few months to do so, and the patient’s thyroid status should be monitored. Some patients are left hypothyroid after the inﬂammation has settled. Propranolol may be considered if palpitations or anxiety are particularly severe. A Carbimazole Carbimazole is used for Graves’ thyrotoxicosis. It is a pro-drug which, after absorption, is converted to the active form, methimazole. Methimazole prevents thyroid peroxidase enzyme (TPO) from coupling and iodinating the tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, hence reducing the production of the thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). In De Quervain’s thyroiditis, the transient rise of T3 and T4 is self-limiting and doesn’t require antithyroid medication. B Propylthiouracil This is used in Graves’ thyrotoxicosis. It shares the same mechanism of action as carbimazole, but moreover inhibits the enzyme 5’-deiodinase which converts T4 to the more active form T3. D Radioiodine This is used in Graves’ thyrotoxicosis when not complicated by thyroid eye disease, as there is a chance that it may aggravate its course. E Subtotal thyroidectomy This is considered in the case of a toxic adenoma or when the cytology results following ﬁne-needle aspiration (FNA) of a nodule raise the suspicion of malignancy.

stem: A 72-year-old woman is discovered at home by her family, demonstrating confusion and poor responsiveness. She is brought into the hospital and assessed in the Emergency Department. Her family cannot recall her past medical history, but they think that she may have asthma and depression. When they last saw her, 3 days ago, she had a productive cough. On examination, the junior doctor thinks her face appears puffy, and they ﬁnd a small scar in the middle of her neck, shown below: She is hypothermic, has a heart rate of 45 beats per minute (bpm), and a blood pressure of 92/65 mmHg. Her Glasgow coma score (GCS) is 9/15. An arterial blood gas conﬁrms type II respiratory failure. Investigations revealed the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 112 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.2 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 165 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 131 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 114 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Blood glucose 3.2 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l TSH 25.2 μm/ml 0.4 - 5.0 μm/ml T3 2.6 pmol/l 4.0 - 7.4 pmol/l T4 3.6 pmol/l 12.0 - 22.0 pmol/l What is the most likely primary diagnosis?
explanation: D Myxoedema coma Myxoedema coma may develop following a long history of undiagnosed hypothyroidism or may occur in a patient with known hypothyroidism with an additional decompensating event such as infection or surgery. The clues in this scenario that point to this diagnosis are the scar on her neck which could be a thyroidectomy scar (which would mean the patient is likely to have hypothyroidism) and the report of a productive cough 3 days before the admission. The other clinical signs are consistent with myxoedema coma, including type II respiratory failure, hypothermia, hypotension, bradycardia, tissue oedema and reduced Glasgow Coma Score (GCS). In severe hypothyroidism, it is common to ﬁnd hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia. B Serotonin syndrome Serotonin syndrome ought to be considered as the patient has a history of depression, and therefore, it is possible that she takes a medication that raises the level of serotonin. While serotonin syndrome can cause impaired consciousness, the other clinical ﬁndings are not consistent with this diagnosis, as you would also expect hyperthermia, hypertension and tachycardia. A Adrenal crisis The past medical history of asthma, for which it is possible that the patient takes a long-term steroid inhaler, coupled with the presentations of hypotension and hypoglycaemia are consistent with an adrenal crisis. However, this diagnosis does not explain the impaired level of consciousness or the facial oedema. It is possible to have adrenal insufﬁciency in addition to myxoedema coma, but the primary diagnosis is myxoedema coma. C Subclinical hypothyroidism Subclinical hypothyroidism tends to be asymptomatic; this would, therefore, not explain these clinical ﬁndings. In subclinical hypothyroidism, the thyroid-stimulating hormone level is elevated, but the thyroxine level is in the normal range. E Thyroid storm In a thyroid storm, patients experience reduced consciousness but will also have hyperthermia, tachycardia, diarrhoea and jaundice. These signs do not typically occur in myxoedema coma.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with tiredness, weight loss, and diarrhoea. She has also been suffering from heavy periods over the past few months. On examination, she looks tanned, but is very thin and emaciated. Her blood pressure (BP) is 115/80 mmHg. Her pulse is 84 beats per minute (bpm) and regular and she has a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb g/l (normocytic) 115–155 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l PLT 195 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Na+ 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Ferritin 25 µg/l 10–120 µg/l Folate 4.0 µg/l 2.0–11.0 µg/l Correcte calcium (Ca2+) 2.35 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Albumin 28 g/l 35–55 g/l ALT 42 U/l 5–30 U/l TSH 8.3 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Glucose 8.5 mmol/l (fasting) < 7 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Polyglandular syndrome type 2 Type 2 polyglandular syndrome is characterised by adrenal insufﬁciency, hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes; hypogonadism, coeliac disease and myasthenia gravis may also be seen. The hyponatraemia, elevated fasting glucose and elevated TSH all support this as the diagnosis.

B Polyglandular syndrome type 1 This is characterised by mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufﬁciency. A Coeliac disease This may explain the diarrhoea, but it would not explain the hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia seen here, nor the postural drop in blood pressure. D Polyglandular syndrome type 3 Type 3 polyglandular syndrome is characterised by autoimmune thyroiditis, but the other associated autoimmune diseases don’t ﬁt with a diagnosis of either type 1 or type 2 disease. E HIV infection Although HIV infection may present with signiﬁcant weight loss and diarrhoea, the abnormalities seen on blood testing are much more consistent with autoimmune polyglandular syndrome.

stem: A 37-year-old man with a 30-year history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He takes a basal bolus insulin regime of 22 units of long-acting insulin (Insulotard®) per day and 6 units of short-acting insulin (Actrapid®) with each meal. His main problem is unpredictable hypoglycaemic episodes, which occur during the day, normally a few hours after each meal. He has peripheral neuropathy affecting the soles of both feet, but is otherwise well. Examination reveals a BP of 105/80 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. His BMI is 21. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 132 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 199 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 102 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 6.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l HbA1c mmol/mol (7.0%) 9.29 - 53.0 mmol/mol (3 - 7%) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange a 72 continuous glucose monitor recording
Change the Insulotard® to insulin glargine
Reduce the dose of the Actrapid®
Refer for Dose Adjustment for Normal Eating (DAFNE) education.
explanation: E Refer for Dose Adjustment for Normal Eating (DAFNE) education. In this situation it is possible that the patient has never been educated about matching short-acting insulin to the carbohydrates consumed with the meal. In the ﬁrst instance he is likely to beneﬁt from DAFNE education, teaching him to take appropriate short-acting insulin for the meal he has eaten. Reducing the dose of his insulin is likely to lead to deterioration in his glycaemic control. D Reduce the dose of Insulotard® This would have most impact on nocturnal rather than daytime hypoglycaemia. A Arrange a 72 continuous glucose monitor recording Although continuous glucose monitoring may elucidate the daytime hypoglycaemia episodes, it won’t initiate the change in behaviour which is driven by DAFNE education. B Change the Insulotard® to insulin glargine This is more likely to impact on fasting hypoglycaemia during the overnight period, rather than daytime hypo episodes. C Reduce the dose of the Actrapid® A blanket reduction in the dose of Actrapid® is likely to drive hyperglycaemia; as such, it should be avoided here if possible.

stem: A 40-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) where she asks for her cholesterol to be measured. She has a past history of polycystic ovary disease (PCOD) and dietcontrolled diabetes mellitus. She drinks a glass of wine each night and swims most days. She is currently on the oral contraceptive pill. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value LDL 5.5 mmol/l < 3.5 mmol/l Triglycerides 2.5 mmol/l 0–1.5 mmol/l HDL 0.8 mmol/l > 1.0 mmol/l Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the low HDL cholesterol levels?
explanation: D Diet-controlled diabetes Low levels of HDL are associated with an increased risk of ischaemic heart disease. Diabetes causes low HDL and raised triglycerides. HMG CoA reductase inhibitors are used in primary and secondary prevention of coronary events. Statins are particularly considered for patients with diabetes mellitus and are recommended now for all diabetics above 40 years of age in the JBS2 guidelines. They are also used in other patients with high calculated cardiovascular risk. A Alcohol Mild to moderate alcohol consumption is associated with an increase in HDL. B Exercise Exercise is an effective way of increasing HDL cholesterol levels. C Oral contraceptive pill Increased oestrogen levels, as caused by the contraceptive pill, lead to higher HDL levels. E Female sex Women have naturally higher HDL levels compared to men, due to higher oestrogen levels.

stem: A 54-year-old taxi driver presents to the Diabetes Clinic for review. He is ﬁnding it increasingly difﬁcult to work because of increased drowsiness and episodes of sweating and nausea. He reports having to take sugary snacks to work with him to help him focus. His current medications for type II diabetes are metformin 1 g twice daily (bd) and gliclazide 80 mg bd. He has symptoms of erectile dysfunction, for which he takes sildenaﬁl, and numbness in both feet. He is otherwise well and works ﬁve days a week as a bus driver. His BP is 135/82 mmHg, and his BMI is 35 kg/m2. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 132 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 113 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c mmol/mol (7.1%) 20–42 mmol/mol (4–6%) Urine microalbuminuria stix: Positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
A Change the Gliclazide for Sitagliptin This patient has symptoms of hypoglycaemia, characterised by drowsiness, sweating and nausea, combined with the need for sugary snacks. In this situation, it is the sulfonylurea (SU) that is driving hunger and episodes of hypoglycaemia and potentially contributing to weight gain. Over time, this will drive an increase in insulin requirements and lead to a deterioration in glycaemic control. As such, the best option is to change the SU for a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitor, given HbA1c control is relatively good. An alternative to sitagliptin would be a sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor, which now has associated class beneﬁts in heart failure and renal impairment. He should, of course, also be encouraged to lose weight. B Change the Gliclazide for Liraglutide Although liraglutide will improve glycaemic control, it is injectable and would at least initially lead to signiﬁcant gastrointestinal upset. In this patient, therefore, it would usually be considered as another option after the second oral failure. Furthermore, the addition of a GLP-1 mimetic, such as liraglutide, should not be considered until failure of diabetic control with triple therapy (eg metformin, sulfonylurea, SGLT-2 inhibitor). C Reduce the dose of Metformin Metformin per se does not lead to hypoglycaemia and has a positive impact on diabetes outcomes. As such, it is gliclazide that should be substituted, rather than reducing the dose of, or stopping, metformin. D Stop Gliclazide Reducing to one medication only may drive a signiﬁcant deterioration in glycaemic control. For this reason, substitution of gliclazide, rather than stopping it, is the most appropriate next step. E Stop Metformin

It would be inappropriate to commence this patient on an insulin regimen at this stage. He is describing symptoms of hypoglycaemia and is working as a courier. Insulin may further exacerbate his symptoms of hypoglycaemia and affect his ability to work (patients must stop driving group 2 vehicles until the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency has made a formal decision). Alternative methods, such as adjusting his oral hypoglycaemic regimen, should be considered initially.

stem: A 36-year-old female who is 36-weeks pregnant attends hospital in labour. She has a tense, woody abdomen and the cardiotocograph (CTG) conﬁrms fetal distress. She is found to have a placental abruption and has an emergency C-section. The major haemorrhage protocol is activated due to heavy blood loss in excess of 3 litres. After being discharged from the hospital, she visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining that she is unable to produce any milk. She has also been feeling fatigued. Her GP suspects that she may have Sheehan syndrome. Which anatomical structure has infarcted, resulting in this syndrome?
explanation:
D Pituitary gland Sheehan syndrome results from profound postpartum blood loss which causes an infarction of the pituitary gland. Most commonly, this disrupts the production of growth hormone and prolactin, which results in agalactorrhea. However, production of the other anterior pituitary hormones may also be disrupted (gonadotropins, adrenocorticotropic hormone and TSH). C Hypothalamus Hypothalamic dysfunction can disrupt the release of hormones that act on the pituitary gland and result in the release of ante-

rior pituitary gland hormones. However, in Sheehan syndrome, it is the pituitary gland itself that infarcts and not the hypothalamus. A Adrenal gland The pituitary gland infarcts in Sheehan syndrome, which can result in hypopituitarism. This can result in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) deﬁciency, which causes secondary adrenal insufﬁciency; the adrenal gland itself, however, does not infarct. B Breast lactocytes Breast lactocytes are the normal site of milk production. The insult in Sheehan syndrome is not to the lactocytes themselves but rather to the pituitary gland which secretes prolactin, which stimulates the lactocytes to produce milk. E Thyroid gland Sheehan syndrome is due to infarction of the pituitary gland. This can cause hypopituitarism (including TSH deﬁciency), which will give rise to the symptoms of hypothyroidism. The thyroid gland itself is unaffected.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to clinic and complains of tiredness, weakness and loss of body hair. He has recently split up with his partner and he cites loss of sexual function as one reason for this occurring. There is no past medical history of note apart from mild essential hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine. On examination, pulse is 90 beats per minute (bpm) and blood pressure (BP) 100/50 mmHg. He is of normal appearance and has normal secondary sexual characteristics, although his body hair is ﬁne and sparse. He also has bitemporal hemianopia. Routine bloods reveal mildly elevated potassium of 5.5 mmol/l. TSH is in the normal range. What test would be most useful from those listed?
explanation: C Serum prolactin This clinical history is highly suggestive of a pituitary macroadenoma. As the patient is of normal appearance, the differential diagnosis is that of prolactinoma or a non- functioning pituitary adenoma. Therefore, serum prolactin is therefore of great importance. A Synacthen™ test is an adequate measure of cortisol reserve and would be the next most important test. MRI pituitary is important to document the size and invasion of the pituitary tumour, but would be done after a Synacthen™ test and serum prolactin to conﬁrm the diagnosis and evaluate the most appropriate surgical approach. A High-dose dexamethasone suppression test A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used in the diagnostic workup for Cushing syndrome, which is effectively ruled out here by the normal appearance and normal blood pressure. B Insulin tolerance test Insulin tolerance testing is used in the work-up for growth hormone deﬁciency, which at this stage isn’t appropriate until an MRI has taken place and other pituitary hormones have been proﬁled. D Random serum cortisol Cortisol is subject to pulsatile release, and therefore random measurement is not useful in the work-up for possible pituitary tumour. E Serum glucose Both hypo- and hyperglycaemia may be associated with pituitary disease, although a random glucose is unlikely to be helpful here.

stem: A 32–year-old woman is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic by the Emergency Department. She has had three episodes of collapse over the past ﬁve months. There is also a history of increased hunger, which has been accompanied by gradual weight gain. On further questioning, family history reveals no useful information. You elect to admit her for a period of fasting. The morning after admission, some 16 hours without food, she complains of feeling faint. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Glucose 2.1 mmol/l < 7 mmol/l Insulin 7 mU/l with increased proportion of pro-insulin C-peptide Elevated Cortisol 550 nmol/l am: 140–500 nmol/l Midnight: 50–300 nmol/ Which of the following diagnoses ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: C Insulinoma After a 15 h fast, the cut-off normal limits for glucose are 2.5 mmol/l and 5 mU/l for insulin. As such, this patient has an inappropriately low glucose and raised insulin level. By 24 h, fasting leads to a detection rate of 78% for insulinoma. If the fast is extended to 72 h, this detection rate increases to 98%. Insulinomas have an incidence of 1-2/million/year, are commoner in women and may be associated with the MEN-1 syndrome in around 10%; 90% of them are less than 2 cm in size. More of the insulin released by an insulinoma remains as proinsulin, so that pro-insulin levels are often raised as a proportion of total insulin levels. D Glucagonoma A glucagonoma would lead to hyperglycaemia, rather than hypoglycaemia. A Abuse of insulin secretagogues As she is in hospital, abuse of insulin secretagogues is unlikely. B Abuse of insulin Abuse of insulin would lead to raised insulin levels without a corresponding rise in c-peptide. E Addison’s disease The cortisol levels in this patient are appropriately towards the upper end of the normal range, making Addison’s disease very unlikely.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the Hypertension Clinic with difﬁcult-to-control blood pressure. He is now taking ramipril 10 mg daily and amlodipine 10 mg, but his blood pressure is still 153/88 mmHg. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal values Na+ 145 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Renal ultrasound scan Kidneys normal size Which of the following represents the best investigation for this patient?
options: Plasma renin, aldosterone and cortisol level
Plasma renin, aldosterone and cortisol levels after washout of antihypertensives
explanation:
B Plasma renin, aldosterone and cortisol levels after washout of antihypertensives ACE inhibitors may increase plasma renin activity, and calcium antagonists may reduce aldosterone. Hence, renin, aldosterone and cortisol should be measured after a 2-week washout period to conﬁrm primary hyperaldosteronism, the most likely diagnosis here. Resection of adenoma leads to resolution of hypertension in around 70% of patients where a discrete adenoma has been identiﬁed. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia may be managed with spironolactone for many years; dexamethasone is the treatment of choice for those with glucocorticoidsuppressible hyperaldosteronism. A Plasma renin, aldosterone and cortisol level These investigations are in the context of suspected secondary hypertension (young patient requiring three antihypertensive agents). These need to be performed after washout of his medication, since ACE inhibitors may increase plasma renin activity and calcium antagonists may reduce aldosterone. C Echocardiogram It may reveal end organ damage (left ventricular hypertrophy) but it will not clarify the cause of the hypertension. D Renal angiogram In young patients with hypertension that is difﬁcult to control, renal artery stenosis is one of the differential diagnoses. In this scenario though, normal-sized kidneys preclude this diagnosis. E Oral salt loading This is one of the tests used to detect autonomous aldosterone secretion. Patients should increase their sodium intake to more than 6 g/day for 3 days with diet and sodium chloride tabs. Potassium supplementation and daily potassium measurements are required for patients with hypokalaemia. Patients perform 24 h urine collection starting on day 3 for sodium and aldosterone. A 24 h urinary aldosterone excretion of more than 12

mcg is consistent with primary aldosteronism, whereas 24 h urinary sodium of 200 mEq indicates adequate intake. This test should not be performed in patients with uncontrolled hypertension, congestive heart failure or arrhythmias.

stem: A 51-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of hot ﬂushes and night sweats for the past few weeks. In addition, she states that she has not been able to concentrate and that her sleep is disturbed at night. She is accompanied by her husband who states that she has been having mood swings of late. On examination, her blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg and her heart rate is 78 bpm. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m2. Abdominal examination is normal. She is started on hormone replacement therapy. However, she wants to know more regarding the beneﬁts of hormone replacement therapy. Which of the following is associated with hormone replacement therapy?
options: Decreases the risk of colorectal cancer
Decreases the risk of dementia in older women
Decreases the risk of gall bladder disease
Increases the risk of diabetes mellitus
explanation: A Decreases the risk of colorectal cancer The incidence of colorectal cancer is decreased in women taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT), making this the most likely answer. Long term follow up of patients taking HRT demonstrated that when colorectal tumours do occur, however, they are found at a more advanced stage. This indicates that the underlying pathophysiology of colorectal cancer may be altered by HRT, although the mechanism remains unknown. C Increases the occurrence of osteoporosis The risk of fracture and occurrence of osteoporosis is decreased (33% decreased risk for hip fracture) by hormone replacement therapy. B Decreases the risk of dementia in older women Consistent, statistically signiﬁcant changes to the risk of dementia have not been demonstrated in patients taking hormone replacement therapy. D Decreases the risk of gall bladder disease Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) causes a deﬁnite increase in the risk of cholecystitis (57% increased risk). For every 185 patients treated with HRT, it is estimated one extra patient will require a cholecystectomy. E Increases the risk of diabetes mellitus There is a decreased risk of type II diabetes mellitus (up to 19%) in individuals taking hormone replacement therapy. A reduction in insulin resistance has been proposed as an underlying mechanism.

stem: You are called to interpret the results of a synacthen test on the Oncology Ward. The patient is a 60-year-old woman who is in hospital for chemotherapy for breast cancer. She has tolerated her therapy poorly and is currently suffering from multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, pulse 120/min regular, BP 90/60 mmHg. Her JVP is not seen, her heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. There is evidence of a right mastectomy. Abdominal and neurological examination is normal. Short synacthen test: Time (min) cortisol (nmol/l) Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most important component of your immediate management?
options: Hydrocortisone oral 20 mg AM, 10 mg PM
explanation:
C Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV QDS This patient’s rise in cortisol demonstrates an inadequate response to synacthen. The 30 min value should rise above 550 nmol/l. Therefore, this lady has acute adrenal insufﬁciency. The treatment for this is intravenous saline - at least 6-hourly initially, as her blood pressure is on the low side. Hydrocortisone should be given at a dose of 50 mg IV QDS. Lower doses will not be sufﬁcient. Fludrocortisone should be started but is not necessary for emergency treatment. The aetiology of the adrenal insufﬁciency should be elucidated, but in this lady is likely to be due to metastatic spread, most commonly from a

breast or lung primary. A 1 litre IV dextrose over 6 IV dextrose may further exacerbate any underlying hyponatraemia, and is unlikely to represent adequate ﬂuid replacement for this patient. B 1 litre IV normal saline over 12 Although normal saline will contribute to total body sodium, this represents an inadequate ﬂuid replacement regimen and won’t correct underlying hypoadrenalism. D Hydrocortisone oral 20 mg AM, 10 mg PM This is an adequate maintenance regimen for hypoadrenalism, although it is inappropriate here due to vomiting, and because of likely greater corticosteroid requirements due to her intercurrent illness. E Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV OD This patient is acutely unwell with a very poor cortisol response to synacthen, and thus higher doses of corticosteroids will almost certainly be required.

stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with confusion. He has a background of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and is on home nebulisers and oxygen. His relatives have noticed increased breathlessness and vomiting, which has meant he has been unable to keep down his rescue course of prednisolone. General examination reveals skin bruises and dry mucous membranes. Other past history of note includes treated hypothyroidism. On chest auscultation, there are bibasal inspiratory crepitations with prolonged expiratory wheeze. His pulse is 78/min, blood pressure 85/54 mmHg, temperature 37.5 °C. Chest radiography shows chronic obstructive airways changes and an electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus rhythm. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 132 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 14 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 470 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ K+ 125 mmol/l 5.3 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 17.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 2.8 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l You give him a bolus of IV glucose and start IV ﬂuid replacement with normal saline. Which of the following is the next best immediate management step?
explanation: A IV hydrocortisone Acute adrenal insufﬁciency in this patient is most likely due to a chest infection and prior suppression of the adrenocortical axis by exogenous steroids. Patients present with hypotension and confusion. Examination may reveal evidence of prior treatment with steroids. Biochemistry shows hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and an increased urea. Treatment includes correction of hypoglycaemia, administration of glucocorticoids and adequate hydration. B IV antibiotics Whilst these may be appropriate, antibiotics should follow corticosteroids in this case in terms of urgency given the signiﬁcant electrolyte disturbance and hypotension. C IV calcium gluconate Potassium is towards the upper end of the normal range and is likely to fall rapidly as a result of rehydration and initiation of corticosteroid therapy. D Oral calcium resonium Calcium resonium is unpleasant to take and is not required here, because potassium will almost certainly fall once ﬂuid replacement and steroid therapy is initiated. Its main use is in the management of hyperkalaemia occurring as a result of acute on chronic kidney disease. E IV aminophylline IV aminophylline use is not encouraged in acute exacerbations of COPD because of the high risk of atrial arrhythmias; it may be used in cases where other options have been exhausted.

stem: A 20-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of excess facial hair and acne. On examination, her BMI is elevated at 29 kg/m2. Her BP is raised at 155/92 mmHg and her pulse is 80/min and regular. You notice excess hair around her beard line, upper chest and lower abdomen. There are no purple striae on abdominal ex- amination. The examination of external genitalia is normal. On further questioning, she tells you that her periods are irregular, only occurring every 3 months, and they are heavy when they do occur. Which one of the following would be an appropriate initial investigation?
explanation: C Testosterone levels The suspected diagnosis here is polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). According to the Rotterdam Consensus, two of the following three criteria are required for the diagnosis of the PCOS:  oligo-/anovulation hyperandrogenism  clinical (hirsutism or less commonly male pattern alopecia) or  biochemical (raised free androgen index or free testosterone) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. D High-dose dexamethasone suppression test This is used when Cushing syndrome is clinically suspected and the overnight dexamethasone suppression test results are equivocal. A Plasma ACTH There is no clear clinical evidence of cortisol excess in this scenario. Even if Cushing syndrome was suspected, an overnight dexamethasone suppression test or high-dose dexamethasone suppression test would be the initial investigation in order to establish the presence of hypercortisolism. If hypercortisolim was conﬁrmed, a suppressed ACTH would point towards an adrenal cause whereas raised ACTH would indicate a pituitary cause. B MRI pituitary This would be useful only if Cushing syndrome was conﬁrmed via overnight dexamethasone or high-dose dexamethasone suppression test and a central cause for hypercortisolism was suspected. E 17-hydroxyprogesterone This is usually raised (>1000 ng/dl) in cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deﬁciency. Females with severe CAH due to deﬁciencies of 21hydroxylase, 11-beta-hydroxylase or 3-beta- hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase have ambiguous genitalia at birth (classic virilising adrenal hyperplasia). Females with mild 21-hydroxylase deﬁciency are identiﬁed later in childhood because of precocious pubic hair, clitoromegaly or both, often accompanied by accelerated growth and skeletal maturation (simple virilising adrenal hyperplasia). Females with still milder deﬁciencies of 21-hydroxylase or 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity may present in adolescence or adulthood with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism and/or infertility (non-classic adrenal hyperplasia).

stem: A 25-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic by his General Practitioner (GP) with weight loss and polyuria. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 125/82 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. His body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. You also note that he has vitiligo. Investigations conducted by the GP revealed the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Na+ 125 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 6.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 8.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 12.5 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.35 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Free Thyroxine fT4 8.0 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l TSH 7.2 mU/l 0.17–3.2 mU/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Polyglandular syndrome type 2 Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 is the association of primary adrenal insufﬁciency with primary hypothyroidism and type 1 diabetes. Sometimes, primary gonadal failure is present as well. Both type 1 and type 2 polyglandular syndrome are associated with vitiligo and pernicious anaemia. A Lysosomal acid lipase deﬁciency LAL deﬁciency, also known as Wolman syndrome, is characterised by primary adrenal failure, hepatosplenomegaly and steatorrhoea. B DIDMOAD syndrome DIDMOAD syndrome is characterised by Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy and Deafness and is a mitochondrial rather than an autoimmune disorder.
