E Parathyroidectomy Parathyroidectomy is the next step in patients who fail to respond to medical intervention for hyperparathyroidism.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with an ulcer over the left medial malleolus on her left leg. She has a history of obesity and hypertension, and has been recently diagnosed with type II diabetes. On examination, she has obvious bilateral varicose veins; there is no evidence of diabetic neuropathy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 140 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 310 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 140 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l ABPI 0.9 Her leg is shown below. Which of the following options offers the best chance for complete healing of the ulcer?
explanation:
B Multi-layer bandaging The shallow pre tibial lesion with exudate is consistent with venous ulceration. Multi-layer bandaging is most useful in reducing lower limb oedema and improving the chances of healing of venous ulcers. It is also crucial for patients to rest and keep the leg up where possible. An ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI) measurement is essential before beginning bandaging, as if there is signiﬁcant arterial insufﬁciency, blood supply to the lower limb may be threatened. An ABPI of 0.8 has become a pivotal ﬁgure in the management of leg ulceration, deﬁning the cut-off point for high-compression bandaging, and is frequently taken as indicating the presence of a socalled 'mixed ulcer'. A Lower limb angioplasty Lower limb angioplasty will improve arterial supply and has no signiﬁcant impact on venous insufﬁciency. C Maggot therapy

Although maggot therapy may be useful for debridement, it isn’t the primary driver for healing of venous ulcers. D Surgical debridement Surgical debridement is only useful where there is signiﬁcant necrotic tissue that risks extensive soft tissue infection. E Fucidin ointment Antibiotic ointment has not been shown to drive faster healing of venous ulcers.

stem: A 59-year-old woman presents to the clinic with tiredness. She takes no medication, and her thyroid- stimulating hormone (TSH) level is in the normal range. She has had a pituitary adenoma in the past that was found to be prolactinsecreting, and she tells you she had some benign tumours removed from her neck. She takes calcium and vitamin D supplements.
explanation: C Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1) MEN-1 is associated with the development of parathyroid adenomas (linked to the neck scar and vitamin D and calcium supplementation seen here). The syndrome is also linked to pituitary adenomas, particularly prolactinomas, and endocrine pancreatic tumours. The history seen here is therefore consistent with MEN-1. Around 60% of islet cell tumours do not originate from beta cells, and these are more common in the over-40 population. A Familial medullary thyroid cancer Medullary thyroid cancer would not explain the presentation with prolactinoma and, as part of a syndrome, is associated with MEN-2. It is not associated with parathyroid adenomas. B Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome An autosomal dominant inheritance pattern for familial hyperparathyroidism does exist, although it would not explain the presentation with a prolactinoma seen here. D Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2a (MEN-2a) MEN-2 is associated with primary hyperparathyroidism, but it is also associated with phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid cancer, rather than the pituitary tumour reported here. E Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2b (MEN-2b) MEN-2b is associated with a marfanoid habitus, medullary thyroid cancer and phaeochromocytoma.

stem: You review a 28-year-old woman with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis in the thyroid clinic. She has been stable on 100 μg of thyroxine for the past few years and recent TSH was measured at 2.9 mU/l some 6 months ago (normal range 0.4–5). The reason for this appointment is that she is 12 weeks pregnant. How would you manage her thyroxine therapy during this pregnancy?
options: Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 100 mcg
Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 25-50 mcg
Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 25 mcg
Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 50 mcg
explanation: B Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 2550 mcg In patients already on thyroxine when they become pregnant, thyroid function tests should be assessed at 6–8 weeks’ gestation and then at 16–20 and 28–32 weeks. Average increase in thyroxine requirements is 25–50 μg, and the increased need for thyroxine ceases immediately after delivery. In patients with positive thyroid autoantibodies there is a twofold increased risk of spontaneous abortion. In patients who are suboptimally treated for hypothyroidism there is a 21% risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension. Maternal hypothyroidism is also associated with increased risk of pregnancy-induced anaemia and postpartum haemorrhage; for these reasons it is crucial that patients with hypothyroidism are followed up appropriately during pregnancy. TSH should be monitored, and guidelines suggest aiming to keep TSH below 3.0. D Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 50 mcg Even if this patient wasn’t pregnant, halving her thyroxine dose risks symptomatic hypothyroidism. A Increase her thyroxine dose by an average of 100 mcg This runs the risk of symptomatic hyperthyroidism in pregnancy, increasing the risk of spontaneous abortion. C Reduce her thyroxine dose by an average of 25 mcg Thyroid hormone requirements increase by an average of 30% in pregnancy; as such, this is not the appropriate course of action. E Keep her thyroxine dose unchanged The 30% increase in thyroid hormone requirements in pregnancy will mean this patient slips into hypothyroidism as her pregnancy progresses.

stem: A 70-year-old man with a history of type II diabetes, cardiovascular disease and depression is admitted to the Emergency Department with confusion which his partner has noticed over the past two to three weeks. Medications include metformin, sitagliptin, bendroﬂumethiazide, lisinopril and ﬂuoxetine. On examination, his blood pressure is 138/72 mmHg and pulse is 70 bpm and regular. He appears to be euvolaemic. He is mildly confused when you review him. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 281 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l CRP 12 mg/l < 5 mg/l Na+ 128 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 6.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l His chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the best way to manage this patient’s hyponatraemia?
explanation: E Stop bendroﬂumethiazide This patient has hyponatraemia, which is commonly seen in conjunction with long-term use of thiazide diuretics. Since his blood pressure is relatively well controlled, and there is no sign of ﬂuid overload on the chest x-ray, there are therefore likely to be no adverse consequences of discontinuing treatment with bendroﬂumethiazide. Taking this step will improve the chances of ﬂuid restriction correcting his serum sodium levels over subsequent days. A 3% saline infusion 3% saline is reserved for the treatment of life-threatening hyponatraemia. In this situation, ﬂuid replacement must happen in a high dependency setting, so that it can be tightly controlled, with regular monitoring of serum sodium levels. B Demeclocycline Demeclocycline, which induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, is the most appropriate option in the event that the patient fails to respond to ﬂuid restriction alone with respect to his serum sodium level. C Intravenous furosemide The chest x-ray is normal. Furosemide is usually only considered appropriate for treatment of hyponatraemia where there is salt and water overload, eg in cardiac failure. D Sodium chloride (NaCl) tablets Salt tablets are unpleasant to take and may negatively impact on this patient’s blood pressure. They are therefore not an appropriate option here.

stem: A 72-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He is managed with metformin 1 g BD and pioglitazone 30 mg. On examination, he has a large necrotic, malodorous ulcer over the right medial malleolus. You notice that he has bilateral peripheral oedema and varicose veins. Peripheral pulses are easily palpable and capillary return is normal. Dopplers done by the chiropody team in the clinic are also within acceptable limits. His pioglitazone is discontinued and a transition to insulin therapy is planned. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 182 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 27 mg/l 0–10 mg/l Wound swab scanty faecal ﬂora Which of the following treatments is likely to be the most effective?
explanation: B Multi-layer compression bandaging The fact that peripheral arteries are palpable and the normal Dopplers exclude the ischaemic origin of the ulcer. The location strongly suggests that this man’s ulcer is venous. As such, the optimal management is compression bandaging. His white count is normal and the CRP is only just above normal, and thus infection is not likely to be the primary cause of his ulcer. Dressings may be employed that encourage de-sloughing, rather than progressing to deﬁnitive surgical debridement. A Surgical debridement under GA Surgical debridement is usually performed on diabetic foot ulcers that are infected and neuropathic, ischaemic or mixed in origin. C Oral metronidazole Depending upon sensitivities, an antibiotic with broadspectrum activity, such as co-amoxiclav, may also be required. Metronidazole is reserved for ulcers where anaerobic infection is strongly suspected. D Varicose vein stripping This procedure is done under general or local anaesthetic to aid in the treatment of varicose veins and other manifestations of chronic venous disease. It is mainly performed when the symptoms are quite severe (pain/discomfort). E Mobilisation Rather than mobilisation, elevation of the leg above the level of the heart and rest, to reduce peripheral oedema, is the recommended course of action.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with central chest pain suspicious of angina. She has a history of resistant hypertension, currently managed by her GP with Ramipril, amlodipine and indapamide. She tells you that her mother suffered from Conn syndrome and she is concerned she may have the same problem. Her BP is 155/95, pulse is 84 and regular. Her BMI is 22. What abnormality would you expect to ﬁnd in the patient’s workup if she was suffering from Conn syndrome?
explanation:
D Hypokalaemia Conn syndrome, a cause of secondary hypertension, is usually due to an aldosterone-secreting adenoma which leads to hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism. The rule of thumb is that in patients prescribed an ACE inhibitor, hypokalaemia is highly suggestive of the condition. It was previously thought that adrenal adenomas were responsible for the majority of cases of hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism, but it’s now realised that the split is much more 50:50. Aldosterone has an action on the distal tubule of the kidney to increase sodium resorption and enhance potassium and hydrogen ion loss. Renin levels are suppressed and do not rise with an upright posture. Medical treatment includes a low-sodium diet with an aldosterone receptor antagonist (spironolactone). Surgical therapy is usually indicated after localisation of adenoma. C Metabolic acidosis Mineralocorticoid excess leads to presentation with elevated

bicarbonate and a metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis. A Hyponatraemia Hyponatraemia is associated with adrenal insufﬁciency, not with hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism. B Elevated serum creatinine This patient may yet develop intrinsic renal damage as a result of chronic hypertension, and thus creatinine values may well be normal. E Hypernatraemia Although serum sodium may well be at the upper end of the normal range, frank hypernatraemia is often not seen in patients with Conn syndrome.

stem: An 18-year-old girl with a history of anorexia presents to her General Practitioner with nausea and abdominal pain. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Urea 20 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Na+ 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 3.64 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l PTH 9.8 pmol/l 0.9–5.4 mmol/l Fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride is started. Following ﬂuid resuscitation, what would be the next step in management?
options: Referral for admission to inpatient Psychiatry Unit
explanation: C Pamidronate infusion The initial diagnosis here is hypercalcaemia, which can cause a severe gastrointestinal disturbance. Serum levels of > 3.5 mmol/l are associated with cardiac arrhythmias, coma and pancreatitis, and urgent treatment is required. The raised PTH level suggests that the elevated Ca2+ level is secondary to primary hyperparathyroidism, and in a young woman, the most likely cause would be parathyroid adenoma. Hypercalcaemia is often associated with severe dehydration which increases the risk of renal damage. Following aggres- sive rehydration to prevent renal tubular damage, the bisphosphonate pamidronate is the treatment of choice to reduce osteoclastic activity, and hence bone resorption of Ca2+. A Emergency surgery Emergency surgery is only required in cases of resistant hypercalcaemia not responding to intravenous ﬂuids and pamidronate. Indications for elective parathyroid surgery include the following:  serum Ca2+ level > 0.25 mmol/l above the upper limit of normal  marked hypercalciuria (> 400 mg/day) or renal stones creatinine clearance < 30% of normal  marked bone density reduction with a T-score < 2.5 at any site  age < 50 years (if the problem is left untreated, many of these younger patients eventually develop complications of primary hyperparathyroidism)  a patient for whom surveillance and follow-up are difﬁcult or impossible. B Oral prednisolone This can be used in the management of hypercalcaemia due to sarcoid or lymphomas. In this case, the cause of hypercalcaemia is most likely primary hyperparathyroidism due to an adenoma or gland hyperplasia. D Referral for admission to inpatient Psychiatry Unit Although this patient has a history of anorexia, which can present with electrolyte abnormalities, this patient only presents with isolated hypercalcaemia. As this patient also has a raised PTH level, this is unlikely to be due to anorexia, and therefore, inpatient Psychiatry Unit admission is not an appropriate course of action. E Subcutaneous calcitonin Calcitonin reduces Ca2+ levels via inhibition of osteoclastic activity in bone and inhibition of renal tubular cell reabsorption of Ca2+ and phosphate, allowing these to be excreted in the urine. It can be used as ﬁrst-line, along with ﬂuids and bisphosphonates, in cases of hypercalcaemia due to multiple myeloma or cancer.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with frequent headaches, excessive sweating, reduction in peripheral vision, deepening of her voice and amenorrhoea. She has also noticed a prominence of her lower jaw. On examination, there is mild hirsutism. Visual tests show bitemporal hemianopia. Investigations reveal a fasting blood glucose of 7.8 mmol/l and a 2 hour post-prandial value of 12.5 mmol/l. Prolactin is elevated at 1000. Her blood pressure (BP) is elevated at 165/99 mmHg. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan shows a 20 mm pituitary adenoma. What would be the most appropriate ﬁrst line management in this case?
options: Somatostatin analogue followed by trans-sphenoidal surgery
Pegvisomant in combination with a somatostatin analogue
explanation: B Trans-sphenoidal surgery Tumor resection via transsphenoidal surgery is the optimal primary treatment in most patients. Data supporting use of endoscopic over microscopic approaches remain incomplete and further comparative outcome studies are needed before one approach can be recommended over the other. Currently, the choice of technique depends on neurosurgeon expertise and preference. Craniotomy is very rarely indicated in patients with acromegaly. Intraoperative MRI and other techniques to aid in intraoperative visualization of tumor remnants remain investigational. C External radiotherapy followed by octreotide Radiotherapy is not the ﬁrst-line treatment of choice in patients with a pituitary adenoma and has been shown to reduce prolactin levels in only approximately 25% of patients. There is also the risk of hypopituitarism as well as localised neurological damage. Radiotherapy can be considered further down the line if the patient is hypersecretory and if the tumour is not fully resected. Octreotide can be used to treat patients with acromegaly, but again this option would not be the ﬁrst-line treatment. A Cabergoline followed by trans-sphenoidal surgery Cabergoline is a very effective treatment for prolactinoma. This patient has a raised prolactin level, but this is likely to be due to pressure effect rather than as a result of a primary prolactinoma. Regardless, carbegoline is likely to be given in isolation rather than with trans-sphenoidal surgery. D Somatostatin analogue followed by transsphenoidal surgery Medical therapy is recommended for patients who do not achieve biochemical control after surgery. Primary medical therapy is reserved for those with contraindication to or who refuse surgery, and may be considered in select patients considered at poor risk for good outcomes and surgical success. Randomized studies suggest improvement in postoperative remission after pretreatment with SRL for 3–6 months. However, data are conﬂicting and, in many instances, results were not sustained during long-term follow-up. E Pegvisomant in combination with a somatostatin analogue Pegvisomant and somatostatins are commonly used individually in clinical practice, but are only licensed for use in combination in patients where there is an effective response with somatostatin analogues alone.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 2-week history of lower leg pain, particularly his left leg. His legs feel heavy when he walks, and his left ankle is more swollen than usual. Despite taking shorter walks, the pain has persisted and is only relieved on elevation. His past medical history includes hypertension, irritable bowel syndrome and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. The ankle–brachial pressure index (ABPI) is 0.9. His lower limbs are examined and there is a noticeable lesion on his left lower leg, shown below: What is the next step in the management of this patient?
explanation: A Compression bandaging This patient has evidence of venous insufﬁciency, given the increased pigment deposition around the lower leg and foot, with venous eczema. There is a moderately-sized venous ulcer with less well-deﬁned margins on the lower aspect of the leg. Usually, the medial malleolus is most commonly affected. A history of aching lower legs that feel heavy and swollen with the improvement of symptoms is also suggestive of chronic venous insufﬁciency and venous ulcer development. Provided the ABPI is 0.8 or above, compression bandaging can be safely applied to the affected limb(s). This is one of the most effective ways of treating venous ulceration. C Topical corticosteroids Topical corticosteroids are used in the management of some cases of dermatitis and pyoderma gangrenosum. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare skin disorder characterised by a painful nodule that rapidly progresses to a large, ulcerative lesion. It is associated with autoimmune conditions, such as inﬂammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis. A classical presentation is a lesion with purple-coloured outer edges. This is not seen here, making pyoderma gangrenosum a less likely diagnosis. B Oral ﬂucloxacillin Oral ﬂucloxacillin is used in the ﬁrst-line treatment of cellulitis. Evidence of cellulitis includes lower limb erythema, swelling, pain and fever. The mild redness that can be seen surrounding this patient’s ulcer most likely represents inﬂammation and venous eczema rather than an infective process. D Topical fusidic acid Topical fusidic acid is used in the treatment of infective lesions. However, the lack of cellulitic changes and signs of chronic venous insufﬁciency make venous ulceration the more likely diagnosis. E Urgent angioplasty Urgent angioplasty is the treatment of choice for critical limb ischaemia, which is characterised by a cold, pale, pulseless, painful limb with paraesthesia and paralysis. Arterial ulceration usually appears more deﬁned, with punched-out edges. Although this patient has a history of smoking, which increases the likelihood for peripheral vascular disease, the appearance of the ulcer, combined with the presentation, makes arterial disease less likely. Pain relieved on elevation is more typical of venous insufﬁciency than arterial.

stem: A 54-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with a history of ‘funny turns’ over the last two years. She complains of intermittent episodes of feeling sweaty and faint and having double vision. She tells you that she often feels better after a strong cup of tea with three sugars. She has no medical history of note and is taking no tablets. Her mother had diabetes mellitus and her father had epilepsy. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol occasionally. Her examination is completely normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Urea 6.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.93 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 0.84 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Na+ 136 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 84µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.3 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Multiple endocrine neoplasia type-1 An insulinoma should be suspected in this patient, given her 2year history of ‘funny turns’ and the fact that she feels better after a strong cup of tea. Furthermore the blood tests reveal an elevated calcium, raising the suspicion of associated hyperparathyroidism. Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN)-1 should be suspected here, which may be a combination of a pituitary tumour (often a macroadenoma), hyperparathyroidism and a pancreatic islet tumour. Of course all these conditions may not necessarily occur at the same point in time. The MEN 1 gene has an autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance. Any individual with a relative with MEN 1 should be screened. Mutational analysis of the coding region has a sensitivity of about 95% in MEN 1 patients. Relatives without the mutation can be reassured and do not require regular screening. Screening includes serum calcium and

prolactin in all patients; 90% of MEN 1 patients present with hypercalcaemia. A Petit mal epilepsy This is a common type of epilepsy syndrome presenting in children in the ﬁrst decade. A seizure is characterised by a brief staring episode with behavioural arrest. A 3 Hz spike-andslow-wave discharge on electroencephalogram (EEG is generally associated with this seizure. B Recurrent TIAs Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is deﬁned as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord or retinal ischaemia, without acute infarction. The duration of symptom/sign is <24 h and resolution is not related to consumption of any food/beverage. D Paroxysmal atrial ﬁbrillation Paroxysmal AF (PAF) is deﬁned as an episode of AF that reverts to sinus rhythm spontaneously or with intervention within seven days. Symptoms can be irregular palpitations, shortness of breath, dyspnoea on exertion, a sensation of lightheadedness or less commonly fatigue, weakness or generalised malaise. In acute presentations, heart rate is controlled by a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker. If spontaneous reversion doesn’t occur and there is haemodynamic compromise, electrical cardioversion is considered or, alternatively, pharmacological conversion with ﬂecainide or amiodarone. E Phaeochromocytoma Phaechromocytoma are rare catecholamine-secreting tumours occurring in <0.2% of patients with hypertension. Most (about 70%) are sporadic. Classical symptoms are headaches, sweating and tachycardia. Other symptoms include palpitations, tremor, pallor, dyspnoea, generalised weakness, and panic attack-type symptoms. Most common sign is sustained or paroxysmal hypertension. Symptoms usually resolve spontaneously without intervention.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who has a history of hypertension is operated on by Neurosurgeons for an intracranial haemorrhage. Over the next few days her serum sodium level progressively declines and by the third day has fallen to 118 mmol/l despite ﬂuid restriction to 1 litre per day. Her blood pressure (BP) has maintained steady at 145/85 mmHg. Her chest X-ray is shown below. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Urine osmolarity 700 mOsmol/l 50–1200 mOsmol/l Urine Na+ 80 mmol/l < 20 mmo/l Serum K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Which of the following ﬁts best with the diagnosis in this patient?
explanation:
B Secretion of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) The chest x-ray here is normal, with no signs of ﬂuid overload or tumour. SIADH is well known to occur after head injury, central nervous system (CNS) infection or intracranial haemorrhage. It is associated with hyponatraemia and hypotonic plasma, raised urine osmolality and excessive urinary sodium excretion (often >50 mmol/l). SIADH is often a transient phenomenon and resolves after a few days; in patients who fail to respond to ﬂuid restriction, demeclocycline, which induces partial diabetes insipidus, may be a treatment option.

D Hypovolaemia The steady maintenance of blood pressure above 140 mmHg systolic effectively rules out signiﬁcant hypovolaemia. A Addisonian crisis Addisonian crisis is associated with signiﬁcant salt wasting and consequent hypotension, not present here, making Addison’s less likely as the underlying cause of her hyponatraemia. C Cranial diabetes insipidus Cranial diabetes insipidus is associated with hypernatraemia and hypotension, rather than the picture seen here. E Fluid overload Fluid overload is both associated with hyponatraemia and signs of heart failure or peripheral oedema, neither of which is seen in the scenario here.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a three month history of diarrhoea. On examination, he is found to have blood pressure (BP) of 180/100 mmHg. A ﬁrm, enlarged thyroid is also noted. On taking his history, the patient mentions that his father had an operation to remove a gland and had a scar on his neck. His uncle also had the same gland removed due to cancer and has also had kidney failure. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 450 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 135 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 3.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 5.5 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.72 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l What is a possible unifying diagnosis?
explanation: C MEN 2a It is important to note that this patient has a thyroid mass, hypertension and hypercalcaemia. MEN 2A is deﬁned by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), which causes diarrhoea; pheochromocytoma, which causes hypertension; and hyperparathyroidism caused by parathyroid gland hyperplasia, which causes hypercalcaemia. MEN 2A is a unifying diagnosis for this patient. A Carcinoid syndrome Carcinoid tumours arise from the enterochromafﬁn cells in the intestine and the main bronchi and do not usually manifest as thyroid masses. These tumours secrete peptides such as 5hydroxytryptophan. Carcinoid syndrome is a manifestation of advanced disease and is characterised by facial ﬂushing, diarrhoea and wheezing. B Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) 1 MEN 1 affects the parathyroid glands, the pancreatic islets and the anterior pituitary. Associated tumours include lipomas, angioﬁbromas or those located in the adrenal gland cortex. This patient has a distinct thyroid mass which is not in keeping with MEN 1. D Phaeochromocytoma Phaeochromocytoma is an adrenal tumour known to secrete large amounts of catecholamines. It is associated with a variety of symptoms including headache, palpitations, sweating and anxiety. Hypertension, which may be sustained or paroxysmal, is believed to be the most consistent clinical sign. E Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)oma VIPomas in adults are neuroendocrine islet cell tumours of the pancreas that produce high amounts of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). Other secreted hormones may include secreted gastrin and pancreatic polypeptide. Episodic diarrhoea is often the presenting symptom. These presenting symptoms do not ﬁt with this patient’s symptoms, making it an unlikely diagnosis.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with a 2-month history of decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. He has no known past medical history of note and does not take any regular medication. On examination, his vital signs are within normal limits. He is noticeably tall, with pronounced gynaecomastia and sparse body hair. Investigation Result Normal value FSH 45 mIU/ml 2–20 mIU/ml Luteinising hormone (LH) 130 mIU/ml 1.1–110 mIU/ml Testosterone 3 nmol/l 10–30 nmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Klinefelter syndrome Klinefelter syndrome is characterised by an extra X chromosome (47,XXY). The condition is associated with primary testicular failure and hypogonadism. Patients with Klinefelter syndrome typically present with small testes, gynaecomastia and sparse body hair. They may also be tall, with weaker muscles, and some patients may have learning disability or behavioural disturbances, particularly in childhood. Laboratory tests show low testosterone levels and elevated LH and FSH levels due to primary testicular failure. A Androgen insensitivity syndrome Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is a condition characterised by resistance to the action of androgens, resulting in incomplete masculinisation of the external genitalia in individuals with a 46,XY karyotype. AIS typically presents with female external genitalia or ambiguous genitalia in phenotypic females. The presence of gynaecomastia and sparse body hair in this patient is inconsistent with AIS. B Kallmann syndrome Kallmann syndrome is a type of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. The condition is characterised by inadequate production of testosterone secondary to hypothalamic dysfunction and failure to produce gonadotrophin-releasing hormone. It is typically associated with low serum testosterone levels and low or normal LH and FSH levels. The presence of elevated LH and FSH levels in this patient makes hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism less likely. D Leydig cell tumour Leydig cell tumours are rare and typically present with signs of androgen excess rather than with hypogonadism. Signs and symptoms of Leydig cell tumours include virilisation and precocious puberty. Additionally. Leydig cell tumours usually result in elevated testosterone levels rather than in low levels, as seen in this patient. E Prader–Willi syndrome Prader–Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disorder with multiple clinical features, including short stature, global developmental delay and hypogonadism. Patients may experience incomplete sexual development, including genital hypoplasia. However, this patient’s presentation is not in keeping with Prader–Willi syndrome.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic. She has had type I diabetes for eight years, and until recently it has been well controlled; however, recently, she has been having numerous hypoglycaemic attacks. These 'hypos' can be at any time of the day and follow no pattern. Her periods are regular. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 100/60 mmHg with a postural drop of 10 mmHg. She is on a basal- bolus regime, taking insulin eight units three times per day and glargine insulin 15 units at night. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 100 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.3 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l PLT 193 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Na+ 130 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l MCV 93 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ Urea 8.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Which of the following is most likely to determine the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
D Short Synacthen test Type I diabetes is associated with many autoimmune diseases, including Addison’s (primary autoimmune adrenal failure). It commonly presents with weight loss and malaise. In patients with diabetes, it presents more commonly as hypoglycaemia. Hyponatraemia is present in 90% and hyperkalaemia in 65%. A normocytic normochromic anaemia is often present, sometimes with an associated eosinophilia. B Paired serum and urine osmolality The presence of unexplained hypoglycaemia in the presence of a low serum sodium steers us more towards adrenal in-

sufﬁciency, which must be excluded before a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) can be considered. A Serum ferritin This patient has normocytic anaemia, which is much more likely to be related to adrenal failure rather than to low iron stores. C Continuous glucose monitoring CGM will conﬁrm a diagnosis of unpredictable hypoglycaemia, although won’t contribute to elucidating the cause. E Transferrin saturation However, haemochromatosis does present with diabetes mellitus and can be associated with adrenal failure, due to the effect of the menstrual cycle it presents in older women, usually post-menopause.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease as a result of long-standing reﬂux nephropathy goes to her GP complaining of tiredness. She currently takes ramipril and indapamide for hypertension. On examination, her BP is 142/88 mmHg and she looks pale and washed-out. Her pulse is 72 bpm and regular. Investigations: Hb 104 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l PLT 198 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l K+ 5.2 mmol/l Creatinine 232 µmol/l TSH 1.5 U/l (< 0.5-4.5) Total T4 45 nmol/l (58-161) Free T4 24 pmol/l (9-27) Total T3 0.8 nmol/l (0.9-2.8) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Thyroxine-binding globulin deﬁciency Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) deﬁciency is a nonharmful condition that is either acquired or inherited. The thyroid hormones – T4 and 3,5,3'-T3 – circulate in the blood by reversibly binding to carrier proteins. Although only 0.3% or less of T3 and T4 circulates unbound, it is this free hormone fraction that is metabolically active at the tissue and cellular level. The three main proteins that carry the majority (>95%) of thyroid hormones are TBG), transthyretin (TTR, or prealbumin) and albumin. Thyroid hormone binding to TBG is characterised by low capacity but high avidity. Inherited or acquired variations in the concentration and/or afﬁnity of these proteins may produce substantial changes in serum total thyroid hormone levels as measured by commercially available assays. Notably, these changes do not result in illness (i.e. hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism), because the concentration of free thyroid hormones does not change. A deﬁciency in thyroid hormone-binding proteins is suspected when abnormally low serum total thyroid hormone concentrations are encountered in clinically euthyroid subjects in the presence of normal serum TSH. More speciﬁcally, low TBG is suggested because this protein carries the majority of the serum thyroid hormones. Thyroid function tests (TFTs) in patients with TBG deﬁciency show normal TSH and free T4, but low total T4 and, occasionally, low total T3 serum concentrations. The most important clinical aspect of TBG deﬁciency states is recognition of these disorders and avoidance of unnecessary and potentially harmful thyroid hormone replacement therapy. D Iodine deﬁciency Iodine deﬁciency results in a goitre. In terms of thyroid function tests, it is characterised by low fT4 and raised TSH. Sometimes fT3 can be normal/raised because of the increased fT3 to fT4 conversion as a compensatory mechanism. A Hashimotos’s thyroiditis Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is an autoimmune condition causing hypothyroidism with low fT3 and fT4 and raised TSH. The anti-TPO antibodies are also raised. In this scenario, the thyroid function tests are not in keeping with Hashimoto’s. B Pituitary failure In cases of pituitary failure resulting in secondary hypothyroidism, the TSH is below the lowest limit of normal, with low fT3 and fT4. Pituitary disorders usually affect ﬁrst the gonadal axis, then the adrenal axis and lastly the thyroid axis; therefore secondary hypothyroidism would also be associated with symptoms of gonadal and adrenal failure (amenorrhea, hyperpigmentation, nausea and vomiting). C Sick euthyroid syndrome Sick euthyroid syndrome is particularly common in patients with chronic kidney disease, and is characterised by small reductions in both free T3 and free T4 and normal or suppressed TSH. It is also seen in the context of severe illness in

patients admitted to the ITU, severe sepsis, cardiac and liver failure, end-stage malignancy and starvation. Whether thyroid replacement is of any value in this situation is a subject of continued debate. What persuades us against sick euthyroid syndrome here is the normal free T4 against a background of reduced total T3 and T4, and the lack of a precipitant acute illness.

stem: A 21-year-old student with type 1 diabetes is brought to the Emergency Department by her ﬂat-mates. She has been suffering from a cold for a few days. On examination, her GCS is 12, and she has a respiratory rate of 40/min. Finger-prick blood glucose in the department is measured at 38.1 mmol/l and this is conﬁrmed on venous sampling. Arterial blood gases reveal a pH of 7.05 and serum bicarbonate of 12 mmol/l. Electrolytes are abnormal, with potassium of 5.9 mmol/l, urea of 15.5 mmol/l and creatinine of 193 mmol/l. She is 63kg in weight. Which of the following options would represent the most appropriate initial treatment for her?
options: 1 litre of normal saline over 8 h
1 mmol of sodium bicarbonate/kg IV over 30 min
explanation: B 1 litre of normal saline stat This patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis, the likely precipitant of which has been her recent respiratory infection. Initial investigations of choice for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) include blood for urea, electrolytes and glucose, full blood count, arterial blood gases, blood and urine cultures, chest radiograph and electrocardiogram (ECG). Initial management involves 2 l of 1 M saline administered over 2 h unless the patient has cardiovascular or ﬂuid management issues. Potassium administration is set according to serum potassium (intravenous (IV) insulin may result in rapid potassium reduction); the recommended dosage ranges from 40 mmol/l K+ added per litre bag of 1 M/saline if serum potassium is <3 mmol/l, to no potassium added if serum potassium is 6.0 mmol/l or above. Where potassium is <3, management on the ITU where central venous access delivery of potassium can be carried out, is preferred. An IV ﬁxedrate insulin infusion is also started to combat hyperglycaemia. E Intubation and ventilation This patient’s GCS is 12, so although she is confused, her conscious level can be monitored for deterioration at this stage. There may be rapid improvement in response to ﬂuid resuscitation and insulin. A 1 litre of normal saline over 8 h Patients presenting with DKA may be ﬂuid depleted by up to 5 l. As such, delivering 1 l over 8 h is far too slow an infusion rate. C 1 litre of Hartmann’s over 4 h It’s argued that Hartmann’s shouldn’t be used as initial ﬂuid replacement because it delivers a lactate load, and patients already have a high lactate/pyruvate ratio in DKA. D 1 mmol of sodium bicarbonate/kg IV over 30 min At this stage the initial response to aggressive ﬂuid resuscitation and insulin delivered IV should be assessed before commencing sodium bicarbonate. In practice for DKA, sodium bicarbonate is only really considered in the peri-arrest situation.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with thirst, polyuria, and constipation. Her family also feel that she has been depressed over the last few weeks, which is unusual for her. Examination is unremarkable apart from generalised abdominal tenderness and a scar noted on the left breast from a previous lumpectomy for breast carcinoma. Investigations reveal the following: Invetsigation Result Normal value Urea 10.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l Na+ 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 3.84 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l PTH levels 0.8 pmol/l 0.9–5.4 pmol/l Which single initial management choice would be most appropriate from the list below?
explanation: A IV ﬂuids The initial diagnosis here is hypercalcaemia, which can cause severe gastrointestinal disturbance. Serum levels >3.5 mmol/l are associated with cardiac arrhythmias, coma and pancreatitis and urgent treatment is required. The low parathyroid hormone precludes parathyroid disease as a cause, and in this age group (particularly with a previous malignancy) metastatic bone disease would be high on a list of differential diagnoses. Hypercalcaemia is often associated with severe dehydration that increases the risk of renal damage. The bisphosphonate pamidronate is the treatment of choice to reduce osteoclast activity and hence bone resorption of calcium, but should always be preceded by aggressive rehydration to prevent renal tubular damage. In the case described here, these would therefore be used as a next step following IV ﬂuids. B Oral furosemide In cases of hypercalcaemia, furosemide is not routinely recommended in the Society for Endocrinology Guidelines, and it should only be given with ﬂuid resuscitation if there is evidence of ventricular strain and pulmonary oedema. C IV steroids Prednisolone is used to treat hypercalcaemia associated with sarcoid. D IV pamidronate Pamindronate is a bisphosphonate used in the acute management of hypercalcaemia after the initial phase of ﬂuid resuscitation; therefore, it would be a good second-line treatment option. E Denosumab Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody used in the treatment of osteoporosis. It is a RANKL inhibitor and works by inhibiting the osteoclastic activity in bone, thereby preserving the bone mass.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic. He presents with short stature (less than the lower 3rd centile) with his weight being between the 10th and 15th centiles. On examination, he has no pubic hair and pre-pubertal testes. There is no family history and he is currently well apart from a six month history of headaches. Appropriate investigations and imaging studies are arranged for the patient, and the result of the computed tomography (CT) scan of the head shows the presence of a suprasellar calciﬁed cyst with the cyst content having the same density as the cerebral spinal ﬂuid (CSF). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Craniopharyngioma Craniopharyngioma is a slow-growing, calciﬁed cystic tumour arising from the remnants of the craniopharyngeal duct. It compromises 4.2% of all childhood tumours and is slightly more common in males than females. The symptoms develop very slowly and usually manifest once the tumour has attained a diameter of 3 cm. The commonest presentation in young patients is growth failure and delayed puberty. The radiological hallmark of a craniopharyngioma is the presence of a suprasellar calciﬁed cyst, with calciﬁcation being more common in children than in adults. Using imaging studies, CT is most useful in demonstrating the calciﬁcations whereas MRI is essential for deﬁning the local anatomy prior to surgical intervention. Surgery is the management of choice and may attempt to resect the tumour in total, or to reduce the size followed by postoperative radiotherapy treatment. C Low-grade astrocytoma Astrocytomas commonly present with headaches and seizures, or with other symptoms of raised intracranial pressure. A Idiopathic intracranial hypertension The most common symptom of idiopathic intracranial hypertension is headache, but it should not cause developmental delay. CT of the head may show ventricles that are slightly reduced in size. D Neurosarcoidosis Neurosarcoidosis presents with a cranial neuropathy in 6070%, usually involving the 7th cranial nerve. Aseptic meningitis occurs in around 20%. E Tolosa-Hunt syndrome Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is also known as superior orbital ﬁssure syndrome. It describes a rare, granulomatous inﬂammatory process adjacent to the cavernous sinus or within the superior orbital ﬁssure and/or orbital apex. The syndrome manifests as hemicranial or periorbital pain, ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.

stem: A 60-year-old woman on long-term therapy for depression has been referred by the Psychiatric Services. She presented acutely via the community psychiatric nurse with increasing drowsiness and confusion. According to her carer, she had complained of increasing thirst and going to the bathroom over the past few days, and appeared to have been drinking more ﬂuids over the past few weeks. Investigation Result Normal values Na+ 156 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Urea 20 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 205 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Chloride (Cl–) 112 mmol/l 98 - 106 mmol/l Glucose 6.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.6 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Which of the following medications is likely to be responsible for this lady’s presentation?
explanation: C Lithium This lady’s long history of depression is likely to be related to bipolar disorder, which has resulted in a long- term script for lithium and her presentation with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI), as shown by her hypernatraemia and picture of dehydration on blood testing. Causes of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus include an X-linked inherited disorder, an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance, lithium, demeclocycline, chronic renal disease, post-obstructive uropathy, hypercalcaemia and hyperglycaemia. Therapy should only be stopped with the advice of her psychiatrist, although her symptoms are highly unlikely to improve unless the lithium therapy is ceased. Bendroﬂumethiazide and indomethacin may be useful in nephrogenic DI due to their local action on the kidney in cases that fail to respond to cessation of lithium: because both increase lithium levels they can’t be given at the same time. Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a treatment for cranial diabetes insipidus and so is of little value here. B Fluoxetine Like paroxetine, ﬂuoxetine is an SSRI and is not associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. A Paroxetine Paroxetine is a selective serotonin uptake inhibitor (SSRI), which is rarely associated with the serotonin syndrome but is not associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. D Amitriptyline Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant which may be associated with syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) rather than diabetes insipidus. E Chlorpromazine The main concern with chlorpromazine, a dopamine antagonist, is the development of tardive dyskinesia.32917

stem: A 40-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic complaining of an eight month history of constant sweating and occasionally being feverish. She found her recent summer holiday to Turkey unbearable and had to return to the UK early. She has also noticed that she has lost weight over the last year, though her appetite remains ﬁne. On examination, she is afebrile but tachycardic. Her palms are sweaty. No goitre is palpable. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Routine full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E) and liver function tests (LFT) are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Thyrotoxicosis Episodic bouts of sweating may be due to hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma or carcinoid. However, a patient reporting night sweats suggests a diagnosis of Hodgkin’s disease or tuberculosis. Hodgkin’s disease tends to feature localised lymphadenopathy, weight loss, pruritus and fever. Patients with thyrotoxicosis report constant sweating and heat intolerance. There may be no evidence of enlargement of the thyroid gland. Taking her age and sex into account, thyrotoxicosis is the most likely diagnosis. D Infection – undeﬁned organism Apart from the weight loss and the sweats, there are no other symptoms which would point towards an infection. Moreover, the FBC is normal (no neutrophilia, or lymphocytosis in the

case of viral infections). Also, liver function tests are normal, which precludes hepatitis or Epstein–Barr. The natural history of the disease is also too long (8 months). A Hodgkin’s lymphoma Hodgkin’s disease tends to feature localised lymphadenopathy, weight loss, pruritus and fever, splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly. In our case, the physical examination is not in keeping with Hodgkin’s lymphoma. B Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma Signs and symptoms of low-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas are:  peripheral adenopathy: painless and slowly progressive; can spontaneously regress  primary extra-nodal involvement and B symptoms: uncommon at presentation; however, common with advanced, malignant transformation or end-stage disease  bone marrow: frequent involvement; may be associated with cytopenias(s); fatigue/weakness more common in advanced-stage disease. In our case, FBC is normal and there is no evidence of lymphadenopathy. E Phaeochromocytoma Classically, pheochromocytoma manifests as spells with the following four characteristics:  headaches  palpitations  diaphoresis  severe hypertension. In our scenario, apart from weight loss and sweating, which are non-speciﬁc, there is nothing else pointing towards a diagnosis of phaechromocytoma.

stem: You are asked to check the blood results on a 32-year-old man who was admitted earlier in the day on the medical take. He is very overweight and has been admitted with an infective exacerbation of asthma. He is being treated with oral prednisolone 60 mg once a day, four hourly 5 mg salbutamol nebulisers with amoxicillin 500 mgs twice a day and erythromycin 250 mg twice a day. Besides his normal inhalers, he does not take any regular medications. He is a smoker. The team commented that it was very difﬁcult to gain venous access. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 6.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 4.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 82 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 139 mg/l < 10 mg/l Glucose 5.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l You visit him on the ward. He is having a nebuliser and reading the newspaper. What is the best course of action?
options: Urgent calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% intravenous (iv) followed by insulin/dextrose infusion
Urgent electrocardiogram (ECG), followed by calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% iv followed by insulin/dextrose infusion
Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample, and hold off further treatment until this result is returned
Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available
Urgent ECG. Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available in the meantime
explanation:
E Urgent ECG. Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available in the meantime This young man has no recognised reasons for hyperkalaemia. He is not on any medications which would predispose him to high potassium; indeed, his regular salbutamol treatment is likely to give him low serum potassium by driving potassium into the cells. His urea and electrolytes are otherwise normal. His glucose is normal. The most likely cause of the high potassium in this case is either mild haemolysis not picked up in the laboratory, or the long use of a tourniquet during blood taking, leading to relative tissue acidosis when the sample was taken and therefore a high potassium. It is likely to be artefactual. However, it would be prudent to check for evidence of cardiac toxicity which is easy to do with an ECG. It would also be worth rechecking the potassium, and if a blood gas machine is available it may be worth rechecking the potassium locally pending the formal laboratory result. C Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample, and hold off further treatment until this result is returned If hyperkalaemia is true, then cardiac toxicity could be fatal; therefore although a repeat sample is need, an urgent ECG should be performed. A Urgent calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% intravenous (iv) followed by insulin/dextrose infusion As explained above, it is important to determine whether there

is any cardiac toxicity and also to conﬁrm hyperkalaemia. B Urgent electrocardiogram (ECG), followed by calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% iv followed by insulin/dextrose infusion Calcium gluconate is given if there are any cardiac electrical changes. The high potassium may be an artefact therefore it is important to check validity. D Repeat laboratory urea and electrolyte sample and check potassium on an arterial blood gas machine if available As above, urgent ECG is needed to check for any cardiac toxicity.

stem: A 53-year-old man with type II diabetes attends the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has had diabetes for ﬁve years and is currently managed with metformin 1 g twice a day and pioglitazone 30 mg daily. You understand that he suffered a myocardial infarction (MI) while on holiday some ﬁve months earlier and has suffered very minor episodes of angina since. He is treated with atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 75 mg, ramipril 10 mg and glyceryl trinate spray, and most recently has had trouble with increasing shortness of breath and peripheral oedema. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 142/80 mmHg. His body mass index (BMI) is 29 kg/m2. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 134 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 x 109/l PLT 299 × 109/l 150–400 x 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1C 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%) < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) Which of the following represent the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Add a sulphonylurea to the regime
Switch to basal bolus insulin therapy
explanation: C Change the pioglitazone to empagliﬂozin This man has a history of ischaemic heart disease and evidence of heart failure. As such, a glitazone is likely to be dangerous with respect to the possibility of worsening his heart failure and increasing the risk of cardiovascular events. For these reasons the pioglitazone should be discontinued. Because his HbA1c is only modestly elevated, a trial of SGLT-2 inhibitor is reasonable, which will control HbA1c and promote modest weight loss, accompanied by a mild diuresis. The class has also now been shown to reduce heart failure, with empagliﬂozin also having a positive impact on MACE events. A Leave the diabetes therapy unchanged Leaving therapy unchanged runs the risk of worsening heart failure and ﬂuid retention because of the pioglitazone. B Add a sulphonylurea to the regime Adding a sulphonylurea risks increasing the risk of hypoglycaemia for this patient, driving weight gain, and it is not associated with positive cardiovascular outcomes. D Switch to basal bolus insulin therapy Switching to basal bolus insulin therapy may drive tighter glycaemic control, but it also drives hypoglycaemia and weight gain and may increase the risk of sudden cardiac death because of episodes of severe hypo. E Add liraglutide Without stopping the pioglitazone, it’s inappropriate to move straight to adding a GLP-1 agonist.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with ulcerated lesions over both shins. He has a history of type I diabetes mellitus. He has recently lost his job and has poor standards of personal care. He is on multiple daily insulin injections (insulin detemir [rDNA origin] injection as basal insulin and insulin aspart with his meals) and his diabetes control is poor (HbA1c: 79 mmol/mol). His right leg is shown below. Which of the following represents the most appropriate treatment to the non-atrophied areas?
explanation: A Topical steroids The image shows shiny pale yellowed lesions with telangiectasia and an erythematous border consistent with necrobiosis lipoidica. Necrobiosis lipoidica is seen in 0.3–1% of patients with diabetes and is more common in females. Around 40– 60% of patients with necrobiosis lipoidica have diabetes, and the condition may predate the development of abnormal blood sugar. Treatments with topical steroids, injectable steroids, skin grafting and camouﬂage creams have been used as therapies. In practice, however, the areas of already atrophied skin respond poorly to steroid therapy. C Azathioprine Azathioprine, sold under the brand name is an immunosuppressive medication which is used in rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, and in kidney transplants to prevent rejection. Common side effects include bone marrow suppression and vomiting. Bone marrow suppression is especially common in people with a genetic deﬁciency of the enzyme thiopurine S-methyltransferase. Other serious risk factors include an increased risk of lymphoma. Azathioprine is in the purine analogue and anti-metabolite family of medication. It works via 6-thioguanine to disrupt the synthesis of RNA and DNA by cells. B Oral prednisolone Oral prednisolone would deteriorate his diabetes control even further. D Flucloxacillin This is mainly used in cases of cellulitis which would manifest with an area of erythema accompanied usually by tenderness and increased skin temperature. E Compression bandaging This is used for the treatment of venous ulcers. A venous ulcer tends to occur on the medial side of the leg, typically around the medial malleolus, and is usually shallow with irregular, sloping edges. Venous ulcers are typically 'wet' with a moderate to heavy exudate. The skin surrounding a venous ulcer may be oedematous, and there may be evidence of varicose veins.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with a phaeochromocytoma by the general physicians visits you for a specialist endocrinology appointment. She is on adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine and is awaiting surgery. They are concerned as her calcium is elevated, at 2.75 mmol/l. On examination her blood pressure (BP) is elevated at 148/88 mmHg. You feel a hard mass on the right-hand side of the thyroid. Which test is most important for conﬁrming the diagnosis?
explanation: B Pentagastrin stimulation test There is a high index of suspicion that this patient has MEN2a, and she may well have both parathyroid hyperplasia and medullary thyroid carcinoma. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is the most important diagnosis to conﬁrm, with the pentagastrin test the best way to do this. It measures calcitonin levels at 2 and 5 minutes, however, and a rise in calcitonin is suggestive of medullary thyroid carcinoma. E PTH assay PTH may be elevated, but wouldn’t conﬁrm or refute an underlying diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma. A Tc-sestamibi parathyroid scan Parathyroid hyperplasia is much commoner than medullary thyroid carcinoma, and it’s most important to conﬁrm or refute medullary thyroid carcinoma and hence MEN-2a. C Ultrasound of the neck Ultrasound of the neck is relatively insensitive with respect to identifying small neck masses, and doesn’t provide a biochemical diagnosis. D Random calcitonin Random calcitonin is much less sensitive versus pentagastrinstimulated calcitonin to identify medullary thyroid carcinoma.

stem: A 16-year-old girl of Greek origin comes to the Endocrinology Clinic with failure to maintain normal growth and development. She has Beta-thalassaemia major and receives regular blood transfusions to maintain her Hb in the range of 90-100 g/l. You arrange some blood tests: Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 95 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 174 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 130 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Free T4 6.5 nmol/l 11–22 pmol/l 9 am cortisol 52 nmol 140–500 nmol/l IGF-1 2.5 nmol/l 9.3-56 nmol/l FSH 0.2 U/l 1–25 U/l Which of the following is the most appropriate replacement therapy to begin with?
explanation: B Hydrocortisone This patient has pituitary dysfunction, which has almost certainly been caused by iron overload. Her blood testing is consistent with a diagnosis of pan-hypopituitarism, but it is corticosteroid replacement that is essential ﬁrst to avoid the possibility of precipitating an adrenal crisis. C Oestrogen Sex hormone replacement is important, particularly to enable this patient to maintain good bone health, but it can be commenced later. A Growth hormone Although chronic growth hormone deﬁciency is associated with tiredness, lethargy and a reduction in muscle mass, it is hydrocortisone that is the more important replacement therapy to start ﬁrst. D Thyroxine Thyroxine replacement is essential, but should be begun shortly after hydrocortisone has commenced to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis. E Fludrocortisone This is only necessary in patients with adrenal insufﬁciency who are unable to maintain normal blood pressure control.

stem: A 52-year-old man on a visit to his GP has been noticed to have a blood pressure of 145/90 mm Hg. He has a 7-year history of type 2 diabetes, which is currently managed with metformin 1 g twice daily and gliclazide 160 mg twice daily. His BMI in the clinic was 26. Systemic examination otherwise was normal apart from bilateral peripheral sensory loss and loss of vibration sense up to his knees, consistent with diabetic neuropathy. He has also had laser photocoagulation treatment in both eyes. Other medication of note includes ramipril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin and aspirin, which were started approximately 5 years earlier. Investigation Result Normal values HbA1c 70.49 mmol/mol (8.6%) g/dl 9.29 - 53.0 mmol/mol (3 - 7 %) Urea 16.7 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 1.02 mmol/l 1.1 - 1.45 mmol/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 225 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.27 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Albumin 38 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Chloride (Cl-) 115 mmol/l 98 - 106 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 18 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l Urine protein 0.8 g/24 h Urine albumin/creatinine ratio 25 mg/mmol < 3 mg/mmol Which next step in his management would be the most appropriate?
options: Stop gliclazide and metformin and start a basal bolus insulin regime
Reduce the dose of ACE inhibitor by 50%
explanation: A Stop gliclazide and metformin and start a basal bolus insulin regime This gentleman’s renal function precludes the use of metformin. Moreover, the fact that despite being on the maximum dose of gliclazide and a high dose of metformin, his suboptimal HbA1c points towards the need for insulin initiation. A basal bolus regimen would be ideal given his poor renal function. Moreover, it will provide ﬂexibility in terms of dose adjustment and will optimize his glycaemic control. Tight glycaemic control is crucial given that this gentleman has already diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy. Improved control of his hypertension is required, therefore reducing or stopping his ACE inhibitor would be inappropriate. Additionally, the ECG is normal and does not indicate a need for beta-blockade at this point. B Reduce the dose of ACE inhibitor by 50% The target blood pressure for diabetics is recommended as <140/80 mmHg, or 125/75 mmHg in type 1 diabetic patients and individuals who have at least micro-albuminuria. ACE inhibitors are renoprotective in patients with a history of diabetic nephropathy, and thus continuing the ACE inhibitor at maximal tolerated dose is recommended. They also have signiﬁcant effect on reducing the albuminuria. C Stop his ACE inhibitor It is likely that the creatinine seen here is chronically elevated in the context of diabetic nephropathy and has not been worsened by ACE inhibition. D Start beta-blockers This patient needs better management of his hypertension, and the use of a second agent would be necessary. Beta-blockers would not be a ﬁrst choice unless there is history of atrial ﬁbrillation or coronary artery disease (the ECG is normal here), given the potential worsening effect of some of these on glycaemic control. E Start furosemide There is no evidence of ﬂuid overload that could justify its use, and it could potentially worsen the renal function.

stem: A 73-year-old man comes to the clinic as a referral from his GP, having presented with severe headaches and ischaemic pain in his ﬁngers and toes. The pain increases with heat, and improves if he keeps his hands and feet cold. Most striking is that just taking a few aspirin tablets seemed to improve things for a signiﬁcant time period. He has a past medical history of hypertension for which he takes ramipril. On examination his BP is 142/87 mmHg and the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Investigations (sent by the GP): Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 123 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 821 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 6.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 130 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate way to deal with his hyperkalaemia?
options: Start a small dose of furosemide
Re-check a fresh sample at the hospital
Reassure the biochemistry department that it is related to the high platelet count
explanation: C Re-check a fresh sample at the hospital Pseudohyperkalaemia is known to be associated with essential thrombocytosis, the most likely diagnosis here. It is also likely that the sample taken at the GP surgery had spent a considerable amount of time in transit, allowing for in-tube cell lysis to further increase potassium levels. As such, it is sensible to recheck a sample. A Stop the ramipril Given that the creatinine is almost in the normal range, it’s most likely the elevated potassium is due to pseudohyperkalaemia; as such, the potassium must be re-checked before considering treatment discontinuation. B Start a small dose of furosemide This may lead to volume depletion and actually increase the risk of a thrombotic event related to the high platelet count. D Reassure the biochemistry department that it is related to the high platelet count It must be re-checked at the hospital to exclude signiﬁcant hyperkalaemia. E Start calcium resonium This should be started for hyperkalaemia either in the acute setting or where other options for reducing hyperkalaemia in the chronic setting, such as discontinuation of other therapies, have been excluded.

stem: A 69-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes man- aged with metformin 1 g BD, liraglutide 1.8 mg daily and glargine 30 mg nocte. He complains of burning pain affecting both feet, much worse at night. Other history of note includes problems with intermittent urinary retention. On examination his BMI is 32, and his BP is 149/82 mmHg. His feet feel warm and his peripheral pulses are easily palpable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 116 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 244 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 145 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%) < 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Which of the following represents the most appropriate ﬁrst line treatment in this case?
explanation: A Duloxetine There is no indication of peripheral vascular disease, and the most likely diagnosis appears to be peripheral neuropathy. NICE guidelines recommend duloxetine, amitriptyline or gabapentin as potential initial therapies. Duloxetine is preferred to amitryptiline because it is associated with a lower risk of urinary retention. C Capsaicin It is a topical agent used for the treatment of neuropathy in addition to systemic agents, or for patients who are unable to take them. B Carbamazepine This is thought to be less effective than amitryptiline and is associated with increased risk of hyponatraemia. D Sodium valproate Sodium valproate is an alternative therapy for peripheral diabetic neuropathy, but isn’t recommended as a ﬁrst- line option by NICE guidelines. E Amitriptyline This isn’t preferred here because of a higher risk of urinary retention versus duloxetine.

stem: A 70-year-old man visits his General Practitioner (GP) complaining of vague left ﬂank pain without any evidence of diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. He is aware of intermittent sweats, particularly at night, that improve with eating. On one occasion, he has fainted between meals. An ultrasound (US) of his abdomen was technically difﬁcult to perform and a computerised tomography (CT) scan was recommended. This revealed a 3 cm mass in the tail of the pancreas. Blood biochemistry was normal. A blood glucose taken after an overnight fast and period on an exercise bike was recorded as 2 mmol/l. A CT guided needle biopsy of the pancreas reveals ill-deﬁned nests of cells separated by vascularised stroma, which stain strongly positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Insulinoma Insulinomas are the most common pancreatic endocrine tumour, the incidence being about 1 case per 250 000. Approximately 50% of islet cell tumours are insulinomas. Patients with insulinomas may present with neurological or psychiatric disturbances. An important feature is that symptoms tend to occur at night or early in the morning. The diagnosis is made by demonstrating inappropriately high concentrations of both insulin and C- peptide in the blood, and a blood glucose level of < 2.0–2.2 mmol/l, together with the clinical picture of a hypoglycaemic episode (confusion, altered consciousness, visual disturbances, weakness, sweating, tremulousness and, less commonly, seizures). Provocative testing with an overnight fast followed by exercise on a static bike can be done in a hospital setting. Frequent measurements of the blood glucose concentration should be made during the fast. Only when a low value is recorded should a sample be taken to provide serum for insulin and C-peptide assay. C Somatostatinoma Somatostatinomas are associated with glucose intolerance, increased risk of gallstones, diarrhoea and steatorrhoea. A Vasoactive intestinal peptide endocrine tumour (VIPoma)

Patients suffering from a VIPoma present with large-volume secretory diarrhoea, not seen here. B Gastrinoma Gastrinomas are associated with development of the Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, and multiple peptic ulcers. E Glucagonoma Glucagonomas are associated with glucose intolerance, increased risk of venous thromboembolic disease and the characteristic rash (necrolytic erythema migrans).

stem: A 59-year-old man is referred to the Emergency Department by his General Practitioner (GP). He has recently started ramipril 5 mg for diabetic nephropathy, and the GP is concerned by a deterioration in his creatinine level. According to the GP letter, he has had type II diabetes for the past seven years and was diagnosed with microalbuminuria some three years ago. On examination, in the Emergency Department, he looks well; his blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg, and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values K+ 5.0 (4.8 mmol/l on ACEi initiation some 10 days ago) 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 220 µmol/l (185 µmol/l on ACEi initiation some 10 days ago) 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Continue ramipril 5 mg and re-check urea and electrolytes (U&Es) in one week
Stop ramipril for one week and re-check U&Es
explanation: A Continue ramipril 5 mg and re-check urea and electrolytes (U&Es) in one week Although physicians generally consider a rise in creatinine levels of > 20% to be clinically signiﬁcant, a rise of > 30% is considered signiﬁcant, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines. The rise seen here (185–220 µmol/l) is below 20% and ramipril can therefore be continued. It is, however, prudent not to increase the dose of ramipril at this stage but merely to re-check the U&Es to ensure that no further rise in creatinine has occurred. C Increase Ramipril to 10 mg daily Blood pressure is in the target range, and there has been a rise in creatinine level. For this reason, a further increase in dose should be avoided at this stage. B Decrease Ramipril to 2.5 mg daily The rise in creatinine level seen here on ACEi initiation is below the 20% guidance for possible clinical harm. As such, there is no indication to decrease the ramipril dose at this stage. D Stop ramipril for one week and re-check U&Es This would have been a reasonable approach, had the creatinine level risen by 30% or more. Given the rise is below the guidance level for concern, there is no indication to discontinue ramipril. E Withdraw Ramipril completely Withdrawal is only indicated for a signiﬁcant rise in creatinine level that can be linked to the ramipril prescription. This patient could derive signiﬁcant potential outcome beneﬁt from an ACEI. Therapy should therefore be continued.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department because she has felt increasingly tired over the past three to four weeks, and now is virtually unable to leave the house due to tiredness, has signiﬁcant nausea and has been unable to eat for the past 48 hours. She has Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, for which she takes 100 mcg of thyroxine daily, and type 1 diabetes, for which she takes a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/70 mmHg, with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Her pulse is 90 bpm and regular. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 179 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 127 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 8.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l HbA1c mmol/mol (7.2%) 20–42 mmol/l (4– 6%) TSH 1.2 u/l 0.17–3.2 u/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 2 (APS ll) APS II is the most common form of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome and presents most commonly in the third or fourth decade. It consists of Addison’s disease plus either an autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus, and may be associated with a number of other autoimmune phenomena such as gonadal failure or coeliac disease. The clinical picture seen here is consistent with a diagnosis of Addison’s disease. C Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 3 (APS lll) APS III is not associated with adrenal insufﬁciency. The backbone of APS III is autoimmune thyroiditis, in conjunction with diabetes mellitus, pernicious anaemia or vitiligo. A Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome Type 1 (APS I) The three major components of APS I are: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and autoimmune adrenal insufﬁciency. D Pituitary failure This patient’s symptoms are consistent with autoimmunemediated glandular failure, rather than secondary failure due to pituitary disease, as exempliﬁed by Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. E Renal tubular acidosis Type IV Renal tubular acidosis is characterised by deﬁcient aldosterone action. It would ﬁt with the urea and electrolytes picture observed, but it would be inconsistent with the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and Hashimoto’s disease seen here.

stem: A keen junior doctor studying for his MRCP examination shows the medical registrar an electrocardiogram (ECG) recorded on a 36-year-old woman in the Medical Clinic in the morning. Examination of the patient reveals a normal body habitus with a body mass index (BMI) of 23 kg/m2, but she is hypertensive with a blood pressure of 165/95 mmHg. She takes no medications and apparently complains of lethargy and muscle aches most of the time. The patient had been referred urgently by the general practitioner for investigation for a metabolic abnormality. The ECG is shown below. Based on the ECG, what is the most likely underlying metabolic abnormality?
explanation:
B Hypokalaemia This ECG demonstrates the classical picture of a prominent U wave – a small deﬂection immediately following the T wave, usually seen in V2 and V3. A U wave on the ECG is thought to correspond with after-depolarisation events in the ventricles. A normal U wave is of the same polarity as the T wave, but one-third of the amplitude. The differential diagnosis of prominent upright U waves includes hypokalaemia, left ventricular hypertrophy, some cases of mitral valve prolapse, hyperthyroidism, and quinidine and other type 1A antiarrhythmics. Conn syndrome is characterised by increased aldosterone secretion (primary hyperaldosteronism) from the adrenal gland from a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma. Metabolically, this manifests as suppression of plasma renin activity, hypertension and hypokalaemia. Bartter syndrome is a cause of congenital salt wasting, which presents in childhood with failure to thrive, polyuria and polydipsia. C Hypercalcaemia

The main abnormality associated with hypercalcaemia is shortening of the QT interval. When the calcium level is very high, J waves may also be seen. A Hyperkalaemia Hyperkalaemia is associated with peaked T waves and later, as the potassium level rises further, with bizarre broadened QRS complexes. D Hypocalcaemia Hypocalcaemia leads to QT prolongation, although arrhythmias are surprisingly rarely reported in association with low calcium levels. E Hypomagnesaemia Like hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia is associated with QT prolongation. The risk of rhythm disturbance is thought to be higher than for hypocalcaemia.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with bilateral gynaecomastia. He apparently had surgery as a child to correct bilateral undescended testes. On examination, he is tall, with increased arm and leg length. He does have evidence of bilateral gynaecomastia, with small testes bilaterally. Apparently there have been problems with anxiety and bullying at 6th form and he has now left to begin a job. Which of the following would be the most appropriate investigation?
explanation: C FSH, LH The suspicion here, based on history and physical appearance, is a diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome. Both FSH and LH are raised in Klinefelter syndrome, and elevation would be a strong pointer to conﬁrming the underlying diagnosis. Chromosomal analysis would be an obvious further step. Management centres on androgen replacement, cosmetic procedures and access to psychosexual counselling. D Progesterone Progesterone levels are not useful in the evaluation of Kline- felter syndrome. A Oestrogen Although oestrogen levels are elevated in patients with Klinefelter, they are less useful vs raised gonadotrophins in conﬁrming the diagnosis.
