B GNRH GNRH levels are reduced in Kallmann syndrome; this syndrome is associated with absence of sense of smell, which isn’t reported as part of the scenario here. E Testosterone Although testosterone is reduced in patients with Klinefelter syndrome, measuring this wouldn’t indicate whether the defect was at the level of the pituitary or the testes and hence FSH and LH measurement is more useful.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a past history of atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) and periods of paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia (PVT) on a 24 hour tape is referred to the Outpatient Clinic with weight loss and tremor. He is clinically hyperthyroid. He takes warfarin and amiodarone. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value T4 100 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l TSH < 0.01 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l
options: Start prednisolone 30 mg OD and carbimazole 40 mg OD
explanation:
C Start carbimazole 40 mg OD This is an example of type 1 amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism (AIT). The high iodine content of the amiodarone induces release of thyroid hormone (Jod–Basedow effect) and causes hyperthyroidism. In type 2 AIT the amiodarone causes a destructive thyroiditis. Colour ﬂow Doppler ultrasound can be used to differentiate the two: blood ﬂow is increased in type

1 and decreased in type 2. High-dose anti-thyroid drugs are needed to treat type 1 AIT as they have less effect due to the high iodine load. D Arrange a thyroidectomy Thyroidectomy is rarely recommended as ﬁrst-line treatment for thyrotoxicosis. Thyroidectomy in a thyrotoxic patient may precipitate thyroid storm. A Stop amiodarone Amiodarone should be discontinued if possible, but in this case, given the VT, this decision should be considered carefully in conjunction with a cardiologist. Withdrawal of amiodarone alone will have no immediate effect due to the long halflife of amiodarone. B Start prednisolone 30 mg OD and carbimazole 40 mg OD Steroids in combination with anti-thyroid drugs help to treat type 2 AIT. However, these have no role in type 1 AIT. E Arrange radioiodine therapy Radioiodine is not usually effective because of reduced uptake by the thyroid due to high iodine levels.

stem: A 42-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of a three week history of a sore throat associated with lethargy, a reduced appetite and general viral symptoms. She has also felt frequent palpitations recently and increased sweating but these appear to be settling, with the patient now complaining of occasional palpitations. Other symptoms include pain in the lower part of her neck made worse with swallowing and an occasional hoarseness of her voice. She is otherwise ﬁt and well, is not on any medications and is a non-smoker. There is no signiﬁcant family history. The only positive ﬁndings on examination were residual tenderness over her lower anterior neck to palpation and mild tachycardia associated with warm skin to touch. No lymphadenopathy was palpable. Thyroid function tests (TFT) show a T4 level slightly above normal and a TSH level of < 0.1 mU/l. The GP diagnoses a viral illness and then commenced carbimazole 20 mg twice a day on the basis of her TFT results. Two months later, the patient again attended her GP but this time complaining of increased lethargy, weight gain and a minor discomfort in the lower part of her neck. What would be the next most appropriate management step?
options: Adjust the dose of carbimazole to control the patient’s symptoms
Stop carbimazole and consider replacement thyroid hormone therapy if symptoms don’t recover
Refer the patient for an ultrasound scan of the thyroid gland
Refer patient for a ﬁne needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid gland
explanation:
B Stop carbimazole and consider replacement thyroid hormone therapy if symptoms don’t recover De Quervain thyroiditis is the most common cause of a painful thyroid gland and causes hyperthyroidism initially, sometimes followed by transient hypothyroidism. The underlying cause is felt to be either a viral infection or the post-viral inﬂammatory response. The condition is more common in females. The typical course of the disease consists of an acute phase, in which the main complaint is pain, although signs of hyperthyroidism may also be present. This is followed by a transient asymptomatic and euthyroid phase, which evolves into the hypothyroid phase. The hypothyroid state may become permanent in 5–10% of patients, but the vast majority go on to the recovery phase, characterised by normalisation of thyroid structure and function. The treatment is consequently directed towards the control of pain and thyroid symptoms. Initial symptomatic hyperthyroidism can be treated with betablockade. Beta-adrenergic blockers are usually the sole form of treatment indicated/required in cases of thyroiditis, although severe, persistent symptoms/signs in may require additional therapy with salicylates and/or glucocorticoids. If hypothyroidism occurs in the late stages, replacement therapy is required and is guided by the TSH levels. D Refer patient for a ﬁne needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid gland Fine needle aspiration should always be performed on solitary nodules >10 mm, those <10 mm with suspicious imaging characteristics or on dominant nodules. A Adjust the dose of carbimazole to control the patient’s symptoms The patient’s symptoms are caused by the hypothyroid phase of De Quervain’s thyroiditis, rather than the carbimazole. C Refer the patient for an ultrasound scan of the thyroid gland Ultrasound scanning should be performed in patients presenting with a single palpable nodule. E Change carbimazole to proplythiouracil The patient’s symptoms are not due to carbimazole. Propylthiouracil and carbimazole are both associated with agranulocytosis and must be stopped if this complication is suspected, and

only restarted if a blood count has conﬁrmed that the white cell count is in fact normal.

stem: A 27-year-old woman who is 22 weeks’ pregnant with her second child comes to the clinic complaining of anxiety and palpitations. She is concerned as she is ﬁnding it difﬁcult to maintain an adequate weight. On examination, she has a BP of 135/70 mmHg and a resting pulse of 88/min. You palpate a nodule on the left- hand side of her thyroid. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 114 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 172 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l TSH < 0.05 < 0.5–4.5 Free T4 31 pmol/l 10–22 pmol/l Ultrasound Solitary left-sided thyroid nodule FNA reveals an adenoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for her?
explanation: D Anti-thyroid medication In this scenario, options are limited to manage her thyrotoxicosis. Anti-thyroid drugs would form the mainstay of intervention until after delivery. Both propylthiouracil and carbimazole are options, although the former is not recommended in late pregnancy because of the risk of maternal liver dysfunction. A Subtotal thyroidectomy This is the option for patients who are unable to tolerate antithyroid medication. B Propanolol Propanolol offers symptomatic relief only, and will not reduce the risk of fetal loss due to thyrotoxicosis. C Radioiodine Radioiodine is contraindicated during pregnancy, and is likely to be unsuitable for this patient for a considerable period of time because of the need to avoid exposure to young children. E Lugol’s iodine Lugol’s iodine is used to acutely control thyrotoxicosis when urgent surgery is considered.

stem: A 72-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with severe dehydration and weight loss. She reports that she has had steatorrhoea for several months and her relatives report that the weight loss has occurred over the same time period. Over the course of her admission, she is found to have a metastatic somatostatinoma. Which of these complications is she most likely to have due to the somatostatinoma?
explanation:
C Diabetes mellitus Glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus occurs in around 95% of patients with somatostatinoma and is often the ﬁrst symptom to develop. The classic triad includes diabetes mellitus, diarrhoea and gallstones. Patients commonly also experience weight loss and hypochlorhydria. D Polycythaemia Patients with somatostatinoma are likely to be anaemic, rather than polycythaemic, which may be due to malabsorption owing to the diarrhoea. A Hyperchlorhydria Patients with somatostatinoma often experience hypochlorhydria, not hyperchlorhydria, a state of reduced gastric secretions, since somatostatin inhibits the secretion of gastrin in the stomach which results in reduced chloride levels. B Hypoglycaemia The most common ﬁnding of a patient with a somatostatinoma is glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus. This would cause hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia. E Renal stones

Patients with somatostatinoma commonly experience gallstones rather than bladder stones. This occurs because somatostatin inhibits cholecystokinin release in the gallbladder which therefore reduces biliary motility and predisposes to stone formation.

stem: A 38-year-old physiotherapist attended for a routine follow-up in the Diabetes Clinic. She was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus at the age of 11 and unfortunately had a history of both diabetic maculopathy and early diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria. She complained of a 6-week history of raised, tender plaques over the shins (shown below) and, on further questioning, described painful wrists and ankles for the past 6 months. Examination conﬁrmed the presence of the plaques, over which there was clear skin thinning and telangiectasia. Her blood pressure is 147/84 mmHg. A urine dipstick revealed protein +1 and glucose +1. What is the most useful next investigation for her painful joints?
explanation: B Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody testing The patient's plaques are probably unconnected to the wrist and ankle pain but are due to necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. The condition is more common in women and presents in young adults or in early middle life. These erythematous plaques are due to small vessel damage causing partial necrosis of the dermal collagen and connective tissue, with a resulting histiocytic cellular response. The lesions are usually managed with support bandaging and use of topical steroids. The wrist and ankle pain is suggestive of possible arthritis. Both rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes may be associated with the human leukocyte antigen HLADR4. Anti-CCP is speciﬁc for rheumatoid arthritis, the most probable diagnosis here, and may be positive in advance of any joint destruction. It also stratiﬁes those with rapid disease progression. It is therefore the most useful next step. C Serum complement measurement Necrobiosis lipoidica is not associated with generalised complement activation, and so this parameter is likely to be normal. A Anti-nuclear antibody testing Anti-nuclear antibody testing is useful when systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is considered as the underlying diagnosis, although given that joint pains are limited to the wrists and ankles and there is an absence of a photosensitive rash, this is less likely vs a new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. D Ankle and wrist X-ray Although ankle and wrist X-rays are useful in deﬁning rheumatoid arthritis, the absence of changes should not delay treatment. Hence, CCP testing is potentially more useful at this stage of the disease. E Immunoglobulin E (IgE) measurement Necrobiosis lipoidica is associated with neither Churg– Strauss vasculitis nor generalised hypersensitivity, and thus IgE measurement has little utility here.

stem: A 54-year-old alcoholic is admitted to the Emergency Department complaining of numbness and weakness affecting his hands and twitching affecting his face and jaw. He drinks one bottle of whisky per day and has been suffering from severe diarrhoea for the past 48 hours. On examination, his blood pressure is 105/70 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. He is clearly malnourished, has multiple spider naevi over his upper chest and back and his abdomen isdisplayed below. While you examine him, he is complaining of numbness and tingling affecting his hands, feet and around his mouth. Serum calcium level is measured at 1.98 mmol/l. You institute calcium replacement; however, 60 minutes later, his calcium has not recovered completely and reads at 2.05 mmol/l. He still has signiﬁcant symptoms of hypocalcaemia. Which of the following next interventions is likely to be most effective?
explanation: A Give magnesium replacement The patient has ascites and multiple spider naevi, which, in the context of alcohol abuse may indicated chronic liver failure. Such patients are often malnourished, resulting in electrolyte loss. This is particularly the case when patients have severe diarrhoea. Hypocalcaemia will often be resistant even to intravenous supplementation when there is concurrent hypomagnesaemia; therefore, magnesium replacement is the correct answer. B Give furosemide Furosemide is hypercalciuric; it directly increases renal calcium excretion in both the acute treatment and long- term usage. Therefore, this would be an inappropriate drug choice. C Give a thiazide diuretic Although thiazide diuretics have metabolic effects contributing to increased calcium uptake as a result of sodiumchloride transport inhibition, these effects will not be enough to adequately increase the calcium levels. Therefore, this is not an appropriate treatment option. D Give recombinant PTH Recombinant PTH is a theoretical option requiring several days to take effect. Given this patient is symptomatic, it is not an appropriate treatment option. E Repeat intravenous (IV) calcium replacement Although this patient may require further calcium replacement, because of the resistance associated with hypomagnesaemia, further calcium replacement without magnesium electrolyte correction would not be appropriate.

stem: A 24-year-old man with a history of previous injury in a motorcycle accident comes to the clinic with his mother. She looks after him as he has been left with a right arm and leg weakness after a skull fracture and intracranial haemorrhage. He also has epilepsy for which he takes carbamazepine. They complain that he is thirsty all the time and can’t stop drinking litres of water and squash each day. His mother herself has signiﬁcant chronic illness, suffering from chronic left ventricular failure. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 134 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 149 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 143 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bicarbonate 22 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Plasma osmolality 350 mosmol/kg 280–295 mosmol/kg Urine osmolality 270 after water deprivation, rises to 810 after DDAVP Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Cranial diabetes insipidus here

It is highly likely that this man’s head injury has led to cranial diabetes insipidus. Whilst it is possible given the clinical history that he may have psychogenic polydipsia, the osmolality results only ﬁt with cranial DI as the diagnosis. Treatment is with intranasal vasopressin; given the possibility of overdose and consequent hyponatraemia, monitoring of U&E is recommended. Carbamazepine may exacerbate hyponatraemia with vasopressin therapy, and therefore close monitoring of U&E and symptom response versus vasopressin dose is even more essential in this case. B SIADH SIADH is associated with relative salt and water overload, accompanied by hyponatraemia rather than the elevated sodium seen here. A Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Nephrogenic DI would not show a positive response to DDAVP and is therefore excluded here. D Psychogenic polydipsia This is the alternative diagnosis, although the history of head injury and strong response to DDAVP makes cranial diabetes insipidus much more likely. E Diuretic abuse Diuretic abuse may be associated with symptoms of dehydration, but elevated bicarbonate would be expected

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with lethargy on a background of depression and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She takes metformin and gliclazide. Her blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg and she is clinically euvolaemic. Routine biochemical investigations reveal: Investigation Result Normal value Na+ 120 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 3.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 5.6 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 76 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Thyroid function test Normal Which biochemical test would be most useful in determining her state of water balance?
explanation: E Serum and urine osmolality Urine osmolality relative to serum osmolality gives an accurate assessment of the state of the ADH axis. In the absence of other causes (eg CCF), a high urine osmolality relative to serum osmolality in the setting of hyponatraemia is inappropriate. Other tests, such as plasma ADH and detailed urine electrolyte studies, can give similar information, but at much greater expense and difﬁculty. Sulphonylureas are recognised as a rare cause of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH); the condition is seen most commonly with chlorpropamide and, while this has been replaced by more modern agents such as gliclazide, it is still occasionally seen. C Fractional excretion of Na+ The fractional excretion of sodium is the percentage of the sodium ﬁltered by the kidney which is excreted in the urine. It is measured in terms of plasma and urine sodium, rather than by the interpretation of urinary sodium concentration alone, as urinary sodium concentrations can vary with water reabsorption. Therefore, the urinary and plasma concentrations of sodium must be compared to get an accurate picture of renal clearance. In clinical use, the fractional excretion of sodium can be calculated as part of the evaluation of acute kidney failure in order to determine if hypovolaemia or decreased effective circulating plasma volume is a contributor to the kidney failure. A 24-hour urinary protein and creatinine This investigation is for measurement of total protein, it would be useful to diagnose nephrotic conditions. However this investigation would not give any indication of volume status. B Erect/supine renin and aldosterone estimation The aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) (ie the ratio of plasma aldosterone to plasma renin activity) is the most sensitive means of differentiating primary from secondary causes of hyperaldosteronism. It is not useful for volume status assessment. D Plasma ADH Plasma ADH would be high in dehydration because it controls the amount of water that is excreted in the urine. ADH levels may be raised and low in certain pathological states such as SIADH or diabetes insipidus therefore it is not the best method to assess ﬂuid status.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department, having been found on the ﬂoor by her carer. She is mor- bidly obese and is prescribed long-term therapy for manic depressive psychosis and hypertension. She arrives with a medication bag containing risperidone, bendroﬂumethiazide and bisoprolol tablets. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 100/75 mmHg and a pulse of 95 bpm and regular. Her temperature is 38.1 °C. There are signs of right-sided consolidation on auscultation of the chest. The abdomen appears soft, and bowel sounds are present. She is drowsy and responds to questions by mumbling incoherently. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 10.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 189 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 146 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 161 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 17.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 32.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l Bicarbonate 25 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/l pH 7.35 7.35–7.45 Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for ﬂuid replacement?
explanation: B 0.9% saline The joint British Societies guidelines on the management of hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic non-ketotic state (HHS) recommend 0.9% saline as the ﬂuid replacement of choice. Assuming insulin replacement is commenced at the same time as saline replacement, there is no reason to expect that use of 0.9% saline will signiﬁcantly increase serum sodium levels. C 1.8% saline Concentrated saline is only indicated where there is lifethreatening hyponatraemia, where it should be given in a High Dependency Unit setting to allow for close monitoring of any increase in the serum sodium level, to prevent it from rising too quickly. A 0.45% saline 0.45% or half normal saline should only be used where osmolality is not declining despite achieving euvolaemia with 0.9% saline replacement. D 5% dextrose Hypotonic ﬂuid replacement with 5% dextrose should only be considered, like 0.45% saline, when osmolality is not correcting despite adequate 0.9% saline replacement. E Hartmann’s solution Studies suggest that Hartmann’s solution (compound sodium lactate) offers no advantage in the treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); the guidelines therefore do not recommend its use in HHS.

stem: A 38-year-old man attends the Endocrinology Clinic with long-standing type I diabetes mellitus. Unfortunately, he has developed nephropathy, with a recent creatinine (Cr) level measured at 180 µmol/l, and microalbuminuria. Last year he received laser treatment to his left eye for severe retinopathy. He is currently treated with a Novomix 30 at a dose of 12 units twice a day. A recent HbA1c was measured at 59.56 (7.6%). You review his home glucose record and ﬁnd that two hour postprandial glucose is high, at 12 mmol/l, yet he appears to be suffering attacks of hypoglycaemia late in the afternoon before his evening meal, and occasionally before breakfast. His body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m2. Which of the following represents the best advice with respect to his treatment irrespective of patient preference?
options: Reduce his portion size in an attempt to take in fewer calories
Alter his insulin to a basal bolus regime involving glargine and aspart
Increase his BD insulin to 14 units
Increase the proportion of short-acting insulin in his mixed insulin dose and increase the dose to 14 units
Advise him to snack more in the middle of the afternoon and prior to going to bed
explanation:
B Alter his insulin to a basal bolus regime involving glargine and aspart This man has documented microvascular disease with proven retinopathy and nephropathy. In this population, optimal glycaemic control would be indicated by an HbA1c of 47.54 mmol/mol (<6.5%) if possible. Aspart, as a short-acting insulin, and glargine as an insulin analogue are associated with less hypoglycaemia, would be the most appropriate choice for

him. D Increase the proportion of short-acting insulin in his mixed insulin dose and increase the dose to 14 units This may improve his postprandial blood glucose levels but may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. A Reduce his portion size in an attempt to take in fewer calories Reducing his portion size may impact on his postprandial blood glucose levels but will increase the risk of late hypoglycaemia. C Increase his BD insulin to 14 units Increasing his BD insulin would only exacerbate the problem of late between-dose hypoglycaemia. E Advise him to snack more in the middle of the afternoon and prior to going to bed Snacking, but remaining on BD insulin, would only serve to increase his total energy intake and may worsen his glycaemic control.

stem: A 42-year-old man visits his General Practitioner (GP) complaining of a history of watery diarrhoea over the past three months and intermittent facial ﬂushing. He does not have any past medical history, has not been abroad in the last six months, and does not take any medications. He appears very dehydrated and is referred to the Acute Medical Unit (AMU) in the local hospital. On admission to hospital, he has blood tests which reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Arterial pH 7.32 7.35 - 7.45 Arterial pCO2 4.3 kPa 4.7 - 6.0 kPa Arterial pO2 14.2 kPa > 10.5 kPa Arterial HCO3 18.1 mmol/l 22.0 - 26.0 mmol/l Investigation Result Normal value Na+ 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 93 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 2.74 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Magnesium (Mg2+) 0.45 mmol/l 0.6 - 1.1 mmol/l In addition, a stool culture returns negative for bacterial and fungal infections. A computed tomography (CT) scan ﬁnds a lesion on his pancreas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E VIPoma VIPoma is a rare neuroendocrine tumour which hypersecretes vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) causing watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia and acidosis. The tumours are found on the pancreas, and more than half are malignant. Other features of VIPoma include facial ﬂushing, and therefore, this diagnosis explains all the clinical ﬁndings for this patient. A Bacterial infection A bacterial infection is unlikely given the absence of fever and the negative stool culture. A bacterial infection could cause dehydration and explain the biochemical results, but it would not explain the facial ﬂushing or the pancreatic mass. B Insulinoma An insulinoma would explain the ﬁnding of a pancreatic mass, but it would typically cause episodes of hypoglycaemia or the diarrhoea and ﬂushing that this patient is experiencing. C Laxative abuse Laxative abuse could cause the diarrhoea and the biochemical abnormalities but would not explain the pancreatic mass or the ﬂushing. There is also no indication from the patient’s history to suggest an abuse problem. D Pancreatitis Pancreatitis could explain the biochemical derangement seen here, but this is usually due to vomiting rather than diarrhoea. Pancreatitis causes inﬂammation of the pancreas but does not tend to cause a pancreatic mass or ﬂushing.

stem: A 56-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is admitted for an arthroscopy of the right knee. His admission to the Emergency Department reveals potassium of 5.9 mmol/l, creatinine of 450 μmol/l and urea of 28 mmol/l. Which of the following stems represents the best plan with respect to his surgery?
options: He should be commenced on calcium resonium and surgery can proceed
He should be given nebulised salbutamol and surgery be postponed by 6 h
He is safe to continue with surgery
He should be given insulin and dextrose and surgery may proceed
Surgery should be delayed until his potassium is below 5.5 mmol/l
explanation: E Surgery should be delayed until his potassium is below 5.5 mmol/l Guidelines for surgery in patients with chronic kidney disease suggest that surgery should be postponed until serum potassium is <5.5 mmol/l. In addition, in patients undergoing surgery potassium should be monitored immediately after and then again 4–6 h later. Where surgery is likely to involve signiﬁcant circulatory compromise and acute or chronic kid- ney disease may be precipitated, such as in coronary artery bypass surgery, patients should ideally be stabilised on dialysis ﬁrst. A He should be commenced on calcium resonium and surgery can proceed Calcium resonium would not work quickly – it takes at least 48 h to signﬁcantly lower the potassium. B He should be given nebulised salbutamol and surgery be postponed by 6 h Nebulised salbutamol is only an interim measure to lower potassium as it moves potassium into the cells. However, because it is likely to leak from the cells hours later it is not a deﬁnitive treatment. C He is safe to continue with surgery Hyperkalaemia can precipitate arrhythmias when patients are given anaesthesia during surgery. Therefore it must be treated pre-surgery. D He should be given insulin and dextrose and surgery may proceed Insulin and dextrose is only a ‘holding’ measure and does not remove potassium from the body, and therefore the patient may become hyperkalaemic later. Dialysis should thus be given ﬁrst prior to surgery.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. She recently suffered a fall whilst at a nightclub and was knocked out for a few minutes. Since then, over the past few weeks, she has suffered polyuria and polydipsia. She has no past medical history of note, and her only medication is the oral contraceptive pill. On examination, her BP is 122/72 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. She has a postural drop of 15 mmHg on standing. Her BMI is 21. Neurological assessment is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 131 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 191 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 146 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 9.1 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Glucose 5.4 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.21 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: B Urine and plasma osmolality The diagnosis to exclude is diabetes insipidus (DI) due to the head injury, and urine and plasma osmolality is an appropriate non-invasive ﬁrst step in excluding DI. Inappropriately low urine osmolality in the presence of a raised plasma osmolality is suggestive of the diagnosis, and a water deprivation test would be the obvious next step after this. A Computerised tomography (CT) head In the absence of focal neurology, a CT head isn’t indicated before further biochemistry is obtained. C Thyroid function The lack of signs of hypo- or hyperthyroidism implies that thyroid function testing is most likely to be normal. D Urinary sodium Urinary sodium is more useful in the assessment of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) and of acute tubular necrosis. E Water deprivation test A water deprivation test is the default next investigation after a spot urine and plasma osmolality.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She has a history of hypertension which is resistant to dual therapy with 20 mg of lisinopril and 10 mg of amlodipine. Other past medical history of note includes asthma for which she takes a Chinese herbal remedy and a ﬂuticasone/salmeterol inhaler. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 162/95 mmHg and a pulse of 78 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal. The chest is clear, and there are no signs of peripheral oedema. Abdominal examination reveals no palpable masses. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 3.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate 34 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Aldosterone 60 pmol/l (sample taken standing up) 55–250 pmol/l Renin 5.4 mU/l (sample taken standing up) 5.4–60 mU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Liquorice poisoning As well as being used in a range of sweets and as a tobacco additive, liquorice is also used as a cough suppressant as a component of Chinese herbal medicines. In this patient, exposure to liquorice is therefore likely to have come via her traditional asthma medicine. Liquorice poisoning results in low renin and aldosterone, hypertension and hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis because glycyrrhizic acid has mineralocorticoid activity. The treatment of choice in this case is removal of the herbal medication; this is likely to result in gradual resolution of her hypertension. B Conn syndrome Conn syndrome is associated with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypertension and hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism, which does not ﬁt with the clinical picture seen here. A Bartter syndrome Bartter syndrome is associated with normal blood pressure, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. Both renin and aldosterone are elevated in patients suffering from Bartter syndrome. C Gitelman syndrome Gitelman syndrome is associated with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis and normal blood pressure or hypotension. It is also associated with magnesium wasting and borderline low calcium levels. E Renal artery stenosis Renal artery stenosis is associated with hypokalaemia, hypertension and elevated renin and aldosterone, which does not ﬁt with the clinical picture reported here.

stem: A 21-year-old student nurse is admitted to the Emergency Medical Unit having suffered a collapse while on attachment in the Acute Medical Unit. This is the third episode to occur over the past six months. Her past medical history includes mild eczema and infrequent menstruation, which is under investigation. Her grandfather and uncle are noted to have type II diabetes mellitus. On examination, her BP is 110/70 mmHg; her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. Her oxygen saturations are 96% on air. Her cardiorespiratory, abdominal and neurological examinations are normal. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l CRP 12 mg/l 0–10 mg/l ALT 42 IU/l 5–30 IU/l ESR 8 mm/1sth 0–10 mm/1sth Albumin 31 g/l 35–55 g/l Bilirubin 17 µmol/l 2–17 µmol/l
explanation: E Sulphonylurea abuse Sulfonylurea abuse relies on access and intent. Given that this nurse’s grandfather has type II diabetes mellitus, she is very likely to have access to sulfonylurea. The elevated C-peptide level in the presence of hypoglycaemia suggests a process which has stimulated endogenous insulin production. This may be a personality disorder or an example of acute psychological stress and an attempt to seek help. C Insulin abuse Insulin abuse presents with hypoglycaemia and a suppressed C-peptide level. C-peptide is a by-product of insulin production. In insulin overdose, the body stops making endogenous insulin and levels are decreased. This patient has a high C- peptide level and it is, therefore, unlikely that insulin abuse is the cause. A Addisonian crisis Although Addison’s disease can cause hypoglycaemia, there is nothing in the clinical history to suggest it as a possible diagnosis, with only mildly abnormal blood pressures and no electrolyte abnormalities. Therefore, it would be unlikely to have caused the collapse. B Hypopituitarism Although this patient has a history of irregular menstruation, which could suggest hypopituitarism, the ﬁndings of hypoglycaemia and an elevated C-peptide level do not support this diagnosis. Rather, it is more likely that starvation and the physiological stress from sulfonylurea abuse (that would cause hypoglycaemia and an elevated C-peptide level) are contributing to her oligomenorrhoea. D Insulinoma Insulinoma is a possible cause. However, it is signiﬁcantly rarer as a cause of hypoglycaemia in comparison to sulfonylurea abuse. Given the patient likely has access to sulfonylureas (note the family history of type II diabetes mellitus), as well as the elevated C-peptide level in the presence of hypoglycaemia, this would tend to suggest sulfonylurea abuse rather than insulinoma.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is admitted to the Admissions Unit. She has a long history of type II diabetes. On examination, her foot is warm and swollen, and she has been suffering vague bony pains in it over the past few months. There is no history of trauma and no obvious skin break. Fundoscopy reveals diabetic retinopathy, and examination of her lower limbs reveals absent sensation to vibration and pinprick to the knees. Her blood pressure (BP) is 155/95 mmHg. A HbA1c level is recorded as 65 mmol/mol.
explanation: C Below-knee cast This subacute presentation, with joint swelling and chronic joint pains against a background of long-standing and poorly controlled diabetes, suggests possible Charcot’s, in this case of the talo-navicular joint. Non-weight bearing in a cast is the intervention of choice. Bisphosphonates may also be of value in reducing bone turnover. A IV ﬂucloxacillin and metronidazole The subacute history is more consistent with Charcot’s, especially as there is no obvious potential site of infection. B Lower limb venous ultrasound scan The localised swelling around the ankle joint is more consistent with bony deformity than a venous thrombosis. D Oral clindamycin Clindamycin is optimal oral therapy for osteomyelitis, although it is associated with high risk of development of pseudomembranous colitis. E Class 3 compression stockings Compression stockings are used in the treatment of chronic venous insufﬁciency. The picture reveals no evidence of venous ulceration to suggest they are of value here.

stem: A 51-year-old man presents to the Ophthalmology Clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly deteriorating vision. He has not had previous eye concerns and does not regularly wear glasses. His eyes are not painful but his vision is constantly blurred. He has not seen his General Practitioner for the past 12 years but reports that he has a past medical history of hypertension for which he takes amlodipine 10 mg once daily, and he has no known allergies. His BMI is 35 kg/m2. His eyes are examined and shown below: What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
C Pan-retinal photocoagulation

This patient’s fundoscopy shows multiple ﬂame haemorrhages and neovascularisation with associated pre- retinal haemorrhages. This is in keeping with a diagnosis of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, a retinal consequence of chronic and under-controlled diabetes mellitus. Although there is not a known diagnosis of diabetes mellitus, the raised BMI puts this patient at higher risk for having the condition. The most important treatment of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, particularly in advanced disease, is with pan-retinal photocoagulation. This is because proliferative disease puts the patient at risk of vitreous haemorrhage. A Antivascular endothelial growth factor Antivascular endothelial growth factor plays an important role in the management of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. However, in severe diseases with multiple pre-retinal haemorrhages and neovascularisation, the treatment of choice is with pan-retinal laser photocoagulation. B Escalate antihypertensive treatment Hypertensive retinopathy is a reasonable differential diagnosis to consider, given the history of hypertension and onset of blurred vision. However, the ocular ﬁndings in hypertensive retinopathy include arteriolar narrowing and, in severe cases, cotton-wool spots and retinal haemorrhages. However, proliferative disease is not a feature of hypertensive retinopathy and suggests an alternative diagnosis. D Topical corticosteroids Topical timolol is a beta-blocker used in the management of acute angle-closure glaucoma. It works by reducing aqueous humour production and, therefore, intraocular pressure. Fundoscopy ﬁndings of acute angle- closure glaucoma include an increased cup-to-disc ratio. However, proliferative retinopathy is not a feature and suggests alternative pathology. E Topical timolol Topical corticosteroids are used in the management of inﬂammatory ocular conditions (eg anterior uveitis associated with inﬂammatory bowel disease). However, it is not used in the management of proliferative diabetic retinopathy and should be avoided in this case.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with feelings of anxiety. She has lost weight over the past few months and describes palpitations. She has visited her General Practitioner (GP) three times over the past six months and been prescribed a selective serotonin uptake inhibitor (SSRI), although her condition continues to worsen. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 122/70 mmHg. Her pulse is 88 beats per minute (bpm) and regular, and she has a ﬁne tremor. The GP conducted some thyroid function tests, which reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value TSH 0.05 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Free T4 20.1 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l Free T3 12.5 pmol/l 3.5–5 pmol/l What is the best treatment for this woman's underlying condition?
explanation:
D Carbimazole This woman has T3 thyrotoxicosis. Isolated elevation in T3 accompanied by a T4 in the normal range is associated with around 5% of cases of thyrotoxicosis. Thyrotoxicosis is 10 times more common in women than men in the UK. Prevalence is approximately 2% of the female population, with an annual incidence of 3 per 1000 women. Graves’ disease is the commonest cause of thyrotoxicosis; other causes include toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma. Assessment of thyrotoxicosis includes thyroid function tests, thyroid autoantibodies and radionucleotide thyroid scanning, where the diagnosis is uncertain. Carbimazole is the mainstay of initial management of thy-

rotoxicosis, with propylthiouracil an alternative in patients who fail to tolerate carbimazole or for whom it is unsuitable. C Paroxetine Therapy for depression may be required, but her mood should be reassessed once thyroid equilibrium is established. A Reassurance Reassurance alone is inappropriate here, since with suppressed TSH, T4 at the upper limit of normal and elevated T3, this patient has conﬁrmed thyrotoxicosis. B Propranolol Although propranolol may be useful for relief of symptoms in the early stages of thyrotoxicosis, use as monotherapy is not appropriate in this situation. E Thyroxine Thyroxine is not indicated, given that TSH is suppressed, T4 is at the upper end of the normal range and T3 is elevated.

stem: A 29-year-old woman who is 30 weeks’ pregnant comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She has found it increasingly difﬁcult to maintain her weight during the past few weeks, and has been suffering from palpitations and anxiety. She has no past medical history of note. Examination reveals a BP of 122/72 mmHg, with pulse 88/min and regular. She has a ﬁne resting tremor and a smooth, nontender goitre. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 119 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 181 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 84 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 4.8 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l TSH < 0.05 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Free T4 20 pmol/l 6.5 - 13.0 pmol/l Anti-thyroid antibody + Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: A Carbimazole This patient has thyrotoxicosis, potentially due to underlying Graves’ disease. The recommended treatment approach is to give enough anti-thyroid drug therapy to maintain thyroid hormone levels in the upper third of the normal range. Carbimazole is the recommended option in late pregnancy because of reports of hepatotoxicity associated with propylthiouracil. C Radioiodine Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy because administration would lead to uptake in the fetal thyroid. B Carbimazole and thyroxine (block-replace) Thyroxine does not cross the placenta to any appreciable degree, and therefore block-replace is not recommended in pregnancy. D Propylthiouracil Propylthiouracil may be used in early pregnancy, but in late pregnancy it is not recommended because of risk of hepatotoxicity. E Propylthiouracil and thyroxine (block-replace) Block-replace is not indicated because of thyroxine not crossing the placental barrier.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant is referred by her General Practitioner to the Endocrine Clinic. Over the past week, she has developed symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection and has pain over the thyroid, more marked on the right-hand side than on the left. She has also been feeling rather anxious with palpitations. There is no signiﬁcant past medical history of note and no family history of autoimmune disease. On examination, her BP is 105/70 mmHg; her heart rate is 89 bpm and regular. She has a ﬁne tremor at rest. There is generalised tenderness on palpation of the thyroid, more marked on the right. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelets 191 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 82 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l TSH < 0.1 U/l 0.4–5.0 U/l Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation: B Ibuprofen This patient has subacute thyroiditis, for which analgesia with a non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drug (NSAID), such as ibuprofen, is an appropriate initial intervention. Typical symptoms are present, including symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection, pain over the thyroid gland and features consistent with thyrotoxicosis. Symptoms of hyperthyroidism are transient and related to increased thyroxine release rather than to overproduction. Ibuprofen should not be used in the ﬁrst trimester (risk of miscarriage) or third trimester of pregnancy (risk of closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus in utero and possibly persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn). Maternal use of NSAIDs should be avoided until the beginning of 20 weeks’ gestation. If NSAID use is necessary between 20 and 30 weeks’ gestation, use should be limited to the lowest effective dose and the shortest duration possible; ultrasound monitoring of amniotic ﬂuid should be considered if treatment extends beyond 48 hours and the NSAID should be discontinued if oligohydramnios is found. Because NSAIDs may cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, the prescribing information for ibuprofen speciﬁcally states its use should be avoided starting at 30 weeks’ gestation. A High dose carbimazole and thyroxine High-dose carbimazole and thyroxine is incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is transient, not due to overproduction, and block– replace therapy is not recommended in pregnancy. C Prednisolone Prednisolone is incorrect. Corticosteroids are avoided in pregnancy, if possible, because of their adverse event proﬁle. D Radioiodine Radioiodine is the ﬁrst-line treatment for Graves’ disease. However, given the history of a recent upper respiratory tract infection, combined with a tender thyroid, a diagnosis of subacute thyroiditis is more likely. Furthermore, use of radioiodine is not recommended to treat Graves’ disease in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal complications. In such instances, carbimazole is preferred. E Reassurance This patient’s pain has precipitated her presentation to hospital. Therefore, it is not considered appropriate to leave her without advice/access to pain-relieving medication.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with decreased libido, vaginal dryness and absence of periods for the past 4 months. Most recently, she has begun to suffer embarrassing milk leakage from her breasts on only minor nipple stimulation. Medication history includes use of the oral contraceptive pill. Prolactin level is 4300 microIU/L and she maintains that she could not possibly be pregnant as she has bought a home test, which is negative. Her BP is normal at 132/72 mmHg, pulse is 74/min and regular and her BMI is 23. Which of the following is most likely to yield the diagnosis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the pituitary fossa
explanation:
A Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the pituitary fossa Prolactin levels are too elevated to be due to the oral contraceptive pill; with this symptomatic picture it is important to rule out a prolactinoma or other pituitary tumour leading to raised prolactin levels due to pressure effects. MRI scanning is needed to determine tumour size and location. Given her prolactin level, the most likely diagnosis is a micro-adenoma producing prolactin; as such, the management of choice is with a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine or cabergoline in the ﬁrst instance. C Thyroid function testing Hypothyroidism is associated with elevated prolactin levels, but usually not to this extent, which is more indicative of a prolactinoma. B Laboratory pregnancy test Shop-bought pregnancy tests have an accuracy of above 95%, so pregnancy is unlikely; however, it would be reasonable to perform a re-test to make absolutely sure that it is negative. D Abdominal ultrasound scan Elevated prolactin levels are noted in some ovarian and endo-

metrial cancers and with pregnancy, although these are unlikely diagnoses given the absence of abdominal symptoms and negative pregnancy test. E Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) testing This is used in the work-up primarily of precocious and delayed puberty associated with low LH and FSH levels.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic with hypercalcaemia and hypophosphataemia. She has no past medical history of note and only complained to her general practitioner of tiredness and increased thirst over the past few months. Examination is unremarkable. Blood pressure is 122/72 mmHg, and pulse is 70 bpm and regular. The body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. Primary hyperparathyroidism is suspected. Which of the following would be considered an indication for surgical referral?
explanation: D Creatinine clearance 35% below predicted This question is based on the criteria from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for surgery in asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism. These include creatinine clearance reduced by 30% or more. A Age 62 Young age, rather than older age, is a driver for parathyroid surgery, with age younger than 50 years considered the driver for surgery in the absence of other factors. B Corrected calcium 2.80 mmol/l Serum albumin-adjusted calcium > 0.25 mmol/l above the upper limit of normal is considered the cut-off for recommending surgery. Given most hospitals quote a normal range of up to 2.61 mmol/l, this is below that threshold. C 24-hour urinary calcium 8 mmol/day A cut-off of 10 mmol/24 hours is used as the urinary calcium excretion threshold for recommending surgery in asymptomatic hyperparathyroidism. E T score -2.0 The cut-off for bone mineral density is a T score < – 2.5, indicating a signiﬁcant risk for fracture linked to loss of bone mineral density.

stem: A 44-year-old man is referred to clinic with headaches and a raised fasting glucose of 7.5 mmol/l. He has also noticed a change in his facial appearance and enlargement of his hands. Examination reveals prognathism, enlarged digits and bitemporal hemianopia. His BP is elevated at 155/90 mmHg. An oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone levels showed a blood glucose of 11.5 mmol/l at 120 min and also failure to suppress growth hormone levels. An MRI scan of the pituitary fossa revealed an adenoma that was abutting the optic chiasm. Treatment options were explained to the patient and he opted for medical therapy rather surgery (transphenoidal resection of the adenoma). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical therapy for him?
explanation:
D Somatostatin analogue This gentleman has acromegaly. Acromegaly is usually related to a pituitary adenoma, although it is occasionally caused by ectopic secretion of growth hormone from malignant cells. This results in coarsening of facial features, prognathism and macroglossia. Patients are at increased risk of cardiovascular disease with hypertension and diabetes. Transphenoidal removal of the adenoma would be curative and is the ﬁrst-line treatment option. B Glucagon This is used for the treatment of severe hypoglycaemia when the patient is unconscious or unable to receive glucose orally. A Insulin The excess secretion of growth hormone in acromegaly results in increased insulin resistance and diabetes. Some patients require dietary intervention only, oral hypoglycaemic agents or insulin. In this case, there is insufﬁcient information regarding the glycaemic control of the patient and whether he will

require insulin or not. In any case, priority is the treatment of acromegaly since diabetes usually subsequently resolves. C Bromocriptine This is a dopamine agonist used for the treatment of prolactinomas as an alternative to cabergoline. E Pegvisomant This is a growth hormone receptor antagonist and is a third-line treatment when surgery, radiotherapy and somatostatin analogues are not effective.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with a history of ischaemic heart disease treated with multiple medications is admitted to the Emergency Admissions Ward with diarrhoea and lethargy. She apparently became unwell with gastroenteritis some 48 hours before admission. Colleagues in the Emergency Department have begun potassium replacement therapy, but the nurses ask you to see her because she still feels ‘washed out’. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 105/67 mmHg and a pulse of 85 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft, but there is left-sided tenderness, in keeping with the diarrhoea. Despite 3 litres of ﬂuid replacement (with potassium), the potassium level is still 3.2 mmol/l (2.9 on admission). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Check calcium and treat if low
Check magnesium and treat if low
Give more potassium via central line
explanation: B Check magnesium and treat if low Hypokalaemia is often resistant to correction with replacement therapy where there is coexisting hypomagnesaemia. Bearing in mind that diarrhoea is associated with substantial magnesium loss, the magnesium level should be measured and corrected if hypomagnesaemia is noted. C Give more potassium via central line This will be less effective than ﬁrst correcting any coexisting hypomagnesaemia. A Check calcium and treat if low Coexisting hypocalcaemia should have no effect on the body’s ability to correct potassium levels. D Start Amiloride Given diarrhoea is associated with volume loss, amiloride, a potassium-sparing diuretic, is inappropriate in this situation. E Start oral potassium supplements This will be less effective than ﬁrst correcting the magnesium level.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the Pregnancy Diabetes Clinic having failed a trial of two weeks’ diet and exercise. Her ﬁrst child was a normal size at birth. She is now 20 weeks pregnant. She has no prior medical history of note. Investigations reveal the following: I nvestigation Result Fasting plasma glucose 6.9 mmol/l Oral glucose tolerance test at 2 hours 11.4 mmol/l What is the most appropriate next step in this case?
explanation:
C Oral metformin This woman has gestational diabetes, as evidenced by a raised fasting and 2 h blood glucose. Abnormal glucose tolerance occurs as a de novo event in around 2–3% of pregnant women; unfortunately their long-term risk of subsequent type 2 diabetes is as high as 40–50%. The aim of treatment is to keep blood glucose readings to around 7 mmol/l or below, and to allow mothers to give birth normally (although a number should deliver at 38 weeks’ gestation due to excess fetal growth). Women should be offered a further glucose tolerance test at the 6-week check, to rule out the possibility of continued abnormal glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes. Studies have demonstrated that where metformin is instigated as initial therapy, maternal and fetal outcomes are no worse than where patients are prescribed insulin ﬁrst line, and wom-

en gain less weight in pregnancy with greater overall treatment satisfaction scores. D Basal bolus insulin therapy Basal bolus insulin therapy is the next intervention when blood glucose levels escape target despite maximal tolerated oral metformin. A Oral glibenclamide Although one trial has shown that glibenclamide is effective in controlling blood glucose in pregnancy, it is associated with weight gain and risk of hypoglycaemia, meaning that metformin is preferred. B Diet and exercise advice only Diet and exercise advice only runs the risk of uncontrolled hyperglycaemia and subsequent adverse fetal outcomes. This is particularly a problem as further weight gain in pregnancy will only exacerbate insulin resistance and worsen glycaemic control. E Oral acarbose Although oral acarbose does reduce GI carbohydrate absorption, no large trial of effectiveness in pregnancy has been carried out.

stem: A 58-year old man is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) following collapse. In his possession are empty prednisolone boxes, and he has a steroid user card. He has obvious rheumatoid features on examination and his chest X-ray (CXR) is shown below. He is given intravenous (IV) ﬂuids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 100/60 mmHg on lying and 75/40 mmHg on standing. His pulse is 95 beats per minute (bpm). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Na+ 131 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 7.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 105 umol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which one of the following would be the most useful addition to the current management?
options: Thyroid function test before giving steroids
Oral prednisolone 20 mg and ﬂudrocortisone 50 μg
Oral prednisolone 40 mg and ﬂudrocortisone 50 μg
explanation:
C IV hydrocortisone 100 mg The history of rheumatoid arthritis and steroid user card suggests the patient is on steroids. The fact that he has empty boxes in his possession may mean that he has run out of steroids. As he currently has a pneumonia (the CXR shows multifocal consolidation, worse in the right upper lobe), his need for steroids will be higher than normal. These should be given IV to ensure they are absorbed. D Oral prednisolone 20 mg and ﬂudrocortisone 50 μg Fludrocortisone is often used in the treatment of Addison’s disease at a dose of 50-300 μg. There is no indication that this patient has Addison’s. Even in new diagnoses of Addison’s, mineralocorticoid replacement is not necessary in the acute phase. This is because high-dose hydrocortisone has a mineralocorticoid effect. A Thyroid function test before giving steroids It is important not to delay the administration of steroids as the patient is systemically unwell and may have missed a number of doses. B Oral prednisolone 40 mg Oral formulations of steroids are inadequately absorbed and therefore not appropriate in patients who are systemically unwell. E Oral prednisolone 40 mg and ﬂudrocortisone 50 μg Fludrocortisone is often used in the treatment of Addison’s disease. There is no indication that this patient has Addison’s. Even in new diagnoses of Addison’s, mineralocorticoid re-

placement is not necessary in the acute phase. This is because high-dose hydrocortisone has a mineralocorticoid effect.

stem: You review a 32-year-old man with a history of type 1 diabetes who is complaining of tiredness, lethargy and weight loss. He also tells you that he has fainted on three occasions over the past 2 months. He admits to nausea and vomiting. He has been working in Spain for some months. On examination, he is very thin and you notice he is tanned. His blood pressure is 102/65 mmHg, with a postural drop of 12 mmHg on standing. Investigation Result Normal values T4 5.7 pmol/l (1022) 10 - 22 pmol/l Na+ 132 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 5.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Glucose 5.8 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Urea 9.1 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l He has a normochromic, normocytic anaemia. Which one of the following is the best way to diagnose the cause of his symptoms?
explanation: A 9 am cortisol and ACTH measurement This man has adrenal insufﬁciency until proven otherwise. This is illustrated by his blood picture of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia (levels may have been blunted by vomiting), raised urea and normochromic normocytic anaemia. Nine am cortisol and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) levels are a very sensitive way to detect adrenal insufﬁciency, with inappropriately low cortisol levels compared to raised ACTH levels indicating a positive diagnosis. Around 70% of cases of adrenal insufﬁciency occur due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands, adrenal insufﬁciency occurring with increased frequency in patients with a history of type 1 diabetes or other autoimmune disease. Malignant destruction and infection by tuberculosis are other possible causes. C CT head scan Given this patient has increased skin pigmentation, hy- poadrenalism related to adrenal rather than pituitary failure is much more likely here, and hence CT head is not of value. B Thyroid auto-antibodies Thyroid dysfunction is likely to be as a result of the severe non-thyroidal illness, and antibody testing is therefore of no value here. Raised TSH and reduced T4 levels are often seen at the point of diagnosis of hypoadrenalism. Commencing thyroid hormone replacement may actually worsen the adrenal crisis, and thyroid function testing should be repeated a few weeks after stabilising glucocorticoid replacement. D Urine sodium and osmolality Relative dehydration and increased urinary sodium loss are both likely consequences of hypoadrenalism. Urine assay of sodium and osmolality won’t, however, determine the underlying cause. E Transferrin saturation Transferrin saturation is useful in diagnosing haemochromatosis, which does present with increased skin pigmentation, although this is against a background of a type 2 diabetes-like picture with arthritis and erectile dysfunction due to low levels of testosterone.

stem: A 34-year-old woman sees her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of persistent fatigue and difﬁculty losing weight. She often feels cold and has been constipated. She discussed these symptoms with her mother, who advised that she see her GP because she had experienced similar symptoms when she was diagnosed with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Which autoantibody is she most likely to have in her blood?
explanation: C Thyroid peroxidase antibody These antibodies occur in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are found in patients with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Thyroid peroxidase oxidises iodide ions which is needed for the production of thyroxine and antibodies against this enzyme, therefore, prevent the production of thyroid hormones. This therefore results in autoimmune hypothyroidism. The exact cause is unknown, but Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is thought to be more likely to occur if there is a family history of the condition. E Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor stimulating antibody (TSAb) TSAb antibodies are usually present in Graves’ disease and result in stimulation of TSH receptor. This results in the overproduction of thyroid hormones, and leads to symptoms associated with thyrotoxicosis (tremor, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhoea etc) rather than hypothyroid (proximal myopathy, bradycardia, hypothermia, constipation etc). A 21-Hydroxylase antibody This autoantibody is most common in patients with primary hypoadrenalism (Addison’s disease). It occurs in 80-90% of patients with this condition and is not associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. B Glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody These antibodies are associated with type I diabetes mellitus and stiff person syndrome and are not associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. These antibodies are typically measured when type I diabetes is suspected and is particularly useful if there is diagnostic doubt about which type of diabetes the patient has. D Tissue transglutaminase antibody (anti-TTG)

stem: A 78-year-old woman signs on with a new General Practitioner (GP) and has some routine blood tests. It is after these blood tests that the GP notices a raised corrected calcium level of 2.80 mmol/l and a raised PTH at 9 pmol/l. There is no history of renal stones, fractures or psychiatric disturbance. Other renal and liver function testing is unremarkable, full blood count is normal and there is no suspicion of underlying malignancy. Bone mineral density is at the lower end of the normal range. Which is likely to be the most appropriate way to manage this woman?
explanation: C Observation Deﬁnite indications for surgery in hyperparathyroidism, the most likely diagnosis here (American National Institutes of Health consensus) include markedly elevated corrected serum calcium (>3 mmol/l), previous marked hypercalcaemic episode, impaired renal function, renal stones, nephrocalcinosis, substantially elevated urinary calcium and reduced bone mineral density. Patients with hyperparathyroidism kept under observation require annual plasma calcium, renal function and blood pressure checks, repeat bone mineral density check every 2–3 years and renal ultrasound scan. Any signiﬁcant deterioration in the clinical condition would be an indication for surgery. Surgery should be carried out by a surgeon who does more than 20 parathyroidectomies per year. In parathyroid adenoma the affected gland should be removed; hyperplasia may be managed with partial parathyroidectomy or complete parathyroidectomy, with medical treatment for hypoparathyroidism. A Neck exploration for parathyroidectomy In this scenario the patient has mild hypercalcaemia, with no symptoms and no end-organ damage (i.e. nephrocalcinosis, osteoporosis), and therefore there is no indication for surgical intervention. B Hormone replacement therapy Common clinical indications to commence menopausal hormone replacement therapy are:  to relieve vasomotor symptoms  to improve urogenital symptoms (long-term therapy is required)  to prevent osteoporosis. Oestrogen therapy in postmenopausal women has been shown to cause a small reduction in serum calcium (up to 0.25 mmol/l) without a change in parathyroid hormone. Oestrogen also has beneﬁcial effects on lumbar spine and femoral neck bone mineral density. However, due to risks associated with oestrogen replacement, it should not be used for the sole purpose of treating primary hyperparathyroidism. D Calcium and vitamin D therapy Calcium replacement is not indicated in primary hyperparathyroidism, since it would deteriorate the hypercalcaemia. Vitamin D can be administered cautiously and at a lower dose in the context of deﬁciency. E Oral phosphate Primary hyperparathyroidism can cause mild hypophosphataemia through increased phosphaturia. Phosphate replacement therapy is not indicated.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is reviewed in the Endocrinology Clinic with a 4-month history of lethargy and increased urination, particularly at night. She has a past medical history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, for which she takes levothyroxine 125 μg daily. She denies smoking, alcohol and recreational drug use. Her vital signs are within normal limits. On examination, her cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Na+ 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.8 mmol/l 1.8–7.1 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Glucose 5.5 mmol/l 4–7 mmol/l Free T4 8.1 pmol/l 7.9–14.4 pmol/l Plasma osmolality 320 mOsm/kg 275–295 mOsm/kg Urine osmolality 220 mOsm/kg 500–800 mOsm/kg Results following water deprivation test: Investigation Result Normal value Plasma osmolality 340 mOsm/kg 275–295 mOsm/kg Urine osmolality 290 mOsm/kg 500–800 mOsm/kg What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Diabetes insipidus

This patient has a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus, given the history of lethargy, polyuria and nocturia, combined with high plasma osmolality and low urine osmolality. Diabetes insipidus can have a central or nephrogenic origin due to deﬁciency in vasopressin or renal resistance to vasopressin, respectively. There are numerous risk factors for developing diabetes insipidus, including pituitary disease, traumatic head injury, autoimmune disease (eg Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) and chronic kidney disease. The initial investigation of choice for diabetes insipidus is a water deprivation test that classically shows an inability to concentrate the urine to preserve plasma osmolality. The persistently low urine osmolality following a water deprivation test conﬁrms a diagnosis of diabetes insipidus. C Primary adrenal insufﬁciency This patient is at higher risk of primary adrenal insufﬁciency, given her autoimmune history. Patients may present with similar symptoms, including fatigue and signs of hypotension. However, due to a lack of mineralocorticoid production, these patients are often hyponatraemic and hypotensive due to salt wasting secondary to lack of Na+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. B Iatrogenic diuretic use Iatrogenic diuretic use is a possible differential diagnosis and would cause a similar picture of low urine osmolality and raised serum osmolality. However, there is often a history of a mental health condition or an eating disorder. A common diuretic that is taken is a loop diuretic such as furosemide. Furosemide can often cause hypokalaemia, making it less likely to be the underlying cause of this patient’s presentation. D Primary polydipsia The presentation of diabetes insipidus and primary polydipsia can be similar. However, following the water deprivation test, there should be an expected rise in urine osmolality (> 700 mOsm/kg) in those with primary polydipsia. The lack of response is more suggestive of diabetes insipidus. E Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH) presents with low plasma osmolality and raised urine osmolality, as patients have higher serum concentrations of antidiuretic hormone. Therefore, patients with SIADH have increased water reabsorption in the collecting ducts of nephrons and dilutional hyponatraemia.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with amenorrhoea. She has not had her ﬁrst period and feels concerned as her friends all went through puberty several years ago. There is no known medical history or family history of note. On examination, she is 125 cm tall with a weight of 55 kg. Her chest is broad with absent breast development. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen with no palpable masses. Investigation Result Normal value Oestradiol 40 pmol/l 75–1000 pmol/l FSH 40 mIU/ml 2–20 mIU/ml Luteinising hormone (LH) 221 × 109/l 1.1–110 mIU/ml Prolactin 200 IU/ml 59–619 IU/ml T4 6.5 pmol/l 7.9–14.4 pmol/l TSH 10 mU/l 0.5–5 mU/l Total human chorionic gonadotropin 1 U/l < 3 U/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Turner syndrome This patient has presented with primary amenorrhoea. She has a primary ovarian insufﬁciency, given the low oestradiol and raised gonadotropin (LH, FSH) levels. This is combined with a short stature of 125 cm, raised BMI (35 kg/m2), absent breast development and a broad chest, which are all features of Turner syndrome. Autoimmune disorders are associated with Turner syndrome, including hypothyroidism and it is not uncommon to see a raised TSH or low thyroxine level. D Pituitary adenoma A pituitary adenoma can cause primary or secondary amenorrhoea. The most common cause of a pituitary adenoma is a prolactinoma. However, the normal prolactin level makes this diagnosis unlikely. Other features of a prolactinoma include lactation, which is not seen here. A Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is an autosomal-recessive disorder associated with virilisation at birth, premature adrenarche and precocious puberty. It does not cause primary ovarian failure or absent development of secondary sexual characteristics. B Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism is an important differential diagnosis to consider, as it is a cause of primary or secondary amenorrhoea.

The blood tests show there is a low thyroxine and raised TSH level which indicates hypothyroidism. High BMI is another feature of hypothyroidism. However, short stature and absent breast development are more likely to represent an alternative diagnosis, such as Turner syndrome. It is important to remember that Turner syndrome is associated with autoimmune conditions, including hypothyroidism and this is the most likely reason for the deranged thyroid function tests. C Polycystic ovarian syndrome Polycystic ovarian syndrome is a common endocrinopathy in young women and is a cause of primary amenorrhoea. It is associated with hyperandrogenism, oligomenorrhoea and metabolic syndrome, with high BMI and insulin resistance. Although it is very important to consider as a differential diagnosis given its prevalence, polycystic ovarian syndrome does not cause short stature or absent breast development.

stem: A 56-year-old woman was admitted to the Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU) after a road trafﬁc accident. There were multiple long bone fractures and signiﬁcant bleeding, and she required a period of mechanical ventilation due to a chest injury. Past medical history of note includes hypertension, which is managed with indapamide, and obesity with a BMI of 31. During her recovery, the orthopaedic surgeons noticed a small goitre. Results obtained 6 days after admission: Investigation Result Normal values Free Thyroxine (FT4) 4.1 pmol/l 5.8 - 17.8 pmol/l Free triiodothyronine (T3) 1.5 pmol/l 5.0 - 10.0 pmol/l TSH 0.5 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Random cortisol nmol/l at 0900 h 200 - 700 nmol/l at 0900 h Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her thyroid disorder?
options: Repeat thyroid function testing in 3 months
explanation: E Repeat thyroid function testing in 3 months This patient has a normal TSH level, which suggests that she is suffering from ‘sick euthyroid’ syndrome. This condition, characterised by low tri-iodothyronine (T3) and T4 and low or normal TSH, is associated with severe illness and frequently occurs in patients admitted to the ITU. Most physicians advise repeating thyroid function testing in a few months; there is no evidence that patients beneﬁt from thyroid hormone replacement. This patient’s level of cortisol is entirely appropriate given her admission to the ITU and road trafﬁc accident. While she is obese, the possibility of co-existent Cushing’s disease is unlikely. It might be appropriate to repeat a morning cortisol level a few more weeks into her recovery. A Thyroxine 50 mcg/day Resolution of the underlying illness (in this case the trauma and subsequent surgery) is enough to correct thyroid function. Replacing thyroid hormone, even at low dose, risks driving symptoms of thyrotoxicosis and potentially hindering recovery. B Thyroxine 100 mcg/day Thyroxine 100 mcg/day will drive suppression of TSH and symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Resolution of thyroid dysfunction, accompanied by restoration of T3 and T4 levels, occurs within a few weeks. C Carbimazole Thyroid hormone levels are depressed as a result of the acute illness, and thus there is no value in suppressing thyroid hormone production further. D Propylthiouracil Given that T3 and T4 are low, like carbimazole, there is no reason to institute therapy here.

stem: A 31-year-old man with type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for advice about his blood glucose control. He has suffered a number of signiﬁcant hypoglycaemic episodes over the past 2 months, which have corresponded with a wish to increase his exercise. He is currently running 15 km per week in 5 km blocks. He takes BD mixed insulin and doesn’t alter his dose on the days he exercises. On examination his BP is 125/78 mmHg and his BMI is 27. There are no signs of peripheral neuropathy. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.6 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 210 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c mmol/ml (6.73%) < 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in his management with respect to glucose and weight management?
options: Reduce his BD mixed insulin dose on the days he exercises
Advise him to reduce his exercise
Advise him to transfer to a basal bolus regime
Advise him to maintain the same insulin dose and take a source of sugar with him when he runs
Reassure him that he will adjust to the lower blood sugar and his hypos will subside
explanation: C Advise him to transfer to a basal bolus regime Whilst some patients with type 1 diabetes prefer to take a BD mixed insulin regime because of convenience and number of injections, it is not responsive to changes in routine such as taking intensive aerobic exercise. As such, he should be persuaded to change to a basal bolus regime where he can alter his short-acting insulin dose just prior to when he is planning exercise. D Advise him to maintain the same insulin dose and take a source of sugar with him when he runs This will blunt some of the beneﬁts of exercise in driving a calorie deﬁcit. A Reduce his BD mixed insulin dose on the days he exercises Reducing his BD insulin is likely to precipitate an increase in his HbA1c because his glucose outside periods of exercise will increase signiﬁcantly. B Advise him to reduce his exercise Exercise is important with respect to maintaining ﬁtness and reducing cardiovascular risk in type 1 diabetes. As such, aiming to reduce his exercise is inappropriate. E Reassure him that he will adjust to the lower blood sugar and his hypos will subside This runs the risk of reducing awareness of signiﬁcant hypoglycaemic episodes.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred to the clinic for review by her GP. She has been worried as she has suffered weight gain of 3 kg over the past 3 months and has not had a period for the past 2 months. There is also some breast tenderness and a feeling of fullness. On examination she looks well and has a normal BP of 125/75 mmHg; other features are entirely normal. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 192×109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Prolactin 1600 mU/l < 400 mU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Pregnancy Prolactin levels rise rapidly in pregnancy, and the symptoms of amenorrhoea, breast fullness/tenderness and weight gain ﬁt very well with this underlying diagnosis. A urine pregnancy test is easily accessible, and should represent the investigation of choice for this patient. C Microprolactinoma Prolactin levels in microprolactinoma are usually slightly higher than those seen here. A Hypothyroidism Although hypothyroidism classically presents with weight gain, it also usually features menorrhagia, whereas this patient reports a two-month period without a period. D Macroprolactinoma In macroprolactinoma a much greater rise in prolactin would be expected, with symptoms of optic chiasm compression. E Polycystic ovarian syndrome PCOS is associated with weight gain, irregular heavy periods and symptoms of hyperandrogenism.

stem: A 25-year-old postman presents for review. He is 6 feet 4 inches tall and has signs of delayed puberty and infertility on examination, notably small testes with scanty pubic hair. Investigation Result Normal values FSH 35 u/l 1 - 7 u/l Testosterone 5 nmol/l 9 - 25 nmol/l Which diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: A 47XXY This is 47XXY, or Klinefelter syndrome. Klinefelter syndrome which is leading cause of primary hypogonadism (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) affects 1 in 1 000 males and involves the loss of Leydig cells and seminiferous tubular dysgenesis. Treatment is with androgen replacement unless testosterone levels are normal. No treatment is possible for associated infertility. Chromosomal disorders such as Klinefelter syndrome, which occur due to loss, gain or rearrangement of one or more chromosomes, have no clear pattern of inheritance and carry a low risk of inheritance in relatives. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism occurs in hypopituitarism, selective gonadotrophin deﬁciency (eg Kallmann syndrome), systemic illness or severe weight reduction. Fragile-X syndrome is associated with macro-orchidism and learning difﬁculties in males. D Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism We can see from the blood results that FSH is signiﬁcantly elevated, ruling out hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism.
