B Down syndrome Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 and is of course associated with learning difﬁculties, rather than the speciﬁc features of hypoandrogenism seen here. C Fragile-X syndrome Fragile-X syndrome is associated with learning difﬁculties and macro-orchidism rather than the small testes seen here. E Kallmann’s syndrome Kallmann syndrome is caused by defective release of GnRH, due to failure of development of the olfactory bulb. LH and FSH are reduced, and patients suffer from anosmia.

stem: A 27-year-old man with a history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. He is managed with a basal- bolus insulin regime comprising glargine and Novorapid™. He has had type I diabetes since the age of ﬁve and has trouble with peripheral neuropathy. On examination his BP is 115/70 mmHg with a postural drop of 10 mmHg, and his BMI is 29. There is gloveand-stocking peripheral neuropathy. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 184 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 80 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c 56 mmol/mol <53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Urinary ACR 7.5 mg/mmol <3.5 mg/mmol Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step with respect to reducing the risk of renal progression of microvascular complications?
explanation: D Ramipril 2.5 mg Evidence suggests that even with normal blood pressure, patients with type 1 diabetes derive beneﬁt with respect to progression of renal disease after micro-albuminuria has become established from angiotensin- converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition. As such, even though his BP is in the normal range it is appropriate to trial this patient on ramipril. B Insulin pump therapy Although HbA1c is slightly above target, a dose adjustment for normal eating (DAFNE) course is more appropriate initially versus moving to an insulin pump. A Amlodipine 5mg Although attaining BP target is important with respect to reducing the risk of microvascular complications, in this case with a systolic BP of 115 mmHg, ACE inhibition is the more appropriate intervention. C Metformin 500mg BD Metformin may help with weight control in patients with type 1 diabetes and have a small impact in reducing HbA1c, although studies are not powered to detect any impact on outcomes. E Reassurance Given that there is evidence to support use of ACE inhibitors in this situation, reassurance alone is not appropriate.

stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She is overweight and has problems with acne and hirsutism affecting her face and upper chest. She only has a period once every three to four months, and when they occur, they tend to be very heavy. She currently abstains from sexual intercourse and does not wish to become pregnant. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/90 mmHg and a pulse of 75 bpm and regular. You conﬁrm a male pattern of hirsutism and acne affecting her face and upper chest. Her body mass index (BMI) is 32 kg/m2. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 197 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.6 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/ Creatinine 103 mmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Fasting glucose 6.2 mmol/l < 7 mmol/l/ FSH 30 IU/l 1–25 U/l Luteinising (LH) : FSH ratio 2.1 U/l 1.1 U/l Testosterone 4.2 nmol/l 0.2–2.9 nmol/l Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to control her symptoms?
explanation: E Weight loss This woman has polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), for which weight loss is the mainstay of therapy. Greater than 5% loss in weight is associated with improvements in acne, hirsuitism and menstrual regularity, and will also impact on the elevated fasting glucose seen here. In patients who cannot achieve weight loss by lifestyle alone, pharmacological intervention using agents such as high-dose liraglutide may be appropriate. C Finasteride Finasteride is primarily used for reducing hirsuitism and acne in PCOS. In this patient, weight control and managing impaired fasting glucose are important, and only weight loss represents a holistic solution for acne, hirsuitism and impaired fasting glucose. A Clomifene Clomifene is the most appropriate option for ovulation induction. In this case, given her BMI of above 30 and impaired fasting glucose, weight loss is the most appropriate option with respect to long-term outcomes. B Combined oral contraceptive pill Given this patient’s BMI, she is at an increased risk for venous thrombosis with the oral contraceptive pill, although it may help regulate her menstrual cycle. D Metformin Metformin is less effective than weight loss in reducing progression to type II diabetes, although it may impact on hirsutism and acne. It could be added in the event that weight loss is insufﬁcient to improve symptoms and fasting glucose.

stem: A 28-year-old woman was referred to the Genetics Clinic after presenting with intermittent nausea and vomiting and associated abdominal pain. There is concern that she has an inherited disorder, the pattern of which is demonstrated in the genogram below. She has had depression since her teenage years and a peptic ulcer requiring hospital admission last year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
B Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)

This is the correct answer, as the presenting symptoms are all encompassed by this diagnosis. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is a hereditary endocrine cancer inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. While cancers begin to develop from the teenage years, symptoms tend not to present for several years. The abdominal symptoms with the long history of depression are secondary to parathyroid hyperplasia (95% of patients) and resulting hypercalcaemia. The peptic ulcer is secondary to Zollinger–Ellison syndrome, occurring in 75% of MEN1 patients. D Familial isolated hyperparathyroidism Familial isolated hyperparathyroidism is an overarching description for genetic disorders which cause hyperparathyroidism without accompanying pathology and is a diagnosis of exclusion. There is no one gene associated with this disorder, and inheritance patterns are uncertain. Additionally, it does not explain the peptic ulcer disease described in the stem. A Familial benign (hypocalciuric) hypercalcaemia (FBHH) FBHH presents with hypercalcaemia and moderately raised PTH. This presents in an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Typically, most people with FBHH do not present with symptoms; the diagnosis is made based on biochemistry. Furthermore, this diagnosis would not explain the presence of the peptic ulcer, secondary to Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. C Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2) While the symptom pattern could be explained by MEN2 (speciﬁcally MEN2A), which is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, there are no symptoms of medullary thyroid cancer such as a thyroid nodule or cervical lymphadenopathy. Nearly all patients with MEN2 have medullary thyroid cancer. Furthermore, there is no clear explanation for the peptic ulcer with this diagnosis. E Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (HDGC) HDGC is an umbrella term used to describe a number of genetic anomalies linked to gastric carcinomas. They follow an autosomal dominant method of inheritance. While HDGC has been linked to breast and prostate cancers, there is no link to parathyroid adenomas or depression.

stem: A 36-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED), having suffered a very severe headache after chasing a man who was stealing his car. Previously ﬁt and well and of normal stature, he was noted to be hypertensive on admission with a blood pressure (BP) of 165/90 mmHg, which later settled to 155/85 mmHg. On further questioning, it was noted that his mother was known to have had ‘thyroid cancer’, and died at an early age. His GP did routine bloods after he moved house a few months earlier and noted his calcium was elevated at 2.84 mmol/l. What is the most likely unifying diagnosis behind his presentation?
explanation:
C MEN-2a The history of marked hypertension in this gentleman, coupled with a family history of thyroid carcinoma, should raise the possibility of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN). MEN2a is characterised by medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid chief cell hyperplasia. It is likely that both this man and his mother carry the same mutation. Around 30% of carriers of an MEN-2a mutation never develop the associated clinical syndrome. The initial diagnostic investigation of choice for phaeochromocytoma is 24 h urinary catecholamine assay. Where the diagnosis is proven, it is sensible to screen for medullary thyroid carcinoma via pentagastrin testing. Conversely, where patients present with medullary thyroid carcinoma, they should be screened for phaeochromocytoma prior to consideration of surgery. Where adequate alpha blockade is not in place prior to surgery, there is a very real chance of hypertensive crisis and possible on-table myocardial infarction. E Von Hippel–Lindau disease VHL is associated with phaeochromocytoma, although it often presents earlier with balance disturbance due to the presence of CNS haemangioblastomas. A Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1) MEN-1 is associated with multiple parathyroid adenomas, pancreatic islet cell tumours and pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas being most commonly seen). B MEN-2b MEN-2b tends to occur as a sporadic mutation; additional features compared to MEN-2a include a marfanoid habitus and multiple mucosal neuromas. D Familial medullary thyroid carcinoma syndrome Familial medullary thyroid carcinoma syndrome is associated with the RET mutation, although presentation with phaeo-

chromocytoma would not be expected.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents to the endocrine clinic for review. He has been taking amiodarone for the past few months for short episodes of VT diagnosed after a myocardial infarction. During the past 2 months, he has noticed weight loss and heat intolerance, with short runs of an irregular, fast heartbeat. In the clinic he has a BP of 112/82, pulse is 88 and regular. His BMI is 21. Thyroid function testing is abnormal, with a suppressed TSH suggestive of thyrotoxicosis. Radioiodine uptake scan is normal, as is serum interleukin 6 (IL-6). A most recent ECHO cardiogram ejection fraction is 38%. His amiodarone is discontinued by the cardiologist after the repeat ECHO cardiogram and a 72 h tape, which shows paroxysmal AF but no episodes of VT. Which one of the following options is the best initial therapy for him?
explanation: B Carbimazole and potassium perchlorate therapy This man probably has amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) type 1, as exempliﬁed by the presence of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, normal radioiodine uptake and normal interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels. AIT type 1 results primarily from iodine excess and therefore increased hormone synthesis. Type 1 AIT is treated initially with a combination of anti-thyroid drugs and potassium perchlorate therapy. D Radioiodine Radioiodine is ineffective at least initially in amiodaroneinduced thyrotoxicosis, because of the iodine load already delivered by amiodarone therapy. A Prednisolone 40 mg/day Prednisolone is a component of therapy for AIT type 2, which is thought to result from a direct toxic effect of amiodarone and is associated with thyroiditis, decreased radioiodine uptake on thyroid scan and raised IL-6 levels. Patients may eventually become hypothyroid because of the destruction of thyroid hormone-producing cells. C Thyroidectomy Surgery should be avoided if possible in a patient with relatively unstable cardiovascular disease; in the event that it is required, acute control of thyroid status is ﬁrst achieved with perchlorate therapy. It may be considered particularly in cases where amiodarone cannot be withdrawn. E Partial thyroidectomy Partial thyroidectomy still involves surgical risk, and hence should be reserved for patients who fail to respond to medical therapy where there are no other options.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department for the second time in a month with a syncopal episode. She admits to tiredness, which has increased over the past few months, and says that she has never been keen on physical activity, even at school, because of muscle cramps and easy fatigue. Apparently, one other relative has similar symptoms. Examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 100/60 mmHg, with pulse 85/min and regular. There is a postural drop of 10 mmHg on standing. Her BMI is 22. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 130 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 222 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 2.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 33 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l Glucose 4.3 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
E Gitelman syndrome Gitelman syndrome is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal-recessive manner. It presents with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and a metabolic alkalosis. The mutation causing this condition results in a loss of function of the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney. This history provides clues to the genetic nature of the diagnosis by highlighting other relatives with the same symptoms.

A Bartter syndrome This is a condition characterised by hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and hypotension, as seen here. However, typically Bartter syndrome presents in early childhood making the diagnosis less likely here. B Classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia This is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder in which the production of mineralocorticoids is impaired. This leads to hyperkalaemia as well as signiﬁcant dehydration from saltwasting. Further virilisation is a key presenting feature, resulting from increased production of excessive sex steroids. These symptoms typically present in childhood. C Conn syndrome This is the eponymous name for primary hyperaldosteronism, in which excess aldosterone is released from the adrenal gland. This leads to hypokalaemia. Unlike this clinical scenario, Conn syndrome presents with hypertension. D Cushing syndrome This results from excess corticosteroids and can lead to hypokalaemia. However, typically patients develop obesity and hypertension (neither of which is present in this case).

stem: A 33-year-old female auxiliary nurse presents for review. She has had difﬁculty with managing her hypertension and is currently taking atenolol 100 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and ramipril 10 mg, yet her blood pressure is still raised at 165/80 mmHg. She takes beclomethasone 100 mcg BD for asthma, but nil else of note. On examination, she has a body mass index (BMI) of 29, with no obvious abdominal striae. Fasting blood results: Investigation Result Normal values Na+ 140 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 2.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3–) 40 mmol/l 22 - 29 mmol/l Glucose 7.1 mmol/l < 5.9 mmol/l What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: C Conn syndrome Adrenal adenomas can account for hyperaldosteronism, the likely cause of the profound hypokalaemia and resistant hypertension seen here. Small aldosterone-producing adrenal adenomas are commoner in young women, whereas bilateral adrenal hyperplasia tends to occur later and is commoner in men. The best test for Conn syndrome is to look at renin/aldosterone levels, with antihypertensive medication having been discontinued for around 3 weeks if possible. This is because the preexisting antihypertensive medications can impact upon the renin:aldosterone ratio. Clearly the diagnosis would be supported if aldosterone levels were raised in the presence of depressed renin levels. A Fibromuscular hyperplasia Fibromuscular hyperplasia is a cause of hypereninaemic hyperaldosteronism. Although it does cause hypertension, the marked reduction in potassium despite angiotensinconverting enzyme (ACE) inhibition as seen here would not be expected, and a rise in creatinine associated with ACE inhibition would be likely. B Diabetic nephropathy This patient ﬁts the criteria for diabetes mellitus, although this is most likely early and is a chance ﬁnding here and not the cause of her hypertension. Renal dysfunction in type 2 diabetes is more commonly seen in older individuals and is a product of both sustained hypertension and diabetic nephropathy itself. D Cushing syndrome Her BMI of 29 and the lack of obvious serious truncal obesity both count against Cushing as the underlying diagnosis here. E Essential hypertension The marked hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis on blood picture do not ﬁt with a diagnosis of essential hypertension.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents complaining of loss of libido and impotence. He ﬁnds work and entertaining clients very stressful. Results of blood tests from GP were prolactin 3200 mU/l (< 360), normal thyroid function tests, MCV 100 ﬂ, testosterone low. He admits on further questioning to drinking three glasses of wine per night. There is no reported visual ﬁeld disturbance. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his impotence?
explanation: B Microprolactinoma This patient’s prolactin results are above 3000 mU/l, which is suggestive of a prolactinoma. The diagnostic test of choice would be MRI pituitary; microprolactinomas appear as hypointense lesions within the pituitary on T1- weighted scanning. Given the fact that there are no signs of optic chiasm compression, and this patient’s thyroid function tests are normal, it would be reasonable to give him a trial of dopamine agonist therapy. Surgery would be kept in reserve for this man if he was resistant or intolerant to drug therapy. E Compression of pituitary stalk Elevation in prolactin due to compression is smaller than that seen here. A Craniopharyngioma Craniopharyngiomas are less likely to present with hyperprolactinaemia and more likely to present with diabetes insipidus, adrenal failure or pituitary-dependent hypothyroidism. Other focal neurological deﬁcits as a result of local compression are also more likely to be seen. C Alcohol abuse Although there is evidence of alcohol abuse, including the raised MCV, this is unlikely to be the main cause of his problems. D Macroprolactinoma Levels of prolactin are usually above 6000 mU/l in macroprolactinoma.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with intermittent double vision on upward gaze. He has diplopia, maximal on looking left and looking down. Examining his eyes, he has mild bilateral proptosis and his eyes look normal, looking straight ahead. His pupils are equal and have normal direct and consensual light reﬂexes. He is able to look up and down for 10 seconds without tiring. He has no weakness or fatigability in any peripheral muscles. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Free Thyroxine FT4 18 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l TSH 3.2 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Graves eye disease The differential diagnosis for an eye movement abnormality, which cannot be explained by a single or multiple cranial nerve palsy, is either myasthenia gravis or Graves’ disease. Myasthenia is unlikely, as the patient can look up freely for long periods of time. Graves’ eye disease can occur with normal thyroid function. The diagnosis can be made by looking for thyroid-stimulating receptor antibodies in the serum. A Left abducens nerve palsy Sixth nerve palsy, or abducens nerve palsy, is a disorder associated with dysfunction of cranial nerve VI (the abducens nerve), which is responsible for causing contraction of the lateral rectus muscle to abduct the eye. The inability of an eye to turn outward results in a convergent strabismus or esotropia, of which the primary symptom is diplopia (commonly known as double vision) in which the two images appear side by side. The condition is commonly unilateral but can also occur bilaterally. The unilateral abducens nerve palsy is the most common of the isolated ocular motor nerve palsies. B Left oculomotor nerve palsy A complete oculomotor nerve palsy will result in a characteristic down-and-out position in the affected eye. The eye will be displaced outward and downward – outward because the lateral rectus (innervated by the sixth cranial nerve) maintains muscle tone compared to the paralysed medial rectus. The eye will be displaced downward because the superior oblique (innervated by the fourth cranial or trochlear nerve) is non-antagonised by the paralysed superior rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique. The affected individual will also have a ptosis, or drooping of the eyelid, and mydriasis (pupil dilation). C Myasthenia gravis Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction in which circulating antibodies cause ﬂuctuant skeletal muscle weakness. Ninety per cent of pa-

tients with myasthenia gravis develop ophthalmologic manifestations of the disease, characterised by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. Variability in the muscle weakness is a hallmark of myasthenia. The pathophysiology of adult MG is a reduced number of acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the postsynaptic muscle membrane due to circulating anti-AChR antibodies or, less commonly, to antibodies to muscle-speciﬁc tyrosine kinase (anti-MuSK), LRP4 and agrin. Myasthenia gravis can mimic almost any painless, pupilsparing ocular motility disorder, including internuclear ophthalmoplegia. Ptosis may be unilateral or bilateral. The ptosis may be elicited with sustained upward gaze, as shown in the image below, or on repeated eyelid closure. In this case, the patient didn’t display any fatigue on physical examination. E Left trochlear nerve palsy Fourth cranial nerve palsy, also known as trochlear nerve palsy, is a condition affecting cranial nerve IV, the trochlear nerve, which causes weakness or paralysis to the superior oblique muscle that it innervates. This condition often causes vertical or near-vertical double vision, as the weakened muscle prevents the eyes from moving in the same direction together. Since the fourth cranial nerve is the thinnest and has the longest intracranial course of the cranial nerves, it is particularly vulnerable to traumatic injury.

stem: A 27-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of difﬁculties with conception. She is overweight, and has acne and hirsutism. She had an ultrasound recently which noted polycystic ovaries supporting a diagnosis of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Which hormone excess has caused the hirsutism?
explanation: A Androgens Androgens are excessively produced by the ovaries in PCOS. This is in part due to an increase in luteinising hormone (LH) levels which are secreted from the pituitary gland. Raised androgens cause symptoms such as hirsutism, conception difﬁculties and acne. D Prolactin Elevated prolactin might be measured in a patient who is struggling to conceive, or in patients with known PCOS, since prolactin will be raised in around 30% of patients. However, while raised prolactin would impair the chances of conception, it would not account for the hirsutism seen in this patient. B Anti-Müllerian hormone Anti-Müllerian hormone is made by preantral follicles and therefore may be raised in PCOS, but it does not cause hirsutism. It does not cause any speciﬁc symptoms itself, but a raised level would point towards PCOS. C 17 hydroxy-progesterone Elevated 17 hydroxy-progesterone may be measured in a patient who presents with hirsutism, as this would point towards a diagnosis of late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia which would cause excessive androgen production, resulting in hirsutism. However, in this case, the patient has known PCOS. E Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) SHBG tends to be low in PCOS, rather than circulating in excessive levels. The low level of sex-hormone- binding globulin contributes to the excessive free androgens which circulate and cause hirsutism.

stem: A 65-year-old man is admitted to hospital with pneumonia and hyponatraemia with a sodium of 116 mmol/l. He was treated with antibiotics and rapid infusions of 3% hypertonic sodium chloride, but despite initial improvement deteriorated neurologically with ﬁts and subsequent coma the following day. What is the possible cause of his deterioration?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
explanation:
C Osmotic demyelination syndrome Osmotic demyelination syndrome, previously known as central pontine myelinolysis, occurs as a result of too- rapid correction of hyponatraemia; ideally correction should not exceed more

than 10-12 mmol/l in 24 hours. There is demyelination of the central basal pons or other areas of the brain. Various types of neurological deﬁcits have been described from quadriparesis to coma and death. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the investigation of choice to demonstrate classical demyelination. D Normal pressure hydrocephalus Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a clinical symptom due to a build-up of cerebrospinal ﬂuid. It is characterised by an abnormal gait, urinary incontinence and potentially reversible dementia. A Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion SIADH is deﬁned by hyponatraemia and hypo-osmolality due to inappropriate, continued secretion of ADH despite normal or increased plasma volume, which results in impaired water excretion. In this scenario the sodium was corrected prior to ﬁts. B Acute cerebrovascular event Stroke would not occur as a result of rapid correction of sodium. E Encephalomyelitis There is no indication of viral infection in this case. Encephalomyelitis is not associated with sodium correction.

stem: A 75-year-old lifelong smoker is seen by his General Practitioner (GP) with a ﬁve day history of wheeze and ankle swelling. He is prescribed diuretics along with some other medications but continues to deteriorate. His blood pressure (BP) is 110/60 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg. His pulse is 90 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Na+ 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 28 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 200 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 16 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Arterial blood gas reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal values pH 7.11 7.35–7.45 pCO2 7.0 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa pO2 6.5 kPa 10.5–13.5 kPa Which one of the following diagnoses best explains the clinical picture and these biochemical results?
options: Mixed picture of COPD and cardiac failure with renal hypoperfusion
Acute kidney disease and ﬂuid overload
explanation: A Mixed picture of COPD and cardiac failure with renal hypoperfusion This patient has a respiratory acidosis (p(CO2) >6.5 kPa, pH <7.35 and hypoxia) and a metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate). It's very likely that he has an element of COPD with chronic CO2 retention and a degree of pulmonary oedema. Treatment with diuretics then leads to renal hypoperfusion, resulting in metabolic acidosis. B Severe COPD This would produce a respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation, which would be reﬂected by raised bicarbonate level on the ABG. C Pre-kidney disease secondary to diuretics Pre-kidney disease on its own would not cause carbon dioxide retention and hypoxia. D Aspirin poisoning Symptoms of acute aspirin (acetyl salicylic acid) toxicity include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, tinnitus, vertigo, altered mentation, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, hyperpyrexia and coma. Salicylates stimulate the medullary respiratory centre leading to increased rate (tachypnoea) and depth of respiration (hyperventilation). This leads to a fall in pCO2 and respiratory alkalosis. Later, metabolic acidosis occurs due to accumulation of lactic and other organic acids. The most common acid–base presentation is that of mixed respiratory alkalosis– metabolic acidosis. E Acute kidney disease and ﬂuid overload This would lead to a metabolic acidosis, with perhaps a degree of disordered gas exchange related to pulmonary oedema. It would not directly cause carbon dioxide retention and wheeze.

stem: A 34-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) because she has fallen twice in the past 2 days. On one occasion, this occurred when she got up out of bed in the morning, and she felt light-headed before falling to the ﬂoor. On the other occasion, she had been sitting in a long business meeting, and when it ﬁnished, she stood up and again felt light-headed before collapsing. She does not think she lost consciousness on either occasion, and she was not drowsy after the episodes. She did not experience incontinence or bite her tongue. She has otherwise been well recently and does not report any fever. She has a history of poorly-controlled type I diabetes mellitus, for which she takes insulin although she sometimes forgets doses. She has an unremarkable cardiovascular, abdominal, and ear, nose and throat examination. There is no nystagmus. The GP performs an electrocardiogram (ECG), shown below. What is the likeliest cause of the falls in this patient?
explanation: A Autonomic neuropathy Autonomic neuropathy is a common complication of diabetes, which can result in postural hypotension and falls. Characteristically, the blood pressure falls rapidly after standing due to a neuronal failure to ensure vasoconstriction. Lying and standing blood pressure measurements would conﬁrm this diagnosis. A fall of ≥ 20 mmHg in systolic pressure or of ≥ 10 mmHg in diastolic pressure within 3 minutes of standing is abnormal. The fall in blood pressure typically occurs within 2-5 minutes of it being measured. The ECG here shows normal sinus rhythm and a QTc interval of 434 milliseconds (normal). D Peripheral neuropathy Peripheral neuropathy may occur in many diabetic patients, and this may lead to ulcers which may cause falls, but this would not cause dizziness, as seen here. B Arrhythmia Autonomic neuropathy is a common complication of diabetes, which can result in postural hypotension and falls. Characteristically, the blood pressure falls rapidly after standing due to a neuronal failure to ensure vasoconstriction.The ECG here shows normal sinus rhythm and a QTc interval of 434 milliseconds (normal). This, along with the lack of any mention of palpitations and the convincing history for postural hypotension, makes an arrythmia less likely. C Labyrinthitis Labyrinthitis can cause dizziness which may cause a person to fall. Typically, dizziness tends to be constant, particularly at ﬁrst; this is in contrast to this patient, whose dizziness is episodic and situational. The absence of nystagmus also makes this diagnosis less likely. E Seizures There are no features to suggest that seizures are the cause of this patients falls. She did not experience any loss of consciousness, tongue biting, incontinence or postictal symptoms, and the context of this patient’s history on a background of diabetes makes autonomic neuropathy a more likely cause of the falls.

stem: A 56-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of galactorrhoea for the past few months. She has a past medical history of chronic kidney disease (requiring peritoneal dialysis), previous hyperthyroidism (successfully treated with carbimazole which was subsequently stopped 2 years ago), and Raynaud’s syndrome for which she takes nifedipine. The GP performs a blood test which conﬁrms hyperprolactinaemia (1250 mu/l). What is the most likely cause of hyperprolactinaemia in this patient?
explanation: A Chronic kidneydisease (CKD) In CKD, patients may develop hyperprolactinaemia. This is due to the effect of uraemia on the hypothalamus, reducing the release of dopamine which promotes prolactin release. In addition, there is an impaired ability to metabolise prolactin in the kidney; this also contributes to the hyperprolactinaemia, which can cause galactorrhoea. E Sexual abstinence Sexual intercourse, and in particular orgasm, causes a transient rise in prolactin levels, not sexual abstinence. This is thought to be due to negative feedback following orgasm on neurons that regulate sexual motivation and function and therefore contributes to sexual refractoriness. B Dopamine receptor agonists Dopamine receptor agonists, such as bromocriptine, reduce the secretion of prolactin as they increase the inhibition of prolactin secretion. Dopamine receptor antagonists, such as metoclopramide, have the opposite effect and can cause hyperprolactinaemia. C Hyperthyroidism Hypothyroidism can cause hyperprolactinaemia, while hyperthyroidism does not. The cause of this is not clear, but hypothyroidism causes thyrotropin hyperplasia in the pituitary gland and sometimes lactotroph hyperplasia as well, which results in hyperprolactinaemia. D Nifedipine treatment Verapamil can cause hyperprolactinaemia, but not other calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine. The cause of this is not clear.

stem: A 30-year-old man attends the Endocrine Clinic along with his wife with a history of infertility. His General Practitioner (GP) had noted that the patient has gynaecomastia. He had mumps at age eight, and broke his arm aged 14. Otherwise, he has no past history of note. He is on no regular medications. On examination, he is tall, with sparse secondary sexual hair pattern. His testicular volume is less than 5 ml. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value 9 am testosterone 4 nmol/l 6-27 nmol/l Luteinising hormone (LH) Elevated Follicle stimulating-hormone (FSH) Elevated What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: E Klinefelter syndrome Low testosterone in the presence of raised LH and FSH suggests gonadal failure. Gynaecomastia and infertility are the two commonest presentations of Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY karyotype), which is often but not inevitably associated with reduced secondary sexual characteristics. D Adrenal tumour Oestrogen-producing adrenal tumours are rare and should not result in primary hypogonadism. Adrenocortical adenomas are associated with pituitary tumours in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, but in this case would cause hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. A Kallmann syndrome Kallmann syndrome is typiﬁed by either anosmia or severe hyposmia. It is also associated with hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. B Mump’s orchitis Testicular failure following mumps is a rare complication and only occurs following mumps orchitis when contracted after puberty. C Pituitary adenoma A pituitary adenoma will cause hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, resulting in both the LH and FSH being reduced.

stem: A 43-year-old man is reviewed in the Endocrinology Clinic and given a diagnosis of Cushing’s disease with a 0.9 cm pituitary adenoma. He has multiple medical problems including severe hypertension currently managed with three agents, poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and morbid obesity. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 166/95 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. His body mass index (BMI) is 38. He has bilateral lower limb swelling with severe varicose veins. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 141 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 258 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 15.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: C Start ketoconazole This patient has severe Cushing’s with multiple complications including poorly controlled hypertension, diabetes and obesity. As such he is at signiﬁcant operative risk. Ketoconazole is an effective agent for control of cortisol synthesis prior to surgery. It acts on several of the P450 enzymes, including the ﬁrst step in cortisol synthesis, cholesterol side-chain cleavage, and conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. A daily dose of 600- 800 mg often decreases cortisol production signiﬁcantly and will help in controlling blood sugar and blood pressure before moving to pituitary surgery. A Proceed directly to trans-sphenoidal resection Whilst this is the preferred option given the presence of a pituitary adenoma, the patient is a high operative risk given his comorbidities of severe hypertension, poorly controlled diabetes and morbid obesity making this option not the best of those available. B Start mitotane Mitotane is used in the treatment of adrenal cancer, rather than in the treatment of pituitary adenoma or Cushing’s. D Pituitary radiotherapy Pituitary radiotherapy is considered in patients who have persistently raised adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), but this is usually reserved for patients who have undergone surgery. E Proceed directly to adrenalectomy This patient is too high an operative risk given his multiple medical problems. In addition, he does not have an adrenal adenoma requiring adrenalectomy. The mechanism for ACTH production is via the pituitary adenoma.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department (ED) by the police. She is convinced that her husband is trying to poison her. Her husband tells you that she is hardly sleeping and seems almost hyperactive at present. She has a ﬁrst child who is four months old. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 150/85 mmHg, with a pulse of 100 beats per minute (bpm) and atrial ﬁbrillation (AF). Eye examination and thyroid palpation are normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 125 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.7 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 282 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l TSH < 0.05 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l T4 31.2 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l Anti-microsomal antibody + Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
C Post-partum thyroiditis Post-partum thyroiditis presents with hyperthyroidism in around 1/3 of sufferers some 1-4 months post- delivery. In rare cases thyrotoxicosis may be associated with a psychotic presentation, as seen here. The period of hyperthyroidism is followed by hypothyroidism and then resolution of the condition in the majority of patients; however, 1/3 of women develop permanent hypothyroidism, in which case permanent thyroid replacement is required. B Graves’ disease Graves’ disease is associated with TSH receptor antibodies. However 50-80% with graves disease may have positive anti microsomal antibody. This patient does not have any other features of graves disease and hence it is less likely. A Hashimoto’s thyroiditis The time of presentation is more consistent with post-partum thyroiditis, and patients with Hashimoto’s present with hypo-, not hyperthyroidism.

D Post-natal depression Post-partum psychosis can be excluded because of the abnormal thyroid function tests, suggesting that the psychological disturbance is related to thyrotoxicosis. E Atrophic thyroiditis Atrophic thyroiditis is rare, occurs in women aged 40-60 years and is associated with hypothyroidism.

stem: A 49-year-old woman with a history of type II diabetes mellitus comes to the Diabetes Clinic for review. She has been taking metformin for the last three years but is gradually losing control of her blood sugars, with multiple readings of > 10 mmol/l throughout the day. Her current metformin dose is 1 g twice daily (BD). She has a history of hypertension, which is currently managed with ramipril and indapamide. On examination, her BP is 155/85 mmHg and her heart rate is 67 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 124 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 102 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l HbA1C 62 mmol/mol < 48 mmol/mol Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: A Dapagliﬂozin This patient is obese and is outside the guidance for good HbA1C control set by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) at 58 mmol/mol for HbA1c; as such, she requires therapy intensiﬁcation. Out of the options given, the sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor is the most appropriate option because it results in modest calorie spillage into the urine and has positive effects on BP control. Patients, on average, see around 2% weight loss over six months, although in some, much greater weight reduction is seen. Evidence from cardiovascular outcomes among the class (the EMPA-REG study for empagliﬂozin) suggests a positive impact on cardiovascular outcomes. B Glimepiride Sulfonylureas promote weight gain and increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. Glimepiride is therefore suboptimal as a therapy option for this patient. C Liraglutide Although liraglutide is likely to drive greater weight loss compared to SGLT-2, it is not recommended by NICE guidelines to introduce a glucagon-like peptide 1 at this stage. It is recommended for patients with a BMI of over 35 kg/m2. D Pioglitazone Glitazones promote weight gain and ﬂuid retention, and over the longer term, have a negative impact on bone mineral density. They are therefore best avoided in a relatively young, obese woman. E Saxagliptin Dipeptidyl peptidase type IV (DPPIV) inhibitors are a possible option after metformin and do not increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. SGLT-2 inhibition, however, is preferred because it promotes greater weight loss and may be associated with positive cardiovascular outcomes, whereas DPPIV inhibitors have a neutral effect on cardiovascular outcomes in reported studies.

stem: A 73-year-old man visits his General Practitioner (GP) for his yearly medication review. He has a past medical history of osteoporosis, depression and heart failure. His medications include alendronate, bisoprolol, citalopram, furosemide, ranitidine and spironolactone. His GP performs some routine blood tests, which reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 144 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.3 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 173 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Urea 6.3 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 73 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Na+ 142 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 2.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Which medication is the most likely to be causing the hypokalaemia?
explanation: C Furosemide Furosemide is a diuretic that acts on the kidney and causes electrolyte disturbances, most typically hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and hypochloraemia. It does this by inhibiting the luminal sodium-potassium- chloride cotransporter which prevents reabsorption of sodium, chloride, and potassium in the thick ascending loop of Henle. It is, therefore, the most likely culprit medication in this case. D Ranitidine Ranitidine is used to treat acid reﬂux and does not tend to cause electrolyte disturbances. It may be given instead of omeprazole, which may cause hyponatraemia and hypomagnesaemia. Ranitidine may cause nausea or constipation. A Alendronate Alendronate is used to treat osteoporosis. It reduces the action of osteoclasts and may cause hypocalcaemia, but not hypokalaemia, as seen in this patient. B Citalopram Citalopram is used to treat depression and is a potential cause of hyponatraemia as it can cause syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). It does not, however, cause hypokalaemia. E Spironolactone Spironolactone is used to treat heart failure and can cause hyperkalaemia rather than hypokalaemia.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the Emergency Department (ED) after collapsing at home. She remembers walking to the dining room when she felt faint, had chest tightness and collapsed. When she woke up she called an ambulance. Over the last two years, she has seen her General Practitioner (GP) for chest tightness, palpitations, and dyspnoea, which lasted for minutes at a time. In the last few months, she had developed non-speciﬁc pins and needles in her extremities and ‘spots before her eyes’. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol socially. Her GP started her on a tricyclic antidepressant two weeks ago for depression. Her mother died of a stroke at age 48. On examination, she is alert, but notably restless, afebrile and has moist palms. Her pulse is 108 beats per minute (bpm) and regular and her blood pressure (BP) is 180/70 mmHg. She has a 2/6 pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex. Chest (including chest X-ray (CXR)) and abdominal examinations are normal, as is a neurological examination. An electrocardiogram (ECG) shows sinus rhythm. Urine testing reveals glucose++ and blood+. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Values Hb 189 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.0 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 471 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 75 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 4.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Glucose 9.5 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.56 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l CRP 6 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Phaeochromocytoma Phaeochromocytoma is a rare, catecholamine-producing tumour within the adrenal gland. (The ‘rule of tens’, ie 10% familial, 10% are bilateral, 10% are extra-adrenal, 10% are malignant, is no longer tenable, as approximately 30% of phaeochromocytomas are familial; the tumour location and malignancy risk are variable). There is an association with multiple endocrine neoplasia type II in familial cases, and also with the von Hippel– Lindau syndrome. Von Hippel–Lindau syndrome predisposes patients to renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and retinal and cerebellar haemangioblastomas. As a result, patients may have raised haemoglobin due to a secondary increase in erythropoietin production. This patient does have a raised haemoglobin and therefore needs to be screened for von Hippel–Lindau syndrome. Patients present with a variety of symptoms including episodic hypertension, chest tightness, abdominal pain, vomiting, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, pallor and weakness. Symptoms are precipitated by sneezing, stress, surgery and by agents such as cheese, alcohol and tricyclic antidepressants. Glycosuria occurs during attacks in 30% of cases. Tests that help in diagnosis include 24-hour metanephrines measurement, meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) and CT/MRI of the adrenal glands. B Transient ischaemic attack Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is deﬁned as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction. Duration of

symptom/sign is < 24 h. A normal neurological examination makes this diagnosis unlikely. A Cardiac arrhythmia Cardiac arrhythmias mimic several medical disorders as they can present with symptoms of palpitations (due to arrhythmia per se) or may be due to the haemodynamic consequences (dizziness, syncope, chest pain, light- headedness, weakness, breathlessness, anxiety). In this case, the presence of other features suggestive of phaechromocytomas makes this answer unlikely. C Systemic mastocytosis Mastocytosis is a condition characterised by excessive mast cell accumulation in one or multiple tissues, and is further divided into two categories: cutaneous mastocytosis (limited to the skin) and systemic mastocytosis, which involves extracutaneous organs like the bone marrow and gastrointestinal tract. The most common symptoms are pruritus on exposure to heat or physical irritation and the presence of urticarial pigmentosa, which are yellowish to reddish-brown papules seen on the extremities, chest and abdomen. E Coronary vasospasm Coronary vasospasm always presents with predominant chest pain with or without symptoms of nausea, sweating, dizziness, dyspnoea and palpitations. Diagnosis is based on ECG changes of transient ST-segment elevation at the time of an episode and absence of high-grade coronary stenoses on coronary arteriography.

stem: A 42-year-old man with a 30-year history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic complaining of frequent falls. On two occasions he has fainted and knocked his head and had to be taken to the Emergency Department, and at other times he was dizzy, but a short period sitting down improved things for him. He has a history of peripheral neuropathy and erectile dysfunction. He takes a basal bolus insulin regime involving insulin glargine and meal time Novorapid™. He also takes ramipril 5 mg/day for renoprotection and indapamide 2.5 mg. On examination his BP is 145/80 mmHg with a postural drop of 35 mmHg systolic. He has signs consistent with peripheral sensory neuropathy to the mid-shin. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 122 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 122 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c mmol/ml (6.73%) < 53 mmol/mol (<7.0%) Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation: E Stop indapamide This patient has peripheral neuropathy and almost certainly has signiﬁcant autonomic neuropathy, which accounts for the large postural drop in his blood pressure. A standing BP of 110 mmHg systolic is clearly acceptable, and therefore the most obvious ﬁrst step is in stopping his indapamide and monitoring his blood pressure over the subsequent 2–4 weeks. If he still has signiﬁcant postural hypotension then the next steps would be to add elastic stockings, followed by ﬂudrocortisone. The history of pre-syncope is much more suggestive of changes in blood pressure rather than changes in blood glucose. D Reduce background insulin Excess background insulin is primarily associated with fasting hypoglycaemia, which is not the cause of this patient’s collapse given the obvious postural hypotension. A Elastic stockings Elastic stockings are a potential intervention for patients who have persistent postural hypotension despite discontinuing the thiazide-like diuretic. B Fludrocortisone Fludrocortisone is considered for patients who fail to respond to conservative measures such as elastic stockings. C Reduce prandial insulin The postural drop in blood pressure points to hypotension rather than hypoglycaemia as the cause of this patient’s collapse.

stem: A 28-year-old woman consults her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of lethargy. She is currently taking ﬂuoxetine for postnatal depression, her child now being ﬁve months old. Other past history of note is type I diabetes mellitus, for which she is using a basal bolus insulin regime. Her thyroid hormone tests reveal a TSH of 7 mU/l (normal range: 0.4-5.0 mU/l) and a free T4 of 8.0 pmol/l (normal range: 10-22 pmol/l). Anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Which of the following most accurately represents her prognosis?
options: She is likely to progress rapidly to thyrotoxicosis
She is more likely to become euthyroid than to remain hypothyroid
She is more likely to remain hypothyroid than to become euthyroid
Corticosteroids can improve the chances of becoming euthyroid
Permanent thyroxine replacement therapy is likely to be needed
explanation: B She is more likely to become euthyroid than to remain hypothyroid Postpartum thyroid dysfunction is said to occur in 5-10% of women during the ﬁrst year after the birth of a child. Hyperthyroidism is said to occur within the ﬁrst 4 months of pregnancy, the only symptom of which may be tiredness, with hypothyroidism occurring later, at the 3-7-month stage. Often symptoms are mild and non- speciﬁc. Spontaneous recovery occurs in the majority of patients within 6-12 months of delivery, although around 40% eventually go on to develop permanent hypothyroidism. Risk of permanent hypothyroidism isn't closely related to the anti-TPO titre at the end of pregnancy because titres progressively fall during the course of pregnancy. D Corticosteroids can improve the chances of becoming euthyroid In patients with postpartum hypothyroidism, low-dose thyroxine (e.g. 50 μg) may be used to allow for spontaneous recovery to occur with re-checking of thyroid function off therapy after 6 months of treatment. There is no role for corticosteroids in treatment. A She is likely to progress rapidly to thyrotoxicosis The hyperthyroid phase presents with non-speciﬁc symptoms and may pass undetected. Patients either then become euthyroid or hypothyroid. C She is more likely to remain hypothyroid than to become euthyroid Around 40% of patients develop permanent hypothyroidism. E Permanent thyroxine replacement therapy is likely to be needed Long-term thyroxine replacement is only necessary in those patients who develop permanent hypothyroidism.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of lethargy. She works in the local pharmacy and has had to ask for increasing amounts of time off work. Apparently there is no past medical history of note, apart from some trouble due to an eating disorder as a teenager. On examination, she looks normal. Her BP is 105/64 mmHg. Her BMI is 20 kg/m2. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 121 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 200 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO32-) 34 mmol/l 24–30 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
D Thiazide abuse This patient works in a pharmacy, so it is possible she has access to medicine, and we hear she has a history of an eating disorder as a teenager. Thiazide abuse would result in exactly this picture, with normal BP, hypokalaemia and high bicarbonate. C Conn’s syndrome Primary hyperaldosteronism is associated with hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, rather than the normal blood pressure seen here. A Bartter syndrome Bartter syndrome may present with a similar biochemical picture, although access to diuretics given she works in a pharmacy is much more likely to be the cause of her symptoms. B Gitelman syndrome Although Gitelman syndrome may also present with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, it differs from Bartter in that it is associated with reduced calcium excretion. E Liddle’s syndrome Liddle syndrome is associated with hypertension, and hence cannot be the diagnosis here. It is caused by a mutation in the

epithelial sodium channel.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for a 6month review after surgery for a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma. She presented to the General Practitioner originally with changes in her facial appearance, soft tissue swelling affecting her hands and feet, and impaired glucose tolerance. Her glucose metabolism has returned to normal. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 70 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m2. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 130 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.1 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) Just above the upper limit of normal Which of the following would be most likely to occur as a long-term consequence of acromegaly?
explanation: C Left ventricular hypertrophy The underlying diagnosis here is that of acromegaly due to the history of the typical clinical features of growth hormone excess in the setting of a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma. Cardiovascular complications are common in acromegaly, including hypertension, arrythmias, biventricular hypertrophy, systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction. This is in direct response to increased levels of growth hormone and IGF1 causing increased cardiac contractility and increased calcium uptake. The cardiovascular effects have been indicated to reduce life expectancy as much as ten years on average in comparison to the general population. Uncontrolled acromegaly (evidenced by high IGF-1 level) also leads to higher rates of sleep apnoea and insulin re- sistance. A Colon cancer While there is an association between acromegaly and colon cancer (up to 5% of all acromegalic patients) a much higher number of patients have premalignant polyps (up to 30% of all acromegalic patients). B Duodenal ulcers Duodenal ulcers are associated with gastrin secreting pancreatic cancers; however, these tumours are rare and duodenal ulceration is not the commonest association with acromegaly. D Sleep apnoea The soft tissue swelling associated with acromegaly gives rise to sleep apnoea. Up to one third of acromegalic patients suffer from obstructive sleep apnoea and treatment of acromegaly variably effects rates of sleep apnoea, but there does tend to be some remission in symptoms following surgery, as per this patient’s presentation. E Uterine cancer Benign uterine tumours are associated with acromegaly rather than uterine cancer.

stem: A 32-year-old woman who is known to have autoimmune hypothyroidism presents with nausea, vomiting and lethargy. Medication of note includes thyroxine and the oral contraceptive pill. On examination her BP is 110/70 mmHg, with a pulse of 70/min; she has a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing and her pulse increases by 10/min. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 105 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 124 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 2.56 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l There are areas of depigmented skin, as seen in her right hand below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: B Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 This is the commonest subtype, and includes autoimmune Addison’s disease in combination with thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus. There are associations with other autoimmune conditions such as coeliac disease and pernicious anaemia, which could explain the anaemia, and primary hypogonadism, vitiligo and myasthenia gravis are also commonly observed. C Gastroenteritis Gastroenteritis is a self-limiting infectious illness causing diarrhoea and vomiting, and is not normally associated with anaemia or hyponatraemia. A Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 Type 1 polyglandular syndrome is associated with mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison's disease. The normal calcium here effectively rules out hypoparathyroidism. It also encompasses both autoimmune hypoparathyroidism and hypoadrenalism. D Isolated new onset Addison's disease This lady possibly does have a new diagnosis of Addison’s disease, but in view of her other autoimmune history this option is incorrect. E Pernicious anaemia Patients with this condition typically present with progressive symptoms of anaemia (breathlessness, chest pain, lethargy) or symptoms of B12 deﬁciency (motor-sensory polyneuropathy and eventually subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord). It is caused by autoimmune atrophic gastritis, with the presence of anti-parietal cell antibodies.

stem: A 54-year-old man with a seven year history of type II diabetes has been diagnosed with background diabetic retinopathy at his annual review. He was also recently admitted to hospital with an episode of cardiac failure after an anterior myocardial infarction (MI). He is taking gliclazide 80 mg twice a day as he has failed to tolerate metformin. On examination, his body mass index (BMI) is elevated at 35 kg/m2. A recent Hb A1C reading was 7.1%. His blood pressure (BP) 154/85 mmHg. Proteinuria is positive and total cholesterol is 5.4 mmol/l with a high- density lipoprotein (HDL) level of 0.7 mmol/l. You are considering switching his blood glucose-lowering medication because of recent weight gain. Which of the following is the most appropriate switch therapy with respect to overall cardiovascular risk in this patient?
explanation:
B Empagliﬂozin Blood glucose-lowering medications in the GLP-1 and SGLT2 inhibitor class have been shown to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). As such, empagliﬂozin, which causes glucose excretion and can have positive effects on weight, reduces cardiovascular death and incident cardiac failure, is the most appropriate choice. C Lixisenatide Although liraglutide has shown a positive effect on MACE,

lixisenatide has not shown an impact on MACE events in a secondary prevention type 2 diabetes population. A Insulin Insulin has no effect in reducing cardiovascular risk, and indeed may increase the risk of heart failure in patients with type 2 diabetes. As such, it is best avoided here. D Saxagliptin Saxagliptin showed no positive impact on MACE events, although its use was associated with a small increase in cardiac failure episodes during the course of a cardiovascular outcome trial. E Sitagliptin Sitagliptin shows no positive impact on MACE events, although unlike saxagliptin the use of sitagliptin did not increase the risk of cardiac failure in the context of its cardiovascular outcome trial.

stem: A 38-year-old South-Asian man is referred to the Outpatient Clinic. He is currently undergoing treatment for tuberculosis, which is known to involve the renal tracts in this case. The only other past history of note is hypertension, for which he takes ramipril 10 mg daily. The infectious disease doctor has referred him to you because of some abnormal tests, which reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value TSH 6.5 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Free T4 8.4 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l K+ 5.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Na+ Computed tomography (CT) scan 131 mmol/l Adrenal calciﬁcation 135–145 mmol/l His blood pressure (BP) in the clinic is actually low with a systolic of 100 mmHg. Which of the following actions would be most appropriate in this case?
explanation: C Arrange a short synacthen test This man is not acutely unwell and you have time to conﬁrm the diagnosis of hypoadrenalism with a short synacthen test. If this is positive then you would consider commencing hydrocortisone replacement. The low BP, coupled with the low sodium and raised potassium, raise the suspicion of hypoadrenalism in this case. E Check anti-adrenal antibodies Adrenal antibody testing can be extremely helpful in elucidating the cause of suspected adrenal failure. The adrenal calciﬁcation suggests the possibility of tuberculosis infection, so that anti-adrenal antibodies are unlikely to be helpful here. A Commence 50 mcg thyroxine/day His thyroid function tests are abnormal, but you would not commence thyroid hormone replacement at this stage. Commencing thyroxine in a patient with hypoadrenalism may precipitate a rapid deterioration in their condition. It would be most important to conﬁrm the diagnosis of adrenal insufﬁciency, commence steroid hormone replacement and then re-check the thyroid function testing later. B Check anti-TPO antibodies Autoimmune thyroid dysfunction is commonly associated with Addison’s. Although the suspicion is that this patient is hypoadrenal, this is likely to be secondary to TB rather than an autoimmune cause. D Commence ﬂudrocortisone 100mcg/day Fludrocortisone replacement is not normally required in the acute stage in the treatment of hypoadrenalism, but can be added once the dose of hydrocortisone is reduced after a few days.

stem: A 18-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with diabetic ketoacidosis. He is subsequently diagnosed with type I diabetes mellitus and commences insulin, to which he adapts well. After 3 months of treatment, he begins to feel very dizzy, and, upon checking his capillary blood glucose (CBG), he ﬁnds that it is 2.8 mmol/l. This happens on three consecutive days. On the fourth day, he decides to stop his insulin treatment, and he subsequently monitors his CBG throughout the day. During the day, his CBG ranges between 5.3 – 10.2, and he feels well with no dizziness. What is the likeliest cause of the hypoglycaemia seen in this patient?
explanation: C ‘Honeymoon period’ Many patients experience a ‘honeymoon period’ after they are diagnosed with type I diabetes. This typically occurs after around 3 months of treatment and occurs because residual beta islet cells in the pancreas are still able to synthesise a small amount of insulin. The precise mechanism is not understood, but patients tend to require less insulin or even no insulin while it lasts, which can be from months to years. D Insulinoma An insulinoma is a rare cause of hypoglycaemia and would not be consistent with the episode of diabetic ketoacidosis and the subsequent diagnosis of type I diabetes. Insulinomas typically present with repeated episodes of unprovoked hypoglycaemia. A Adrenal insufﬁciency Adrenal insufﬁciency does not cause diabetic ketoacidosis, which is what led to the diagnosis of type I diabetes in this patient. Adrenal insufﬁciency can cause hypoglycaemia, but he would need steroid treatment to feel better, whereas this patient felt better simply after he stopped the insulin treatment. B Error with insulin administration It is possible that the patient was administering himself too much insulin, but this is less likely to occur suddenly after 3 months of treatment, and this patient adapted well when he was started on insulin. E Misdiagnosis of diabetes Since this patient was admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis and was then successfully treated for type I diabetes for 3 months, it is unlikely that he was misdiagnosed. Given the timing of the symptoms, it is more likely that the hypoglycaemia is due to a ‘honeymoon period’ and in the future, he will require insulin when this period ends.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who is 10 weeks’ pregnant is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic by her General Practitioner (GP). She is suffering from a great deal of tiredness and morning sickness. The GP is concerned about her thyroid function. She has lost 2 kg in weight over the past month. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 115/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 65 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value TSH 0.2 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Free T4 27 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Ask GP to repeat thyroid function tests in 2 months
explanation: A Ask GP to repeat thyroid function tests in 2 months Suppressed TSH with a small rise in free T4 is a normal ﬁnding in 13.5% of women in the ﬁrst trimester, and 4.5% of women in the second trimester. Hyperemesis gravidarum is the most likely underlying condition. The suppressed TSH with slightly elevated levels of T4 is due to the partial thyroidstimulating action of beta-HCG. No speciﬁc management is indicated. Thyroid function tests are likely to have returned to normal on retesting. D Refer for partial thyroidectomy Thyroidectomy is indicated for Graves’ disease in pregnancy where medical therapy with thionamides is ineffective or contra-indicated. B Start propylthiouracil At this stage of pregnancy, without overt symptoms of hyperthyroidism and with TSH and T4 only slightly outside the normal range, thionamides aren’t indicated. C Start carbimazole Like propylthiouracil, carbimazole isn’t indicated, because the overserved thyroid blood tests seen here are a normal physiological ﬁnding. E Consider radioiodine Radioiodine is contra-indicated in pregnancy, and treatment isn’t indicated because the thyroid function tests seen here are not as a result of thyrotoxicosis, but as a result of excess betaHCG.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology clinic with a 3-week history of anxiety and palpitations. She reports that even when she is resting, she ﬁnds that she is tremulous. There is no history of chest pain or shortness of breath and she is eating and drinking well, although she is having difﬁculty maintaining her weight. She is 18 weeks pregnant. Examination reveals a BP of 125/82 mmHg and a heart rate of 95 bpm and regular. She has a ﬁne resting tremor bilaterally. There is a small, smooth goitre, which is mildly tender on palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal values TSH < 0.05 U/l 0.4–5.0 U/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for the likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Carbimazole It seems this patient has Graves’ disease presenting in pregnancy. Although block–replace is the standard intervention outside pregnancy, it cannot be used here as thyroxine does not cross the placenta and there will be a risk of fetal hypothyroidism. Carbimazole is the safest option in the second and third stages of pregnancy, and the dose is titrated to a target TSH level of 0.2–3.0 IU/l. C Propranolol Propranolol is a beta blocker that is generally prescribed with signiﬁcant caution in pregnancy, as beta blocker use in pregnancy has been shown to be associated with intrauterine growth restriction, fetal bradycardia and neonatal hypoglycaemia. B Naproxen Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are indicated for pain relief in patients suffering from subacute thyroiditis. They are less useful in treatment of Graves’ disease and should be avoided in pregnancy. D Propylthiouracil Propylthiouracil has been reported to cause maternal hepatotoxicity after the ﬁrst trimester. As such,carbimazole is the preferred option for antithyroid therapy. E Thyroxine and propylthiouracil Propylthiouracil is not recommended after the ﬁrst trimester, and thyroxine does not cross the placenta. Therefore, if block– replace is used where antithyroid drugs are maximised, fetal hypothyroidism is precipitated. This is not an appropriate option because of the use of propylthiouracil and because block– replace is not recommended.

stem: A 48-year-old man is referred to the Endocrinology Clinic with newly diagnosed type II diabetes. He reports that he leads a healthy lifestyle and is surprised about the diagnosis. His past medical history includes hypertension, which is managed with amlodipine and indapamide. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg and his heart rate is 88 bpm. His cardiorespiratory examination is unremarkable, although he appears to be clammy and sweating. His abdomen is soft and non- tender. There is soft tissue swelling of his hands and he reports having had to remove his wedding ring due to it feeling tighter than usual. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 149 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 300 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50 – 120 µmol/l Random glucose 12.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial investigation to conﬁrm this patient’s likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
B IGF-1 measurement This patient has a clinical picture consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. Usually, IGF-1 measurement varies with age and nutritional status; however, reference ranges exist for comparison. Additionally, IGF-1 has a long half-life and, as such, is a useful measure of growth hormone status. Failure of growth hormone to suppress in response to an oral glucose challenge is the other diagnostic method of choice for assessing patients with possible acromegaly, although this is less convenient following an initial clinic appointment. A Fasting plasma glucose

Although an elevation in fasting plasma glucose level may indicate a diagnosis of diabetes, it will not reveal the underlying cause, which, in this case, is likely to be acromegaly. C Prolactin measurement Prolactin levels may be elevated because of local pressure effects from a pituitary adenoma. However, it will not conﬁrm elevated growth hormone levels. D Random cortisol measurement The symptoms seen in this patient ﬁt better with acromegaly, rather than with elevated cortisol levels as a result of hyperadrenalism due to either an adrenal or a pituitary tumour. E Random growth hormone measurement Growth hormone is released in a pulsatile fashion and has a short half-life. As such, random measurement is not useful in conﬁrming a diagnosis of acromegaly.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of tiredness and malaise, which came on after a short viral illness. She also has pain which appears to be referred to her lower jaw. On examination of the neck the thyroid gland appears to be generally tender and is nodular on palpation. Her TSH is measured at < 0.05 mU/l (normal range: 0.4-5.0 mU/l), while her ESR is raised at 45 mm/hour and a technetium scan reveals decreased thyroid uptake. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D de Quervain’s Thyroiditis De Quervain’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of a painful thyroid gland and causes hyperthyroidism initially, sometimes followed by transient hypothyroidism. The underlying cause is felt to be either a viral infection or the postviral inﬂammatory response. The condition is more common in females. The typical course of the disease consists of an acute phase, in which the main complaint is pain, although signs of hyperthyroidism may also be present. This is followed by a transient asymptomatic and euthyroid phase which evolves into the hypothyroid phase. The hypothyroid state may be- come permanent in 5–10% of patients, but the vast majority go on to the recovery phase, characterised by normalisation of thyroid structure and function. The treatment is consequently directed towards the control of pain and thyroid symptoms. Initial symptomatic hyperthyroidism can be treated with betablockade, but anti-thyroid drugs are of no value since the excess circulating thyroid hormone is due to the release of preexisting thyroid hormone because of follicular damage rather than from increased synthesis. If hypothyroidism occurs in the late stages, replacement therapy is required and is guided by the TSH levels. Radionucleotide scanning reveals decreased uptake from the thyroid gland. A Hashimoto’s thyroiditis Hashimoto’s presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism. On examination there is often a hard goitre which is non-tender. Anti-thyroid peroxidise antibodies are usually raised. B Riedel’s thyroiditis Riedel’s thyroiditis is characterised by intense ﬁbrosis of the gland. Most patients remain euthyroid. Symptoms of tracheal compression can occur. C Graves’ disease Radionucleotide scanning is useful in distinguishing between Graves’ and other causes of thyrotoxicosis: it will show increased uptake in the whole gland in Graves’ disease. E Pyogenic thyroiditis Pyogenic thyroiditis is rare and is associated with a pyogenic infection elsewhere. Patients can present with pain and swelling in the neck. and fever. TFTs are often normal.

stem: A 46-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) complaining of polydipsia and polyuria. He is careful with his weight and regularly visits the gym, but still feels that his health is deteriorating and he is actually ﬁnding it difﬁcult to maintain his weight and muscle mass. He also complains of diarrhoea and a skin rash which seems to break down and bruise/bleed easily. He has no past medical history, apart from a recent fall from his bike after which he sustained a head injury. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 135/85 mmHg. His pulse is 68 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. His body mass index (BMI) is 25 kg/m2. On dipstick urine testing, there are 2+ of glucose. Which of the following would best explain these ﬁndings?
explanation: D Glucagonoma Glucagonoma is vanishingly rare, with an annual incidence estimated at 1 in 20 million, but it ﬁts the bill here as the only potential cause of secondary diabetes mellitus from the options listed. The fact his weight is normal and he has developed diabetes whilst still maintaining a healthy weight and lifestyle is suggestive of secondary diabetes. A Head Injury Head injury can be a cause of transient diabetes insipidus that usually recovers slowly over the course of a few weeks. B Hypothyroidism Autoimmune thyroid disease is associated with type 1 diabetes, but wouldn’t account for the glycosuria seen here. C Hyperparathyroidism Hyperparathyroidism may be associated with diuresis related to hypercalcaemia, but we are given no evidence here of elevated serum calcium. E Insulinoma Insulinomas present with recurrent episodes of collapse due to hypoglycaemia, and gradual weight gain because of compensatory eating.

stem: A 17-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhoea. She has never had a menstrual period and reports no cyclical abdominal pain. She denies symptoms of hot ﬂashes or night sweats. She has normal breast development (Tanner stage 4) and scant pubic hair (Tanner stage 2). Physical examination reveals a tall stature, a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus, but absent ovaries. Investigation Result Normal value FSH 85 IU/l 1.5–12.4 IU/l Luteinising hormone (LH) 40 IU/l 1.7–8.6 IU/l Oestradiol Undetectable 20–50 pg/ml Karyotype 45,X – What is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient?
options: Perform MRI of the brain to evaluate pituitary func- tion
Schedule surgical evaluation for ovarian transplantation
explanation: A Start combined oestrogen–progesterone therapy The patient has primary ovarian insufﬁciency likely due to Turner syndrome (45,X karyotype), which causes gonadal dysgenesis and leads to elevated FSH and LH levels. Combined oestrogen–progesterone therapy is recommended to promote secondary sexual characteristics, support bone health and initiate menstrual cycling. E Initiate cyclic progesterone therapy alone Progesterone alone would not be appropriate because the patient requires both oestrogen and progesterone for complete hormone replacement. Oestrogen is necessary for developing secondary sexual characteristics, and progestin is added to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. B Perform MRI of the brain to evaluate pituitary function MRI of the brain is not necessary here because the elevated gonadotrophin (FSH and LH) levels indicate that the amenorrhoea is due to primary ovarian failure, not a pituitary issue. Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism would present with low FSH and LH levels. C Begin growth hormone therapy Growth hormone therapy may be considered earlier in childhood for Turner syndrome to improve height, but it is generally less effective after puberty. This patient has already a tall stature, and hormone replacement is the priority at this stage. D Schedule surgical evaluation for ovarian transplantation Ovarian transplantation is not a treatment option for Turner syndrome-related amenorrhoea. Instead, hormone replacement therapy is the standard management to prevent complications of oestrogen deﬁciency.

stem: A 32-year-old woman complains that she urinates around 6 litres a day and is constantly thirsty. She has a past medical history of diabetes mellitus and bipolar disorder. She takes insulin and lithium and no other medications. She is referred to an Endocrine Clinic.
