Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 134 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 8.3 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 183 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Urea 6.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 93 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Na+ 162 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Random glucose 13.5 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Water deprivation tests reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Urine osmolarity after ﬂuid deprivation mOsm/kg 800 - 1200 mOsm/kg Urine osmolarity after desmopressin administration mOsm/kg 1000 - 1200 mOsm/kg What is the likeliest cause of the hypernatraemia seen in this patient?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
explanation: B Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI) NDI would explain all the clinical ﬁndings of excessive urination and polydipsia along with the hypernatraemia and the results of the water deprivation test. The pathological problem is the reduced responsiveness of the kidney to antidiuretic hormone (in this case probably caused by lithium). Therefore the urine osmolality does not improve after the dose of desmopressin. A Cranial diabetes insipidus (CDI) CDI would result in hypernatraemia and the same symptoms, but the urine osmolality would improve to greater than 800 mOsm/kg after desmopressin administration. This is due to their being a cranial defect in the production of antidiuretic hormone, so when a synthetic hormone is given, there is a full renal response and improvement in the osmolality. C Partial diabetes insipidus An improvement in urine osmolality would evidence partial diabetes insipidus after administration of desmopressin where the osmolality increases to above 300 mOsm/kg but remains less than 800 mOsm/kg. D Primary polydipsia Primary polydipsia is caused by excessive drinking of ﬂuids and may be seen in patients with a history of psychiatric disease such as this patient. However, the water deprivation results are not consistent with this diagnosis since the urine osmolality would be expected to be greater than 800 mOsm/kg, both after water deprivation and after desmopressin administration. This is because there is no defect in the production or sensitivity to antidiuretic hormone in this condition. Therefore when the ﬂuid intake is reduced, there is a normal physiological secretion of antidiuretic hormone, which increases the osmolality. E Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) SIADH typically causes hyponatraemia rather than hypernatraemia. In SIADH, there is an excess of antidiuretic hormone, whereas diabetes insipidus is caused by a lack of, or resistance to, antidiuretic hormone.

stem: A 65-year-old woman is brought into hospital critically ill and with a reduced level of consciousness. Her relatives state she has been increasingly lethargic over the past month and had put on weight. She had been slightly confused, with constipation, and was commenced on antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection. She currently takes no regular medication. Her pulse is 55/min, blood pressure 125/98 mmHg, temperature 34°C, respiratory rate 8/min, oxygen saturations 98% on air. Examination reveals coarse facial features with dry skin, thin hair and brittle nails. Initial investigations: Investigation Result Normal values ECG Sinus bradycardia Glucose 5.9 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Urea 15.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Na+ 127 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 5.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 223 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l After giving her IV hydrocortisone, which other therapy would you consider?
explanation:
B Intravenous T3 Myxoedema coma can be the initial presentation of hypothyroidism, but more usually occurs against a background of long-standing disease where patients are unable to comply with their thyroxine replacement. Patients will have a history of cold intolerance, weight gain, increasing lethargy and constipation. Facial features include general coarsening with periorbital oedema and hair thinning. This is an emergency, and treatment involves intravenous thyroxine and slow rewarming. It is also important to take serum for thyroid function and adrenal function. Coexisting hypoadrenalism is suggested by the hyponatraemia, the hyperkalaemia and a raised urea. Patients may also be hypoglycaemic, although that is not the case here. Treatment with hydrocortisone is recommended until Addison’s disease can be excluded. It is important to provide hydrocortisone until Addison's is excluded, as just giving thyroid hormone alone may precipitate an adrenal crisis. C Rapid rewarming

The patient is hypothermic and she should be rewarmed slowly in order to improve the chance of neurological recovery. A Rapid intravenous ﬂuids The patient has a normal blood pressure with bradycardia, and therefore there is no indication for aggressive ﬂuid resuscitation. Moreover, she is hyponatraemic, and therefore the correction of sodium levels should be gradual in order to avoid central pontine myelinolysis. D Hypertonic saline This is indicated in cases of severe hyponatraemia (Na <115 mmol/l) presenting with seizures. In all other cases, hypertonic saline should be administered on ICU or after discussion with an endocrinologist. In our case, the patient is mildly hyponatraemic (Na 127 mmol/l) and this doesn’t account for her level of consciousness. E Demeclocycline This is a semi-synthetic tetracycline antibiotic that can be used off-licence for the treatment of hyponatraemia caused by SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion). It works by reducing the responsiveness of the collecting tubule cells to ADH. In this case, the cause of the hyponatraemia is unknown although it could be due to adrenal insufﬁciency, and therefore demeclocycline would not be effective.

stem: A pregnant woman at 26 weeks of gestation has clinical evidence of hyperthyroidism. She is very anxious and complains of palpitations, heat intolerance and difﬁculty maintaining her weight during the pregnancy. On examination her BP is 120/70 mmHg, with pulse 95/min regular. There is no obvious goitre on neck examination. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 190 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 94 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l TSH <0.05 μU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Anti-thyroid antibodies +ve How would you propose to manage her?
explanation: A Carbimazole There are associated risks for both the fetus and the mother associated with untreated maternal thyrotoxicosis. Unfortunately, thionamides may also cross the placenta and precipitate fetal goitre and hypothyroidism. For this reason patients are usually managed with a dose which keeps their T4 just within the upper limit of the normal range. Carbimazole is associated with rare reports of fetal abnormalities, meaning that propylthioracil is often used in early pregnancy (3 months) with a later switch to carbimazole after the ﬁrst trimester. C Propylthiouracil Propylthiouracil is now rarely used in late pregnancy because of case reports of maternal hepatotoxicity. B Radioiodine This is contraindicated in pregnancy because of accumulation in both the fetal thyroid and the mother’s thyroid gland. D Propranolol Although propranolol will treat symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, it won’t signiﬁcantly impact on the risk of miscarriage. E Prednisolone Prednisolone doesn’t signiﬁcantly impact on the progression of autoimmune thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy and therefore has no role here.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with headaches, sweating, anxiety and palpitations. She states that members of her family on her father’s side have had similar symptoms and have required surgery. She is also complaining of polydipsia and constipation. On examination, her blood pressure is elevated at 165/92. She had two 24 h urinary collections for catecholamines, which were above the upper limit of normal. Her bone proﬁle revealed: Investigation Result Normal values Corrected (Ca2+) 2.71 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 1.1 mmol/l 1.1 - 1.45 mmol/l PTH 19 pmol/l 0.9 - 5.4 pmol/l Her physician would like to send her for genetic testing. Which condition would he like to test her for?
explanation: B MEN 2A Type 2 Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN 2) is a rare familial cancer syndrome caused by mutations in the RET protooncogene. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. MEN 2A patients present with phaeochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia and medullary thyroid carcinoma. C MEN 2B This condition is characterised by the presence of mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, along with phaechromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma. A Von Hippel-Landau disease Clinical hallmarks of this disease include the development of retinal and central nervous system haemangioblastomas, which are absent in this case. Moreover, hyperparathyroid hyperplasia is not part of the condition. D MEN 1 The main components of MEN 1 are hyperparathyroidism and pituitary and pancreatic tumours. From the pituitary tumours, 25-90% are usually prolactinomas although growth hormone or ACTH secretion has also been described. The pancreatic tumours can be non-functioning, originating from the beta-cells (insulinoma) or originating from non-beta-cells and secreting other peptides such as glucagon, pancreatic polypeptide, somatostatin, chromogranin or gastrin. E Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia This is a genetic condition caused in the majority of cases due to loss of function mutations in the calcium- sensing receptor (CaSR) gene, expressed in parathyroid and kidney tissue. The perceived lack of calcium levels by the parathyroid leads to constitutively high levels of parathyroid hormone and therefore hypercalcaemia. Urine calcium/creatinine ratio has to be less than 0.01 in order to consider this condition as a cause for primary hyperparathyroidism. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid • Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2A: medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, phaeochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism (inherited in autosomal dominant fashion) • MEN type 2B: the above features which are found in MEN 2A and mucosal neuromas (most likely to be sporadic, although where inherited follows an autosomal dominant pattern). They are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Phaechromocytomas are also associated with other conditions: von Hippel–Lindau disease, neuroﬁbromatosis, and tuberous sclerosis.

stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of chronic cough with haemoptysis comes to the Emergency Room with severe vomiting and dehydration. His relatives tell you that he has suffered from the cough for over three months and has progressively lost weight. He smokes 40–50 cigarettes per day. On examination, he looks unwell and has a BMI of 18, with a BP of 95/70 mmHg and a pulse of 75/min. There are coarse crackles on auscultation of both lung ﬁelds. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 119 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 198 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 124 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 145 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l His chest X-ray is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: C Adrenal metastases This patient has an underlying bronchial carcinoma, and whilst adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH)- producing tumours are seen which lead to a Cushing-type picture, hypoadrenalism is usually related to the presence of metastases. Severe gastroenteritis with vomiting leads to hypokalaemia; in this case, given that the potassium is at the upper end of the normal range, another cause such as Addison’s is more likely. This patient has likely got a lung malignancy, as evidenced by the left hilar mass seen on his CXR and the history. He is hypotensive and hyponatraemic, which is suggestive of adrenal insufﬁciency. The most common cause in this case would be adrenal metastases, and therefore adrenal metastases is the correct answer. A staging CT will help conﬁrm the diagnosis. A Autoimmune adrenal failure This diagnosis is possible but incorrect, as in the context of possible lung cancer, metastases is more likely. B Paraneoplastic syndrome Small cell lung cancer has an association with inappropriate secretions of anti-diuretuc hormone (ADH), but it would not explain his symptoms of vomiting and hypotension. It also does not normally present so acutely. D Severe gastroenteritis There are no infective symptoms to suggest that gastroenteritis is the underlying diagnosis in this case. You would also expect the electrolytes to reveal hypernatraemia associated with dehydration, as well as hypokalaemia from electrolyte loss E Acute tubular necrosis We have no abnormal blood tests to suggest an acute kidney injury.

stem: A 26-year-old woman who is 36 weeks pregnant presents to her General Practitioner with a history of palpitations, sweating, and diarrhoea. She has no past medical history of note and her pregnancy has otherwise been unremarkable. On examination, she has a resting tremor. Her pulse is 100 bpm and regular. Her BP is 118/68 mmHg. Heart sounds are normal. Her chest is clear and abdominal examination reveals a gravid uterus correct for her dates. Investigation reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 126 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 214 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l MCV 86 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ Na+ 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 62 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urea 4.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Bilirubin 6 μmol/l 2–17 µmol/l Albumin 38 g/l 35–55 g/l ALP 68 U/l 30–150 U/l ALT 26 U/l 5–30 U/l TSH 0.01 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Free T4 36.4 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l She plans to breastfeed her baby after delivery. What is the most appropriate therapy?
options: Carbimazole till delivery and then switch to PTU
Propylthiouracil till delivery and then switch to carbimazole
Radioiodine therapy after delivery of the baby
Blocking dose of carbimazole with supplemental thyroxine
explanation:
B Carbimazole till delivery and then switch to PTU The choice here is between carbimazole and propylthiouracil at a dose to control thyroid hormone levels without blocking them completely. What drives the choice between propylthiouracil and carbimazole in this situation is the adverse event proﬁle. Cases of fatal hepatotoxicity have been described with propylthiouracil, and for this reason carbimazole is always recommended in late pregnancy. Neither is recommended in breastfeeding, although if the patient still wishes to breastfeed, switching to propylthiouracil post-partum is potentially the safer option. A Lugol’s iodine Lugol’s iodine is occasionally prescribed for patients undergoing thyroid surgery, but causes goitre in infants. It is primarily used for short-term control of thyrotoxicosis. C Propylthiouracil till delivery and then switch to carbimazole Propylthiouracil is not recommended here because of the risk of maternal hepatotoxicity. D Radioiodine therapy after delivery of the baby Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and it is recommended that patients avoid be-

coming pregnant for six months after therapy. It also presents logistical difﬁculties in that the woman would not be able to remain in close proximity to her baby for some time after dosing. E Blocking dose of carbimazole with supplemental thyroxine Carbimazole crosses the placenta but thyroxine does not, so the ‘block and replace’ approach could render the neonate profoundly hypothyroid.

stem: You review a 62-year-old type 2 diabetic who is taking metformin 2 g per day and gliclazide 160 mg per day and ramipril for renoprotection. Recent HbA1c was 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4%) and his blood pressure was 140/75 mmHg. You review his eye photograph that reveals dot-and-blot haemorrhages, cotton wool spots and micro- aneurysms. None are within close proximity to the macula. Which of the following treatments represents the best option for reducing the probability of further deterioration of his diabetic retinopathy over the long term?
options: Addition of valsartan to his blood pressure regime
Addition of amlodipine to his blood pressure regime
explanation: A Gradual transition to insulin therapy This patient’s blood pressure is relatively well controlled, yet there is room for signiﬁcant improvement in his blood glucose. Achievement of the target HbA1c of 53.0 mmol/mol (7.0%) would be associated with signiﬁcantly reduced progression of retinopathy. D Laser therapy Although laser therapy reduces progression of retinopathy, there are no high-risk features currently identiﬁed on retinal photography. B Addition of valsartan to his blood pressure regime Addition of ARB to an ACE inhibitor brings little added impact on blood pressure control, with signiﬁcantly increased risk of hyperkalaemia. As such, it should be avoided. C Addition of amlodipine to his blood pressure regime The next step in further intensiﬁcation of blood pressure con- trol is addition of a calcium antagonist such as amlodipine, although amongst the calcium antagonist class, only diltiazem has been shown to impact signiﬁcantly on proteinuria. E Increasing gliclazide to 320 mg/day The dose–response curve for gliclazide above 160 mg is fairly ﬂat, and hence there is little value in a further increase in sulphonylurea dose.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with a left Colles’ fracture after a relatively minor fall at work. He lives alone and admits that he has difﬁculty maintaining sexual interest in women. He holds down a normal job although he has recently had time off work with depression. On examination he has sparse secondary sexual hair and small testes. His BP is 138/88 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 126 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 197 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.7 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 124 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected Ca2+ 2.2 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l T-score -3.1 Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage him?
explanation:
E Testosterone From the history we are given, the suspicion is that this patient has underlying hypogonadism, most probably due to Klinefelter syndrome. Small testes, sparse sexual hair, problems with depression and sexual function are all in keeping with the diagnosis. Testosterone is known to improve bone mineralization and is the treatment of choice here; it is also likely to impact on his sexual function and may consequently improve his depressive symptoms. Unfortunately, due to late diagnosis of Klinefelter, a signiﬁcant number of patients begin testosterone replacement therapy far too late. D Raloxifene This is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator used in the

treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis where bisphosphonates are not tolerated. A Weekly alendronate This would be considered a standard intervention for postmenopausal osteoporosis, but hormone replacement is more important here. B Teriparatide This synthetic PTH analogue is primarily used in the treatment of severe osteoporosis, with a T-score of below either -3.5 or – 4.0 contingent upon age, and is a daily injectable. Replacement with testosterone, usually via an intermittent implant, is more appropriate. C Calcium and Vitamin D Calcium and vitamin D status isn’t the primary driver of fracture risk in this patient; hormone replacement is the crucial ﬁrst intervention.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with vomiting, anorexia, and polyuria. She is a non-smoker. Her GP has been treating her for anaemia with iron supplements, although she tells you this has had little or no effect on feelings of increasing lethargy over the past few months. On examination, her BP is 122/82, pulse is 88 and regular. She looks pale. Investigation Result Normal values Na+ 141 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Bilirubin 20 µmol/l 1 - 22 µmol/l Urea 12 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l ALT 30 u/l 7 - 55 u/l ALP 280 u/l 30 - 150 u/l Creatinine (Cr) 154 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Albumin 30 g/l 35 - 55 g/l Total protein 85 g/l 60 - 83 g/l Corrected (Ca2+) 3.0 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 1.3 mmol/l 1.1 - 1.45 mmol/l You start her on IV normal saline. Which one of the following would be the best initial investigation to contribute to the underlying diagnosis?
options: Sesta MIBI scan of the neck
explanation: E Skeletal survey This woman has hypercalcaemia without hypophosphataemia. Therefore, malignancy must be considered. The LFTs show increased globulin fraction (TP-ALB) indicating the possibility of myeloma. Therefore, the most appropriate management in this case is IV saline and a skeletal survey. Treatment of myeloma-induced hypercalcaemia is IV saline rehydration. Furosemide therapy with IV saline can be used as an adjunct to increase calcium excretion. IV pamidronate is also useful in reducing the calcium. In myeloma, hypercalcaemia is primarily due to increased osteolysis and high-dose steroids - e.g. prednisolone 40 mg od can rapidly reduce the calcium level. IV pamidronate is also useful in reducing the calcium in resistant cases. The emphasis should be on treating the myeloma with chemotherapy, which will in turn lead to a reduction in the calcium. B CT chest CT chest is most useful in patients with suspected bronchial carcinoma; the absence of a history of smoking and any reports of a cough counts against this as the underlying diagnosis. A Sesta MIBI scan of the neck This is most useful if a parathyroid adenoma is suspected. Given the phosphate is in the normal range. this is much less likely versus malignancy as the underlying cause of her hypercalcaemia. C Abdominal X-ray Her symptoms are entirely consistent with hypercalcaemia, and an abdominal ﬁlm is unlikely to contribute to determining the underlying diagnosis. D Ultrasound of the neck Ultrasound is a poor investigation with respect to detecting underlying parathyroid adenomas, and these are not likely to be the cause of hypercalcaemia given that the phosphate is within the normal range.

stem: A patient comes to your clinic complaining for 2 months of abdominal pain. He has lost signiﬁcant weight. He complains of feeling dizzy on standing. He has had a normal upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy, colonoscopy and barium follow-through. His blood pressure from lying to standing dropped by 30 mmHg – from 120 mmHg systolic to 90 mmHg. He has abnormal mucosal pigmentation, which is shown below. Which one of the following blood test results might you most expect to see?
explanation: A Glucose 3 mmol/l (3.5–5.5) Addison’s disease, the most likely diagnosis here, can present with hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, uraemia, hypoglycaemia, mild acidosis, hypercalcaemia, neutropenia, lymphocytosis, eosinophilia, anaemia and abnormal liver function tests. It also presents with darkening of the skin in a number of areas, including palmar creases and the buccal mucosa, as seen in this case. In the United Kingdom, noniatrogenic Addison’s disease is most commonly due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal glands. Adrenal autoantibodies are present in about 75% of cases. The next most common cause is tuberculosis. Other causes include haemorrhage (including during pregnancy), sepsis (including Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome from meningococcaemia), shock, coagulopathy and metastases. Other causes are metastases in over 90% in both glands, human immunodeﬁciency virus (HIV) and opportunistic infections associated with acquired immune deﬁciency syndrome (AIDS). B Calcium 2.1 mmol/l (2.12–2.65) The most likely diagnosis here is Addison’s disease, which can be accompanied by hypercalcaemia. The mechanism is uncertain but is thought to be a combination of increased calcium input into the extracellular space and reduced calcium removal by the kidney. Reduction in calcium removal is probably due to decreased glomerular ﬁltration and increased tubular calcium reabsorption. Both renal factors are secondary to volume depletion. The enhanced calcium mobilization is thought to be of skeletal origin. C Lymphocytes 15% (20–45%) In Addison’s disease, relative lymphocytosis and eosinophilia may be present, which respond to glucocorticoid replacement therapy. D Neutrophils 90% (40–75%) In Addison’s disease, relative lymphocytosis and eosinophilia may be present, which respond to glucocorticoid replacement therapy. E Sodium 148 mmol/l (135–145) In Addison’s disease, the most prominent ﬁndings are hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a mild non-anion gap metabolic acidosis due to the loss of the sodium-retaining and potassium- and hydrogen ion-secreting action of aldosterone.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic as she has become increasingly concerned about her weight. She has always been overweight, but has gradually gained 3kg over the last six months. She claims that her diet has remained unchanged and her physical ﬁtness is good. She is taking topical erythromycin for her acne. A pregnancy test is negative, although she does admit to a somewhat erratic menstrual cycle. She has also noticed increased coarse, dark, hair growth on her upper lip. In the clinic, her random blood sugar measurement by ﬁngerprick is 8.0 mmol/l. Which investigation is most likely to point to the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
E USS pelvis The history is consistent with Cushing syndrome or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). If not caused by pregnancy, weight gain is most likely in young people to be caused by increased fat. The causes are: increased caloric consumption disproportionate to energy expenditure; sedentary lifestyle, contributing signiﬁcantly by TV watching and video gaming; endocrine disorders such as Cushing syndrome; PCOS; hypothyroidism; hypothalamic dysfunction; medications; environmental factors such as poor sleep; gut microbiota; and viruses. Women with PCOS often present with hirsutism and menstrual irregularities. PCOS is also associated with insulin resistance. As per the Rotterdam 2003 criteria for PCOS, two out of the following three should be applicable for a diagnosis of PCOS.  Oligo- and/or anovulation  Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism  Polycystic ovaries (by ultrasound). The ultrasound criterion for deﬁning polycystic ovarian morphology is the presence of 12 or more follicles in each ovary measuring 2–9 mm in diameter and/or increased ovarian volume (>10 ml; calculated using the formula 0.5 × length × width × thickness). One ovary ﬁtting this deﬁnition is sufﬁcient to deﬁne PCOS. D MRI brain MRI brain would be helpful if pituitary disease, such as Cushing syndrome or hypothalamic disease, was suspected. Here the patient has no speciﬁc features to suggest the former. Hypothalamic dysfunction with secondary hypopituitarism is mostly seen in patients with a history of previous surgical treatment for a hypothalamic/pituitary lesion; other causes for hypothalamic dysfunction include inﬂammatory disease, history of trauma and neoplasia. A Urinary cortisol levels The typical physical signs of Cushing syndrome, such as facial plethora, round face, abdominal striae, dorsal fat pad and easy bruising (ecchymoses), have not been described in this case. Screening tests would be one of the following: latenight salivary cortisol (two measurements), 24 h urinary free cortisol (UFC) excretion (two measurements) or the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST). B TSH level Although menstrual irregularities and weight gain are commonly seen in hypothyroidism, the other characteristic features of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin and myalgia have not been mentioned in this case. The hair be-

comes coarse due to accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the interstitial matrix, and there is a tendency for hair loss. The distribution of the affected hair is diffuse and does not limit itself to androgen-sensitive distribution like the upper lip. C Oral glucose tolerance test Women with PCOS have insulin resistance and are at increased risk of ischaemic heart disease, type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia. An oral glucose tolerance test will help assess the risk for type 2 diabetes and current glucose regulation, but per se it is not useful for diagnosing PCOS.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) with recurrent episodes of penile thrush. He has no other signiﬁcant symptoms indicating hyperglycaemia. A strong family history of type 2 diabetes is noted and the GP arranges to check fasting plasma glucose. Two samples are checked and the laboratory glucose results are 8.1 and 8.2 mmol/l. Urine is negative for ketones. Haemoglobin A1C, also checked by the GP, is elevated at 74 mmol.mol (8.9%). His BMI is 22 and his BP is 105/72. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
explanation: B Gliclazide This man is most likely to have maturity onset of diabetes of youth 3 (MODY3) due to HNF1-alpha mutation (hepatic nuclear factor-1). MODY3 is the cause of 1–2% of type 2 diabetes and makes up around 70% of MODY cases. It presents most commonly in early adulthood and is associated with severe hyperglycaemia in some cases and frequent microvascular complications. One-third of patients require insulin therapy and around one- third may be controlled on oral hypoglycaemic drugs. Sulphonylureas (SUs) would be the initial drug of choice because, at least for the ﬁrst few years, the capacity to secrete insulin is preserved and the use of SUs restores insulin release, avoiding the need for insulin therapy. The next commonest MODY variant is MODY 2, which results from a glucokinase mutation leading to altered glucose sensing in pancreatic beta cells. In contrast, 90% of MODY2 patients are controlled on diet therapy alone. C Sitagliptin Sitagliptin potentiates the incretin effect by preventing the breakdown of endogenous GLP-1; it is used as adjunctive therapy in type 2 diabetes. A Metformin Metformin primarily reduces hepatic glucose output and has minor positive effects on weight control. As such, it is the initial therapy of choice for overweight and obese patients with type 2 diabetes. D Basal bolus insulin Basal bolus insulin therapy may well not be required for the majority of patients with MODY for a considerable period of time. E Acarbose Acarbose prevents the breakdown of complex carbohydrates in the gut. Its main use is in patients with type 2 diabetes who have a diet high in starches, such as those who follow a diet high in rice-containing foods.

stem: A 75-year-old man with a background of a localised squamous cell lung cancer is admitted to the Emergency Department with worsening confusion. He is thirsty, and, on examination, he has peripheral muscle weakness. His blood results reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 102 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 167 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.7 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 6.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 145 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 3.2 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l PTH 1.9 pmol/l 0.9 - 5.4 pmol/l You are concerned that the patient may have pseudo hyperparathyroidism. After treating the acute hypercalcaemia, what is the most appropriate long term management of the pseudohyperparathyroidism?
explanation: D Lung lobectomy Pseudo hyperparathyroidism is often a neoplastic syndrome, whereby the cancer produces parathyroid-related- peptide (PTH-peptide) which has the same effect as PTH. After the acute treatment of hypercalcaemia, the most appropriate management is to treat the underlying disease. In this case, the squamous cell lung cancer might be amenable to surgical excision if it is localised. B Calcimimetics Calcimimetics, such as cinacalcet, may be given if the hypercalcaemia does not adequately respond to bisphosphonate therapy; this is, therefore, is part of the acute management of hypercalcaemia, rather than pseudo-hyperparathyroidism. A Bisphosphonate therapy Bisphosphonate therapy is part of the acute management of hypercalcaemia. Intravenous (IV) ﬂuids should be given ﬁrst, and if the patient continues to demonstrate hypercalcaemia after 24 hours, he should be treated with bisphosphonate therapy, eg IV zoledronic acid. C Loop diuretic therapy Loop diuretics may lower calcium levels but are rarely used in the management of hypercalcaemia and do not have a role in the long-term management. E Parathyroidectomy In this condition, the parathyroid gland is acting appropriately. The mechanism for the hypercalcaemia occurs outside of the parathyroid feedback loop, and therefore a parathyroidectomy would not be helpful.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic because of an inability to achieve a pregnancy. She and her husband have been trying for some three years for a child, without success. Her General Practitioner has measured a prolactin level of 2600 mU/l (normal < 360). Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is arranged that demonstrates a microprolactinoma. She elects for treatment with pharmacotherapy. Which one of the following best represents the recommended follow-up for this patient?
options: General Practitioner to monitor prolactin levels
explanation: E Yearly MRI Initially, pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be arranged yearly for patients with microprolactinomas. For patients with macroadenomas or those whose serum prolactin level fails to respond to dopamine agonist treatment (cabergoline or bromocriptine), imaging may be indicated more frequently. The frequency of imaging can reduce once there is suppression of serum prolactin level to the normal range and tumour size remains stable. D Regular visual ﬁeld examination Patients with visual ﬁeld disturbance secondary to optic chiasmal compression should have regular visual ﬁeld examination until maximum improvement is achieved. However, this patient does not have any visual ﬁeld loss, as she is suffering from a microprolactinoma. A General Practitioner to monitor prolactin levels Periodic measurement of serum prolactin level is an essential part of monitoring for microprolactinomas. As this patient wishes to achieve pregnancy and has been started on pharmacotherapy, she is best managed in an Endocrine Clinic during initial treatment and through pregnancy. B Monitoring of pituitary hormone axes In patients with macroprolactinomas (> 10 mm) which have caused hypopituitarism, patients may be started on hormone replacement. They will therefore require monitoring of the pituitary axes (including testosterone and thyroid function). This patient has a microprolactinoma and this is therefore not required. C MRI 2-yearly Initial monitoring of the tumour should be via yearly magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and periodic prolactin level measurements. The frequency of MRI monitoring may be reduced once the patient is stable on treatment.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Clinic with a 10-month history of right iliac fossa abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea up to 15 times a day. He had been a heavy drinker in the past, consuming 40 pints of beer a week, but has cut back to 1 pint a day for several years. He has recently noticed that his symptoms became worse when drinking alcohol so has now stopped completely. His wife had noticed that that he has lost weight recently but he was unable to quantify this. He has never smoked but his wife has noticed that he has had some attacks of wheeziness. Examination of his abdomen revealed 3 cm hepatomegaly and an indistinct mass in the right iliac fossa. Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and full blood count were normal, but a small-bowel barium examination revealed a submucosal mass in the ileum. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Carcinoid syndrome Carcinoid tumours are neuroendocrine tumours that most commonly occur in the GI tract. They secrete many vasoactive molecules (particularly serotonin), which, in the absence of hepatic involvement, are metabolised in the liver. If these tumours metastasise to the liver, the liver's ability to break down the serotonin produced by these tumours may be overwhelmed; it may then enter the systemic circulation, and symptoms will subsequently develop. It is the phalanx of symptoms produced through serotonin entering the circulation that deﬁnes the carcinoid syndrome. Of these symptoms, debilitating diarrhoea – often associated with abdominal pain – is the most common. Flushing (which commonly affects the neck and face) may be associated with wheezing, and telangiectases may result. Alcohol and food intolerances, and exacerbations of symptoms by stress and some drugs, are not uncommon. The classic cardiac ﬁndings are of right-sided heart disease, namely tricuspid incompetence or pulmonary stenosis. Examination often reveals hepatomegaly; imaging of the liver reveals metastatic disease. Urinary levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) are normally increased. Treatment with somatostatin analogues (such as octreotide) may improve symptoms, and chemotherapy may also be helpful. Men and women are equally affected by carcinoid tumours, and presentation tends to occur between the ages of 50 and 75 years. Carcinoid tumours are mostly commonly found in the ileum and appendix, but can be located in many other sites, both intestinal and extra-intestinal. Approximately only one-third of tumours metastasise and, consequently, many are asymptomatic. A Coeliac disease-related lymphoma Lymphoma is a recognised complication of coeliac disease, but his lack of GI symptoms prior to 10 months earlier makes underlying coeliac disease unlikely (although coeliac disease may be subclinical). B Chronic pancreatitis Chronic pancreatitis tends to cause upper abdominal pain and malabsorptive (as opposed to watery) diarrhoea. It is not likely to cause the associated symptoms described in the presentation. C Villous adenoma Villous adenomas of the rectum are not likely to cause the associated symptoms described in the presentation. E Immunoproliferative small intestinal disease IPSID is a proximal small bowel lymphoproliferative condition that tends to present with malabsorption and weight loss. As with coeliac disease, it may progress to lymphoma. It does not describe the full pattern of symptoms described in the scenario.

stem: You are asked to see a 24-year-old woman who is 8 weeks into her ﬁrst pregnancy. She has suffered vomiting and is ﬁnding it difﬁcult to maintain weight. On examination, she is clearly anxious. Her BP is 105/70, with pulse 75 and regular. Her BMI is 22. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 119 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.7 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 212 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 144 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 3.4 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Glucose 4.8 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Total T4 185 nmol/l 58 - 174 nmol/l TSH 0.6 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Which of the following is the most appropriate management in this case?
explanation: E Observe This patient has increased total T4 with a TSH which is in the normal range. There are no clinical signs of hyperthyroidism. The weight loss and vomiting are most likely to be related to hyperemesis gravidarum. Although normal in this case, TSH itself may be suppressed in 13.5% of patients in the ﬁrst trimester due to the thyrotrophic effects of beta HCG. There is a twofold increase in thyroid-binding globulin levels in pregnancy due to a combination of reduced hepatic clearance of thyroid-binding globulin and increased synthesis in response to oestrogen. The increased level of thyroid-binding globulin plateaus at 20 weeks and then gradually falls. In this case thyroid binding globulin may be useful in conﬁrming the diagnosis. A Start propylthiouracil Although thyrotoxicosis may occur in early pregnancy, the lack of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis here makes that much less likely as the underlying diagnosis, as does the fact that TSH is at the lower end of the normal range rather than being completely suppressed. Propylthiouracil is the treatment of choice for thyrotoxicosis in early pregnancy. B Start carbimazole Carbimazole is the preferred intervention for thyrotoxicosis in late pregnancy because of the risk of maternal hepatotoxicity associated with propylthiouracil use. C Start propylthiouracil and thyroxine (blockreplace) Block replace regimens are not used in pregnancy because thyroid hormones do not readily cross the placenta. D Start thyroxine therapy This patient is not hypothyroid and there is no indication for commencing thyroid hormone.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department (ED) by her General Practitioner (GP). She gives a history of malaise and weight loss. Most recently she collapsed at home and has suffered from persistent vomiting over the past 24 hours. Other past history of note includes a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in pregnancy and positive screen for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome. Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, pulse is 100 and regular. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Na+ 128 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 6.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 9.1 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 128 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Hb 101 g/l 115–155 g/l Mean corpusuclar volume (MCV) 99 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ ESR 41 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Glucose 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.5 mmol/l You arrange for a blood sample to be sent for cortisol and give a bolus of 20% dextrose. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
options: Arrange a short synacthen test for the following morning
Start IV ﬂuid replacement with 5% dextrose
Start IV ﬂuid replacement with 0.9% saline and give a bolus of IV dexamethasone
explanation:
E Start IV ﬂuid replacement with 0.9% saline and give a bolus of IV dexamethasone This woman has anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome, which may have led to adrenal infarction, precipitating this presentation with an Addisonian crisis. Autoimmune disease is the commonest cause of Addison’s in the developed world, although malignancy and infection (e.g. with tuberculosis) may also be responsible. Initial treatment is with rehydration, and several litres of normal saline may be required during the ﬁrst 24 h of therapy. A bolus of dexamethasone 4 mg IV should also be given because unlike hydrocortisone, this won’t interfere with a synacthen test. C Start ﬂudrocortisone 100 mcg PO OD

Fludrocortisone replacement is not normally required in the acute stage, but can be added once the dose of hydrocortisone is reduced after a few days. A Arrange a short synacthen test for the following morning This lady is presenting with an Addisonian crisis – you should not wait for a synacthen test prior to commencing therapy. B Start prednisolone 30 mg PO OD Hydrocortisone is the steroid of choice in the treatment of Addison’s. D Start IV ﬂuid replacement with 5% dextrose Hypotension should be managed with aggressive ﬂuid resuscitation with 0.9% saline. Blood glucose should be monitored and hypoglycaemia corrected appropriately, but this usually improves with glucocorticoid therapy.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is referred to the clinic by the Emergency Department, having been admitted after fainting in the local supermarket. On further questioning it transpires that she has been feeling weak and washed out for quite some time. On examination, her BP is 105/60 mmHg, pulse is 75/min. Her BMI is 18. She has calluses on her knuckles but tells you these are due to her job as a landscape gardener. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 194 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 3.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 115 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Urinary potassium 0.7 mmol/l/24 h 25–100 mmol/24 h Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Laxative abuse This woman is underweight and has symptoms of fatigue which are consistent with hypokalaemia. The fact that she is underweight with a BMI of 18, and has calluses on her knuckles, may point towards induced vomiting and a diagnosis of bulimia, which would ﬁt with possible laxative abuse. Laxative abuse leads to increased GI potassium loss and renal conservation of potassium, a urinary concentration of potassium of less than 1 mmol/l being highly suggestive of laxative abuse. Urine screening exists for a range of possible laxatives, and the patient should be consented for a urinary laxative screen with appropriate counselling. C Diuretic abuse The use of thiazide diuretics leads to hypokalaemia through increased potassium excretion in the urine. A Bartter syndrome This is an autosomal recessive renal tubular disorder characterised by hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, metabolic alkalosis and hyper-reninaemia with normal blood pressure. Urinary potassium excretion is high due to the inability of the kidneys to retain potassium. B Liddle syndrome This is a rare hereditary disorder involving increased activity of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) which causes the kidneys to excrete potassium but retain too much sodium and water, leading to hypertension. Symptoms are of hypertension, ﬂuid retention hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. The urinary potassium excretion is high. E Conn syndrome Conn syndrome, or primary hyperaldosteronism, occurs due to excess production of the hormone aldosterone by the adrenal glands, resulting in low renin levels. Around 66% of cases are due to enlargement of both adrenal glands and 33% are due to an adrenal adenoma that produces aldosterone. Most people have hypertension requiring treatment with more than three agents. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypernatraemic, hypokalaemic, metabolic alkalosis. The urinary excretion of potassium is high.

stem: A 48-year-old man is referred to the clinic with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. He also complains of excessive sweating and worries that his hands have swollen so that his wedding ring no longer ﬁts him. Past medical history includes hypertension, which is managed with amlodipine and indapamide. On examination, his blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg and he has a very prominent lower jaw. There is also soft tissue swelling of his hands. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 149 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.0 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 300 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.0 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 μmol/l 50 – 120 µmol/l Random glucose 12.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial investigation towards conﬁrming this man’s likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
E IGF-1 measurement There is obvious frontal bossing and prognathism which along with the soft tissue swelling in the hands, hyperhidrosis and hypertension is consistent with a diagnosis of acromegaly. IGF-1 measurement varies with age and nutritional status, but reference ranges exist for comparison. IGF-1 has a long half-life and, as such, is a useful measure of growth hormone status. Failure of growth hormone to suppress in response to an oral glucose challenge is the other diagnostic method of choice for assessing patients with possible acromegaly, although this is less convenient following an initial clinic appointment.

A Fasting plasma glucose Although an elevation in fasting plasma glucose may indicate a diagnosis of diabetes, it won’t reveal the underlying cause. B Random growth hormone measurement Growth hormone is released in pulsatile fashion and has a short half-life; as such, random measurement is not useful in conﬁrming a diagnosis of acromegaly. C Prolactin measurement Prolactin may be elevated because of local pressure effects from a pituitary adenoma, but it won’t conﬁrm elevated growth hormone. D Random cortisol measurement The symptoms here ﬁt better with acromegaly rather than with elevated cortisol as a result of hyperadrenalism due to either an adrenal or pituitary tumour.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department after her neighbours found her confused at home and called an ambulance. She is unable to give much history. However, her General Practitioner (GP) records state that she has diabetes and hypertension and she has previously suffered from a stroke. Her GP records also note a number of regular medications, including clopidogrel, atorvastatin, linagliptin, Humulin® I, Toujeo® and amlodipine, which were last dispensed two months ago. On examination, she is disorientated and appears dehydrated, but is otherwise well. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value pH 7.34 7.35–7.45 p(O2) 12 kPa 9.5–14 kPa p(CO2) 7 kPa 4.6–6.0 kPa Bicarbonate (HCO-3) 21 mmol/l 22–30 mmol/l Glucose 27.8 mmol/l 4–10 mmol/l Urea 8 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Sodium (N+) 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4 mmol/l 3.5–5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 286 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Ketones 1 mmol/l < 0.6 mmol/l Lactate 2.1 mmol/l 0.6–2.4 mmol/l What is the likely cause of this patient’s presentation?
explanation: E Poor adherence to medications This patient likely has type II diabetes. With many years of insulin resistance commonly experienced in type II diabetes, the pancreatic endocrine function is reduced, meaning that many patients end up on insulin therapy. It is likely that this patient has not been taking her regular insulin regime for many weeks, which has resulted in hyperglycaemia and dehydration. The treatment of choice for this patient would be to start her on a variable- rate insulin infusion (VRII) and intravenous ﬂuids. Once her blood sugar levels have normalised and she is eating and drinking normally, she can be started on an insulin regime based on her requirements from the VRII. C Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state Hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state (HHS) is diagnosed with plasma osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg; this can be approximated using the calculation for the plasma osmolarity as: [2(Na2+ + K+) + urea + glucose]. This patient’s osmolarity is 307.8 mmol/l. Usually, in HHS, the glucose level is > 30 mmol/l and there is no signiﬁcant ketonaemia or acidosis. Sodium is frequently raised in HHS, as the raised glucose level causes osmotic diuresis and severe dehydration. A Alcohol excess Alcohol excess may cause poor adherence to medications and mildly raised blood glucose levels in the acute setting. However, blood sugar levels would not be expected to be this high and there is nothing in the scenario to suggest alcohol misuse. B Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) This patient is only mildly acidotic with mildly raised ketone levels. A diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is based on blood glucose level > 11 mmol/l with ketonaemia (blood ketones > 3 mmol/l or urine ketones 2+ or more) and acidosis (pH < 7.3 and/or venous bicarbonate < 15 mmol/l) would not be appropriate. It is more commonly seen in patients with type I diabetes. D Intracranial haemorrhage Intracranial haemorrhage secondary to a fall and clopidogrel may cause a presentation with confusion. However, it is not known whether the patient has not collected her medications for at least two months, making this less likely.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a two-week history of malaise and anterior neck pain. She explains that she has been suffering from what seems like a severe ﬂu-like illness. On examination, her pulse is 118 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. Her blood pressure (BP) is 132/74 mmHg. She has a ﬁne tremor and her palms are moist. She has a slightly enlarged, smooth tender thyroid. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value T4 40 nmol/l 11–22 pmol/l TSH <0.01 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l ESR 40 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Subacute thyroiditis This is a description of subacute (De Quervain’s) thyroiditis, which usually presents with malaise and neck pain. The neck pain can radiate to the ear or occiput. There is often tenderness and nodularity of the thyroid. ESR is often elevated. A Technetium-99m scan shows no technetium uptake by the thyroid. Mild cases can be treated with non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs), but more severe cases associated with hyperthyroidism should be treated with prednisolone 30 mg/day. The prednisolone can be stopped when the T4 normalises. Treatment with carbimazole is not indicated. D Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is a C-cell (calcitoninproducing) tumour. It is not associated with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. A Toxic multinodular goitre A nodular enlarged thyroid gland is expected in toxic multinodular goitre, with a more prolonged period of symptoms of hyperthyroidism. B Graves’ disease Graves’ is associated with smooth enlargement of the thyroid, often with only mild tenderness. Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis also occur over a more prolonged period. C Toxic solitary nodule Toxic adenoma is not associated with generalised tenderness of the thyroid gland, and symptoms of thyrotoxicosis build up over a period of weeks and months.

stem: A 65-year-old woman comes to the Endocrinology Clinic complaining of weakness and lethargy. She has gained 5 kg in weight over the past four months and is ﬁnding it increasingly difﬁcult to look after her granddaughter, particularly when she needs to go up and down the stairs. There is a history of mild hypertension which is managed with indapamide, but she is otherwise well. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/92 mmHg; her pulse is 55 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. She appears to have thinning hair. Her body mass index (BMI) is 32 kg/m2 and neurological examination reveals evidence of proximal myopathy. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 112 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.1 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 127 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Creatine kinase (CK) 352 IU/l 23–175 IU/l Glucose 6.1 mmol/l 3.8–5.4 mmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate way to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
E TSH There are several clues in the history to point towards the underlying diagnosis of hypothyroidism, including weight gain, proximal myopathy, hyponatraemia and slight CK elevation. TSH is the most appropriate test to conﬁrm the diagnosis - which is likely to be Hashimoto’s thyroiditis as the underlying pathophysiology. B Prolactin

The clinical scenario supports the possibility of hypothyroidism. Prolactin may be useful to support the possibility of a prolactinoma, which is unlikely in this case. A Muscle biopsy While there is a slight elevation of CK, it is not sufﬁciently raised to contribute signiﬁcantly to a diagnosis of myopathy. A muscle biopsy in this case would therefore not be the most appropriate way to conﬁrm the diagnosis. C Serum and urine osmolality Although this patient has a low sodium, the serum and urine osmolality are useful in patients in whom you are considering syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), it neither conﬁrms the diagnosis or ﬁts with the clinical scenario in this case. D Synacthen test Although patients with a low sodium and lethargy should be considered for a short synacthen test, Addison’s disease is not consistent with weight gain and therefore is unlikely to be the diagnosis in this case.

stem: A 42-year-old Portuguese woman presents to her GP with increasing lethargy. He had seen her twice in the past few months and commenced antidepressants at her last appointment. Most recently, she had been complaining of increasing nausea and vomiting and had lost a considerable amount of weight. On examination, her blood pressure was 105/65 mmHg and her BMI was 21. There was a postural drop of 20 mmHg in her blood pressure on standing, with a corresponding increase in her pulse rate. Investigation Result Normal values Sodium (Na ) 126 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l Potassium (K ) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l TSH 7 mu/l 0.4 - 5.0 mu/l Free Thyroxine (FT4) 7 pmol/l 10 - 22 pmol/l Urea 10.1 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Haemoglobin (Hb) g/l (normochromic, normocytic), eosinophilcount raised 135 - 175 g/l Which of the following is the initial treatment of choice in this patient?
explanation: C Hydrocortisone This patient has the clinical features of adrenal insufﬁciency, with hyponatraemia, a raised urea, normochromic normocytic anaemia with eosinophilia and a relatively high potassium level despite repeated episodes of vomiting. She should not be treated with thyroxine at this stage: thyroid function testing should be repeated after treatment with corticosteroids. She should be rehydrated, but with N saline. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause of primary adrenal insufﬁciency. Metastatic carcinoma from lung, breast or kidney primaries is also known to result in adrenal failure. Inﬁltration due to amyloid, infection due to tuberculosis, vascular haemorrhage or infarction are other documented causes. B Fludrocortisone This is used for mineralocorticoid insufﬁciency leading to postural hypotension. In Addison’s disease, because corticosteroid replacement therapy usually exerts a mineralocorticoid effect, ﬂudrocortisone is not ﬁrst-line treatment. A Thyroxine Mild biochemical hypothyroidism often accompanies adrenal insufﬁciency, but early treatment of abnormal thyroid numbers, particularly before corticosteroid stabilisation, may further decompensate the adrenal insufﬁciency. D IV 5% dextrose Adrenal insufﬁciency manifesting with adrenal crisis is associated with volume depletion, and therefore normal saline is the appropriate intravenous ﬂuid. E Fluid restriction Addison’ s disease is characterised by volume depletion. The hyponatraemia is in the context of the condition, and therefore the most appropriate therapy is ﬂuid replacement with normal saline rather than ﬂuid restriction.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a chest infection. The GP undertakes routine blood tests and notices that her glucose is just into the range for diabetes. He refers her to the Diabetic Clinic, where you see her and take a full history. At the time of the test, she had been unwell for one week with a chest infection. She has no other medical history and is normally ﬁt and well. Her grandmother, mother and sister all have diabetes, which presented when they were young. Her mother’s and sister’s diabetes is diet-controlled only. Her grandmother has only started to need insulin recently. She has two older brothers who also have diabetes. Her family are all very health conscious and do not smoke, do not drink excessive alcohol and exercise regularly. They all maintain a body mass index (BMI) around 20 kg/m2. Her fasting venous glucose is 12 mmol/l. How would you best describe the likely diagnosis in her case?
explanation: E Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) Maturity-onset diabetes is a genetic subgroup of diabetes characterised by autosomal-dominant inheritance, early onset, non-insulin-dependent diabetes and results from a monogenic defect leading to defects of either insulin sensing or insulin release. MODY3 is particularly important to diagnose as many patients initially treated with insulin can in fact be managed with sulphonylurea. C Type-2 diabetes mellitus The fact that her BMI is 20 makes type 2 diabetes very unlikely as the underlying diagnosis. A Incidental hyperglycaemia The FPG result of 12 is well into the abnormal range. Coupled with the probable autosomal-dominant inheritance of diabetes, MODY is the more likely diagnosis. B Type-1 diabetes mellitus The symptoms of hyperglycaemia such as polyuria, polydipsia and lethargy are absent from her presenting complaint. D Metabolic syndrome Given the BMI of 20 and the autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern, MODY is more likely than metabolic syndrome to be the cause of the hyperglycaemia seen here.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with episodic abdominal pain and a recent episode of acute pancreatitis. He has a history of obesity, hypertension and type II diabetes mellitus, for which he takes metformin and amlodipine. He reports consuming alco- hol occasionally. Family history is signiﬁcant for cardiovascular disease in his father, who had a myocardial infarction at the age of 50 years. Physical examination reveals central obesity and hepatomegaly. Investigation Result Normal value Fasting triglycerides (TG) 15.2 mmol/l < 1.7 mmol/l Fasting blood gglucose 8.4 mmol/l 3.9–5.8 mmol/l Total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/l < 5.0 mmol/l HDL 0.8 mmol/l > 1.0 mmol/l (men) Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol 2.2 mmol/l < 3.0 mmol/l Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 30 U/l 10–35 U/l ALT 35 U/l 10–40 U/l What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s hypertriglyceridaemia?
options: Type II diabetes mellitus with metabolic syndrome
explanation:
C Type II diabetes mellitus with metabolic syndrome Metabolic syndrome, often associated with obesity, type II diabetes and insulin resistance, commonly leads to hypertriglyceridaemia, low HDL cholesterol levels and other lipid abnormalities. The patient’s obesity, diabetes and elevated TG levels are consistent with this diagnosis. B Alcohol-induced hypertriglyceridaemia Although excessive alcohol intake can cause elevated TG levels, this patient reports only occasional alcohol use, making it an unlikely primary cause of the severe hypertriglyceridaemia observed here. A Familial hypercholesterolaemia Familial hypercholesterolaemia is typically associated with elevated LDL cholesterol levels and does not commonly present with high TG levels. This condition is unlikely to explain the high TG and low HDL levels in this patient. D Familial combined hyperlipidaemia Familial combined hyperlipidaemia can present with elevated TG and cholesterol levels, but it typically results in modest TG elevations and is not usually associated with acute pancreatitis at such levels.

E Drug-induced hypertriglyceridaemia Certain drugs, such as beta-blockers and some antipsychotics, can elevate TG levels, but neither metformin nor amlodipine is associated with signiﬁcant hypertriglyceridaemia, making this an unlikely cause.

stem: A 58-year-old man who has both type 1 DM and chronic kidney disease managed with haemodialysis comes to the clinic for review. He was previously noted to have raised PTH and started on CaCO3 and twice weekly vitamin D at the high dose. He has recently begun suffering from depression. He has suffered two previous myocardial infarctions and had a spinal anaesthetic for a total hip replacement in the past year. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 4.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 199 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.2 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 634 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l PTH 87 pmol/l 1-6 pmol/l Corrected Ca2+ 2.2 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 1.45 mmol/l 0.70–1.40 mmol/l Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step for this patient?
explanation: D Cinacalcet This man has hyperparathyroidism, with a PTH that has failed to suppress in response to calcium and vitamin D. As such, the next most appropriate step is cinacalcet. It works as an agonist at the site of the calcium sensor on the parathyroid gland. This leads to a suppression of PTH levels. Cinacalcet may currently be used in patients on renal replacement therapy as an adjunct to vitamin D or phosphate binders. A Parathyroidectomy Given this patient’s history of end stage renal failure, myocardial infarctions and the fact he received a spinal anaesthetic for a hip replacement last year, they are strongly hinting at him being high risk from operative intervention for hyperparathyroidism, and other treatment options should be explored ﬁrst. B Increased dose of vitamin D PTH is in not in the treatment range, but calcium is in the normal range. They are on high doses of vitamin D and calcium carbonate and supplementing further with vitamin D is very unlikely to drive down levels of parathyroid hormone. C Sevelamer Sevelamer is a phosphate binder, and given that phosphate is only just above the normal range, it’s not going to signiﬁcantly impact on the clinical picture seen here. E Aluminium hydroxide Aluminium hydroxide, an alternative phosphate binder is now used less frequently because of risks of accumulation and the impact on cognitive function.

stem: An 63-year-old woman from Saudi Arabia attends the Endocrinology Clinic with her son after referral from her General Practitioner (GP). He has noticed that she has symptoms of hypercalcaemia, and is worried about hyperparathyroidism. On further questioning, you ﬁnd out she has been taking Rennie anti-indigestion tablets three or four times per day, and has increased these as she has felt progressively more nauseous. Additionally, she is taking a calcium supplement to guard against bone fracture as her mother suffered from fractures late in life. Additional symptoms include fatigue, and, apparently while in Saudi Arabia she was started on sertraline for depression. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 129 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 145 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l ESR 18 mm/hour 1–20 mm/hour Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 185 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected corrected Ca2+ PTH 2.85 mmol/l Low 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Chest X-ray (CXR) No focal lesion seen Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: E Milk-alkali syndrome This patient has a markedly elevated oral calcium intake, as illustrated by her propensity to take both calcium- containing indigestion medications (Rennies is a mixture of calcium and magnesium carbonate) and calcium supplementation to reduce the risk of bone fracture. Additionally, she has various symptoms of hypercalcaemia including the nausea, lethargy and depression reported here. The condition can lead to mild renal impairment, as we’ve seen with her elevated serum creatinine, but this may well return to normal once calcium intake is reduced. D Hypercalcaemia of malignancy Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is a possibility given the patient’s age, but the lack of other symptoms, apart from indigestion, and relatively normal blood picture including ESR and haemoglobin, count against this. A Familial hypercalcaemic hypocalciuria FHH is usually asymptomatic, although some patients may present with renal stones, or very rarely with acute pancreatitis. B Hypoparathyroidism Hypoparathyroidism is associated with hypocalcaemia rather than the elevated calcium seen here. C Primary hyperparathyroidism In the absence of the strong history of excess calcium and alkali ingestion here, primary hyperparathyroidism would be considered the main differential, although a normal or slightly elevated PTH, rather than the low value seen here would be expected.

stem: An overweight 68-year-old woman with a ﬁve year history of type II diabetes mellitus attends for her annual review. She is currently being treated with metformin (2 g total daily dose). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value HbA1C 98.91 mmol/mol (11.2%) < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) EGFR > 60 Creatinine (Cr) 240 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Total cholesterol 7.5 mmol/l <5.2 mmol/l Which of the following represents the most appropriate therapeutic option for this patient?
options: Start gliclazide in addition to metformin
explanation: E Start insulin and stop metformin This patient has kidney disease and thus metformin is contraindicated. In addition, her HbA1c is out of control at 98.91 mmol/mol (11.2%). It is highly unlikely that gliclazide would achieve the necessary level of glycaemic control, and therefore initiation of insulin therapy is the most appropriate therapeutic option. Most patients with type 2 diabetes are initiated on a twice-daily mixed insulin regime, with conversion to a basal bolus regime as an option if sufﬁcient control is not achieved. D Start a statin The priority is to improve the glycaemic control. Once this is achieved, lipid management with a statin can be considered. A Start gliclazide instead of metformin Her HbA1c is very high, and therefore the initiation of insulin is more appropriate in order to achieve more rapid glycaemic control. In terms of her renal function, gliclazide could cause hypoglycaemia since its clearance will be delayed. B Start gliclazide in addition to metformin Metformin has to be discontinued once eGFR is <30. Gliclazide can be used, but there is the risk of hypoglycaemia C Start insulin and continue metformin Although metformin enhances insulin sensitivity and can be used as adjunctive therapy to insulin, it has to be discontinued in our case since eGFR is <30.

stem: A 42-year-old man sees his General Practitioner (GP) due to a persistent and gradually worsening headache over the previous few months. On examination, he is noted to have bitemporal hemianopia, and he is sweaty to touch. His blood pressure is 165/95 mmHg. The patient has no past medical history. An image of the patient is show below: His GP sends a range of blood tests, including Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF-1) as they suspect a diagnosis of acromegaly. Investigation Result Normal value IGF-1 53 nmol/l 7.7 - 28 nmol/l What is the most likely cause of acromegaly in this case?
options: Hypothalamic hypersecretion of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH)
explanation: D Pituitary macroadenoma Pituitary macroadenomas (diameter more than 10 mm) that secrete growth hormone are the most common cause of acromegaly, accounting for 60-80% of cases. This is often caused by a spontaneous mutation in the somatotroph cells which are responsible for growth hormone secretion. Excessive growth hormone secretion causes the symptoms of acromegaly and the size of the tumour can cause local tumour effects such as headaches, visual ﬁeld defects (such as bitemporal hemianopia) and cranial nerve palsies. A Ectopic growth hormone secretion Some rare conditions, such as pancreatic islet cell tumours or non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, may result in ectopic production of growth hormone, which may lead to the symptoms of acromegaly. On investigation, no mass will be seen on the pituitary gland, and therefore the typical symptoms of mass effect in acromegaly will be absent. It is also possible to have ectopic production of GHRH. This is also rare and most commonly caused by bronchial carcinoid. B Hypothalamic hypersecretion of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH) Hypothalamic tumours, eg gliomas, can secrete excessive quantities of GHRH, which results in pituitary hyperplasia, excessive growth hormone secretion and acromegaly. This is a rare cause of acromegaly. C Pituitary carcinoma Pituitary adenomas causing acromegaly tend to be benign lesions. It is rare for the lesion to be malignant. E Pituitary microadenoma Pituitary microadenomas (diameter less than 10 mm) are the second most common cause of acromegaly. They account for between 20-40% of cases and, due to their small size, they tend not to cause symptoms of mass effect, eg bitemporal hemianopia, which is more typical of a macroadenoma.

stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has been referred by his General Practitioner (GP) for an obvious slowly enlarging mass in the left lobe of the thyroid. He is concerned he might have cancer. Which of the following would increase the likelihood in this patient of underlying thyroid malignancy?
options: Strong family history of breast cancer requiring multiple check-up mammograms
Abuse of thyroid tablets as a teenager
Family history of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
explanation:
D Family history of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) FAP is caused by an APC gene mutation on chromosome 5, and is also associated with increased risk of developing thyroid cancer. A Family history of hyperthyroidism Endemic goitre, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and thyroid adenoma, not hyperthyroidism, are associated with increased risk of thyroid malignancy. B Strong family history of breast cancer requiring multiple check-up mammograms A familial history of breast cancer is most closely associated with increased risk of ovarian cancer. C Abuse of thyroid tablets as a teenager

Thyrotoxicosis factitia, or abuse of thyroid hormone, is not associated with increased risk of thyroid cancer. E Male sex Females are three times more likely to develop thyroid cancer than males.

stem: A 28-year-old single woman presents to the Endocrine Clinic with recent symptoms of sweating, weight loss and palpitations. She tells you that there is a history of thyroid disease in the family and she has recently applied for a job as a nurse because she wants to help people. On examination, she has a BMI of 20, there is no palpable goitre and a tremor is noted. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 125 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 6.5 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Glucose 5.7 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l TSH < 0.05 mu/l 0.5 - 4.0 mu/l Free Thyroxine (FT4) 32.1 pmol/l 10 - 22 pmol/l Thyroid scintography revealed decreased uptake Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation: D Thyroglobulin levels One possible cause of recent-onset thyrotoxicosis is thyroiditis. Thyroglobulin levels can be used to differentiate thyroiditis and other causes of hyperthyroidism from thyrotoxicosis factitia. Low thyroglobulin levels are associated with a diagnosis of thyrotoxicosis factitia (inappropriate abuse of thyroid hormone), and this is also associated with absence of thyroid enlargement and suppressed TSH in the presence of elevated T4 levels. Decreased isotope uptake is seen on thyroid scanning. Expert psychiatric input is advised in cases such as this one, as presentation of the diagnosis may be met with a hostile reaction and appropriate psychological assessment is required. C Beta HCG There are no signs of pregnancy, where elevated beta HCG which suppresses TSH is seen. It doesn’t normally cause symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. A Thyroid ultrasound scan Thyroid ultrasound scanning is most useful in identifying small thyroid masses that can’t be detected on palpation alone. B Fine needle aspiration biopsy Fine needle aspiration biopsy is most useful in identifying the histology of cold nodules, identiﬁed on ultrasound scan. E Abdominal ultrasound scan Abdominal ultrasound scanning is useful in identifying intraabdominal tumours producing thyroid hormone, although these are extremely rare and unlikely to be the cause of symptoms seen here.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department some two weeks after discharge following the birth of her second child. Unfortunately, she suffered a signiﬁcant period of hypotension due to post-partum haemorrhage and required a 4-unit blood transfusion. She has been feeling increasingly tired with nausea and symptoms of pre-syncope. She looks pale and her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg with a postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. Her pulse is 85 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 22 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.9 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 171 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 128 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following is the pathology underlying her presentation?
explanation:
D Pituitary infarction

Due to increased blood supply during pregnancy, the pituitary gland is susceptible to infarction during a period of hypotension. In this case, a gradual decline of ACTH is likely to have led to reduced cortisol production and driven the adrenal failure. A short synacthen test and pituitary MRI would be useful in conﬁrming the diagnosis, but investigations should not delay corticosteroid replacement. B Bilateral adrenal infarction Although there was a signiﬁcant period of time where the patient was hypoperfused, this would be rare to occur in an otherwise well individual. A Autoimmune adrenal failure The clinical history indicates there was a signiﬁcant period of hypotension. During this time, the pituitary gland can be prone to infarction which is therefore more likely than autoimmune adrenal failure. C Pituitary haemorrhage Pituitary haemorrhage, also known as pituitary apoplexy, occurs suddenly and presents in a dramatic fashion as opposed to the subacute presentation above. Typically, patients present with sudden-onset severe headache, visual loss and diplopia. Treatment is surgical. E Renal tubular acidosis type 4 Renal tubular acidosis type 4 would explain the hyperkalaemia. While acquired forms occur in the context of patients with primary adrenal failure, it does not explain the clinical history and therefore is unlikely to be the diagnosis.

stem: A 61-year-old man, who has had type II diabetes for the past eight years, presents to his General Practitioner for review. He has found it increasingly difﬁcult to maintain his glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) at target on metformin 1 g twice daily (BD) and empagliﬂozin 25 mg. He has also gained 6 kg in weight over the past year. His past medical history includes hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and benign prostatic hypertrophy. On examination, his blood pressure is 142/90 mmHg and his heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. The respiratory examination is unremarkable. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and his body mass index is 36 kg/m2. There is bilateral pedal oedema. Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.0 × 109/l 4.0–1.0 × 109/l PLT 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 12.1 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l HbA1c 62 mmol/mol < 48 mmol/mol [for diabetics] Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Stop oral treatment and transition to basal bolus insulin
explanation: B Add liraglutide In this situation, with a body mass index of > 35 kg/m2, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines allow for a trial of a glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP1) analogue. They recommend a reassessment of response to therapy after three months to ensure that adequate HbA1c reduction (> 1%) and weight loss of ≥3 % has been achieved. D Refer for bariatric surgery Although this patient would qualify for bariatric surgery, a trial of GLP-1 agonist therapy is indicated ﬁrst, given the morbidity associated with a permanent surgical solution. A Add intermediate-acting insulin at night This patient is signiﬁcantly obese. As such, although adding intermediate-acting insulin at night may improve his HbA1c, it is likely to result in signiﬁcant further weight gain and adverse effects, including hypoglycaemia. In particular, in patients with long-term diabetes, hypoglycaemia may risk cardiac arrhythmias, which is an undesirable outcome in a patient with ischaemic heart disease. C Add pioglitazone Pioglitazone is contraindicated in patients with a history of heart failure due to the risk of ﬂuid retention. Given the presence of oedema on examination and the history of ischaemic heart disease, it is likely that this patient has an element of cardiac failure. E Stop oral treatment and transition to basal bolus insulin Although basal-bolus insulin can optimise insulin delivery, continuing metformin and the sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor seems sensible in this case to limit weight gain on insulin initiation.
