stem: A 57-year-old non-insulin-dependent diabetic man presented to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of shortness of breath. He was commenced on insulin 4 months ago due to persistent hyperglycaemia despite being on metformin 1 g twice daily (bd) and gliclazide 160 mg bd, and the oral medications were continued. Since being on insulin, he has noticed a weight gain of about 10 kg. He has been a heavy consumer of alcohol and has been treated on multiple occasions for withdrawal symptoms. Other medication includes ramipril, aspirin and atorvastatin. On examination, he had bilateral pitting oedema up to the knees and facial pufﬁness. Auscultation revealed bilaterally decreased air entry and widespread crackles. Jugular vein pressure (JVP) is elevated. Investigations revealed a normal renal, liver and cardiac proﬁle. Electrocardiogram (ECG) was normal. An echocardiogram revealed a slightly reduced ejection fraction. An admission chest X-ray is shown below Investigation Result Normal values Hb 102 g/l 135 - 175 g/l MCV 80 - 100 WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 110 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l HbA1c 55 mmol/mol 9.29 - 53.0 mmol/mol Which of the following would be the most appropriate management step for his symptoms of cardiac failure?
options: IV furosemide and oral thiamine supplementation
explanation: D IV furosemide and oral thiamine supplementation This is a well-established but largely under-recognised clinical scenario of insulin-related worsening of heart failure and ﬂuid overload, which occurs because insulin itself promotes salt and water retention. Thiamine deﬁciency may also have contributed to his heart failure symptoms. Management of choice is with furosemide to promote salt and water excretion, and thiamine in view of his excessive alcohol consumption. Once his ﬂuid status is stable, if he still has symptoms of heart failure, addition of a cardioselective beta blocker such as bisoprolol may be of value. B Reduce the insulin dosage Reducing the insulin dose without additional blood glucose lowering therapy runs the risk of deterioration in HbA1c. A Discontinue insulin HbA1c is virtually at target, and discontinuing insulin risks a signiﬁcant negative impact on target attainment. C Fluid restriction Fluid restriction alone won’t provide sufﬁcient impact on ﬂuid status to reduce symptoms of heart failure. E Trial of bisoprolol Beta blockade may improve symptoms of heart failure, but only after ﬂuid overload has been treated with diuretics.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of a lump at the base of his neck. He has noticed that this has become particularly prominent with swallowing and has grown signiﬁcantly over the past 8 weeks. There is also a problem with diarrhoea over the past few months. Clinical examination reveals a thyroid nodule. On further questioning, it transpires that his mother died during a thyroidectomy some years ago. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 121 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 5.2 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.85 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Ret oncogene positive Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Medullary thyroid carcinoma Ret oncogene positivity raises the possibility of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN-2). Occasionally patients suffer troublesome diarrhoea in response to increased calcitonin levels that cause increased gastrointestinal secretions. We are not given the calcitonin levels here, but it is to be assumed that they are likely to be raised. The thyroid nodule is most likely to be a medullary thyroid carcinoma. Given that his mother died on the operating table, the possibility of MEN-2 with coexistent phaeochromocytoma is further raised. The most appropriate initial screening test would be 24 h urine for catecholamines. MRI with or without meta- iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scanning is useful at a later stage for localising the site of a potential tumour. It is crucial to rule out a phaeochromocytoma, or to manage it appropriately with maximal alpha blockade, before progressing to thyroid surgery. C Follicular thyroid carcinoma Only a very small proportion of cases of follicular thyroid cancer (<5%) are thought to be related to a familial cancer syndrome. Associated syndromes include (PTEN)-hamartoma tumour syndrome/Cowden syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis/Gardner syndrome, Carney complex type 1, Werner syndrome and Pendred syndrome. B Papillary thyroid carcinoma Papillary thyroid carcinoma may be associated with RET mutations, but is also associated with mutations in RAS, BRAF and NTRK. The hypercalcaemia here is also more suggestive of MEN-2 because of co-associated hyperparathyroidism. D Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma This is undifferentiated, fast growing and occurs most commonly in an elderly population. E Thyroid adenoma Thyroid adenomas are not rapidly growing and would not ﬁt with the picture seen here of a potentially cancerous lesion.

stem: A 49-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. Most recently, he has noticed swelling of his hands and is unable to keep his wedding ring on. His brother also visited from Australia, and thought that his appearance had changed a little. Medication includes ramipril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g BD and gliclazide 160 mg BD. On examination he has soft tissue swelling of his hands and a prominent lower jaw. He is hypertensive, with a BP of 162/90 mmHg. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 139 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 4.6 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 200 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmo/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.8 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 155 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l HbA1c 68.31 mmol/mol (8.4 %) 9.29 - 53.0 mmol/mol (3 - 7 %) You arrange for him to undergo a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. You look at the low point reached in terms of growth hormone level during the test. Immunoradioassay reveals a growth hormone level of 1.6 mcg/l and you diagnose a growth hormone- producing adenoma. He progresses to surgery, but he then presents 1 year later with a raised IGF-1 level. His diabetes control has worsened a little and again his blood pressure is proving difﬁcult to control. Which of the following would be the most appropriate option for ﬁrst-line medical therapy for him?
explanation:
C Somatostatin analogue Dopamine agonists are somewhat less effective in the treatment of acromegaly than they are in the treatment of hyperprolactinaemia. For this reason, somatostatin analogues are considered ﬁrst-line medical therapy.

Treatment failures may be considered for pegvisomant, a growth hormone antagonist. Indeed, pegvisomant may be more suitable for patients with particularly marked features of hyperinsulinaemia, as in this gentleman, but currently it is considered a choice only for those who have failed therapy with a somatostatin analogue. B Bromocriptine It is a dopamine agonist and the alternative to cabergoline as ﬁrst-line treatment for prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas. A Selegeline Selegiline, at normal clinical doses, is a selective irreversible MAO-B inhibitor. In larger doses, it loses its speciﬁcity and also inhibits MAO-A. It is available in tablet form and is used to reduce symptoms in early-stage Parkinson's disease. A transdermal patch is used to treat depression. D Pegvisomant Pegvisomant is a growth hormone receptor antagonist used in the treatment of acromegaly. It is primarily used if the pituitary gland tumour causing the acromegaly cannot be controlled with surgery or radiation, and the use of somatostatin analogues is unsuccessful, but is also effective as a monotherapy. E Pergolide Pergolide is an ergoline-based dopamine receptor agonist used in some countries for the treatment of Parkinson's disease (PD). PD is associated with reduced dopamine activity in the substantia nigra of the brain. Pergolide acts on many of the same receptors as dopamine to increase receptor activity.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has some blood tests as part of a medical examination for life insurance. She is completely well and takes no regular medication. Apparently another member of her family is noted to have high calcium levels, but has required no intervention. Investigations revealed the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Corrected (Ca2+) 2.88 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Her General Practitioner (GP) therefore conducted some blood tests, which revealed the following: Investigation Result Normal values PTH 4.7 pmol/l 0.9-5.4 pmol/l Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio < 0.01, indicating relative hypocalciuria Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) 30 U/l 25–82 U/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) This lady is well but has elevated calcium. Her parathyroid hormone and serum ACE are normal. Her calcium- tocreatinine ratio is <0.01, indicating reduced excretion of calcium. This is characteristic of FHH, which is a defect in the calcium-sensing receptor (plasma membrane G-protein coupled receptor). No treatment is usually needed. FHH is characterised by hypercalcaemia, relative hypocalciuria, slight hypermagnesaemia and inappropriately normal to high levels of PTH. D Sarcoidosis Where there is signiﬁcant sarcoid disease activity, leading to a raised serum calcium, angiotensin-converting enzyme levels are usually elevated. Normal levels seen here count against sarcoidosis as the cause of hypercalcaemia. A Bronchial carcinoma Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus is associated with production of parathyroid hormone-related PTH (PTHrP), which is a cause of hypercalcaemia, but should actually suppress endogenous PTH production. Other features suggestive of bronchial carcinoma, such as a cough or smoking history, are also absent in this scenario. B Primary hyperparathyroidism Relative hypocalciuria was previously thought to differentiate between primary hyperparathyroidism and FHH, although population analyses of patients with primary hyperparathyroidism cast doubt on this as a differentiating factor. The inheritance pattern indicating other affected family members does, however, support a diagnosis of FHH. E Paget’s disease Paget’s disease is associated with elevated alkaline phosphatase and joint pain, and is usually only associated with hypercalcaemia when patients spend a signiﬁcant period of time recumbent in bed.

stem: A 32-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) with a two-day history of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. He has returned from a week’s holiday in Crete two weeks ago. He says he is worried because he had numerous episodes of unprotected sex. He is feeling weak, has lost his appetite and has lost 6.3 kg (1 stone) in weight. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and often drinks a bottle of red wine for dinner. His mother has type I diabetes mellitus and his father has had a stroke. On examination, his clothes hang loosely and he has a suntan. He is afebrile. His pulse is 60 beats per minute (bpm) while his blood pressure (BP) is 80/40 mmHg. His heart sounds are normal and his chest is clear. His abdomen is soft but tender on palpation. Bowel sounds are present. His neurological examination is normal, as is a chest X-ray (CXR). Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Hb 110 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 3.2 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 143 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 121 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 65 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 2.72 mmol/l 2.20–2.60 mmol/l Urea 7.2 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Albumin 34 g/l 35–55 g/l Glucose 9.8 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l MCV 101.3 ﬂ 80–100 ﬂ Blood ﬁlm Macrocytosis What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Addison's disease Over 90% of patients diagnosed complain of weakness, hyperpigmentation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting and hypotension. In addition, the accompanying macrocytic anaemia suggests a diagnosis of pernicious anaemia. Between 70 and 90% of cases of Addison’s disease in the UK are caused by autoimmune adrenalitis. The combination of a high ACTH concentration (> 80 ng/l) and a poorly responsive Synacthen test is diagnostic of Addison’s disease. The raised glucose raises the possibility of co-existent autoimmune diabetes, but the glucose isn't high enough to indicate ketoacidosis. B IV drug abuse There would be signs of injection drug use, including scars at injection sites (so-called ‘track marks’) on the skin. When acutely unwell, patients can present with medical conditions affecting one or more system – the cardiovascular system (infective endocarditis, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, etc.); renal system (kidney failure); gastrointestinal system (pancreatitis, cirrhosis, chronic liver disease, infective hepatitis, etc.); central nervous system (dementia, memory impairment, cerebrovascular events, etc.); or respiratory system (lung abscess, pneumonia, chronic obstructive airway disease, TB, etc.). A Gonococcal sepsis Gonococcal sepsis affects 0.5–3% patients with a sexually transmitted Gram-negative organism called N. gonorrhoeae. It presents as one of the two common syndromes: a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgia without purulent arthritis (also called the ‘arthritis–dermatitis syndrome’); or purulent arthritis without associated skin lesions. D Gastroenteritis Diarrhoea and frequent vomiting are usually present together, but the former symptom conspicuously is absent in this case making this diagnosis less likely. Vomiting can present in isolation in some cases of viral gastroenteritis, but the incubation period is usually shorter (< 72 h).Weight loss in not present in the acute phase. E Diabetic ketoacidosis There is no weight loss as the presentation is acute, and the patient is signiﬁcantly dehydrated. Laboratory investigations to conﬁrm the diagnosis include the following: elevated plasma glucose (> 11 mmol/l), arterial pH ≤ 7.3, serum bicarbonate ≤ 15 mmol/l, positive urine ketones, blood ketones ≥ 3 mmol/l.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP), complaining of severe problems with central obesity. Her past medical history includes manic depression, hypertension and chronic alcohol abuse. Medication includes sodium valproate, ramipril, indapamide and amlodipine. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 165/90 mmHg and her body mass index (BMI) is 38. She has moon- like facial features, buffalo hump and abdominal striae. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 122 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.6 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l Platelet (PLT) 230 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Sodium (Na) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 123 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l ALT 105 U/l 25–55 U/l Fasting glucose 8.2 mmol/l < 5.6 mmol/l 0900 hours plasma cortisol 1000 nmol/l 130–690 nmol/l Midnight plasma cortisol 400 nmol/l < 50% of morning level Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Pseudo Cushing’s disease The answer is Pseudo-Cushing’s disease (Option C). It can be challenging to distinguish Cushing’s disease from pseudo-Cushing’s disease as the clinical presentation is similar. The main clinical clues to pseudo-Cushing’s disease in this case are the chronic alcohol abuse and depression. The key biochemical evidence is that there remains diurnal variation in the cortisol level, which would not be seen in Cushing’s disease. Often, treating the underlying cause will result in resolution of the symptoms and biochemical disturbances. B Cushing syndrome Cushing syndrome (Option B) is incorrect. In a patient with Cushing syndrome, the plasma cortisol level would not show diurnal variation, ie the midnight plasma level would not be < 50% of the morning level; this patient’s biochemistry clearly shows a drop of > 50%. With her background of chronic alcohol abuse and depression, the best answer would therefore be pseudo-Cushing’s disease. A Cushing’s disease Cushing’s disease (Option A) is incorrect. In a patient with Cushing’s disease, the plasma cortisol level would not show diurnal variation, ie the midnight plasma level would not be < 50% of the morning level; this patient’s biochemistry clearly shows a drop of > 50%. With her background of chronic alcohol abuse and depression, the best answer would therefore be pseudo-Cushing’s disease. D Impaired glucose tolerance Impaired glucose tolerance (Option D) is incorrect. A raised glucose level is expected as a result of raised cortisol levels. Diagnosing impaired glucose tolerance requires a fasting blood glucose level of < 7 mmol/l and an oral glucose tolerance test level of 7.8–11.0 mmol/l, which is not the case here. E Simple obesity Simple obesity (Option E) is incorrect. The patient clearly presents with an abnormal picture and abnormal biochemistry, which simple obesity alone would not satisfactorily explain. There is no doubt that this patient should lose weight.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with type II diabetes comes to the Emergency Department for review. She is not due for followup in clinic for two months but has recently started insulin therapy and now has burning pain and weakness affecting her left thigh. Her diabetes has been poorly controlled over the past two years, with an HbA1c of > 69 mmol/mol (> 8.5%) over the follow-up period. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 145/90 mmHg, and pulse is 75 bpm and regular. Neurological examination reveals evidence of weakness and wasting of the left quadriceps. There is loss of the left knee jerk and slightly diminished sensation over the medial aspect of the thigh. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 130 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.2 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 295 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 118 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1c mmol/mol (8.0%) < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) ESR 32 mm/ﬁrst hour 0–10 mm/ﬁrst hour Creatine kinase (CK) 64 IU/l 23–175 IU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A Diabetic amyotrophy The classical picture of proximal pain and weakness in a femoral nerve distribution is suggestive of diabetic amyotrophy. The underlying pathology is unclear, although the presentation

is associated with rapid changes in blood glucose such as those associated with commencing insulin therapy after a period of poor diabetic control. Physiotherapy, coupled with medications, to manage neuropathic pain is the intervention of choice. C Lumbosacral disc prolapse This is associated with sudden-onset back pain and radiculopathy, usually more marked on one side than the other, rather than the symptoms described here. B Injection site reaction This is very unlikely, given that patients are not encouraged to inject directly into the thigh on a regular basis and there is no indication of skin changes. D Polymyositis This is associated with raised CK and generalised proximal muscle pain (in around one-third of patients). E Polymyalgia rheumatica This is associated with more generalised proximal muscle symptoms affecting both the hips and shoulders, usually worse in the mornings, and a much greater rise in markers of inﬂammation than that seen here.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with increasing nausea and vomiting over the past 72 h. She has a history of autoimmune hypothyroidism controlled with thyroxine replacement, but has no other signiﬁcant past medical illnesses. On further questioning, it transpires that she has lost weight and been feeling increasingly lethargic, having passed out twice at work, in the last three months. Examination reveals a BP of 100/80 mmHg, which falls to 85/65 mmHg on standing; her pulse is 80/min and regular. She is slim and tanned with a BMI of 20. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 119 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 188 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 130 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 110 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Urea 10.2 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Glucose 4.1 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l TSH 2.1 u/l 0.4 - 5.0 u/l Which of the following is the most important step?
explanation: A IV hydrocortisone The presentation here is consistent with Addison’s disease. Given the signiﬁcantly abnormal clinical chemistry, coupled with worsening nausea and vomiting, there is no opportunity to delay initiation of therapy whilst awaiting a Synacthen test. Commencing IV hydrocortisone is therefore the initial intervention of choice. In this case, given the previous history of autoimmune thyroid disease, autoimmune adrenal failure is the most likely cause here. Adrenal insufﬁciency is excluded in the Synacthen test by an incremental rise in cortisol of > 200 nmol/L and a 30 min value > 600 nmol/L. One dose of hydrocortisone the previous evening is unlikely to affect interpretation of the test. C Oral ﬂudrocortisone Oral ﬂudrocortisone is used in patients who fail to maintain postural blood pressure despite adequate corticosteroid replacement. B IV normal saline Although IV normal saline may temporarily improve blood pressure, it won’t impact on the underlying cause, in this case adrenal insufﬁciency. D Synacthen test the following day Delaying intervention until after a Synacthen test is inappropriate given the signiﬁcant hypotension and E Abdominal ultrasound scan (USS) This may reveal adrenal atrophy or calciﬁcation, but it won’t provide an estimation of adrenal function.

stem: A 68-year-old woman who has been taking long term amiodarone therapy comes to the clinic complaining of palpitations at rest. On examination her BP is 135/75 mmHg, her pulse is 90/min at rest. Thyroid gland examination is normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 119 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 6.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 182 × 109/l 150–400 ×109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 130 μmol/l 50–120 μmol/l TSH < 0.05 U/l < 0.5–4.5 U/l Thyroid autoantibodies Negative Interleukin (IL-6) Elevated You change her amiodarone for another agent. Which of the following is the mainstay of therapy in this situation?
explanation: D Corticosteroids This patient has amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) type 2, as evidenced by the relatively normal thyroid on clinical examination, lack of marked signs of thyrotoxicosis, elevated IL-6 and negative thyroid autoantibodies. Management of AIT type 2 is very different to the management of AIT type 1, with corticosteroids being the mainstay of therapy. This is because AIT type 2 is the result of a direct effect of amiodarone, which leads to thyroiditis. E Propylthiouracil This is an alternative to carbimazole as a mainstay of intervention in AIT type 1. A Carbimazole Anti-thyroid drugs are the mainstay of therapy for AIT type 1, which is more usually associated with positive thyroid antibodies and there is no rise in IL-6. There is no practical difference in efﬁcacy between propylthiouracil and carbimazole. B Potassium perchlorate Potassium perchlorate is utilised to gain acute control of thyroid function in patients who require urgent intervention, for example because of unstable cardiovascular disease. C Thyroidectomy This is considered for patients who fail to respond to medical intervention alone, usually for AIT type 1.

stem: A 21-year-old student nurse presents with frequent episodes of collapse. One of these occurred during a placement in the Emergency Department at the same time as a cardiac arrest. Blood glucose at the time was noted to be 1.4 mmol/l. Other blood tests were unremarkable. On examination straight after an event, her BP was 123/82 mmHg, withpulse is 95/min and regular and she was cold and sweaty. Blood taken at the time conﬁrmed a venous blood glucose of 1.2 mmol/l, C-peptide level was low-normal and insulin levels were markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation: C Insulin misuse Hyperinsulinaemia in the presence of a normal or low Cpeptide is suggestive of insulin misuse, which is unfortunately a more common occurrence in healthcare professionals who are seeking attention, as is the case here. As here, measurement of insulin, glucose and C-peptide at the time of a collapse is crucial for making the diagnosis. D Alcohol misuse Hypoglycaemia does occur in association with alcohol misuse, but this is commonly following a period of binge drinking and it’s unlikely this person could work in a hospital environment whilst having consumed signiﬁcant amounts of alcohol. A Insulinoma Insulinoma is a rare occurrence, and is associated with elevated insulin and C-peptide. Overnight fasting, coupled with supervised exercise, is the most commonly used protocol to drive a hypoglycaemic episode. B Sulphonylurea misuse Elevation in both C-peptide and insulin may raise suspicion of sulphonylurea abuse. It is possible to assay levels of commonly used sulphonylureas in urine, and this should be considered. E Retroperitoneal sarcoma Hypoglycaemia associated with retroperitoneal sarcoma is extremely rare and is associated with increased levels of IGF2.

stem: A 67-year-old patient who is visiting from West Africa attends the clinic with her daughter. She has had hypertension for a number of years and is managed on a range of agents, including ramipril, indapamide, amlodipine, aspirin and simvastatin. Other past history of note includes a recent left forearm fracture after a fall, an episode of kidney stones and a short period of drug treatment for depression. Her daughter is extremely worried, as she has noticed a change in the appearance of her mother’s hands since she last saw her 18 months earlier. Examination in the clinic reveals a blood pressure of 149/85 mmHg and a pulse of 78 bpm (in atrial ﬁbrillation). Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Abdominal and neurological examinations are unremarkable. She appears to have telescoping of the ends of her ﬁngers, although there are no obvious signs of arthritis elsewhere. Investigations: Investigations Results Normal Values Hb 124 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 8.0 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Calcium (Ca2+) 2.95 mmol/l 2.2–2.6 mmol/l Phosphate (PO4–) 0.7 mmol/l (0.8– 1.5) 0.8–1.5 mmol/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: C Primary hyperparathyroidism This patient has a relatively normal creatinine level, elevated serum calcium level and reduced serum phosphate level. This clinical picture is most consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism driven either by a single adenoma or four-gland hyperplasia. The X-ray shows the beginning of reabsorption of the terminal phalanges of the ﬁngers on both hands. The intervention of choice is surgery, following localisation of any adenoma with magnetic resonance imaging, technetium scanning or a combination of both. B Pseudohypoparathyroidism Pseudohypoparathyroidism classically presents with shortening of the fourth ﬁnger of both hands. It leads to calcium levels below the limit of normal. It is caused by G protein-coupled receptor resistance to activation by PTH. A Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (FHH) FHH is often a benign condition, which presents incidentally with mild to moderate elevation in calcium level on routine blood testing. D Secondary hyperparathyroidism Secondary hyperparathyroidism is driven by hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia and is seen in patients with chronic renal failure. The normal renal function here effectively rules it out. E Tertiary hyperparathyroidism Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops in some patients with secondary disease, when production of PTH becomes autonomous and cannot be limited by correction of calcium and phosphate levels.

stem: A 16-year-old boy comes to the Endocrine Clinic with his parents. They are concerned about his excessive height. Apparently, he has grown signiﬁcantly in the past six months and his parents are unable to buy shoes to ﬁt him. He has no signiﬁcant past medical history apart from severe myopia. On examination, his blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. He is 1.92 m tall and has size 12 feet (his parents are shorter at 1.8 m and 1.62 m). He has large hands, a prominent lower jaw and appears to be perspiring excessively. You note normal secondary sexual characteristics. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 131 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 7.8 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l PLT 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 6.8 mmol/l (fasting) < 7 mmol/l Growth hormone ng/ml post oral glucose tolerance test < 10 ng/ml Bone age Consistent with age 19 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Pituitary gigantism The rapid growth, large hands and feet and normal secondary sexual characteristics alongside failure for growth hormone to be suppressed with an oral glucose tolerance test is highly suggestive of a growth hormone producing pituitary adenoma. A pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is the next investigation of choice. B Familial tall stature His parental height and oral glucose tolerance test result effectively rule out familial tall stature as a diagnosis. A Ehlers–Danlos syndrome Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is a connective tissue disorder that is associated with extensive elastic skin, joint hypermobility and abnormal scar formation. This is not consistent with the clinical scenario – especially the rapid growth. C Marfan syndrome Although patients with Marfan syndrome do have tall stature, it would be unusual for there to be such rapid growth. Aside from the myopia, this patient does not meet any of the other features in the revised Ghent nosology. E Weaver syndrome Weaver syndrome is a bone overgrowth disorder with associated developmental delay. This does not ﬁt the clinical scenario in this case. The patient's rapid growth and the failure for growth hormone to be suppressed is highly suggestive of a growth hormone producing pituitary adenoma.

stem: A 42-year-old man is reviewed in the Lipid Clinic some 6 weeks after a second episode of acute pancreatitis. He has no past medical history of note apart from hypertriglyceridaemia. He denies signiﬁcant alcohol consumption. Examination reveals a BP of 135/85 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. His BMI is 23. Investigations; Hb 139 g/l WCC 8.1 x109/l PLT 231 x109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l K+ 4.3 mmol/l Creatinine 105 micromol/l ALT 62 U/l HDL 0.8 mmol/l LDL 2.3 mmol/l TGs 8.1 mmol/l Which of the following is the best way to treat his triglycerides?
explanation:
C Fenoﬁbrate The answer is Fenoﬁbrate - Fibrates can lower triglyceride levels by up to 70% in patients with signiﬁcant hypertriglyceridaemia, and are the initial therapy of choice here. They are also thought to impact positively on plasma viscosity in this situation, hence reducing the risk of vascular events. In patients with mild elevations in TGs, fenoﬁbrate should not be used as it may actually increase the risk of pancreatitis events. A Atorvastatin Atorvastatin, is incorrect, because statins primarily impact on levels of LDL cholesterol. B Cholestyramine Cholestyramine, is incorrect because bile acid binding resins have very modest effects in reducing cholesterol and triglycerides, and are unlikely to signiﬁcantly impact on this person’s markedly elevated triglycerides. D Niacin Niacin is incorrect. Niacin and nicotinic acid derivatives can signiﬁcantly reduce triglyceride levels. They are poorly tolerated at high dose, however, due to ﬂushing and itching, and

may increase the risk of diabetes. In the EU they are only available at low dose as a food supplement. E Omega 3 fatty acids Omega 3 fatty acids is incorrect, this can have very positive effects on triglyceride levels, but in this situation would be the add in of choice to patients not achieving triglyceride target on ﬁbrate alone.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of symptoms of pain and tingling in her hands, which is particularly worse at night. She has an unremarkable past medical history. On examination, Tinel’s sign is positive and there is some vague sensory loss over a median nerve distribution; there is also some weakness of the muscles of the thenar eminence. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be the cause of this problem?
explanation: A Hypothyroidism This patient has symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, with pain and tingling at night, thenar eminence wasting and positive Tinel’s sign (reproduction of pain and tingling on tapping over median nerve). Associated conditions include hypothyroidism, raised oestrogen levels (oral contraceptive pill or pregnancy), Cushing syndrome and obesity, amongst a number of additional related diseases. Treatment of choice for carpal tunnel syndrome is surgery, although in patients who are surgically unﬁt, non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs, locally injected corticosteroids and nocturnal splints may be usefully employed. Even with treatment of hypothyroidism, or birth of the child, symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome may not resolve. E Menopause High oestrogen levels, such as during pregnancy or whilst taking oral contraceptives, are associated with carpal tunnel syndrome. B Anorexia nervosa Obesity is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome, due to compression of the median. C Hyperthyroidism Hypothyroidism is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome due to excessive soft tissue/collagenous deposition associated with myxoedem. D Addison’s Cushing syndrome (i.e the ‘opposite’ of Addison’s) is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.

stem: A 42-year-old type II diabetic woman presents with recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs). She has been treated with a number of antibiotics, including trimethoprim and amoxicillin. She still complains of dysuria and some soreness in her groin. Her most recent Hb A1c was 108 mmol/mol (12%). Ultrasound (US) scan abdomen demonstrated no structural abnormalities or evidence of pyelonephritis. What is the most likely causative agent?
explanation:
A Extended spectrum beta-lactamase-producing coli Data from the American Diabetes Association have shown that 9.4% of people diagnosed with type 2 diabetes had a UTI compared to only 5.7% of those without. The most common pathogens isolated from the urine of diabetic patients with UTI were E. coli and other Enterobacteriaceae such as Klebsiella spp., Proteus spp., Enterobacter spp. and Enterococci. Multiple courses of antibiotic therapy in these patients, and increased incidence of hospital-acquired and catheterassociated UTI, induce the development of antibioticresistant urinary pathogens. Infection with ESBL-producing E. coli is an increasingly recognised cause of infection in diabetes patients and is associated with poor outcomes. ESBLs are enzymes that open the betalactam ring, inactivating the antibiotic and consequently conferring resistance to most beta-lactam antibiotics such as pencillins and cephalosporins. Some ESBL isolates have been shown to be resistant to antibiotics commonly used for UTI,

such as trimethoprim. Ciproﬂoxacin is no longer recommended for use in uncomplicated cystitis if there is an appropriate alternative available, due to an increased risk of long lasting or permanent side effects such as tendonitis; however ciproﬂoxacin may also be ineffective against some strains of ESBL isolates. Carbapenems are generally considered the drug of choice for the treatment of ESBL/E. coli (ESBL–EC) infections. With a half-life of 4 h, ertapenem is commonly used as it is administered only once daily. Fosfomycin is an oral antibiotic agent that has broad activity against multi-drug-resistant pathogen, including ESBL–EC. Another oral antimicrobial agent that can be considered for the treatment of ESBL-EC cystitis is nitrofurantoin. D Neisseria gonorrhoea N. gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted Gram-negative organism that causes infection in 0.5–3% of patients acquiring it. It presents as one of two common syndromes: a triad of tenosynovitis, dermatitis and polyarthralgias without purulent arthritis (also called the ‘arthritis–dermatitis syndrome’); or purulent arthritis without associated skin lesions. B Methicillin–resistant Staphylococcal aureus (MRSA) MRSA prevalence has risen dramatically in hospital and community settings. Methicillin resistance is mediated by PBP-2a, a penicillin-binding protein encoded by the mecA gene that permits the organism to grow and divide in the presence of methicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics. Risk factors for infection are long-term care residency; recent surgery/hospitalization; long-term indwelling catheters such as in haemodialysis patients; prolonged and repeated use of antibiotics such as cepaholosporins and quinolones; HIV infection; and sharing of needles. C Candida albicans Candida urinary tract infections (UTIs) also occur commonly in uncontrolled diabetic patients, but the frequency of occurrence of infection with this organism is lower than that with E. coli. E Chlamydia trachomatis Chlamydia trachomatis is a Gram-negative organism that is sexually transmitted. It causes trachoma, a sight- threatening eye disease endemic to Asia and Africa; urogenital infections; and lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), which is a condition characterised by the development of a painless, stellate genital ulcer followed by the development of inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is the leading cause of infertility in women. Chlamydial urinary tract infection occurs in a small proportion of sexually active women who present with typical symptoms of UTI, but in whom urinalysis reveals pyuria but no bacteriuria.

stem: A 19-year-old student presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with delayed puberty. He has so far been unable to form relationships and feels any time he meets a potential female partner everything breaks down at the physical stage. On examination, he has sparse body hair and an underdeveloped penis with small testes. His blood pressure (BP) and body mass index (BMI) are both normal. He is also anosmic. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Testosterone 5 nmol/l 9–35 nmol/l FSH 0.69 U/l 1–25 U/l LH 0.57 U/l 1–70 U/l TSH 1.2 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
A Kallmann syndrome Kallmann syndrome results from disordered migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-producing neurons into the hypothalamus. This leads to failure of episodic GnRH secretion and subsequent failure of luteinising hormone (LH), FSH and testosterone production. Seventy-ﬁve per cent of sufferers have absent sense of smell (anosmia). It occurs in 1 in 10 000 males, being rarer in females (male : female ratio 4 : 1). The syndrome is also associated with an increased risk of cleft lip and palate and sensorineural deafness. The main differential diagnosis is constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), which is far more common than Kallmann syndrome. A deﬁnitive diagnosis of IHH in the absence of a family history or prior genetic testing is difﬁcult to make until the patient reaches at least 18 years of age, unless other suggestive features are present (ie, prior microphallus and/or cryptorchism, anosmia, renal agenesis, skeletal defects, etc). The management of GnRH deﬁciency includes replacing sex steroids to develop secondary sex characteristics and to build and sustain normal bone and muscle mass. Exogenous gonadotropin or pulsatile GnRH therapy are used for ovulation induction in women and for induction of spermatogenesis in men. C Androgen insensitivity syndrome AIS is associated with female external genitalia, rather than the male phenotype seen here.

B Klinefelter syndrome Klinefelter syndrome is associated with small testes and low levels of testosterone, but isn’t associated with loss of sense of smell. D Pan-hypopituitarism The normal-range TSH in the absence of symptoms of hypothyroidism counts against a diagnosis of pan- hypopituitarism. E Turner syndrome Turner syndrome is associated with short stature, cardiovascular abnormalities and female external genitalia.

stem: A 18-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP) complaining that she has not begun began to menstruate and that she has severe acne. On examination, she is found to have hirsutism, a deep voice and severe acne.
explanation: B 21-Hydroxylase Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is caused by defective 21-hydroxylase in around 95% of cases, due to a gene mutation. This may be classical CAH - where there is a failure to make cortisol and also salt-loss due to a failure of the adrenal glands to synthesis aldosterone; or non-classical CAH - which is milder and causes androgen excess which causes symptoms such as hirsutism, a deep voice and severe acne. Classical CAH tends to be diagnosed when the patient is very young due to failure to thrive, whereas non-classical CAH may be diagnosed later, in late childhood or early adulthood. C Apolipoprotein B This enzyme defect may be seen in some patients with familial hypercholesterolemia. However, as we suspect that she suffers from CAH, it would therefore not be seen in this patient. A 17-alpha hydroxylase This enzyme may be defective in CAH, but this is a rare occurrence. In contrast, 21-hydroxylase deﬁciency is responsible for around 95% of cases of CAH and is, therefore, more likely to be defective in this scenario. D Thyroid peroxidase Thyroid peroxidase deﬁciency occurs in patients with congenital hypothyroidism, and not in those with CAH. E Menin Menin is defective in multiple endocrine neoplasia type I as a result of a mutation in the MEN1 gene. This affects the pituitary gland, parathyroid gland and pancreas, but not the adrenal gland, which is affected in CAH.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Endocrinology Clinic with headaches and excessive sweating. She also reports joint pain and has noticed progressive enlargement of her hands and feet. She has a past medical history of carpal tunnel syndrome and hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 10 mg once daily and ramipril 10 mg once daily. On examination, she has frontal bossing, prognathism with an underbite and an enlarged tongue. What is the most appropriate initial investigation to aid in the diagnosis of this patient?
explanation: D Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 This patient has a likely diagnosis of acromegaly, given the history of headaches, sweating, joint pain and enlargement of the hands, feet and facial features. The condition is usually the result of excess growth hormone secretion from the pituitary gland. Growth hormone stimulates the production of IGF-1, the main tissue mediator of growth hormone. Therefore, the most appropriate initial investigation is to measure the serum levels of this hormone. A raised IGF-1 level is indicative of acromegaly. E Serum prolactin Often, cases of acromegaly are caused by a growth hormonesecreting pituitary adenoma. Large adenomas can affect the secretion of other pituitary hormones. Therefore, as part of a general workup of the condition, the levels of pituitary hormones, such as prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone, are measured. However, such measurement is not indicated at this stage. A Oral glucose tolerance test The oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is used to conﬁrm the diagnosis of acromegaly in those with a marginally raised IGF-1 level. Since growth hormone levels are normally suppressed by glucose, patients are given a 75-g glucose load and their growth hormone levels are monitored. If the growth hormone level remains elevated, this conﬁrms the diagnosis of acromegaly. Although this investigation is used in the early diagnosis of acromegaly, it is typically used after the measurement of IGF-1 levels. B MRI of the pituitary gland Acromegaly is often caused by a pituitary adenoma. As they enlarge, additional symptoms may present such as headaches or visual ﬁeld defects. Therefore, imaging of the pituitary gland is often necessary. However, MRI of the pituitary gland is not an initial investigation needed to diagnose acromegaly. Additionally, correlation of the imaging ﬁndings with biochemical results (eg IGF-1 levels) is needed. C Random serum growth hormone level Although an elevated random growth hormone level suggests acromegaly, growth hormone levels vary throughout the day, with a short half-life, and are therefore unreliable. For this reason, growth hormone levels are not usually tested in isolation and other measures (eg IGF-1 levels) are used instead.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of thirst and lethargy. She has been feeling unwell for some time, and is now suffering from an erythematous rash that began on her groin but has now spread to involve the buttocks, lower limbs and perineum. The rash is shown below, there is associated glossitis and vaginitis. Fasting blood glucose is raised, at 8.1 mmol/l. On further questioning she admits to weight loss of a few kilograms over the past few months. What would be the most useful investigation to elucidate the reason of presentation in this patient?
explanation:
B Glucagon level This lady has diabetes mellitus, with the characteristic rash of necrolytic migratory erythema. The rash results in itchy lesions which blister before eroding and crusting over. Whilst it can affect any body area, it commonly occurs around the genitals, buttocks and lower legs. Her diabetes, therefore may be secondary to a glucagonoma. Glucagonomas are extremely rare, with an annual incidence estimated at 1/20 million. Diagnosis is conﬁrmed on ﬁnding raised plasma glucagon levels. Most primary tumours are >3 cm in diameter, 70% are malignant in nature and more than 50% have metastasised at the time of diagnosis. Tumour localisation is usually possible with abdominal ultrasound and/or computerised tomography (CT); where tumours are small, or metastatic spread is being assessed, octreotide scanning may be utilised. The potential for surgical cure is only 5%; octreotide is useful for controlling the rash, although its effects on associated diabetes and weight loss are more variable. Palliative chemotherapy using strepto-

zocin and ﬂuorouracil does produce acceptable reductions of glucagon over a 1-year period. Selective tumour embolisation via the hepatic artery may be of additional value. E Insulin tolerance test Insulin tolerance testing is used in the evaluation of patients with growth hormone deﬁciency. A Insulin level Insulin levels are most useful in assessment of hypoglycaemia, checked in conjunction with a c-peptide and glucose at the time of an episode. In insulinoma elevated insulin and cpeptide are seen with a low blood glucose. C Somatostatin level Although a somatostatinoma may be associated with the development of impaired glucose tolerance, it is not associated with the characteristic skin rash of glucagonoma seen here. D Oral glucose tolerance test This will merely conﬁrm the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus without elucidating the underlying cause.

stem: A 34-year-old woman visits the Diabetic Clinic. She was diagnosed with type II diabetes 18 months previously and has been on treatment with metformin modiﬁed release 1 g twice a day, pioglitazone 45 mg once a day and gliclazide 80 mg once a day. On examination, her HbA1c level is 75 mmol/mol (9.0%), and blood pressure (BP) is 136/75 mmHg. She has no microalbuminuria. In spite of dietary advice and modiﬁcation, she remains obese, with a body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention with respect to weight and glucose control?
explanation: E Liraglutide 3 mg This patient is obese with poor HbA1c control; as such, rather than an intervention for glucose control and weight loss is appropriate. Liraglutide is licensed for weight loss at the 3 mg dose and was shown in the SCALE diabetes study to drive signiﬁcant weight loss (6% versus baseline over 52 weeks; see link for JAMA article). D Orlistat Orlistat does achieve modest weight loss, but it is often poorly tolerated due to side effects related to fat malabsorption. Tolerability issues are also seen more frequently in patients where there is concomitant use of metformin. There will also be no short-term impact on glucose control. These factors drive us more towards the use of liraglutide. A Further diet and exercise Given this patient has not lost a signiﬁcant amount of weight with lifestyle intervention, further measures are required. B Dulaglutide 1.5 mg Dulaglutide 1.5mg is used for glucose control in type II diabetes; although it does impact on weight, effects are more modest versus liraglutide 3mg. C Canagliﬂozin Canagliﬂozin is primarily an SGLT-2 inhibitor which reduces glucose reabsorption in the kidney, promoting carbohydrate loss. It is licensed for control of blood glucose in type II diabetes, not for weight loss.

stem: A 24-year-old woman who is 24 weeks’ pregnant is referred to the clinic complaining of increasing tiredness, emotional lability, tiredness particularly in the evenings, and episodes of palpitations. Her GP has put this down to the normal stresses and strains associated with a ﬁrst pregnancy. On examination she looks tired, her BP is 125/78 mmHg and her pulse is 90/min at rest. You notice that she has sweaty palms. There is a small, smooth goitre on palpation. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal value Hb 110 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.4 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 182 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l TSH < 0.05 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Graves' disease Thyrotoxicosis, of which 85% of cases are due to Graves' disease, occurs in 0.1-0.4% of all pregnancies. Whilst her reported symptoms may be reﬂective of the anxiety experienced by many pregnant women, they seem particularly severe, and the presence of a suppressed TSH points towards the diagnosis. B Anxiety The goitre, signs of thyrotoxicosis and suppressed TSH effectively rule out anxiety as the cause of symptoms here. A Hyperemesis gravidarum This may be associated with TSH suppression, but it isn’t usually suppressed below the lower limit of quantiﬁcation, and is not usually associated with frank symptoms of thyrotoxicosis. C Hashimoto’s thyroiditis Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is of course associated with hypothyroidism rather than the picture of thyrotoxicosis seen here. E Toxic adenoma A toxic adenoma isn’t associated with a goitre, but with a discrete nodule. The suppressed TSH would, however, ﬁt with a toxic adenoma.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to her GP with complaints of fatigue, weight gain and sensitivity to cold over the past few months. She reports no signiﬁcant changes in her diet or activity level. On examination, she has dry skin and mild periorbital pufﬁness. Her thyroid gland appears mildly enlarged on palpation, with no nodules. Investigation Result Normal value Hb 120 g/l 135–175 g/l WCC 6.5 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 250 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 132 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l TSH 18 mIU/l 0.4–4.0 mIU/l Free thyroxine (FT4) 8 pmol/l 12–22 pmol/l What is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's symptoms?
options: Increased thyroid hormone production due to TSHsecreting adenoma
Decreased synthesis of TSH in the pituitary
Increased conversion of T4 to triiodothyronine
explanation:
B Autoimmune destruction of thyroid tissue Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) is a common cause of primary hypothyroidism where immune- mediated destruction of the thyroid gland reduces T4 production, leading to a compensatory increase in TSH level. The patient’s symptoms and laboratory results are consistent with hypothyroidism due to autoimmune destruction. C Decreased synthesis of TSH in the pituitary If TSH production were low due to pituitary dysfunction (secondary hypothyroidism), both TSH and FT4 levels would be low. Here, the TSH level is elevated, indicating that the thyroid, not the pituitary, is the primary problem. A Increased thyroid hormone production due to TSH-secreting adenoma TSH-secreting adenomas typically cause hyperthyroidism, leading to high levels of TSH and thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), causing symptoms including heat intolerance and weight loss. This patient’s low FT4 and elevated TSH levels indicate primary hypothyroidism. D Increased thyroxine-binding globulin

Increased thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) levels would raise total thyroid hormone levels, but FT4 (the active form) levels would remain normal. TBG changes do not account for the low FT4 and high TSH levels in this patient. E Increased conversion of T4 to triiodothyronine Increased T4 to T3 conversion is not relevant to hypothyroidism, as it would not explain the elevated TSH levels or the symptoms of reduced thyroid hormone levels. In hypothyroidism, both T4 and T3 production are generally low due to thyroid gland dysfunction.

stem: A 44-year-old woman comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath and a choking sensation, particularly when she goes to bed. She has seen the GP, been given a diagnosis of anxiety and started on sertraline. On examination, she has an obvious multinodular goitre. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 127 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 5.9 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 194 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l TSH 3.5 U/l < 0.5–4.5 U/l Ultrasound (US) Multiple thyroid nodules, very large goitre Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation: E Sub-total thyroidectomy The fact this woman has symptoms of thoracic outlet obstruction when she lies ﬂat in bed raises the possibility that she may have signiﬁcant tracheal compression because of her goitre. There is some debate about whether sub-total or total thyroidectomy is the most appropriate option, with slow re-growth and the possibility of malignant change favouring the latter, but this is countered with increased potential risk of postoperative hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy. A Radioiodine Radioiodine is less effective in patients who are euthyroid; it is effective in patients with thyrotoxicosis where increased uptake of iodine is seen. B Carbimazole Anti-thyroid drugs will result in hypothyroidism without resolving the goitre seen here. C Propylthiouracil Like carbimazole, propylthiouracil will result in hypothyroidism without signiﬁcant resolution of the goitre. D Observation This woman has signiﬁcant symptoms of thoracic outlet obstruction and is at risk of nocturnal hypoxia.

stem: A 52-year-old man who has suffered 5 episodes of pancreatitis related to alcoholism presents to the Emergency Department with thirst, lethargy and loss of weight which has increased in severity over the past 2 months. On examination his BP is 132/90 mmHg, there is a postural drop of 20mmHg on standing. His abdomen is soft and non-tender; his BMI is 21.5. Investigations; Hb 131 g/l WCC 7.1 x109/l PLT 203 x109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l Creatinine 132 micromol/l Urea 10.2 mmol/l Glucose 20.1 mmol/l HbA1c 84 mmol/mol (9.8%) Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his diabetes?
explanation:
A Basal bolus insulin The answer is Basal bolus insulin - This patient shows signiﬁcant features of insulinopaenia, probably related to beta cell loss as a result of repeated episodes of acute pancreatitis. Given he is losing weight and has a

very elevated glucose, basal bolus insulin is the only practical intervention. Due to alpha cell loss patients are at signiﬁcant risk of hypoglycaemia, basal bolus allows much tighter targeting of insulin to requirements versus other regimens such as a BD mixed insulin prescription. E Sitagliptin Sitagliptin, is incorrect because DPPIV inhibitors have very modest effects on glucose, only in patients with signiﬁcant residual beta cell function, and are associated with increased risk of pancreatitis. B Gliclazide Gliclazide is incorrect because given the random glucose, HbA1c and symptoms, sulphonylureas are likely to be inadequate with respect to controlling blood sugar levels versus insulin. C Liraglutide Liraglutide, is incorrect because of the likely very low levels of residual beta cell function, and risk of pancreatitis associated with GLP-1 agonist use. D Metformin Metformin, is incorrect because the primary role of metformin is to reduce hepatic glucose output, which is not the cause of the diabetes seen here.

stem: A young woman comes to the clinic with the diagnosis of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and decides she would like some treatment. She tells you that her facial hair and acne cause her a great deal of stress. She has a BMI of 23. She is not currently interested in having children and is currently on the oral contraceptive pill (COCP). Which one of the following would be the most appropriate advice?
options: Losing weight will signiﬁcantly impact on her symptoms
Clomifene is the most appropriate intervention
Metformin is effective in controlling hirsuitism and acne
Co-cyprindiol may be more effective than the COCP
explanation: E Co-cyprindiol may be more effective than the COCP Co-cyprindiol because it contains cyproterone, an anti- androgen, may be more effective than the COCP in controlling acne and hirsuitism and acne in PCOS. C Clomifene is the most appropriate intervention Clomifene is used to induce ovulation in PCOS; hence it is not of value here. A There is no treatment available Co-cyprindrol may offer incremental beneﬁt versus the COCP alone in managing symptoms of hyperandrogenism. B Losing weight will signiﬁcantly impact on her symptoms This patient’s BMI is in the normal range, hence weight loss is likely to have very little impact on her current symptoms. D Metformin is effective in controlling hirsuitism and acne A Cochrane meta-analysis has suggested that metformin is not effective in controlling hirsuitism and acne versus other options such as the COCP or co-cyprindrol.

stem: A 25-year-old woman comes to the clinic with her 5-monthold baby. Over the past few weeks she has been feeling increasingly tired, but the GP has dismissed the problem as the usual tiredness after having a baby. She tells you she feels tired, has put on weight and is constipated all the time, feeling the cold when she goes out. On further questioning, she tells you this wasn’t always the case, and that in fact during the ﬁrst few months she actually felt like she had more energy and could survive on hardly any sleep at all. On examination her BP is 142/70 mmHg, with pulse is 65/min. Her BMI is 28. You notice that her hair and skin are quite dry. Investigations: Hb 109 g/l WCC 6.7 x109/l PLT 190 x109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l Creatinine 100 μmol/l Cholesterol 6.2 mmol/l TSH 7.1 U/l Free T4 7.1 pmol/l Anti-thyroid antibody +ve Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: D Post-partum thyroiditis The history here suggests that an early period of possible thyrotoxicosis has now been followed with symptoms of hypothyroidism, with hypothyroidism conﬁrmed on biochemical testing. The timing after the birth of her child suggests this is post-partum thyroiditis. Treatment is with thyroxine replacement, although withdrawal may be possible in some patients who recover normal thyroid function. Recurrence of thyroiditis is common in subsequent pregnancies, however, and in up to 40% permanent hypothyroidism develops. The presence of anti-thyroid antibodies does put her at higher risk of permanent hypothyroidism. C Hashimoto’s thyroiditis Hashimoto’s disease is the main differential here, although this patient’s recent pregnancy makes post-partum thyroiditis more likely. A Graves' disease Graves’ disease is characterised by thyrotoxicosis rather than the picture of hypothyroidism seen here. B Subacute thyroiditis Subacute thyroiditis is associated with symptoms of a ﬂu-like illness and pain over the thyroid gland. An initial period of thyrotoxicosis is followed by transient hypothyroidism and then recovery. E Sick euthyroid syndrome Sick euthyroid syndrome is associated with a signiﬁcant intercurrent illness where abnormal thyroid function tests are noted, for example, in a patient with a prolonged stay on the ITU.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations which have worsened in frequency over the past week, a BP of 130/80 mmHg and she is found to have atrial ﬁbrillation on her ECG. On examination, she has a palpable, smooth thyroid goitre. She is two months postpartum and is currently breast-feeding. Her daughter is very healthy. She has no past medical history. TSH is supressed at less than 0.05 mU/l and is TSH receptor and TPO antibody positive. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis of her goitre?
explanation: A Postpartum thyroiditis This patient has clinical hyperthyroidism and is in the ﬁrst few months after pregnancy. As such, the most likely diagnosis is postpartum thyroiditis. In women who present with postpartum thyroiditis and have symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, TSH receptor antibodies are found with increased frequency, although TPO antibodies are classically described in association with the condition. A transient period of hypothyroidism follows the episode of thyrotoxicosis, and up to 30% of patients may eventually develop permanent hypothyroidism. D Struma ovarii Struma ovarii is caused by ectopic thyroid tissue, so there is no goitre present. B Pregnancy Pregnancy may be associated with the development of a goitre but thyrotoxicosis is, of course, pathological. C Graves’ disease Postpartum thyroiditis may be a harbinger of permanent thyroid dysfunction in some women, but the timing here points us towards postpartum disease rather than diagnosing Graves’ at this stage. E Subacute thyroiditis Subacute thyroiditis is associated with symptoms of a ﬂu-like illness, pain over the thyroid gland and thyrotoxicosis. It is not associated with pregnancy.

stem: A 18-year-old woman comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. She is concerned because although she feels she has developed normally as a woman and has a normal sex drive, she has never had a menstrual period. There is no past medical history of note. Examination reveals a BP of 105/72 mmHg; pulse is 75/min and regular. She is 1.8 m tall, and has a BMI of 23. Breast development is normal although pubic and axillary hair appears absent, vulval development also appears to be normal. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal values Hb 131 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.1 × 109/l 4.0–11.0 × 109/l PLT 181 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 85 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Glucose 5.4 mmol/l 3.9–7.1 mmol/l Testosterone 21.2 nmol/l 15–70 nmol/l Karyotyping 46 XY Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Androgen insensitivity syndrome The answer is Androgen insensitivity syndrome, (AIS). AIS is associated with normal external female genitalia, (although pubic and axillary hair is absent), primary amenorrhoea, and 46 XY karyotype. Ovaries are absent, undescended testes are common, and some patients present in the ﬁrst few months with bilateral inguinal hernias, (where testes are identiﬁed at hernia repair). As here, testosterone is in the normal male range, although individuals are insensitive to its effects. B Congenital adrenal hyperplasia Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, is incorrect. This is associated with XX karyotype, later presentation with normal sexual development with symptoms similar to PCOS in the case of nonclassical CAH, or virilisation in women with classical CAH. C Kallmann’s syndrome Kallmann’s syndrome, is incorrect. Kallmann’s is associated with absence of sense of smell due to failure of the olfactory bulb to develop properly, and lack of GnRH production, leading to delayed puberty with an XX karyotype. D Primary ovarian failure Primary ovarian failure, is incorrect. This is associated with XX karyotype, and normally with secondary amenorrhoea. E Turner’s syndrome Turner’s syndrome, is incorrect. Turner’s is associated with XO karyotype, hypertension, and short stature, with female external genitalia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She is otherwise well, apart from lesions on each tibia and some loss of sensation in her feet. The lesions are shown below. Biopsy reveals granuloma formation, with inﬁltration of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
D Topical corticosteroids The appearance in the picture of these ulcerated lesions with their yellow-brown appearance, along with the history of diabetes, points towards the diagnosis of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. These erythematous plaques are due to small vessel damage causing partial necrosis of the dermal collagen and connective tissue, with a resulting histiocytic cellular response. While topical corticosteroids can worsen atrophy, they may be of value in reducing inﬂammation in early lesions. As such, in this situation, they are the intervention of choice, and systemic steroids are best avoided, if possible, due to their impact on

glycaemic control. Small trials support the use of both ciclosporin and hydroxychloroquine as second-line agents. E Hydroxychloroquine It can be used as second-line treatment for the management of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. It can also be used for the management of rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. A Aspirin Antiplatelet agents, such as aspirin, have only limited efﬁcacy in treating necrobiosis lipoidica. A 2016 Cochrane systematic review concluded that further research is necessary before this treatment option can be conﬁrmed to be safe and effective. Most venous ulcers respond to patient education, elevation of foot, elastic compression and evaluation. B Oral prednisolone Topical steroids are indicated for the management of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. Oral steroids can signiﬁcantly impact on glycaemic control. C Oral ciclosporin Ciclosporin can be used as a second-line agent for the management of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum. It can also be used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease and nephrotic syndrome and in organ transplants in order to prevent rejection.

stem: A 28-year-old man is admitted to Intensive Care following a motorcycle injury. His computed tomography (CT) head conﬁrms extradural, subdural and subarachnoid haemorrhages. After 6 weeks, he is discharged from hospital. One year later, he is followed up in an Endocrinology Clinic. On review, he is depressed and feels fatigued. On examination, his skin is thin and dry, and he has developed central obesity. He also complains that his sexual libido has markedly reduced.
explanation:
C Growth hormone Chronic growth hormone deﬁciency can be caused by a TBI and results in symptoms that include fatigue, depression, reduced muscle mass, increased fat mass and reduced libido. This ﬁts the clinical picture presented in this case and explains all of his symptoms on review at the Endocrinology Clinic. B FSH Gonadotropin hormones, including FSH, may be chronically deﬁcient after a TBI which can cause poor libido and fatigue, similar to the symptoms observed in this patient. However, this would not explain the skin symptoms or the central obesity, whereas growth hormone deﬁciency can explain all of these symptoms. A Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) Levels of ACTH may be deﬁcient in the acute phase after a TBI, but it is rare for this to persist more than a year after injury. The symptoms that this patient has are more in keeping with growth hormone deﬁciency (fatigue, depression, reduced

muscle mass, increased fat mass and reduced libido) rather than ACTH deﬁciency (abdominal pain, weight loss and nausea). D Prolactin TBI can cause hyperprolactinaemia, particularly acutely. This may cause reduced libido but is due to a hormone excess rather than deﬁciency. E TSH TSH may be reduced following a TBI, although this is the least common anterior pituitary hormone to be affected. This would cause many of the symptoms that this patient has experienced, such as low mood, fatigue, poor libido, dry skin and weight gain. Still, it is much more common for these patients to experience chronic growth hormone deﬁciency and not TSH deﬁciency.

stem: A 53-year-old woman visits the Medical Outpatient Clinic for advice. She is hypertensive and has been treated with atenolol for the last two years. While in the clinic, she asks for advice regarding the use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT). She suspects that she is menopausal due to hot ﬂushes, mood swings and lack of periods for the last ﬁve months. She has no past medical history of thromboembolism, stroke or breast cancer. However, having read conﬂicting results about HRT in the press, she is concerned about the risk of deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and heart disease. Which of the following statements is correct with respect to HRT (combined oestrogen–progestin therapy)?
options: HRT reduces the risk of coronary artery disease
HRT has a protective effect on the risk of DVT
Risk of strokes is reduced by HRT
Risk of DVT is 2–4 times higher in women on HRT
HRT has no effect on the risk of DVT
explanation:
D Risk of DVT is 2–4 times higher in women on HRT The WHI is the largest available clinical trial on HRT. It was stopped after 5 years – 3 years early – because it revealed increased dangers. Older age and obesity added to the risk associated with a regimen of oestrogen plus progestin. Thinner and younger women were at a low absolute risk of DVT, although their risk was still twofold higher among women taking oestrogen plus progestin, compared with women taking placebo. A HRT reduces the risk of coronary artery disease HERS has shown no reduced risk of coronary artery disease in women taking HRT. B HRT has a protective effect on the risk of DVT Clinical trial evidence from the Heart and Oestrogen/Progestin Replacement Study (HERS) and the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) have shown that oestrogen therapy, with or without progestin, is associated with an increased risk of DVT. C Risk of strokes is reduced by HRT The WHI has shown that the risk of having an ischaemic stroke is increased in those taking HRT due to an increased risk of blood clotting. E HRT has no effect on the risk of DVT As explained above, the relative risk of DVT is increased 2–4

times in those taking HRT.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP) complaining of a painless lump in the lower part of her anterior neck, which was found incidentally as she was ﬁddling around with her necklace. She is otherwise ﬁt and well and denies any recent chest or throat infections. She is a non-smoker. On examination, the GP conﬁrms the presence of a solitary hard, immobile lump measuring approximately 2 cm in the patient’s lower anterior neck, which moves with swallowing and appears to be positioned in the thyroid gland. The patient is apyrexial and the remainder of the physical examination is normal. The patient is referred for a ﬁne needle aspiration biopsy and relevant laboratory studies. The biopsy conﬁrms that the patient has a papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. She undergoes total thyroidectomy and radioiodine treatment. Which of the following is the most useful marker of tumour recurrence?
explanation: C Thyroglobulin Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is the most common thyroid carcinoma and accounts for 80% of such cases. It is a slowgrowing and well-differentiated carcinoma but it has a propensity for spread to the cervical lymph nodes. The male to female ratio is 1:3, with females having an overall better prognosis. Risk factors for developing this condition include excessive intake of iodine and external radiation to the neck. Thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation are the mainstays of therapy. Since thyroglobulin is synthesised by welldifferentiated thyroid carcinomas, it can serve as a useful tumour marker for assessment of recurrence of the tumour, but only after total thyroid ablation. D Thyroxine Given that this patient requires thyroid hormone replacement, thyroxine is not useful as a marker of tumour recurrence. A Alkaline phosphatase Alkaline phosphatase is elevated in the presence of bony metastases from well-differentiated thyroid cancer, although this would be a very late feature. B Beta-HCG Beta-HCG is useful in the monitoring of malignant germ cell rather than thyroid tumours. E Thyroid-stimulating hormone Like thyroxine, TSH cannot be used as a marker of tumour recurrence, given that this patient is treated with exogenous thyroid hormone.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is refered to the Endocrinology Clinic by her General Practitioner (GP) for the management of her type II diabetes mellitus and persistent hypertension. In addition to insulin and metformin for her diabetes, she is also on sertraline and lorazepam for her depression, and carbamazepine for her agonizing post-herpetic neuralgia. On examination, she is obese with a round face and moderate facial acne. She is a heavy drinker. An overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows failure of suppression of cortisol. A provisional diagnosis of Cushing syndrome is made. However, computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen reveal normal adrenal glands and no evidence of malignancy, and the serum cortisol measurement shows normal daily variation. Further investigations including a midnight cortisol later exclude Cushing syndrome. What was the reason for her failed initial dexamethasone suppression test?
options: Interference of metformin with the cortisol radioimmunoassay
Variance of baseline cortisol due to ﬂuctuating glycaemic control
The induction of the cytochrome p450 system by alcohol and carbamazepine
Fluctuating level of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol due to non-compliance with insulin treatment
explanation:
C The induction of the cytochrome p450 system by alcohol and carbamazepine The overnight dexamethasone suppression test is usually used as a screening test for Cushing syndrome. This test has a false-positive rate of up to 2–12% (meaning that a diagnosis of Cushing is suggested incorrectly). Dexamethasone is primarily metabolised by the cytochrome p450 system, speciﬁcally by the CYP3A4 isoenzyme. Several

drugs such as phenobarbital, carbamazepine and rifampicin are enzyme inducers, and therefore lead to increased activity of CYP3A4 enzyme, and can thus result in false-positive dexamethasone suppression tests. Considerable increases in cytochrome 450 enzyme activity can be seen in smokers and people who drink alcohol regularly. A Interference of metformin with the cortisol radioimmunoassay Patients need to be off all oestrogen-containing medication for six weeks prior to any measurements of serum cortisol, but metformin is not known to effect cortisol. B Variance of baseline cortisol due to ﬂuctuating glycaemic control Whilst patients with diabetes often have slightly higher baseline levels of cortisol, there is no link between raised cortisol levels and poor glycaemic control. D Fluctuating level of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol due to non-compliance with insulin treatment Non-compliance with insulin treatment is likely to lead to poor glycaemic control, but there is not known to be a link between this and levels of ACTH or cortisol. E Ectopic ACTH production Ectopic ACTH secretion is most common from a bronchial tumour, and we are given no suggestion in the history of one here. Very high ACTH levels are highly suggestive of an ectopic source of ACTH. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used by some units to help differentiate between pituitary and ectopic sources of ACTH in difﬁcult to diagnose Cushing syndrome, where ACTH fails to suppress when the production is ectopic. Useful mnemonic Enzyme inducers = SCRAP GP (sulphonylureas, carbamazepine, rifampicin, alcohol, phenytoin, griseofulvin, phenobartbitol)

stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and a recent HbA1c of 83.61 mmol/mol (9.8%) asks for urgent clinic review. He complains of a hot, swollen left foot, which has gradually got worse over the past month. On examination, there is increased heat over the tarsalmetatarsal joint and the foot is swollen. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and there is obvious neuropathy. Investigation Result Normal values Hb 121 g/l 135 - 175 g/l WCC 12.1 × 109/l 4.0 - 11.0 × 109/l PLT 204 × 109/l 150 - 400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 101 μmol/l 50 - 120 μmol/l CRP 9 mg/l < 10 mg/l Which of the following represents the investigation of choice with respect to the likely diagnosis (where available)?
explanation:
B Indium-labelled white cell scan Although not widely available, an indium-labelled white cell scan is the best way to differentiate between infective causes of this clinical presentation and Charcot’s arthropathy. It is more stable with respect to labelling of white cells versus other techniques such as technetium, and is therefore less likely for example, to label areas of increased bone turnover. Charcot’s is thought to occur due to increased blood ﬂow as a result of neuropathy. This results in increased osteoclast activity and bone turnover; the foot is then susceptible to often very minor trauma and destructive changes take place. Experts recommend immobilisation for at least 3 months in an aircast-type non-weight- bearing plaster. This is to allow bone remodelling/repair to occur. Bisphosphonates are a useful adjunct to the healing process as they reduce osteoclast activity. Whilst insulin therapy is likely to improve glycaemic control and slow further progression of neuropathy, it will not affect recovery of the Charcot’s joint. A Technetium isotope scan Technetium is more likely to label areas of increased bone turnover associated with Charcot’s, as well as areas of infection. C Plain radiograph Plain X-rays may show areas of joint destruction but won’t differentiate between infection and Charcot’s-driven inﬂammation. D ESR Although ESR may be elevated, it is a non-speciﬁc marker of inﬂammation and therefore won’t deﬁnitively conﬁrm osteomyelitis here.

E Joint aspiration Joint aspiration of a foot is technically difﬁcult and painful. Whilst it may deliver a diagnosis of osteomyelitis, where indium-labelled white cell scanning is available, it’s preferred.

stem: A 25-year-old man attends the clinic with his partner as they have difﬁculties with fertility, having tried for a baby for over 24 months with no success. He admits to decreased libido and some problems maintaining his erection. He has also had difﬁculties with his sense of smell for as long as he can remember. On examination his BP is 120/70 mmHg, with a pulse of 75/min. He has a small penis and sparse secondary sexual hair.
