Investigations: Hb 124 g/l WCC 7.1 x 109/l PLT 203 x 109/l Na+ 139 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l Creatinine 110 µmol/l TSH 1.2 U/l (0.5-4.5 U/l) Free T4 12 pmol/l (10-22) Testosterone 7.0 nmol/l (9–35) FSH 0.4 U/l (1-7) LH 0.2 U/l (1-10) Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Kallmann syndrome This patient has classical symptoms of Kallman syndrome including anosmia, loss of libido, gonadal deﬁciency, erectile dysfunction and absent secondary sexual characteristics such as pubic hair. The low LH, FSH and testosterone in the presence of a normal TSH ﬁt with the underlying diagnosis of isolated gonatrophin deﬁciency. GnRH or pulsed gonadotrophin therapy can be used to achieve fertility; in those patients who don’t desire fertility, testosterone replacement is an appropriate option. C Mumps orchitis Orchitis (inﬂammation of the testicle) is associated with pain, fever, blood in ejaculate, dysuria and penile discharge. None of these symptoms are discussed in the question, nor are there any symptoms associated with mumps infection (swelling of parotid glands, fever, joint pain). Mumps is now quite rare due to current immunisation protocol. B Klinefelter syndrome Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal disorder characterised by an XXY genotype. Patients tend to present earlier with poor sexual development, small or undescended testes and gynaecomastia. These patients are infertile. The condition is associated with learning disabilities, predisposition to diabetes, breast cancer, long leg height and tall stature. Treatment is with androgen replacement. D Pituitary failure In this condition you would expect deﬁciency in all anterior pituitary hormones in addition to GNRH (LH, FSH, TSH, ACTH). E Androgen insensitivity syndrome In this condition you would expect the FSH level to be normal, smell would be intact and there may be the presence of ambiguous genitalia.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of headaches for the past two months. She has no signiﬁcant past medical or family history and there is no history of smoking or consumption of alcohol. On examination, her blood pressure is 152/92 mmHg and her heart rate is 90 bpm. Auscultation of the abdomen reveals an abdominal bruit left lateral to the umbilicus. Her body mass index is 22 kg/m2. Investigation Result Normal value Urea 3.8 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 120 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Which of the following best describes the changes expected to be seen in this patient?
explanation: A Hyperreninaemia, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemia Hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism is characteristic of renal artery stenosis. The patient is a young woman with newly diagnosed hypertension, along with an abdominal bruit on phys- ical examination. This patient likely has renal artery stenosis, most probably due to ﬁbromuscular dysplasia causing hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism, along with hypokalaemia. D Hyporeninaemia, hypoaldosteronism, hyperkalaemia These ﬁndings are typically seen in type 4 renal tubular acidosis. The most common cause is uncontrolled diabetes mellitus which leads to dysfunction of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA). This, in turn, leads to hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism. B Hyperreninaemia, hypoaldosteronism, hyperkalaemia Hyperreninaemic hypoaldosteronism may be seen in patients with septic shock. It could possibly indicate ﬂuid depletion and is associated with an increased incidence of acute kidney injury in such patients. C Hyporeninaemia, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalaemia These ﬁndings are classical of primary hyperaldosteronism. However, this patient likely has renal artery stenosis due to ﬁbromuscular dysplasia. E Hyporeninaemia, hypoaldosteronism, hypokalaemia Renal artery stenosis results in hyperreninaemia, rather than hyporeninaemia, due to decreased renal perfusion, hence activating the JGA to secrete renin.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the Endocrinology Clinic for review. He has told his general practitioner (GP) that he consumes up to 8 or 9 l of ﬂuids per day and is constantly up during the night and day to pass urine. The GP has checked some routine bloods; a fasting blood sugar is 3.4 mmol/l. You arrange a water deprivation test, which reveals the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Maximal serum osmolality after ﬂuid deprivation 290 mOsmol/kg 278–300 mOsmol/kg Urine osmolality after ﬂuid deprivation 830 mOsmol/kg > 750 mOsmol/kg Urine osmolality after desmopressin 841 mOsmol/kg > 750 mOsmol/kg What diagnosis ﬁts best with this clinical picture?
explanation: B Primary polydipsia Results of the ﬂuid deprivation test are crucial in determining the correct diagnosis here. In this test, patients are deprived of ﬂuids for a period of 8 h or until 5% of body weight is lost. Patients should be weighed hourly. Plasma osmolality is measured 4-hourly, with urine volume and osmolality measurements occurring every 2 h. The patient is then given 2 μg intramuscular (i/m) desmopressin, with urine volume and urine and serum osmolality measured over the next 4 h. Where urine osmolality reaches levels >800 mOsmol/kg without desmopressin, then the diagnosis is primary polydipsia. This patient should be offered behavioural advice about slowly reducing his ﬂuid intake. C Nephrogenic DI Urine osmolality <300 mOsmol/kg in the water deprivation test, remaining at <300 mOsmol/kg after desmopressin, indicates nephrogenic DI. A Cranial diabetes insipidus (DI) If serum osmolality rises above 305 mOsmol/kg in the water deprivation test, then the patient is said to have DI and the test is stopped. Urine osmolality <300 mOsmol/kg after ﬂuid deprivation, rising to >800 mOsmol/kg after desmopressin, indicates cranial DI. D Partial nephrogenic DI Where urine osmolality at the end of the water deprivation test is intermediate (300–800 mOsmol/kg), and fails to rise above 800 mOsmol/kg after desmopressin, the diagnosis may be partial DI or polydipsia. E Hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism A picture of hypokalaemia and hypertension, rather than polyuria and polydipsia, would be expected in hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with a long history of Type 1 diabetes presents to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of diplopia. Her diabetes is poorly controlled, despite basal bolus insulin a recent HbA1c has been recorded at 76 mmol/mol (9.1%). She has had previous therapy laser for diabetic retinopathy, has numbness affecting both feet, and a resolved left common peroneal nerve palsy. On examination the right eye is looking down and out, there is a ptosis on the right hand side, and the pupil appears spared. Investigations; Hb 120 g/l WCC 7.1 x109/l PLT 201 x109/l Na+ 137 mmol/l K+ 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 micromol/l Glucose 9.3 mmol/l ESR 9 mm/1st hour Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her cranial neuropathy?
explanation:
C Diabetes mellitus The answer is Diabetes mellitus - This patient has previous mononeuritis (common peroneal nerve palsy), and poorly controlled T1DM; as such the most likely cause of the oculomotor nerve palsy seen here is mononeuritis related to diabetes. Symptoms may gradually resolve over a period of 6-8 weeks, and improved diabetes control may positively impact on the degree of improvement seen. B Cerebral infarct Cerebral infarct, is incorrect, it is very unlikely given that only one cranial nerve is affected. A Anterior communicating artery aneurysm Anterior communicating artery aneurysms, is incorrect, usually result in visual ﬁeld defects, (a bitemporal hemianopia) because of optic chiasm compression. D Intracerebral tumour Intracerebral tumour, is incorrect, it would be associated with gradually worsening symptoms including increasing headaches and other focal neurology, neither of which are seen here. E Vasculitis Vasculitis is incorrect, it is a possible alternative cause of mononeuritis, although the normal ESR and lack of other features aside from the oculomotor palsy, counts against vas-

culitis as the alternative pathology.

stem: A 32-year-old man who has had type I diabetes mellitus for 27 years comes to the clinic for review. He has bilateral lower limb sensory loss consistent with peripheral neuropathy and background diabetic retinopathy, but is otherwise well. Current insulin regime is 8 U TDS of short-acting insulin (Actrapid®) with 20 U/ day of intermediate insulin (Insulatard®). Apart from recurrent nocturnal hypoglycaemia (4 times/week), he feels he is doing well. His BP is 135/70 mmHg, with pulse 80/min and regular. His BMI is 23. HbA1c is 66 mmol/mol (8.2%) and a recent creatinine was measured at 135 micromol/l. Morning glucoses are in the range of 6–22 mmol/l. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in his regimen?
options: Change his Insalotard® to insulin glargine at 20 units/day
Change his regime to 12 units of Mixtard® twice/day
explanation: C Change his Insalotard® to insulin glargine at 20 units/day This patient is missing his HbA1c target and suffering nocturnal hypos, as evidenced by his symptoms and some of the morning glucose values (22 mmol/l being potentially reﬂective of a counter-regulatory response to hypoglycaemia). Because he is missing the HbA1c target, it would not really be appropriate to reduce his insulin dose. Switching to glargine is likely to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia whilst improving target achievement, because it is a ‘peak-less’ insulin. E Change his regime to 12 units of Mixtard® twice/day BD mixed insulin is not tailored as appropriately to meal times as a basal bolus regimen, and as such it isn’t recommended for patients with type 1 diabetes. A Reduce his Actrapid® by 6 units/day The proﬁle of glucose testing suggests possible episodes of hypoglycaemia at night; as such, reducing the dose of Actrapid® won’t impact signiﬁcantly on this patient’s glucose control. B Reduce his Insalotard® by 6 units/day Given that the HbA1c is above target, this is suboptimal versus switching to an insulin analogue. D Increase his Actrapid® by 6 units/day This won’t signiﬁcantly impact on nocturnal hypoglycaemia, but may drive increased food intake and suboptimal weight control.

stem: A 34-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of extreme fatigue and increasing generalised abdominal pain. He reports a 3-day history of vomiting, diarrhoea and dizziness. He was recently diagnosed with HIV and was started on antiretro- viral therapy 3 weeks previously. On examination his pulse rate was 120 beats/min and blood pressure was 100/50 mmHg. His cardiovascular, neurological and abdominal examinations were normal. Investigation Result Normal Values Na+ 128 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 5.6 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 100 µmol/l 50 - 120 µmol/l Glucose 3.0 mmol/l 3.9 - 7.1 mmol/l Urea 8.5 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Virology at the time of HIV diagnosis: Cytomegalovirus IgG + HbsAb + HbsAg - Previously his electrolytes had been within the normal range. What is the most useful bedside test to aid in diagnosis?
explanation: D Postural blood pressures This patient is suffering from an Addisonian crisis, as evidenced by the low sodium and raised potassium, low blood pressure and dizziness, abdominal pain and vomiting. This is probably due to an immune reconstitution syndrome after starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV. In this patient’s case, he is CMV IgG positive and therefore the cause may be CMV adrenalitis. If this was felt to be the case, ganciclovir should be used in treatment. Postural blood pressures will demonstrate a signiﬁcant drop. He should be treated with IV hydrocortisone and ﬂudrocortisone. C Exercise oxygen saturations These are sometimes used as a bedside test to gather evidence of PCP pneumonia in HIV-positive patients. This patient has presented in an Addisonian crisis: this explains his low sodium and raised potassium, abdominal pain and vomiting, dizziness and low blood pressure. The most appropriate bedside test would be postural blood pressures, expecting to see a signiﬁcant drop. Patients can develop Addisonian crises as a result of an immune reconstitution syndrome after antiretroviral therapy is started; in this case, the patient is CMV IgG posi- tive and therefore this may be as a result of CMV adrenalitis. A Blood pressure in each arm This patient has developed an Addisonian crisis, as evidenced by the low sodium, raised potassium, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, and low blood pressure. This can occur as part of an immune reconstitution syndrome once antiretroviral therapy is started in HIV; it may have been caused by CMV adrenalitis, as this patient has previously been exposed to CMV (hence he is IgG positive in serology). The most appropriate bedside test would be postural blood pressures: you would expect to see a signiﬁcant postural drop in an Addisonian crisis. B ECG This patient is in the midst of an Addisonian crisis: this explains the low sodium and raised potassium, low blood pressure and abdominal pain, vomiting and dizziness. An ECG will not help in the diagnosis of Addison’s: instead the patient should have postural blood pressures taken, expecting to see a signiﬁcant drop. Addisonian crises can occur as a result of an immune constitution syndrome after antiretroviral therapy for HIV is started: in this case, the patient is CMV IgG positive and therefore this may be CMV adrenalitis. E Urinalysis This patient has developed an Addisonian crisis: he has a low blood pressure, tachycardia, hypoglycaemia, dizziness, abdominal pain and vomiting, and bloods show a low sodium and a high potassium. This is probably due to an immune reconstitution syndrome as a result of starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV; in this patient’s case, he is also CMV IgG positive and therefore it is possible that this has been caused by CMV adrenalitis.

stem: A 40-year-old man attends the Hypertension Clinic describing a three month history of episodes of headaches and dizziness. In addition, he often experiences vague central abdominal discomfort. He feels that he has lost some weight recently, though this may be related to a low-fat diet he has been trying. On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 152/90 mmHg. In addition, there appears to be thyroid swelling which has not previously been noted. His bone proﬁle reveals a corrected calcium of 2.74 mmol/l. He also had an oral glucose tolerance test with his General Practitioner (GP), who was concerned about the weight loss, which was normal, hence excluding the diagnosis of diabetes. Which one of the following is most likely to be the cause of his hypertension?
explanation: D Phaeochromocytoma The episodic symptoms of headache and dizziness, the hypertension, the hypercalacaemia and the thyroid mass ﬁt better with a phaeochromocytoma in the context of MEN 2A. MEN 2 presents with medullary thyroid carcinoma and phaechromocytoma. The third component could be parathyroid hyperplasia (MEN 2A) or mucutaneous neuromas and marfanoid habitus (MEN 2B). E Graves’ disease Graves’ disease can cause a diffusely enlarged, non-tender goitre and also mild hypercalcaemia in the acute phase (thyrotoxicosis). However, dizziness, abdominal pain and hypertension are not features of the condition. A Cushing’s syndrome Cushing syndrome is a cause of secondary hypertension but would not cause weight loss. The typical feature is weight gain with central distribution. B Addison’s disease Addison’s could be considered in the context of dizziness and abdominal pain, but hypertension would be unusual in this condition. It mainly resents with postural hypotension, nausea, abdominal pain and hyperpigmentation. C Abuse of growth hormone Abuse of growth hormone is another cause for secondary hypertension. It may also lead to weight gain, insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance, which is not the case in this scenario.

stem: You review a 52-year-old man who describes having undergone pituitary surgery (and ‘some treatment’ after the operation), a while ago. He now complains of feelings of lethargy, reduced energy and vitality. On examination, he has increased central abdominal adiposity and has reduced grip strength. He is already taking thyroid and cortisol replacement, and blood testing suggests these are adequate. Full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E) and liver function tests (LFTs) are unremarkable. Which of the following would be the best investigation to perform next?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa
explanation: E Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) In light of this man’s previous pituitary surgery, it is possible that he has growth hormone (GH) deﬁciency. Clinical features of growth hormone deﬁciency include impaired well-being, reduced energy and vitality, reduced muscle mass and exercise tolerance, decreased sweating, increased cardiovascular risk and increased fracture risk (osteoporosis). A serum IGF-1 concentration lower than the lower limit of normal in a patient who has pituitary disease conﬁrms the diagnosis of GH deﬁciency. Even a normal value does not exclude GH deﬁciency; further investigations would be indicated here. A Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary fossa We know that pituitary anatomy is likely to be abnormal in relation to previous surgery, and further imaging won’t inform as to abnormalities of gland function. B Insulin tolerance test Insulin tolerance testing to induce hypoglycaemia is a potential option for investigation, although this is unpleasant for the patient. Other options, such as the arginine-growth hormonereleasing hormone test, are preferred where these are available now. C Glucose tolerance test Oral glucose tolerance testing is utilised in the evaluation of acromegaly, not growth hormone deﬁciency. D Serum prolactin An elevated serum prolactin would neither conﬁrm or refute growth hormone deﬁciency, and this is not therefore a preferred next investigation.

stem: A woman is 32 weeks’ pregnant. She is taking propylthiouracil 150 mg daily for thyrotoxicosis. On her check-up, she complains of heat intolerance and palpitations, and repeat thyroid function tests conﬁrm that TSH is < 0.1, and T3 and T4 are also elevated. Which of the following is the next most appropriate management step?
explanation: D Stop propylthiouracil and start carbimazole In pregnancy, PTU is only recommended in guidelines for the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy. After this time, a switch to carbimazole is recommended because of the risk of maternal liver toxicity associated with PTU use. This patients should be switched to carbimazole and the PTU not up-titrated. E Arrange for partial thyroidectomy Thyroidectomy should be considered in cases of allergies/contraindications to both anti-thyroid drugs in patients who are not compliant with drug therapy, and in women in whom euthyroidism cannot be achieved even on large doses of anti-thyroid drugs. If surgery is indicated, the second trimester is the optimal time. Thyroidectomy is often followed by a gradual, but not immediate, disappearance of TSH receptor antibodies, and withdrawal of anti-thyroid drugs in the mother after thyroidectomy may lead to isolated foetal hyperthyroidism. A Increase propylthiouracil dose Both carbimazole, at a suggested daily dose of 10–20 mg, and propylthiouracil (PTU), at a dose of 150 mg bd, are acceptable for use in pregnancy, although PTU tends to be the more popular choice. PTU may be more protein-bound and so less is transmitted to the foetus, but compliance with carbimazole is generally better. In addition, there is evidence that PTU may be associated with maternal hepatotoxicity in late pregnancy, precipitating a change to carbimazole as the most appropriate in that case. B Radioiodine treatment Radioiodine treatment is contraindicated in pregnancy, since radioiodine crosses the placenta and can cause congenital hypothyroidism. Following radioactive iodine treatment, men should avoid fathering a child for four months, and women should avoid conceiving for six months. C Induce delivery In cases of thyrotoxicosis not responsive to anti-thyroid drugs, or in cases of non-compliance, thyroidectomy is then recommended (ATA Guidelines 2017).

stem: A 48-year-old woman is reviewed after attending for a well woman clinic. She ﬁnds it difﬁcult to control her weight, often feels tired, and currently has very heavy periods. Apart from this she doesn’t have any particular concerns. On examination her BMI is 32 and her BP is 155/92 mmHg. Otherwise clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 132 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 4.5 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 201 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 132 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l Fasting serum triglyceride 3.2 mmol/l 0–1.5 mmol/l Which of the following tests is most likely to contribute to determining the underlying diagnosis?
explanation: E TFTs The difﬁculty with weight control, menorrhagia and hypertriglyceridaemia are all features consistent with hypothyroidism. TSH is likely to be elevated above the normal range, with low T3 and T4. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism, and the condition is managed with thyroid hormone replacement. Once thyroxine is commenced, periods improve and hypertriglyceridaemia usually begins to resolve without intervention with statin therapy. B HbA1c measurement Signiﬁcantly elevated blood glucose is unlikely to be seen, and even if HbA1c is abnormal it won’t illustrate the reason for her weight gain and menorrhagia. A HDL measurement HDL may be low but it’s not contributing to the underlying diagnosis. C LFTs There may be a small elevation in transaminases, but this won’t conﬁrm the underlying cause of her symptoms. D Prolactin Prolactin is elevated in hypothyroidism, but thyroid function tests should exclude hypothyroidism as the underlying cause before other investigations are undertaken.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred to the Endocrine Clinic after she complains of urinating ‘constantly’ during the day and night. She estimates that she urinates 5 litres of urine a day. Two years previously, she was involved in a road trafﬁc accident (RTA), where she suffered a traumatic brain injury (TBI) and was admitted to intensive care (ITU).
explanation:
D Vasopressin analogue Diabetes insipidus (DI) is caused by a deﬁciency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and may occur idiopathically or due to a precipitating cause, such as a TBI. DI may occur as a result of a deﬁciency in production of ADH from the pituitary gland (cranial DI) or due to impaired renal responsiveness to ADH (nephrogenic DI). The treatment of cranial DI is with desmopressin, which is an ADH analogue. It primarily acts on V2 receptors in the renal collecting ducts, which rapidly increases the reabsorption of water into the bloodstream, providing symptomatic relief. A Dopamine receptor agonist An example of a dopamine receptor agonist is bromocriptine, which may be used in the treatment of a pituitary prolactinoma since it suppresses the release of prolactin and gradually causes shrinkage in the size of the tumour. This has no value in the treatment of DI. B Somatostatin analogue Somatostatin analogues, such as lanreotide, stimulate the somatostatin receptor and may be used to treat acromegaly which results from a pituitary growth hormone-secreting tumour. Somatostatin inhibits the secretion of growth hormone and has no value in the treatment of DI. C Tetracycline antibiotic

Demeclocycline is a tetracycline antibiotic and is used in the treatment of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). It acts on the collecting tubules in the kidneys and reduces their responsiveness to antidiuretic hormone (ADH). In DI the problem is reduced ADH secretion rather than the increased ADH. E Vasopressin antagonist Vasopressin receptor antagonists, such as vaptans, are used in the treatment of SIADH, where there is an excess of ADH, rather than the deﬁciency of ADH, seen in DI.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the clinic because of problems with the physical side of her relationship. She is concerned that her breasts leak milk after only minimal stimulation from her boyfriend, and that intercourse is difﬁcult as she has signiﬁcant problems with vaginal dryness. She also reports that she has not had a period for the past 4 months. The only other history of note is that she was given metoclopramide by a locum doctor for a recent episode of gastroenteritis. On examination her BP is 142/82 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination is unremarkable. You can produce milk on minimal breast stimulation. She has some peripheral ﬁeld visual loss. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin 127 g/l 115–155 g/l WCC 7.6 × 109/l 4–11 × 109/l Platelets 203 × 109/l 150–400 × 109/l Na+ 138 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l K+ 4.4 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 100 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Prolactin 1005 mU/l < 400 mU/l TSH 7.2 µU/l 0.17–3.2 µU/l Free T4 16.2 pmol/l 11–22 pmol/l FSH 0.5 U/l 1–25 U/l LH 0.5 U/l 1–70 U/l Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A Non-functioning pituitary adenoma The prolactin isn’t raised enough to be consistent with a macroprolactinoma, and the peripheral visual ﬁeld loss raises the possibility of a large tumour. The low FSH and LH are consistent with this; the raised TSH may be due to the fact that non-functioning adenomas may occasionally secrete small amounts of TSH. This woman should undergo a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to further characterise the tumour. However, it is likely that surgery will be the mainstay of therapy as the tumour is highly unlikely to respond signiﬁcantly to somatostatin or dopamine agonists. The elevated prolactin here is likely related to pressure on the pituitary stalk. Pressure on the pituitary stalk causes an elevation in prolactin levels which stimulates milk production. B Metoclopramide-related hyperprolactinaemia Drug-related hyperprolactinaemia is usually associated with a lesser rise in prolactin, to <1000. C Microprolactinoma Microprolactinomas are not associated with visual ﬁeld loss, and a greater rise in prolactin would be expected in microprolactinoma. D Macroprolactinoma Macroprolactinomas are associated with the visual disturbance seen here, although a rise in prolactin to at least 5000 mU/l would be expected. E Pregnancy Although pregnancy is associated with a rise in prolactin, it isn’t associated with the visual ﬁeld defect seen here.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. She is usually managed with basal bolus insulin but has omitted a number of doses due to a row with her boyfriend. On examination her respiratory rate is 35/min, she is drowsy, confused and smells of pear drops. Which of the following results would ﬁt best with her arterial blood gases?
explanation: D pH 7.1; pCO2 3.0 mmol/l; pO2 11.1 mmol/l The characteristic picture of metabolic acidosis with hyperventilation and the smell of pear drops is typical of diabetic ketoacidosis. Hyperglycaemia with a relatively normal pH is of course seen in patients with hyperosmolar non-ketotic coma, typically found in the elderly population with type 2 diabetes who retain enough residual insulin production to avoid becoming ketotic. A pH 7.4; pCO2 3.0 mmol/l; pO2 12.1 mmol/l Drowsiness with respiratory compensation accompanied by a pear drop smell would always imply a metabolic acidosis due to diabetic ketoacidosis until proven otherwise. B pH 7.5; pCO2 3.0 mmol/l; pO2 7.4 mmol/l This implies an alkalosis, and with a low CO2 this would be respiratory in origin. C pH 7.25; pCO2 6.7 mmol/l; pO2 7.4 mmol/l The pCO2 here is elevated, which implies a respiratory rather than a metabolic acidosis. E pH 7.4; pCO2 6.7 mmol/l; pO2 6.7 mmol/l A normal pH is inconsistent with this presentation, and the elevated pCO2 implies a respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner for a check-up for his type II diabetes mellitus which is controlled by metformin. He was diagnosed with diabetes 11 years ago after an inferior myocardial infarction (MI). On examination, his blood pressure (BP) is 160/95 mmHg and his body mass index is 26 kg/m2. He has normal fundi and examination of his feet shows normal sensation and peripheral pulses. As well as his metformin he takes ramipril 2.5, amlodipine 5 mg once a day and simvastatin 40 mg at night. Investigation Result Normal value Cholesterol 4.6 mmol/l < 5.2 mmol/l Urea 7.4 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 109 μmol/l 50–120 µmol/l HbA1C 57.38 mmol/mol (7.4%) < 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%) Albumin : creatinine ratio 3.8 mg/mmol < 3.5 mg/mmol Which of the following is likely to have the greatest impact on this patient’s future risk of complications?
options: Adding a ﬁbrate to statin therapy
Escalating the dose of ramipril to 5 mg once daily
explanation:
C Escalating the dose of ramipril to 5 mg once daily The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest a target blood pressure (BP) of 140/80 mmHg in type II diabetes. First-line antihypertensive drug treatment should be with an angiotensin- converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. This patient also has microalbuminuria; a sign of diabetic nephropathy. Normally, ACE inhibitors signiﬁcantly reduce the risk of allcause mortality in patients with diabetic kidney disease and the dose should be escalated to the highest dose tolerated by the patient. D Starting a sulfonylurea The NICE guidelines suggest a target HbA1c of <53 mmol/mol (< 7%) in patients with type II diabetes mellitus. However, the ACCORD trial showed no beneﬁt of aiming for an HbA1c of < 47.54 mmol/mol (6.5%) in late- stage disease in patients who also have a positive cardiovascular history. A Adding a ﬁbrate to statin therapy The action to control cardiovascular risk in type II diabetes (ACCORD) trial investigated the addition of fenoﬁbrate to statin therapy but found no impact on future macrovascular events. B Adding insulin If initial drug treatment with metformin has not continued to control HbA1c to below the person's agreed threshold for intensiﬁcation, consider dual therapy with metformin combined with one combining a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone or a sulfonylurea. Insulin is only normally considered if dual therapy has not achieved adequate glycaemic con-

trol. E Switching from ramipril to losartan For adults with chronic kidney disease and type II diabetes, an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) or an ACE inhibitor (titrated to the highest licensed dose that the person can tolerate) should be offered if the ACE is 3 mg/mmol or more. Given that this patient appears to be tolerating treatment with an ACE inhibitor, there is no indication to switch to an ARB, although the dose should be intensiﬁed to the highest dose that can be tolerated.

stem: A 21-year-old man who was previously diagnosed with type I diabetes mellitus visits his General Practitioner (GP) for his yearly review. He checks his feet for ulcers occasionally and recently forgot to attend for retinal screening. His urine protein creatinine ratio (PCR) shows evidence of microalbuminuria. He asks his GP whether his diabetes will be lifelimiting. What is the most likely cause of death for a patient with type I diabetes?
explanation: A Macrovascular disease Macrovascular disease is the biggest cause of death in diabetic patients, accounting for around 75% of deaths. This includes coronary heart disease, cerebrovascular disease and peripheral vascular disease. Atheromas develops more rapidly and progress more quickly in diabetic patients which leads to morbidity. D Neuropathy Neuropathy develops in many diabetic patients and includes both autonomic neuropathy and peripheral neuropathy which can lead to ulcers and ultimately amputation. Neuropathy can have a signiﬁcant effect on quality of life. It can lead to ulcers which are prone to becoming infected, which can lead to death, but it is not as likely to cause death as macrovascular disease. B Malignancy Diabetes is a risk factor for many malignancies, including colon, breast and pancreatic cancer. This does not, however, account for the majority of deaths, unlike macrovascular disease. C Nephropathy Nephropathy occurs in a signiﬁcant number of patients with diabetes, and this can lead to a requirement for renal replacement therapy. Ultimately, nephropathy itself is not the biggest cause of death as it causes death in around 5% of diabetic patients. However, the diabetic population with nephropathy are at greater risk of developing cardiovascular disease. E Retinopathy Diabetic retinopathy may lead to sight loss in patients with diabetes, and this underlines the importance of yearly retinal screening. This has a signiﬁcant effect on quality of life but does not directly lead to death.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of weight loss and headaches. On examination, he is noted to have a blood pressure (BP) of 175/110 mmHg and 180/102 mmHg on three successive readings at the general practitioner (GP) surgery, despite having been started on an angiotensin- converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor and calcium channel blocker. He smokes ﬁve cigarettes per day. His body mass index (BMI) as measured in the clinic is 23. Investigation Result Normal values Na+ 145 mmol/l 135 - 145 mmol/l K+ 4.1 mmol/l 3.5 - 5.0 mmol/l Urea 10.6 mmol/l 2.5 - 6.5 mmol/l Corrected (Ca2+) 3.1 mmol/l 2.2 - 2.7 mmol/l Phosphate (PO43-) 0.4 mmol/l 1.1 - 1.45 mmol/l What is the likely cause of his presentation?
explanation: D Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2 The patient in this case is young, hypertensive and has hypercalcaemia. The high calcium level can be explained by the presence of parathyroid hypertrophy, and the hypertension is secondary to the presence of a phaeochromocytoma. Both abnormalities may be visualised on ultrasound imaging. Clearly the presence of hyperparathyroidism will be clariﬁed by normal or raised levels on blood testing in the presence of hypercalcaemia. Medullary thyroid cancer doesn’t cause hypercalcaemia, it is due to cancer affecting the thyroid C cell line, (which produce calcitonin). There are two forms of MEN II, A and B. Patients with MEN2A and MEN2B experience two main complications, medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) and phaeochromocytoma. MEN2A patients have a predisposition to hypertrophy of the parathyroid glands and subsequent tumour development. MEN2B patients show a variety of additional conditions: a characteristic facial appearance with swollen lips; tumours of the mucous membranes of the eye, mouth, tongue and nasal cavity; enlarged colon; and skeletal abnormalities. MEN2A shows no distinct physical features and must be identiﬁed by either measuring hormone levels or ﬁnding endocrine tumours. A Extra-adrenal phaeochromocytoma Although this may explain the hypertension seen here, it wouldn’t explain the hypercalcaemia. B Small-cell lung cancer Small cell lung cancer is associated with the production of ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), leading to features of hypercortisolism. Although hypertension may be a feature, the lack of signiﬁcant weight gain or dysglycaemia and the modest smoking history count against this. C Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 1 MEN1 is associated with pancreatic endocrine tumours, not with phaeochromocytoma. E Zollinger–Ellison syndrome This is the syndrome of hypergastrinaemia and recurrent peptic ulceration related to a gastrinoma.
